TLDR at the bottom
The hours shown on steam for project zomboid is way off. I've been playing since it showed up on Desura and I must have clocked 400+ hours. It's up there as one of my favourite games.
It's easy to die if you aren't careful, from being bitten by zombies to cutting yourself on broken glass and bleeding out. This makes building a base rewarding, as it gives you a "safe" place... if you can build it well enough (barracade windows, doors, create rope ladders to windows, destroy stairs).
Create a farm to ease the need to look for food, which has it's own mechanics e.g. crops get diseased/stunted and don't grow in winter.
The health system is indepth, from moods (scared, tired, sad, bored) to injuries (broken bones, scratches, bites and bleeding). Any injury you need to treat.. by making splints and bandages etc.
There are RPG elements...you gain stats the more you do something (sneaking, running, blade weapons, blunt weapons, carpentry and a ton more) which you can also boost if you find the correct books to read.
Combat is different but feels fun and fluid, there are several different weapons you can find or craft which are more effective depending on the weapon and skill level.
TLDR :- A solid survival game that keeps you on your toes.

Please bear with me, I do not write reviews often. It really takes a very bad, or very good product or service to make me stop and take the time to let the originators know what I think. As an artist, I know how a critique can sting, or salve. So with that being said, let me continue by letting you off the hook. This is a rare game indeed.
I have tried multiple other survival games, and none are as challenging, or easy to play endlessly as The Long Dark. The atmosphere is one of tense expectation; will the radios suddenly make an announcement if left on? Why can you open the gas cap and hood of the cars? Is there a way out of this forsaken valley? Is there a secret way across the ice? Will a different strategy change the outcome of my survival next time? With as many ways to plan your survival scenario as in real life, and with the expectation of more to come, I think the alpha is worth getting in now. It will help you learn the game and activities available and the timelines, and other difficult real world situations that come up as the game develops into what appears to be a highly challenging and thoroughly exhilarating game.
I would say more, but long reviews get boring, and I have a new battle plan I want to go try out..oh yeah..if this game goes pvp though, I hope they leave the option of Pilgrim in effect for humans too. I like the pensive exploration and food hoarding and crafting and hunting aspects more than the constant fighting like in other survival games. Now I understand that not all humans will be aggressive or passive, I just don't want to constantly run and hide or fight. Other people could be an asset or a liability, it would add an entirely new dimension to the game play. It would take a group to survive in the long run. I would like to see plantable indoor greenhouse type features for long term survival and in reality without replenishment there can be no survival...maybe like onions, potatoes, carrots...citrus for scurvy and rickets, maybe milk goats, chickens, and pigs for livestock? Kind of a catch and tame thing? Dig to discover the tubers, hidden sheltered valley with fruit trees and fragrant herbs/berries. Ok, so that got a little wishy. Well, that is my two cents worth, try it out folks, it is addicting.

I should preface this with the fact that I'm a pretty big fan of old shooters. I mean, hell, F.E.A.R. is one of my favorite shooters of all time and it only came out 2 years before Bioshock 1. Games being "dated" doesn't bother me at all.

The Long Dark is a really fun experience with a lot of well polished mechanics but ultimately suffers from a lack of direction which leaves me feeling a bit unsatisfied with the game.
On the plus side, it hast a great art style that definitely makes you feel like you are trudging through the snow alone in the wilderness. The fantastic weather effects help with this ambiance while also having a huge impact on gameplay. While of course the survival aspects are very gamified and not really that realistic, the gameplay does result in a lot of interesting decision making and risk balancing that you'll have to make all the time. As the survival mechanics are quite punishing, this leads to a great mix of strategy and risk. For instance: push ahead down the road when the weather looks like it may start to turn bad in hopes of finding food and shelter around the next bend, or hole up safely in a cave but risk running out of food and starving if the storm ends up lasting days. The various survival mechanics also combine to create very unique and dynamic crises, where you'll go from feeling well stocked and safe to at risk of dieing very quickly.
The main negative problems behind the game are a lack of direction and no way to get strong enough to survive sustainably. The only goal is to survive as long as possible, but unlike many other survival games (such as subnautica, don't starve, minecraft, etc) there is no base building at all and crafting is extremely limited with only a handful of items that can be built. There is no way to gain a foothold in the game and beef up -- every gain is temporary. There are a few rare and powerful items, such as the rifle, but ammo is extremely limited (and non craftable) making finding a rifle or a few bullets more of a temporary boost rather than a lasting upgrade to your character's state. Loot does not respawn either so everything is of finite supply. The result is that unlike many other survival games, there is no fun to be had in world building, base building, crating, or the general feeling of mastering one's environment. The only fun is from surviving for a finite amount of time and exploring the different regions of the game. Make no mistake though, there is a lot of fun to be had here as the game map is very large and entertaining to explore which negates the lack of purpose or direction to the game.
The bigger issue that leaves me feeling unsatisfied with the experience is that there are no fully sustainable strategies to survival in the game. Every item in the game (every one!) has a condition meter that is ticking down to ruin due to either time or usage. Even if you get lucky and find a ton of fantastic gear, it is only so long before it decays away. There are also items that can repair gear (like a whetstone to repair a knife), but these items also have condition meters that decay even faster than the items they are repairing, or are dependent on finite resources. Certain tools are really necessities for surving sustainably via hunting in the game, but as they decay with use you soon realize that there is only so long you can spend in the game before you've used up all the knives and whetstones and will starve.
On the up side, this decay meter dynamic does a good job of keeping players on the move and encouraging them to explore the world. I started one game and happened across a couple of rabbit snares and a nice shelter close to good trapping grounds, and ended up doing some homesteading just trapping rabits, killing a few wolves, curing pelts, and fashioning a few key fur clothing items that made my character a lot more hardy. I might have been tempted to stay put indefinitely, but with all my tools and gear decaying steadily away it was only going to be so long before my knife and hatchet ran out and I starved there. Down the road, I even found a rifle, killed a bear and a few deer, and had a cubard full with several weeks of cooked meat, but still felt compelled to move on as eventually no matter how much I stockpiled my tools would all decay and I would need to move on to more areas I hadn't looted yet.
In short, there is no real purpose to the game and you will eventually die due gear decay even if you are playing perfectly. It's a good bit of fun early on due to the stylized graphics and atmosphere as well as a well made world with solid survival mechanics, but no matter how long you survive it doesn't quite feel rewarding as you know that there is no direction and no possibility for sustainable survival. In the mean time, its fun to explore and deal with the day to day challenges of survival, but the game really suffers from the lack of purpose. There is a "story mode" planned by the developers that could be fun, but as the game has been in early access for two years and development has been fairly slow, it's hard to know how big of an impact this will have.
I would recommend this game only to those that are really interested in the survival aspects of the survival genre, as there is no world building or purpose to the game. The closest cousin to this game is probably DayZ without the zombies or other players but with much more punishing survival mechanics and more dynamic storm weather.

A beautiful, slightly melancholic jrpg. The overall plot follows a young girl named hinako who is dealing with the loss of her dream to be a ballet dancer due to a knee injury. After recovering from the injury she begins school where she encounters two sisters who give her the ability of a "Reflector" in order to fight demons in humanities collective unconscious. The game is somewhat similar in theme to persona, but rather than fight with the power of your "other self" you fight as a magical girl anime type character and become stronger through fragments of emotion you receive. Now then, onto gameplay, at its core is a fairly basic turn based rpg with a distinct leveling system. Rather than level up through fights you level by gaining fragments of emotion from "Common" and using them to increase stats, which in turn unlocks skills. You get these by resolving issues for other characters and through crafting them. Its a simple system, but it works well and deciding which stst to up can be difficult. Exploration is bare bones and doesn't feel wholly necessary outside of gathering crafting items. Overall tje gameplay falls into the average jrpg tier, nothing top notch but solid enough to stay interesting. The story is where the game truly shines, the plot is melancholic yet uplifting and the light, almost watercolor, color scheme really helps set the feeling of it all. Game is fairly short, but worth the money for old fashioned jrpg fans or fans of persona. Would love yo see a sequel/similar game from the developers with more content. All in all I give it a solid 8/10.

Limbo is a 2D platform game. You play as a young boy lost in the forest, then later in a derelict urban environment, solving puzzles and struggling to stay alive.There are no coins to collect or mushroom power-ups in Limbo’s monochromatic, eerie world. There are no limits to the number of lives you can have. That latter point is crucial.
Many platform games are about learning a few moves perfectly so you can race through level after level. Limbo deliberately messes with that mechanic. There are places where doing the same thing twice in a row will simply get you killed.As you play through Limbo, dying becomes a fact of life – dying in ever more gruesome ways. Sometimes it will be the result of terrible accidents, other times you’ll fall into the clutches of giant monsters. Other children occasionally appear to thwart your character’s progress by luring him into traps.
It’s a game that will haunt you long after you’ve switched off your pc.

A game for the introspective thinker.
First and foremost this game is not for everyone, it is not multiplayer, it is not an RPG, it's not a survival crafting game. The term walking simulator comes to mind, however it really doesn't fit that bill either. It is a hardcore loner survival game, intended to be challanging, beutiful, simple, and occasionally nerve racking.
Let's start with what I do and do not like. I love the atmosphere, while it may not be bleeding edge graphics the use of specific methods with textures and atmospheric effects make this game simple, yet beutiful, a type of elegance few developers pull off, though many try. The enviorment itself is a challange, monster and zombies can be annoying, but when the world around alone is enough to kill you just for trying to push your character a bit too hard, requries careful use of your time and resources, to me is far more intimidating than a wave of enimies when you have a practically unlimited supply of ammunition for an assult rifle. Resources are sparce and not every little thing is useful, many take days just to be useable for anything. You can find a hunting rifle but it will become useless to due wear or a lack of ammunition. As for the wildlife, it's not only hard to kill a wolf, bear, or deer, but you actually have to find them, and survive them if they see you first (for wolves and bears).
What you may not like. Their is a planned story mode to be used later, but not yet. You cannot make ammunition, that would be OP in this world. You cannot make your own shelter, I personally would like to see snow caves, they would need to take hours to make so again even this would take careful consideration, and wildlife and your condition would be factors. It's not likely you can survive indefinately, and when you die you die for good.
So if you can understand what this is and is not, and still think it's worth a go, I doubt you will be dissapointed.

One thing you should note before buying Cuphead, is that the game is not for people who play games casually, and it certainly isn't for the faint of heart. This game is the most difficult game I have ever played, to the point where I spent around an hour stuck inside of the first level, which is pretty insane. The boss battles are equally, if not more challenging than the platforming sections, and are the most fun bosses that I have ever seen in a game. Cuphead's music is brilliantly executed, mainly consisting of Jazz and Ragtime, and the sound quality is also top notch. The visuals are breathtaking, with hand-drawn animation, as well as colorful and creative characters. My only downsides with this game is the "Parry" move, which can be extremely annoying in boss fights, and also the fact that it almost feels like you need an Xbox controller in order for the controls in the game to actually feel solid. Other than that, I have no issues with the game. So if you want an amazing, colorful and rage-filled experience, go ahead and buy it.

I love this game. It's one of the first games in years that I'd been anticipating, and it was def worth it. That said, my favorite joy I've gotten from this game is seeing all the salty reviews on the MS store giving it 1/2 stars bc of how difficult it is. One person even talks about how they wish they were more informed about it before preordering. The salt is so real and I love every bit of it. Now for the actual review.
This game is a mainly boss rushesque (each level is a boss, not an actual boss rush per say) platformer with 6 sidescrolling levels. Don't let the games appearance fool you, it's hard as♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ The main thing to do is, if you think of a new strategy, why not give it a go. I spent probably 20-25~ hours on the normal mode, the rest is on achievement hunting.
The art style and music is great, I believe everything was hand drawn hence why it took hella long for it to come out and the quality shows. It's really weird seeing this style in a 2017 game. It feels like this game is a lot older. The music is great if you love old timey swing/jazz/ragtime type stuff.
The bosses take a while to get used to but I always felt good when you hear that "KNOCKOUT" from the annoucer because you earned that it. It'll take an average game probably about 700~ deaths for a completion, I'd say, depending on skill level. I think I'm pretty good at platformers I'd say, but I got my ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ rocked by all of these bosses at least 10 times. That said, there aren't any fights that seem to really drag on with the exception of one towards the end but that's fine bc there's a lot of variety, if you catch my drift.
I'd say that one complaint that I'd have is that you can't progress on simple mode, which just cuts off the final stage of the boss. That said, just get good and kill the boss on normal. If all else fails, just take the health buffs and dmg reduction if needed. That and the controls kinda suck. I just switched shoot to RT so my thumb is free on A B & Y for jumping, special and dodging.
Get this game. It's dope if you like this genre.
This may be a bit of a spoiler if you want to go in completely blind, but these are just some tips for what people seem to think are some of the harder bosses and in general:
You should use the purple gun on the Bee and the Dragon, and similarily the alternate bombing gun in the birdhouse level. They make those levels a lot easier since the bosses are under you in the case of the bee and Bird, and in the case of the dragon you want to stay in the top part of the screen. That's all I'll say for actual strategy bc it's one I don't see a lot of people doing and it helps out immensely. Also, for the flying levels, the Coffee upgrade is probably the most useful as the other ones (other than health) won't really change anything while you're in the plane. The extra hearts aren't really worth the trade for damage, so I usually use th P. Sugar in normal levels. Which makes jumping a lot less dangerous in a lot of situations as there are plenty of times where you'll be under a parry object, but won't be able to double tap A fast enough.

Like clockwork. Highly original gameplay, highly atmospheric and stylish, "Dungeon of the Endless" provides a rogue-like experinece in an entirely new way. By crafting a two-man party at the start, constructing defense structures, recruiting new people (max party size: 4), equipping items, encountering dungeon elements benevolent, neutral, malevolent ,and risky, you aim to ascend through 12 floors and escape. Thing is, each of those parts has their own layers: party memebrs may be better by themselves ina  room, some may not like each other, they have different types of items they can equip, they have levels and abilities to gain, etc. It goes on and on for a multitude of possibilities.
That depth extends to each end of the game: Will you focus on your towers for this floor? Will you have enough resources to have a good footing for the next one? Will you explore more of the current floor or move on?
In addition, the combat is real-time (though with a pause function); you can actively manuever, advance, retreat, repair, etc. as the heat of the current turn shoots up. Monsters can have differing priority targets, and your abilities may very well change that.
All the parts are painted in a beautiful pixilated, Alien-esque styling (though with much more color!) and puncuatued by lovely music. This game is will worth the money, whether you want something to occasionally come back to or something to bite deep into.

The achievements are letters so if you 100% this game, you will have the English alphabet at your disposal should you want to spell something on your profile using the showcase achievememt option. Oh, and the puzzles are fun and challenging.

This game is an old school mmo based on social interaction rather than just farming mobs and getting drops like 99 % of all mmos out there.
Pros:
-Cute and light hearted graphic style based on chinese mythology.
-Very versatile class system where you can get all class at the same and mix and match by choosing one main job and then choosing different skill paths to add to your play style from your other jobs. Each job levels independently point. Making it easy to join all kind of level ranges to play with your friends of different levels. Perfect game for anyone who hates gender locks, race locks, character locks or class locks.
- 2 main story quests filled with old gen hilarious and messy cutscenes.
-You can catch mostly all enemies pokemon style on top of the regular pet system with evolutions for egg based pets (Pets are totally OP in this game) They can also become mounts and flying mounts as well as used for super fast grinding for your lower level jobs.
-Game relies on a crafting system that is actually essential to the game and encourages exploration and social interaction. Pots with recipes are scattered around the game making it a challenge for low level characters to venture into much higher level areas to try and nab recipes. Durability and max durability is finite and will crumple down with time, making material gathering and alchemists indispensable for fast cheap weapons and armor especially in late game.
-The game relies a lot on quests and objectives that will make you activly seek out other players.
-EXP gain is based on damage done rather than enemies killed. (Which is a way better system in my opnion) So if you are about to be killed while the enemy is almost dead, you can run away without the frustrating feeling of having wasted your time.
-Seems like alot of server based events are still running.
-Female shura heavy armor bare bottoms.
Cons:
-Lack of options for grapchis/chat/fonts/etc.
-Stylized yet very dated graphics and poor drawing distance.
-Game is slow and grindy in most parts you will be spending hours just vaccuming up all enemies into a perpetual mob grinding machine called a "party", just chatting away, or doing whatever(pron? i don't know you but im pretty sure it's pron. Isn't it?).
-Lack of end game content.
-There is no super rare drops/weapons/armor or anything, this game is mostly about collecting recipes and materials.
-Some very outdated systems regarding items, item management and so on.
-Underwear quest is tedious.
-Pink lines.
I would recommend it for you just to check out the skill/class system, but I doubt this game will have any longetivity in the long run.

So, in conclusion, WATCH SOME GAMEPLAY BEFORE BUYING. It is that simple. Have fun.

Coop has no ability to save your game, and with a full playthrough requiring a few hours of gameplay, you better make sure you set aside some time. I recommend playing at least a game or two on singleplayer, as this will allow you to unlock some characters before trying multiplayer. Also, the game had a few connectivity problems where players lost connection with each other about an hour in (In our case, two players maintained connection, while two players lost connection, while still able to view each other's movement. Some sort of host desynch...)
Overall, worth the $13.

It's a shame that "Sinister City" is marred by technical issues.  It's a tongue-in-cheek vampire Hidden Object Game (HOG) that's got good graphics, nice puzzles and mini-games, and darn good voice acting (far better than the norm for the HOG genre).  The story is simple but interesting and the poking of fun at normal HOGs is really well done.  But, the game does suffer from bugs and some irritating design decision.
The poor design decisions are firstly that if you're playing the game in either Easy or Advanced mode, the cursor does not change to indicate hot, live, or actionable areas.  That means that as you search the scene, you have no idea if you can pick something up, use something, open a HOG or mini-game, talk to someone, or even just leave the scene.  Easy mode puts a sparkle on the screen after a few seconds for the next thing you should be doing.  But, you end up watching for that and blindly following it instead of thinking about what's showing.  In Advanced mode, there's no sparkle.  So, you're essentially reduced to just clicking on everything possible in the hopes that something will happen.  Secondly, the mini-games have no instructions at all.  It's not just that there's nothing telling you how you need to manipulate things.  It's also that there's no explanation of what the win-state (i.e., what you're supposed to do) is.  And finally, In the HOGs, the items you're searching for can be so small as to be indistinguishable.  Similarly, the HOG scenes usually have in-focus/out-of-focus, lighted/non-lighted areas implying where you're supposed to be looking for things.  Nope.  The items can be anywhere at all (the out of focus ones were a real treat).
As for bugs, I first tried playing the game in Advanced mode.  I quickly got to a point where nothing I clicked on would activate anything.  I could do no HOGs nor leave the scene.  I had to start a new game in Easy mode to play.  There are also several places where the character floats over the pavement.  In one such scene, there IS no pavement.  The characters are both floating in air.
It's a shame that those issues are spoiling an otherwise very good game.  But, at the current list price of $0.99, I can live with it (it took me 2.4 hours for my playthrough on Easy -- but I still have to go through on Advanced to get 100% Achievements).  So, I'm recommending the game.
EDIT:  I've confirmed the bug I ran into earlier.  In Advanced mode, once you're given the task to collect the magic keys to unlock the mirror, none of the active points will activate.  IOW, you can't enter the two HOGs in the area to get what you need and you can't leave the area to get some other items and unlock the mirror.  I worked around this by exiting the game, re-entering it, and selecting Continue.  When the game loaded up the scene where I was, I could finish the scene (and game) without further problems.

Vampy and campy, twitchy and glitchy, and if this game was a movie it would be shown during the late night double feature creature picture shows where all good "bad" B-rated flicks were shown.
Spoof parody of vampires and B-rated flicks in Hollywood, complete with an otaku vampire fan boy of Bela Lugosi and Nosferatu who wants to become an actor and play Count Dracula in his own film.  Since the otaku fan boy is having a mid-life crisis (at 500 years old), he is causing grief for his daughter and her fiance, who has come to find her.
For the amusement value alone this game is worth the playthrough (and the price of 99 cents).  How serious can the storyline (or the characters, for that matter) really be when the News Station is called "Plan 9"?
Trivia 1: Plan 9 from Outer Space (1959) starring Bela Lugosi directed by Ed Wood is considered to be the worst creature feature ever made.
Trivia 2:  Bela Lugosi's protrayal of Dracula (1931) in some circles is still considered one of the best.
Trivia 3: The 1922 black and white German silent film 'Nosferatu: A Symphony of Horror' is considered to be a cinematic influential masterpiece, and even by today's standards is still considered to be one of the best Dracula movies ever made.  (Dracula's name in the film was changed to Count Orlock.)
Trivia 4: Jonathan Harker and "Mina" Murray were the bethrothed and eventually married "lovers" in Bram Stroker's 'Dracula'.
Gameplay is twitchy and glitchy (if stuck just exit the game then hit continue when coming back).  There are no  instructions for any puzzles, so previous puzzle experience and a bit of intuition is needed.  (I got stuck once and had to look up the solution, which is randomized I discovered on a different playthrough.)  Plenty of HO scenes to do, and not the usual type of getting an object at the end.  I sorta wondered the entire time why the HOs scenes were even there but they do serve a purpose.  In some ways this game feels like an experiment in third person play by Jet Dogs Studios and reminscent of how Syberia and Niburu plays, without defined instructions on what to do or where to look.
Worth a look and at least one playthrough just for the campy cheesiness of it.  (This would be perfect fodder for MSTies  (Mystery Science Theatre 3000)).

I should preface this with the fact that I'm a pretty big fan of old shooters. I mean, hell, F.E.A.R. is one of my favorite shooters of all time and it only came out 2 years before Bioshock 1. Games being "dated" doesn't bother me at all.

This game is just not my thing, although I suspect I'll force myself to finish it anyways.

I pirated this game way back in 2009-2010, of course it was a stupid idea but the unforgettable moments I had playing this game was truly amazing. The first time using plasmids, the first time receiving ADAM. It was amazing.
Bioshock is set in an underwater city called rapture, built by Andrew Ryan. The place goes mad, people become spliced and insane craving for ADAM and all hell broke lose. You play as an unnamed plane crash survivor and you swim to a near-by lighthouse, this is the beginning of your trip down into the depths of rapture.
The combat is smooth as can be, weapon upgrade stations are far and scarce and are a one use only so you better chose which upgrade you want wisely, the upgrades can range from accuracy increases to damage increases. Splicers use their environment to attack you, weather it be hiding in the shadows or climbing on the ceiling like spiders, they will find a way to get you by surprise. Plasmids are an amazing addition to spice up the gameplay, they're genetic modifiers that can give you specific abilities e.g. electric or fire, with these abilities you can do environmental damage to your enemies, weather it be an oil spill conveniently set under the enemies feet or they might be standing in water.
The levels aren't linear but you will have to leave at some point, the levels are huge and you can find all sorts in them. Maybe some extra cash or a big daddy or two, who knows?
The sound is great however I did experience some issues when too much was going on, some sounds cut out completely breaking the tense moments.
The overall graphics are still breath taking, the first time you enter rapture you see glowing neon lights and buildings covered in sea life. As for the inside the place is dark and secluded. How ever nice and bright in some huge places.
Overall, this game is amazing. Can't wait for the
remaster.

Red Faction: Bug Hunt is more in line with the original games than Guerilla was.  It's a linear story-focused experience that I found much more enjoyable than Guerilla.  It doesn't suffer from any of the drawbacks of that bland open world and has a much larger variety of gameplay experiences.
The game has a wide variety of weapons, and they're all far more useful than anything in Guerilla.  The addition of the magnet gun is also fantastic, giving you another way to tear down buildings rather than burning through precious explosive ammo or slowly chipping away with a hammer.  There's even a gun that collects nearby debris and shoots it towards your enemies (in the DLC.)  This time around, only certain objects drop scrap when destroyed, but the upgrade systyem is much more robust allowing you to acquire and upgrade special nanoforge powers along with general upgrades.
The destruction system is great fun like always, and feels improved since Guerilla, with buildings more realistically falling down when supports are destroyed rather than hanging in the air supported by one lone pillar.  In addition, you also have the ability to reconstruct destroyed objects.  Some people think this cheapens the destruction but I find it gives the level designers more options so they don't have to worry about whether you'll be able to continue after a structure is destroyed and also gives you more tactical options, being able to construct cover during combat.
The graphics are quite good, and the game even has full DX11 support.  It even manages to run well even when buildings are exploding all around you.  Unfortunately the game uses an extremely low FOV, though it can be fixed by editing some game files as with all Volition games.
The multiplayer is pretty fun, though I doubt you'll find anyone playing public games so it's best to bring friends.  There is a set of 8 survival maps, where you fight of waves of enemies to either survive, or defend key structures.  It shares upgrades with the single player so you'll have an easier time if you play the single player first.
Overall a fantastic game and I hope Volition keeps working on Red Faction at their new home with Deep Silver.

SUPERHOT has captivated me since the playable alpha version years ago.  It's often described as a "Puzzle Shooter," but the entire time I felt like Neo from The Matrix.
The campaign's story is... odd, but still a complete blast to play, taking 3-4 hours.  The main content of the game, however, are the Challenges and Endless Mode.   Challenges change the game to make you play certain ways, such as making movement faster but limiting you to the Katana, or defeating X number of enemies under a Real-Time time limit.  Endless mode is straightfoward, providing levels to try to last as long as possible - although I find it more fun to use it as a playground to try stupid tricks. (New arenas are unlocked based on total kills overall, so you don't need to do well or cheese for unlocks).
If you enjoy the basic gameplay, you'll love playing through all the content and/or turning it on to mess around on Endless or to try a new Challenge here and there. Hi, guys.
I decided to write a review because there seems to be a lot of negative comments on the game from people who tried the game for 5 minutes, got frustrated, and quit. Which, coincidentally, frustrates me.
First things first, this game is one of my favorite games. I have played this game for multiple thousands of hours (before it came out on steam, before this server even existed), so understand that this is coming from someone who knows what they're talking about, but may also be a bit corrupted by my love for it. I will try to be objective, but it is one of my most-played and favorite games.
I would like to go in to a few points I mentioned earlier and expand on them, because bulleted points don't really cover the breadth of them.
This game comes with 14 classes, you do simple quests to receive the class "qualification", then you can talk to an NPC to change your class. You can have all classes on one character, and they all level individually. Classes have 3 sets of skills, two tend to be active skills the third is always passive skills. Along with these skill sets, classes come with 2 extra open active and passive slots, where you can drag and drop other classes' skills. Multiclass systems are fairly uncommon in general, and I've never found an MMO with a a class system quite this involved and unique.
The easiest way to level for most of the game is in a 6-person team. Along with this, the highest level of content is only available to guild parties. By design, the game is very social, and there tends to be a very strong feeling of community. People will often help newbies, crafting them free armor/weapons or giving them pets.
For all of these cons, there is a fairly simple explanation. This game was made in 2005,
by a Chinese company. Look at the system requirements if you don't believe me. Does that excuse them? Not really, but it does give some context for them. In my experience, though, most people who put a little bit of time in can get past these issues.
If you managed to read this far, congratulations, you've finished my review.

Lemme get this out of the way first.  Even though Steam says I've only played this game for half an hour, it doesn't account for all the time I spent on it when the game was new, nearly ten years ago.  I have some pretty fond memories of playing it with my friends, but it was in the barrage of all the different MMOs we tried together and we didn't really tend to stick with any of them all that terribly long.
A lot of the MMORPGs from that time played similarly and bled together to the point you really couldn't tell that much of them apart, and while DOMO was no exception to that, I liked it for its unique job system.  You can change jobs at any time in the game, level up that particular job enough to learn skillsets from that job permenantly and use them with other jobs.  Essentially, it's a game where you hybridize your job classes, much like Final Fantasy V.
That being said, there's really not much else that sets this game apart from other MMORPGs, and it suffers for that now as much as it did then.  So it's not just that it's dated (though it most certainly is), it was just never that interesting to begin with.  The job system was great, the game itself just wasn't strong enough to support it.  For a while, the North American server cancelled the game and it could only be played in Europe and other regions, so it's frankly kinda surprising to me to see it on Steam all these years later.
Would I recommend it?  Sure, but it's not for everyone, and it probably won't appeal to many people anymore.  But it does have flirty zombies.  That alone might make the game worth playing for, at least for a little while.

This game is a zelda-esque RPG with simple but charming pixel graphics. It doesnt look like much at first glance, but its really fun. If you are a fan of pixel art or top-down realtime RPGs, take a look at this one. Overall, its totally worth the completely reasonable asking price, even with a few minor flaws.
In depth
+++++++++++++
You move around with the WASD on a top down screen and aim you guy's facing with the mouse pointer, so you can run backwards while attacking or in circles or what have you. Its actually quite entertaining to run circles around a mob dodging their weapons while you hit them repeatedly. It is controlled simply. RMB is any ranged weapon, LMB is use (the cursor changes to a situational icon when you are pointing at something you can interact with) and melee. A few other keys round out the commands (questlist, char sheet, quickbar, inventory, menu), and all are mappable.
All weapons have a slight cooldown and even melee weapons have a range difference based on type (ie a sword has more range than a dagger) identified by how far away your "attack" animation travels. There is a simple char screen any RPG'er will pick up immediately, where you can add stat points, learn talents and generally make your guy better. It has a niceinventory and item system, and there is even a crafting menu. The enemies respawn, so farming and grinding is an option if you wanted to, but not strictly needed. There is also a lot of tongue in cheek humor, but it never feels like it beating you over the head with "trying too hard to be funny"
It does have a few flaws, some people may consider them major, some people may not care at all. One of the ones I consider major is the M+K only configuration. For people like me with physical disabilities that make it so using WASD is difficult, JoytoKey is a must. But even then JoytoKey never works as good as native controller. Another one is that the game is obviously written by someone without complete fluency in English. Grammar mistakes and odd phrasing abound in nearly all dialogue. It isn't as badly written as many games I've seen, but its definately noticeable. There are still many jokes that are greatly amusing, and some of the stilted odd dialogue adds a certain charm.
If you are fluent enough to play it in French, I suggest you do that.
Another thing I noticed is that walking into the bed at the inn is how you regain health and save. It costs 4 gold every time you touch it. There have been times when I bounced off it accidentally while leaving, causing me to spend 12 gold I didnt want to in 2 seconds. I have also been pinned by NPCS in certain areas (the crafter's bench in the miscellaneous store is horrible for this one), and was unable to get out due to the configuration of the area. It could also stand to be a little longer and have wider variety of items and crafting receipes as well as not have everything you can craft visible from the start (although that is a matter of personal taste, I like to gain/learn receipes instead of seeing everything right away). YOu;ll probably get 3-5 hours of gameplay out of it, more if you explore and mess around.
Even with these flaws - which I would call more of a lack of polish than anything - the game is definately worth it. With a seeming trend of indie developers charging ridiculous prices for games far less polished and fun than this one (especially 99c mobile games being badly ported to the PC and sold for $10), its a breath of fresh air to see a non-greedy dev charging a fair price for a game.
Its worth the $5 for any top-down RPG or oldschool fan. Get it.

Star Wars Empire at War is one of my favorite games of all time and an incredibly fun RTS. I've been playing it for around 8 or 9 years now (most of that was a physical disc) and it has *never* become boring. It has very good balancing with a rock-paper-scissors strength/weakness system, and the strategic elements aren't too simplistic yet aren't as in-depth as, say, Sins of a Solar Empire.
In the base game you play as the Empire and the Rebels, and in the Forces of Corruption expansion (which is what I'll be talking about during this review) you get the added Zann Consortium. They all have the gameplay styles and strengths as you'd expect from the movies. Empire is very straightforward in their attacks, can produce massive ships and use their superior technology to crush their opponents. The Rebels are more cautious and use methods like stealing technology from the Empire and relying on fighter support more than huge battleships. The Consortium is essentially the Rebel's stealing mechanic amplified, with systems like bribing and actively stealing money. All are fun to play as- it's satisfying to send a Super Star Destroyer into a weak Rebel base and dominate them, beat a seemingly-unstoppable Empire with a few squadrons of well-coordinated Y-Wing and X-Wing strikes, and to cripple powerful factions through espionage.
The battles themselves are entertaining. Even if the same general scenario has played out before, it's still captivating to watch the ships on-screen battle and blow up system after system until one explodes and falls towards the nearby planet. Personally I think the space battles are MUCH better than ground battles. I usually have the game auto-resolve ground battles, but they are still enjoyable nonetheless.
Oh, also, mods. The mods for this game are absolutely incredible, and if for whatever reason the base game doesn't satisfy you enough, perhaps the mods will. Want to add campaigns based off of the Thrawn Trilogy and play as factions like the New Republic, Pentastar Alignment, or the Empire of the Hand? Want to fight through the Vong War, and all the other awesome EU events that happened post-Return of the Jedi? (Or, sorry, our overlord Disney says those aren't canon anymore. But let's pretend they still are.) Get Thrawn's Revenge. Want to COMPLETELY convert the game from the Galactic Civil War to the Clone Wars? Get Republic at War. Want the same thing but you're not that good at strategy games and don't want to be brutalized by AI Opponents? (That would be me) Get The Clone Wars mod.
In conclusion, just buy it. You won't regret it. And if you're that /one guy/ who DOES regret it and thinks that Disney's EU is better than the old EU, you can use that handy refund button.

Sir, You Are Being Hunted is a stealth-survival game taking place on a small chain of islands. The premise is really simple: find all the runes necessary to activate a monument in the center of the map so that you can return to your home. There is a heavy emphasis on utilizing cover as much as possible and avoiding making noises or startling creatures, as either can give your position away. You also have to maintain a positive vitality score through eating good quality food and drink (poor quality will poison you). For the most part, you are fairly defenseless and will almost certainly need to retreat if spotted.
Thankfully the game gives you various buildings to search for supplies and weapons as well as plenty of high cover (bushes/tall grass) to hide in until enemies pass. As far as items go, you can get either weapons/ammo, food, junk, and distraction items. Distractions, like the clock and empty bottle, are very useful for moving hunters away from runes or just changing the direction of a patrol heading directly for you.
The game features a pre-built map that randomizes parts of each island at the start of every new game. Each island has a certain number of pieces that must be collected and returned to the obelisk at the center in order to win. As you collect pieces (and as time passes) the game will introduce greater numbers of hunters in addition to more dangerous varieties of hunters, such as the hounds which can detect you at close range without line of sight, and the scarecrow who functions similar to the enderman from minecraft. You’ll also find more powerful weapons capable of destroying almost all of the hunters in only a shot or two.
Towards the end of the game I found myself practically sprinting through areas as there are so many hunters and it got pretty hectic a few times especially when I thought I could pick off a few hunters only to find myself being chased by a group of 10 as they chipped away at my health, forcing me to duck behind rocks to stop the bleeding. Still, I never felt like the AI was acting unfairly although there were a few instances where I was able to slide around a tree in between myself and a hunter until he gave up.
While the game does have some replayability due to the randomized levels, I can’t really say I will be coming back to it again after playing it as there’s really not much else to see once you’ve beaten it. I would recommend grabbing this one on sale for 50% off so you really get your money’s worth.

The game will give roughly 3 hours of gameplay which is ill suited for an RPG.  It gives you just enough time to figure things out but not enough time to advance any sort of story or bring your character to a reasonably customizable point.  I hit Level 6 when I finished the game, which gave me 5 points to distribute.  I put two in stamina which ended up being a completely useless stat to me, 2 in health and one in mana... which also ended up being a completely useless stat to me.
The final boss of the game was killed by left clicking it over 10,000 times.  My right hand is still suffering from carpal tunnel, but thankfully I'm left handed and can do fine without.  But if you have carpal tunnel and are right handed.... you probably should just not buy this game.
The game starts you off in a room where you left click on what appears to be a flower until you look a little closer and find out that it's your dead wife.  You find out she's dead and receive your first quest to avenge her.  Throughout the game you will pick up 8 quests which will get you to 8 different boss-like entities that are all killed in roughly the same way.
The game advertises crafting... which it does have.  However since the game is so short and you don't actually need it, it doesn't make up a very important part of the game.  I killed the final boss with a weapon I picked off of an enemy, crafting seems like it is tacked on.  It is the way in which you get all higher quality goods, but because you can beat enemies by using a microing technique, it's simply not necessary.  It's kind of like how I found out I could block shots with the shift key... and then never used it because I barely ever got hit.
Each story is very rushed.  You talk to a person and they tell you two sentences, and then you are on your way.  For an RPG it's very lacking in plot development.
The pixel graphics unfortunately hinder the game in such a massive way.  Pixel art can be very beautiful.  In this case it looks like most of the pixel art was taken from royalty free artists and slapped into the game.  Nothing looks like what it should be.
If this was a free to play browser game I'd play it.  But I don't think I'd ever pay for something that looks like it was made at a game jam.

Not unless you are willing to spend $100 on an "average" gaming experience, that will quickly drop to "below average" once they release hunters and monsters you won't have.
EDIT: Changed to positive as the game moved to F2P and seems to be going in a more respectable direction.

Sir is an excellent example of how a short game can be very memorable and very good. The game is a survival-stealth title that features British Robots and an overall British theme. Your first playthrough will be full of tense moments and take about 7-10 hours, though anyone accustomed to stealth games may have much more favorable results. As with most survival games you need to consume food and avoid skirmishes with your robotic rivals. If you're interest is lessened by screenshots featuring guns have no fear, you will never become an overpowered thriving individual able to engage 10 robots at once. Using guns will send robots in your vacinity charging towards you. Reload times are long and the clips are very small.  Killing robots is a big component of the game, but you have to use hit and hide tactics. Very often you have to investigate a house's defences before you're able to make a move. You'll need to use distractions, traps and a few choice weapons to outwit the robots. Gameplay is very enjoyable, allbeit very short.
There are a few issues that can detract from your experiance however: death, poorly placed device parts and an invincible enemy. The game uses a save point system and there are five spots to save your progress. Upon death you return to your last save with everything you did undone. This causes some serious balance issues: suicide runs to find things can have no risk, and 3 hours of inventory management and storing items in houses become totally irrelivent if you forgot to save. I'd honestly prefer some kind of perma-death system to being flat out ignored by the game. The device parts also tend to get clustered togeth on the coast. You can basically beat the game by walking around each island and you'll find 80-90% of the needed parts in most instances. There are two invincible enemies in the game one is a hot air baloon that shines a light on you and makes a ton of noise, but can be temporarily disarmed by shooting the light or easily avoided. The other can one shot you, track you to the ends of the earth, and is difficult to evade. I don't like that one. Usually if I get caught I just save and quit and then reload.
The game has been finished and the final product is similar to it's beta. I still recommend the game, though I am disappointed in how little content there is. Wait for a sale. Less than $15 is worth a buy.

Written in 2008:
I was waiting for Bioshock since late-summer. I knew that the producers of such great games as Ultima Underworld, System Shock I & II and Freedom Force were involved and couldn’t help but have high expectations.
To say they delivered would be an understatement. I believe that this is the best, single-player videogame I’ve ever played. And that’s saying something because I’ve got records going back to the Atari 2600.
[Playing Quake and other id games online is still my #1 videogame experience but connectivity being what it is and the call of more adult activities, have me sidestepping online play since my clanberries days. Fix the box Marion!]
You can get an in-depth review from Gamespot so I’ll just hit you with my impressions in bullet time format:
Atmosphere: Great games create an atmosphere that consistently suck you in and won’t let you out. The developer’s desire to go all 1950s with Bioshock, I initially thought was a mistake. That was before I played the game. The voice-acting, the ambient sounds, the level and object designs… were all superlative. I can’t really say enough about how well they captured the feel of the 50s. This coming from someone who wasn’t even alive then.
Storyline: Another essential component to great games is having a viable premise and attainable goal. Bioshock’s story is completely compelling. I don’t want to give any of it away. In fact, if you are thinking about buying this game, don’t read the reviews. They inevitably give away too much of the surprise. It’s better to go in blind.
Gameplay: One of my biggest gripes about the game was it’s video requirements. My computer is fairly new, dual-core and all that stuff, but I had to tone it down to 800×600 to get a decent frame rate. Even then, the game stuttered on me at certain points. It’s hard to imagine what kind of beast of a machine someone would need in order to play this game at 1280×1024.
Realism: A pet-peeve of mine is a lack of realism in game designs. I’ve started to capture some of these concepts in my Real Life Manifesto document. (Feel free to send me some of yours!) Bioshock falls down on several of these. For example, your character has no problem carrying a wrench, pistol, shotgun, machinegun, rocket-launcher, flame-thrower, plenty of ammo for all, a camera & film, 9 first aid kits and 9 syringes of Eve, all the while running and jumping at the same speed as you did at in the first minutes of the game when you merely held the wrench. Stuff like this kills me. Anyway, all of these lapses are common to most games these days, so they’re (mostly) easy to forgive.
The game was immersive and addictive. As soon as I finished it the first time on Hard, I played it again on Medium so I could check out of more of the characters and environment. I give it the highest rating I’ve ever given a game, 9.5 out of 10.
Note: I do need to mention the game is rated “M” for mature and that’s due primarily to the harsh language “provided” by the games characters. The game is certainly violent which added to the rating but not to the point of being gory.

A game for the introspective thinker.
First and foremost this game is not for everyone, it is not multiplayer, it is not an RPG, it's not a survival crafting game. The term walking simulator comes to mind, however it really doesn't fit that bill either. It is a hardcore loner survival game, intended to be challanging, beutiful, simple, and occasionally nerve racking.
Let's start with what I do and do not like. I love the atmosphere, while it may not be bleeding edge graphics the use of specific methods with textures and atmospheric effects make this game simple, yet beutiful, a type of elegance few developers pull off, though many try. The enviorment itself is a challange, monster and zombies can be annoying, but when the world around alone is enough to kill you just for trying to push your character a bit too hard, requries careful use of your time and resources, to me is far more intimidating than a wave of enimies when you have a practically unlimited supply of ammunition for an assult rifle. Resources are sparce and not every little thing is useful, many take days just to be useable for anything. You can find a hunting rifle but it will become useless to due wear or a lack of ammunition. As for the wildlife, it's not only hard to kill a wolf, bear, or deer, but you actually have to find them, and survive them if they see you first (for wolves and bears).
What you may not like. Their is a planned story mode to be used later, but not yet. You cannot make ammunition, that would be OP in this world. You cannot make your own shelter, I personally would like to see snow caves, they would need to take hours to make so again even this would take careful consideration, and wildlife and your condition would be factors. It's not likely you can survive indefinately, and when you die you die for good.
So if you can understand what this is and is not, and still think it's worth a go, I doubt you will be dissapointed.

Disgusting tier weeb trash.  But it's pretty fun.  My first Warriors game and I have to say I'm pretty impressed at how satisfying the gameplay is in general.  Disclaimer:  Detailed review for newcomers and the like.
For those not in the know, the Warriors game series is primarily focused on conquest styled gameplay where you take control of a Hero Character and mow through thousands (literally) of enemies to get to your actual targets; be it a boss or a capture point in order to win a match.  All this is done against computer controlled enemies.  Warriors All-Stars is sort of like the Smash Brothers of Koei Tecmo's series
One of the greatest strengths of the series, as far as I know, is the massive roster that's packed into it.  I don't know *any* of the characters here (save for Ryu Hayabusa) or have played any of their games but they all belong to Koei Tecmo.  Many if not all of the characters have relatively unique animations and combos and skills to suit your playstyle and or your fanservice needs.  I'm generally not a fan of modern iterations of whatever constitutes as the inbred artstyle of anime in not only anime itself but the vast majority of Japanese video games.  That being said, there are a few good character designs that don't fall into this generic art style (primarily those of older IPs, if you can spot them) so if you're not a fan of that, you stll have options.  That being said, the roster does *appear* relatively one note if this were one's first game.  If you're not a fan of a purely eastern-asian art style, it can put you off if you find few characters that you like.  This was how I felt at first, but there were two or three characters (out of 30) that I found myself playing and enjoying, which kept me playing as long as my hours indicate.
*Buying Point 1:  Look up the game's roster of characters, but not necessarily how they play; do you like any of them?  How many of those characters do you actually see yourself playing at all?  This will be one of the biggest parts that determines the longevity of gameplay and how much you'll get out of the game.
The story in Warriors All Stars is pretty generic, almost to a fault.  It's fairly cut and dry but it's enough to at least weave a narrative that can motivate you to play.  There are some (quality-ish) pre-rendered cutscenes that are well done but the story isn't much to laud.  A lot of the actual maps seem to be lifted off of other Warriors games as well, which feels somewhat flavorless and disappointing.  It definitely negatively impacts the presentation of the story because it simply doesn't make sense.  The maps can be fun to run about in, though.
All Stars does have some interesting mechanics I didn't expect to encounter; there's a slight social element to building a friendship between characters which not only provides a small bit of dialogue between the two, but can introduce new skill combinations and improve passive bonuses.  This mechanic is also tied to parts of the story itself which can branch off in a number of different ways.  Some of the endings in the game are obvious cop-out "endings" that inflate the potential endings you encounter, but they're easily avoided and the game provides you tooltips to actually navigate around that, so it's guilt free to look up how to attain an ending or characters you're interested in.   I might be mistaken but the impression I got was that most characters had at least ONE specific mission dedicated to them while others got entire chains and even endings.  It's particularly impressive on that note.
The gameplay of Warriors is satisfying, yet almost sadly repetitive if you're stubborn about a particularly limited set of characters.  The meat of the gameplay revolves around beating up as many mooks as possible, while having a level of tactical control of the battlefield, defeating enemy Heroes and taking over certain capture points.  It's not particularly challenging, and the bravery system encourages a more tactical approach to addressing certain situations and combat.
(In brevity, you build up a "bravery" rank that starts at 1 at the beginning of every level; boss units on the field have one, and even if they're comparatively weak, going against an enemy with a higher bravery level puts you at a disadvantage at times.  This bravery is leveled up by destroying large amounts of enemies or boss units (be it higher or lower than you).  This allow you to plan how you approach a level.  It's not completely mindless and neither is the Bravery system anything less than a boon.)
You can equip up to 4 other player characters at a time and actually use them in a variety of dumb and fun ways, such as getting the equivalent of a phalanx of all 5 of your character roster.  You can then (temporarily) play one of them as if they were your main player character, with their full set of combos and abilities, *simultaneously alongside the other PCs in a literal phalanx.*  It's absolutely ridiculous the amount of power it offers and can be very fun.  Personally, I found it more of a tool than something I enjoyed because I couldn't give a crap about most of the characters.
The progression system to Warriors All Stars isn't fantastic and once you unlock combos for a character through level ups (can be bought with gold and doing battles), there's not much else for them to do.  There are "cards" that you have to pick up for specific characters that act as passive buffs.  They not only provide attack power, but they also can provide unique passive defenses or elemental effects, an extra life, and so on.  They resemble RPG passives not unlike earlier Final Fantasy iterations (IE, resist more damage when knocked down, or do more damage under certain contexts or gain other buffs under certain contexts, etc.)  However, I found the cards to be unsatisfying rewards and a means of progression.  It's by no means bad, but it just felt utterly tasteless, like bland oatmeal with the occasional cinnamon packet.
*Buying point 2: The gameplay can be repetitive but the variety of characters is what can let you enjoy the mindless combat over and over again.  It's particularly fun to see how each character can address some situations compared to others.  However, the game's level types are rather limited, especially when compared to the somewhat more directed story missions.  The tactical element, while a boon to the game, isn't the biggest selling point but provides flexibility to first buying point (Characters).
Graphics are neat, runs well on my laptop at max quality @ 1080P with an I7 4720HQ and an NVIDIA 960M 2GB.  You're not buying Warriors Games because they're crysis.  HOWEVER, the game's combat is essentially an anime mook-fest slaying so that's fun and neat.
Buying point 3: Presentation and my most understated point.  You should know what you're getting yourself into.  It's anime ya'll, the good and bad.  It's got the good (over the top) and satisfying combat that's got all the fancy bells and whistles.
Sound, working, passable, nothing I care to note.  Minus the generic anime girls squealing obnoxiously.  Even the princess character, who I fully expected to dislike, was more bearable and sensibly VA'd than some of the roster.  But that's just my opinion; if you don't mind it then consider this a boon for yourself.
If a 5/10 is an average game (scores vary according to personal preference, personal enjoyability, and some objective measures like DOES IT WORK or IS IT ANNOYING?), then Warriors All Stars is an 8/10 enjoyable experience to relax and feel cathartic with some unexpected interesting curveballs the game threw at me.  Repetitive to a fault, but a fun repetitive.  The developers knew what kind of game they were maknig and they acheived it.  That, I can respct and appreciate.  A great "mileage" game if you're looking for a high playtime to cost investment ratio IF you get into it.
If not, then I suggest looking elsewhere.

Guess it's time I write my review, even though there's another 12k for this game and you'll probably already buy it (and love it!)
Let's start off with what makes this game
: The visuals and soundtrack. The art-style is amazing and unique, those qualities are put even more into perspective when you learn that the game was
The soundtrack is most certainly impressive, being live composed, and always giving off the right vibe for each part of the game you're currently at. The vintage atmosphere surrounding this game is amazingly nostalgic; remember when you were a kid on a sunday morning and you would eat your favourite cereal and then rewatch your favourite taped cartoons for the 1000th time on VHS?
Each boss is unique, and will require patience, but it is not a game that you'll tediously memorise. Quite the opposite, the boss evolutions are always interesting, keeping you on your toes. Also a tiny thing I love about this game is there is almost no RNG that will randomly screw you over.
The main complaint I've seen about this game (aside from scrubs complaining about how hard it is...to that I say: git gud), is about the weapons/charm system saying that one or two are overpowered and the rest are futile. Honestly, that's just stupid when you realise most of them are saying different weapons are OP. The thing here is that, there are weapons for people with different playstyles, and people usually prefer what they're comfortable with, of course they're going to say what they use is better. So yeah, I think the variety available here is awesome, especially when you are playing in co-op mode and you can have four different weapons (trust me, when you get a good combination in 2 player, you can
it).
The storyline is simple, but that's not a bad thing. The beauty of this game is its simplicity and originality. It ties together with the general mood of the game: simple and straightforward. It wouldn't make sense for it to have a complex storyline. It's like if someone complained about the story line for Mario being too simple.
One last quick thing, the amount of tiny details put into this game is astounding! With references to all sorts of things, to cool easter eggs such as the barbershop quartet and unlockable visual options, it's safe to say a lot of effort and love was given on behalf of the devs.

To this date, this is the last game in the Red Faction franchise. It has performed rather poorly in sales and it's easy to see why.
There is no more revolution or fight against oppression (which would mean human opponents), in it's stead - bug-like aliens take place. It reminds me of Alien Swarm or Alien Breed but with a much higher level of quality and that AAA feel to it. It's a rather decent game with the physics and destruction being improved, some very nice weapons and fairly challenging difficulty.
The storyline isn't bad. In fact it's much better then any of the new blockbusters.
A special place holds the music in my mind, it's not only a new style for the franchise, but a very well made artistic move that revolves around a more claustraphobic environement - like the first Red Faction and second Red Faction games to a degree.
It feels as if the identity on first glance changed, leaving nothing but the destruction aspect as a standing-out feature. In the end THQ went bankrupt and Nordic games took it's place releasing a little bit of content for free. Thank you Nordic Games!
The style is much too different. But don't be fooled by that, it's still a worth conclusion to a story that went on for 10 years with an amazing aesthetic value.

My hook to get you to read this review: I am NOT a veteran player, I am a Steam user just like you so my review is not a circlejerk of nostalgia.
Edit: Alright, I might as well fix this review now that I have 97 hours played. SO, this review will be divided into 2 sections. The first part you will read is my SECOND impression of this game where I actually experienced a bit of it. My first impression (which is mainly just me raging about being stuck in a bug) will be at the bottom with it's current rating. So why keep it in instead of just editting it out? Well that's because my rage was REAL. And I want everyone to know that this MMO is old and it has it's own set of problems. I wasn't planning on rewriting this review until one of the big bugs were fixed but since I'm pretty much up to 100 hours, why the hell not. What are you going to get from this review over others? Absolutely nothing because every review on here says the same things, but here goes:
This game is pretty good. It runs well on low-spec toasters because it's old and the community is literally one of the best group of people I have ever seen on the internet. Which says a lot. Within my first week being on this game I have been invited to a great guild, had people help me with literally everything and people have even given me cosmetics that they paid for with real money. Awesome.
-So this game has 15 classes. 1 starting class with basic harvesting skills and then at lv10 you can start unlocking the rest of the jobs and switching to them whenever you want. Now, I've never really been interested in games where you can just change jobs whenever because it sort of took away what type of character you were. But this game does it right. You level each class and then you can mix and match skill trees together.
Example: level your doctor a decent amount, switch to a class you haven't leveled yet and carry over the healing spells from doctor. Great.
-I won't really go into the community because I already stated it's perfect except for the Shiithead steam trolls that are Running Amok using le cool kid 4chen terms. (Also the game seems a little dead at night and when you're not in Eversun City. Mainly because this game was washed away in all the steam releases and it's launch on here was coincidentally ruined by the spawn bug.)
-Graphics aged well. Looks decent compared to other recent anime-inspired MMOs. And plenty of rare costume piece to customize your char with. Given you have the time and patience to either grind gold to buy them off players or reach into your wallet and buy CHANCE boxes to try and get some yourself vs. The RNG.
-Gameplay is your typical MMO except for the fact that mobs do not drop gold, they only drop items which can either be sold or kept for collection quests, etc. Closest I can describe it to any other MMO is maybe FlyFF because at lv15 you get a flying quest and I♥♥♥♥♥♥you not once you start flying, if you've ever played FlyFF, you'll be thinking about that game.
-The GMs are actually active with their community. More than I've seen from a lot of other teams out there.
-Biggest negative in my book is: There are a few bugs. I think the spawn bug is fixed but there's also this inventory bug THAT'S NOT VERY COMMON. I've only seen it happen to 1 of my friends where you get disconnected and lose your equips. But it has never happened to me personally and that was quite awhile back and there's been a few updates since then. If it does happen to you let me know. And also submit a ticket on their site if you lost something valuable.
Idk, best advice I can give is to try it yourself. Download is pretty small.

I picked this game up after having brain surgery, in the hope that it would help me regenarate some of my cognitive abilities, and I can honestly say that it has been invaluable in helping me recover. At its core this game is so simple, just draw a line to tiles of the same colour and fill in blank tiles with whichever colour fits. Sounds easy on paper, but in practice this simple puzzler can leave you stumped for ages. It's so satisfying when you finally complete a puzzle that you've been stuck on for ages, and it can keep you entertained for hours. It took me over 40 hours to finish every puzzle and get all the acheivements, about the same time it took me to complete one playthrough of dying light, so for a game that cost me under £1 it's pretty cost effective. I didn't encounter any bugs, the game runs smoothly, it looks beautiful, it has a calming and serene soundtrack, and genuinly makes you think. Brilliant little game, I can't really find a fault with it.

This is an old school game, many, many years old.
Although granted the game is dated, there are many points
worth at least considering here.
--Pros--
Graphics - Old Anime styling, cuteness factors that attract a variety of people.
Gameplay - Organized, your average tank/dps/healing/support all exist.  Each class can be made how YOU desire it with ease.
Job/Class - Unique, through leveling more than a single class, you have the ability to use other classes skills on another class.  Playing DPS but not surviving too well?  Level up doctor a bit, gain a healing spell or regenation.  This will ease your gameplay fairly, though there are many combinations you can use to maximize DPS and supporting/tanking abilities.  Find what works best for you!
Patches/Updates - Suba has promise a certain amount of patches, and from launch to now has been delivered as promised.
Social Aspects - The community is fairly large, people communicate regularly and are quite fun.  Get to know others, make friends.  Your overall gameplay will improve phenominally.
--Cons--
Grinding - Granted this is in most every MMO you see, that hasn't had every ounce of challenge nerfed out of it.
UI - A bit small and hard to read for players with higher resolution settings.  Easily resolved by reducing native resolution setting.
Lack of good instructions/directions - While i can't expect this to be improved upon much, i've ran into my fair share of moments where i had no idea where to go, or what exactly to do.  Try roaming a wiki or asking other players, if you're unsure of an objective.
Overall rating - 9/10

Endearingly awful...  :)
Cheesy B-movie acting, a plot that doesn't even pretend to take itself seriously, and some amusing jokes - for a mere $0.10 on sale I really can't complain too much!  It was a little dull at times, and the excuses for making you go find stuff were lame, but it was a couple of hours of mild entertainment for almost nothing.
The characters who inhabit Hidden Object Games are some of the messiest people I've ever seen - I'm no longer surprised by the piles of junk they seem to have in all their cupboards and corners and desks.  Unfortunately in this game, some of the objects you were asked to find were barely visible behind other objects (just a tiny piece poking out), were hard to see clearly, were named oddly, or were completely hidden behind other objects that you probably wouldn't know you could move unless the hint sparkles told you so...
Speaking of which, the 'easy' mode was far too easy.  Pause in your random clicking for mere seconds and the game would show you what you needed to find, without you asking it for help.  That said, though, some tasks or locations seemed so obscure that I'm not sure I would have known I could look closer at a particular spot in the room if it hadn't shown me.
I did encounter one bug, where the game refused to respond to my clicking and I thought I'd have to restart, but it was fixed by going to the main menu and then continuing the game.  Other than that, the only issues I encountered were with the clicks picking up objects I wasn't actually clicking on in some cases, which may have something to do with it apparently being a mobile port (I presume, what with it telling you to 'tap here' or to swipe the screen in order to complete a mini game).
I had a few laughs while playing, and especially at the end credits - I'm not sure I would have been happy to pay full price even though it IS cheap, but on sale it's worth a play through.  Just don't expect anything serious and you'll be okay!  :)

A great asymmetrical with lots of depth. Each character is strikingly different in tactics and play style, even within the same class, and the monsters are very unique and equally fun to play. Playing as the monster is a completely different experience, depending on a mix of stealth and brute force, and even some finesse with the Wraith.
It does have an offline mode where you can play against bots which is nice, but not enough to entice those who don't have reliable online access. The AI for both the hunters and monsters is decent but gets predictable after awhile; this game is definitely best enjoyed online, with the offline best served as practice or for ranking up.
Evolve has a clean menu system, tutorial videos that automatically play the first time you play as a new character. The game also boasts great graphics and excellent sound design that works well with the premise; a lot of the time I am listening for the monster's location, or hearing the hunters on my tail. It's all very slickly presented.
As for the biggest complaint about this game, the DLC. Like most, I'm not a fan of the game's DLC model, but I also don't think that detracts from the game as it is, and piling on this game seems a bit unfair considering DLC has been around for a long, long time now, and done more egregiously. All the current DLC is cosmetic only. Future DLC is on par (price-wise) with map packs or booster packs that other games pump out. At least Turtle Rock seems to have a more thoughtful approach to DLC, with all of the future maps and game modes being free, preventing the community from being fragmented (a la Payday or COD) because some don't have the DLC (you can always play against new monsters or have people in your party play as the new hunters).
My only other gripes would be slow updates and lack of game modes. The modes there are fun (Nest, Rescue, Defend, and Hunt) and the attempt at a campaign is admirable, but more variety would always be nice.
However, as far as the package as it, I feel like I got my money's worth with the depth of gameplay and character development/unlocks, variety of maps, and just the overall presentation. I played in the alpha and the beta and loved every minute and keep coming back for more. I'm looking forward to future monsters, maps, game modes, and hunters to keep things fresh.
