At first glance What Lies Beneath looks like Realm of the Mad God, but the visuals are the only similarity. Myrne plays a lot slower. It wants you to take your time and explore!
I'll do my best to describe the good and bad points, but with such a simple game, it's a bit tricky..
THE GOOD:
-The story doesn't take itself seriously. If you've played DLC Quest, the sense of humour will seem very similar with goofy jokes and calling attention to the fact that it's a game. The main character likes to break the forth wall while the NPCs struggle to stay in character.
-Questing is fun! You could probably count the total number of quests with one hand, but the game does a good job varying them up. Most of them involve killing bosses or other creatures, but you might have to solve a puzzle to reach them.
-Very lengthy for what it is. You can finish it in a little over 4 hours. I got stuck on a quest which took me a while to figure out, otherwise everything else was easy :)
-The Music is awesome! The soundtrack in What Lies Beneath will surprise you! Seriously, it's steps this game up to a whole other level.
-Walking speed doesn't suck! This might seem trivial, but for a game like this, moving slow can test your patience. You can spend stats to increase movement speed and there's plenty of items that warp you to your last checkpoint (touching a bed saves your game and sets spawn)
-Easy to grasp crafting system! In this day and age, crafting has become a strange standard in gaming, which a lot of times requires loads of research on the games wiki. Song of Myrne has descriptions for every item and effect in-game so you won't be scratching your head and taking notes.
THE BAD:
-I've ran into a couple bugs. One completely locked my hotbar. I could walk around, but I couldn't attack. Reopening the game resolved the issue.
-The second bug isn't an issue, but it's quite cruel. I was killed inside a dungeon (being killed will respawn you in town and cost gold) and while the screen was fading out to respawn, the monsters continued to attack my corpse. Each hit counted as a "death blow" so kept losing gold over and over as the game thought I died multiple times.
-The Hotbar can get a bit confusing. Say you have an item tied to 1 on the keyboard. If you have 6 of that it shows your reserve on the hotbar. The problem is there's no visual que letting you know which number is which, so until you get used to it, you might press the wrong key a few times. This is an easy fix if the numbers on the hotbar were a different colour than the item number.
If you'd like to see the game in action, here's my First Look :)
FINAL THOUGHTS:
If you're in the mood for a casual single player RPG, you can't go wrong with Song of Myrne. $5 is a perfect price for this game. Any bugs I ran into weren't game breaking or annoying, I just noticed them. I really don't have anything bad to say about this game.
-Thanks for taking the time to read this review!

Outlast is a first-person survival horror.
You play an investigative journalist investigating a psychiatric hospital or Asylum, trying to uncover what has been going on in this place while running, hiding and trying to survive.
Intersting gameplay.
The camcorder is there for a reason. Both story-wise and gameplay-wise.  You are meant to record whats happening and uncover the truth. And it helps you see in the dark. This drains battery. You can only carry 10 batteries.
Apart from batteries you collect files. Filming certain events will unlock notes.
The characters are interesting, some bizzare, some strange, some disgusting, some entertainingly funny.
One of my worries was that the twist would be supernatural. Im not gonna spoil the twist.
As for the ending its pretty much what you'd expect from a horror movie ending.
This typically is not my type of game. But a good game nonetheless.
NEGATIVES:
You have a brightness setting but you cant make the game too bright which is understandable.
But unfortunately there isnt a separate slider for the music.
This can be a pain when you want to listen for footsteps.
Those obvious cheap jump-scares where something/someone jumps in your face, with loud music in your ears.
The game doesnt need those jump-scares since the game already has tense moments. And so I wish they werent there.
The stealth element. Enemies can see you in the dark. I dont know if standing or crouching makes any difference. I dont know if noise is a factor. They always tend to investigate an area whenever you activate something. But thats more a scripted thing rather than a noise based thing.

So I play basically all the Musou games that come out. SW4-2 was pretty great, maybe the height of the series in terms of character design and gameplay concepts. How does this stack up to that?
Well, it's iffy.
The story is terrible, it's an obvious excuse to just have different characters in one universe. Very little - if any - effort seems to have been made to have it all make sense, or to give it a purpose beyond allowing for the setting. The original characters are bland stereotypes you've seen a million times in anime. They're cardboard cut-outs of cute little girl, motherly figure with huge boobs, cold tall guy with long hair and glasses, and generic enthusiastic teen leader #4.
The card system is the new equipment management system, and it's okay.
There's a loyalty system, how friendly you are with your teammates, which is okay. It's not great, its mechanics are a little needlessly obtuse, but whatever.
There's a quest system, which ties into the loyalty and card system, and it's okay.
So what about the combat, which is basically the whole reason for the entire series? Well, I enjoy it more than I dislike it. Here are some pros and cons:
Pros: Having teammates join in after you finish a charge combo allows for weaker characters to still seem competent. Having a mechanic where you constantly summon a nigh-infinite amount of enemies to always be surrounding you means you get to really fulfill that "kill a zillion people" itch the game seeks to scratch.
Cons: Character movesets are severely limited, it's actually really disappointing that we only get up to five squares and a triangle as the highest combo there is, with previous Musou games going up to six or seven, having multiple kinds of movesets focusing on normal chain attacks or weird delayed projectile placement, changing it up to keep things interesting, and this entry also doesn't have the R1 special move that further allowed each character to feel unique. All of those things are gone.  And since only combos above square-square-triangle give you the teammate followup moves, it makes it so there's not really ever any point to using square-triangle or square-square-triangle, ever. At all. Not even for niche situations or in 1v1 fights. So what you're left with is the three-square-triangle, four-square-triangle, and five-square-triangle moves. Each character effectively only has three moves, with the five-square-triangle move almost always being the optimal one to use in every situation, so you'll mostly be spamming that one move for your entire play experience with that character. The Bravery system is completely unnecessary and serves only to annoy you - it's like the level of your character matters less than the Bravery level you've achieved within the battle, which makes no sense at all.
And you might notice that there's way more under the "Cons" bit than under the "Pros" bit, so why did I say I enjoy it more than I don't? Because there's more people on screen to fight at once than there ever has been in any other Musou title. Remember in ye olden days when you'd be fighting like five guys at once, at most, and then more would fade into existence around you as the system allowed for it? No longer! If there's dudes there, you can see them. You can attack them. You can kill them. I don't think I've noticed any kind of cap regarding how many are allowed to be on-screen at once. It feels good to kill a thousand guys in a few seconds.
Loading times are really fast, I'm very happy with that.
I do wish they'd made different choices, and they certainly aren't trying anything new as far as movesets are concerned. It feels more like Dynasty Warriors 4, honestly. So it's a step backwards there.
Overall it's a decently competent kill-a-million-people simulator. It'll kill some time. (Note: review written Jan 2017, after ~2.5 years in Alpha.)
TL;DR: Good? Yes and no. Slightly yes for me :) It depends on what you look for in a game. If you've played a bunch of crafting/survival games you may find this slow and want more gameplay, but for everyone else I recommend it for being pretty easy and immersive, with lots to explore - especially if you're interested in survival, but don't think zombies and raiding belong.
- Full review follows -
This is proper Four Core survival! With very little gameplay. There's hunting and hiking, but the main game is inventory management and crafting (no building), i.e. menu-clicking.
It's a walking simulator with *lots* to explore, and the weather and audio creates quite immersive moods that can make you feel the urgency of nightfall, a whiteout, a broken leg, or starvation!
The slow pace is relaxing at first and sets a good mood, but you can't trigger a craft and then go do other things; you have to watch a meter until it's done... I wish the skill-leveling system would speed up crafting, but it doesn't.
For most of the game, you will be inside, managing your backpack. Actions here are well thought out and detailed! But it will make you look at 1998 resolution objects and textures a lot, which is just too bad. But the excellent coherent and driven art design helps here too - and outside, almost everywhere you go, it will make screenshots look like a watercolor painting scene. Very nice :)
Despite this, you may get the 20-40 FPS bug on a great gaming PC. Until the bug is found, try 60Hz+Vsync. (Probably, the game can run 60 FPS on a 2011 graphics card.)
"Accurate description, OK, but all I wanted to know is if you had fun??"
I had fun the first 7 hours, got loot+shelter. I had survived. So I left it. Came back to it some months later, same game, no Story mode, OK. So I played a couple evenings, and still liked how it made you plan trips or think twice about even going outside, even if you have to :) Tried some things and leveled. But overall I found the pace too slow, and there's nothing you can do to play it more skilfully to fix that; you do the same old things in the inventory all the time. I'm not sure I'll come back to it at all. I think it depends on how interesting the Stories are and above all whether more gameplay is added.
So maybe you'll get 20 hours out of this, more if you explore everything, maybe 10+ hours on top of that if the Stories turn out great.
And that's pretty good! My thumb tilts slightly upwards then, for these 2 main features that I'm glad I experienced:
+ proper survival feel
+ good immersion

When I first saw Limbo on the Steam store page a couple of years back, I was interested in the eerie ambience it projected. This minimalistic, indie game was unique in the sense where most 2D games offer a fast-paced, brutal action-packed gameplay; Limbo deviated from this and focused more on exploration and curiosity immersing the player into a very dim world.
I finally tried it thanks to the Steam sale and after spending 12 hours to explore every nook and cranny, as well as obtaining all the achievements, this is my overall opinion of the game:
The lack of a background story makes it all the more intriguing. It's one of those games where the whole scenario never gets explained. So leaving something open-ended, gives players a chance to come up with their own interpretation.
In terms of gameplay, I believe the linear mapping of the "base" levels accomodate towards casual players: meaning if you're just after the story, you'll be able to manage the whole playthrough at your own pace without too much stress or frustration on consequences.
All in all, the sucess of this refreshing game, I think inpired other indie developers to also delve into the dark-themed 2D genre in the succeeding years.

Project Zomboid is a unique game with a lot to offer.  The developers are active on this game, there are tons of fun Workshop mods, and some pretty fun multiplayer.
The gameplay is simple, yet unique and enjoyable.  You have limited vision, stamina, the ability to freeze or overheat, all adding to the realism.  You aren't some super soldier like in Call of Duty, you're a regular guy, who has his own unique personality, with traits.
Traits, this is another great feature.  They can completely change the gameplay.  There are good traits, such as "Brave", which makes you less proned to panic, and bad traits, such as "Obese", which slows your running speed.
Crafting in this game is pretty realistic, but I depended on online guides at first.  There is a wide range of things to craft, such as food, medical supplies, barriades, and more.
Combat may seem bulky, but that's part of the game's realism.  You can't go in like Rambo and take out an entire horde of 20 zombies.  This also can encourage strategy when dealing with large hordes.  Also, in combat, you're going to get injured, and the medical system in this game is realistic, and certain tools can help you and prevent you from dying, such as tweezers, to pull out broken glass.
Okay, this game certainly doesn't have dazzling graphics, but I don't care.  Graphics aren't everything in a game, and Project Zomboid proves this.
- Fun and Enjoyable Gameplay
- Great Amount of Realism
- Large World to Explore
- Crafting can be tedious
- Not the world's best graphics (A minor point.)

You play a small boy who wakes up in limbo… I assume. You then start traversing purgatory towards an unknown goal. As you travel, you encounter monsters, traps, murderous children, an empty city and brain-controlling parasites.  Limbo is one of those indie games where nothing is said or explained, relying on what happens in the game to convey a sense of meaning.
I do not need my hand-held as I’m led down a narrative path, but I certainly need signposts or hints as I’m going. First of all, in a linear game, I would like a motivation to keep going, some kind of plot hook or story. My desire to complete a game does not come solely from the desire to complete a game. Second of all, endings can be open-ended, but they should still explain everything that has occurred so far. Like a “Bruce Willis is a ghost moment”, or the last ten minutes of Shutter Island.
That is my gripe with the story of Limbo. However, I was impressed by all other aspects of the game. For a 2D game entirely in grey scale, the graphical style was really impressive. Multiple layers gave the impression of depth, with a clever use of shadows and beams of light around that. I was never confused about what I could interact with. Also, a lot of effort has been placed into making things like water, rain, dust motes and grass look good.
The puzzles themselves are well-thought out, and most of all, actual puzzles. In other words, once you know the solution, they’re not that hard. Sure, it’s a platformer, so there is always going to be well-timed jump here and there, but that part of it isn’t overly challenging. I never failed a puzzle because the solution was unintuitive, or because I failed to grasp a ledge properly (looking at you Monochroma).
Limbo is a fun, short game to play, if not a little bleak in themes. If you are looking for a story, you will not find it here. But you will find some well-polished and engaging puzzles, all holed up in a game that does a lot visually with no colour.

TL'DR: Good game that stands above the rest; but it is not about beating the zombie apocalypse. We LOST! Now, how long until you die too? That's it!
The game is a stand out veteran of the horror zombie sandbox survival genre. However, rather than compete with Minecraft, or Dayz, or the over saturation of countless others... Project Zomboid is original in its spin on things.
The graphics are isometric, god perspective: think The Sims. They are also purposefully retro and pixelated, nearly 2.5D! This allows a huge savings in rendering, processing, and video memory. All of which is converted to progress and in game content.
The base game mechanics are solid and as you'd expect: scavenging for food, resources, crafting/building supplies, etc. Where it stands out is: the character creation, threat detection, zombie AI, and combat.
Character creation: aside from your gender, name, and appearance; you can choose a career which will come with certain perks and penalties. You can then assign character traits or flaws. These will have varying costs depending on their stats. Example: you can make a character disorganised. This, will reduce your carrying capacity but allow you 2 extra trait points. Then, you can select a positive trait like: sneaky. Obviously, this means it is harder for zombies to detect you. Impressive and complex stuff!
This brings me to threat detection: Depending on your traits and flaws your character will have a given awareness radius around them. You can only see things in front you; depending on your hearing you may or may not be aware of things behind you AT ALL! You cant see over fences, or through walls. Even looking through windows will only give you a narrow view. Amazingly, given the game graphics and rending: there is no way to know what is beyond your senses. The engine simply does not render what you can not see or hear! This is a huge competitive advantage over other games. Just because you can't see the zombie, does not mean he cant see you. Watch your back! Remain alert, clear rooms methodically, know your escape routes (note the plural!) Always be ready to HOLY MOTHER OF GOD, GTFO!!!
Fortunately, zombies are pretty dumb. Their programming however is amazing! A single zombie will hear, see, OR SMELL you. Each one, like players, has its own stats and traits. Once you are detected, a zombie will move towards your location; or last known location if you slip away. Freshly turned mobs will be quick, generally though you can walk to get away. You should walk! It makes less noise, and doesn't drain your stamina. Running is simply making tendering your innards while ringing a loud dinner bell! Which is next flaw in your plan! Any other zombie, that sees that first one move, will become curious as to what it's up to... You will quickly find yourself facing a swarm! Keep quiet, stay out of sight, try not to panic. If you are detected, do NOT try to hide! They will not stop looking for you. They will break down doors, climb through windows, and they will eat your face off!
In the event that you can't escape; you'll need to fight. I hope you found a weapon! Empty handed, you'll only be able to kick and shove zombies away from you. You might be able to create an opening and slip through: good luck! If you do have a weapon, you'll need to ready it with CTRL (default) and make strategic attacks. Only headshots will stop a zombie. Be quick however, the struggle will be noisy and will draw even more attention. Not only that but you will get tired; they wont! The longer you run or fight the more exhausted you get = the less damage you do and you'll move slower too!
In the end, the game is brutal and unforgiving, but that is the point! It is not about winning back the planet or saving the human race... We've already lost! It's over, they win! The only question left is how long until you die too?

Dream of Mirror Online is a cute MMORPG with an anime style. The game is originally from 2006, so people should stop comparing it to new games - for me the graphics are great, i love it's style and everything about it.
I recommend using the window-mode, as there might be some issues with the fullscreen (not-windowed) mode. It also allows you to drag around the game-window on your screen, what is a plus for me (i like to watch anime/series on the same screen i'm playing at).
The game starts with an tutorial, that is very informing when you actually take a few minutes and read trough it.
What i've read often in the negative reviews is that the game starts without WASD-movement. Well, when you read this before you start the game and you are a fan of wasd: use ctrl + N to open the actions (or click on the down-right button in the menue), go to control and enable the wasd-movement.
The game has 4 races that distinguish only in looks, and so far 14 implemented different classes (jobs) to play. The player starts with the basic job: commoner. The commoner is the only class without active skills, because this class is bound to the crafting-system in the game. It allows your to level your alchemy (crafting skill), or material-collection skills. Once lvled to lvl 10, you can qualify for the other jobs via quests, and start the "real game". There are tank-classes, sorcerer/mage, healer/support, and of course dps/damage dealer, so everyone can find his/her passion. Now the Jobsystem gives everyone the opportunity, to lvl each job seperatly, and sub-equip the skills from another class (e.g. once learned, you can use the doctor's healing skills on another class to heal yourself).
Besides all the classes, the player can own pets that support the player when fighting and represent the main classes as well: there's mage pets (ruby, sapphire pet), tank (jade, metal pet), blademaster (rock pet) and support (love pet).
I advise everyone who wants to try out this game: please don't judge it after playing like 10 minutes, as it takes a while to get used to it in the very beginning.

Playing this game is like playing an unfinished product. Mainly because it is one.
With my experience, the gameplay is the same - either too balanced, or too unbalanced. What do I mean?

Well, this game would have been tons more fun if you could upgrade your player to specific stats, so training rooms and teams could require a specific level cap (so it isn't too unbalanced).This would create strategy (that is missing from the game) and complexity, trying out new styles and possibly being a fun experience. However, we settle for this - a really basic unfinished product where every character plays the exact same.

When in matches, unless you're teamed up with people who aren't selfish ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, you'll find that the only person defending is your keeper (who is CPU controlled), every teammate ever would just act like a hero and come up forth, ignoring basic offside rules, ultimately screwing up the team. This could be countered by adding a ratings system based on the player's performance in his positon, so these ratings stick to a player after each game so people could know how much of a♥♥♥♥♥♥he is. But I'm not here trying to convince the devs to put a little bit more balance (or fun complex unbalance) to the game even though it would be great. I'm here to advise you whether this game is worth it or not.
In conclusion, this game is an unsuccessful attempt at a minimum viable product, every player plays the same, basic physics and rules aren't that well implemented, slide tackles are too op (since there isn't any fouls) so you find everybody just lunging at each other at the speed of light, and the whole experience is just the same every time. This game neither showcases the random exciting nature of the real sport, nor does it showcase the players' skills. And that would be a good thing, if the game was just a simple fun experience, but it definitely isn't one. I'd advise the devs to take what they've learned from this failed attempt and focus on improving on the core formula, since this could be a great title, until then - I wouldn't recommend this title.

Evolve is a highly fun and unique multiplayer game about the thrill of the hunt and the changing dynamic of the hunter vs. the hunted. Many of the negative reviews have left me disheartened, as complaints about optional DLC and core game pricing have likely prevented many potential players from enjoying what's actually important about Evolve: it's extremely novel gameplay. Sure, the DLC sucks, but it doesn't detract in the least from the solid core game experience. Furthermore, the argument for the pricing of games like Titanfall and Evolve is that people are completely happy to pay $60 for a ~15 hr AAA single player game, so $60 for 30+ hrs of extremely polished multiplayer is a fine deal. If you're an FPS gamer looking for a fresh, fun, and challenging multiplayer shooter in a somewhat stagnant genre, look no further.

'Detailed' Review
DO NOT FALL FOR THIS GAME'S TRICKS
It starts rather strongly, with flashy gameplay gimmicks, fun interactions with the characters, the promisse of a lot of alternate story paths and such...
but this is all a trick; this game is built in a way to hide its flaws until its too late to get a refund
as its only after playing it for a few hours that you realize that all the flashyness it showed at the start, is all it has to offer
the character interactions fall apart, stages get CONSTANTLY re-used (to the point where I have come to realize this game only has a tiny few stages, and many of those stages are copy and pasted directly from other warriors games, only with a slight asset change here and there) mission objectives are recicled completely and constantly re-used (like the stages, there seem to be 14-16 mission variations in the game)
the meager 30 characters (and yes, that is a relatively small number, one that is entirelly stacked towards the DOA series, even.) in this title are wasted, similarly coming off great at first, but quickly falling apart the more you invest in them.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding cheese cake recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1 cup digestive plain sweet biscuit crumbs
3 tablespoons sugar
3 tablespoons melted butter
40 ounces softened cream cheese
1 cup sugar
3 tablespoons flour
1 tablespoon vanilla
1 cup sour cream
4 eggs
Directions:
For The base:.
If you're using a dark pan, preheat the oven to 350. If you are using a shiny pan, 375.
Combine the crumbs, melted butter and 3 tbsp sugar well and pat onto the bottom of a 9 inch springform pan. I also like to very very lightly butter the sides of the pan so that the cheesecake will not stick later on.
Bake for 10 mins in your preheated oven and remove. Let it cool while you prepare your batter.
For the batter:.
Make sure everything is at room temperature.
Combine sugar, cheese, flour and vanilla in a big bowl and mix on medium speed till well combined. Don't forget to scrape the bowl as you're doing this.
Mix in the sour cream till its incorporated well. Then, add the eggs one by one, mixing well after each addition.
Pour the batter into the springform and let it bake for 1 hour and 10 minutes After the baking time, turn off the oven and leave the door ajar. Let the cake cool in there for about 1 1/2 hours.
Remove the cake and let it cool thoroughly. Refrigerate overnight.
Release the sides of the springform.
Eat.

Sinister City is a ghoulish adventure that will frighten you to the bone, seize your soul, and cause your blood to run cold. You will spend the entire hour or so of this game in constant fear and...Whoops!
Got my intros mixed up.
Your fiance has been kidnapped by a vampire! Are you a bad enough dud to rescue your fiance?! Action and adventure await in Sinister City!
Hmm..Nope...That one kinda sucks too.
Truth is, there's not much to discuss when it comes to Sinister City. Not too long ago, this game was on sale for around 10 cents. On top of that, it has cards, so you're all but guaranteed to profit off of the purchase. Therefore, I'm going to assume that you already own this game, and are just reading this review because you assume there will be some funny jokes.
You know what they say about assumptions right?
In the interest of being "helpful" I'll talk about the actual game. Sinister City is a hidden-object puzzler. Look for the object, find the object, click on the object, become a winner. I must warn you though, the objects tend to be hidden. Occasionally there are puzzles to break up the monotony, but nothing too strenuous. For those exceedingly rare situations that you're actually stuck, a handy "HELP!" button is always nearby.
Not all hidden-object games are equal, and Sinister City is IMO an example of a mediocre one. The images are of a lower resolution, which makes objects muddy and difficult to spot. Yeah I know, it sounds ironic when you think about it, but bear with me on this. Another unfortunate technical issue is the prevalence of bugs. These can range from disappearing images to the game no longer properly responding to your inputs. Thankfully, these are usually cleared up by quitting to the main menu. The game saves automatically and constantly, so all you have to fear is those wacky vampires, not the possibility of losing progress.
The following couple paragraphs include SPOILERS!
----SPOILERS----
This next aspect is not so much a complaint about Sinister City, but about adventure games in general. All too often they rely on this logic that is baffling to normal human behavior. At one point in this game you have to find some books so that somebody will talk to you. There is an abandoned bookstand nearby, but the protagonist doesn't want to steal the books. In order to pay for these $20 books, he finds 75 cents in loose change scattered on the ground. If that made too much sense, consider that the protagonist steals a key from the bookstore to open a mailbox.
Sinister City's attempts at humor are also...pretty laughable. Early on the protagonist acquires some vampire hunting equipment. He's getting geared up to kill a vampire, but then some guy points out that not everything is as it seems. The protagonist takes a closer look at a stake he picked up, and he finds the words "MADE IN CHINA" engraved on it. The "Made in China" gag is as old as time, but it doesn't work when written on a stake. A stake is a piece of wood sharpened to a point. It's possible that the Chinese stake is actually made of soft rubber, but wouldn't the protag notice that? Here's a thought: Crosses are also commonly used to fight vampires. So how about having the Cross say "MADE IN CHINA". Eh? Eh? Okay whatever. The point is this, when you're trying to make a gag out of something that's almost impossible to screw up, it doesn't really work. Yes, I have a nasty habit of nitpicking. What can I say? I love talking about mistakes.
----END OF SPOILERS! YOU CAN BREATHE EASY NOW.----
Even with its faults, Sinister City is still an enjoyable romp. It doesn't take itself seriously at all, the voice-acting is amazing, and the game ends before you get tired of it. I'm not usually one to recommend bad games - even the ones that are "purposefully" bad - simply because they take too long to complete. This game delivers on hidden objects and puzzles, which is always nice to have when you're not in the mood for more Counterstrike or DOTA2 or Sakura Angels. It's nothing difficult, but at least it'll give you something to do if you have an hour or so to burn.

My hopes for Armageddon weren't high, which is why it’s taken me so long to actually play the game. I was pleasantly surprised though :)
The game is very well made, the environment design, the lighting, the animations and weapon effects. It’s all made to a very high standard, similar to the previous game, Red Faction: Guerrilla. Unlike Guerrilla though, this is a corridor shooter but with some seriously innovative features.
Returning from the previous games is the geo-mod technology that allows the player to destroy the environment. I’m so happy they've brought this back and even enhanced it! The new features include a  magnet gun, which allows objects to be pulled into other objects with great force. This creates a gameplay style I’ve never experienced before! Using a house to crush your enemies never gets old!
The new nano forge ability allows the player to regenerate the environment after you have destroyed it. This I found particularly cool, destroying the environment and then rebuilding to create cover or access new areas. Clearly a lot of thought has been put into new gameplay features for this game.
The story is probably the weakest point here. There are many links to previous Red Faction games (which is always great to see), but the characters are somewhat stale and the story feels as though it’s moving too fast at times. The low res cut scenes don’t help either.
But overall, a very good game. It’s always great to experience new and interesting gameplay mechanics, which Armageddon pulls off very well.

Project Zomboid is a hardcore survival game with the works. You have to manage the usual things like hunger and thirst, but also new considerations like sleep, overheating, freezing, fear, sickness and infection. It's a balancing act that has lasting appeal with an ever growing variety of ways to deal with your situation. Which brings me to Early Access.
I personally don't find the distinction between a finished game and an unfinished one to be all that useful. The feeling of fun that I have while playing a game doesn't care if it's "finished" or not. If your game is functional and enjoyable before it is officially released, then I'll happily give you money to continue creating a product that I would have probably bought anyway. After all, this same method is how we have come to enjoy many games that likely wouldn't have been made. Some games, perhaps most famously Minecraft, will likely
be finished, with new content being added on a regular basis. Project Zomboid is possibly in the same situation. If being in Early Access
one of your considerations against buying a game, then I hope this review is at the very least informative for you.
Zombie survival often turns into dumb action, so it's nice to see a game that is more
than
. The Zombies themselves aren't that threatening in small clusters, but the real danger comes in numbers. I had an experience where I had boarded up a house with a small vegetable garden, only to wake up in the middle of the night to a horde migration on its way to the city. I escaped, but my stash became inaccessible. After the initial frustration, I looked back and thought, "that's a really cool feature". Coming across an event as catastrophic as a migration or even something mildly hazardous like finding a zombie behind a door that you weren't expecting add excitement to the gameplay. Once your character is dead, you have to start a new game, so even being scratched by an unnoticed zombie can be devastating, and in more than one case, lethal. I love this. You approach scavenging cautiously. You pick your targets and pass over ones that you think would end badly. It's an elegantly designed difficulty curve that while not unique to Project Zomboid, has been well implemented.
A large part of the game is character progression. You create your character with a basic background and positive and negative traits, customise the games difficulty settings to your preference and then are dropped into rural America to fend for yourself. There are a selection of skills available to you. The way they improve is simple. The more you use a skill, the better you get at it. Thats it. This encourages variety in the way you play your game as new options open up the better you get at a skill. Currently there are 20 skills. Most are related to different physical abilities, but there are ones that affect how well you can farm, build, cook, trap, fish etc. While the system itself works mostly without player interaction, it's still nice to see something going on under the hood in a genre where most games are just content with a hunter-gatherer style of gameplay.
So what actually is the scope of the game? Well, when you start you literally just have the clothes on your back. Among your first concerns are food, water and a safe shelter to sleep through your first night. You will scavenge for anything of use and try to carry as much as you can without making you a slow, easy target for nearby zombies. Once you've found a nice place, preferable close but not actually in a town, you'll probably want to go about barricading it to reduce the risk of zombies breaking your windows or even worse, just wandering through the back door you forgot to close. Once you have found your new home, you'll go about nicking as much as you can and dropping it off for later use. Eventually, the utilities will be shut off, so you'll have to find alternatives to using refrigerators to keep food fresh and taps for easy access to water. Long before this, you'll need to consider actually growing and catching food yourself, a task made difficult by roaming walkers. This status quo balancing act can go on for months until you finally run out of bandages or meds to keep you going. I found the variety of things to manage to be really immersive, thanks in no small part to the attention to detail. If zombies are banging on your door, your character will become anxious so you need to give him sedatives or risk him being less effective when it comes time to run.
I really liked Project Zomboid. It has a wealth of content in its current state and still has new things added to it each time I play. It is everything that I want from a survival game in a package that clearly has had a lot of care and attention put into it. Again, being an Early Access title, you'll have to decide for yourself whether you'll find value in this purchase. I certainly feel like I got my money's worth.

Horror, Survival, RPG, Action, (Dying Simulator)
I would give it
due to being a unique and different style of the overused zombie survival genre.
Project Zomboid is an isometric 2.5-D (A 2D image that simulates depth much like 3D) zombie survival game that is very much different from all of the other...generic zombie games, including a realistic medical system in which you MUST keep an eye on your wounds else you might not wake up the next morning!
Everything! I mean from the configurable settings to the weather and the amount of things you can do in the game, looking after yourself is vital to your survival from depression and boredom to stress & temperature, every aspect of the human condition is counted as a survival mechanism and for you to truly survive & thrive in this environment you must manage all of this effectively, failure to do so results in death, and not just "you die, and then respawn" once you die in this game the whole world is gone, you could call it permadeath, all of your hard work gone, just because you decided to investigate that abandoned police station. (Police stations are dangerous; I did this once, and died almost instantly).
But that's not all, you have to scavenge for vital supplies such as food, water even rope & weapons, because after a while has passed (6 in-game months by default) water and electricity will be cut off to the town and you are left to fend for yourself. However you can build defences to not only hold off the advancing zombie hordes but to provide sustenance, shelter, warmth & storage.
Food spoils and water becomes tainted, so what do you do? You build makeshift water catchers to provide clean & safe water, find seeds and plant crops in a safe place...look after them and maybe one day, they will flourish into clean, edible food!
And to top it all off, updates, and the community, updates on game come out every Monday (They are called the mondoid) usually these don't include any game updates (they're usually once a month) but instead just what they have been working on for the past week, and they are usually interesting!
I can't really think of much that is wrong with this game, other than that there are no NPC's (Non-player characters) and there are also no cars, but it has been confirmed that these things are going to be integrated into the game in the coming months.

This is an infinitely charming 2D puzzle-platformer which proves that "less" done right can be infinitely more deep, enjoyable and satisfying than "more" (hear that, Ubisoft?).
I'll start with sound design this time - it's very, VERY minimal, but that's what makes this game feel even more eerie and creepy. There is very little music and mostly you hear your footsteps, the sound of the objects you are interacting with and some sort of idle noise in the background (wind in the forest area, industrial sounds in the factory-like areas etc.) and sounds have a lot of reverb, which creates an unmatched sense of loneliness, despair and to an extent, scale. Excellent.
Visually, this game is stunning, but not in the way that you might think. Performance wise there are absolutely no issues and the game runs smoothly on pretty much anything save a toaster. In terms of graphics, this game puts much more emphasis on style than hardcore texturing and models. Everything is black and silhouetted, even your character, but the atmosphere and mood this sets is quite unique: dark, depressing, foreboding and grim, which is in stark contrast to the game's protagonist, a young boy looking for his sister in Limbo (hence the title). The environments are actually fairly varied for such a short journey - you start in the forest, move to a sort of cave-like complex and a kind of pseudo-urban setting, finally going to an industrial area of sorts. The world is marvellously detailed and the animations are super smooth. The physics are simply superb as well, which is absolutely crucial to the gameplay.
Speaking of which - although this game is relatively short (I doubt you'd need more than 4-5hrs to complete this title, maybe even 3hrs without going for all the achievements), the gameplay is excellent, varied and pleasantly challenging. The controls are bare-bones, you move with your analog stick, jump with A/Y and use or grab with X/B (I strongly recommend playing this game with a controller). The puzzles are great and some of them require some out-of-the-box thinking, but there's nothing infuriatingly difficult or obscure. It's a puzzle platformer and you can run, jump and grab onto ledges, hit buttons, pull/push objects, swing on ropes... not much more I can say really, you have to experience it for yourself. One last thing to note is game relies heavily on "die first then try", and it adds to the relentlessly grim atmosphere. You will die. A lot. And that makes solving the puzzles that much more satisfying.
The only downside I can think of is the short length, but to be fair, it has decent replay value for such a concise title. There are secrets which take some extra braining around (if you're not following a guide) that you might have missed on your first playthrough, and when you find all the secrets, there is one extra chapter, which is a lot harder than the rest of the game - the majority of it is played in pitch darkness and the only thing you can rely on are sound cues and timing. Part of me wishes there were more moments like this in the game, but on the other hand, I think that once may have been enough in this case or it could've gotten old, fast. Then, there's the "No Point in Dying" achievement, which you get for playing the game through in one sitting and dying a maximum of 5 times which should keep you busy for a fair amount of hours more than the standard 3-5 if you choose to go for it.
Long story short, this game is great and you should definitely give it a try. Because of it's rather short length, I'm on the fence about whether or not it's worth 10€, but during a sale, go for it, it's more than worth sale price.

Hi All!
I first played DOMO back in 2008 with Aeria and I am really glad Suba gave it an other chance.
I like how the game gives you to choice to solo or party up and keeps both paths viable. The class system is nothing I have ever seen before or since. You can level up all 14 classes on the same character (classes open up at lvl 10), and you can mix and match their skills. You can sub 2 skill groups from other jobs to our current one.
The maps are decent sized but with flying available from lvl 15 and teleports to all cities getting around is easy. For the lazier or richer folks there are the item mall Teleport to Parties or Go Anywheres. If you are bored of murdering creeps hourly events can keep you entertained (quiz show/treasure hunt/pupu darts/flying race etc.) for quite some time.
Pets are an other highlight of the game. Other than they help you fight with each having their strength and weaknesses once you level and evolve them to lvl 61 they can become mounts (both riding and flying). Riding a huge metal bear or flying on a winged cat (my personal favourite) are both great. Or if you so prefer get one of the cute/handsome humanoid pets. ;)
It is true there are technical issues and things the game can improve on. However several of the negatives have a sollution ready if people were willing to look around.
- WASD is available from options
- Screen resolution can be fixed in the game files
- The font the game uses can be downloaded to fix the text issue lot of people has
- Start village is instanced, that is why you do not see anyone, the game is not a ghost town
- While only a few hair colours are available from the character creation you can buy a lot more later from the Item Mall or other players.
Item mall is just what you would expect from a free to play game. XP and loot boosters, luxury items and of course countless cosmetics.
As for end game there are several guild based raids with billboards to show off your times (while pocketing loot) and compete with other guilds. If you are the bloodthirsty kind you can also hop in the Arena for some PvP action (also with billboard). Or, if you are one of the clumsy you can try climbing the death billboard. :)
There are no perfect or bugless games. But if you really want to give DOMO a try there is a way to run it without most of the issues mentioned in reviews. Please keep in mind the game is old, and due to that it cannot race with modern games in a lot of aspects. Should you like it the main concern would be how long the developer (SoftStar) will support such an old game.
If you want some nostalgy, or want to have something to pass time with give it a try.

A great asymmetrical with lots of depth. Each character is strikingly different in tactics and play style, even within the same class, and the monsters are very unique and equally fun to play. Playing as the monster is a completely different experience, depending on a mix of stealth and brute force, and even some finesse with the Wraith.
It does have an offline mode where you can play against bots which is nice, but not enough to entice those who don't have reliable online access. The AI for both the hunters and monsters is decent but gets predictable after awhile; this game is definitely best enjoyed online, with the offline best served as practice or for ranking up.
Evolve has a clean menu system, tutorial videos that automatically play the first time you play as a new character. The game also boasts great graphics and excellent sound design that works well with the premise; a lot of the time I am listening for the monster's location, or hearing the hunters on my tail. It's all very slickly presented.
As for the biggest complaint about this game, the DLC. Like most, I'm not a fan of the game's DLC model, but I also don't think that detracts from the game as it is, and piling on this game seems a bit unfair considering DLC has been around for a long, long time now, and done more egregiously. All the current DLC is cosmetic only. Future DLC is on par (price-wise) with map packs or booster packs that other games pump out. At least Turtle Rock seems to have a more thoughtful approach to DLC, with all of the future maps and game modes being free, preventing the community from being fragmented (a la Payday or COD) because some don't have the DLC (you can always play against new monsters or have people in your party play as the new hunters).
My only other gripes would be slow updates and lack of game modes. The modes there are fun (Nest, Rescue, Defend, and Hunt) and the attempt at a campaign is admirable, but more variety would always be nice.
However, as far as the package as it, I feel like I got my money's worth with the depth of gameplay and character development/unlocks, variety of maps, and just the overall presentation. I played in the alpha and the beta and loved every minute and keep coming back for more. I'm looking forward to future monsters, maps, game modes, and hunters to keep things fresh.

Dungeon of the Endless (DoTE) is a strange mix of genres that works surpisingly well. Part tower defence, part squad management and part roguelike.
DoTE presents an interesting dilemma for the player; should I open this door? Ever door you open has the chance to make your escape to the next floor harder. Every room you don't run power too, and very rarely will you have enough power for every room, has a chance to spawn hordes of aleins who want you dead. You can slow their assault by building towers in powered rooms. You must also choose which resources to generate so you can afford more towers, tower upgrades or character levels. Everything in DoTE comes down to a simple choice: how hard do I want to make this for myself? All of this, with a helping of humour and increasing difficulty results in very rewarding risk/reward gameplay.
There is a wealth of characters in DoTE, all with their own strengths and weaknesses. Their combined flavour texts makes for an interesting narrative and the various interactions between the characters in the post level screen is a very nice touch and makes the world feel alive. You will rectuit additional squad members  the deeping you dive into the dungeon, but you will have to decide who to sacrafice in order to create room for them as you can onyl have 4 squad members. Even unlocking new characters for future playthroughs has a risk/reward aspect to it as you must dive at least 3 floors into the dungeon with your new compainion before they are available to you for other playthroughs.
The only downsides to DoTE are in the multiplayer. At the time of writing this here are my issues:
You cannot create private multiplayer matches. This has resulted in me kicking many people (sorry!) when I only wanted to play with a friend.
You cannot trade items between player's characters outside of selling the items to the shop keeper and having them buy them.
The game tends to drop connections often and you cannot rejoin a game which effectively ends it.
You cannot save your progress in a multiplayer game and a game of DoTE can take a few hours so make sure you have nothing else you need to do before you start a game up.
I hope that the devs iron out the technical issues so that multiplayer can be a more enjoyable experience.
In conclusion, I would highly reccomend this game despite its flaws in multiplayer. If you like rogue-likes and tower defence games you should definitely try this one out. It is a steal at only $14 (CAD) and some of the most fun I have had with a game in recent memory!
TL;DR: Rogue-Like, Squad Management, Tower Defence. Very fun. Very cheap. Broken multiplayer. Go buy now.

It was a chilly, spring evening in O'Lution Manor when this first came to my attention and I must say, that my interest in gaming had been waning a bit, snatching short plays of casual titles rather than putting in any significant time playing anything of depth. Indeed, with my eldest son having largely commandeered the console, leaving me with the laptop and mobile devices, it seemed I was wandering into the realms of the casual gamer.
And then I came across Sir, You Are Being Hunted. The visual style and sense of humour lulled me in in and when I saw, yes, my word, it will run on my laptop, I decided to take the plunge.
Buy, install, test. Yes, it seems to be working fine. I'll give it a proper go tomorrow.
Well, maybe tomorrow.
Tomorrow.
After a month of tomorrows I finally sat down to play it properly and... yes.
This game has it all for me, a veteran of stealth since Tenchu and Metal Gear Solid, here was a game that allowed greater flexibility than even they allowed. Sure, it allows you to make more mistakes and it can be very unforgiving when it wants to be, but what we have here is a very solid game.
You, a gentleman or lady of apparently some standing have been transported to a strange alternate Britain, populated by a variety of robots who seem focussed on making your days end. Gentleman hunters, with synthesized Upper-Class British accents are you initial foils, but soon a whole range of robotic country-pursuits types are also on your trail, from poachers to foxhunters and of course, the robotic force-of-nature which is the Landowner.
To escape, you need to collect several parts of a machine scattered across the five islands, returning them to a set of standing stones at the heart of the map.
You have weapons and traps available to find, as well as a number of items to help distract your opponents and, of course, food to keep yourself alive.
Vastly outnumbered, stealth is the key to victory here. Sure, you can try to slog your way through the robotic hordes but that is unlikely to end well for anybody. Rather you are encouraged to explore and retrieve what you need by subterfuge, or perhaps through use of a rusty trombone.
So, the gae itself. Lets look at the negatives first. The world is precedurally generated, which is great for variety but it sometimes seems that this makes the landscape you biggest enemy from time to time. I've never had a problem with beyond some locations being fiendishly difficult to get to, but it seems others have been completely stymied by this.
The graphics are great for such a small team and have an excellent visual identity of their own, but especially at night there are a couple of glitches that sometimes give you cause to pause, was that the flash of something significant, or just a glitch in the landscape.
And of course, thr focus, this isn't a big narrative game, this is a game that gives you a world and a mission and lets you get on with it. Don't expect AAA production values here...
...but...
that's a good thing. You see, the designers have come up with a good idea. This is a clever open-world stealth game that rewards ingenuity, careful planning and the occasional bout of gung-ho bravado. This is a game that is not afraid of stacking the odds against you and leaving you to your own devices. If there are insurmountable odds between you and your target do you wait it out, try and sneak through anyway, or just back off and live to fight another day? The game is certainly challenging in this way and with this in mind, the ones who will be most disappointed with it are those who like to be led through a game by their noses, or rely on quick reflexes to blast their way through a horde of opponents.
As a stealth game, its a welcome return to form from a genre that had lost impetus in recent years and as the kind of person who would once upon a time sit patiently watching guards waiting for that perfect moment, this game has rekindled my enthusiasm.
As mentioned, Graphically you are not looking at detailed character models, but beautifully stylised creations that can bring a smile to yoru faces with their occasional nuances and the scenery fantastically evokes the British countryside. Sound is equally well thought out, with a balance of excellent natural cues and some brilliant audio for the hunters themselves (The gentleman hunters somehow manage to come across as upper-class Cylons). The sound design will be as much of an ally in this game as anything else and playing with headphones is warranted.
The Keyboard/Mouse controls are responsive and clean and the HUD and inventory interfaces are straightforward and intuitive.
Frankly, Sir or Madam, this game has brought be a lot more joy than the last few TripleA games I bought and that is an achievement in itself. Now, if you don't mind, I'm going to set my hat at a jaunty angle and go and explore the North Island again. Toodle Pip!

I highly recommend Dungeon of the Endless. The game combines action rpg, tower defense, and resource management elements into a rogue-like structure.  It's hard to get a bead on what the gameplay is like from watching trailers.  There is a lot of planning that goes into each turn.  Then once the turn is executed, you have to manage the waves of enemies in pausable real-time.
At first I felt like I was easily mastering the early levels.  Then I realized the game challenged me more than expected.  As I play, I continue to discover more nuggets of strategy and unlocked content.  Dungeon of the Endless provides a ton to explore, and you find it naturally as you go.  I have yet to find tedium in that exploration.
Graphics and sound form a retro sci fi atmosphere that I find a pleasure to spend (a lot of) time in.  The style and humor tell me the devs put a lot of love into their project.
I've run into a few minor bugs, but am more than happy to ignore them.  I once couldn't get an item to equip or sell, but then it started working later (possibly my misunderstanding).  Another time I saw a variable name for a line of dialogue instead of the actual text (dev: it was the mini-story between the doctor and warden).
In a nutshell, you won't regret giving this a try.  Play it!

Warriors All-Stars is the newest hack & slash game from KT. In short, this game is a dumbed down version, the gameplay is more shallow than the same games in this series like Warriors Orochi series. Here is the breakdown of my review.
Graphic, music and sound:
Overall, graphic is nice, nothing ground breaking but character's design are clearer and more detailed. In terms of music, this game has some good tracks, but nothing worth remembering. And sound, yeah, not much is happening in this department.
Story:
This is one of the things that makes Warriors All-Stars is just a quick cash grab, story is bad, after finishing the game for the 1st time, I didnt bother with it on my next playthrough. The character rooster is sadly very few, event DW8XL has more characters than this game. Though the character rooster isnt much, it has some awesome characters like Nobunyaan Oda, Williams from NiOh, Sophie from Atelier series, etc.
Gameplay:
This is the main problem why I said Warriors All-Stars is dumbed down, first there is no weapons, instead of weapons, we get cards, which acts like weapons, you can get cards by defeating enemies, finishing missions, finishing character's quest. Cards can be enhanced or combined to raise certain attributes, also can be sold or destroyed to get materials. Materials are needed to add your choice of attributes (enhanced cards). In battle, you can bring 4 other characters with you, you can use their skills in battle or summon all of them to battle (they will stand side by side with your characters in battle, sort of a human chains). They took some mechanics from Warriors Orochi. There is also rush battle, you can activate it if you have a star by pressing R3/RS, you can get rush star every 1000 kills you make.
Availables missions can be selected in World Map, including story and final missions. Also, everytime you finish certain missions, the map will be highlighted wider and wider. This game has multiple endings with 3 main story branch depending which sides you choose when selecting your first character everytime you start a new game.
Conclusion:
TL;DR Warriors All Star isnt a bad game, but its not for everyone, too simplified, and not much content, especially for 60 bucks. If you are new to this kind of games and want to try, go ahead. But if you like DW or SW series to death, you might want to wait for sale, this game isnt as good as the main DW series. If you are a KT die hard fan, well, what are you waiting for? In short, "Wait for a sale"

Welcome, Sir/Madam, to the most haunting and horrifying hunting game; where YOU are the ultimate prey.
Your helpful butler will explain things more fully, but suffice to say that this game is not your standard survival fare. I'm sure you'll be informed about the striking resemblance of the Archipaelago to some nightmare post-apocalypse Britain, and you'll likewise be educated about the wonderfully dreary atmosphere whihc makes this game stand out from the crowd of survival-horror titles. You'll be instructed how to avoid detection by the cold, calculating automatons that will relentlessly pursue you. You'll endure the elements, and learn to prepare impromptu meals from dubious ingredients. You'll learn to outwit those hunting you, and to fight back against them. You may even discover the hope of a safe trip home.
I'm sure you'll learn of all these things in good time. However, I'd like to draw your attention to another matter.
You see, you are no longer alone with the robots. Others have made their way to the accursed place, and while that may be an opportunity to band together; it could equally be the sign of a new and far more dangerous threat. Not all your fellow prey are interested in working together, and it seems there may not be a way to bring everyone home...
Ignore the cut-throat ruffians who spread rumours of "abandonment", for the hunt is very much on.
... ok, breaking character now for the sake of a more complete opion. Sir, You Are Being Hunted is a phenomenal game where you must combine stealth, guile and brutal combat tactics in order to escape a relentless horde of very British robots on a group of very British islands, while a very British butler guides you in a quest to recover the fragments of a mysterious machine. The stealth action is extremely tense and clever; and you'll be rewarded for keeping a cool head. The survival aspects are basic, but they get the job done -- and when you're running from crazed robots with shotguns, feeling a little nip of breeze is your last concern. Keep calm and carry on, and all that.
The controls and menus are intuitive and functional, and the world of Sir is far from hideous. If you get a chance to stop and admire the sunset, it's quite nice really. However, most of the game is spent crawling, creeping, sprinting and dodging; so the view doesn't always need to be the most spectacular... soon enough, the sight of hard cover and safe shelter will be more attractive than the most breathtaking vista. As such I'd suggest you ignore anyone complaining about low production values or a supposed lack of polish -- there's a definitive rustic and gritty tone, but that's kind of the whole point.
The real sense of excitement and enjoyment comes from that moment you turn the tables and begin laying your own traps, making your own plans, and visibly progressing towards your escape. Everything in the game points towards that end -- from the not-so-subtle reminders that most of the "loot" you find will be utterly irrellevant to your quest, to the way that the robots force you to keep moving, and even the barren-ness of the landscape.
That said, there are plenty of moments of levity mixed in; and the addition of multiplayer adds a whole new dimension to that. Items which were previously useless (or as good as useless) can now be used inventively; both for pure shenanigans or for a tactical purpose.
Furthermore, multiplayer adds a new element of competition -- the robots can be outsmarted and outmanouvred, but fellow players are a whole different matter.
Sir, You Are Being Hunted combines the best elements of horror, stealth and survival; and wraps them all up in a quirky British package. It's not everybody's cup of tea, but if you're into that kind of thing then it will do very well indeed.

This is the first early access game that I've actually enjoyed playing - I've dumped all the others I've tried.  The part that works is the sandbox, a mode with selectable difficulty levels and a SKYRIM-sized fully explorable area.  It's divided into half a dozen inter-connected areas, so it's not all continuous but it's all accessable and so counts as a largish map to investigate, gather, snare, hunt, fish, craft, and dodge dangerous animals in.
The idea is that you've been dumped, unharmed, in the mostly trackless Canadian wilderness.  It's perpetual Winter and darn cold.  It's your job to survive, all by yourself, without even a pocket knife.  Explore to find some essential tools, like that kife, some matches, a hatchet, and eventually, if you're lucky, a rifle.  There's some crafting, handy for creating a new fur suit to brave the cold white North in, some minor skills to develop, like fire-starting, cooking, and knife sharpening, but there are no perks or levels to advance your player.  There's also no magic, dragons, or enemy hordes to contend with; this game is more realistic to true life.  It's you against the cold in the wild.  It's challenging, especially so for the first week, but if you can manage to find shelter, keep a fire, and find something to eat then by the second week, and certainly after the first month, it gets a lot easier.
This game is a blast just the way it is but the developers are quite active and have big plans - rumor has it that user feedback will strongly influence those plans - and the experiences gained now in the sandbox should prove invaluable when the developers publish their 'story' mode.  This could be the best currently available survival game out there.

World of Soccer, the successor to Netsoccer and Netsoccer 2, brings you an unmatched experience in virtual football. It allows you to play the sport we all love in a way that most games do not let you. It removes the arcadey experience of "Be a Pro" modes in larger games and gives you full control over your player's actions. Like the best games, it's easy to learn and hard to master. It will take some time for you to learn the intricacies of the game, but when you do, and you actually find a team and "click" with them, it makes for one of the most satisfying gaming experiences you'll ever know.
The controls might not be the most obvious for people who haven't played it before, but you can quickly learn what is possible and then, practice makes perfect.
Having played its predecessor since 2006, and having spent an embarassing amount of hours on it, I can only recommend to you from experience that it's something you should try if you feel like playing football with your friends and make sick plays, but don't feel like getting kicked in the shins.
The game itself does feel like it's not yet completely functional, some things aren't very intuitive (like chat) and it can definitely become a lot better, but I still recommend you try it.

...Hi all...
Okay, so i see a lot of negative reviews for this game.  This actually makes me a little upset, as to this day, this game remains one of my favorite mmos.  I understand its not perfect, and I also understand a lot of the launch problems are partially due to crappy default options.  I'll go over how to fix the main issues i found first.  Honestly, I feel like Suba dropped the ball a little bit, but hopefully, it wont ruin the experience that much if you know how to handle it.
One of the main complaints that I see, and actually came across myself, was the screen going below the start bar.  This makes it so you can't access the options panel to fix said screen resolution.  A real problem.  To fix this, press Ctrl+n in game to bring up the options menu and change the resolution from there.  My personal favorite is Windows-Full screen, which resizes the window to exact area of your screen minus the start bar. Feel free to pick whatever works for you.
Let's fix another complaint I see a lot: lack of sound.  This game has a beautiful soundtrack (obviously my opinion, but still).  However, for some reason, the music defaults to muted.  You can go ahead and fix that in the sound options while you have the menu open.  No big deal.
Other random stuff I want to address: The character creation in this game IS good...if you look at it a certain way.  There are four races and genders, and while they are all basically 'humanoid', they're fine as they are really.  When I hear people talk about lack of customization options in this game, I think they must be talking about face and hair styles, for which each race and gender has only 5.  However, this is the only game I've played that gave full character proportion control to the player.  Not only that, but the Eversun Elder quests make these decisions early on important.  In the end, you're left with what can only be described as 'your character'...and really, that's exactly what it's supposed to do.  It's not as great as it could be, but I've seen much, much worse...
Now that Sound and Image are fixed, lets continue down to controls.  This is where you can turn on ASWD if that is you prefered gaming style.  This will deactivate your chatbox, and make it so you can use the keyboard to move.  For the record, even if you have ASWD off, the arrow keys on the keyboard will move your character just fine. Anyway, fine tune the rest of the options as you want.  After all, the key is for you to enjoy it.
Now on to the review proper.  I'll start by saying, DoMO is one of those games that requires team work and patience from the get go.  And I don't just mean in repetative questing (but, yeah, that too). One monster in the well that is required for a title spawns once every 45 minutes to an hour.  The best option is to team up so everyone gets the title...and wait for it to spawn...and wait...and wait... Grinding is a staple in mmos, and its in full force here.  There is no real easy way to get experience as a soloer past a certain point.
Waiting might sound like a pain, but in a way, its brilliant.  When your forced to wait collectively in a group for long stretches of time, inevitably, bonds will be formed.  I have met so many people through this game over the last 3 years, and the strongest bonds I have are with my guild mates, who kept me company over time that i otherwise would have been fiddling my fingers... My point here is, join a guild.  Any guild is fine.  A good, active guild, even if they aren't in a team with you, will keep you entertained even when the game itself slows down.
What's that? Sounds like a lot of time you don't have? That's fine.  Even a casual player can find value in game as an alchemist.  The crafting in this game, while not always making sense (The only thing that is used to make a wooden sheild...is glass...) is pretty easy to figure out.  Weapons and armor are made using monster drops and Collection items.  Collection includes Mining, Meditation, Fishing, etc. and can easily be done while your away doing your business (I'm collecting iron bars myself right now actually).  When collection is done, you can use your items for crafting, or sell you finds to other players.
Oh, and there are currently 13 classes in game...should prolly mention that.  You start the game as a commoner, and have to make it to lvl 10 before you can earn any of the other ones.  During this time, you'll learn no attack skills, but just getting thru the tutorial area should get you somewhere between 6-8 easily.  Completing the Eversun Guide missions when you reach the city should easily get you high enough for your first job.  There are 3 rows of hot keys for a reason.  While you have a main job equiped, you can substitute jobs from other classes to help you out.  I recommend learning doctor skills early, so you can sub a healing spell for whenever you need it.  Not all skill work the same on every class, and many skill require certain weapons that your main job may not be able to equip by default.  However, with enough grinding, technically you can use any skill on any job to some degree.  Finding your favorite class and sub combination can be a game all in itself.
I feel like I've devolved into ranting... so final thoughts:  This game is NOT perfect.  If you want proof, ask anyone in game about the stairs... However, for what it is, DoMO is an enjoyable experience, especially if you choose to take part in the community.  I may be disappointed in the Suba launch on Steam, but I still recommend people at least try this game.  It might not have the flashiest graphics, or the fastest action, or extreme whatever, but in terms of a nice, slow way to enjoy a day, this is one of my favorite options.
-Timreh

SUPERHOT is a Sci-Fi Augmented Reality Shooter (you are essentially Neo in the Matrix) that is incredibly immersive. It breaks many 4th walls and although isn't really neccessary for this sort of game, is executed flawlessly. The clever lore, beautiful aesthetics and simplicity add up for a great game, although it seems to pump itself up a bit much with the price tag. There is some replayability with "The Endless" and a "Challenge Mode" but for the most part you'll be replaying the same levels with minor tweaks.
As you can tell by my hours, I LOVE this game. I can't get enough of it. When playing through the story for the first time I was truly focused and in awe as I discovered the truth behind this game. The graphics are very clean and sharp; the only colours you'll encounter are red, black, and white. In the menu screens, you will also find a very aesthetically pleasing ASCII-inspired 'Operating System'.  Performance is also not too much of an issue due to it's minimalist design. There are easter eggs scattered throughout the game which if you can find will allow you to really see what this game is actually about. As you can tell, I
don't want to spoil it for anyone, because it's so well done.
As you discover easter eggs, you will learn more about the nature of the game, although most answers you receive are very open-ended and if anything, ask more questions than they answer. In the end, there is some interpretation to the reality of the game, but if you talk with someone who has also completed SUPERHOT you will be able to agree on most things.
In terms of gameplay, the SUPERHOT Team have nailed it square on the head. Dodging bullets, slicing, bashing and blasting away red dudes is very satisfying both visually and aurally.
I would rate SUPERHOT a 9, possibly a 9.5/10 if it wasn't so expensive. Even I, one who fell in love with the series from the first free demo think that 25 USD is too much for most players.
- Beautiful graphical design and execution
- Immersive and detailed lore
- Highly satisfying gameplay
- Aesthetically pleasing in all aspects
- Very high price-to-hour ratio.
- Levels are VERY bright; exploring for easter eggs may require you to adjust the in-game gamma settings or contrast on your monitor, especially if you are photosensitive.
OH MY GOD, SHRL.exe (a free standalone expansion for SUPERHOT) IS IN EARLY ACCESS! YEEEEESSSSS!

Outlast is a first-person survival horror.
You play an investigative journalist investigating a psychiatric hospital or Asylum, trying to uncover what has been going on in this place while running, hiding and trying to survive.

You have a brightness setting but you cant make the game too bright which is understandable.
But unfortunately there isnt a separate slider for the music.
This can be a pain when you want to listen for footsteps.
Those obvious cheap jump-scares where something/someone jumps in your face, with loud music in your ears.

The stealth element. Enemies can see you in the dark. I dont know if standing or crouching makes any difference. I dont know if noise is a factor. They always tend to investigate an area whenever you activate something. But thats more a scripted thing rather than a noise based thing.

TL:DR The game was fantastic when it came out however it did not age well but if you want a good Star Wars RTS this is it.
-The Galactic conquest mode was fantastic for it's time, a real-time X4 type of game in which you have to manage armies, fleets and planets in order to grow and conquer your enemy. Story mode took place pre Episode 4 until the end of Episode 4 (this was before Rogue One and everything got retconned by Disney)
The space battles were great, large ships were split into different hardpoints (weapons, shield generator, engine etc...) so you can focus on which ever target in order to give it a negative effect after it's destroyed. And all the fighters were in dog fights when they approach another squadron of fighters. (However it's hard to tell if you're winning or losing those dog fights.)
The mods for this game were fantastic, mods that included new races like the CIS and clone troopers, to new ships and units for exisiting factions.
Some maps (ground and space) and special points on them that you must go near to capture them, points like Abandonned Factories, Sensor Pods, Communication Array, turret points, Hutt Palace, etc... each brings an advantage to the owner of the point.
So the issues now:
-For land maps there's a pathing issue with every map, meaning units can get stuck while moving. This is especially true in long skirmish matches.
-RTS games were never visually appealing but there's something off about looking at ground unit models that have triangular shapes. Even Darth Vader looks to funny to take him seriously.
-If the Rebels can reach Tier 3 in a skrimish match it's pretty much game over as their T-4B tanks are juggernauts that can't be beat, even with AT-ATs and Darth Vader. Basically the game is unbalanced at that point.
-There is no online community anymore so unless you have friends to play with, you'll only get this for the single player.
-The AI in the Galactic conquest mode is a bit... silly. They will send a fleet of rebel transports without protection into your Imperial controlled space (space station and whatever ship you have stationned there.) And then will attempt to flee after the map loads. Vindicator cruisers with gravity well generators can prevent them from escaping... meaning they just lost an army because they decided not to bring ships to protect them...

The balance between tower defense and dungeon exploration is excellent. Both paths are equally viable. If you wish to set up a series of traps that monsters have to crawl through to get to your crystal, you can. In short, what are you waiting for? Buy it now!
