I'm not really practiced in the art of writing reviews and other such things,hence I can be quite hectic with my writing's quality,as a matter of fact,most of the time,my writing is all over the place,digressing and sidetracking a lot from the original point. So,with that in mind,I hope you can bear with me here,as I attempt to form a coherent review of sorts for Red Orchestra 2 ,my favourite multiplayer/fps/WWII game to date.
The game was released in September,2011 and takes place in the Second World War,specifically,the Eastern-Front,even more specifically,the battle of Stalingrad. [This event comes off as a bit personal for me,because my ancestors fought there,alongside with the germans,italians,spaniards,romanians,and croatians. I hasten to add that I have nothing but the utmost respect for both sides of the war.]
With that out of the way,let's look at the game,how it manages to recreate this hellish environment.
When the game came out,it was really buggy,it had performance issues,it was prone to crashing,and there was barely enough content to quell the gamers needs. Since then,the game saw a dramatic improvement both performance and content wise (even though the content is still a bit lackluster,but it can be expanded,more on that later).
The gameplay itself is a perfect mix between casual fps shooters and mild milsims. It's got a cover system,squads,chain of command,one shot killing mechanics. It can be either infantry only,or combined arms,meaing that there is vehicle and tank based combat in the game present. So I'd say it is a fusion of Battlefield and Insurgency/ArmA. It is hardcore enough that you feel a bit more involved and tactical,and it is casual enough to not get frustrated. You can either choose to LARP as a soviet/russian in the Red Army or a national socialist/german in the Wehrmacht. The game has native voices,meaning both sides speak their native language,respectively. I highly recommend turning this feature on,not only it increases immersion,but it helps you identify your opponent.
Speaking of immersion,this game delivers in every department: the sound design is stellar,as is the soundtrack,the graphics are realistic,animations and gore are sufficient enough so that you get your daily dose of PTSD.
Now onto the content: the game has a respectable amount of maps (although some of them are played over 9k times a day,I'm looking at you Bridges),a good amount of weapons and classes to choose from,there is a leveling system (separate for weapons,classes and overall level,eventually reaching Hero status lvl 99) ,some veterans find this to be superficial and needless,but I have no grudges against this gameplay mechanic. Other than the vanilla maps,you can download custom maps,mods,and complete overhauls through the steam workshop,which is a huge plus. A few years back,the devs held a map competition,so the best custom maps could become a part of the vanilla game,and the content creators were rewarded greatly. After that,they did not abandon their game,but further improved upon it,adding a few more maps,a territory based campaign (which is the most popular game mode as of now),new weapons for both sides,and some new vehicles.
One simply cannot afford not talking about the community in a game where the main pulling force is multiplayer.
It is quite small (2000-3000 tops),but all the more dedicated. You will find all kinds of people from all walks of life. There is an abundance of memers,trolls,casuals,hardcore elitists,friendly veterans,LARPers,commies,nazis,so on and so forth. I can say with confidence,that I have mostly positive experiences with the guys playing the game. Some server admins can be total ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s,abusing their powers,but other than that,you will definitely find your place and your role you are comfortable with.
Some thoughts about the downsides: minor bugs,glitches,sometimes clunky movement,rare occasions of wonky cover mechanics,the load times can be a bit long,vehicle physics are not the most polished,and the sorts. Nothing game breaking but aggrovating little things nonetheless. The devs have a small studio with limited funds (hopefully that will change with Killing Floor 2 and Rising Storm 2 : Vietnam),so it is understandable to an extent.
All in all,if you want an authentic WWII experience with a friendly and welcoming community,good amount of content,and you are tired of all the other popular fps franchises with the same carbon copies every year,and can look over a few bugs,and minor annoyances,I can definitely recommend this game. Thank you for reading,I hope this wall of text was helpful.

This is a stealth action title, with emphasis more on the former than the latter.
The game meets its concept well and even /plays/ well, but the only people I can recommend this to are serious fans of the stealth genre. Inventory is limited, as are your opportunities to save the game - a simple misstep in a crowded area can bring half a dozen hunters to your location and may cost you 20 minutes progress in the blink of an eye. Think NES levels of frustration at times.
The procedural generation sometimes leaves a bit to be desired; I attempted to visit the northern island only to find the island had generated with sheer cliff walls. A piece of the machine is in there for me to find. Can't wade in the water, because water robots will get me. Can't climb a sheer wall because the game isn't set up that way. Hard to progress, under such circumstances.
Controller support felt loose and lackluster. Keyboard WASD was fine, and felt more natural. Remember, inventory doesn't pause the world, so good luck using those rags while you're bleeding out!
In all, things I'd have liked to have seen:
* A few more save opportunities for those of us who aren't particularly great at Stealth
* tighter controls on a gamepad
* some basic fairness would be pleasant, though certainly not required
For: Stealth fans
Not for: People that like tight control, people who feel a game should stop destroying your hopes and dreams, or people who want a more cinematic/triple-a experience.

So this is a first person shooter / stealth game set in a robocalpytic British islands scenario. You have to find mysterious parts that are strewn about the landscape while avoiding different types of robots that will try to kill you on sight.
The islands are procedurally generated, and the parts you have to find are dropped in random locations on the map. They are made easier to find by emitting a pillar of smoke, and are usually guarded by a couple of robot huntsmen. You can either rush in and try to demolish them or you can sneak in and steal it from under their nose. Or maybe it's safer to create a distraction, in the form of an alarm clock going off that you previously dropped some place else, or maybe a little choo choo train that you let go somewhere in the hope that the robots will go and investigate the disturbance.
The game has a day and night cycle, so it's obviously better to wait until it's dark for your pick up attempts. The problem is, you will get hungry while waiting. So you have to find food, maybe in the form of a glass of pickled eggs that you found in an abandoned house, or you might stumble over a pheasant in the fields, which just tastes splendid when cooked over a campfire. Too bad you haven't found any matches yet to get the fire going.
The default settings generate 5 islands that are connected by boat (which serve as the loading transition), and measure about a square kilometer in size. The British landscape is well represented, with rocky coasts and small, but thick forests, rolling countryside with some agriculture, some castle ruins, and so on. The weather is also well represented, rainy, with a chance of clouds. There are small abandoned hamlets, hunting cottages and other buildings strewn about the maps, which can unfortunately not be entered, but if you activate the doors, you can find useful items within. They range from junk like bones or souvenirs over dubious food items like dead rats or strange mushrooms to useful stuff like guns, ammunition, bandages or cans of tea.
The robots are pretty deadly, they only take a short moment for aiming, then you are blasted with shotguns, blunderbusses or other weapons, which leads to a quick demise. If you start bleeding, you better have some bandages on you, or your health slowly runs out until it's game over. The AI is pretty good, the robots investigate all kinds of noise and movement; for instance if you startle a rabbit while your sneaking towards a guarded piece, a robot might see it run away and start looking for trespassers in the area. Sometimes a robot can get stuck in an obstacle, but I only saw it one or two times. The different robot types require different approaches to deal with them or to avoid them, which creates a bit of variety in an otherwise pretty repetitive game (you walk around looking for the smoke pillar of a piece in the distance, sneak there, deal with the robots who might guard it, get the piece, rinse and repeat 15 times).
Technically, the game is solid, the controls work well, the AI behaves like it should, and video and audio is well implemented. It obviously doesn't have triple A graphics, but it gets the job done, and art assets are stylish and support the British setting beautifully. The soundscape supports the feeling of being alone and hunted by a superior foe and sometimes even creates a mildly creepy feeling, when you are sitting in the high grass and listening to the distorted electronic voices of your hunters all around you.
There is no free save system. You can only save at the place where you have to return the pieces to (a spot in the middle of the central island), or at the boats. This obviously creates some tension, because if you get detected while going for a piece and die in the aftermath, you will start again at the boat and have to travel the whole way to the piece again (which doesn't take very long, fortunately).
I finished the default 5 islands scenario in about 7 hours, but it's probably doable in less time.

This is one hell of a RTS wargame - especially for the price (4.99).  I've been gaming for 30 years now and this is one of my favorite RTS games.  I wasn't paid to write this review, and I didn't get the game for free.  I played this game on a tablet for several months and when I saw it available on Steam I bought it and added it to my library.  You will be hard pressed to spend $5 any better than you could by purchasing this game.  It's straightforward: build extractors to mine money and then build units and mechs as fast as you can.  Defend your bases and go after the enemy.  There are air, land, and sea units, as well as some units that are amphibious.  The graphics are not cutting edge but the game-play mechanics are rock solid and it has high replay value.  When I get that ol' RTS itch, this is my go to fix right now.  I would recommend this game to every single person on Steam.  I purchased a copy of this for my son and we just got done with a multiplayer game where we teamed up against a computer opponent.  It was fun coordinating our attacks and then upgrading to build better units to counter the computer's newer units.
Rusted Warfare absolutely has that classic RTS feel.  The production buildings and economy are simple enough that you focus mostly on the battles and your strategy - not micromanaging a ton of other things that keep you from fighting.  The battles can get pretty intense and involve over a 100 units at a time - even more if you're doing multiplayer.  You do need to keep your armies balanced though so that you can deal with a multitude of enemy units with different capabilities.  Overall it is a totally refreshing game that provides a challenge in a classic RTS format.  This game ought to be trending right now - it just needs a little more exposure and word-of-mouth recommendations.  I'm doing my part with his review.  Pick this game up you won't be disappointed.

Five Nights at Freddy's is a point-and-click, horror survival game created by Scott Cawthon. The game centers on a fictional pizza restaurant called "Freddy Fazbear's Pizza", where the player must act as a night security guard, defending themselves from the malfunctioning animatronic characters by tracking their movement through the facility using security cameras.
The player must survive their shift, lasting from midnight to 6:00 a.m. without being attacked by one of the animatronics roaming the facility. The player, who sits in an office and is unable to move, is given access to a network of security cameras throughout the facility to track the movement of the animatronics. Four of the five characters have distinct movement patterns while the fifth, "Golden Freddy", only appears when certain actions are taken, however, most of the characters' movements take place off-screen. The player cannot leave the guard room, but can close the doors to defend themselves, and briefly turn on lights in the hallways to check for animatronics.Use of these actions consume the player's limited electrical power; if the power runs out, the cameras become inoperable, the doors open, and the lights go out, leaving the player with no defense against an attack.
FNAF is actually a fantastic game. Even if the animatronics aren’t scary, the lore behind the series is the most talked about, most researched, and perhaps the biggest lore of any game ever. Heck, it’s the only thing that keeps Game Theory running! (No offence to MatPat.)
If you have never played FNAF, you really should. Even if you don’t enjoy the games, the lore behind the whole thing, is something worth checking out. 10/10
Three sequels have been released:

Five Nights at Freddy's 4 and soon,

First, let me say that the majority of the negative reviews stem from bugs that the devs have since patched out (i.e. a lot of reviews are now out of date)
Second, let me warn you that a game controller is highly recommended due to a bug (this is coming from a hardcore PC, keyboard and mouse person who happens to own and XBox 360 controller).
Unlike other survival games, you don't do any of the crafting yourself. You're simply the person who finds the required materials and then your team of 4 undertakes the crafting once you've collected all the necessary items. Each of the 4 team members has their own unique role to play: one is a chef, one is a car mechanic, one is a survival expert, and the last is an electronics/computer expert/hacker. The chef can turn basic ingredients into complex meals that are much greater than the sum of their parts, offering more sustenance and possibly a much-needed morale boost to those who eat them. The mechanic, amongst other things, can build upgrades for the church that help to keep the team and its belongings safe from looters, and stave off the freezing temperatures outside. The survivalist will craft you items that will make your solo expeditions into The Void easier and safer, and the hacker will upgrade your robotic companion making it even more useful.
On top of this, each team member has their own story line to follow. These are all completely optional, but are recommended to pursue, as completing their missions will unlock further upgrades and crafting options along the character tech trees. These unlocked craftables not only increase your chance of survival, but also improve the quality of life for each of the survivors and even you the player. Yes, the game can become less of a chore for us playing it at home. For example, you start the game with a very limited inventory space for loot. Completing the first story mission for the computer hacker gives you the opportunity to increase its size. This means that you can then carry more, and so have to make fewer trips between a particular loot location and the church to transfer all the goods you feel you need to have to survive.
The survival is pretty standard fare for the genre with a couple of exceptions. Stave off hunger, keep thirst at bay, sleep whenever you're tired, and keep the fire burning. However, there is no base building (just base updgrading), and there's no hacking away at trees and rocks. Food can be found by looting abandoned buildings and by hunting. Drink is found through the scavenging process as well.
Being in a post-apocalyptic "nuclear winter", hypothermia is also a permanent threat. But in reality, unless you spend a ridiculous amount of time in a very cold area (e.g. -30 centigrade) it's not actually a problem for your character. The cold is principally a problem for your companions back at the church. If you fail to keep the base camp fire burning at all hours, they'll quickly become cold, their morale will drop, and they could end up abandoning your party.
In addition to the hunger, thirst, warmth, and morale meters, each character has an overall health gauge. This depletes when attacked by a hostile creature, or when someone is dying from starvation, dehydration, or hypothermia. The health bar replenishes when each of your needs is sufficiently met.
In addition to assigning crafting/cooking tasks to your fellow survivors, you also get to assign them a particular role, and have to ration their food and drink supply. They have ration boxes that are separate from the church's main storage area.
Each available role can be taken by only one survivor at a time (that's worth noting right now, as I thought this was bugged when I was trying to assign the same role to more than one person), roles can greatly assist in your team's survival (someone assigned to hunt will bring in a very nice stash of raw meat), and each role has a positive and a negative effect. Not only do you have to weigh up the pros and cons when assigning a particular role, but you also have to decide when the best time is to allocate that role. For example, it would be a waste to designate someone as a hunter if you're urgently waiting for them to finish crafting a vital upgrade.
The ration boxes are a very important way of ensuring that your team members remain hunger-free, well hydrated, and happy. Plus, you can assign a specific foodstuff to just one person if you know that person happens to love it and will get an important morale boost from consuming it. Keeping a happy team will ensure that it's productive, and will keep depression at bay. A depressed member will lose faith in your leadership and will wander off away from the church and disappear, thereby permanently depriving you of the strengths they brought to the group.

In addition to being your portable inventory, your robotic companion acts as a source of light, and can scan and dig for buried caches of loot. You must use good judgement of where and when to scan for such an underground anomaly, as every scan drains the battery, and battery life is limited. Once having found a buried treasure trove, you still need to decide whether it's worth Ako Light using the energy to dig for it there and then, as running out of battery disables Ako's radar, causing you to lose your only immediate means of navigation. You must then find your way back to the church to safety with no asistance. Returning to the church recharges Ako Light immediately.
+ Excellent survival game in which you have to scavenge for every last scrap of food, every last drop of water, and any items which could be of any crafting use.
+ Very nice crafting progression system, which truly does reward you for keeping a keen eye out for potentially valuable items.
+ Excellent visuals that immerse you in the post-apocalyptic world.
+ The game provides you with a rather large map to explore with a good variety of looting locations.
+ On top of the "open world" freedom for exploration, the crafting unlocks and progressions of each of the other 4 survivors allow you to focus on what you feel is most important for your team, and how you want to play the game.
+ Good team management aspect that adds a meaningful extra layer of gameplay to what could have been "just another ordinary survival game."
+ Good soundtrack that adds to the atmosphere.
- Impact Winter still has several bugs that persist even after all this time, and after several patches e.g. getting stuck on terrain and having to reload your game from the last checkpoint.
- The game involves a lot of hiking back and forth between the church and looting and mission locations. This could be a big turn-off for some people. There is a snowmobile in the game for high-speed travelling, but you have to advance quite a way through the crafting projects for it to become available to build.
- A controller is highly recommended, and does work very well. The keyboard and mouse support has improved a lot since launch, but still contains some bugs that could negatively affect your game. You have been warned!
- The weather seems to be rather clement too much of the time and so the world itself never truly feels threatening. Not once have I found myself stranded because of a whiteout or at risk of death due to hypothermia.
- Only one real level of difficulty. An option to choose how many days you have to survive to complete the game would be very welcome, as 30 days can pass rather quickly.
An excellent wintery survival game with good team management elements. Any enhusiast of the genre will enjoy it immensely, but do expect to be hiking back and forth a lot, seeing the same places over and over again.

I'd recommend this game purely on the novelty in the gameplay and the style of the system.  This is a strategy FPS, and I don't mean an FPS with turn-base gameplay, but rather an FPS where time slows down (not stops) when you aren't moving.  So when you move the game runs at normal speed, or turn around to look behind you the game again moves. What makes this phenomenal is you're able to stop and plan your next step, attack or movement.
And this works.  Holy crap, there's only one small problem with this idea, and it's a FPS so sometimes I feel like I missed a bullet, and the game says I got hit.  Alright, fine, I'll live with that.   However the execution and gameplay is so tight and sweet, I absolutely love it.
When you finish you get a replay of you running through the level and getting each kill in "real time" and it looks super slick.  It could have had a little more variety or a little difference in your attacks, but overall I love that feeling of moving through the level like a Neo from the Matrix.
Then there's the challenge, man a few of the final levels are hard.  I mean there's at least a few levels I restarted 20 times, but for the most part I had a great time playing it. (There is an elevator level I could do without).  Overall though, this game is slick as hell, and really shines.
Now as for the rest of the game's package that the game is a little mixed.   I love the gameplay, but the story starts well but then gets a little too clever, then painfully clever.  God I want to love this whole package but the story really turned on me, rather than super slick gameplay, I'm forced to go through these little hoops out of game, and they aren't exactly thrilling moments.  "Guess this password" which the game does for you by you pressing random keys?   The ending is also cringy...
But I won't spoil the story people will likely like, I know some people have, however I came for the game, and the game is what's really enjoyable.
The other problem is the price.  25 bucks is ENTIRELY too much for this game, it's longer than people say, I played it for about 10 hours, maybe a little less, but with the DLC coming, this deal gets better.  I did pay 15 bucks for it, and enjoyed the hell out of it, but it's not a long game and the value is a little light depending on how many challenges (each are pretty good) you're going to play after the game.
But is it good?  Well yes, like I said, the gameplay is fantastic.  Any time I got a katana in the game is awesome, most of the levels are fantastic, and if you like secrets, there's hidden objects all throughout the game.   The aesthetics of the game are beautiful and I love the entire experience.
So yeah grab it, but maybe wait for a small sale.  15 bucks is a really good deal in my opinion, I love the strategic FPS idea, and the game plays really well, but anyone expecting a ton of time to put into the game will likely be disappointed.   Still it's an enjoyable experience while it lasts.

A relentless pseudo-turn based dungeon crawler, with no end of challenge. The game features only two immediate and apparent difficulties: Too Easy, and Easy. Don't let these difficulty titles fool you, they're a lot more daunting than they seem. The dungeons are unforgiving, one mistake or failure to prepare can ultimately lead to your cascading loss of the dungeon. The already challenging difficulties can be further multiplied by selecting different escape pods that give new rules to your dungeon. The greatest enemy you will face in the dungeons isn't the monsters, it's the random number generator. What's in the next room? Monsters? Dust? A much needed damage-per-second, or utility hero? I really like this game.   It is a 100%  stealth and strategy game.  I have played using all the different character types  available which does not change the gameplay just the items in your inventory at the start of the game.   You can change the landscape and the buildings and throw in the amount of robots that you want.   I really like the ability to be able to modify and change landscapes and structures because you have a different game each time.  I will strongly advise not to start the game with the max amount of robots  if you are a beginner as it will be almost impossible to play.  Between the dogs and the horsemen you will  running  for your life and may not enjoy the game.  Horsemen  sometimes  do not appear if the fields (hayable, stonewall,  hedge, woodfence) are not checked or turned on.  They will appear outside of fields obviuosly but many times I have constructed landscapes with no fields with horsemen added in  the mix of robots and none were ever seen during the game.   If  you  really want a challange give it a go because almost every single field will have a horseman.    Horsemen are not limited to the fields and they will roam the woods and villages as well but prefer the fields it seems.   It does not matter where you are  if the horsemen see you run.  In the landscape menu you have a variety of landscape types to pick from and to modify.  Only one landscape pattern per island.    Be careful when choosing dramitic with mountains and valleys as it can make extreme pits and  canyons to fall into and mountains that are very tall and hard to climb.     Also, if you choose large islands for all your islands sometimes the game will have trouble loading and then other times there may be  one of the docks that is off in the corner of the screen (map) or way out in the water where you will always be killed by the mechanical arms (bog monster) before you can reach the dock.     However, not all of the arms will bite you causing damage.    I have found that they tend to rotate damage vs non-damage.   The first one you encounter will make noise and that is all but when it goes away the very next one will bite and cause severe damage and death if  you do not run away.   Sometimes you will have a piece of the artifact (teleporter) on an island that is only a few yards away from your main island and you will have to walk through the water.   There are no boats to use for these situations you must wade through chest high water and sometimes go underwater.  You do not swim or drown just walk or run through the water.   I have spent alot of time in and under water and never drowned in this game but anything is possible I suppose .   Jump in the water and wait for one of the bog monsters to  pop up.  If it does not bite then keep going but if it does, retreat back to shore and wait for it to go away.  Do not stand at the waters edge cause they can hit you on land.   Once it goes away try again and the next one should be harmless.   There is so much to this game that I love and appreciate.   My hats off to the makers of this game at Big Robot.  Great job and well done.   I  know some people do not like this game because they cannot save game progress anywhere anytime in the game or they say there are not enough weapons or they want massive damage weapons.   This IS NOT a "shoot'em up" type of game.   It is a stealth and strategy game.   I love the fact that you can only save at the standing stone or at one of the boat docks.    Also,  if you are bleeding or starving you cannot save either so make sure you have rags and food.    I like the challenge this puts on the player.   Its 100% all about STEALTH and strategy.   If you use your noise makers wisely ( clocks, trains, bottles, rocks and trombone)  you can distract the hunter bots to accomplish your goals.  I  know its just a game and that the robots can be predictable sometimes, but you still have to plan  and think ahead about how you manuver.   Happy hunting.

Roguelike that appears to be a mixture of FTL's pause based gameplay, tower defence and a few other interesting elements.
Pseudo real-time, in the sense that combat happens dynamically but resource generation is gated to 'turns'. A 'turn' is triggered when you open a new door, and once you open all doors on a floor (unless there is some other way to generate resources outside of discovery and 'turns'), you're at an impasse until the next floor.
The visuals appear retro in their pixelated designs, but are exquisitely intricate. Shadows move dynamically, lasers illuminate the environment, lights glow eerily in darkened rooms; it's really something to lay eyes upon and it looks spectacular in motion.
I'm yet to complete this game on what I think is the highest difficulty (labelling everything with variants of easy doesn't distill much confidence), but I've had a blast doing it.
It doesn't take much time for a single playthrough (even less so if you're terrible at it like I am), and it is cruel but rarely unfair. Be ready for the monster house that you unleash with the removal of your crystal.
Only real gripes with the game are minor ones: the fonts used in the menus does not align with the visual aspect (modern vs retro), and anyone that has played Endless Space is going to notice the FIDS icons used to denote the currencies for research, levelling up and construction in all of their crisp glory which clashes wtih the game's general aesthetic. I get that the Endless (currently at a trilogy: Space/Dungeon/Legend) games are linked (which I think is cool), but it's still a little jarring given the overall style of DotE.
All-in-all, I love what I've played of this game thus far (Steam game time is not 100% accurate as I have spent some time playing this on my daily train rides to work), and look forward to continuing to fail miserably in the future. Well worth it for the cost.

LYNE is a visually simplistic and minimalistic puzzle game where you have to connect shapes in certain patterns in order fill the board, similar to the classic game of connect-the-dots. Although it’s quite restricted in its gameplay, the combination of the polished, intuitive interface, conciliating, dynamic audio and simple concept makes this one of the best casual games available on Steam.
As you progress further into the game, the puzzles increase in difficulty and complexity, thus, players will ultimately resort to the drawing board on several puzzles. However, even though it’s very limited in terms of its variety, the game never felt tedious or mundane and I was able to appreciate the challenging, yet addictive nature of LYNE, whilst simultaneously solving the ingeniously designed puzzles.
Even after completing all the achievements and unlocking all the colour palettes there isn’t really anything to stop you from playing this puzzler. With the addition of 50+ daily puzzles, this game also serves as a pleasurable mental exercise and I would be lying if I said my analytical thinking skills haven’t improved since experiencing LYNE. If you may not know, I don’t hand these out like candy but this game impressed me enough that I’m comfortable giving it a 9/10.

AI is quite predictable (isn't it always the way in stealth games, though?) but the scarcity of defense measures and variety of enemy behaviours allow the game to remain challenging (run on default bot population:  I have no intention of playing on the hardest settings, thank you very much)
Overall, probably not worth the full $20 but it filled four hours and I don't consider that time wasted.

So this Game I'm sure everyone has at least heard about by now but if you havent. It's been a looked forward to game for awhile made by the same people that made Left 4 Dead. With somewhat the same concept in mind, in this game its 4v1 with really level playing grounds on all fronts. A game that can be competetive or just fun, you can play it with friends or by yourself with randoms all being really fun at least through my eyes.
The Pros:
-Really balanced classes on all sides. Which in a game like this it's a must need otherwise it can end up a tilted game.
-Short games, typically these games run between 10-20 minutes on average(depends on the team and the person playing the monster)making it easy access for people that can't play games for too long
-The community, the community in any game is pretty important and sense it's a game primarily run on its community for match ups its important to have a decent one. From my experience this game has a pretty decent community
-The updates often balance things that my seem a little off in classes the Devs stay close to this game they didn't just release it and leave it to build a new game. They take in account how many people play the game etc.
-Classes you play in the game take a bit of time to find the right one that suits you but once you do. It's just extremely fun to be able to play a game where you can pick it up and say "Yep this is mine" to a class.
The Cons:
-Games that last over 20 minutes seem to feel too much like a drag to play past the point when a team won't co-operate
-Matching is kinda wonky getting paired up with a team at your first level and going against someone that has maxed out all his abilities
-There is much room for improvements on weapons i feel like a bit of customization to make a class truely feel unique to your playstyle needs to be incorporated
Now this isn't some game you have to enjoy a story or anything, so if your looking for that try something like Skyrim or an RPG because this game doesnt have it. This game is a primary multiplayer game its meant to be played with a team/friends which isnt bad just know that you are buying a multiplayer game not anything else. Nothing more nothing less.

I'd buy this for a dollar, or actually a euro... or actually I just paid around 0,09€ for this since it was on -90% discount. You get what you pay for I guess. I recommend this since I was happy with my purchase, see the pros and cons though to see what exactly you're getting with the buck this game costs. Some of the things listed are strong matters of taste.
The review
This game is an extremely short and extremely easy hidden-object puzzle game. It's very silly and the whole plot is just finding your girlfriend, freeing her and [spoilers]kickstarting her vampire father's film career[/spoilers]. Voice acting is bad and the texts don't match the lines, but due to overall campy feel of the game I really didn't mind.
Gameplay consists of you mostly clicking a person / object and seeing what he / it wants / needs, finding the items from nearby and then usually solving a puzzle of sorts. Some of these necessary items are often hidden behind some other items that are involved in a hidden object game, totalling to about 11-16 items (5 at a time), the last of which usually has the final items you are looking for hidden behind them. It's really simple and usually you can just get through most of it by randomly clicking the obvious items in the scene. If you want all of the achievements though, check the items required and then click through 5 of them (the hidden objects, not the quest items) in 10 seconds to get the achievement, that's basically the only one needing bit more effort.
The puzzles are the most interesting part in this game (beside just seeing the silly plot and clunky conversations go by). Unfortunately there were like 2 or 3 puzzles requiring actual thought while the others were passable by randomly doing stuff or just matching things together. There's not much explanation to them, but they're so simple a child will understand their point, you really don't need the included hint system. (also there's an achievement if you don't!)
- Funnily, you can actually tell the main character to walk somewhere in the scene, but it really has no function as clicking on hotspots trigger them immediately.
That's about it. Game really doesn't span far. I played it 100% through on hardest difficulty in ~2h. More lucky person can probably do it in less time. Well, here's the pros and cons.
Pros:
+ Cheap (like really, got it for 9 cents)
+ Campy (got a few chuckles from some events, couple unexpectedly silly ones too)
+ Money's worth of entertainment and ultra-light brain exercise
+ Achievement icons look pretty cool
+/- Easy even on hardest difficulty
Cons:
- Some bugs (backgrounds messed up or characters floating in the backgrounds, also one time (in the psychic dimension) game didn't let me click any hotspots, closed and restarted the game and it worked again though)
- Typos
- Lame story (and there's barely any of it)
- Harder puzzles can be calculated with a single quaternary digit
- Finger got tired from all the basically useless random clicking
+/- Bad acting
+/- Easy even on hardest difficulty
Score 6 / 10

This will be one of my favorite games, it's exactly the kind of experience I want and believe needs to be explored more often by developers. Where to start....
Let me preface this review by saying I really do like the concept of the game, but it is very difficult to enjoy when you are just constantly losing progress due to bugs.
This is a survival game reminiscent of This War of Mine. So if you enjoyed that type of game play then I think you will enjoy this game too. You are the leader of a group of survivors that have taken shelter in a church after the world has gone to♥♥♥♥♥♥because a meteor strike has dumped enless snow all over the planet.
This game's survival mechanics are pretty straightforward. You need to keep track of your usual things like health, stamina, food, water, and temperature, for you as well as your group. The game gives you various ways of keeping you and your group alive.
In this game you will be battling against the cold weather constantly. You will need to keep you and your group's warmth high or you may catch the flu or hypothermia. The weather can change at a moment's notice, and certain locations will be much colder than others, making exploration much more difficult to carry out. I will say that temperature is handled in a counter-intuitive manner. I would think that it would be much colder roaming the void where the high winds would increase the chill factor dramatically, and the shelter of abandoned houses/buildings would be warmer. This may have been a deliberate design decision by the developers to encourage exploration of the void but I think it makes exploration of the void too easy.
Exploration is the key to surviving in this game. You will need to brave the void and find locations to scavange for much needed supplies. Gas stations, diners, hotels, houses, parking lots, and offices are among some of the areas you can find in this game. Each location will have groups of items that are available to that type of location. So if you are looking for food supplies, hitting up a diner or gas station is the most logical choice. There may be dangers lurking within said locations so you will need to decide whether you'll want to carry some kind of weapon to defend yourself with, but doing so comes at the cost of reduced inventory space, which means your supply runs will yield less. I do like this aspect of the exploration very much. Some areas or parts of areas may be inaccessible to you as well. You will encounter areas that require you find a key to proceed. Other areas can be lockpicked, and some areas require you blow your way into. All I can say is lockpicking can kiss as my♥♥♥♥♥ There can be a location I have to get into and I have 6 lockpicks on me, and all will fail to open the door. The game doesn't denote if some locations are just more difficult to lockpick, so it can result in a very frustrating experience after failing a bunch of attempts since you won't know if it was a bad date with RNG or not.
Throughout your survival journey you'll encounter many different items, most of which will be useful in crafting. The game allows you craft all kinds of devices which will help your survival become just a bit easier. Some devices will help your fire last longer, while others will allow you to collect and melt snow into drinkable water. Each member of your group has different specialties allowing them to craft different items, some of which may craft quickly while others may take much longer. Also, ordering your group to craft drains their energy and morale. The only aspect of crafting I do not enjoy is tracking which items you need to gather to complete a recipe. The game does allow the tracking of items but only if they are part of a quest, not if they are just part of recipe you are trying to build. This seems like a giant design misstep as there are too many items to remember and you may find yourself accidentally ignoring a rare item because you forgot it was one of the 5 required components.
While exploring the world of Impact Winter you may encounter situations where you'll need to defend yourself. The game has various ranged weapons which you may run into, such a rifles, handguns, and bows. I have not seen any melee combat so I don't know if that's available or not. I will say that the combat is incredibly clunky, and something you're better off just avoiding unless you have no other choice. There's no skill involved in aiming your weapons. You'll pick a target and shoot until RNGeesus says it's ok for it to hit.

I'm constantly getting stuck in terrain. Sounds pretty awesome since it could potentially save you a long run home, except I've actually only managed to get this working once. Most of the times the items just disappear and dont' get put in the church inventory. Other times he doesn't even attempt to deliver the items.
Accessing containers is also a complete pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ The textual messaging that says something like "A to access TV" is usually spot on when you are facing the TV, but pressing A doesn't do anything. You'll have to re-adjust multiple times until you're able to access it. I'm not sure what's up with this but it can get quite frustrating after 12 hours of play.
The whole mechanic of assigning roles is a joke. Now, it's possible I may not fully understand how roles are supposed to work, so bear with me. If I give someone a particular role, then move to the next NPC to assign a role, the previous NPC  will not have a role assigned anymore. This happens so frequently I've stopped using it. I was basically having to assign roles every time I interacted with these NPC's.
I've heard talk about loading times being too long. I put the game on my SSD so I haven't really experienced this as drastically as other people have. That being said, The Witcher 3 still loads faster, which boggles my mind.
I've run out of time for now, but I will come back to the review later and finish it. I'll just summarize my opinion for the moment. The game has lots of bugs that completely hinder your otherwise wonderful experience. I wish I could give it a thumbs up, but I can't unless these bugs are fixed. On a positive note, it does seem like the developer is actively updating the game trying to address some of it's most prevalent issues, so perhaps just give them some time to iron these things out. I think this game will be well worth the 20 dollars once that happens.

I had this in my collection from a sale a while back and finally got around to playing it. I should have played it sooner. Absolutely brilliant, excellent and amazing game.
Things I Liked
- The gameplay. Throws you in at the deep end with intense battles against super freaks. Use guns, melee attacks with the wrench, and extremely cool plasmid attacks (that are effectively like spells from similar games)
- The atmosphere. Creepy yet cartoony. I'd describe it as vintage comic horror. Definitely unique.
- The character design. Enemies are grotesque and varied. Animations and lighting effects on the various plasmids are stunning even by today's standards.
- Big Daddys and Big Daddy battles. Tough, but rewarding.
- The difficulty level. Normal setting was PERFECT for first playthrough. I was never overpowered or underpowered. Money for health and ammo was common enough to get by but scarce enough to keep me on my toes. For this reason, what would be just an action game also has probably the best feeling of surviving than other survival games I've played.
- The endless configurations of weapons, power ups and plasmids. No player will play the same way twice!
- Hacking lock/gun turrets etc. There is a LOT of it and I wouldn't be surprised if a lot of people didn't like it. But something about getting the pipes in order just in time was always satisfying. Also it's extremely useful. You can't beat walking down a hallway with three hack flying turrets and a hynotised Big Daddy fighting your corner!
- I could go on here. So if you're reading this just play it...
Things I Didn't Like
- The map!!!!! Horrible thing. Since parts of the game left me without the handy little navigational arrow I found myself using the map a lot. And boy is it annoying! It insists on opening zoomed in, forcing me to have to zoom out every time! Sounds minor, and it is. But hey, I have to find things I didn't like... Also the way it shows how stairs lead to different levels is just so confusing.
- Switching between ammo types takes far too long. I wouldn't be surprised if there was a power up and I just missed it, but I lost count of the amount of times I'd die due to running backwards while switching ammo!

I'm very critical when it comes to games, and all I can say is they must have fixed quite a bit since the negative reviews were written. Overall, I'm very impressed.

If you don't have friends to play with and aren't looking to socialize with this game's playerbase, then this game isn't for you -- solo play becomes a grindy, arduous chore and all but the most dedicated MMO players will grow bored before hitting Lv. 20, and oftentimes the sluggish feeling is only mitigated by purchases from the currently-lackluster Item Mall.
If you're a socialite and tend to stick around to play with friends and meet new ones, then you'll be all over this game for sure. Partying up for a good grind is much more enjoyable -- relaxing between punching sessions nets some fun conversations and memorable moments, and joining a guild makes for the opportunity to establish real connections with some of these people. While the in-game social structure isn't used quite as much as it was intended (to my knowledge), it certainly lives up to its promise of emphasis on social interaction.

Let me share a story with you, one of a survivor who accidentally ended his own life by being overly ambitious.
It is well known that zombie bites are terminal and deadly. After one is bitten, it only only a matter of time staving off what you already know is coming. It all started waking up on the couch hearing moaning from outside the front door. Arming himself with a rolling pin, Ben walked up and opened to door to be greeted by what once was his neighbors. 3 good swings took care of Jim, and another 4 Took out Carol. Neither had anything of value, so Ben moved on before any more of the biters could find him.
Ben slowly became more confident while looting. He grabbed everything, stuffing his treasures in several dufflebags. Many trips back and forth to a nearby store filled his cache to the brim, until one fateful evening. The stove was left on, and Ben became and Accidental Pyromaniac. He watched with sadistic joy as all of his treasures went up in flames. Disappointment soon ran its course, as Ben had nothing left but the food and dufflebags on his back. He set off to rebuild.
With his cache once again established, Ben downloaded a mod to make zombies drop more loot. The newfound power went right to his head, and the biters swarmed him. He took every single one of them with him, all 37. The victory was short lived, however. Ben suffered multiple serious injuries, not to mention the previous burn wounds from the fire. A bite to the stomach, and multiple lacerations all over his body bled freely as he rushed to bandage his wounds. Most of them were infected already, and ben knew his time would be short. Ben made multiple feeble attempts at survival, keeping the bandages clean. Good intentions only go so far... Ben survived 12 hours from his final battle with the biters. He bled out doing what he loved, drinking orange soda and eating his favorite stir fry, Steak and salmon with some bacon sprinkled over the top.

I love this game. It was challenging, beautiful, and rather fun to play. Still, it hurts me that I have to mark this as a not recommend because it has some serious design flaws and is still in need of a decent amount of polish.
From a visual and audio perspective, this is a masterpiece. The inspiration it takes and the delivery of the design is top notch. Beautiful characters and animations.
The part that breaks the game is a fair number of glitches kept in the game to keep it overly challenging to the point that the game thinks you're doing too well and then uses a glitch to say "Oh you're dead! Git gud!"
Sure, plenty of trolls will tell you to git gud, and if you're willing to be patient enough the game is still beatable despite this, and overcoming some of the cheaper areas of the game gives you satisfaction for overcoming these flaws, but the frustration is simply not worth it. Being frustrated because of your own lack of skill is one thing, but to lose over and over because of a broken game just has no appeal.
Probably the best example of this in the game is a battle you will face against a ghost who possesses a train. In the first phase of the battle, several bullets are thrown at you that you can shoot at and hopefully destroy before they hit you. However, these bullets have two problems. The first being that they have no set amount of hits to destroy them. Sometimes four hits will do it, and sometimes it might take as many as eight. If it happens to be the latter, then it's possible that the bullet has reached you and hit you for damage already, which is a huge disadvantage in the first seconds of a long battle. I found myself restarting bosses far more than being killed by said bosses simply because of the unlikelihood I could take on an entire battle with 2 hp (as well as my desire to achieve the higher grades in battles, which of course requires full health).
Now, that alone isn't worth the flak I'm giving the game, of course. But the problems in this part alone get even worse. There was a particular glitch that would randomly take a bullet that you destroyed, and immediately respawn it just above your character so that it turns into an unblockable attack. There is just simply no defense against this, and no particular reason it happens, but it does. If the goal of a battle is to dodge the bullets, that's fine. That's a challenge. But if there is a system set in place to destroy the weapons coming at you, but it requires you to literally roll the dice and hope it means that the game doesn't decide to hit you regardless of your actions? Well, that's pretty broken.
But, I mean... Git gud, right? Sure. Don't listen to internet trolls. There's hundreds upon thousands of games out there that are beautiful and not broken, and ultimately it's your money. If you want to throw down twenty bucks for an unfair amount of frustration and that makes you happy, then cool, this game is perfect. But if you want challenging, there's better options. Don't pay for a pretty package. Demand decent structure and polish to your games.

Anyways, SUPERHOT is a game about a very simple concept: Time moves when you do. Basically, The Matrix. Bullets fly, people explode, you kill. The minimalist art style does a service to this game as it helps to emphasize the "story" or feel of the game, seeing as you assess information in the fastest possible way with the artstyle in place. You'll pick up the suitcase, throw it at the person with the gun, throw a punch at the person without a gun, grab the gun, shoot the one on the right, throw the gun at the person who once had it, and beat them down. This game really makes you feel like a professional badass, especially when you see the real time replay the game gives you. The game is beautiful. The art and animation are clever, and a perfect imitation of that done in the 1930's. The music is top-notch as well. The artistic accomplishments of Cuphead are beyond reproach.
The game is hard, in the style of early Nintendo Entertainment System games, or the arcade quarter-plunkers that came slightly prior. This isn't a reflex game, it's a pattern-learning game. There are a handful of run-n-gun levels, but the bulk is boss fights, and the vast majority of the play is learning those bosses, recognizing their telegraphs, and then avoiding their attacks over time.
The thing is, while I found the game to be a challenge, and I played it through for the sake of completing that challenge, I did not actually find Cuphead fun. I enjoyed seeing each boss, and marveling over their design and animation. But the process of actually fighting and beating them was frustrating, punishing, and often...boring. There's no fanfare, no interesting context. The story of Cuphead is totally bare-bones, the characters simply there, a parade of things that are more interesting to look at than to interact with.
Cuphead is an achievement, no argument there. In the end I do recommend it. It's probably going to be many people's and gaming publications' game of the year, and deservedly so. But is it an enjoyable game? To look at, yes. To play, in my opinion, no.

I'm recommending this, but it's not a strong recommend. Picked it up during a monster Steam sale -- I think for like 90% off or something -- and it was definitely worth the ~$3CAD but probably not the full price of >$20.
Sir (or Madam), You Are Being Hunted is a sandbox first-person stealth game set in a vaguely Edwardian time period where you, the protagonist, get stranded on a series of islands and are hunted by murderous robots. Your goal -- to travel to each island (five in all) and acquire pieces of a machine to transport you to safety. All the while, you have to mind your hunger and scavenge for items like food, bullets, weapons, and alarm clocks. The islands are procedurally generated with each game with a choice of one of five biome types. I really like the procedural islands; each biome is different and they feel natural and well thought out. On the default setting, the game starts with a few robot  hunters and, as you collect more pieces, ramps up the difficulty until finding those last pieces becomes seriously difficult.
The good and the bad (caveat: I haven't finished the game yet because of the serious difficulty mentioned above):
Good:
Procedural generation: I'm a sucker for it, my favourite game genre of all time is roguelikes, and this is roguelike-y in random generation of the islands, the buildings and the enemies.
Stealth: this game is at heart very stealth oriented, inasmuch as even if you do find weapons going in with guns blazing, even on the lower levels, is not a winning strategy. Bullets are scarce, weapons are scarce, and there are way more of the enemy than there is of you. It's entirely possible to play the game without shooting any weapon at all, which I find refreshing.
Graphics: I game on Linux, which okay, I'm already at a disadvantage, and I game with a low-endish business model Thinkpad, which again, problematic, but the game is smooth as anything on my machine and still is graphically nice to look at. Well, "nice" in that the game is simulating a depressing English countryside, so colours are muted and browns, grays, dull greens abound, but that's ok.
Sound: Surprisingly this game is *very* sound oriented. Don't try to play without having your sound on; you'll get clobbered. You'll need to hear the robots approaching -- each type has a distinctive sound -- in order to avoid them. There's an option in the game to turn on an indicator, which puts a little Metal Gear Solid-ish "!", "?" above the robots' heads to gauge how aware they are of you, and this is *invaluable* - at least if you're playing the game without headphones -- but even so you'll have to listen hard to survive.
Repeatability: There are *lots* of options to tune the robots appearances and numbers. I haven't messed with this yet as I want to finish the game on the default, but it's great to have something beyond "Easy, Medium, Hard" for difficulty.
Gender: It's a small thing, but the fact that you can pick your gender is a good one. More games should do this.
Bad:
Stealth: hey wait, didn't I just put stealth in the "good"? Yeah. But in this game you spend a *lot* of time crouched in reeds or ducking behind buildings while all the while your vitality trickles to zero. This does present a nice amount of tension to the game, but the islands are *big* muthas and finding the pieces without the piece detector is hard enough; trying to find them blind is *really* hard. And when you've spent hours combing an island to find that last piece, while all the while the *hordes* of robots that populate the endgame are shooting you, trapping you in bear traps, running you over with rocket horses, and biting your foot it gets real frustrating real fast.
Sound: I have a mild hearing disability and I don't particularly like games that are super dependent on sound, so I sort of resent the fact that I *have* to have sound turned on in this one. Not sure how it would work without it though.
Items: The primary way one gets ahold of things is by searching buildings for them, and there are a *lot* of junk items you can't actually do anything with. I would love an option to turn off junk items because it's annoying to go to a door and just find bones. You can't do anything with junk -- not even throw it as a distraction -- so I'm not sure why the designers included the junk items in the game at all. As far as I can see, they serve no purpose beyond annoying window dressing.
Buildings: The buildings look great, but you can't go inside them. They exist solely as a cache for (mostly) junk items. The game would be improved greatly if you could enter a building and peek out a window, or have, say, fixed items to heal damage, like beds or something. Instead they're basically giant crates.
I'd say, eh, three and half stars out of five to four stars out of five depending on your tolerance for frustration in the difficult endgame.

I love what indie studios are doing in taking risks and pushing the envelope on bringing challenging and/or novel ideas to life. This is why I support them and purchase their products. I really, REALLY want to recommend this game, but I cannot in it's current state (even after the patching).
There is a very nice gem here under the large pile of bugs. Right now it can be a very frustrating experience. The mouse controls are still off (can tell it is expecting a console controller interaction), collision detection issues (keep falling through the ground, have to reload the game and hope I didn't lose anything), items disappearing from inventory as you transfer them, design problems (menus flipping around selections in wrong sections or becoming unselectable), optimization problems, etc... etc... I enjoyed the story (so far), loved the art direction, and loved the core gameplay mechanic/ideas. Unfortunately, that solely doesn't carry a game. It's current state is a war of attrition on patience and fun. You shouldn't have to continue to tenaciously push through the painful muck a QA team should have nailed down. If you need backing or want your community to assist, that is what Early Access, Kickstarter, etc... are for and customer expectations align. I hope the devs turn it around quickly and will gladly edit my review. I'll revisit it again later in hopes they pulled it out of the ditch. I wish them them the all best as this does have potential.

With the game graphics maxed out, and resolution at 1920*1080, the framerate goes from 60 to ~30 depending on how much action there is on screen. It doesn't affect gameplay, and I never had a point where the game become choppy in four hours on gameplay.
As for the game itself it's kinda like Pirate Warriors 3.
You have your team of characters, you only control one, and you can temporarily summon the others on the battlefield to do their specials or to do some finishers after ending your combo with an heavy attack.
As for the new stuff you have the musou rush, which doesn't make much sense but is fun nonetheless : you become invincible for a time, there's suddenly an overflow of ennemies coming from nowhere (the normal ennemies are still here though), you just kill them all at a really fast pace while the rest of the team is cheering on the side, and when it ends the extra ennemies disappear, you do some big damage in the area, and get a ton of loot.
No horses, no second character going around with the player switching with one he controls.
Also no free mode it seems, but there's free missions to do inside the story mode itself, with different benefits.

There's definitely fun to be had here and I did enjoy a lot of the characters (William from Nioh is great in it, as is that... guy with the sword that I can't remember. Hajime something), but the framerate and the mission design can really drag it down - or at least they did for me.
It's a tough question. I think if you're in the mood for some Warriors action and you can keep your expectations in check, you'll get something out of the game, mostly because the playable characters are pretty cool across the board.
For me personally, I think the characters are just enough to warrant a look if you're a big Warriors fan, but again, don't expect anything amazing.
The framerate fluctuates constantly, hitting its target 60 frames-per-second and then dropping to what feels like half that every few seconds or so. It never quite seems to hit anything too low, so it's an issue that doesn't directly damage your ability to play the game, but things can get so choppy that at one point, we almost felt sick turning the camera. It's bizarre, and honestly, pretty unforgivable given how unremarkable the game's visuals are to begin with.
Yukimura and Mitsunari kind of have their triangle combos from Samurai Warriors 4, but as far as I can tell, they're not quite as fast. I guess this was done to balance them with the rest of the cast, but having said that, the movesets vary quite heavily across all playable characters.
the actual story doesn't carry much weight, and the members of the royal family -- the title's only original characters -- adhere to tired anime archetypes. You've got Tamaki, the shy and distressed princess, Setsuna, the energetic and enthusiastic hero, and Shiki, the stern and brooding older brother. There are some interesting character interactions here and there, but by and large, this isn't a release that you'll be playing purely to see what happens next.
Despite its relatively small playable character roster, Warriors All-Stars does a fine job of offering varied playstyles and interesting movesets. From simplistic melee fighters such as Zhao Yun of Dynasty Warriors and Yukimura Sanada of Samurai Warriors to more complex additions like the rifle wielding Tokitsugu of Toukiden fame, unlocking new characters and levelling them up is enjoyable.
Conclusion:
Warriors All-Stars is a colourful hack and slash title that can be fun in short bursts thanks to its varied cast of playable characters, but it just has too many problems to be considered a good Warriors game. Frustrating, tedious mission design,repetitive skill sets, a throwaway story, and a wildly unstable framerate make it very difficult to recommend when there are so many better Koei Tecmo titles on the market.

This game is great. The servers have a bad history, but after a bit the creators got new servers up and running and logins are working flawlessly. The person making this game is a previous developer of Net Soccer, and it shows. The UI is the most painful thing in this game, expecially when it was back when the servers were trashy, but since the game just went up from greenlight it's okay to have some inconvience riddled inside.

You can call to them to pass the ball to you, but I wish it made some notification so that you could notify other players as well.
The community isn't that great according to some people, but I haven't seen one person that is too rude or plain annoying yet. The team system is well made too, You can make your own custom jerseys, which look actually nice in game. The organised matches are the bread and butter of this game and I love to play in them. With good communication you can make great plays and tactics, and its overall very well done.
Overall I think this game could DEFINITELY use some changes over time, but for only 3 days on steam, it looks amazing and plays very well. The reason for my lower score is that the UI needs some serious reworking to be usable. He possibly needs to find some community members to help with that, most of them would know how it should be done to fit to the player, considering they are the community.

Let me give an initial look at the game through my eyes during my first start-up of this MMO and you can decide whether it's worth the hassle to you.
(((Skip to the bottom if you want a simple bullet list of pros and cons.)))
I downloaded the game and booted it up. Oddly, though, I had a very thin window for the game, but long enough that it went under my taskbar and hid some options. As I had little way to fix this, I had to go to the discussion boards and (luckily) found someone with a post on it. They suggested hitting Ctrl + N to open up the resolution options.
I then proceeded to enter the game and set my resolution, but unfortunately there wasn't one for my monitor (1366 x 768), so I tried one that was close enough and chose the fullscreen variant of said resolution. For some reason the game decided that "Fullscreen" meant "No Border" and I could still see my desktop to the right. This wasn't acceptable, so I just chose a small resolution that wouldn't reach the edges of my screen (top, bottom, left OR right).
Not wanting to judge a game purely on technical difficulties, I decided I'd jump into the game itself and make my character.
No real issues there. I just made my account as the game wanted and it automatically linked it to my Steam account. Simple as can be. I then proceeded to create a Sylph and got into the game itself.
Now here's where things are a little more annoying.
1. The chat menu is constantly active. That's right, you can't use WASD to move around or it'll just type it.
2. The abilities (if there are any) are nowhere on the screen. I hovered over all the menus, but there wasn't a hotbar for spells/abilities, so I have to assume either I hadn't unlocked them or there just aren't any. (I only reached 3, so it's likely I just didn't have any. I just find it odd that there isn't a hotbar at all.)
I don't expect World of Warcraft quality controls, but the above two are a tad bit of a problem for me.
Gameplay-wise, I have to say the game isn't bad. It seems like any other basic MMO and the graphics are simple with decent animations. I don't worry too much about graphics, though, so maybe most wouldn't agree that they're "nice". I think they are.
I ended up relying on clicking to go places because for some reason right-clicking DOES drag the camera, but doesn't hold the cursor in place like you would think.
At first I clicked on the wrong NPC and got a chat bubble above their head and nothing. I thought I was doing something wrong until I remembered I was supposed to talk to some "Grandpa" character. I don't know whose grandfather he is, but not mine.. I think.
After accepting the quest, it seemed to obstruct my view of the chat bubble with its confirmation "Quest Thingy Here Accepted" and I looked past that and moved on.
Then I killed a few piggies (Click and your character moves to them and attacks. Nothing special.) called "Pupu" and turned in their bones for a reward. Whatever reward that was, I am not sure.
My next quest led me to a tailor and I found him by his giant name on the map at the top-right, which is convenient, as there doesn't seem to be any sort of directional quest-tracker (WoW doesn't have this either, which can be dismaying for new players, but you can click the map to find things).
The tailor asked me to collect something from "flying Pupus" but I decided I wasn't going to invest more time in the game. The small window was a big factor, but the controls weren't helping.
End of story? Update your product before releasing it on Steam.
MMOs should constantly try to improve, both technologically and visually (the latter doesn't have to be 60fps Modded Skyrim graphics, just better models or lighting).
------------------------------------------------
Pros
- Nice Graphics
- Smooth Animations
- Functional Gameplay
Cons
- Limited Resolution Options
- No Hotbar
- Minor UI Complaints
- Limited and Unimaginative Race Options (Mage-like Thin Race, Brawny Fighter Race, Child Race, Humans)
Recommend?
I'm going to say no, but I want to say that if any of the complaints I've made seem minor to you, I would actually recommend giving it a shot. I've heard some interesting things about the game (pets that level with you, growing in power and eventually becoming mounts) and combined with the simple anime look, I think the game could be fun if you invest time in it or play with friends.
If you're not data-capped on your internet, there's no reason why you couldn't download the game, give it a whirl, and come up with your own conclusion. I'm just trying to give you a heads-up on what to expect.
Sorry if it seemed like a long read!

Awesome game. Very challenging, totally unique and fresh.
Here's some tips. Learn how the game works. There is a ton to take in, but the game is so addicting it only takes one session to learn all the hidden rules. Think 32 bit arcade Dark Souls Co-op.
A tip on movement. If you need to gain some distance from an enemy to fire ranged shots. Click to a different room, (away from mobs) than reclick the room that you and the mobs are in and you'll turn back around and start firing.
Criticism: Game is likely at it's funnest when playing with competent friends. However, there are a few functionalities that put a direct negativity to multiplayer.
1: Not being able to save the game while in multiplayer is dissapointing. I agree it shouldn't be so simple as "oh lets save a 3 player progressed game and I'll just finish it later by myself." But we were at it for 3 hours and only got to the 7th level of the 12 levels on the first dungeon. Now the idea is kind of cool to do it all in one sitting, which if you can do, that'd probably be best. But some gamers are workers too, and might not be able to commit 6 hours for on session game. What I'd like to see is a "group save" function, where the save file is only accessible if all involved players are present.
2: Keeping criticism 1 in mind with how long the session can last and how you can't save, you also can't re-join any game you somehow DC from. 3 and half hours of progress then "poof." Gone. You lost the hero you almost earned, and your mates will have to try and carry on without you. This happened to me and it was extremely dissapointing (because this game is extremely good.) After surviving hordes and hordes of some of the most difficult mobs, no one wants to die indefinitely to server problems.
3: It's far easier to earn new heroes playing solo, since in a party of 3, there can be only one more hero added to the party and can only be controlled by a single player and only that single player will earn  that hero. Which from a different perspective may seem like "only the ones who earn the hero get the hero" but to me it's just a reason to not play multiplayer, which this game shouldn't be doing.
In summary, embrace the multiplayer. Make it a bit friendlier. Other than that, awesome game. 4/5 stars.
One more thing. The 32 bit art in this game is gorgeous.

Полный обзор читаем тут:

The game features a number of single-player modes: scripted missions, balanced skirmishes, and endless survival matches. In addition, maps can be edited in the game, and cross-platform multiplayer is available allowing players on Windows, Linux, and Android systems to play together. The interface is very basic and lacks some features, like infinite queues (or even queueing up things in advance without paying for them) and auto-explore. Rusted Warfare only features one resource (cash), extracted from specific locations on the map (or produced at a lesser rate anywhere). Cash is used to build factories (land, air, sea, and mech), defensive turrets, repair structures, and shields. Cash is also used to upgrade structures to higher tiers so they can produce more advanced units. The AI is a decent competitor. Rusted Warfare doesn’t offer anything innovative to the genre, instead producing some combination of Red Alert and Supreme Commander; shallow economics and simple unit countering (along with extremely tedious end-game clean-up) limit potential strategies. That said, the price is very reasonable and cross-platform multiplayer is a nice feature. But overall, the limitations of Rusted Warfare hold it back just enough from being a satisfying take on the classic real-time strategy game.
