Simply put, I expected an impressive experience that would hold my interest and have me caring about survival.
Simply put, I'm incredibly disappointed. I’ll be VERY thorough about the result of having cautious optimism.
Cons:
> Rife with grammatical/spelling errors. These are breaking immersion when BASIC INSTRUCTIONS on how to play the game contain things auto-correct finds. Here are a handful I found in just 90 minutes: 'modifers', 'availible', 'finish-up', 'details of you team'. Also, when a single team member is injured by a scavenger, the event screen describes needing to aid "them". Not gender police here, just reference to a single person is needed, not multiple people. (Wonder how many Not Helpful's I'll get for that.) Sorry folks, I enjoy being literate, so this poked me the wrong way.
> Lightning-fast Exposition. The first five minutes of the game has me waking up in The Church, the base for character interaction. No cut-scene like Jacob’s descending the ladder from in the game trailer. No such event or script for Jacob becoming the leader through conversation or initial discovery of the church. Just wake up, find out what the robot does, know how to read the menus, and off I go to retrieve some tech or a cookbook. Funny, as the lagging loading screens come up, I have a brief chance to view ‘hints’. Such things include back-story which I would have been happy to sit through at the beginning of the game. Sadly, character and environmental depth take a backseat to chucking the player into tedious mechanics of this wasteland wanderer’s doddle across the endless white. How enchanting was facing realism, like not sleeping for 3 days by eating canned beans and drinking water for an hour of gameplay straight.
> The g. o. d. d. a. m. n. keyboard + Mouse controls. Perhaps on Steam, most games that don’t use a K+M require virtual reality headsets/joysticks of some kind. But for a PC game, after an initial release without proper K+M controls, and a broken promise for releasing updated K+M support by a given day on a PATCH ROAD MAP, I still have problems. Problems such as: Hovering mouse over menu options is improperly spaced (I have to hover my mouse next to/away from the buttons for them to be counted as highlighted). Opening up menus often auto-highlights particular random menu keys. When cycling through team member conditions/crafting, the next/previous arrows skip ahead two characters per click, rather that one. Not being able to hover my mouse over an item needed for crafting, needing to use my arrow keys instead. Little things like this dampen my playtime and take away from the decent inventory storage dimension/sorting system.
“Uh well the game only just came out from a small team, you expect it to be perfect?” No homeboy, I expect a game built properly before it’s released. It’s hard to feel emotions while playing a game that doesn’t even cooperate with you on a fundamental level. I guess I don’t have a fetish for A E S T H E T I C, like the people that enjoyed No Man’s Sky knowing full well it's a single player time-waster.
After a shallow introduction to the game’s world and broken controls, there are few pros to this game. SPOILERS, none of them salvage the game for me.
Pros:
> Character art. The avatars look nice, as do the character models. The outdoors hold a particularly good atmosphere. Having limited sight and little to see at times allows points of interest to arrest my attention easily, reminding me of my options and priorities (whatever those seem to be).
> Concept. The core idea for a story/gameplay looks good on paper. This game leaves me reminiscing about Carpenter’s “The Thing”, a favorite of mine - and the mild edge of going into underground environments blind (with no Ako-Light radar) is intriguing. The idea of trekking the unknown without having to embrace it is easy to repeat, but not unpleasant (if it's executed properly).
Having a brain, I knew I couldn’t judge the game properly based on a mere 90 minutes of gameplay. Across three days after release, I indulged in hours of captured gameplay on youtube. Watching other people meander was alright, because I knew I would be doing the same thing. Honestly I enjoyed watching people play it over actually playing it, which is a first for me since I loath typical cookie-cutter, “quirky lets-play personality” channels. Any interest I would have felt doing something myself, I found in watching other people play as well. Choices, obstacles and perks for team story completion all felt dull and futile stretching across the landscape (while watching gameplay and actually doing it). While actually playing the game, upgrading the church was easier than expected, and did not feel rewarding. I took my time, and I managed to do a lot with so little, which felt unnatural. (On a side note, anyone that claims a person can’t criticize a game unless they play it themselves, and can’t truly understand it until then, might as well be saying you can’t know anything about breasts until you touch one. That line of thinking results in losers leaving recommends on games like this after realizing they past their two-hour refund limit and start feeling synthetic awe, and base the quality of the game on personal enjoyment as a way to cope with having flushed $25.)
Ah, but what about the soundtrack? The man partially responsible for establishing Kung Fury’s tone, and a killer bandcamp discography. Surely that’s good. Yes, it is superb. It’s part of the reason I made the mistake of pre-ordering. I still don’t know when it’ll be available for download/purchase, so good luck getting it anywhere besides youtube or the game files.
What else can I say, quarters are falling out of my A. S. S. because I played myself. I felt the pain No Man Sky left me with, just on a smaller scale. Those cruel pre-order blues. I would only recommend this game if you enjoy tedious scavenging missions, on sale. I may very well buy this again if it's drastically changed and fixed. Until then, hello refund.

This would be a beautiful beta.
But it's not. It's a fully released game. And as someone who has played 9 hrs on release day, I've got more feelings than an animal rescue commercial.

This game is visually great. The music goes well with the theme and I'm not sick of it yet. I'm an inventory management junkie (ie in-game hoarder). I play PC games with an Xbox controller, much to the shame of my family. I'm having a lot of fun with this game. Its a little This War of Mine, a dash of fetch questing, and a hint of "Will there be zombies? Your messages say no, but your wink says yes."
That said, I've rage quit. Five times. I'm a glutton for punishment, you see.
As of May 23rd 2017, the game is riddled with bugs. As someone who has done QA for video games, I get it. With releases you have priorities and as long as it doesnt crash the game or completely kill gameplay, you just patch it as fast as possible. But the bugs I've encountered keep me from progressing and force me to restart. I'm on Day 13 with 9 hours into it. I've had faster days being eaten by cannibals in The Forest. A few of the issues I've encountered:
- MIssing collision where my character literally falls off the map in the diner
- Collision where there shouldnt be, forcing my character to get stuck in a snowbank with no way out (main example, by the bridge near the traders camp to the north)
- Quests not updating after completion, making me unable to continue a storyline
- Tech vans resetting and not producing items vital for the quest
- When a support asks if they should eat a can of food without a label, being unable to select yes or no, and also being unable to get away from that menu
There are also things like filler character names popping up, and the annoying problem of selecting Enter multiple times to go into a building, but something just isnt registering or lining up, so you move your character a little to the left, then the right, until finally it decides you've done well.
There's no intro, cutscene, or immediate backstory. Dont know why that bugs me, but to just be thrown into You Wake Up is unnerving to me. Just personal preference.
Even with the tutorial, there is very little hand holding. Which I actually like. It allows you to explore and experience the wilderness, which is think is a key component to the game. You dont have this gigantic map that shows where you are all the time, and you have to really watch your stats. They arent always on the screen. There are some things that still havent been explained to me, like why the robot will glow red and do the Hotter/Colder noise at times, but my hope is that it is the result of a quest that I cannot complete.
So why do I recommend it? Potential. Yeah, it sucks that I wouldnt consider it fully playable in the state that it is in. As someone that the last 5 purchases have been betas that have no actual "release date", I'm used to going with the flow of monthly updates. Hell, I dont know if those games are ever actually going to be considered fully released! Why bother when, if you do fully release the game, the moment there is a bug people jump down your throats?
So my recommendation is this. Try it out. Know that you need a controller. Go into it with an open mind. Put a few hours into it, and then shut it off. Wait a month. Let the dust settle and they can figure it out. Because when this is what we all thought it was going to be (and I really think it will), it's gonna be a great game.

Bought this when the grand RPG maker shovelware apocalypse happened and everything was on sale.
Its got about 15 hours of gameplay for one playthrough, with four difficulty modes. I think the intent is that you play it once on each, but I don't see how someone could stand that.
Its a pretty neat take on a JRPG though. Encounters don't respawn, Most are mobile and can be avoided and the rest are static and must be fought to physically progress. The characters are cute and the game play is basically like a mix of a point and click adventure/puzzle game and a JRPG. Its neat and the story is decently engaging.
There's an endurance element to it also. Vendors are rare and all but two sell only stat ups. Their inventory is fixed so once you buy them out they're done. Recovery is mainly through picking up items that are autoconsumed when picked up, and recover a small amount of HP or MP. Same for curatives. There are dmg/poison proc ones, sometimes the game tricks you wtih them or makes them required to walk through, or just requires you to always weave through a maze of them. Which is blah.
Its not without some serious flaws though. Like most point and click games it can be frustrating to know where to go, since the path through is so backtrackey (get a thing that lets you break rocks, redo everywhere breaking the rocks to go new places, etc). Keys or key-like items (there are quite a few) have to be equipped to offhand to use, and the things that let you break the 3 different kinds of rocks (for real) have to as well, and later on the jumping item. That means you spend a lot of time in your menu scrolling through a big♥♥♥♥♥list to equip the key then immediately take it off and put back on your shield/good weapon/good charm.
As a consequnce of the lack of one shot recovery at an inn or resting it makes things like getting poisoned or statused very frustrating. Especially early on, having someone die (all the pickups rez them but at one heatlh) or getting your team poisoned blows, it can be a hard stop on your playthrough. It also means later one when your last party member gets an in combat heal thats cheap (she has 3x your mana and it costs 1/4 what your protagonists heal does), you sandbag lots of routine fights to slowly heal.
Your protagonist ends up being the tankiest by a wide margin, and has a free taunt and a counterattack proc when hit. Lots of fights especially lategame devolve into your protagonist just murdering everything on the crackback, including all the bosses. It leads to hilarious fights with some bosses and the non-boss enemies that use their sprite (they're all just recolors) since they can too, so once one of you hits the other you sit there counterattacking until someone dies.
There was a really bad difficulty curve on mobs. A lot of areas are a pretty std level of strength with large jumps, which usually means you get to backtrack in the harder areas to go heal up and then slog back in. This is partially alleviated by two teleport items but you don't acquire them until right at the end of the game, since you would otherwise have to slog back through a really long empty room.
The ending, to cap it off, is rather unfulfilling.
Thats a lot of negatives and no praise really, but despite that this game was very engaging, very charming, and fun. It had some really well done levels and sets, great music, and the cutest theme imaginable. This is definitely worth playing if you think you can deal with the negatives ( or don't consider them to be, different strokes for different folks).

I don't remember exactly when I first bought this game (long before it arrived on Steam), but it was at least 7 years ago.
Very little seems to have changed since then. They spent two years working on a whole new game engine and map tools, which perhaps was of long term benefit, but what have they done in the other 5 years? Added some crafting and farming (fair enough, good), multiplayer (could have waited in favour of other stuff), redid interfaces, stats and other minor stuff.
If you buy the game, you will get some enjoyment out of it for a while. You'll enjoy exploring the town, breaking in to various buildings and searching for useful stuff to help you survive, dodging or fighting off zombies along the way. You'll enjoy trying to build your zombie proof home.
And then you'll get bored of it. The developers might keep you interested in how the development is going with their weekly essays on how awesome the game is going to be once they add the extra features that they've been working on for the last X years, but even that will wear thin sooner or later.
If you're bored and want a distraction for a little while, then perhaps buy this and play it until you get bored again. But don't buy it based on promised content or improvements 'cos it'll be years away, if it arrives at all.
Edit: For those questioning my time frame. I moved house about 5 years ago, and I played Zomboid at least a year or two before that, back when it was using Java (before the change of game code/engine, as stated above). Long before Steam EA (as stated above), so don't bother quoting that at me.
Plenty of other games just as complex have been fully developed on EA and released in that time, so the argument "development takes time", yes it does. But for someone who has been following this game on and off for so long, this is just getting silly.
Give it a couple more years, we'll see if you're still as zealous then.

I love this game. It was challenging, beautiful, and rather fun to play. Still, it hurts me that I have to mark this as a not recommend because it has some serious design flaws and is still in need of a decent amount of polish.
From a visual and audio perspective, this is a masterpiece. The inspiration it takes and the delivery of the design is top notch. Beautiful characters and animations.
The part that breaks the game is a fair number of glitches kept in the game to keep it overly challenging to the point that the game thinks you're doing too well and then uses a glitch to say "Oh you're dead! Git gud!"
Sure, plenty of trolls will tell you to git gud, and if you're willing to be patient enough the game is still beatable despite this, and overcoming some of the cheaper areas of the game gives you satisfaction for overcoming these flaws, but the frustration is simply not worth it. Being frustrated because of your own lack of skill is one thing, but to lose over and over because of a broken game just has no appeal.
Probably the best example of this in the game is a battle you will face against a ghost who possesses a train. In the first phase of the battle, several bullets are thrown at you that you can shoot at and hopefully destroy before they hit you. However, these bullets have two problems. The first being that they have no set amount of hits to destroy them. Sometimes four hits will do it, and sometimes it might take as many as eight. If it happens to be the latter, then it's possible that the bullet has reached you and hit you for damage already, which is a huge disadvantage in the first seconds of a long battle. I found myself restarting bosses far more than being killed by said bosses simply because of the unlikelihood I could take on an entire battle with 2 hp (as well as my desire to achieve the higher grades in battles, which of course requires full health).
Now, that alone isn't worth the flak I'm giving the game, of course. But the problems in this part alone get even worse. There was a particular glitch that would randomly take a bullet that you destroyed, and immediately respawn it just above your character so that it turns into an unblockable attack. There is just simply no defense against this, and no particular reason it happens, but it does. If the goal of a battle is to dodge the bullets, that's fine. That's a challenge. But if there is a system set in place to destroy the weapons coming at you, but it requires you to literally roll the dice and hope it means that the game doesn't decide to hit you regardless of your actions? Well, that's pretty broken.
But, I mean... Git gud, right? Sure. Don't listen to internet trolls. There's hundreds upon thousands of games out there that are beautiful and not broken, and ultimately it's your money. If you want to throw down twenty bucks for an unfair amount of frustration and that makes you happy, then cool, this game is perfect. But if you want challenging, there's better options. Don't pay for a pretty package. Demand decent structure and polish to your games.

This is a well thought out zombie survival game that has plenty of developer support and modding/community support as well.  That's a combination to a sustainable and successful game which is what Project Zomboid is achieving.  For me I found the game refreshing because this game already has what many other zombie survival games strive to become.  There's a great crafting system, base building, various levels of difficulties, single player, co-op, or play as multiplayer.  One thing I particularly enjoyed is that the game doesn't hide the fact that you will die at some point(as the game becomes increasingly more difficult as times carries on and resources start to reduce(such and utilities being turned off permanently).  So every time you go out to scavange when you have survived for a while is a legitimate risk of the effort you have put in.
Some issues with the game is the game is extremely harsh to new players, although this is getting better from the developers via tutorials.  I also suggest reading up on guides and the forum(something I didn't do initially, I jumped right in and turned into zombie food).  Some mechanics feel clunky, especially if you're used to playing with a controller, it feels more favorable towards mouse and keyboard, so be prepared for some adapting.
With that all said I would highly recommend getting this game if you're a zombie fan, survival fan, or both.  You will find it rewarding and challenging at the same time.

The game is beautiful. The art and animation are clever, and a perfect imitation of that done in the 1930's. The music is top-notch as well. The artistic accomplishments of Cuphead are beyond reproach.
The game is hard, in the style of early Nintendo Entertainment System games, or the arcade quarter-plunkers that came slightly prior. This isn't a reflex game, it's a pattern-learning game. There are a handful of run-n-gun levels, but the bulk is boss fights, and the vast majority of the play is learning those bosses, recognizing their telegraphs, and then avoiding their attacks over time.
The thing is, while I found the game to be a challenge, and I played it through for the sake of completing that challenge, I did not actually find Cuphead fun. I enjoyed seeing each boss, and marveling over their design and animation. But the process of actually fighting and beating them was frustrating, punishing, and often...boring. There's no fanfare, no interesting context. The story of Cuphead is totally bare-bones, the characters simply there, a parade of things that are more interesting to look at than to interact with.
Cuphead is an achievement, no argument there. In the end I do recommend it. It's probably going to be many people's and gaming publications' game of the year, and deservedly so. But is it an enjoyable game? To look at, yes. To play, in my opinion, no.

This is how Early Access should work. Now I only bought this game two weeks before release, but at that point it was already more polished and complete than most on release and now that is is officially out I am blown away by the quality!
I just love this game for the randomness, but usually that isn't enough for me what makes this game special is every game feels like a new story. "Does this group have what it takes?" I find myself asking, "Is luck on my side today?" sometimes I find my way through the maze and beeline to the exit, (happened on floor 10 kinda scared me because its so damn huge and I found the exit so fast couldn't even power half the rooms on the way to the exit) and the writing for the characters is awesome! Sure they don't talk much but the descriptions, plus the few intertwining stories that you may or may not hear in the elevator really flesh out the characters to a point where I find myself making up relationships between them that might fit, or thinking about how much they must hate having to work together and I will even make up friendships between heroes that end up working together throught multiple floors. (sometimes i can even encorperate one of the "canon" stories into it and it just feels great)
On top of all that. is an amazing game that doesn't really have any peers (at least to my knowledge) sure it feels like FTL or Space Marines or what have you but it combines them all in such a way that it creates something revolutionary. I see this as almost a difficult story generating game, where the goal isn't to win but to create a good story.

The Gameplay.
The gameplay of this game can be amazing, and frustrating. When it works, this game is one of the funnest games i've ever played, but that's only when it works. I think i can better explain how the game works by explaining how it doesn't work. The game can be frustarting. Its very annoying when the game has red guys come out of nowhere, as an example some levels have you in a small area where there are some guys, but the annoying thing is when you kill them new one spawn in all around you, so when you are fighting 3 guys in front of you, you get shot in the back from nowhere. Not to mention that the spawns are random depending on where you are, so you just keep on trying and hope you get lucky and there's no one behind you. Or you could just stay at a spawner and wait for the guys to come at you, but that ruins the action and makes the game a grind.
The Game Length.
Im not that great at games, and i died a ton on the last level, but the fact that at the time i bought the game for 24.99 and finished the game in 3 hours is ridiculous, your telling me when they have like 3 textures and all the level designs are just simple polygonal shapes, that they couldn't add more levels? But after you beat the game you can now do challenges and endless mode, they both suck for the most part. Endless mode is hide in a corner killing guys as they come to you because if you leave your corner some one will kill you from behind while you are fighting some one that's attaking you with a machine gun (because they spawn right behind you, and you have to turn around every 10 seconds which moves time so you can't do it in a firefight). And the challenges, some of them are fun, some aren't, but the annoying thing is that to unlock new challenges, you have to beat levels in challenges you have unlocked, so if you hate playing one of the challenges to bad because you have to beat half the levels to unlock a new challenge.
The Story.
The story is ok, i don't really think its good or bad, but if you don't care about the story it can get annoying. The game pulls you out of the action and gives you the story, so if you just wana play the game it can get annoying.
If you really want it just get it and make sure you don't play over 2 hours, then if you don't want to spend 25 bucks on it just return it. But i regret playing over 2 hours.

is a stealth survival FPS with random map generation. You step into the role of a high-classed gentleman/ lady scientist/ inventor of some sort who's latest experiment has gone horribly wrong, and has this Sir or Madam stranded on a group of islands in an alternate reality. If things didn't look bleak enough, your butler informs you that you are being hunted by denizens of this strange new land; they are Victorian England robot hunters looking to fill in a space on their den wall. Keep a pistol in your hand and an ear to the ground as you venture forth in this funny yet freaky adventure.
The goal of the game is to repair the Standing Stones, the relic that went haywire during your tests, in order to use them to warp you back home. To repair the Stones, you need to locate the missing pieces which where dislodged during your failed experiment, and gather them back to the Standing Stones. The catch, however, is the presence of the manhunting automatons that are more than happy to riddle you with buckshot, catch your♥♥♥♥♥up in a bear trap, and otherwise just ruin your unexpected journey. Their forces grow larger and more dangerous with the more progress you make.
As a survival game implies, you have to manage needs like hunger. It is called Vitality in
and it is basically a calorie meter combined with your potency to regain lost health over time. You use various food and drink items you gather from looting and hunting wild game to restore Vitality.
Even though the game supports a decent variety of weaponry, from a simple axe to a high-powered rifle, the best weapon is stealth. Ammo can be difficult to find as the game goes on and can be very cumbersome on your inventory, so sticking to the shadows pay be the most safe and economic way to play. If you're one who isn't worried about saving every bullet and shell, then you can employ guerilla tactics and Rambo your way to victory. There are also other means to gain advantages against your predators, such as bear traps and noise makers.
This game stands out fairly in the survival game scene nowadays, with its somewhat simple yet surreal/steampunk art direction, witty humor and Easter eggs, the haunting feeling of being watched and hounded down, moments of "what the hell..." and robotic gentlemen with shotguns instead of zombies. I give this lovely game a 9/10.

Having completed all three campaigns and one game of conquest my worst fears are confirmed. EAW is an RTS hybrid that tries to be many things but is tripped by technical issues, bad design decisions and a clear lack of testing. The end result is a game that is mediocre at best and only held together by the magic glue that is Star Wars. Only recommended for fans who are willing to suck on a lollypop made out of pure salt just because it's shaped like Darth Vader's helmet.
+Authentic Star Wars music and sound effects that leave nothing to be desired. Sometimes even the voice acting is surprisingly good
+Graphics seem fairly timeless with some space battle effects still looking pretty sweet
+Space battles are fun most of the time
+Asymmetric factions (Empire has bigger ships with free fighters, Alliance has better fighters that require no carriers etc.)
+Multiple campaigns and conquest mode scenarios
+Dropping the screen filling Executor in the middle of a battle for the first time should make any nerds inner fascist climax immediately
-Doesn't seem to play nice with Win10 and has no borderless window support. If played fullscreen while Alt-Tabing can put your Windows in a state where you have to reboot to get anything done. I recommend running it in a maximized window instead.
-Game breaking bugs include disappearing critical characters, inability to task units to campaign critical missions, disappearing units etc. These issues can be somewhat circumvented with furious saving.
-A multitude of UX issues that range from fighters needlessly blocking capital ships from selection to the way save files are handled: latest saves don't always show up first, save files take too much space etc.
-AI blatantly cheats both by its very nature and also seems to gain scripted fleets out of nowhere for the campaigns
-AI sometimes just freezes and does nothing with its ships in battle
-Unit AI is atrocious and does not seem to do any target prioritization whatsoever for any attacks. Pathfinding gets progressively worse with unit size to the point where units like AT-ATs, artillery units and Star Destroyers sometimes require near constant micromanaging so that they move the way you need
-Being unable to assign any movement orders on the galactic map in pause mode makes no sense
-Forces of Corruption doesn't integrate to the main game and is actually a separate game that feels like it was cheaply hacked together in a hurry
-While the original EaW is somewhat balanced, the Consortium faction in FoC is completely out of whack and seems to have the best in almost everything in addition to their frustrating corruption mechanic that requires constant fiddling especially from the opponents
-Ground battles are usually horrendously repetitive and tedious
-Battles can be autoresolved, but the logic for resolving them is completely ludicrous and can lead to massive casualties even if the opponent doesn't actually have any chance of fighting back
-Very limited amount of units and ships in a battle at any given time (for example, you can have 6 Imperial class Star Destroyers if you have almost nothing else) and the rest have to be drip-fed into the battle as reinforcements when previous units are destroyed
-Player can't choose which units enter a battle first in EaW (mostly fixed in FoC though)
-Flying units can't actually fly over many obstacles in ground battles
-Some of the writing and voice acting is very cringeworthy especially in FoC. A few characters also use quotes from the movies to a ridiculous degree even for fanservice
-The Alliance can commit genocide without any issues and can actually get more funds from it

There's something about Dreamscape that's different than most RPGs, especially as an indie title. So far, I've unlocked 4 of the playable characters and all of them are completely different. And I do mean COMPLETELY different, which is really awesome. The story is as simple as the main character searching for her boyfriend that's gone missing, but the story is so compelling that it really is the journey that is more important than the destination. Logistically, this game has unique features that most RPGs do not have. For one, battles can be choose and most enemies do not regenerate at all. This helps you tell where you've been and where you haven't been. Also items are not put directly in your inventory; instead, you have to decide whether you should pick them up now and use them or wait till later to grab them. This adds strategy to the gameplay.
On top of the great story and gameplay, the game is just overall whimsical and colorful and really embarks some of the visual aesthetics of games such as Earthbound.
Overall, if you love RPGs, then this is the game for you. For only $10, you get hours of fun!

I have been revisiting this game since its very early release a couple of years ago and since then i feel that the game has developed more issues then it has enhanced. I know that there was a sitiuation where the developers had lost all of their contents and practically had to start over again, so my negative opinion does not merge from that, but the time after.
I've been playing PZ since its early stages, 2D graphics, Zombies looked all the same, only Male Characters and all that. Back then the game had a lot less features then it has now. But this doesn't always have to be a bad thing. The difficulty level was a bit low after getting used to the game, and it was a little boring after a while so adding features to it was absolutley neccesary. But that is of course OK for a game in early access. Yet the changes it has made degraded the game.
The Focus suddenly was to make the game more realistic and a lot harder, thats not a bad thing as long as it doesn't infect the initial design of the game.
Back then i had a good little tutorial Level wich explained the important bits to me and after that i had to survive on my own... now i have a lot of Textboxes with the companys cheery little mascot telling me about all the stuff i need to know. Thats where the problems startet for me.
I generally don't like reading a lot throug text in order to play a game, not because im lazy but because i think its a huge flaw Designers make these days.
A tutorial is important for us gamers as well as for the Developers themselves. It's the first stage of the game which makes the game appealing to someone, and at the same time explains how it works. I felt that having to look out for Kate was a great way to do that and it set the right tone for the Zompocalypse Theme.
Then there was the decision to upgrade the Graphics from 2D to 2.5D.
Thats not so bad in general but it slowed down the process of the general Development a lot. Also the gameplay has been set to be more realistic. It now consumes time to pick up items, or eat or read.
That aint a bad idea at first but how does that work for the game itself ? It slows down its pace, it makes the player wait unnecessarily. It makes it more boring. Same as with opening windows. I know stand there and have to watch my Character struggeling with opening the window every time i want to enter a house. Be that as it may, it gives me the feeling that development has lost track of what it originally wanted the game to be.

Slow-motion at its finest. This is a game where the time only really flows when the player is moving.
Simple controls: run, grab/throw objects (you can grab the guns from your shot opponents, the game provides very limited ammunitions so you have to switch weapons regularly), fire (or punch/melee). You can also jump but that was rarely useful to me. There is not much more to it, not much interaction generally speaking. The levels are usually small, baddies spawn from portals (that the player can watch a bit too closely imho, but that wasn't game-breaking at all for me). Kill them all, go to the next level - or, if the game requires it, advance the story a little bit using the game built-in console.
The story feels a bit like déjà-vu, but the fact the whole games is about VR (the characters absolutely look like vintage 3D/VR games) makes it more fun. Expect some fourth-wall jokes or allusions.
This game lacks a bit of depth imho (there is no denying level design could have served the main concept -which is slow motion- better, or that the game could have used a few more features). Some of the not-so-obvious-but-cool things you can do are playing with the bullets and try to dodge them (barely !) or even shoot/cut them.
Anyway, it should be pretty fun for you while it last. Pretty short game but the devs included alternative modes.

This most recent offering on Steam from Aldorlea confirms again that these developers are at the top of the list of those making the old school/adventure style games. Dreamscape has everything a fan of these games could want, and much more.
As always, these games are driven by the story, and, IMO, Aldorlea always has this element perfected. In the game you are Erin ---- who is on a mission to save her boyfriend. Sounds simple enough, but to accomplish this seemingly straightforward task she has some magical headphones that allow her to enter the dreams of virtually everyone she comes in contact with including a cat, a mouse, and a plant. Together, they explore the dreamworlds of those within their own dreams (an adventurer, an old man, a dog, a pharaoh, and many others). So much for simplicity ---- yet the story remains tightly organized, and everything makes sense. Some of the dreams are simple, some complex, and they all add up to a story that is beautifully put together with no meandering that completely draws you in and holds your interest in a completely captivating way.
With so much to see and do Dreamscape is a long one, and offers high replay value with 4 levels of difficulty that offer new challenges. The game offers an innovation that is different in that the items you need for good health and magic are not always able to be stored in your inventory, but are found everywhere in the world to be used or left behind for later ---- your decision, and an interesting spin on the ordinary. But there are plenty of items so it never becomes a problem (at least not in the easiest level, which I am playing).
Character development is excellent (even Marine from the Millennium series makes an appearance), and offers a lot of good humor ---- it's easy to like these characters as they offer their comments to one another while exploring ---- especially the cat.
Gameplay is with either the keyboard or mouse, and both work well.
The artwork is very nicely done, and includes some very different and detailed scenes as you travel throughout the various dreams. The music is pleasant and unobtrusive which adds to the enjoyment of the game.
This is a very creative and different rpg that shows great care and attention to detail by the developer that I would enthusiastically recommend to anyone of any age. And, if you have never experienced an Aldorlea game, this one is a fine place to start. But, then, I would say that about any of their games here on Steam. Enjoy.

2 things of note: This is an EARLY ACCESS review of the game, and as a part of a promotion, I got a free copy of the game from
First of all, at this stage of development, the game is in a fairly rough state, but it does have a lot of potential, so this review is both for prospective buyers as well as some suggestions on what to focus on.
The level design for the race map that is in the game so far is very large, and while there are some bugs in the design of the map (ramp edges above the ground, causing a crash when trying to use the ramp)  The map has an ample number of turns and features to make the map interesting, and there are more versions of the map and extra maps incoming according to ingame screens.
The car controls currently are the biggest let down to this game, to put it simply the vehicle is hard to control with the autopilot wanting to drag you back to the center line constantly and the turning seems a bit brick like.  The car does need a reverse gear, as at one point I did get my nose of my car right against a rock and was unable to move since the rocketcar only goes forward.  The autopilot is able to be turned off, but sometimes it feels like it turns itself back on randomly at points.
The default camera angle is fine most of the time, but when you start messing things up is where it goes a bit wonky, the camera seems locked to look at the roof of the car always, and while that's not a horrible thing, when making sharp turns or if you get flipped over, the experience suffers.
Is the game perfect right now? No, but it looks to have quite a lot of potential and if the controls are addressed I look forward to playing this game a lot more in the future!

Cuphead has so much going for it! It is one of the most polished games in recent years, and it boasts such a unique artsyle that will set it apart for what I believe years to come. The controls are sound even though you don't have dual directional aiming. My only gripe with the controls is that when I ducked on a platform and jumped, it seemed unintuitive that I fell through instead of jumping which caused more than a handful of deaths. Similar to the aiming, I got use to it though, but only because the game punished me for thinking. The loadouts are all useful despite me thinking otherwise at first and gave several different approaches to taking on the bosses. Speaking of which, after beating the game on expert, I came to realize that very few of the bosses are plain unfair (especially when trying to S rank), but a majority just require the player with learning the bosses moveset. This gives an artificial difficulty spike that diminishes when the player does learn the patterns. This can be considered rewarding, but when the whole game is like this, it starts to become a grind. A way to alleviate this grind would be to implement a system where you could choose to practice certain phases of the boss, but instead you have to start from the beginning each time. The good does outweigh the bad in this case though as the feeling of overcoming the boss and/or achieving an S rank is satisfying in the highest degree. Overall, Cuphead is probably somewhere between an 8 and a 9 as it gives a fun but frustrating experience that is definitely worth the asking price if you have the perseverance to overcome the bosses.

Fantastic approach to dungeon crawling with some unusual gameplay mechanics featuring semi-turn based tactics and micro-management.
I could call this game 'a mix between a party dungeon crawler and a tower defense' but that wouldn't cover all this game has to offer.
You start off selecting a 'crew' which is to land inside a planet's randomly generated dungeon. Your crew is consisted of 2 to 4 heroes, which have their own skills, stats, intentory, background story and dialogue. Upon landing you explore the dungeon by opening doors to other rooms, which are hidden in a fog of war, until you open them. Every door opening counts as a turn. Each turn you gain resources, which you can then spend on: building modules which generate more resources or assist your heroes in various ways; constructing turrets and such in rooms you have already visited and sent power to; shopping for equipment and leveling up your heroes. Your ultimate goal is to find an exit/elevator on each floor and to deliver the 'crystal' you start off with in a first room to the elevator.
The catch is: every 'unpowered' room you discover has a chance to spawn monsters every time you open a door. Every monster will then proceed to attack your crystal, reducing your 'dust'(A currency, required to power rooms which also serves as crystal's HP) until it's depleted. Also as soon as you take your crystal off its place - there is no turning back, monsters will spawn in every room and begin attacking you until you reach the elevator.
Your progress is not limited to just leveling up your heroes and giving them equipment. Tons of random events occur in a dungeon, which offer you to hire new heroes in your party, trade your resources for a powerful equipment and research over a dozen turrets, modules and other ways to defend your crystal as you proceed through the floors.
The game features a great amount of unlockable content. Characters, starting setups and an artwork gallery. Its replayability is totally on the highest of levels. Especially considering that every piece of equipment found inside a dungeon is generated with random stats.
Game also features a multiplayer mode, which adds more tactical depth since you can divide the roles and do whatever you wanted to but lacked a partner controlling a character in a singleplayer mode.
TL;DR : A great party dungeon crawler with a randomly generated floor structures, deep tower defense features, unique and interesting pre-made heroes and a great replayability value because of the unlocks. Also music. The soundtrack is very good.

I don't have a full hour yet, but I decided to go ahead and make a review because of one thing regarding this game:
The initial impression. Read the whole thing before you go "well, what do you know, with only one hour?"
Upon starting the game up, it tells you to link your account with their site. That's fine, whatever. The big issue is the fact that the game's resolution is automatically set at a messed up number (couldn't tell you what one, exactly), and you can't change this, until you get in game. In fact, there are no options settings at all at the inital menu, and they are only visible once you get in game.
Besides that point, there is also the fact that the music, for whatever reason, is automatically muted, and you have to turn this on as well. Even after the music is turned on, it's still kinda wonky, and doesn't loop very often, so you'll have a thirty-second period of music, then another few minutes of silence (not counting the attacking sound effects).
Character creation is a joke, and I don't know if this was done the way it was AS a joke, or if they weren't finished with it, and never got around to fixing it. You can give your character a large head, and make them taller, shorter, thinner, or fatter. You then have a handful of hairstyles and even less hair colors to pick from. The races seemed interesting, but not too terribly to get me to pick something besides human.
While on the subject of characters, the motions are kinda weird. They don't seem broken, but they don't seem too fluid from time to time. The motions themselves are just weird, and it's hard to explain them without seeing them. Basically, they seem a little bit under par for the course, in regards to them.
Humor is kinda bland. The game tries to throw it in, but it's too forced.
Now, some long term player might say "it gets better at level 15/20/30!" and that may be so, but when you're looking at this game, which is still free of course, against something that did the same thing, such as Mabinogi or Dragon Nest, and did it better, why would you waste your time on this?
The game is rather outdated, that's a given, but there is still a lot about the game that would have been pretty poor, even when it was released.
So, if you're looking for an anime MMORPG (or any new MMORPG for that matter), I wouldn't look here, unless something shifts in the game's favor.

This game is very old, I understand that. But really, it was still just was highly disappointing. I do not recommend it to anyone. I wouldn't call it an "acquired taste" even, it's just bad. I only played for about 10 or 15 minutes after creating my character, but I could already tell it was horrible. Here are a few things I learned while in-game.
1.) One of the first things I noticed about the game was its short amount of customization options for character creation. This wasn't a MAJOR issue to me, but I was just slightly disappointed. However, I've played many MMOs before; some have a good, detailed character creation, and some have this simple customization with not many options. So I worked with what I had and it wasn't TOO big a deal, but if you're like me and you like to make your character unique amongst others, I'm letting you know, this game has very few customization options.
2.) The game has little to no direction at all, even for beginners. There is no way to tell who you are supposed to talk to for a quest. There's no exclamation point, question mark, book icon, or anything above the quest NPC's head. You just have to talk to them and kind of go off of a wild guess, or you have to read your journal constantly to figure out where you're supposed to be going. Not your traditional MMO.
3.) Hotkeys. Oh my god, the hotkeys. You couldn't have made them something simple like 'B' for Backpack (or 'I' for Inventory), 'J' for Journal, 'O' for friend list, 'G' for guild interface? Nope. They made it Ctrl+C for inventory, Ctrl+N for options, etc. SO many confusing hotkeys, nothing simple. And guess what? You can't change them. I tried. I sat on the options menu for a good 3 or 4 minutes trying to figure out if there's a way to change the hotkeys, so that maybe I could rebind them to my preference and be able to get over it and get on with playing the game, but no. So basically you just click on the icons in the lower right of the screen (Most people prefer not to do that. It's just easier to use a simple hotkey to get to your inventory!) or learn all the hotkeys which are completely different from the average MMORPG (Which generally use simple hotkeys like the ones I listed before).
4.) Gameplay = boring. MAYBE this would change if i'd given the game more of a shot. Maybe I would go to the next town, learn my class and get skills, etc. but in the beginner town, it was boring. After looking around wondering what exactly to do, talking to a random guy and getting a quest to kill Pupus (basically pigs), I went ahead and did that. The combat was a very "back and forth" style (your character does one hit on the enemy, the enemy hits him/her, your character hits the enemy again, repeat, until the fight is over). Again, maybe the gameplay factor would have changed if I was more into the game and I was able to get skills and such, but I pretty much knew I wouldn't enjoy the game due to the fact that there is basically no sense of direction. You really have to figure it out yourself, who gives quests and such.
If you're looking for a good anime-style MMORPG to play, go play Mabinogi. I play it from time to time and I love it.

Playing "Sir, You Are Being Hunted!" has been one of the most engrossing and endearing experiences I've had for a while. It makes you feel powerless, but hopeful. It's a game where an empty bottle is more useful than a revolver, where running is usually the best option.
You have to weigh up risk and reward, since you can only save at key locations. It's nailbiting when you're driven to sneak through an occupied village because you're desparate for something to eat, hoping you don't get caught. Although, when you do get caught, it's a rush. You're faster than the standard, common hunters, so you'll be able to shake them if you put enough forest between the two of you.
Overall, I had a lot of fun with "Sir, You Are Being Hunted", a really fun experience, and a great sense of achievement when I made it out of the hunt alive. I'd recommend it to anyone looking for something different.

Do you remember those early moments playing games like S.T.A.L.K.E.R. where the game had just started, and you were travelling along in a desolate ruin of a place feeling tremendously under-armed and vulnerable?
If you loved that feeling of tension and vulnerability, this is the game for you.
In Sir, You Are Being Hunted, well, you get what it says on the tin. You are being hunted. Constantly. At first, if you're cautious, avoiding the patrols of dapper british robots trundling around looking for you in the wake of some robo-pocalypse feels pretty easy.
But the more of the key pieces you gather to get to safety, and the longer you survive, the more dogged and determined the robots get.
Weapons are few in this game. Ammunition scarce. Weapons (on both sides!) are devastatingly powerful. Nothing feels like a peashooter in this game, especially on your meatbag fleshy body. Running and hiding is ALWAYS preferable to combat, not least of all because the sound of gunfire and violence will bring in robots from the surrounding countryside.
This game isn't very fast-paced, but it is tense, and great at punishing you for being too careless. (It will also punish you for being too cowardly, as you've got to keep scrounging and wandering to find/hunt food.)
This isn't a game you'd call a power-fantasy. It's more like a vulnerability-fantasy.

However it has some serious balance issues(ie. submarine vs missile ship) while lack in some fundamental UI structure that any RTS should have, for example when selecting units the game selects everything including engineers and even all buildings, also there's no indication on what types and how many units are selected neither.
For a game with such scale, there's no user-friendly unit marker visible on screen when zoom out to show what kind of unit is there, so I have to either select them all or zoom in again to see what is there, combine with the lack of selection indication, it really creates frustration during my brief playtime.
There's no build queue for factories when fund is low, so I have to go back to factories(I know there are shortcuts, but hey, just trying to make a point:) ) and click to build again whenever I have enough funds to pump out more units. This might be nitpicky to others, but we are talking about TA/SPC/PA level of combat scale with hundreds of units being pumped out every minute, a queue system can greatly improve the combat flow and ease up the micro-managing part so players can focus more on the combat side and greatness of this game.
Lastly the localization, it's good to have more languages for broader appeals, it's extremely business hurting to have languages translated poorly using google or some sort. I can't speak for other languages, but Chinese in game is full of BS and not much of it make any sense.
Unfortunately despite how much I enjoyed this game I need to request a refund due to the reasons above, but I will thumb the game up in the review as it really achieved many that many other games failed to delivered. I'll keep eyes on this game and hope for its success in the near future and buy it back again.

Evolve is a pretty good time killer.
The concept behind the game is pretty good, and no doubt that it will suck you in at first glance. It's got great art, engaging competetive gameplay and a real emphasis on teamwork.
That is, if you choose to look at the bright side most often like me.
But to give it fair criticisim, it's got no engaging storyline whatsoever. It places tidbits of "lore" in between conversations that Hunters have during the fight or before they jump off the plane. It didn't even make sense to have casual conversation whilst jumping and skydiving. The gameplay is great for a few days, but it WILL get boring fast if you don't have a lot of motivation to play. It's designed for multiplayer, and even then it can get boring.
A good monster will almost always slaughter a team of decent hunters. Why? Like I've read on a different review, "80% is fiding the monster, and 20% is the actual fight." Any good monster player can easily outwit and evade the hunters easily enough to reach stage 3. And more often than not, the hunters fighting this stage 3 happen to be newbies or incompetent enough to match the monster. Why? Everyone loves playing as the monster more than the hunters because its assured you will win as long as you don't do anything stupid. But the Hunters? They have to watch their asses and play smart. And even if they do, there's no guarantee they will win. Especially on a planet where everything can help the Monster.
I don't see the bugs like the other players, so I can't criticize for those technical faults. But if there are bugs, then they should be ironed out as soon as possible. And it's always best, as we all know, to release a game AFTER making sure there are no bugs. The only bugs people are allowed to leave in a game is one that can act as an easter egg or something to attract more people. Urban myth spikers that make the people on Creepypasta ♥♥♥♥ their pants, y'know?
The Hunters are too weak. Too squishy. Sure, they're human. And yes, there are 4 of them. But I've played enough times as a Monster to know that once one Hunter is down, the rest of the team CAN'T WIN. That's it. Evolve crew, I know this may be what you intended to happen. But if you can, please make the odds a BIT more favorable for the Hunters. The point of player skill is to fight on equal ground. But where is the equal ground when four humans that can't get out of a Sneak Attack have to do battle against a planet full of these monsters that can't die unless you kill them early or fill every single spot of their skin with five magazines' worth of bullets?
Now, to those DLCs? I understand that the crew is trying to cash in as much as possible on a decent game. But when I saw that there were skins PER HUNTER, I just started laughing. There's a difference between offering something a player might want and blatantly doing something transparent enought to see through the plastic. Hey, I don't mind skins. I mean, look at Savage Goliath. I don't have that skin, but it looks like something I want. But when you have to shell out so much extra that it will cost more than another game that might entertain you more, it gets sad. Besides, they can't even be called Skins. Those are frikkin palette changes. The Hunters could looks SO nice with alternate CLOTHING, not just a change in color. Please, devs?
There are so much Hunters to play as, each with their own loadout. Now, someone please give these Hunters a nice backstory. Come on, there's so much legroom for origin stories and the devs are wasting it. Is it planned? I sure hope so.
To be fair, the game is pretty enjoyable. I've spent fifty hours already, and it's a good time killer. I dislike playing online, mostly because my internet is slow plus the fact that I've hardly met competent hunters. I don't need good graphics to enjoy a good game. The art is incredible, the characters look really awesome, and the gameplay is good for friends. But to be fair, it's not worth too much money at the state it's in now. I bought the Monster Race pack, and I could've just torrented Pokemon Mystery Dungeon and be happy with that.
In short, Evolve. Good game to kill time over, but don't buy the extra unless you really want to. I mean, no one's stopping you.

Dreamscape (DSC) is quite a unique and refreshing game. You are lost in dreams and need to escape (and rescue your boyfriend in the process). But the path is far from linear - in order to progress in one dream you often need to do or get something in another one. This makes the different dreams "linked", and since each of them feel very distinct, the frequent "jumping" helps feel the game various and enjoyable. Plus, there are also dreams in dreams...
So basically, on lower difficulties, DSC is a bit like a puzzle / adventure game. The battles (turn-based, btw) are relatively easy. Exploring the dreams and solving the puzzles is your main goal. And if you should run out of health / spells you just can teleport to the beginning and touch a healing crystal.
If you are a dedicated player, DSC offers much more, though. For completing the game you get a reward - bonus characters, resistance to poison, ... - it depends on the mode you played in.
But, if you complete it without touching the healing crystal, you get better reward. And there's a catch, the game only offers a limited amount of resources. Enemies don't respawn, which means your experience earned (translating into levels) is limited. You earn money by picking coins on the maps, and these are limited, too. And on top of that, the consumables cannot be stored in inventory and are consumed just as you touch them. Plus, you heal a tiny amount after each won battle.
So, on harder difficulties the game becomes very tactical and challenging. Since the enemies are progressively harder and harder as you venture further into the dreams, you need to balance very carefully how to play. Some battles can be too "costly" in terms of healing required, some easier ones can be left behind and used for "healing" later and so on.
The "True Nightmare" (playing on the Nightmare difficulty "from the scratch" (i.e. no bonuses) and without touching the crystal truly deserves its name. I even dare to say it was the hardest game I have ever played.
The other aspects of DSC will be no surprise for those familiar with Aldorlea games - funny characters and dialogues, unexpected plot twists and many secrets. And the music feels really dreamy. Together with the replayability and the great variety of dreams (deserts, cities, some are funny, other ones scary or more adventurous ...), DSC is one of my favorites.

As an RTS (and I've played 90% of them) It's probably one of the most shallow base building games I've come across. Once you get down an extractor or 2 to give you an initial jump start, you can hammer out money fabricators to your hearts content without any penalty other than a high initial cost outlay. There's no power requirements to any building, because there is no power or resource management whatsoever.. so long as you can churn out enough cash generation, it's just a matter of hammering out as many units as you can.
Cost is the main issue you have to manage and that's it. So long as you can protect, upgrade and go nuts building your fabricators, you're laughing all the way to victory. As I mentioned it's just about making sure you can afford high cost, higher tier units up-front. In my eyes this is one of the game's biggest flaws.
Another flaw is map design.. other than water ways to go around, maps are extremely featureless. There are no rocks, trees, hills etc... everything is flat with different colours. There are a few maps here and there with additional terrain height. But there's not nearly enough, and their design is still woefully basic.
The tech tree is a very limited as well. you build the prerequisite factory, and if you want more powerful units, you click the structure then press "Upgrade" for a small fee, after a short time period you have access to all tier 2 units. If you want experimental, you build the factory for that. You don't need higher tier builders to build higher tier buildings. The basic builder will also build your superweapon.. It once again falls down to high cash requirements.
The only real choice really you get in upgrading are the turrets. Levelling those up allows you to choose a turret type.
That said I don't wish to take away from the game any more than that. As an RTS, the combat is incredibly solid, and the usual Rock Paper Scissors mechanics are on point with any other RTS on the market. As you would expect from AAA when it comes to Air , Land, Sea warfare, you'll get the combination layers required to make the breakthroughs you need.
As a single player game, there's plenty of content here. But milage will vary on that because of the shallowness of the building mechanics. To get the most out of the game with the AI, you do have to crank it up to higher difficulties, this will make the game interesting enough to give it legs as the AI will be smarter than your typical RTS. It'll still do it's cheaty thing by having additional bonuses. But it does have elements of actual intelligence here and there, that when you see them, you'll be quite surprised at it.. It doesn't just build to a certain quota of units and then chuck them at you, This is actually a big pro.
The game does shine in the Multiplayer though as the shallow mechanics make more sense here. Facing off against human opposition is as good as any other game. It's your usual yet very solid arms race in creating the best Military Industrial Complex. I would say that if you want this game, this is what you play it for, with fighting higher difficulty AI 2nd...
You get what you pay for really. So you can't expect much at this price point. Might I address this this site first:
This is where I got my info from.
Bought this game to play with one of my friends.
This review is entirely based on the multiplayer perspective. It is intended for people who are looking at this to play with friends or randoms. This review does not in any way take into regard the single player experience.
What I find are the pros:
*Art is simple yet recognisable. You can identify what is what.
*Minimal Controls. A mouse (with 3 buttons) and 'space' bar.
*Doesn't really hold your hand. It gives basic controls and objectives.
*This game is NOT easy.
*Totally replayable. There is progression for each character as far as I have heard. More characters to unlock as you find and hire them. More turrets and structures to research.
*Resource collection is different. You need to consider what you want to power up (turrets, research for new things, level your character and power to power up rooms so you can use them and mobs wont spawn in them).
*Turrets are not your main defense. Your character(s) are. Turrets allow for various 'help' effects.
What I think are cons:
*Characters are set with skills and stat increases. This doesn't annoy me as much as the rest of the cons that follow.
*Bugs. This game locks up at times, sometimes causing my entire computer to freeze. Sometimes your character will lock up and be unable to do anything.
*Characters act on their own. They will fight if enemies are in same room (auto target, you don't get to choose) and collect resources or open chests all on their own. Your involvement constitues to clicking on a door for them, and clicking on a room to move them between places. You don't get to specify where in the room they will stand so all thoise ranged cowboys are getting meleed (no kiting here). If the character has enough levels they will have an activated ability that you choose when it should happen.
*Online only multiplayer. The site I read said it can be local. Same screen. Not a feature in the game at all. At least, it isn't made obvious if it does exist.
*No private servers. You'll have randoms join your game whether you like it or not. There is a kick feature, but you'll be kicking often if you don't have 4 players for your game.
*Someone gets disconnected? Too bad, nobody can join a game in progress or rejoin should they happen to disconnect - and it will happen due to bugs.
*Node placement system. You have limited placement of turrets and types of sturctures per room. I've not found a way to upgrade turrets .
*Once you pick up your power crystal (which you need to carry to the lift to clear the level), it can't be put down except at the lift room. A character with the crystal will only walk (slowly). This makes playing a solo character impossible (because once it's picked up all rooms go dark and monsters spawn like crazy and come for blood). It makes playing 2 players difficult. Should that player be unable to move due to bug or disconnect... good luck completing the level.
*In multiplayer, each person can only play a single character.
I'll review this once things have been fixed up and the game is playable for longer than a few measely minutes.

I had a review for this before. But that was when it was in early access.
Now this is a review for the game now it has been released.
You should be buying this already. Hell, you should have already bought it.
Here's the deal. Do you like tower defence? Do you like roguelikes? Do you like dungeon crawling strategy type games? If the answer to all three is yes, then I can imagine your trepidation at hearing that this game combines all three, as I was nervous too. I mean there IS such a thing as too much of a good thing, and too many cooks spoil the broth, and sometimes many great things added together do not make an awesome thing...
But in this case you can lay your fears to rest. Dungeon of the Endless is an incredible game, so much fun, brutally difficult and very rewarding. It requires quick thinking, strategic planning, and a buttload of blind stupid balls-to-the-walls courage at times.
The BAD parts of this game is that the view is very zoomed in, and there are only two states to the view. Zoomed right the hell in, or zoomed right the hell out so it looks like a map screen. This DOES make things slightly awkward, especially if you have split your party to explore a particularly large dungeon, or if an attack comes from various areas of the map.
Secondly it's unforgivingly hard, even on "Too Easy" mode. The game lies. Too Easy is still brutally hard. You will lose party members. You will get two floors with a new team member unscathed, only to have them die suddenly and unexpectedly during the rush to get the crystal to the next floor before you can unlock him or her fully.
Thirdly the pixelly graphics may not appeal to some. To me, personally, they are amazing, I love them. They've got a lot of charm, BUT I recognise that it isn't always everyone's thing. It CAN also make combat extremely confusing. Granted you don't have to directly target any enemies, but it's still difficult to watch lots of things at once.
Finally the control system takes a little getting used to. It's simple enough to navitage everything via right clicks and left clicks and such but getting used to the UI and how it does equipping and everything is .... well it feels slightly counter-intuitive. An ability to click-drag items about would have been nice for example, and a quicker way to open/close inventory/stat panels too...
Now for the good stuff:
Music? Really nice. Not too epic, sadly, but not annoying at all, or obnoxiously loud and grating, nor does it overwhelm you. The devs know when to use what music and it's very apparent that in that aspect their sound design is definately on the ball.
Gameplay mechanics? rock solid. Resource management and building, turret defence/augmentation placement, power management and placement, the Risk/reward nature of opening just one door or many doors for the added XP/loot multiplier at the risk of being overrun by swarms of enemies, the various different types of enemies and their priority targets, the sheer volume of characters and skills and strengths... The pure joy of opening a door and finding a merchant or item box and being able to equip something awesome is amazing. Finding cool little things like Steles or Research Artefacts is also great fun.
Also this game has an amazing, rather dark sense of humour. Characters make quips as they traverse between levels and as they open certain doors, they talk to each other, they crack jokes... The item/skill/module descriptions as well are ALWAYS worth reading too for a good chuckle.
As for a game that's come through Early Access? Incredible results. It's come out so polished and refined, and so full of meat and bones that it's become an even greater game for all the feedback the fans gave it. This is well worth your money and absolutely a lot of fun.
Just be sure to prepare yourself for inevitable demise.

Evolve is a pretty good time killer.
The concept behind the game is pretty good, and no doubt that it will suck you in at first glance. It's got great art, engaging competetive gameplay and a real emphasis on teamwork.
That is, if you choose to look at the bright side most often like me.
But to give it fair criticisim, it's got no engaging storyline whatsoever. It places tidbits of "lore" in between conversations that Hunters have during the fight or before they jump off the plane. It didn't even make sense to have casual conversation whilst jumping and skydiving. The gameplay is great for a few days, but it WILL get boring fast if you don't have a lot of motivation to play. It's designed for multiplayer, and even then it can get boring.
A good monster will almost always slaughter a team of decent hunters. Why? Like I've read on a different review, "80% is fiding the monster, and 20% is the actual fight." Any good monster player can easily outwit and evade the hunters easily enough to reach stage 3. And more often than not, the hunters fighting this stage 3 happen to be newbies or incompetent enough to match the monster. Why? Everyone loves playing as the monster more than the hunters because its assured you will win as long as you don't do anything stupid. But the Hunters? They have to watch their asses and play smart. And even if they do, there's no guarantee they will win. Especially on a planet where everything can help the Monster.
I don't see the bugs like the other players, so I can't criticize for those technical faults. But if there are bugs, then they should be ironed out as soon as possible. And it's always best, as we all know, to release a game AFTER making sure there are no bugs. The only bugs people are allowed to leave in a game is one that can act as an easter egg or something to attract more people. Urban myth spikers that make the people on Creepypasta ♥♥♥♥ their pants, y'know?
The Hunters are too weak. Too squishy. Sure, they're human. And yes, there are 4 of them. But I've played enough times as a Monster to know that once one Hunter is down, the rest of the team CAN'T WIN. That's it. Evolve crew, I know this may be what you intended to happen. But if you can, please make the odds a BIT more favorable for the Hunters. The point of player skill is to fight on equal ground. But where is the equal ground when four humans that can't get out of a Sneak Attack have to do battle against a planet full of these monsters that can't die unless you kill them early or fill every single spot of their skin with five magazines' worth of bullets?
Now, to those DLCs? I understand that the crew is trying to cash in as much as possible on a decent game. But when I saw that there were skins PER HUNTER, I just started laughing. There's a difference between offering something a player might want and blatantly doing something transparent enought to see through the plastic. Hey, I don't mind skins. I mean, look at Savage Goliath. I don't have that skin, but it looks like something I want. But when you have to shell out so much extra that it will cost more than another game that might entertain you more, it gets sad. Besides, they can't even be called Skins. Those are frikkin palette changes. The Hunters could looks SO nice with alternate CLOTHING, not just a change in color. Please, devs?
There are so much Hunters to play as, each with their own loadout. Now, someone please give these Hunters a nice backstory. Come on, there's so much legroom for origin stories and the devs are wasting it. Is it planned? I sure hope so.
To be fair, the game is pretty enjoyable. I've spent fifty hours already, and it's a good time killer. I dislike playing online, mostly because my internet is slow plus the fact that I've hardly met competent hunters. I don't need good graphics to enjoy a good game. The art is incredible, the characters look really awesome, and the gameplay is good for friends. But to be fair, it's not worth too much money at the state it's in now. I bought the Monster Race pack, and I could've just torrented Pokemon Mystery Dungeon and be happy with that.
In short, Evolve. Good game to kill time over, but don't buy the extra unless you really want to. I mean, no one's stopping you.

In Sum: Playable but not great hidden object game with some glaring flaws. Do not buy at full price.  3/5
This is another grudgingly recommended game, which I would have preferred a neutral rating on.  This is not a horrible game, and I have suffered a share of stinkers on Steam.  It is just a hidden object game, not much more or less than that, and I suspect a lot of the objection here is due to the casual nature of the game.  However even as a genre, within hidden object games, there is something to be desired.
The concept is seemingly inspired by Dracula and early vampire movies that novel inspired, but with a twist that comes off somewhat amusing but not pulled off as well as, say, a similar theme in Magicka.  Unlike most hidden object games, you actually get to play a character and move around some parts of the game.  The visuals are actually decent for the non-searching parts of the game, and the voice acting is not bad.  It feels like it would have been a well-received, even high quality game in 1998.  I am not saying that the graphics are that ancient, just that I can't help but recall the casual  games of that era.
The game consists of exploring very small areas for hidden objects, talking to NPCs, and solving puzzles.  Through playing, you effectively unlock search quests where you must find a certain number of specified items.  In some areas, there are item lists that must also be found before a quest item is revealed.  Once the quest is completed, a puzzle must be solved.  The puzzles are not complicated in the least.
Some HO games are difficult for various reasons, including devious trickery in design, such as putting similar looking objects, wordplay in clues, shifting images, interactive objects, and so on.  This game uses it's own method of frustrating the player, and it unfortunately is not very satisfying.  The objects are often hidden behind other objects that are not related to the puzzle (like a book or a plate), which must be clicked on to reveal the item underneath.  Makes it hard to search for something that isn't there.  Worst of all, the lighting and visibility of the objects is often terrible, to the point where I found myself clicking the screen randomly...and still succeeding!  Despite screen settings, the images can be so dim that they are practially not there, and I am sure on some monitors, would not show up at all.  And with the secret movable items and the poor display of items, and a lack of consequence for random clicking, it can become as much of a clicking game as Cookie Clicker...but without managers.
Some seem to say that the objects are hard to find because they are not what people are expecting.  I have played many hidden object games, and as far as the genre goes, this one is actually very good at properly telling you what you are looking for.
There are two major glitches, however.  If you are using Windows 7 or above, you will need to set the game to XP compatibility mode, or it won't even launch.  Sometimes during the game, you will not be able to interact with environments after a cutscene.  Going to the main menu then resuming will fix this.
All together, it is an acceptable HO game, purely casual and good for destressing or a waste of time.  On the easiest mode, there is no pressure and no consequence for wrong, and the soundtrack is not bad at all.  It was worth the 9 cents, but not the $10 full price by any means.
