“Uncertain of his sister’s fate, a boy enters LIMBO” – honestly, this sparse description given on Steam’s Store Page for this wonderfully understated, creepy game is all you need know of the story when you start playing. To say much more of it would be horribly spoiling what is an amazing and wonderful experience, albeit an unsettling one to say the least.
However, I can give gameplay details and extrapolations. The game is totally in black and white, the only different color being that of the boy’s eyes, being slightly brighter than the other visible elements. You scroll mostly to the right on a 2D plane as you wander through the titular space between Heaven and Hell, through forests, factories, villages and other run-down environs.
EVERYTHING will be trying to kill you, from a ravenous spider to the other native inhabitants of this continuous, load-free realm. And the deaths you experience come quick, soon and gory; thank the developers that not much visual detail is rendered. What you hear, though, more than makes up for what you can’t see; they’re not happy sounds, let’s say.
Don’t let this stop you from experiencing an amazing experience that actually reminds me of the classic game Out of This World; in it you also walked/ran on a 2D plane through bleak environments, death came often though cheaply (passwords provided easy access to most points in the game, and here, the checkpoints are plentiful), and the graphics, while sparse in both, feature amazing animation both of the main character and his obstacles.
As I said before, saying much more about this masterpiece would be doing it a disservice; you owe it to yourself to check it out. Five out of five for this.

Outlast is beautiful and well-presented but badly structured.
It's meant to be a spooky horror game but enemies only exist in pre-determined sections and their arrival into the 'arena' where you encounter them is ALWAYS broadcast by a distinctive noise or their ♥♥♥♥ING DIALOGUE. These sections always clearly end with you climbing through a vent or similar and, once you're out, there's no reason to fear the corridors because you'll never be attacked there.
The AI feels unfairly broken and will either totally ignore you or instantly find you in pitch-black rooms and tear you to shreds. In the sections where you're forced to run from the AI, it's easy to get lost in the dark rooms that the NPCs typically inhabit, leading to you dying several times in the same section. The atmosphere is then destroyed as the focus shifts from horror and fear to rehearsing the section's sprint path. If you're anything like me, the lack of a map will also lead to you getting lost a whole bunch.
In summary, the graphics, sound and atmosphere are all great but the gameplay itself gets boring and repetitive quickly and isn't helped by janky and frustrating AI. IMO this game would have been better as a classic resident evil / silent hill title. Worthy of note is that the Whistleblower DLC does a fair amount of back-tracking through sections seen in the core game.
If you've played Amnesia or Alien: Isolation, you'll probably like this. Outlast is worth picking up in a sale if you're already curious but, if not, give it a miss and try Alien: Isolation instead.

This is probably one of the best survival zombie games I have played. It gets many things right: The atmospheric and unsettling music; the feeling of isolation and lonliness in a zombie-infested world; the game mechanics from crafting, to healing yourself, to combat, and the player creation.
The game is quite unforgiving in its difficulty; a single bite is a death sentence, and scratches have a chance to infect too. You must keep your avatar well fed, sheltered, rested, hydrated, and even sane. Weapons are scarce, so must make do with whatever you can find. A lone zombie isn't much of a threat, but they quickly become extreme dangers in groups -- and trust me, even so much as running too much will draw a horde after you.
The only improvements I would say this game needs is the introduction of NPCs when playing by yourself; the game gets boring rather quickly when its only you and zombies in the world.
Overall though, great game.

In short: A superb blend of RPG Rogue-like dungeon-crawling with light tower-defense (which is a mouthful !).
You start by picking two characters (all characters are unique, with broad classes). With the selection out of the way you procede into the game proper. You explore the "dungeon" you find yourself in by opening doors and building. Once a room is cleared of enemies you can then build turrets -to protect your starting point- and other modules (that do a variety of things, including increasing the resources you gain each time you open another door). You also have limited "power", you can power a room to prevent enemy units from spawning and to enable building. You can also find merchants, extra characters, and "relics" -which enable the ability to spend resources on researching better turrets and modules. The game is pausable at any point, and the game moves forward everytime you open a new room. Once you find the exit (or better yet, explore the entire floor) you must pick up a crystal at your starting point and race to the exit, all while your other characters defend from waves of enemies that spawn from each unpowered room. I have not done this game justice in this short review, but it is definately a must-play with enormous depth and replayability.
The music is excellent, as is the art-style.

Alright, first off you don't play this game with an assault rifle or a shotgun. You take your magnet gun, sticky bomb launcher, missile launcher and portable black hole creator. Why? Because you can pretty much wreck everything.
The magnet gun works like this, you pick an object and shoot the magnet at it. After that you pick another object and attach another magnet, which sends object one flying towards object two. You can drop a ton of rubble on an enemy for instance, send him flying into a ravine or make him collide with one of his friends.
You also have a nice wristband with special powers, it can repair pretty much anything you've blown up, create anti gravity fields, create force fields and more.
The story is not worth noting, the characters aren't either and the dialogue is just alright. At around 50% the game picks up some slack. However you spend 90% of the relatively short campaign (6-7 hours) in underground caves and tunnels. This is not exciting at all, in fact if they had not used different colored lighting it would all look exactly the same. You get to go on the surface a couple of times but before you know it you are stuck underground again.
There are just a few different enemy types, most of them jump from wall to wall or vanish and appear again. You wait for them to sit still and then splatter their insides around the cave. Kind of like chasing a mosquito around your room that's keeping you up at night, you wait for it to sit still and -splat-. Your enemies are nothing more than just a pest.
They put some of the coolest weapons on vehicles that you only get to use once in the game, should've made some portable versions of them.
This game just screams for some more creative weapons, and by creative I don't mean a unicorn that shoots rainbow rays from it's behind. Yes they actually put that in the game after you've finished it. I'm talking weapons á la Ratchet and Clank or Resistance.
If you can get this game for approx. 20 cents I'd say do it.

Short, decent hidden object game with a delightfully silly story. Some minor bugs and annoying mechanics are out-weighed by the exceedingly low price and the genuinely fun story and dialogue. If you enjoy the genre and you enjoy a good B-movie story, you should have a reasonably good time for a low price.
You play as John, a generic American guy looking for his missing bride who apparently got kidnapped by her vampire father. You chase her to the titular Sinister City, the haven of all that is unholy. If that sounds rather silly, don’t worry, that’s the point. Not at any point are you supposed to be taking the game’s story seriously. That, combined with competent voice actors and well-written silly dialogue, provided a good amount of fun for me. Luckily the game does not last long enough (I finished it on advanced mode with all achievements in apparently 2.6 hours according to steam) or use the silliness too ham-fistedly for it to grow stale. I especially liked how they incorporated the silly story with the already silly “go find X items” or “go fix my Z” missions that are the staple of hidden object games. It made it amusing instead of just silly.
The mechanics of the game were not the best admittedly. The hidden objects and mini-games were decidedly average for the genre coupled with an annoying tendency to have items hidden by other items with no indication that you can interact with the covering item. For example you are in a bookshop looking for item X. Item X is hidden behind a book… you need to click the right book to show it, but your cursor will not change as you hover over it. So basically you need to click all the books in the scene to show it. Sometimes it is more obvious which item is the covering one, but quite frequently you need to click a huge number of random items to find the right one. Which is not great design. However, there are no penalties for misclicks and there is a robust hint-system so when you get used to it, it’s not a huge deal (using the hint-system will costs you an achievement though if you care about that).
Though old areas remain open as you open new ones, the items you need to find is always in the new areas or the game makes it obvious that you need to return to an old area (like, a character tells you to go back to the castle) so there is no annoying backtracking.
People have reported a lot of bugs it seems. I only ran into one in one area and it was partially fixed by exiting to the main menu and totally fixed by restarting the game.
Overall, I had a good time with Sinister City. I enjoyed the silly dialogue and story. The mechanics were nothing exciting, but I quite enjoy the genre so that was fine. For the price (I got it for 0.99 euro) I would definitely say it is worth it.

Are there some nitpicks?  Are some bosses rather tough while others are suprisingly easy?  Did I not like the run and gun as much as the boss battles?  Sure, but who cares?  This game is amazing all around.
Get Cuphead, play it, and be happy.

I love this game. It was challenging, beautiful, and rather fun to play. Still, it hurts me that I have to mark this as a not recommend because it has some serious design flaws and is still in need of a decent amount of polish.
From a visual and audio perspective, this is a masterpiece. The inspiration it takes and the delivery of the design is top notch. Beautiful characters and animations.
The part that breaks the game is a fair number of glitches kept in the game to keep it overly challenging to the point that the game thinks you're doing too well and then uses a glitch to say "Oh you're dead! Git gud!"
Sure, plenty of trolls will tell you to git gud, and if you're willing to be patient enough the game is still beatable despite this, and overcoming some of the cheaper areas of the game gives you satisfaction for overcoming these flaws, but the frustration is simply not worth it. Being frustrated because of your own lack of skill is one thing, but to lose over and over because of a broken game just has no appeal.
Probably the best example of this in the game is a battle you will face against a ghost who possesses a train. In the first phase of the battle, several bullets are thrown at you that you can shoot at and hopefully destroy before they hit you. However, these bullets have two problems. The first being that they have no set amount of hits to destroy them. Sometimes four hits will do it, and sometimes it might take as many as eight. If it happens to be the latter, then it's possible that the bullet has reached you and hit you for damage already, which is a huge disadvantage in the first seconds of a long battle. I found myself restarting bosses far more than being killed by said bosses simply because of the unlikelihood I could take on an entire battle with 2 hp (as well as my desire to achieve the higher grades in battles, which of course requires full health).
Now, that alone isn't worth the flak I'm giving the game, of course. But the problems in this part alone get even worse. There was a particular glitch that would randomly take a bullet that you destroyed, and immediately respawn it just above your character so that it turns into an unblockable attack. There is just simply no defense against this, and no particular reason it happens, but it does. If the goal of a battle is to dodge the bullets, that's fine. That's a challenge. But if there is a system set in place to destroy the weapons coming at you, but it requires you to literally roll the dice and hope it means that the game doesn't decide to hit you regardless of your actions? Well, that's pretty broken.
But, I mean... Git gud, right? Sure. Don't listen to internet trolls. There's hundreds upon thousands of games out there that are beautiful and not broken, and ultimately it's your money. If you want to throw down twenty bucks for an unfair amount of frustration and that makes you happy, then cool, this game is perfect. But if you want challenging, there's better options. Don't pay for a pretty package. Demand decent structure and polish to your games.

The game is beautiful. The art and animation are clever, and a perfect imitation of that done in the 1930's. The music is top-notch as well. The artistic accomplishments of Cuphead are beyond reproach.
The game is hard, in the style of early Nintendo Entertainment System games, or the arcade quarter-plunkers that came slightly prior. This isn't a reflex game, it's a pattern-learning game. There are a handful of run-n-gun levels, but the bulk is boss fights, and the vast majority of the play is learning those bosses, recognizing their telegraphs, and then avoiding their attacks over time.
The thing is, while I found the game to be a challenge, and I played it through for the sake of completing that challenge, I did not actually find Cuphead fun. I enjoyed seeing each boss, and marveling over their design and animation. But the process of actually fighting and beating them was frustrating, punishing, and often...boring. There's no fanfare, no interesting context. The story of Cuphead is totally bare-bones, the characters simply there, a parade of things that are more interesting to look at than to interact with.
Cuphead is an achievement, no argument there. In the end I do recommend it. It's probably going to be many people's and gaming publications' game of the year, and deservedly so. But is it an enjoyable game? To look at, yes. To play, in my opinion, no.

A fun cross platform RTS inspired by old classics like Total Annihilation.
TL;DR: Captures the old school feel really well, excels in multiplayer team battles.
The game itself is fairly simple: there's one resource type, which you typically mine at the start of the game, and then build more expensive buildings in later game to produce it. There's a single "race" but you have a fairly varied selection of units (air/sea/land units plus upgrades for each type, experimental mega-units that excel in different aspects, plus of course, nukes). The varied selection of units I feel brings some good strategy to the game - e.g. you might build a big land force, but your opponent might see it coming and counters you with air units etc.
While single player works I didn't spend too much time there, and feel the game shines in Multiplayer. You have varied start options (e.g. start with experimental units, or start with just a builder, start with additional resources etc and plenty of maps to choose from.
Playing with teams is great as you can have teammates playing the early game and pumping out cheap units to keep your opponents on the defence while you build up a mega army for the late game (which can be a hell of a lot of fun :)).
In terms of updates: I played this on android a long while ago and it seems to have come a long way, with more units, more maps, more start options etc. It's early days but looking at the developer responses in greenlight and how far the game has come makes me think the updates will keep coming :)
Also note for linux gamers: game functions perfectly for me on ArchLinux (using steam with runtime).
Disclaimer: I received the game for free, before steam release and did some beta testing for the dev.

Hello there I have played 22.1 hrs as of when I am reviewing this product and currently only have Cabot, a support class hunter left to unlock and I feel that I have played enough of this game to give it a review.Here are my thoughts so far.
Description
Evolve is NOT meant to be played on a low-budget computer as it is a triple-a title and will probably be unable to run smoothly enough for you to get some enjoyment out of the game so please ensure your operating system can run this game before purchasing it.
Evolve is a pretty fun team-orientated 4 v giant♥♥♥♥♥monster game where there are currently a variety of different game modes to name a few we have the classic hunt,defense,rescue and nest.Evolve also includes a "campaign" mode called evacuation which lasts 5 missions which  will vary in map and mode and will also provide bonuses to whomever won the previous mission and provide a buff or de-buff depending on the map.
The hunters comprise of 4 different classes,the medic,assualt,support and trapper.The medic is charged with keeping the team healthy and providing certain buffs for the team (speed or creating weakpoints in the monster's armor).The assualt is the main damage dealer of the group and has a personal shield that he can use to become invunerable for brief moments to essentially act as a tank and become a big-fat,annoying little fly that will pester the monster with his large amount of damage.The support has alot of utility and can buff the team.The trapper as you can guess is in charge of forcing fights with the monster and slowing it down.Last but not least,everyone's favourite,the monster.The monster can feed on the local wildlife to gain armor and evolve upgrading and gaining abilities.
The goal of the hunters is to fufill their mission objective depending on the mode or kill the monster.The monster's goal is the utter destruction of everything and the death of those who dare hunt it.
Thoughts so far
Right now everything is kind of balanced at the moment with each character or monster having its own pros and cons and having a certain playstyle to it.Luck is usually not a big factor in the game but can affect the outcome.The outcome is usually dependent on the player's skill and their ability to evolve depending on the situation(har har) as well as how the hunters are able to operate together as a team.
Being a game where teamwork is vital for the hunters,there is obviously going to be some negative experience from try-hards and the like.However, this also means that if you can get friends to join you,you will be able to get a better experience(and probably more wins as the hunters) when you play together.NOTE:YOU CANNOT SET THE MONSTER AS A PREFFERED ROLE WHEN MATCHMAKING IN A PARTY.
The game is extremely fun to play and the dlc isn't really something you should care about as you can get skins from just ranking up your character.Evolve is also brings a new change in the 4 player co-op genre as it is slightly different in terms of what you have to do for victory to ensue.However, if you play the same game mode it can get slightly repetitive and boring(WHICH IS WHY THERE'S DIFFERENT MODES) so if you want to just play one mode in this game and focus on play only a few characters,YOU WILL BE BORED SOON and I reccomend that you wait for this to go on offer before buying it.

Evolve is a solid game if you like the idea of chasing down a huge♥♥♥♥♥monster with three others...or being the monster yourself and wrecking the hunters.
Positives :
The environments look amazing and play an integral part of fighting.  Various wildlife (even plants) can kill lone hunters, some wildlife even pose a threat to unarmored or weak monsters.   The hunters and monster alike can use the topography to lay an ambush, put up snares, mines, etc.  Unique wildlife called albinos hold various buffs for monsters and hunters alike.  It's often worthwile to kill the creatures that benefit your nemisis before they can find it.
Currently there are twelve hunters split evenly in to four classes (medic, support, assault, trapper) and three monsters (goliath, kracken, wraith).  Each new monster and hunter must be unlocked through play but are quite easy to get.  Each hunter and monster has his or her own strengths and weaknesses.  There are only a few hunters, in my opinion, that are less than stellar but fun to play none the less.  A balance patch is coming out "soon" to address some issues.
The game has a few different match modes.  Hunt is the traditional four hunters versus a monster.  Rescue mode challenges hunters to help NPCs receover from near death and lead them to a safe spot.  The monster's goal is to eat the NPCs.  Nest mode is almost the opposite of Rescue.  The hunters are charged with killing monster eggs and any minions the monster has.  The monster must kill the hunters and can hatch a minion out out an egg for help.  In Defend mode, the goal for the hunters is merely to survive or kill the monster.  Monsters have a much more difficult time as they must destroy defensive base turrets and generators to win.  They do get some help from NPC monster minions, though.
One last positive note, I read on the Turtlerock forums that all future maps are free so no one gets segregated by those that buy DLC and those that don't.
Negatives :
Evolve suffered a lot of negative press from it's DLC bundles.  The majority of the DLC happens to be monster skins and hunter skins.  Unfortunately for the hunters, only their weapons get skins.  The pricing for the next four hunters is around $25 USD.  That's nearly 40% of what it cost to get the 12 original hunters and 3 original monsters.
Possibley the biggest negative concerns the Wraith monster.  This is the only monster that currently causes many hunters to foam at the month when it is in play.  As a hunter expect to spend most of a match chasing after this monster while it sends it decoy at you time and time again to kill you while it runs away.  Repeat until the Wraith is finally at stage three and ready to battle.   It's not an overpowered monster, but it certainly drains the fun of the game to chase decoys around.
The game give you the chance to rank which class you want to play from first choice to last.  It tries to give you your number one choice (and in Co-op mulitplayer is farily good at this) but can frustrate some players.  Premade teams of 2-4 make it difficult for random players to get anything other than monster.  Grouping with a friend also means you can't play as a monster unless you make a Custom game.
TLDR :  This is a fun game with an amazing environment.  Most of the negativity on this game is about the DLC pricing for the next wave of hunters and new monster.   Another major complaint is the Wraith monster's use of decoy spam.  If chasing down a huge♥♥♥♥♥monster sounds like fun, you will enjoy Evolve.  If eating puny humans sounds like fun, you'll enjoy Evolve.  A balance patch is scheduled "soon".

Here's a thing that annoyed me: You're often collecting some number of objects (bulbs, coins, etc) that appear in hidden-object scenes. These are sometimes hidden behind things in the scene, which you have to click on to move & reveal what you're looking for. But these concealing objects won't move out of the way if you click on them before you've gotten the collection task for the object they're in front of, which seems to me like cheating, in a way.
And since there is no apparent penalty for mis-clicks, and no clue that something is moveable in this way, the best strategy is often to just spam the screen with clicks everywhere, in case something comes into view.
The hit zones for hidden objects are also remarkably large, so you just have to click sorta kinda *near* what you're looking for. Several times, I was able to pick up multiple things by clicking repeatedly in exactly the same place.
Aspect ratio is messed up - it's obviously a 4:3 screen stretched to 16:9, in both full-screen and windowed mode. Text size & placement was also messed up on my 3840x2160 screen, and doesn't reset properly when switching from windowed to full-screen without closing & reopening. All-in-all, not one I can recommend.

Ne'er has a Survivial Game been so lonely, frightening, beautiful and compelling as 'The Long Dark'.
Yes, this is still in early access, and the much touted Story Mode has not yet come to pass, but the Sandbox levels that are here so far are challenging and breathtaking all in one.
You will not survive long in this game, and without any real tutorial you will scrape and scarper every last twig and thred you can find in an effort to keep yourself warm; never has finding a can of beans been so exciting, both in-game and in-life.
Graphics (cel-shaded but in their own way endearing) and sound/music work with the gameplay to bring a true sense of solitary isolation to this incredibly compelling game.
There is stuff to work upon sure. The fact that in the Sandbox you can never truly win, simply survive for as many days as you can, may be off-putting to completionists and those seeking an ultimate pay-off, but if you like the look of 'The Long Dark' and think it's something you'll love sinking some hours into, chances are you'd be right.

It isn't ideal, but it is by all means acceptable.
What Bioshock is, primarily, is an experience.  The story is linear and almost non-existant.  The gameplay is shallow, punishing, and not well thought out.  But you aren't playing for those things.  You are playing for a chance to experience such a cool world.
Far from a tepid recommendation, I would say absolutely play this if you don't mind dealing with the oppressive first person shooter aspect.

Simply, Outlast.
EDIT: I have now finished the game.
I have to say the strongest quality this game has is the gameplay. It's extremely fluid, works well as both an action/stealth game. The graphics and controls are by far the strengths here. It kept me coming back for more because it was easy enough to play, as someone who sucks at survival/stealth.
No you can't fight back in Outlast, but you can feel yourself gaining power over these mutants throughout the game. I felt more and more comfortable as time went on. You learn the detection ranges, speeds, dark areas, etc.
By the end, I was able to manipulate many of them to do and go where I wanted them to. It became much more cat & mouse than running away screaming for your life.
Once the uneasiness and fear tactics wear off, this game is surprisingly pleasant to play through.
I'm not a fan of jump scares, but I love horror and atmospheric terror. This game has the perfect mixture of both. Playing through the camera breeds a lot of the terror, as it resembles the found-footage appearance in modern day horror flicks.
I quit a few times but kept coming back and wanting to know more about the story. There are 2 closing scenes that really put the icing on the cake for this game. If not for those two moments, I would have felt negatively about the game overall I believe.
I'd highly recommend for those looking for scares, stealth, and decent horror story. I wouldn't recommend for those who enjoy shooting/fighting, as you're left entirely to survival skills here. Overall, great horror experience.

At this point, I can't do anything but recommend.

I really want to like this game. I really do. Like most people, I was introduced to its inspiration- Kirby's Dream Course- through the Game Grumps lets play and ever since I first saw their lets play back in 2015, I've been hoping someone would do exactly this: make a modern, spiritual succesor to the game that I could get on Steam. I've been looking forward to this game since it was first announced and was so excited when I heard it had finally been released. And if it had been released in early access, like I thought it would, I might still give it a positive review. At present, though, I cannot recommend it.
This review is going to be VERY critical and nitpick a LOT, but please know that I honestly want this game to get better. Somewhere in there is the seed of a game that's actually really charming, if only it could get a little more polish.
Problems:
-The courses are way too small. In Kirby's Dream Course, the courses are massive, sprawling maps that kirby can strategically bounce all over, and it can easily take multiple bounces to get from one side of the course to the other. In this game, though, a single bounce can send you sailing clear across the course, not even getting the chance for a second bounce. On top of the camera being zoomed in way too close, this makes the game feel very claustrophobic, and not at all like the high flying game that inspired it.
-The controls are sluggish. Everything seems to move way slower that in should, from aiming Bulby to waiting for Bulby to wake up, to the loading screens, its like wading though molasses and not nearly as fast paced and exciting as the original. Also, the controls themselves are not great. Arrow keys and ZXC are acceptable, but you have to use a mouse to navigate the menu screens? It's weird. Also, the lack of controller support is just criminal. Playing this type of game with a mouse and keyboard is just criminal.
-Maybe those loading screens wouldn't be nearly as long if you weren't trying to render needlessly photo-realistic water in the background? I'd rather see a simple image of the ground below, like in Kirby, rather than seeing that real-time rendered photorealistic water which clashes with the game's aesthetics.
-Speaking of the aesthetics, they're overall actually very good, but there are a couple of nitpicks there as well. Bulby looks a bit lifeless and bland. It looks like a cheap knockoff brand Kirby. Which is what it is, of course, but I still think his design needs work. The eyes, in particular, are very flat and dead looking. I'd rather see a simple, dynamic design over "Kirby with pants and a toupee." More to the point, the diamonds which replace the enemies after you've hit them are way too small. The stars in Kirby's Dream Course were much larger, and easier to read.
-There seem to be quite a few missing sound effects in this game? And a lot of the sound effects that are present aren't nearly as punchy as they should be. This is a major, all around problem which contributes to the game feeling very flat and less exciting than the original. Hitting launching Kirby set of a resounding "POW!" to let you know you'd really given him a good whack, which is a far cry from the dull thud you get in this game. Everything from menus to movement to hitting things in this game should sound much more alive.
-Altogether, I guess what I'm getting at is a lack of attention to game feel in the games controls, audio, and visuals. Mechanically it's sound, but it all just falls flat. It feels unfinished. The "level cleared" message just kind of slides up in tiny text with barely any fanfare, there's no spark when you hit the enemies, there's barely any sound effects, there's no velocity to the gameplay, and worst of all, the music.
-Biggest complaint that I have: The music. It's terrible, It seriously is god-awful. The cheap, bland, generic, royalty-free easy listening muzak that just drones on and on was actually the final nail in the coffin that drove me away from this game. I would've been critical either way, but I might have kept playing the game if it wasn't for that horrible, mind numbing music. Please, for god's sake, please hire a composer to make your some original music that fits the game. Or at the very least, get some more appropriate royalty free music. I know for a fact that there's better stuff out there. I know that for a FACT. There's no excuse to use music that sets such a terrible atmosphere.
-It is NOT worth $17.99. Not in its current form, at least. Half of that might be ok, but I can not see how you justify selling the game as it is for almost twice the price of games like Undertale.
If these problems are addressed, I will be happy to repurchase this game. But currently, it's just not worth owning, or playing. I really do want to see this game improve. I really do want to see it succeed. Hopefully the devs actually take these critiques to heart and don't just abandon the game. Please, devs. Make me change my review. I really want this game to be good.

Ah fond memories of this classic.
Besides the fact that this is Star Wars, the thing  like about this game is the Strategic vs Tactical balance.  You want poorly defend a planet on your frontier?  When it gets hit with a larger fleet you have to make do defending it with what you have.  No building a fleet of ships or mining ore in the middle of combat.  But on the same token you can hit the other side at a weak point with overwhelming force or just the right mix of weaker forces to deliver a knockout blow.
Don't get me wrong this game isn't perfect.  Outside the main story campaign the number of maps is somewhat limited.  And the AI for those maps really kinda sucks (they're best meant for multiplayer matches).  And in Forces of Corruption the Zann Consortium seems like it wipes the floor against everyone else with respect to balance.  But you can mod this game almost endlessly. And the replayability is pretty good.  The subtle tie ins with SW: episodes IV-VI is also really nice.
In short, great game that won't disappoint if you love SW, RTS, and don't have crazy expectations.

This is a game that I find a huge amount of joy in recommending. I've never really been into tower defence games, but this game successfully combines elements of tower defence games with roguelite elements. The developers are highly dedicated to this and I've noticed they actually care about the community, something some games don't have. They are constantly working to fix bugs and rebalance, and make sure we know about it. They also know some of the dungeons can go on for a while, and as such, they have a save game system that deletes the save when you reload, so you can't just keep reloading to redo a floor.
First, the story:
You have just crash landed on a dangerous planet and are desperately seeking a way off. Your power source and ultimate source of survival, your ship's crystal, is precious, but is constantly being attacked by the monsters roaming the dungeons. To continue to the next floor, you need to move with the crystal, which one of your surviving heroes must carry, and due to its size and weight, its slow moving.
Second, Defending the Crystal:
You have quite a few choices here, mainly dependant on resources, how far through the dungeon you are, and how many heroes you have, as well as what modules you have at your disposal. With strong heroes and not much Tech, will you set up a few turrets, or set up support modules that buff your heroes defences, attack damage, and heal per monster kill? With enough dust, will you save it for a chance at a shop to upgrade your heroes, or will you use the precious resource to light another room, allowing for more turrets to be set up, and soften monsters up until they reach your heroes, which in the later levels, become your main source of defence as monsters will come from every direction. The monsters spawn in dark rooms randomly every time you open a door, so will you light a dead end, allowing for easy protection of a costly module to increase resources gained per door, or leave it dark, hoping your heroes and defences are strong enough to deal with the threat. Will you use the Food to level up a hero or save it for desperate situations to heal and recruit another hero?
Finally, escaping the floor:
You find the exit, now, do you continue exploring, and hope to find good loot, maybe gather resources and not get overrun or do you run for the exit with the crystal?
Onto the bad:
I've noticed that when large amounts of monsters spawn (at least on my pc) the fps has a tendancy to drop a bit. Beyond that, I've not really noticed bugs or anything annoying, the game itself if very well balanced and difficulty builds up gradually enough that you are strong enough to take on later levels when you reach there, as long as your strategy holds out.
Overall Good:
-Dedicated team of developers constantly working to ensure there's no major bugs and that everything is balanced.
-Varied gameplay per playthrough, as is the tendancy with most roguelites.
-Balanced and surprisingly fun gameplay.
-Save system that some roguelites that have longer gameplay could use.
-Fairly minimalistic graphics so older pc's can run it.
Overall Bad:
-FPS drop when there's a lot of monsters that spawn.
Unsure as of right now:
-Due to this being in Early Access, there's something that hasn't been released that I'm kind of curious about, and that is Multiplayer. The developers say they are working to add it in, and will not judge until I've tried it.

Hello there I have played 22.1 hrs as of when I am reviewing this product and currently only have Cabot, a support class hunter left to unlock and I feel that I have played enough of this game to give it a review.Here are my thoughts so far.
Description
Evolve is NOT meant to be played on a low-budget computer as it is a triple-a title and will probably be unable to run smoothly enough for you to get some enjoyment out of the game so please ensure your operating system can run this game before purchasing it.
Evolve is a pretty fun team-orientated 4 v giant♥♥♥♥♥monster game where there are currently a variety of different game modes to name a few we have the classic hunt,defense,rescue and nest.Evolve also includes a "campaign" mode called evacuation which lasts 5 missions which  will vary in map and mode and will also provide bonuses to whomever won the previous mission and provide a buff or de-buff depending on the map.
The hunters comprise of 4 different classes,the medic,assualt,support and trapper.The medic is charged with keeping the team healthy and providing certain buffs for the team (speed or creating weakpoints in the monster's armor).The assualt is the main damage dealer of the group and has a personal shield that he can use to become invunerable for brief moments to essentially act as a tank and become a big-fat,annoying little fly that will pester the monster with his large amount of damage.The support has alot of utility and can buff the team.The trapper as you can guess is in charge of forcing fights with the monster and slowing it down.Last but not least,everyone's favourite,the monster.The monster can feed on the local wildlife to gain armor and evolve upgrading and gaining abilities.
The goal of the hunters is to fufill their mission objective depending on the mode or kill the monster.The monster's goal is the utter destruction of everything and the death of those who dare hunt it.
Thoughts so far
Right now everything is kind of balanced at the moment with each character or monster having its own pros and cons and having a certain playstyle to it.Luck is usually not a big factor in the game but can affect the outcome.The outcome is usually dependent on the player's skill and their ability to evolve depending on the situation(har har) as well as how the hunters are able to operate together as a team.
Being a game where teamwork is vital for the hunters,there is obviously going to be some negative experience from try-hards and the like.However, this also means that if you can get friends to join you,you will be able to get a better experience(and probably more wins as the hunters) when you play together.NOTE:YOU CANNOT SET THE MONSTER AS A PREFFERED ROLE WHEN MATCHMAKING IN A PARTY.
The game is extremely fun to play and the dlc isn't really something you should care about as you can get skins from just ranking up your character.Evolve is also brings a new change in the 4 player co-op genre as it is slightly different in terms of what you have to do for victory to ensue.However, if you play the same game mode it can get slightly repetitive and boring(WHICH IS WHY THERE'S DIFFERENT MODES) so if you want to just play one mode in this game and focus on play only a few characters,YOU WILL BE BORED SOON and I reccomend that you wait for this to go on offer before buying it.

Evolve is a solid game if you like the idea of chasing down a huge♥♥♥♥♥monster with three others...or being the monster yourself and wrecking the hunters.
Positives :
The environments look amazing and play an integral part of fighting.  Various wildlife (even plants) can kill lone hunters, some wildlife even pose a threat to unarmored or weak monsters.   The hunters and monster alike can use the topography to lay an ambush, put up snares, mines, etc.  Unique wildlife called albinos hold various buffs for monsters and hunters alike.  It's often worthwile to kill the creatures that benefit your nemisis before they can find it.
Currently there are twelve hunters split evenly in to four classes (medic, support, assault, trapper) and three monsters (goliath, kracken, wraith).  Each new monster and hunter must be unlocked through play but are quite easy to get.  Each hunter and monster has his or her own strengths and weaknesses.  There are only a few hunters, in my opinion, that are less than stellar but fun to play none the less.  A balance patch is coming out "soon" to address some issues.
The game has a few different match modes.  Hunt is the traditional four hunters versus a monster.  Rescue mode challenges hunters to help NPCs receover from near death and lead them to a safe spot.  The monster's goal is to eat the NPCs.  Nest mode is almost the opposite of Rescue.  The hunters are charged with killing monster eggs and any minions the monster has.  The monster must kill the hunters and can hatch a minion out out an egg for help.  In Defend mode, the goal for the hunters is merely to survive or kill the monster.  Monsters have a much more difficult time as they must destroy defensive base turrets and generators to win.  They do get some help from NPC monster minions, though.
One last positive note, I read on the Turtlerock forums that all future maps are free so no one gets segregated by those that buy DLC and those that don't.
Negatives :
Evolve suffered a lot of negative press from it's DLC bundles.  The majority of the DLC happens to be monster skins and hunter skins.  Unfortunately for the hunters, only their weapons get skins.  The pricing for the next four hunters is around $25 USD.  That's nearly 40% of what it cost to get the 12 original hunters and 3 original monsters.
Possibley the biggest negative concerns the Wraith monster.  This is the only monster that currently causes many hunters to foam at the month when it is in play.  As a hunter expect to spend most of a match chasing after this monster while it sends it decoy at you time and time again to kill you while it runs away.  Repeat until the Wraith is finally at stage three and ready to battle.   It's not an overpowered monster, but it certainly drains the fun of the game to chase decoys around.
The game give you the chance to rank which class you want to play from first choice to last.  It tries to give you your number one choice (and in Co-op mulitplayer is farily good at this) but can frustrate some players.  Premade teams of 2-4 make it difficult for random players to get anything other than monster.  Grouping with a friend also means you can't play as a monster unless you make a Custom game.
TLDR :  This is a fun game with an amazing environment.  Most of the negativity on this game is about the DLC pricing for the next wave of hunters and new monster.   Another major complaint is the Wraith monster's use of decoy spam.  If chasing down a huge♥♥♥♥♥monster sounds like fun, you will enjoy Evolve.  If eating puny humans sounds like fun, you'll enjoy Evolve.  A balance patch is scheduled "soon".

Celestial Tear: Demon’s Revenge is a fantastic JRPG that’s marred down by technical problems. Built on the RPG Maker engine, the game has so many limitations, hardly any customization, and crashes too often to ignore. If you’re willing to wade through it though, and you should, the game offers an engaging and yet familiar storyline, a nice blend of battle systems and some stellar ideas. I felt like I had discovered a lost gem from the fourth generation, and I enjoyed all of the moments that worked. It’s clear that there’s some real passion behind this project, but the technical know-how may not be as strong as their creative drive. Hopefully they’ll get this all ironed out, and possibly consider a more modern engine and a VO director for their next outing.

Unfortunately, despite really really REALLY wanting to recommend Celestial Tear ep 1, after my ten hours of play I can't do it.
Pros:
+Excellent comic-style line art
+Decent production values - original graphics, sound, music, voice acting
+Mostly original combat system that takes inspiration from Xenogears, Legend of Dragoon, and others
+Loads of not-terrible writing in form of dialogue and journal entries
+Indie JRPG on Steam
+Female protagonist (sorta)
Cons:
(As disclaimer, most cons are related to using the RPG Maker engine)
-Low resolution, no graphics scaler options. This makes the game look very grainy and pixelated, despite the art being technically sound.
-Hiccups. Constant hiccups. The longer I play the game, the more frequent and annoying they get. After several hours, don't be suprised if your screen pauses for nearly an entire second every 4-5 seconds.
-Framerate issues. Only one or two maps are designed to allot for full framerate in the RPG Maker engine.
-Bugs. Despite being delayed for several months, I've encountered sloppy scripting issues, text issues (mostly grammar related), invisible barriers, and items that don't do what they say (Stun, for the record is apparently not a "physical status ailment").
-Characters. Characterization is forced and almost everyone fills a trope. You won't find much originality here, except for the female protagonist.
-Heavy balance issues. You'll encounter enemies that can deal 50 damage to one character and 5 to the other. You'll have battles that will take you forever and consume all your items and you'll be rewarded with 7 XP; or you'll fight a battle which is over in one attack and you'll be rewarded with 30-40. I only found one shop in episode 1, and I was only able to shop there once. This is a moot point since you can only carry 8 items of any one type at a time, and if you find any more they will be immediately discarded (even in chests). The Legend of Dragoon-style pinch-defend-heal is actually the most effective way to heal in the game, so I recommend in every battle you get the opportunity to delay killing the last enemy and defend-heal up to max so you don't waste items and MP. Grinding, too, is near-impossible, since it seems monsters only respawn when it's inconvenient, and not when it would be nice to gain XP.
-Dungeons are way too long. There are several areas in every dungeon which is simply a path populated with monsters. I'm pretty sure the devs of Pier Solar would get tired of the dungeons in this game.
-Puzzles are often not very intuitive and the clunkiness of the controls lead you having to repeat them over and over and over.
In short, if you don't mind the RPG Maker engine and a game that is too big for its britches, you'll enjoy Celestial Tear. The plot is interesting enough and combat is challenging (though not exactly rewarding, and unbalanced), but this isn't going to win any awards, especially when the intro cinematic -- the most impressive part of the game -- won't even play without constant stutter. You can't help but think with this level of dedication, scripting and custom assets, a more sensible engine choice (like Unity) wouldn't make more sense. RPG Maker has already been committed though, and that's the primary shame.

This is quite an impressive game (for RPG Maker) with its visuals, philosophy, and voice acting.  The combat system is similar to Xenogears, with being able to combo light, medium and heavy attacks.  The philosophy derives from ethics and seeing that even treating people as equals can result in hypocrisy, or sometimes prejudices can be justified with good intentions (though of course some may be extreme). I also like that the characters can be different and willing to work with one another despite disagreeing on things (can a tree hugger blame someone who lost his family to demons for wanting revenge?) initially.
Only 2 things I didn't like so far: 1) The beginning of the game is a text heavy drag, with you moving really slowly (keep going down past the wall as it is really an underpass once you touch it).
2) Don't mislead players; I already mentioned the bit with the wall that as you walk down you can see it becomes an overpass (was stuck for a little while). I want an initial choice of 3 characters if 3 are shown at 1 time, not have 4 characters with only 3 visible at once to choose 2 from. I don't know if this is an episode based thing as the game only released episode 1 (which I bought) now, and the other 2 characters can be chosen once the other episodes are released, but that is a bit misleading.
To give a sample of the writing, upon choosing the character (the other 2 you can't choose), there are quotes like, "The world breaks everyone and afterward(s) (typo should be fixed), some are stronger at the broken places,", or, "An eye for an eye and the whole world would be blind."
Overall, be patient with the game if you like to read and I find it definitely worth $5. I would wait before episodes 2 and 3 are completed before buying them all at once; episode 1 was pending release on Steam for the longest and I have no idea if/when those later episodes will be released.

Note: This review is for the final patch prior to the full release of the game. There's currently no Coop mentioned, and I have not tried the ships / gametype variants so I will not mention either.
My GOTY candidate. There's a lot more here than what you see at first glance.
PROS:
- Hero choices make the game varied, and engaging.
- Gear and Builds become interesting and somewhat diverse (more on this later).
- Resource management is straightforward, and easy to grasp. Interesting decision on how you use your resources added in later patches.
- Level of difficulty is very high (this might be a con for some)
- Excellent art style.
CONS:
- RNG can definitely kill your run, hands down.
- Balance was lacking a bit. There were some OP builds which made the game easier, though some of these have been addressed in patches.
- The game expects you to learn its ins and outs via investing time. It's not very easy to pick up.
- Unlocking heroes can be fun, though once you get to the latter heroes to unlock, it feels like a time sink.
Overall:
Bottom line for me personally is that I really enjoy the depth of the game. It took me hours of fiddling around with what's possible, and strategizing and using tactics and a relatively high level of micromanagement to beat the game on its hardest difficulty. Though RNG can make this game a bit more tedious than I'd like, I stil find this a refreshing take on the genre (or mash of genre's in this case).
It's really the gameplay and the extreme level of dedication and understanding of the systems in the game that make this  extremely fullfilling to play. Few experiences have pushed me that close to the edge and I enjoyed every minute of it. There's definitely some downsides, but compared to most triple A releases this game packs a huge punch for the price. It does offer a large amount of replayability in the form of heroes, and playing to their strengths plus adjusting strategy to come up with new playstyles on the fly. You won't win on the first go, and chances are it will take you some time to even clear a few floors. But if you're like me, you'll really enjoy the experience.
Once CoOp is added, I'll be back in to spend some time trying to sync with my friends and beat the game for my 7th time.

In addition to looking gorgeous, this is easily the most fun I've had with any tower-defense related game. DoE combines those genre mechanics with dungeon exploration, resource and party management, as well as wave-based PvE combat to great effect.
Carefully distributing your limited resources is the key to making progress as the waves quickly grow stronger and soon threaten to overwhelm your intrepid troupe, and the stress might be too much to bear if it weren't for the clever decision to have waves be triggered by opening the next door to continue your exploration. This effectively separates each wave into turns, allowing you to clear the stage of enemies then take time to regroup, distribute loot, and reorganize your defenses as needed before you push forward.
Having now played it after it's left Early Access, I can only say that the final touches they've put on the game (largely UI updates to give the game that little extra bit of oomph) make this gem shine all the brighter.
It's easy for me to recommend picking up Dungeon of Endless: it's equal parts interesting, entertaining, and goddamn beautiful.

I am a tester for Celestial Tear: Demon’s Revenge and was provided a copy for testing purposes.
The indie scene for games is constantly growing and evolving especially in the PC game market.  White Guardian Studios is no exception.  Celestial Tear: Demon’s Revenge shows promise to deliver a great experience for gamers to enjoy.  Don’t let the RPG Maker tag scare you.  This game is definitely not your average RPG Maker game.  Custom graphics, music, limited voice acting, and completely overhauled combat just to name a few.
The game is an episodic game taking place over 5 chapters.  This is chapter 1 of the series.
Storylines switch between Sen, a human turned demon trying to find her place, and Jagen, an aristocrat type character seeking revenge and justice.  I found both storylines to be interesting but seemed to favor Sen’s character.  While the developer reveals some things about Sen’s past there are parts that are still a mystery.
Combat revolves around use of attack combos (think Street Fighter to an extent) to deal maximum damage.  The characters build up energy to release powerful attacks that can deal more damage than just spam attacking.  You can also utilize “magic” to an extent.  Here is where I feel the game is really trying to do too much.  Allowing for regular attacks, combo attacks, and different levels of magic tends to feel a bit overwhelming.  The key here was finding out what works best for you as a player.  This took a bit of experimenting for me but found using combos and healing with Jagen worked best for me.
I am a firm believer of supporting indie developers in their work if they show promise to deliver engaging content.  I believe that White Guardian Studios can do just that.

Before I actually discuss the game I'll quickly address this whole dlc argument that seems to be all that people focus on.
In my view there is no problem with the use of day one dlc, as it is all cosmetic, with no in game affecting content available so all this controversy is rather out of proportion as this kind of content is unfortunately very common now a days with game publishes/developers even valve with portal 2. Yes I agree, the monsters and hunters that will be released are overpriced, and the fact that there are going to be two season passes is stupid, but the fact that maps and modes are going to be free , makes this an actually good business model as dlc or not, all players can play together and is something I wish more games did.
First I'll address some of the cons, because like any game there are note worthy issues. Firstly the progression system is flawed, forcing you to redo repetitive tactics which is actually a bad way to complete objectives. Some of the maps also tend to resemble one another with only a couple that really stand out. While the hunters feel adequately stocked with options, the monster side feels like it could do with at least one more character to add variety. When you play as the hunters you are very dependent on your team, so one person being unsupportive, getting killed to easily, and relying too heavily on hand holding ways of finding the monster (like Daisy), can lead to frustrating doomed to failure games. While a few more modes would also improve the experience as the can feel quite similar (with defend being the most varied) and having to play the evacuation 5 part match playlist to access the other is not a great idea in my eyes.
While I have found issues, I still think this game is worth experiencing (at least at a reduced price, or when more maps/modes are released if you are unsure) because in my eyes the positives are well worth it. First off while the maps can feel samey, they are well designed and look fabulous, offering a variety of scenarios and tactics for both hunters and monster to utilize such as natural features and wildlife. The characters themselves all feel distinct and require their own finesse in order to better your odds with the monster all requiring different fighting styles to avoid death, with the hunters feeling equally important and balanced, with their own unique personalities (although their remarks to one other can be repeated quite a few times). The gameplay itself is fantastic and is truly unique and refreshing, with a real sense of urgency and power as the monster as you steadily evolve and requires quick tactical decision making in order to pick off the hunters, with the hunter side having a great team aspect that makes everyone feel as valuable as the other in their own way, and allows for a deep metagame due to the shear variety of abilities you can combine to produce a variety of techniques. While the game does lack any form of campaign (similar to the also online based Titanfall which I also enjoyed), the off-line bots and tutorials give the players a great chance to refine their tactics and learn the games intricacies, with the bots giving adequate challenge and support, while also offering a nice way to kill a quick bit of time. Also it's nice to see a multiplayer launch that has been nice and smooth for once, after all the controversy last year, with me finding almost no bugs or glitches in the game, with the experience feeling tight and fair.

This game took me awhile to pick up and give a shot despite having always been fascinated by it. I'm glad I did. It is very unique, rewarding, and difficult in all the right ways. I feel that Hinterland is an ethical studio and are committed to improving the game. Hopefully this allays the concerns for those soured by early access.
The game is very playable in its current form and extremely engaging. it is largely bug-free. It absolutely oozes atmosphere. The different zones are beautiful to explore. It is very colorful despite the white-out blizzards and eerie fog. It's easy to put yourself in your character's shoes. You will notice your own IRL hunger and turn up the thermostat due to your struggles in the game! My heart pounds through my chest when I'm surprised by hostile wildlife. Every rifle round must be made to count, or else.
It is very fair despite the randomness and indifference of mother nature, not to mention extremely realistic. There is a way out of most tough situations if you put your mind to it. You can figure out what to do intuitively and the controls and movement are fluid.
The game has big things on the horizon - story mode, for one. I wish very strongly for co-op and pvp, but it is fine as single player game. All in all, it is a 9/10 in its current state. If able, I would gift each person at Hinterland the Ferrari of their choice.

LIMBO has very good atmosphere and some challenging puzzles.
If you want to try a platformer that's very different from the Nintendo style, this is a good choice (as is Oddword: New 'n Tasty). With 75% of my inventory occupied by bottles and empty guns, but no food or rags, I need to find a source of food. a house to loot, perhaps. I scurry into a forest after the sound of a squadron falls upon my ears; I was in no condition to fight. I wander the forest for a little bit, helplessly watching my vitality droop into the low thirties. I need food, drink, anything.
And fast.
After crawling through the forest for a few minutes, I hear humming. There is a lone robot here. I scope out the immediate area, hoping to set course away from certain doom. Upon laying eyes on the beast, however, I sit in place, carefully calculating where it is traveling.
Because of the shack it was patrolling.
I watch the shack and robot from above, as I am stationed on a hill just out of sight. My vitality is hitting the low teens. This shack is my last shot at life; any village would be too far to not starve. This is my last chance, and I need to spend it wisely. I note the robot's steady patrol around the shack, and sprint when he rounds the corner. I do not care if I am seen; I could run after I retrieved any food in the shack, and any other course of action would leave me dead.
A meter or so away, I note that I can no longer hear the robot humming. This is either my lucky day, or my last. I got within a few decimeters of the door, so close to life once more.
That is all I hear, and all I need to hear. I am dead. The abrupt and loud snap and accompanying crunch can only mean one thing.
I quickly look down to inspect my injured shin, shattered by a perfectly placed bear trap. I quickly try to undo the traps mechanisms, to free myself and run. I am interrupted by a loud click above my head. I look up. I am greeted by the barrel of a large gun, then by a bright light, and darkness. I can feel the ground as I land, I feel it welcome me to a long, peaceful slumber. As I fall into eternal sleep, I am greeted with a lullaby, a familiar song that I am unable to name. It is unsettling, however in the way it is sung, or rather, hummed.
And it sounded oddly robotic.

Jet Racing Extreme is a racing game where you get behind the wheel of a jet powered car and race around one of (currently) four tracks. There's not much else to say about the game itself so I'll crack on with the rest of my review.
+A fair amount of customisation is available for your car, you can change the paint colour which is pretty basic but you can also upgrade the components of your car as well as fine tune them to create the best vehicle possible
+The car's damage models are good and the car breaks apart nicely upon impacts, smashing into things is a big part of the game so this is rather important
+Decent sound effects, the car noises are reasonably realistic in particular
-Keyboard controls are, as expected of a racing game, bad and despite the dev claiming the game is best played with a gamepad the gamepad controls are quite possibly worse with terribly thought out bindings and no way to change the bindings for the gamepad (keyboard bindings can be changed)
-There are currently only four maps available, two of which are just a short section of one of the other maps
-The camera occasionally swaps angle randomly and most of the camera angles in the game are completely useless for a fast paced racing game -
-The driving and general physics aren't even slightly realistic despite the claims on the store page and in the forums
-None of the UI is explained at all making it almost completely pointless
-The point system doesn't really work properly, I sometimes got given stunt points for crashing into objects and spinning uncontrollably which doesn't really make sense
-A few grammatical and spelling errors, obviously not everyone speaks perfect English but it can't be too hard to get someone to proof-read
-Despite not being a mobile port (the devs are planning to port it to mobile however) it does very much feel like a game that belongs on a smartphone or tablet rather than a PC or laptop
-The mouse cursor always stays visible, one of my major pet peeves in games
-You can't reverse so if you crash into a wall and can't turn out of it you're forced to restart
-You can't pause the game! Another of my major pet peeves, seriously it's 2015 and we can't pause our games?
-As you can see from the below comment section, the dev really has no idea how to communicate with the Steam community, telling me, among other things, that I'm wrong because I disagree with him
Verdict:
Avoid it like the Plague (2/10)
Jet Racing Extreme is a poor mobile port that fails at what it sets out to achieve, with poor controls, sub-par graphics and a fair few other issues this game is neither worth your time nor money.

Sir (or Madam), You Are Being Hunted is a survival horror, first-person shooter game where the player is stranded on one of five islands, surrounded by mysterious stones and killer robots.
Players can choose what environment to make the four outlying islands, from dystopian industrial, to crumbling fens. In each, small rows of buildings remain behind, with different types of rural English tropes of robots awaiting. These robots are programmed to hunt down the player, if the player is seen or heard in the vicinity of their paths.
The player, however, begins the game either with a minimal amount of items, or on easier settings, weapons and distractions for the robots. The player can also find more weapons, ammunition, food, bandages, accessories, and plenty of unusable items, in buildings and bins throughout the islands. Since this is a survival horror game, all items are scarce, and the player may only take what can fit in his or her backpack. However, the player can store items in buildings or bins along the way.
The object for the player is to find mysterious rocks that have struck the islands. Taking these to a monolith at the center of the middle island will teleport the player off the island and to safety. Guarding these rocks, however, are very alert robots, knowing the player must try to retrieve these pieces to get off the islands.
To assist the player, wisps spawn and fly toward one of these fallen rocks. A player can always track down pieces by following a wisp, but this also makes the player a bit more visible to robots.
On harder settings, robots also have canines that can run faster than the player and can hear the player farther away than the normal robots. There is also a hot air balloon robot which will sound an alarm and shine a spotlight on the player when he or she is discovered.
The game feels like the player is a game animal, being released for hunters to find and kill. It is a different, but well executed, idea for a survival horror game.
The graphics are mediocre, and the sounds need plenty of work. But the game is still being updated infrequently, so eventually these shortcomings will be resolved.
Recommended for fans of survival horror or challenging FPS games.

As a fan of both Tower Defense games and Rogue-likes I have to say this game is fantastic! It's not that much of a tower defense game (even though it has strong influences from the genre, like waves after waves of mobs and module/tower building) as it is a resource-management and a survival game.
This game is step-based, meaning you have to open doors in the dungeon, and after each door is opened you gain resources depending on how many active modules you have and an action phase starts where mobs rush to your crystal room. Game is real-time during the action phase, but it can be paused to plan your strategy accordingly.
There is a lot of depth in this game from things like:
- many heroes, all of them with stat progressions, levels, abilities and personalities
- many constructable minor and major modules, that offer effects to your rooms, heroes or resources
- research system, that allows you to unlock module tech by spending science
- item system that lets you tweak heroes in various ways (each hero can hold 3 items in special slots)
- though monsters, most of them with special effects
- interesting progressive dungeon rooms, with good visuals, and many bonuses to be explored
Bonus points:
- great minimalistic artstyle
- soothing soundtrack
- great gameplay
- future potential as the devs continue to develop it
- devs are great and they are updating the game frequently
- endless hours of fun
- challenging gameplay
Bad points:
- can be too difficult
- still in early development
I really recommend this game to anyone that wants a challenge and a good old rogue-like, with a modern feel.

The easiest description I can give of Shadow Ops is "Call of Duty Modern Warfare", if done with a less talented team and worse technology.
It's evident that Zombie Studios, the developers of Shadow Ops, wanted to make exactly the same sort of game that Infinity Ward would produce three years later; it's the same sort of spec-ops ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, scripted and liner story-driven adventure as would dominate the genre for nearly a decade, albeit released in 2004 instead of 2007, and not done half as well.
In part, this was a failing of the technology; the graphics engine just couldn't produce the necessary quality of visuals, still being stuck with the "real is brown" graphics and blocky polygonal characters that seemed just a step above Quake's monsters. Better lighting and production values would have greatly improved the effect and immersion of the game, but the aging Unreal engine just was not able to provide these. But the game also suffered from poor level design; not just in how the levels looked, but also in flow and layout, in how it clued the player as to where to go next, and in enemy placement. Gameplay was too frequently interrupted by video cut-scenes (because in-engine graphics couldn't cut it), and the inability to drop or pick up new weapons seems a baffling choice.
The story is the usual Modern Warfare awfulness, with a super-human protagonist soldier-spy mowing down enemies in venues as varied as the Congo, to a Russian research facility, to the streets of Paris itself (none of them very convincingly rendered), all in pursuit of a madman with the eponymous "red mercury" bomb. In this area, at least, the game is on par with the more notable Call of Duty games, which are equally nonsensical and stupid, but that's not much of an achievement.
As a historical footnote, the game is of marginal interest as it evidences the direction the genre was moving, but as a game it is forgettable and unenjoyable trash.

I’ve been waiting for Cuphead since it was first revealed in 2014. Now it’s finally here. Cuphead, a super difficult platformer/run & gun game with outstanding visuals, one which mimics the aesthetics of 1930s cartoons to perfection. The game is pretty, but we knew that for the last 3 years. But is the gameplay any good?
Cuphead is basically a series of boss fights with the occasional run & gun level in between, all accessible via an explorable map. It was originally designed as a purely boss fights game, but when it got a lot of attention at the 2014 E3, StudioMDHR decided to make something bigger and better. And I, for one, am glad they did. Nothing in the game feels as if it was just an afterthought. Every boss and every level is well thought out and just feels great.
If you look at the screenshots, I’m sure you will agree they are absolutely stunning. The game doesn’t just look similar to 1930s animations. It looks exactly like it. Not only is it drawn perfectly, it also mimics the animations spot on. Combined with a nice filter that simulates the flickering of an old film, the illusion is complete, you really feel like you are in an old cartoon.
The sound is equally convincing. The game plays an original song on the title screen and right away it feels like this is a very authentic re-imagination of the cartoons of yore. A style that extends not only in regards to the visuals but also the audio. All sound effects, music and voices sound like they were taken directly from an old film reel.
But how does it play? Responsive controls are very important for this type of game. And they are. Responsive that is.. You have just a few actions, the basic movement itself, a dash move, standard and special attack and a movement lock which keeps Cuphead in place while shooting. Aside from that you can switch through your available weapons, while in the air combat missions you also have the ability to hold down a button in order to morph into a smaller version of yourself that is more agile, just doing lesser damage. That’s as far as the controls go. The game is not about complexity. Quite the opposite. You have a very limited set of moves but need to execute them perfectly in order to succeed. If you die in a level, it’s most likely your own fault.
You may already have heard that Cuphead is supposed to be quite difficult. Indeed, it is. Both the bosses and the run & gun levels are extremely challenging. Sometimes so challenging that it took me 20 or more tries to get it done. So, don’t let yourself be fooled by the kiddy graphics, this game is hard and you will get bogged down on certain stages. If you don’t enjoy fighting a boss over and over just to get a little better every time until you eventually beat him, just barely, better think twice before getting Cuphead. As brilliant as the game is – it is certainly not for everyone. It might look mainstream and even childish when looking at the screenshots, but the reality is that it is a niche title for a niche audience. It is fast, pure and unforgiving. It won’t hold your hand, it won’t help you on the way. However if you can handle the difficulty, you will enjoy Cuphead a great deal. Nothing is more satisfying than beating a boss that you really got stuck on for the last hour.
Cuphead is the game we were all hoping for. The presentation is unique and nearly perfect in both video and audio. The gameplay is simple and precise. It is challenging and addictive, I suffered from ‘just one more try’ syndrome quite a bit. For those who don’t mind challenge and brutal difficulty, it is nearly perfect with very few things to criticize. It may be a simple game, but what it does it does extremely well. If you are even remotely interested in this kind of game and don’t mind the difficulty this is a must-buy.
+ Gorgeous Visuals: A beautiful re-imagination of 1930s cartoons, they couldn’t have done it better.
+ Sound Design: Music, sound effects and speech all feel very authentic.
+ Boss Design: Every boss fight is different in both, the look, and mechanics.
* Difficulty: A welcome challenge to some, but a deal breaker to many others.
- Hectic Gameplay: You have so much to dodge on the screen and the game is so unforgiving that you don’t have the time to admire the beautiful art style.
5/5

I've lived entire lives in this game.  Braved bitter winters.  Sorted and labeled crates of canned food, wondering how long it would last me.  Tended crops and cursed the misfortune of plant disease.  Fractured my leg and holed up in the corner of some dilapidated warehouse dying of thirst since I lacked the speed to get home safely.  I've lived a thousand lives and felt the touch of death so many times, now I'm only surprised when it doesn't come swiftly.
What I've learned is that death isn't failure, no, it's a sweet release.  Make no mistake, I've survived for a long time, built impregnable safehouses with self-sustaining crops, high above where any zombie could reach.  But that is simply a different kind of death, death in the form of boredom, but it is a death all the same.  It makes sense though, doesn't it?  You are the last person on Earth, the world is filled with endless zombies, there is no happy ending to all of this.
But the point isn't to survive, the point is to create your own tale, make a snapshot of experiences that are memorable.  This game is really just an analogy for life and death, compressed into a few hours at a time, and how you choose to spend your time reflects on your personality.  How will you keep death at bay?  Will you build walls, will you hide, will you run as far away as you can, or will you pick up an axe and try to fight it?  It doesn't matter, death will find you in the end, but it will be a hell of a journey.
