Bioshock is a first person shooter developed Irrational Games and published in 2007. It takes the player on an adventure in the fallen underwater utopia of Rapture. You guide the character, Jack, through Rapture and uncover not only the story of the city, but your own story as well.
Story/Characters:
The Bioshock games are known for telling a story through environmental storytelling. By finding audio diaries throughout the game, you uncover the amazing story that is the fall of Rapture and even a broken bottle next to a pool of blood has an entire story to it.
The story of Rapture can generally be divided up into two parts: The story of Rapture and the story of you, the player. Though the story of Rapture stands incredibly strong and is a thrill and joy to experience, the "main story" or story of the player falls short and really only drags the game down. Throughout the game I found myself looking forward to what the next 20 second audio diary (telling of the events of Rapture) had to say more so than what i would have to do to advance to the next level. The main story is, however, somewhat saved by an incredible twist midway through and without spolling it (trust me you want to experience it yourself), let's just say it changed my view on games.
However, it is also here that the game also really takes a dive, storywise. The already not to interesting story of the first half is replaced with an out of place story that I personally did't care for. To put that into perspective, let's just say that I would have preferd to have the game wrap up at that point, even though it meant the game being significantly smaller.
Though my complaints with some of the story aspects, Bioshock truly delivers a gripping story of a city that falls due to the ideals it was build on.
Character wise, I'm not going to say much, for it is truly the city, Rapture, that is the main character.
Gameplay:
Bioshock has an incredibly solid gameplay. There is not much more to say really. Everything works, weapons feels incredibly satisfying and enemies are pleasantly challenging.
Art/Sound:
Bioshock is from 2007 and this is clear when you look on the graphics. Though this is not a bad thing! Even though it doesn't measure up to modern standards set by games such as Uncharted or The Witcher, Bioshocks look only adds to the atmosphere and it gives players with even a small rig a chance to experience it.
Concerning sound and soundtrack, Bioshock doesn't really stand out. the music adds to he creepy atmosphere sure, but unlike games such as 'Everybody's gone to the Rapture' where you'll end up standing still, just taking in the music Rapture never really has such a moment.
Verdict:
Even though the game is nearing its 10 year anniversary, its solid gameplay and captivating story makes it an experience on equal footing of modern games. If you played Bioshock Infinite and are worried about wheter you'll be able to handle the outdated graphics and engine, don't be. Though the main story isn't all that interesting, it should be the story of Rapture that draws players in, for that is truly the strength of Bioshock.
Story/Characters: 7
Gameplay: 9
Art/Sound: 6
Overall: 8

I have never bothered to write a review about any game I have played before.  I have to make an exception for this one.  After playing games like Fire Watch and others I almost didn't pick this one up thinking it would be the same type that is only good for a few hours and then nothing more.  I am so glad I was wrong.  I have had this game for a couple of days now and even though I have died permanently several times already, I can't get enough of this game!  There is a definite sense of accomplishment you feel when you use a snare you found to catch a rabbit, or a well placed shot to bring down your first deer and realize that you just might actually survive.  Yes, you can find things to eat out of cans but the first time you get food poisoning, and there is nothing you can do to stop your dying because you can't find the right thing to counteract the poison, makes you want to rely on fresh consumables.  I couldn't find the ingredients to counteract the food poisoning so I made my way to a place with a bed and let myself pass into oblivion in bed instead of being food for a bear or wolves.  The game brings you to realize how survival is based a lot on luck and where you initially spawn (where you are when it hits the fan) in the game if you have a good cache to start or not.  Spawning out in the woods requires expending too much energy in finding meager food supplies which results in a Christopher McCandless situation and you can almost feel the poignant ending as you fade to black alone.  Spawning in a place like a Trapper's Cabin and you have quite a good start to actually survive this game.  A great combination of food, water, warmth and rest, all easily monitored makes for long endurance with this game.  Clothing, tools and consumables have wear/tear and time percentages that must paid attention to or your clothes, tools and food will degrade.  Bears and wolves are a constant concern as they too are out trying to survive in a harsh environment, wanting to make a meal out of you as in anything else they can find to eat.  The weather is totally unpredictable in that you can start out hiking across a frozen lake in beautiful sunshine trying to check out new areas and then suddenly, snow starts falling, the wind picks up and suddenly you are in a blizzard and can't see more than a few feet in front of you and can't find your way back to where you have a fire, you break through thin ice and you end up freezing to death.  This game is a set of huge interconnected maps to explore that get added to all the time. This game has it all (except zombies, thank god, enough already) and this is only Sandbox.  I can't wait to see the Story line.  Only one thing... since this is set in far north Canada, there really isn't a place to settle down and farm when the weather gets warm, it never gets warm so unless you can build a fence and keep a herd of deer behind it to raise for your food, you will allways have to wander the countryside finding something to eat which means you are scouring each area clean and it will eventually be a zero sum game as you run out of bullets or game or both with no hope of rescue or escape.

I'm writing this review at the tale end of 2016, I still play this game regularly, and there is a very good reason for that. I am hopeful that with the uptick in Star Wars everything with the new episodic series and the Star Wars Stories series that another Star Wars real time strategy game; until then, Empire at War reigns supreme. To start with, the original Empire at War in this pack, it is an in depth yet user friendly real time strategy game that allows you to build massive fleets and land armies with limits for space and land battles so you don't lose track of your units in battle. The game has three modes; story/campaign, skirmish and galactic conquest. The story allows you to choose the Heroic Rebel Alliance or the Fearsome Galactic Empire through many unique missions that allow you to explore the unsung battles of the galactic civil war. This game mode yields to the Galactic Conquest mode which is very similar to the Campaign but without the special missions and cut scenes. This is my personal favorite mode because it allows you to run through the whole galaxy and conquer it for your favorite faction. In this mode, you have to balance the logistics of limits to your troops, money to pay for new units and for developing conquered planets. You work your way up in the tech tree to unlock the more advanced and powerful units and buildings in the game. The Empire and Rebellion have dramatically different capabilities as well; different enough for their strategies are challenging to master but very well balanced. For example, the rebellion can launch special land invasions on Imperial planets called raids that bypass the orbital fleet and if the rebellion is successful then the empire loses that system no matter how good their orbital defenses are. The Empire on the other hand can build the death star that can of course destroy enemy planets. It must have a fleet to defend it while it gets into range and within a few minutes of a space battle, it can fire and destroy the planet. The balance here is that the rebellion can destroy the death star for an automatic win, regardless of the state of the map so the empire is forced to spend many resources defending the Death Star. The final game mode is the skirmish mode that allows the player to engage in a single land or space battle. All units are purchased from the base or space station unlike the previous modes. This mode is great for a quick battle to learn a map, play with units the way you want or simply cut your teeth on new strategies. Unfortunately, the servers for this game have been off for a long time but you can use game ranger to play with your friends who own the game. With the vanilla game covered, I'll briefly cover Forces of Corruption. This add on adds a completely new faction with its own campaign. The unique thing about this circumstance is that it is in the extended universe and has many non-canon units, characters and missions. The Zann Consortium is a criminal syndicate to rival the Hutt gangs and in the campaign builds itself into a formidable faction in the galaxy. It uses underhanded techniques such as sabotage, piracy and other abilities to advance its tech tree and earn credits in the galactic conquest mode. It uses a mix of different ships to form its fleets all with their own unique roles and powers. They add another player faction to the multiplayer as well and is a DLC that adds serious content to an already wonderful game. Overall, this game is king of Star Wars RTS and I highly recommend it to anyone who enjoys both.

Before I actually discuss the game I'll quickly address this whole dlc argument that seems to be all that people focus on.
In my view there is no problem with the use of day one dlc, as it is all cosmetic, with no in game affecting content available so all this controversy is rather out of proportion as this kind of content is unfortunately very common now a days with game publishes/developers even valve with portal 2. Yes I agree, the monsters and hunters that will be released are overpriced, and the fact that there are going to be two season passes is stupid, but the fact that maps and modes are going to be free , makes this an actually good business model as dlc or not, all players can play together and is something I wish more games did.
First I'll address some of the cons, because like any game there are note worthy issues. Firstly the progression system is flawed, forcing you to redo repetitive tactics which is actually a bad way to complete objectives. Some of the maps also tend to resemble one another with only a couple that really stand out. While the hunters feel adequately stocked with options, the monster side feels like it could do with at least one more character to add variety. When you play as the hunters you are very dependent on your team, so one person being unsupportive, getting killed to easily, and relying too heavily on hand holding ways of finding the monster (like Daisy), can lead to frustrating doomed to failure games. While a few more modes would also improve the experience as the can feel quite similar (with defend being the most varied) and having to play the evacuation 5 part match playlist to access the other is not a great idea in my eyes.
While I have found issues, I still think this game is worth experiencing (at least at a reduced price, or when more maps/modes are released if you are unsure) because in my eyes the positives are well worth it. First off while the maps can feel samey, they are well designed and look fabulous, offering a variety of scenarios and tactics for both hunters and monster to utilize such as natural features and wildlife. The characters themselves all feel distinct and require their own finesse in order to better your odds with the monster all requiring different fighting styles to avoid death, with the hunters feeling equally important and balanced, with their own unique personalities (although their remarks to one other can be repeated quite a few times). The gameplay itself is fantastic and is truly unique and refreshing, with a real sense of urgency and power as the monster as you steadily evolve and requires quick tactical decision making in order to pick off the hunters, with the hunter side having a great team aspect that makes everyone feel as valuable as the other in their own way, and allows for a deep metagame due to the shear variety of abilities you can combine to produce a variety of techniques. While the game does lack any form of campaign (similar to the also online based Titanfall which I also enjoyed), the off-line bots and tutorials give the players a great chance to refine their tactics and learn the games intricacies, with the bots giving adequate challenge and support, while also offering a nice way to kill a quick bit of time. Also it's nice to see a multiplayer launch that has been nice and smooth for once, after all the controversy last year, with me finding almost no bugs or glitches in the game, with the experience feeling tight and fair.

I wanted to like this game, I really did. Unfortunately, I just didn't find it fun.
There is just so much wrong. An enemy is placed in pretty much every corner, and surviving pretty much requires knowing the enemy locations, this is proven by how easy the runthroughs become after playing that area once or twice. The AI are practically aimbotting, making combat mostly a contest of lean spamming. There is an extremely bad issue in the second mission where the map is covered in fog, but the AI can see a good few feet further than you. You are stuck charging down a bridge because if you stay back they can easily see you despite the fact that it would be impossible. In the same mission I had AI spawn at least once in places that it would be impossible to be. For instance, I cleared a wooden walkway, had 2 squadmates sitting there up top, but eventually had 3 AI randomly show up behind me. There was only one way down, and it was being watched by friendlies, but nope, I ended up having to restart the mission the first time because the enemy can teleport. The second time, of course, I quickly killed them knowing that they would show up.
Speaking of friendly AI, I don't get the praise. Sure, they actually help, which is a step up from a lot of games. However, they are invincible other than scripted events and overall do a terrible job fighting the enemy 90% of the time. Also, one time I was advancing towards a friendly (in the first mission), only to move up further to find that an enemy (in clear sight of the friendly) was just sitting there with his back turned to him waiting for me to come around the wall further (despite the fact that he couldn't have realistically known I was coming).
Also, though possibly more of a personal preference, you don't get close to enough ammo for the enemies you have to fight. Or, at least if you want limited ammo, make it slightly less of a twich shooter.
Overall, if you want an old school game with frustrating AI aimbot play MoH: Allied Assault. At least it is overall pretty polished and has a plethera of cool concepts. In Shadow Ops' defence, maybe it gets better. But, I already have a headache from it and I don't feel like slogging through annoyingly designed missions to find out.

Red Faction: Armageddon, like its predecessor (Guerrilla), proudly flaunts its massively destructible environment. The player can tear down any building he so wishes and in this new (and perhaps final) iteration of THQ's long running franchise, buildings can now be restored. But is this gimmick enough?
Manipulating buildings isn't the sole gameplay at work here. Armageddon is a third person shooter that plays similarly to any typical third person shooter in the market. Even more generic is its plot that revolves around the uprising of an alien species that threatens human life on Mars.
My biggest grievances though are the removal of Guerrilla's open world. As a consequence, Armageddon is a very linear affair. That's not to say it isn't a blast, but more freedom might have made the game much more engaging.
Armageddon isn't "Game of the Year" material, but I'd be lying if I said it wasn't fun. Just demolishing buildings in this game may be worth the admission price.
Grade: B

Bioshock is a first person shooter developed Irrational Games and published in 2007. It takes the player on an adventure in the fallen underwater utopia of Rapture. You guide the character, Jack, through Rapture and uncover not only the story of the city, but your own story as well.
Story/Characters:
The Bioshock games are known for telling a story through environmental storytelling. By finding audio diaries throughout the game, you uncover the amazing story that is the fall of Rapture and even a broken bottle next to a pool of blood has an entire story to it.
The story of Rapture can generally be divided up into two parts: The story of Rapture and the story of you, the player. Though the story of Rapture stands incredibly strong and is a thrill and joy to experience, the "main story" or story of the player falls short and really only drags the game down. Throughout the game I found myself looking forward to what the next 20 second audio diary (telling of the events of Rapture) had to say more so than what i would have to do to advance to the next level. The main story is, however, somewhat saved by an incredible twist midway through and without spolling it (trust me you want to experience it yourself), let's just say it changed my view on games.
However, it is also here that the game also really takes a dive, storywise. The already not to interesting story of the first half is replaced with an out of place story that I personally did't care for. To put that into perspective, let's just say that I would have preferd to have the game wrap up at that point, even though it meant the game being significantly smaller.
Though my complaints with some of the story aspects, Bioshock truly delivers a gripping story of a city that falls due to the ideals it was build on.
Character wise, I'm not going to say much, for it is truly the city, Rapture, that is the main character.
Gameplay:
Bioshock has an incredibly solid gameplay. There is not much more to say really. Everything works, weapons feels incredibly satisfying and enemies are pleasantly challenging.
Art/Sound:
Bioshock is from 2007 and this is clear when you look on the graphics. Though this is not a bad thing! Even though it doesn't measure up to modern standards set by games such as Uncharted or The Witcher, Bioshocks look only adds to the atmosphere and it gives players with even a small rig a chance to experience it.
Concerning sound and soundtrack, Bioshock doesn't really stand out. the music adds to he creepy atmosphere sure, but unlike games such as 'Everybody's gone to the Rapture' where you'll end up standing still, just taking in the music Rapture never really has such a moment.
Verdict:
Even though the game is nearing its 10 year anniversary, its solid gameplay and captivating story makes it an experience on equal footing of modern games. If you played Bioshock Infinite and are worried about wheter you'll be able to handle the outdated graphics and engine, don't be. Though the main story isn't all that interesting, it should be the story of Rapture that draws players in, for that is truly the strength of Bioshock.

Well, ain't this a blast from the past?
I remember renting this on the Xbox in 2004 after being bombarded by an avalanche of adds for the game on every gameplay video I watched on gamespot (everyone complains about the media player nowadays but the video player back in the day was like a brief glimpse of hell) and to be honest, the premise was quite enticing. Most FPS's back in the day fell into either the Sci-Fi or WW2 categories and most contemporary shooters were TPS's or tactical shooters like Rainbow Six, SOCOM, Counter-Strike, Delta Force or Ghost Recon. All of them were very realistic in terms of difficulty and pacing and were quite hard to get into because of that, so Shadow Op's was interesting as it took the more arcade-like approach to it's combat.
I had a lot of fun with it back in the day so obviously I decided to pick it up many years later only to buy it again once more on Steam.
So, obviously, considering I rented the game multiple times and bought it twice, my review is leaning on the biased side, but I digress. It's a nice blast to the past.
No one ever saw an FPS like this, especially one that was trying super hard to play out like a big dumb summer thriller. While nowadays everyone is so sick of Contemporary shooters we are now gasping for joy at the prospekt of a WW2 shooter like the good ol' days, Shadow Op's is still quite astounding. The sound and production values were pretty crazy for an Xbox game in 2004. The audio itself was pretty damn impressive, with reverb in gunfire and outdoor environs giving your guns a more distant crackle with every pull of the trigger.
Story wise, the plot is pretty forgettable but ironically, is saved by corny cliches that make otherwise crap dialogue unintentionally humorous in hindsight. This, coupled with the ridiculous ragdolls and giggle-inducing death squeals of fallen enemies gives the game an unintentional humorous edge. Which to me isn't a bad thing.
Gameplay wise, the shooting mechanics are tight and the controls are responsive. The player is capable of leaning while using ironsights (an unseen concept back then) but I found crouching had to much of a delay in most firefights.
Speaking of firefights, the game is chock-full of them. While boasting 25 levels you progress through them fairly quickly even on harder settings. On hard, enemies take more of a beating and can knock your health down if you are not as quick on the draw while on easier settings they go down like chumps and tend to spill ammo like blood. Regardless of the settings, I've noticed that their reflexes are still very high. However, there is no quicksaving or checkpoint saving whatsover. You have to get to the end of the level to continue, but if you die inches from the exit door, tough♥♥♥♥♥♥ You have to do the entire level all over again! Offputting, but it's not as crushing as other games, due to the relatively short lengh of most levels and an overabundence of medkits.
All in all, I had a lot of fun with this game back in the day and I still do now. It hasn't aged the best, Unreal 2 was showing its age in 2004 and while its used to good effect here, it's not exactly eyecandy, not to mention the Modern-Military edge may detter modern players due to an overstauration in the market, but I can't deny the fun I had playing this. It's big, it's loud, it's dumb and just like the conspiracy theory it is based off of, the story doesn't hold much water, but screw it. Shadow Op's is a nice relic that tried to be different in a market over-staurated with Sci-Fi and WW2 themes. So I guess I can tip my beercap in Shadow Ops' general direction.

I was really into the original web prototype for SuperHot way back when, but when it finally released it was a whopping $25. I couldn't afford it at the time, but years later it's finally reasonably priced with the Winter Sales.
The theme of SuperHot is sort of unsettling/creepy while also being vague and artsy. The theme is consistant, I'll give it that, but this feels like a bit of a cop-out to avoid drawing real art assets and composing music.
The writing and story of this game is terrible. Usually I don't care much about that stuff but the game really forces you to get invested in it. Whenever cutscenes were happening, I was just wishing I could play the next level. The writing is cringe-worthy and I literally laughed out loud when the credits rolled and I saw that 6 PEOPLE collaborated on it. It's just plain pretentious and awful.
The core gameplay itself is very fun, despite everything else, and once you beat the short campaign you get access to a bunch of very fun challenge modes that switch up the rules. Having a shooter that's almost turn-based is a really cool idea that I think was mechanically executed well. It's a shame that the presentation seems determined to prevent you from enjoying that gameplay.

I have never bothered to write a review about any game I have played before.  I have to make an exception for this one.  After playing games like Fire Watch and others I almost didn't pick this one up thinking it would be the same type that is only good for a few hours and then nothing more.  I am so glad I was wrong.  I have had this game for a couple of days now and even though I have died permanently several times already, I can't get enough of this game!  There is a definite sense of accomplishment you feel when you use a snare you found to catch a rabbit, or a well placed shot to bring down your first deer and realize that you just might actually survive.  Yes, you can find things to eat out of cans but the first time you get food poisoning, and there is nothing you can do to stop your dying because you can't find the right thing to counteract the poison, makes you want to rely on fresh consumables.  I couldn't find the ingredients to counteract the food poisoning so I made my way to a place with a bed and let myself pass into oblivion in bed instead of being food for a bear or wolves.  The game brings you to realize how survival is based a lot on luck and where you initially spawn (where you are when it hits the fan) in the game if you have a good cache to start or not.  Spawning out in the woods requires expending too much energy in finding meager food supplies which results in a Christopher McCandless situation and you can almost feel the poignant ending as you fade to black alone.  Spawning in a place like a Trapper's Cabin and you have quite a good start to actually survive this game.  A great combination of food, water, warmth and rest, all easily monitored makes for long endurance with this game.  Clothing, tools and consumables have wear/tear and time percentages that must paid attention to or your clothes, tools and food will degrade.  Bears and wolves are a constant concern as they too are out trying to survive in a harsh environment, wanting to make a meal out of you as in anything else they can find to eat.  The weather is totally unpredictable in that you can start out hiking across a frozen lake in beautiful sunshine trying to check out new areas and then suddenly, snow starts falling, the wind picks up and suddenly you are in a blizzard and can't see more than a few feet in front of you and can't find your way back to where you have a fire, you break through thin ice and you end up freezing to death.  This game is a set of huge interconnected maps to explore that get added to all the time. This game has it all (except zombies, thank god, enough already) and this is only Sandbox.  I can't wait to see the Story line.  Only one thing... since this is set in far north Canada, there really isn't a place to settle down and farm when the weather gets warm, it never gets warm so unless you can build a fence and keep a herd of deer behind it to raise for your food, you will allways have to wander the countryside finding something to eat which means you are scouring each area clean and it will eventually be a zero sum game as you run out of bullets or game or both with no hope of rescue or escape.

About Controls
You can control your player with mouse or joypad. Keyboard isn't available, becouse its limited just to 8 directions, therefore you cant aim your shots properly.
Mouse:
-Your player moves toward mouse cursor.
-For shooting, hold LMB (left mouse button). More nearer you keep mouse cursor to your player, more higher shoot you will make.
-Direct shot/pass, click your RMB (right mouse button). Power is determined, how far you keep your mouse cursor.
-Slidetackle, click MMB (middle mouse button)
Joypad:
-Button 1: hold to shoot
-Button 2:
with ball: tap to autopass, hold to direct shot
without ball: request pass from bot
-Button 3:
with ball: hold to cross
withoutball: slidetackle
Tip 1: When you control ball, your player moves slower. So when running with ball, make small shots with LMB/Button 1, so you aren't actually holding ball and you can run faster.
Tip 2: There arent actual jumping for header, but hold RMB/Button 2 to make direct shot when ball is in the air.

Its memory will live on, i have no intention of going back in any time soon. Because my god, i dont want to ruin the impact of that first playthough.
There were some very minor annoyances: such as mantling and opening and closing doors mid chase or whilst i was bolting through the pitch dark. When i had to fiddle with my mouse to correctly open or close a door, it unfortunatly pulled me out of the immmersion, usually resulting in my death - sadly reminding me that it infact is "only just a game, afterall"

To summarize in few words - the game is a gorgeous mixture of Chess with Deflektor, taking the best ideas from both. ( (Btw. - does anyone know what the 2nd game is? ;-)
)
Funs of lasers and even light sabres will realize soon that there is not much of an FPS here ;-) Just a 'boring', almost static board with some 2-colour pieces. And some rules that you have to read about - on how to play and win or lose...
Briefly - you have to destroy opponent's Pharaoh. To achieve that you have to use the pieces to reflect a laser beam so that the enemy's Pharaoh is shot with the laser beam. The pieces, depending on their type and orientation (side on which they receive the beam), can either reflect the laser, absorb it without damage or be destroyed. The 2 players play by turns, in which a single piece can be moved or turned. To win the player have to secure his own Pharaoh and find a way either to destroy or to use(!) the enemy's pieces to shoot the other Pharaoh. Before the opponent does it to his of course... So basically often the decision is whether the move can be offensive or defensive (can you afford losing a piece or have to do something to save it, depending on how it affects the situation on the board later - very much like in Chess).
So in each move there is plenty of possibilities and silly movements ends badly very soon. If you are not careful you can actually lose after your own move (yes, you can destroy your own 'Pharaoh'... - not like in Chess ;-). And one of the first things you learn is that you have to be careful maybe even more than in Chess - because your pieces might be used against you! So you have to analyse the position and possibilities of the attack using all the pieces on the board - but you can control movement of half, and any move you do can be then used against you! Really cool, heh? ;-)
Comparing to the mentioned games the rules are:
The game is surprisingly smooth to learn, ie. much easier and faster to learn than chess. And be warned - the gameplay is kind of addictive. I often started the program just to play one-two games... and yeah, sure... At least an hour gone...
Implementation of this kind of game could be very simple (concerning graphics etc), it could be even simple 2D board with symbolic pieces - but most of today's players would not even look at it. So the art part is perfectly OK. (really nothing more needed). Maybe music could be better... Or more ambient (or just could let to choose the genre). But not necessarily, these are really not why you buy and play this kind of game...
I'd say it is a game of the best kind - it has simple rules, but the gameplay can be complex and hard to win. And as I wrote earlier - it is easy to start playing it, much easier than Chess (and therefore it is initially more fun I guess; later - it depends...)
Those who like logic or tactics/strategy games should be delighted - and especially if you like Chess you will definitely like this one!

Fantastic art direction - mediocre gameplay.
A game that (currently) isn't the sum of its parts. All the elements are there, apart from something compelling to do when you play it. The concept is original enough, but the execution is in turns tedious, repetitive and unfair. Playing simply involves repeating the same actions, stage after stage, and hoping the RNG doesn't screw you too badly.
Unlike true Rogue-likes such as FTL and Binding of Isaac, this is essentially a very pretty, but basic, tower defence game with occasional difficulty spikes, or loot drops, as its 'random' element. None of these are compelling like Spelunky's altars or shopkeepers, or FTL's story choices, but simple occasional resource gifts or monster waves.
The problem here is that it misjudges what makes tower defence fun - accurately managing those resources. By tying those into the RNG (level layout strongly dictates your defences and resource gathering) your strategy is always a slave to the RNG, and can often be ruined simply by an obnoxious layout simply starving you of resources, or forcing you to defend more points than is possible.
This makes the game a case of going through the motions, repeating an optimal strategy with little breathing room for experimentation, until you luck into a good run or are forced into an unfair loss. All 10 stages play exactly the same, but just get larger and contain more damaging enemies. Once you've finished stage 1, you've essentially seen the entire game.
A shame, as every other element is dripping with style and polish, and the mixture of TD, dungeon crawling and Rouge-like works as a proof of concept, but unfortunately all you get here is simply a marriage of extremely shallow reprentations of all three genres.

So, why the thumbs-down? On a game with 95% review score?
Well, as nice as this game may be, there are a few problems that make me not recommend it to others.
Sure, it has 500 levels. But after 50 or so, you've seen everything. Sure, there may be nodes with
connections, but it's more of the same, really. The level set names are also quite un-inspired, and the achievements maybe even more so. Also, the unlockable themes are not that much of a novelty either.
The gameplay itself has a problem too though. It's not learnable. There's not really a way to "become good" at this game. Solving levels is merely a case of trying many combinations until you hit the right one. There's a lot of trial and error. Trial and error is usually bad, and I don't see why it's good here.
The third problem is the level solutions themselves. They're too abstract, and don't resemble anything, and after a while, all levels look the same at first glance. Solving a level just doesn't give me that feeling of accomplishment that other puzzles can. When you solve a nonogram, at least you end up with a nice pixel art picture. Here it's just connected shapes - for all levels. It's all a bit too similar.
Also, someone could probably write an algorithm to solve these puzzles. :)
The game sure has its positives though. I like the minimalist look-and-feel, and I think the font choice and color usage are brilliant. Also it's easy to pick-up and play; it hardly requires a tutorial. It's also a nice original idea to toy around with. It's not a bad game. Certainly not! It's just, well, ...not much more than meets the eye?
And it's not overpriced. For 3 dollars it's hard to be disappointed. So sure, pick it up if you think you like it. Just don't expect miracles :)

DLC breaks down into the following:
Maps & Gamemodes - Free for everyone (think of them more as updates to the whole game.)
Skins - paid for DLC. Get them if you give a crap.
Hunters - Bought individually or as a season pass. You can always play with people who have them even if you haven't bought them yourself.
Monsters - Bought individually or as a season pass. You can always play against them too, even if you haven't bought it them yourself.

So Ive own this game for a while now, but now I decided to write my own review.
If you're looking for a good simulation style zombie survival game this is great. The game has some very realistic aspects, for example how the weather effects your character. Even to the extent where food spoils and the electricty shuts off after a time frame (0-2 months Normal). I do think this is a very well made indie game, and is making my veiws on it better and better with each passing update.
This game is extremly difficult if you do not know what you are doing! There is a tutorial which only teaches very basic concepts like moving and fighting. Everything else you will have to pick up as you go. The new "First Bite" Mode actually scales it down quite well and makes the start easier. So if you are looking to find somewhere to learn the ropes this is a very good place. Now im not saying this game is extremely hard just picture it as dark souls, it takes a few deaths before you know how to play properly. To be completly honest the difficult format makes the game quite fun, the game even tells you "This is how you died" when loading the game. Even in the tutorial it says stuff on the lines as "Grab all the food you can before deaths cold hands end you". So you've been warned.
Gameplay and asthetic wise, very well done. Its the old Diablo style mixed in with some modern isometric veiw items. Like where you cant see behind you or through walls. With all that I played I havent seen to many bugs, if so they are mostly visiable, and I havent came across a game crashing one yet. On a diffrent note there is not a whole lot to do but there is enough and the devs are doing very well with the content flow. Even tho its Early Access it could be passed off as a full game in some aspects. Keep up the fantastc work

Honest review, and helpful advice for survivalists.
The Long Dark is an early access game that offers players an interesting survival experience in the world of the post-apocalypse. It takes place in the Northern Regions of Canada, when your plane suffers an accident after a catastrophic geomagnetic disaster, you are the lone survivor. In this stark and desolate wasteland covered in ice and snow, you must gather your wits and hopes, and try to survive the unforgiving conditions Mother Nature has to offer. It's as real as it gets, no holds barred.
Players will experience a survival game like none other, you will have no choice but to strap yourself down and focus, and pay attention to every little detail that going on in your screen. You will not be hand held through it, and no compass or map is offered, no electricity and no A.I to talk you through it. You are alone in this world, you've got nothing else to lose except your life, it will get medieval out there and will not hold back. It's a survival of the fittest.

I start my day like any other as I wake up and look through my bedroom window. Apparently the zombie apocalypse has happened.. The first thing to do on my agenda is scrounge my house for supplies and weapons, sadly the world seems to have a cruel sense of humor, as the only weapon at my disposal is a butter knife. However that and my meager supply of food will have to do. I step out into the dead and lonely world only to find... It's not as lonely as I expected it to be. Only when the "company" is a horde of zombies around every street corner begging for "just a bite" of my flesh I would much rather it to be a lonely world. I was forced to come to the quick realization that walking out the front door was nothing short of ringing a dinner bell and not my most thought out plan, and a butter knife not the most relyable weapon as my life quickly came to an end the very day I started it.
This is pretty much how easily day 1 can come and end in project zomboid, all depending on where you spawn, the zombies in the area, and how sadistic the game wants to be with what spawns in your starting house, along with your own skills of course. This only compounds to the fact the game begins turning off resources such as water and electricity. Also did you establish a well fortified base in a lowly zombie populated area? That's great, except for the fact I think I hear a helicopter flying over said base and now there seems to be an army of the dead shambling your way, I hope there's a backup plan in mind. Zomboid is easily one of the more sadistic games out there right now and funnily enough that is it's greatest appeal.

An excellent indie game.  People looking for some deep backstory need to look elsewhere, it's not really necessary in this game.  You know what you need to know from the beginning:  You are dropped in a procedurally generated world, a group of 5 islands, each with their own "theme" (industrial, feudal, countryside, etc.).  You need to find a bunch of scattered parts for some sort of teleportation machine that will get you home (back to your home dimension, according to the "victory song" at the end).  All the while you must concern yourself with survival, looking for food, weapons, ammunition, and useful items in houses, sheds, and towns.
However, you are being constantly hunted by robots, armed with guns, dogs, and lots of fun British lingo.  They tend to hang around areas that contain items that you need, so you are always looking for ways to sneak past them, distract them, or if you have enough ammo and the numbers aren't too great, taking them out.
The game is a lot of fun.  Lots of things to chuckle at, but also some great gameplay.  It's Day-Z without the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, and with a dark sense of humor.  The environments are varied and look nice, each area having it's own feel.  The robot AI is very good, and strikes a good balance between being not so good that they are impossible to beat, but not so stupid that they are always easy either.  The robot variety is also well done, with various types each posing their own challenge.  Right when you think you've seen every kind, the game surprises you with a new one.
I had this on my wishlist for a long time, but eventually pulled the trigger at full price because I simply got tired of wondering about it.  Glad I did!

The core game of Khet is amazing. If you like chess and other strategy board games, you will most certainly like Khet. Unfortunately, this digital version of the game leaves a lot to be desired. The game is very buggy, and crashed multiple times when I was trying to play an online game with a friend. Good news is, that my friend submitted error logs to the developer and he fixed most problems within a day. But there are still some lagging issues. For one, the game will always crash if you have a browser window open that is playing video such as Netflix or Amazon Video. Also, the interface is not very good. Almost every digital version of chess that's ever been released has allowed players to scroll through all the moves made in the game. This is incredibly useful when you are playing an asyncronous game, and you need to refresh your memory on what the last several moves were. This is a feature that is sorely needed in Khet. Even if you are playing a live game and you happen to look away from the screen for a second while your opponent moves, it can be extrememly difficult to try and figure out where he just moved, and there's no way to click back and see. Overall though, I do recommend this game, simply because Khet is such a deep and interesting game. And hopefully in the future, the interface can be fixed with an update. As of January 2016, I would give this game a 6/10. With some interface tweaks and bug fixes, this game would easily be a 10/10.

Boring gameplay and terrible controls. The hidden object scenes only give you a few items at a time, and you can't move on to the next part of the list until you've found all of them. The mouse pointer doesn't give any indication of what's clickable, so sometimes an object will be behind something else in a scene, and you don't know what you can move unless you just frantically click on everything. There's no indication of area transitions, either, so even the most basic action of moving from place to place gets irritating. Plus there's a bug where sometimes the game won't register ANY area transitions as being clickable, so you're stuck unless you restart the game.
I bought this in a bundle with 6 other games for $1.89 and I still think I paid too much.
EDIT: Went back to finish the game. I think the area transition issue was fixed since I wrote my initial review, but I got some buggy minigames. (At least you can skip those.) The biggest issue for me was still the lack of a context-sensitive mouse cursor.
I do like how the adventure game-style gameplay and art set this apart from the many samey-looking hidden object games out there, but it's not good enough to make this worth playing.

Sinister City, developed by JetDogs Studios, puts you in the shoes of John, and man who is sent on a quest to chase after his Fiancée Nina. The thing is that Nina just up and left John to go to a strange city of darkness and vampires. You will have to find your way through hidden object puzzles, collection puzzles, and many more different types of puzzles if you hope to rescue Nina.
Graphically it feels a bit dated, but then again judging from some of the wording used in the game I'm going to say that this was a port of a tablet game. That being said there's nothing wrong with the look of the game. You will be interacting in a 3d environment broken down into five main areas, and of those areas there are several "rooms" you wil get to interact with in order to advance the storyline. The vampire modeling makes the game feel like a cheesy B-movie, but I think that's what the developers were going for, so in other words they nailed it.
The voice acting was interesting. Almost every character sounded like they were just reading lines, and it just didn't feel like there was any energy put into it. The only character that was really believable was the vampire that was supposed to be the TV star.
You are going to use the mouse for everything in this game, when it comes to controls. Basically you are going to click and drag, or just click your way through this game.
So here's the deal, as cheesy as the storyline was I enjoyed the game, when it worked, and that was the problem with this game. There were several times where after I solved a puzzle and I tried to go on to the next puzzle or thing, I had issues. For example when I am trying to collect items after solving a puzzle, I would go into the next piece of the game where several items are present and after clicking on the screen, anywhere, I automatically exited back out to the area. Then there was the issue of this game only has autosave, which is fine, but I really wish there was a reset button that would reset the scene of a certain piece of the game because during one of the times I had to collect several different items, I was unable to collect the last one, even with the hint indicator highlighting it. I tried restarting the game, steam, and lastly my computer. None of these things work, and so I had to start the game all over again from scratch.
There's also the subtitles, or text that the characters are supposed to be saying, you know when you hear the audio how it is supposed to line up to what is written on the screen? Well its all over the place, sometimes its correct, but most times its hit or miss. The context might be mostly the same but the phrasing and words are completely different. At the end of the day I'm going to have to say that even though this game was enjoyable there were just a couple too many bumps in this game to make it worthwhile for anyone who isn't willing to wrestle with the game doing strange things. So with that I have to give this game a 5.3 out of 10.

When the gaming world was still on a WW2 wave, one developer saw opportunity to take the action in modern days and Shadow Ops: Red Mercury was born. Well, this is what I think happen.
First I want to move out the obvious – graphics. They are bad. There isn't enough video options, but those that are present can't make the game look good. It doesn't matter if you set them on the highest available setting, it's still not a great looker. And the pop in is so obvious at some levels, it's so annoying. This maybe because it's a console port.
In the audio section you can find 4 different sliders. Music, effects, dialogs and voices. For some reason music is off by default, so crank that music to the max, because it's awesome. Also you can rebind keys and customize the HUD, which is a nice surprise.
You are Frank Hayden, an elite Delta Force operative, who is tasked sometimes with his team, sometimes alone, to recover a briefcase nuclear bomb from Vladimir Styanovich a.k.a. Vlady the Vicious, a terrorist mercenery. You will travel around the globe trying to stop him. The story is cheesy, cliché and you can see the twist from a long distance. But the action, music and great variety of places you visit are what can keep you interested.
Shadow Ops: Red Mercury is military FPS. It was made in 2003, before COD: MW. The game is not realistic, it have arcade feel, but make no mistake, this is not Quake. If you try to run and gun, death will come quickly. This game is tough, but fair to a certain degree. This is because of the AI. It is highly accurate. Sometimes enemies are cheaply placed and this annoyed me a lot. There is not enough time to react. You can take quite a few shots (even a rocket), but they may come so quickly and before you know it, you're dead. Because of the AI, there are a lot of tense firefights in and outdoor. You, as one man army will have to kill waves of enemies and it feels so good, when you beat a level, you overcome the odds. The game grabs you for the neck right from the first level. You are pin down by enemies and you have to get out of there fast. There is two more things that will keep the tension. The health is not regenerating, you have to find med packs and ammo is running fast. Enemies can sometimes drop both of them and they also can be found around the levels, but still you have to be careful and accurate in your shots. Some maybe frustraded by that and I was at some point. I had low health, ammo and only a pistol, but I manage to get through this and it was great feeling. Some of the frustration comes from the lack of checkpoints. The levels are not long, but combine with the all things I mentioned above, thing can get annoying. In the end who will pull the trigger first is what matters.
What was suprising to me is the AI of your fellow soldiers. When you are on a mission with them, they can actually kill enemies. But don't expect them to make more kills than you.
Weapons are pretty standard – pisols, sniper rifles, uzi, shotgun, machine gun, granade launcher and so on. They all have recoil and feel good. They kick, so shooting in short burst is recommended . Headshots, of course, are most effective.
Level design is nice. You will visit the jungles in Congo full with shacks and wooden watchtowers, hightech facility in Kazakhstan, streets in ruins in Syria, harbor in Chechnya, ride a train and so on. They are really diverce, but there is nothing suprising. This is not a open world, it's a corridor shooter, but still be on a lookout for hidden ammo or health packs. Sometimes it will the difference between restarting the level and beating it.
What keeps everything together is the soundtrack. It is phenomenal!!! It contribute for the atmosphere a lot. All levels have different theme and fits incredibly well with the pacing and the action on screen. In a snowy level, where is advise to use stealth, the music is calm, but if enemy see you, right at that moment the music picks up seamlessly and so on.
As a whole the sound design is nicely done. Effects are okay. Every gun sound what it supose to, explosion are bombastic, but granades are weak. The voice acting on the other hand is hit and miss. Hayden have gruff voice. It overdone, but it's still pleasant for the ears. But Vladimir Styanovich, if you can hear him, it's just bad. Other voice actor are just okay. They are doing their best with the cheesy writting
I have two more small problems with the game. The cutscene are rendered with the engine, but why they look worse than the in-game graphics is a mystery to me. The other is you can't use aim and move and this makes you easy target. It took me awhile to get use to it.
The game feels like it was inspired from of  90's summer blockbuster movies – tons of action, one man army, tense moments, the main character do imposible things and gets the girl in the end, even the cinematography of the cutscene (they are great) scream 90's. And don't think of the plot too much. If you do, you will find a tons of plot holes. The game is janky, rough around the edges, but the great firefights, amazing sountdrack, nice variety of levels and tension are worth overlooking the pop in, dated graphics, cheaply placed enemies, no checkpoints and the cliché story, although the plot in my opinion is working in favor of the game. And I think the price I right. The campaign will take you b 6-7 hours to beat it. The multyplayer is dead, so keep that in mind. The game have one small, but unique feature – except throwing granades, you can roll them. Despite the flaws, I recommend it.

I have a lot of issues with this game. I am a fan of HOGs (hidden object games) thus it is not the genre that I have a problem with. I believe the devs intended Sinister City to have a B-movie campy feel. In some parts, they succeeded but the storyline ended up feeling jerky - for lack of better term. I can poke a lot of holes at the story but alas, it is not the main problem.
Game issues:
1) In this game, you are simply given items to search, eg. 5 rungs of a ladder, and you have no idea where the HOG scene is. In some games, this is part of the fun. In this game however, the "fun" is marred by the fact that those 5 rungs are spread among various hidden HOG scenes. You have no idea how many rungs this particular scene has.
2) This can actually go hand in hand with pt 1. In usual HOG scenes, there are some items which are doubly hidden. Eg. You are to find a pearl. That pearl could be hidden in a oyster shell. Thus the game will show 'pearl' in your search list in a different color, to let the player know that it is a hidden item. This is the case for ALL the hogs I have played so far and I have played way more HOGs than my fingers and toes could count. Sinister City has NO SUCH THING. Thus you have zero idea if that item you can't find is simply staring at you right in front of your eyes or if it is hidden behind something irrelevant in one of the many HOG scenes.
3) In advanced mode, the game is not supposed to show you your task but on occasions, it shows up and then flickers off. This is likely another bug.
4) The game is pretty much fully voiced. This is supposed to be a good thing but the voice acting in all honesty, is crap. Furthermore, they don't match with the subtitles at all.
5) Despite being a HOG lover, I will be the first to admit that you often do some illogical things in HOGs. However, in this game, it takes the cake. Eg. Your task is to brew a truth potion and get the Count to drink it. What you do actually, is finding all the ingredients and brewing it RIGHT IN FRONT of the Count. After the potion is brewed, you hand it to the Count who actually said something along the lines of, wow, something healthy, give it to me quick. Like...seriously. What.

It's a mish-mash of old and new, an action shooter akin to Modern Warfare far back enough as to have the ability to lean and to have more than 2 weapons but not regenerating health or a grenade indicator.  The game mechanics promote a more tactical approach, as opposed to run-and-gun.  While that's also fairly effective, the best way to proceed through a level without taking is to check around corners, use cover, and use the environment to your advantage.  As there is no checkpoint system and you are forced to restart the entire chapter if killed, this forces you to at least be somewhat mindful of your surroundings.
Teammates are fairly competent at taking out enemies, although they do have issues with spotting them occasionally.  Enemy AI can be compared to the Call of Duty series: they spawn in, rush into cover, then periodically pop out and fire a few rounds in your general direction.  Thankfully, each individual enemy is hard enough that you'll only be up against a couple at a time, since a few well placed shots can potentially take a quarter of your health away in the blink of an eye.
Guns are fairly responsive and the aiming system makes it easy to scope in around a corner without having to move your hands off of the movement keys and scout out an alleyway.  Unlike the earlier Call of Duty games however, you can also lean upwards above cover or downwards if there are gaps in terrain.  While you can still get shot at when leaning your head out, this gives you a much better chance of assessing the situation without exposing too much of your vital organs.
All in all, a fairly decent shooter at its core if one can look past the outdated graphics and lack of proper widescreen support.

Project Zomboid is a zombie survival game with its own twists and turns, effectively separating it from the others.
First off, it takes a bird's eye view that kind of reminded me of the Sims. It's fairly simple to learn the game but at the same time it doesn't hold your hand either. You start off creating your character; their past career, their strengths, and the weaknesses to balance them out. You can even be deaf, which adds a rather unique and fun twist when playing the game. From there I'll let you figure out for yourself.
In Project Zomboid you're not some kind of badass who can slaughter hordes of zombies for days without any worries. A single mistake can end up getting you killed in the future, climbing through a broken window can lead to you getting a cut which can get infected; things such as hunger and thirst can affect your fatigue and how well you'll be at bashing heads in. And what's more, your character can become panicked which will decrease their accuracy. Overall this is not the story of how you came out on top, this is the story of how you died, of your last days, weeks, or months up until your death.
The game comes with a sandbox mode, which allows you to change a lot of different things such as item spawnrate, seasons, how long until water and electricity shut off, etc. What's more is you can even change the limits and behaviors of zombies! Have them blind or eagle eyed, deaf or perfect hearing, sprinters or slow shamblers, it's all up to you if you wish. A fun challenge is to make them like 28 Days Later zombies, nobody survives that one long.
What's more is the developers are always adding more. Soon NPCs will be added which will completely change up how the game can go, more cities will be added, cars, etc.
At first I had some doubts due to the absolute lack of certain essentials spawning, but the developer has actually addressed my concerns about that and they are currently working on it. It's not often a developer cares like that, and I'm glad to see it.
On a side note I don't know if anyone else has encountered this glitch, but according to my friend fire burns and spread forever, even across concrete.

Ive had mixed feelings about this game over the past while, I love it to death but its at such a crawl that it feels like the devs just straight up abandoned the game.
But they didnt.
They may be making very slow progress, and yes its fustrating, but they're still working on it. I wont say hard at work, because I honestly think they could be working harder, but nonetheless they're working on their game still. Most devs would just say the game is finished, and leave it at that, disappointing and angering everyone who was promised all these features like NPCs and such. But the Project Zomboid dev team is still working on their promises. I just hope that with all this time its taking them to release these features, they dont come out all ♥♥♥♥♥♥ and buggy and boring.
Vehicles have been in the works for a lot of time, and its really nice to see it almost finished (I think), but its honestly taking such a long time for these big updates I find myself taking breaks from this game for months, sometimes even a whole year or two. Although I always find myself somewhat hooked just the same as before when I return after that time, even if theres not too many new features, Project Zomboid has a solid base game design.
If you want a game that'll last you hundreds of hours, get this game
If you aren't a fan of extremely slow devolpment, consider this game on a sale
If you believe the game will never be finished at this rate, or that when it is the game won't be able to compare with the competition that the future of gaming holds, never get this game
But no matter what you think of the game, or how you feel about buying it, try to at least appreciate the effort the devs have put into this game and for how long they've been at it. Creating a game can be painfully upsetting, especially if its working on the same game for years and years. I may have a love-hate relationship with this game, but its all love-love with the devs.

At the time of this game (2004), it would be really hard to recommend it over Halo 2, Half-Life 2 or even Call of Duty 1. I would suggest a rental at best.
Yet I enjoyed this game more than the modern shooters today. Today, FPSes have too many crutches like regenerating health, hit markers, and checkpoints. This game has none of that. It's back to health kits and more prudent use of cover. There's no in-game objective markers either, so it's back to paying attention to your objective so you know what to do and where to go. And guess what, there's a BOSS FIGHT at the last level. It may not have been spectacular, but at least it wasn't a QTE boss where you just press a button and that's it.
Three complaints however: 1) the game was quite short. And multiplayer is dead. Yet a second playthough is worth it. 2) You cannot pick up enemy weapons. You must stick to the weapons that is suitable for the mission; and 3) there is no quicksave. If you die, you have to start over from the level. Another extreme.
At it's current price, it's a steal. It is sad that an average shooter from 2004 has more fun than some "highly-rated" shooters today. And no, I didn't play it when I was young. This is my first time with the game around the time of this review.

If youre looking for a cute mahjong puzzle game, this is pretty good.
In total, there are 120 puzzles, some difficult and some easy. My only complaint is that I wish there were some more of the more difficult ones. Some of these almost border on too easy, but for a starter at mahjong, theyre probably perfect. The game scores you on how quickly you can complete the puzzles, givng you a rating of 1 to 3 stars. The achieves are mostly for completing puzzles and completing them and getting 3 stars.
The game music is on a loop and it gets a bit old after awhile, but its pretty nice. Also, if you leave the game sound on, the game "meows" at you each time you match tiles, which can be kind of annoying after awhile.
Bug wise, I only found one. If I ran out of matches and the popup window came up to reshuffle, if I clicked the "shuffle" button too quickly, sometimes the tiles wouldnt respawn. Solution was to slow down and it worked perfect.
Overall, there isnt much to say. If you like mahjong, want a mahjong game thats good for a beginner, or a good kids puzzle game, could do much worse than this game. More than worth a recommend, especially if you catch it on sale

Meow Jong does exactly what it sets out for and provides a simple but fun single player experience. Now it’s really hard to mess up a more simple game I feel and the game proves correct with no bugs or any major glitches through the timescale in which I played. I’d recommend this game to young children and gamers who are looking for something simple and something which provides a little challenge.
Meow Jong provides quite a lot of content with around 120 boards which I found really impressive, navigating through them all was a bit tedious and painful because you have to click the arrow button which takes a long time because of the move animation. I’d love to see just a simple drop down box perhaps instead.
There is also a score system for each boards and the quicker you do them without hints the higher your score can get and you are rated out of three stars, with three stars being the highest. Getting three stars on some of the boards can be pretty challenging. The great thing about the boards is that they range from very easy to actually pretty hard boards, with some of the boards being really challenging for me to hit three stars.
The only downside is the audio track just loops over and over and over until you hum the music with insanity but fortunately you can turn the audio off. It would be nice for a variety of backdrops too or different noises and tiles. This game essentially does exactly what it sets out to do, and does it very well.
Happy Meowing :)

Well that was a bad purchase!
The opening screen looked quite good and I thought this could be a fun pirate hack and slash with a decent story and adventure element. Oh how I was wrong.
The graphics are quite nice and that is probably the only redeeming feature. What we have is a game full of bugs from the off, terrible voice work, dull swordfights, lack of free movement and ridiculous situations....oh...and did I mention the bugs? Gee, how can this be on sale for such a price!
So, after the nice opening screen we are deposited onto a jetty with the instruction of getting to the inn.
The first thing you notice is the lack of instructions for controls. They weren't clear, but could be figured out without too much stress. Then you realise you can only walk left or right. there is absolutely no free movement at all, which is ridiculous at times. One instance is when you enter the inn and go upstairs through a kind of stairway leading to the middle of a landing, you can't walk around the hole making the stairway though there is a clear way...no, you have to jump it. So daft.
Next issue is the voice work. The main character's voice is so horrendously contrived and what makes it even worse is when you die, and you die a lot, you have to suffer the same comments again and again just to get back to where you were.
Then we have the fighting. There are two movements with a sword you can make and no skill involved at all. There is the possibility to throw rum bottles, but I couldn't get the keys to work properly and there is a pistol that is about as much use as a cap gun. And to see it says on the game page on Steam 'Amazing Sword Fights' really does take the p***.
Next we have the absurd. Again in the inn, after a dialogue with what I assume must be the intended heroine, we are told that guards are coming for the character. So down we go into the main bar of the inn and kill two guards. Meanwhile nobody else in the inn is batting an eyelid. They are all (well 4 of them as that's all there are) continuing chatting and dozing while two guards are being killed 1 metre from them. Then the barman casually sells my character another bottle of rum. I mean....woooot?
Now for the bugs. I kept getting trapped in mid walk with nothing happening. Only my characters little legs were wiggling and but he was going nowhere. At the same time the enemies were just standing in front of my character also doing nothing. Another bug example is when my character was on a horse and the instruction flashed up to press the spacebar to make it gallop. Well, the horse continued to walk incredibly slowly, but my character was doing the amazing by shooting into the air by 6 foot from the saddle of the horse, each time I pressed it.
So, as you can see, this game is an absolute rip-off and a waste of money and I would recommend everyone to steer well clear of it and GameIndica.

This game has so much potential. Sure - zombie games are plentiful, but they are a kind of game that provides for endless amounts of joy.
is an overhead view survival game that looks like a polished piece of work. It has the tension and surival feeling that so many of its cousins also have.
Yet it's when one actually starts playing the game that the problems start. Firstly there's the controls. The mouse and keyboard combination works well most of the time, but the lack of conscious feedback from the zombie attacks mean that you cannot tell if you've successfully avoided an assault until the creature is lying on the floor dead. Or you are. Either way, it's difficult to tell until the battle is over.
Next comes the less crucial but still annoying issues of glitchy backgrounds. Whilst walking around, you will see backgrounds with different shaded areas that don't blend at all. This kind of amateur coding is to me evidence that this game needed proper project management and a proper QA system. When I work, things like this are picked up by testers. Here, they seem to be simply disregarded.
There's also the problem of character and weapon sprites lacking clear definition over their backgrounds. This, combined with the lack of proper detection of when the player is walking on the weapons means this game becomes an exercise in squinting at the screen trying to see where certain things are.
I've given NZP enough time. I'm going to delete it and concentrate on the better offerings out there. I'd advise anyone else out there to stay clear of this game too. Go with 7 Days to Die or even Day-Z for your zombie rewards.

This review isn't about the Day-1 DLC, because it's only cosmetic and so doesn't really bother me.  I don't know why you would base your entire marketing campaign around something gamers abhor, but I won't claim expertise on the subject.
This game has the potential to be a whole lot of fun, and I've played a lot of great matches that I really, truly enjoyed.  Why the negative review?  Because fun matches are few and far between.  Matchmaking usually takes around 5 minutes to find a single other player, leaving the remaining slots as bots, which have an IQ hovering somewhere just above potato.  The monster in every match is inevitably a Wraith, which has this ability called Warp Blast which players have complained about since the Beta.  It allows even a semi-competent Wraith to literally never be caught during the hunt.  This means the hunters chase the monster, doing absolutely nothing, for 15 minutes while it stages up.  Those of you doing the math will note that this means 20 minutes of downtime between actual, fun gameplay, whatever the outcome of the match.  This simply isn't acceptable.  The developers have acknowledged that this is a real problem, but instead of correcting it, after a month they released a patch fixing all of one bug that affects gameplay.
You've had consistent community feedback and sufficient time to fix this, TRS, and it saddens me to do this, but your game, in its current state, isn't fun, and I cannot recommend it to other players.

Don't listen to the haters.
It plays beautifully, looks gorgeous and offers a lot of variety right off the bat, since there's 12 very individual hunters and 3 equally individual monsters. You won't know what you're pitted against until the game begins, so people mix up their class/monster choices quite a lot, since it's impossible to know what you're up against.
I, myself, did get pretty annoyed by the skin store with micro transactions. But that was until I realised I actually liked the original skins more + the original monster skins are still the best for stealthing, and it seems like the devs are going to be hosting various community events where players are rewarded with free skins, which is really nice.
But the game is truly a lot of fun, especially when playing with friends. And if your friends are offline, you can always pick monster against a bunch of strangers, which is really intense. You will be extremely paranoid, since the hunters are desperately searching for you before you stage up. And with good reason, For once you reach stage 2, you already become an extremely powerful beast, and if you reach stage 3, then it'll take a pretty coordinated team of hunters to take you down. And let's face it. It feels pretty good to wipe out an entire team by yourself. You are the monster. You are the epic boss fight they talk about the next day.
And when playing hunters with friends, this game has really rekindled my long lost love called cooperative gameplay. In a lot of other recent games I've played with my friends, I felt like something was missing. We were playing together, we were winning and losing together. But we weren't all that dependant on each other. In this game, everyone needs to play their part, and communication is key. It's been a long time since I've played a game with my friends that was so dependant on good communication and tactics, and I absolutely love it.
So don't listen to the haters. If you and perhaps your friends think that this game looks interesting, then go for it. I, and all of my 8 friends who bought the game definitely recommend it.
(And if the price is holding you back, then look around various key retailer sites and find a bargain there. I got the PC Monster Race Edition for $67, still loving the game, and I'm just excited for the content that is to come)
Happy hunting for those of you I will encounter online!

Starting off as a class project from Tulane University in 2004, Khet has its roots buried in academia and education, and boasts an award from MENSA select on its store page and website. Khet 2.0 is a thinking mans strategic board game and plays very similar to Laser Chess, but also has elements akin to the 3000 year old game Go. The concept of Khet is somewhat similar to chess: destroy your enemy's Pharaoh with your Sphinx Laser via positioning and strategy, while protecting your own as he does the same.
The simple principles make for just as much memorization, logic and planning as Chess, but they reduce the emphasis on knowing moves, and as a result tend to make on-the-fly strategy a bit more open and accessible. Overall, Khet was perfect for me because as much as I love battling wits in Chess, I rarely have the time or patience for it and Khet 2.0 offers much faster games for those looking for them, but also offers support for asynchronous play, so I'm never hurried or rushed to make a move when I want to take my time or play casually.
The gameplay and fun of Khet comes down to pitting wits against friends, opponents or AI and approaching a win while mavourering an attack and simultaneously paying attention to defense and if you like the idea of an arguably simpler chess, it's an easy sell. What really matters for Khet 2.0 is the development team and how well they bring the concept to Steam. While there are technical issues and small problems with the title,
and despite flaws, the multiplayer platform is overall solid and works well.
* Asynchronous multiplayer support is a great feature and lets casual players like myself start a few games, play a move against different players and then forget about it for a day or two and only come back to those games when I need to. It also helps to reduce the problems associated with lower numbers of players in multiplayer.
* The choice of cross platform and non-DRM-restricted servers deserve special mention. They mean multiplayer is universal and should the game ever be made on other platforms, everyone would be able to integrate.
* Local multiplayer is also included and a pass-and-play mode for two people playing on the same computer (i.e. controllers or two keyboards, etc).
Khet 2.0 is a fairly simple concept, design and overall game which makes it ripe for improvement and addition over time. Unfortunately it's still slightly rough around the edges and has some minor issues that could affect your choice of a purchase.
The multiplayer functionality works, but it's somewhat lacking in depth, and the number of players online is a concern for a game like this. Matches are listed by tags showing the settings of the game, but there are no filter options whatsoever. I spent some time in the lobby and was only ever able to see the same 20 or so games already in progress, and with no spectator option, this was essentially pointless data to show. Similarly, chatting in game is impossible, and communicating via Steam is the only current option, which pauses gameplay and causes frustration.
An Eye of Horus Beam Splitter game piece was originally launched as an expansion piece for the board game and has been added as a DLC. While it does significantly affect gameplay, and is priced fairly, it's still hard to view this as anything other than a cash grab. Considering the price  of the original title and the presumably small amount of development time this took to add, it should be included in the original title instead of offered as DLC. The big block of DLC promotion on the title screen is also rather jarring.
* The graphics are fairly boring, bland and poor. While it doesn't affect gameplay and isn't a reason not to buy, it would've been nice to had some colour customization, themes, designs, backgrounds or anything to add to the very bland art design.
* The A.I. is somewhat unpredictable, which adds an element of chance, but also makes beating the A.I. very easy in many situations, even on extreme difficulties.
At the time of review, Khet 2.0 is available on Steam for £6.99/9.99€/$9.99 which, if you enjoy chess and are likely to put more than 10-15 hours into this title, is well worth the price. When weighed against competition however, it may feel a little overpriced. Hero Academy, for comparison, is a similarly simple asynchronous strategic board game and comes in at half the price, and Tabletop Simulator, a game with multiple gameplay elements, including Chess, Go, and tons more, is only around twice the price.
When on sale however, Khet 2.0 is a good deal for the strategic thinking lover. There's also a 2-Pack option which saves you a few extra bucks if you have a friend.
The Eye of Horus DLC includes the Beam Splitter piece originally offered as an expansion piece to Khet 1.0. It significantly affects gameplay and you can try it out in multiplayer games by finding someone hosting a game with it included (only the host needs have the DLC to use it). That said, it's, at least in my opinion, a bad move not to include this in the base game, so each to their own.

which comes from the same team under the same academic roots and is worth a look for anyone who liked Khet 2.0
