Let me say, I think Amnesia: The Dark Descent ruined this game for me.
Outlast starts off very strong, but loses tension quickly.  The game starts off with a lot of tension from atmosphere and I think simply not knowing what to expect.  You are then hit with jump scares that will 100% startle you.  The game is scary and disturbing, but by 2-3 hours in, the enemies aren't scary at all and the game becomes a bit of a chore.
Comparing this to Amnesia, Amnesia wasn't scary, it was terrifing.  I remember being a kid laying in bed at night wondering whats in the closet or what's outside the window, but too afraid to open my eyes and see there was nothing there.  That is the feeling TDD gave me, and just like the young me, usually nothing was even there.  It was just absolute raw terror, being so afraid to even move forward.
Outlast never inspired real fear like Amnesia did.  I never found myself hiding, wondering when would I be safe.  Occasionally there would be areas where you simply have to run.  The levels are designed in such a way, that running blindly will easily get you lost and stuck in a dead end room.  Which would be great if I was truly scared, but it ended up being annoying more than terrifing.  With Outlast, I never felt the sense of isolation and I feel it showed too much so it lacked suspense.  Once the suspense was dropped about an hour in, the fear went downhill quickly.

Red Orchestra 2 is possibly the best first person shooter I've ever had the pleasure of playing.
I wanted to write a review for this game for a while, but never got to doing it. Now with the November 2016 Steam Nominations I have a reason to for a badge. I nominated this game for the Test of Time award, because despite me having the game for almost a year now, I still enjoy this game as much as the day I recieved it as a gift from my friend.
[PROS]
+Fun overall
+Extremely realistic gunplay (weapon kick, reloading, MG barrel changes, etc.)
+Realistic and exciting vehicles
+AMAZING voice acting, especially Germans
+Scary artillery (that feeling of fear when you hear an artillery barrage about to land on you)
+Great audio and graphics (and I play on medium graphics)
+Many fun and nice looking maps
+Realisitic fear (flinching when being shot at, grayed out vision, character even yells/screams)
+One of the best damage systems for infantry (need to bandage, each body part is counted as seperate wounded entity)
+Small but (mostly) friendly community
+Historically accurate (if you care about those kinda things)
+Very good DLC (Rising Storm)
+Bayonet charges (For the Fatherland!)
[CONS]
-Rare/minor gunplay glitches (repeating reloading animations)
-Kinda sh*tty cover system
-Hard to get in server with players (they're either full or empty)
-Wierd vehicle physics (can drive straight over tank traps on a few maps)
-Minor bugs, nothing gamebreaking
Overall I love this game and even though Rising Storm 2 is coming out, I think it would be amazing if more people bought this game and got into it. If you're considering buying this game and you're interested in WW2 FPS's or teamwork, I definitely reccomend you buy this masterpiece, especially with the Rising Storm DLC.

I want to like this game.
...let me rephrase that: I want to
this game -- I do enjoy parts of it, like the atmosphere and the art style. It's an artsy game, but one that at least tries to still, you know, be a game.
Unfortunately, the gameplay, while not terrible, is still the weakest part of this game. The puzzles, while interesting brain-teasers, rely WAY too much on trial-and-error -- and in this game, error means death. Now, a lot of deaths in a game aren't necessrily a deal-breaker (think Super Meat Boy), but in this particular instance, they're very frustrating for two reasons. First, the checkpoints are just a bit too far back, meaning every time you die you have to walk back -- not a super long way, but just long enough to be annoying. Second, there's an achievement for beating the game in one sitting while dying no more than 5 times. The "beat in one sitting" part is interesting, but unless you have a walkthrough open constantly or memorize EVERYTHING, that achievement is basically impossible.
So ok, too many deaths are annoying in this case. The funny thing, though, is that I could look past the fact that I die a lot if nearly all of the deaths didn't feal cheap or out of my control. It's understandable to die before you figure out the puzzle -- it's annoying, but that's just how this game is. What crosses the line for me is the fact that it's incredibly easy to die even
you know what you need to do, largely because of how vague and undefined your abilities are. It's never clear exactly what your character is capable of, leading to multiple times when I was asking myself "can I make this jump" as death fast approached. I can
I'm supposed to jump over a buzzsaw, but without a clear sense of exactly what that means, I find myself still dying after the puzzle is "solved," which is what really gets my blood boiling.
On top of that, the aforementioned vageness makes the puzzles themselves unnecessarily obtuse, again because you don't know exactly what will and won't fly in this game. I'm constantly asking questions I should be able to intuit the answers to, from mundane things like  "will falling from here kill me," to more important things like "can I stand on this thing to cross this death-water." Since you never know until you try (and usually die), that just means more and more frustration.
Despite the rant above, I do think this game is worth playing, if only to see firsthand how an atmosphere can be achieved in a game like this. I don't, however, think this game is necessarily worth
, especially at full price. If you do buy it, be fully aware you're in for a frustrating time.

I picked this game up for nostalgia's sake because I remember playing the demo on one of those Original Xbox demo discs when I was a kid. Back then, it seemed like the most amazing thing ever. Any game that was gritty and realistic had to be amazing, right?
No. Today, this game is absolutely laughable.
Your teammates have some of the worst AI that I've ever seen. The most entertaining thing I saw in this game was watching Sgt. Gnucci charge up to an enemy, stop two feet away from him and start meleeing the air above the enemy's head all while being constantly shot. This lasted for about a minute until Gnucci retreated and let me kill the enemy.
This isn't to say that the enemy AI is any better; they constantly shift between having superhuman perception and instantly killing you without you ever knowing where they are and being completely blind and letting you kill them without ever reacting to your presence at all.
The environments are dull, the music is boring, but the voice acting is okay. That's the only positive thing I can say about this game: it has okay voice acting. That's not enough for an FPS to even be considered passable.
One can look at this and say, "It's an old game. It just hasn't aged well." That's a valid argument, but I'd like to point out that this game came out the same year as Halo 2, and that game holds up pretty well. It's at the other end of the decade-old FPS spectrum.
In summary, I'd rather hang out with Sgt. Johnson and kick some♥♥♥♥♥than watch Sgt. Gnucci get his♥♥♥♥♥kicked.

This game consists in hiding/runing away from robots of varied types, or shooting them if you manage to get hold of the appropriate firepower.
There ain't much to it really. Not even humour, which is what I was really looking forward to find. Quite bland references to what the devs believed to be "English culture", that's all this game has. Crikey!
As for gameplay, you'll find mostly anything you'd find in any other so called "survival" title.
There is food and drinks, but the need for them is only noticed via the ever decreasing vitality meter, which upon reaching zero, also decreases your health.
There are bandages you have to use when shot by robots or hurt somehow, otherwise you'll bleed to death.
There is stealth, which consists in hiding and/or moving silently. That includes not upsetting the wildlife, which will scramble all nearby robots in search for whatever caused the stir.
There are 5 different weapons (at least that I could find): a hatchet (melee), a pistol, a double-barrel shotgun, a bayonet and a rifle, this one very difficult to acquire. There is also a bear trap you can set to catch that distracted robot, or your dinner.
There are also a few items you can use to create a distraction so you can run away, or get the robots over so you can ambush them: a rock, empty bottles, a alarm clock (this one gives you time to hide and prepare before it goes off) and a toy train.
The only good thing it has going for it are the huge open world maps, but frankly, there ain't much exploration to be done. For example, you don't get enter buildings, you just access its inventory screen by interacting with the door.
It get's boring very quickly.... you almost forget that your main mission is to find some shiny stones you can stuff into what resembles the Stonehenge, in order to open an escape portal of some sort...
I say, old chap! Game's a load of old cobblers, and you'd be mad to pay more than a fiver for it!

Had this game been a third, or first-person shooter, heck maybe even with better animations and a better enviroment, this game would be mounds better to-- look at.

- The flashlight's batteries must all come from the dollar store, despite the model being that of a car battery; because your flashlight WILL run out in about a minute's time of continual usage.
- For a game supposedly made in the Unreal Engine, it certainly looks unpleasant considering the character models are stiff, lifeless, and lacking of any form of genuine animation. Think I'm talking about the zombies? HO HO! That's ONLY if you're lucky enough to find any. The playable character takes the spotlight on this.
- Be prepared to walk, and walk, and walk with no clear goal, or story to help set the game in motion. You'll be thrown into the game and a random grab-bag of items, and you just "SURVIVE".
- The BIGGEST problem with this game. The meter on the top-right. Apparently, you are infected with... Something... Maybe not, I'm unsure. It's never explained, at all. You have to keep a close eye on what seems to be either '
', or some silly mechanic where blood slowly reaches your brain in hopes of killing you via aneurysm over how boring this game is.
tl;dr -
Maybe if you're high on Percocet, and wish to hold your breath everytime you're chased by zombies.
Not if you think torturing yourself with bad games is worth murdering your wallet.

*This review is written based on the early access beta version 0.9.2. This is by far the most balanced version I have seen them release yet but there may be details in this review that are different in release*
DotE is a deceptively deep and amazingly difficult game. On the surface it appears a simple rogue-like dungeon crawl, however delving deeper in to the mechanics reveals a more in depth gambling game of risk taking and both strategic and tactical decisions.
If you are a fan of knowing what is coming and being able to easily calculate the best odds to victory, this is not the game for you. The critical data you need to formulate exact decisions is hidden from you, hidden behind who knows how many doors you have yet to open. Mistakes and miscalculations are dealt with harshly.
If you are okay at failing and having to best guess decisions and adapting quickly to a changing situation, this is a unique gem of a game that does a fantastic job of blending several genres in to one.
The premise of the game is simple. You are trying to escape a dungeon, starting at floor 1 and exiting somewhere down the line (I believe the number of floors is based on difficulty). Each floor has a number of rooms you can explore by opening doors, which acts as a turn based mechanism. Cooldowns count down by each door opening and your resource production increases on a per door basis.
The idea is you search for the exit to the next level, and then carry your all-important crystal to the exit. Each room can contain any number of surprises both good and bad, and each room can have module nodes that allow you to build your defense/production structures.
The game gets interesting on many levels. You can build tower defense like structures on minor nodes in rooms, and some rooms have 1 major node that allows you to build what is normally a resource producing structure. You have 4 resources to juggle each serve their own purpose. You have industry that allows you to build on major/minor nodes, science, which can allow you to research new modules and upgrade existing, food which you use to heal your heroes and level them up, and dust which is probably the most critical as it is used to power rooms on a floor.
Powering rooms is the most critical element, I have found. Powering a room, allows structures to be built in it and allow those structures to function. If power gets cut to a room, all the modules inside cease functioning. Even more importantly is un-powered rooms are in the dark and if they are unoccupied by a hero can cause monsters to randomly spawn each time a door is opened.
This is where your strategic choices compound. By choosing which rooms are un-powered, and which you power with your dust, you can create choke points and lanes in the dungeon where monsters will spawn. You can use this to build defensive areas that whittle down the monsters as they move towards their target or your crystal, and place combat efficient heroes close to the action in order to respond to the mass of monsters. You will run in to situations where you just simply do not have enough dust to power every room you want to, and you will have to adapt your defenses on the fly to the situation.
You do not know how many more doors are in the wing of the dungeon you are in. You do not know how much dust you will gain in those rooms. You could doom yourself to being hit from two sides without the industry to provide defenses in both directions. You can and will get easily overwhelmed when your decisions do turn against you.
The heroes you are provided with to help you escape are varied and each can do very different things for your group. Some are good front line fighters. Some are very quick and can respond to a crisis in an unexpected area, or even defend a couple locations each turn. Some are very good at making others better. Some can accentuate your resource income. Some can do a little of a couple things. Their system of leveling is pretty straight forward and there are no choices in leveling, only if you want to spend the food to level. Keep in mind food is used for leveling and for healing, so the more efficient you are in your fights the quicker you can level.
The game also does a very good job at tempting you to take risks. Don’t use the food to heal so you can level faster, instead kite monsters to defenses. Don’t build defenses in that far off location to save industry, etc. Usually you pay a hefty cost for taking chances, like starting a new game. However, that doesn’t mean you won’t take one or two of these risks…
When you finally have explored your floor, you must carry your crystal to the exit. One of your heroes picks it up and has to walk it there, taking a penalty to movement while the rest of your team and defenses try to keep the crystal carrier alive while monsters start to spawn from every dark room. This only ends when you either get overwhelmed, when you exit, or when the crystal carrier dies. On to the next floor you go, keeping your industry, science and food supplies however losing your dust.
The game is amazingly addictive and deep. It is also frustrating and unforgiving. You will die many many many times and only win a handful. Most of the times when you die you will realize what went wrong (once you learn the factors of the game). Occasionally you will make a mistake knowing it will cost you in the end and sure enough attrition takes it’s toll.
The game is still in beta, and while an excellent game could still be improved. The random layout of the floors is awesome but sometimes unlucky streaks make a floor painstakingly hard (even for DoTE standards). Other times you can cruise through a floor. Sometimes you get a full party of 4 with excess recruits by floor 3. Other times you are on floor 5 going to 6 with only 1 recruit found and you struggling to keep up.
Tldr; If you get frustrated easily, hate dying, hate losing, and believe only when you win is a game enjoyable this is not a game for you. If you love challenging games with interesting twists, and calculated risks with a simple yet deep resource management this may be your new addiction. I loved FTL and I really love this game too.

The music, as stated, is also intentionally calming.  The background pads drone as each connection is audibly accentuated with a soft syntheized pop. 3: Innovation
Shocker, the creators of L4D decide to make an FPS based around 4 characters, hunting or killing a lot of something. *cough* L4D's exact play style *cough*. Now, no disrespect, but this kind of thing is a one trick pony. Once you know the map, you know where everything is, and how to defeat it or get it. The only innovation was making the hunted not just some lame A.I. and giving the controls to a human.

After a horrendous and frightening experience of an overnight zombie raid, my house was in ruins. All food was consumed, crops destroyed, ammo non existent. My weapons damaged, my body aching, my mind lost. I was wounded and in desperate need of medical attention. After rummaging through piles of bodies, I managed to find a dirty bandage. "I can't use this..." I said to myself, and after long contemplation and painful thinking I decided against it. "If I can clean it, I can use it" I dragged my broken body across half of town, exploring every inch of land in order to find cleaning materials. My last sip of water felt like days ago. I came across a shanty area,  a settlement of plywood, corrugated metal, sheets of plastic, and cardboard boxes. Wildly scavenging through heaps of sh#t, yes! A half empty bottle of bleach.
I moved my way to a quiet and not known location, where I was able to sit and gather my breath. Frantically scouting to make sure I was ok, still sat down. I looked up into the sky and dreamed of what life used to be. "I need this bandage cleaned", opening up my bag to take out both the bandage and the bleach. "There is no threat here, take your time" I wish I had a mouse! I must of double tapped my track pad. With the bandage in my left hand, and the open bottle of bleach in my right, the double tap of the trackpad forced me to consume the bleach. Every last drop.
Stories were told of my valiant display of british grit, fighting off the barrage of zombies and ultimately falling to my death through a 16 hour massacre. At least, thats what the stories told. If only they knew the truth of my stupidity.

An amazing isometric time-killer! The Indie Stone does not fail to deliver when it comes to zombie survival! I've played this for quite some time but lately my time is running low so I don't play it as often.
In a nutshell, Project Zomboid is an apocalypse simulator on the road to greatness. I've dumped quite a few hours into building bases, fighting zombies, and restarting characters. Unlike other zombie games, it's simplified graphics and isometric gameplay allows for more in-depth features such as construction and hunting.
Do not underestimate the ability of this game to scare the pants off of you just because it's isometric. Everything behind you goes black, so you can't use your mystical powers to know what's behind you. Beware your trait choice. If you choose to be hard of hearing or choose poor eye-sight, your game WILL become harder. This game REQUIRES headphones and audio to play. You can't mute the game to listen to music, otherwise you'll be in-game, trigger an alarm without knowing and get swarmed and chewed on because you decided it was a fantastic idea to blast Dubstep, House, or whatever while the zombies were loudly smashing the windows. Audio plays a major role in the game, muting the audio will severely affect the gameplay as the sound of muffled thumping or pounding on the windows are your main signs to get to the heck out now because your character is panicking about that zombie peeping in on your nightly shower.
Aside from zombies munching on your delicious giblets, your character has been given moods. This is the precursor to the much anticipated NPC survivors where bad interaction will put your character into a bad mood. As of right now, your character can become self-destructive through depression, boredom, tiredness, and anxiety. During encounters and explorations Panick, pain, encumberance, and fatigue. Even the elements have it out for you! Sickness and infection added to the stewing pot of hinderence makes it very unwise to step out into the rain or go buck wild naked during the winter. Temperature moodlets make it advisable to grab winter and summer clothes.

Superhot is an original shooter that isn't really a shooter.  It's really something you probably haven't seen before. The writing of the game is very unique and the gameplay is probably a category on it's own. The time based movements and actions have been taken to the next level. When you don't move, time passes very slowly, and when you move, time passes normally. Have you ever watched the Matrix movie and felt like : "Man, this is cool, wish I could do that! " ? Well in this game you can pretty much do that. You can dodge bullets, you can punch enemies really quickly, you can shoot a bullet at an enemy, then throw the gun at another while taking control of an enemy that fired bullets at you, all in just a couple of seconds. This game allows for a crazy combinations of actions, and when you complete the level, it lets you see what you did but in real time, so it looks really neat most of the time.
I however got this game in a bundle and it was really cheap. I only recommend this game if you find it in a cheap bundle or if it is for 5€ or less. While I admire the idea of this game and the exectution of developer's ideas, this game can get really frustrating (especially in the end of the game), and the game is really short (2 hours, and thats when you fail a lot) for the asked price.

Video Review:
Echo of Soul is a very strange MMORPG It was released in 2013, still sees updates bringing fixes and new content to this very day, but I’m not sure how given its playerbase.
Echo of Soul plays kind of like World of Warcraft with its tab targeting system, but it’s abilities seem a lot more thought out. Every class is very unique in the way their skills work. It doesn’t feel like as much of a copy & paste with different effects for each class as other MMORPGs of this style tend to. Rogues are very combo-based where one ability sets up another ability and that ability sets off another, whereas none of the other classes are really set up like that. I consider this a good thing because it really does allow for many playstyles, and that’s something I didn’t really expect from a game with tab targeting. The fact that each class has it’s own path and each path has a branching tree of skills means there’s plenty of customizing you can do to get the perfect gameplay experience for you. Unfortunately though the classes are gender locked. Want to be a male archer? A female rogue? Too bad! So that’s a pretty disappointing.
The story of Echo of Soul is very generic for an MMORPG. Once upon a time a thing happened, now we’re all getting invaded. You play as the chosen one even though thousands of other chosen ones are running around. End of the world scenario. You show up and save the day. That kind of stuff. But I must admit the individual quests have some quality to them as some of them are either really funny or really ♥♥♥♥ed up. The funny comes in because almost every single quest title is pun or a reference that helps give you a laugh every time you start something new. In terms of ♥♥♥♥ed up? There’s an early on mission where you help some guy find his little sister and you find her corpse lying among a bunch of monsters and her clothes are all tattered. You show her amulet to her brother, he screams for two pages of text, and then that’s it story complete. The quests are delivered in the typical read a bunch of text format, no voice acting involved. Some rare quests every hour or so give you a cutscene that’s typically rendered well, but with rancid voice acting. Still, it’s a nice change from MMORPGs that don’t even put the effort into simple cutscenes.
The graphics of Echo of soul are, well, garbage. Look at them yourself. This game released in 2013 yet it looks like it released a decade ago at least. They were bad for when the game released, and they’re even worse now. If you’re looking for a pretty world to experience? It’s not here. The render distance is so bad things are always popping in ten feet in front of you with every step you take. The animations all look rather strange too. The audio is decent in every aspect but the voice acting. All of the voice acting is just bad.
Now a good thing to remember in a review of an MMO is that it is supposed to be an MMO. This brings me to the biggest flaw Echo of Soul has. The game is basically dead. The active playerbase is very small and the way guilds and the chat work makes it hard to find a community to become a part of in-game. It would require ventures to forums at least. If you start up Echo of Soul then you’ll likely be signing up for a singleplayer experience in a game designed for a large community. This isn’t the biggest deal since Party quests are soloable and dungeons are soloable as well as a feature of the game. A very smart feature of the game.
The game is F2P so as you can imagine it has some monetization. There’s a cash shop filled mainly with conveniences so it’s not that bad. What’s really bad is that around level 7 or so and again at level 60, the game gives you a quest that can only be completed by purchasing something from the cash shop. That’s kind of a scummy thing to do. Teaching someone they can buy is one thing, but rewarding them with quest rewards? Kind of bad.
Overall Echo of Soul was a decent game for when it came out. The problem is other than the uniqueness of each class? The game really has nothing special about it. Nothing in this game stands out. It is very very close to being a carbon copy of World of Warcraft. And unless you enjoy reading all the quests it’s really just not fun since the quests are the game’s only big strength. Echo of soul gets a 3/10. By the standards of MMORPGs in 2017, it’s a bad game. While I did have SOME fun in it? I wouldn’t recommend it to most gamers. It’s really not even worth the install.

National Zombie Park promises a realistic survival roguelike experience in a world infested by zombies: you're thrown into a forested area with some loot nearby and asked to survive as long as possible with both zombies and the progressive infection (yes, you start infected) trying to kill you.
What follows is a laggy, uninspired and ultimately quite dull romp in a barebones area while being chased by huge hordes of zombies that'll kill you in one hit.
-none
-unremarkable graphics still manage to create several framerate drops, how this can happen considering the top down perspective and how little is on screen is beyond me
-few sounds and they're all very weak: weapons sound tinny and zombie noises are pretty bad: there's also no music at all, not even on the main menu
-horrible animations, zombies just flail their arms awkwardly, reloads and melee bashes look very artificial
-awkward movement, you're not much faster than a zombie and can't sprint at all thus making escapes impossible
-no story whatsover, no goals, no leaderboards, nothing
-game world feels barren, just a few repeated tree models, some houses, fences, rare bunkers and that's all
-unfair loot spawn could leave you overflowing with batteries for your flashlight but with no antidote whatsoever thus forcing you to die and restart
-one hit kills coupled with bad framerate makes surviving a question of luck
-no way to edit keybinds unless you want to mess with the game files
-game only explains the controls, heck it doesn't even tell you that you're infected or how infection works
-you won't be surprised to know multiplayer is dead
National Zombie Park is functional, apart from the crippling framerate, but the fact it works will just let you experience a game that quickly becomes boring due to the very basic gameplay. Why would you be playing this and starting over and over? There's no story to uncover, no random objectives to complete, no high scores to compare...you just aimlessly wander the mostly empty area hoping to find some ammo and antidote while also praying that the game's framerate won't betray you when a zombie is near.
It's not only boring, it's pointless, and these- in my book-are two cardinal sins in a game: add to this the technical problems and the low production values and you'll see how this game is one I can't recommend at all. Even the devs probably realized this was a total mess since they abandoned it a few days after release.

It seems to me that hybrid-genre games are getting more and more common these days. I've seen RPG/FPS (Borderlands), FPS/TD (Sanctum), FPS/Roguelike (Rogue Shooter), Strategy/Roguelike (FTL), RPG/Puzzle (Puzzle Quest), RPG/TD (Gemcraft), and...whatever the hell kind of mix Desktop Dungeons is, just to name a few.
Now we have Dungeon of the Endless bringing Roguelike/TD to the table. Honestly, it's scary how accurate that genre alone describes DotE. We have RPG characters exploring random dungeons and staying permanently dead when they die (textbook definition of "Roguelike") and a base to protect with towers (textbook definition of "TD"). That's pretty much the entire game.
It's a solid game, which requires you to plan your strategy well; it's scary how quickly a solid game can come crashing down in an instant.

Let me say, I think Amnesia: The Dark Descent ruined this game for me.
Outlast starts off very strong, but loses tension quickly.  The game starts off with a lot of tension from atmosphere and I think simply not knowing what to expect.  You are then hit with jump scares that will 100% startle you.  The game is scary and disturbing, but by 2-3 hours in, the enemies aren't scary at all and the game becomes a bit of a chore.
Comparing this to Amnesia, Amnesia wasn't scary, it was terrifing.  I remember being a kid laying in bed at night wondering whats in the closet or what's outside the window, but too afraid to open my eyes and see there was nothing there.  That is the feeling TDD gave me, and just like the young me, usually nothing was even there.  It was just absolute raw terror, being so afraid to even move forward.
Outlast never inspired real fear like Amnesia did.  I never found myself hiding, wondering when would I be safe.  Occasionally there would be areas where you simply have to run.  The levels are designed in such a way, that running blindly will easily get you lost and stuck in a dead end room.  Which would be great if I was truly scared, but it ended up being annoying more than terrifing.  With Outlast, I never felt the sense of isolation and I feel it showed too much so it lacked suspense.  Once the suspense was dropped about an hour in, the fear went downhill quickly.
It is good for first 2 hours and after it it starts to be boring.

There is a reason Amplitude is the only game company that I trust giving my money to for early access titles, and Dungeon of the Endless is a great showcasing of why.
To start off on early access (so I can remove this part when the game fully releases, or forget and at least have a seperate section for it), it feels complete with the minor exclusion of one or two bonus elements that don't detract from the game experience by missing, it feels polished and not completely unfinished, and most of the game "feel" is there. The only downside to possibly playing this on early access is getting yourself burnt out for when the actual game comes out- there are a few features not implemented yet, but development is speedy and happening every week or two.
The graphics and music are amazing, and stylistically what you'd expect from other Amplitude games. The quirky humour you see in sci-fi games comes along too, retaining a serious feel while putting in the odd joke here and there (for example, there is a convict who is 100% convinced she is a spider and her description says she sometimes attempts to climb up walls), and overall the game is beautiful to look at and listen to.
The gameplay might seem a bit overcrowded with buzzwords by reading the features list (My first thought: "A turn based tower defense roguelike squad based exploration game? Is there mining and crafting and fighting zombies too...?" ) but it somehow gets pulled off perfectly without feeling like there is way too much crap being thrown at you to juggle. Every feature is used and balanced- you need your towers to survive as much as you need to buff your heroes. The game is surprisingly simple, but unforgiving. I never beat the game to the "under construction" point, but I did get close- where it stands in early access, the dungeon is quite short, about 2-3 hours of solid playtime to get as far as you can if you rush.

Will probably appeal to my generation (I'm 30) more than today's gamer, because this game embodies the type of shooters that we grew up with and includes none of today's modern conveniences/handicaps: There's no automatic health regeneration, no automatic ammo refill, and , as far as I can tell, no quicksaving. Instead, you'll have to pick up health packs, scavange dropped ammo from enemies, and complete missions to save your game and progress. Some of the missions can be somewhat challenging, and you never know if there'll be a mob of enemies, a tank, or an RPG around the next corner. The story is okay (so far), and it's complete with decent voice acting and fully animated cutscenes in between each misison.
Kids, if you want to know the kind of game we frittered away hours with before Modern Warfare, then buy this game! Fellas, if you want a trip down memory lane, then you owe it to yourself to buy this game!

This is a great game.  As a big fan of Go (igo, Baduk, etc.) this has a good number of qualities of the go game.  First, its rules are simple. Movement of pieces is very simple and can be understood very quickly.  The format of the game is quite logical and without reading the rules, it only took one or two games to understand all the movement and basic strategy of the game. Second, it has some depth to the game play.  It is not so simple to have standard moves (at least not for me yet), though it may at some point for me in the future.  The good thing is that there is a bit of repeatibility in play because of the different setups for the board.
I have played on all three board types and I can now definitely say that this game has a good future.  The other board types are quite challenging compared to the first, and the strategy definitely has to change for each board type.  That makes it a bit more interesting since there may be even more unique ways to play in the future.
I am quite happy with this game. It mixes the qualities of Chess with go by adopting the simplicity of go, but the faster pace of chess and removal of pieces off the board.  With the rating system, I am also looking forward to playing online at some point.
I should also note, having now played the game a bit and beaten the computer AI on Hard level, the pace is not too slow.  Many times when you get into the harder levels, the AI slows considerably.  One of the things I like about this game is that it has a relatively quick pace (can finish a game within 20 minutes easily), and it still maintains some interesting depth.  I assume the elite and impossible levels will get even slower, though.  It is good to maintain a reasonable pace, and I hope the advanced AI games can still finish within an hour.
Once I play some online games, I will again, update this review.

A surprisingly deep strategic dungeon defense game with excellent pacing, sense of progression, and replayability.
Premise: Your spaceship crashland on an unknown planet. You find yourself burried into an unknown facility, trapped, with only the hope of find an exit out of this treacherous dungeon. WIth a team of heroes, you must plan a strategic escape by moving your ship's powercore to elevator. Along the way, without knowing where your destination lies, you must open doors to dark rooms populated with monsters, hazards, or if you are lucky, treasures, recruits, resources and special events. One of your main decision lies in using the game's main currency to power rooms, preventing monsters from spawning. You also have to allocate resources to build defenses, improve your hero, and invest in long term tech growth.
===Review===
*Note: this is a beta review.
Gameplay:
+++ Great balance betwen Macro and Micro management. Macro involves resource allocation, where and when to power/unpower rooms, tech progression, defense placement and combination. Micro involves allocating heroes to point of defense, creating chokepoints, using abilities, etc. This is a huge plus because at any given point in the game, you will always make meaingful decisions for which you can be rewarded or punished.
+++ Great Pacing. Pacing is determined by opening a door, which begins a new round: you gain resources, monsters spawn, you fight, etc. You can open as many doors and at whatever speed you wish; in doing so you dictate the flow of action. There's definitely as sense of joy as you become better at the game, especially in regards to making efficient decisions and this becomes every evident in your pacing.
+++Customizable experience = Replayability. You can choose heroes and your spaceship in this game, which modifies the starting and persistent conditions of the game. For example one of the spaceship in the game changes the number of starting heroes from two to four and boosts their damage, but disables certain resources/defensive structures.
+++ RNG = Replayability. Many factors are random as you progress through a level, such as what items you find, when/where you find merchants, which/when recruits you find, what special events occur, which monsters spawn, level layout, etc.
--- Uneven difficulty. Do not make this mistake of using difficulty metric from other games. EASIEST difficulty = NORMAL,  play on easiest difficulty to learn game's mechanics. But once you've learned the mechanics, you'll find that easier difficulties take away from the play of the game, as abundent resources, weak monsters invalidates the need for better strategy.
Strategic Elements:
+++ Monsters have differentiated goals. Different monsters will prioritize different targets, be it your heroes, resource producing structures, defensive structures, NPCs. As such their pathing is different. Learning such differences adds depth to  the game.
+++Well defined Hero roles. Most heroes in the game are specialized, which means that for any given situation you'd prefer some heroes over the rest due to their stats and abilities. This is good because your hero composition matters.
+++All Hero stats are relevant. This is impressive because 99% of games out there get this wrong.
+++All but one building in the game is useful.
--- Why is this building in the game???
--- Need more environmental hazards, such as cloud of slowing.  I feel like this aspec has so much potential, as it makes certain locations more strategic.
---Needs more NPC types to protect. The merchant is great for the game since the bonus of keeping him alive is huge. But the game would be better if there are more NPC types that offered different benefits.
Interface
+++ Clutter free
--- Skills need more information
--- Need customization hotkeys
--- Why is the Inventory window separate from hero window
Visuals
+++Great color pallete
+++Stylized characters
--- hard to tell towers apart if build in very close proximity
---hard to tell some lower tier offensive buildings apart from others due to their small size
Theme
+++ Interesting character bios
+++ Flavorful naming schemes
--- Wierd assortment of obsolete technology and futuristic technology for item choices.

Verdict:
Without a doubt, this game is worth a buy if you are interested in the defense genre.  Though it's hardly fair to pin this game down to any one thing in particular, as you'll find many elements from different genres that will add to your enjoyment, be it strategic planning/resource management, hero building/progression, basebuilding/defense, and a small slice of MOBA-esque hero micromanagement. In the end, all these things would be meanlingless if they didnt add up to a cohensive whole, but in this case, they do, and the game shines because all the parts ultimately add up to form a more intricate and interesting whole.

Background story is simple: prisioner ship goes kaput, escape pod is ejected and crashes down on an uncharted planet, you start with two controllable chars and all you need to get out the planet, bringing with you the crystal-shaped generator thru ten levels. Open rooms, power then with Dust, craft modules, buy equips from (eventual) merchants, find survivors to enlist (up to 4 including the 2 you begin with), leave each level (and eventually the place) by finding the exit and getting the Generator there. Easy as pie (you wish!).
The Resources are the useful stuff you'll need to survive; Industry (to make modules), Science (to search for better/improved modules), Food (healing and leveling up) and the most important and difficult to get: Dust. It powers the rooms, keeling then illuminaned, because dangers prown unlit rooms and also important, you buy equipment from the merchants. You can't manufacture it; only finding when opening rooms, killing monsters.
Did I say monsters? Yeah, the place is infested.. the thing is, they stay on dark places until you open a door. They also spawn on unlit opened rooms,
Each char has his/her/its own characteristics and quirks, when you enlist the new ones and keep then alive for 3 levels, they become available when you start a new game
Since it's a rogue-inspired game, I must warn; the chars can (and will) die easly if you don't do it right. If the monsters kill you, game over, if they reach the generator, and destroy it, game over (even if they don't, each hit can eat your precious Dust).
Finally, on winning a 10-lv run, depending on how you did it, you can get a new pod (just got the Infirmary)

I love the concept of this game, the asymmetrical gameplay aspects are what really shine in this game. When you add ontop of that the beautiful graphics that they developed for the game and the relatively low amount of bugs you end up with a very interesting game, in concept. Where Evolve truly falls flat is the gameplay, the gameplay is fun and interesting the first few matches and then you are stuck in a rut of repetition. I had a ton of fun playing this game for the first five hours as I unlocked new hunters/monsters and learned the games mechanics. However once you break through the admittedly short progression wall there isnt much left to do, thats not even calling into light the absolutely ridiculous progression system itself. I cannot stand the fact that I have to depend on Daisy through two tiers of Maggies expertise tree just to level up. Its basically a super out of your favor RNG roll whether or not daisy will revive a team mate when they go down, theres no skill involved to get it to happen, its just whatever she wants to do when she feels like it.
On to my next point, the game lacks content. Theres no story, none. I have no ♥♥♥♥ing clue what any of the game is about, I dont know what the monsters are, who the hunters are, what the planet is, why the planet is valuable, nothing. The only "story" in the game is the quick 10 second blurbs of conversation between the hunters while waiting to drop from the ship. Then once you do drop from the ship either the game lasts 2 minutes and you catch the monster level 1 in a dome and wreck him, or you end up running fruitlessly across the map for 15 minutes until the monster hits level 3 and wrecks you. If there was more interaction between the hunters and the game while the hunting is being done then maybe it would be interesting, but in actuality its just looking for one of four basic queues showing the last known location of the monster. Not fulfilling, not interesting, repetative, over-priced, I have heard this little bit I am about to spew over and over again from so many people and I hate to jump on the band wagon and over hash it as well but its a valid point! The game is not worth the price, it would be a great f2p game or a $20 arcade game but for a AAA $60 box cost its not worth what you get.
TL;DR
Beautiful Scenery
Little bugs/glitches
Asymmetrical Gameplay done well
Lack of Content
Lack of Story
Poor Progression Model
Over-priced
If you have money to burn and want to play a game with a neat concept and very rare spurts of fun gameplay with lots of time to kill inbetween this is for you. If you are like me and you dont have tons of cash to burn and have to budget your game purchases skip this for now and wait for a price drop or more engaging content and story.

Shadow Ops: Red Mercury is one of those shooters that's a lot of modern shooters traced their lineage from, but relied on mechanics that are just too old and unrealistic enemies to provide "challenge", resulting in a game that just doesn't accomodate casual players at all.
The plot is pretty much cliche: a nuke had fallen into the hands of a terrorist, and you've been sent in to neutralize it. Except obviously, you got ambushed this way and that, enemies everywhere, and the enemy's about to get away... and... jump to couple weeks ago, when the whole mess got started.
The missions basically mostly have you running around, alone, though occasionally you'll see your teammates shooting at the rest of the enemies, but mostly it's you, everything from taking out AAA to holding back a wave of enemies with a HMG to go through sniper alley, and so on and so forth. Those who play COD / COD MW will see a lot of similarities between this and their game.
The game is a first-person shooter, though it has rudimentary cover shooting where you can lean around certain covers. How you do it through is a bit dodgy as it involves holding space while pressing left or right. There is no auto-heal. You are constantly on the lookout for first-aid kits and ammo. And enemies can pop up anywhere, even from behind you, as you are constantly looking for enemies around a blind corner and such. Fortunately, there is no "door breach" scenarios (i.e. Matrix-style shoot enemies in the head sequence)
This game is old and the poly count of the models aren't that high, even at max everything settings. But the models aren't *that* bad. Sound is actually quite good, as are the music.
The problem is there are just too many "tired tropes" in the game. There are so many betrayals, and the bad guy always get away... or does he? And then there's the question just how many bad guys are there that there's not enough good guys to deal with them (well, all except you). And enemies that pop up behind you, around corners, and so on? BORING! Add some cliche like "bad Russians", "one-armed merc", "I leave no witnesses", "he's getting away!", "take out that tank", etc. and it's getting a bit tiresome.
All in all, if you want to play a good shooter, play a modern one.

Despite the intimidating 'Realistic' tag, Red Orchestra 2 manages to perfectly blend together the realism and clunkiness of hardcore FPS games with the fast pace and simplicity of more accessible arcade games.
The game does this by introducing to you a very easy to understand tutorial, helping you to get used to the clunky, yet still smooth (Yes, I realize that this is an oxymoronic statement) movement system before allowing you to let loose on the shooting range and giving you a taste of its satisfying gunplay. What follows may be contradictory to some and that is a tutorial of commander/squad leader-based commands which will probably intimidate a newer player, possibly a way of telling them to NOT be a Commander/Squad Leader unless enough experience has been gained. The overall pace and movement system is just right to give a feeling of tension, vulnerability and weight while still being smooth and not too sluggish for someone who is used to arcadey movement systems of other games. Weapons also feel, sound, look and hit hard with full force and momentum with balance being good from what I have experienced. The clunkiness and the nature of one-shot kills also help to reinforce the roles of each weapon with the bipod-restricted, one-shotting rapid-fire Machine Guns being deadly in well-chosen positions and the lack of flashy dodge maneuvers making riflemen vulnerable to Assaults with their SMGs at close range and vice versa beyond that.
The sounds are also top-notch in which they all add up to create an atmosphere that's as comparable to the incredible sound design of Battlefield 1. The guns sound powerful, the screams and voice acting are well done (Atleast in native language) and the incredible, yet very underrated soundtrack helps to further the depressing (Or in some cases, heroic) tone of the game. Linking to the voice acting, the devs have also done a good job humanizing the 'evil' side of the war AKA the Germans and the Japanese with matching soundtracks and depressing voice lines for them. The only issue I personally have with the sound design is the sound of explosions where in some cases, they are quieter than a pistol shot. Other than that, the sound design of this game is one of the best I've heard.
Balance is also well done as each side in the Eastern Front seems to be able to properly counter the other with the exception of the Russian machine gun simply being outmatched by the German MG34/MG42. The balance for Rising Storm AKA the Pacific Theater portion of the game is also well done where the Americans' advantage in technology such as flamethrowers and the abundance of automatics like the M1 Garand being able to be countered by proper use of the unique tactics of the Japanese with their Banzai Charges and booby traps. This is an ideal example of asymmetrical warfare done right in a multiplayer game.
Performance and graphics are really the only things that are keeping me from fully enjoying Red Orchestra 2 as stutters are frequent and overall performance being inconsistent. The graphics are fine for a 2011 game, but I cannot tell you how much money I'll be willing to pay just to play this game on Killing Floor 2's improved version of the Unreal Engine with its very good optimization and visuals.
Overall, I'd say the game is 100%
the full price and the still alive and dedicated community along with the upcoming Rising Storm 2 Vietnam expansion makes it never too late to experience the game.

Now for the real review.
Five Nights at Freddy's is an indie, click-and-point, horror game. You play as the protagonist, Mike Schmidt, who is a security guard at a local Chuck E Cheese-like establishment, Freddy Fazbear's Pizzeria. During the day, the animatronics there, Freddy Fazbear, Chica the Chicken, Bonnie the Bunny, and Foxy the Pirate entertain the children. At night, however, they're out to kill you. Using limited power and security cameras you must survive for five nights from 12 AM until 6 AM. If the animatronics catch you, they'll stuff you into an empty Freddy Fazbear suit. For those hesitant about buying the game because it's scary, it isn't really. There's only jumpscares (turn the volume down, headphone users!), and people over react to the game on YouTube and Twitch all the time. It's a gem of a game, and if you like it, I recommend the other 3 (soon to be 4) games in the series.
It's the most innovative shooter I've played in years.

To Indie Stone (PZ Developers):
The animations were good enough  3 years ago.  I don't play PZ for the visuals, I play it for gameplay depth, simulation aspects and atmosphere.
VOIP  just seems to be a quick and easy way to try to reduce the complaints of emptiness/isolation in the game world.   The real way to solve the feeling of emptiness would, of course, be to add multiplayer and/or non-player-characters.
So focus on the strengths of your game.  If I want visuals, animations and multiplayer, there are plenty of full 3D zombie games that do this far better than PZ ever will.  However none (very few) of them offer anywhere near the world detail, simulation and atmosphere that PZ does.
Oh, and finally, please take the game out of Early Access.  It's getting embarrassing after 5 years.  Since when does releasing a game mean that development cannot continue?
Terraria, for example, shows how happy players are when new features are added for free to a 'released' game., even if they come 2 years later.

The game is very easy to pick up, and you quickly get drawn into plotting out future moves and paths. I very quickly beat the AI on the lowest two levels, but have yet to take on the higher skill levels.
The client itself, from the same developer as the also-excellent Hive, is very well done. I'd add a slight wish for keyboard controls that don't rely on the number pad, to support us laptop users, but that's a very minor complaint.
All in all, a well-written version of a very fun game, at a low price. Highly recommended.

Sir, You Are Being Hunted is one of the very few FPS games that actually feels unique.  While the gameplay is somewhat limited, with only a handful of different enemies, each of them has a lot of personality, and strenghts and weaknesses that make them very distinct from one another, same goes for the limited number of weapons.  The usable items could be more unique... I never found myself using the toy train, or the alarm clock, or the traps at all, as throwing bottles and rocks to draw enemies away from you seemed superior, although you may find better uses for those items than I did.
The game is pretty simple; you start off on the center island, and there are 4 more to explore (N, S, E, W) as you gather all the shards of whatever it is you're collecting that will teleport you off the island to safety.  Sneaking around is FAR superior to engaging in combat, which I really found enjoyable,  because in real life, you can't stand and have a gunfight with 1 or more other people and not expect to die.  The use of the red light emanating from the enemies eyes, as well as their characteristic sounds was perfectly used to help you identify them in the bleak British countryside, as well as build suspense... It's a little difficult keeping your cool and crouching in the weeds while a towering Landowner strolls by, screaming, with hunting dogs swarming around him, waiting to attack and pin you to the ground so others can finish you off with their guns!
I liked that they made building unable to be entered; they would too easily become safe havens against the robots hunting you, and checking them in broad view of passersby while your screen is obscured by the doorways made for some very tense moments... especially knowing that if the big, normally passive robot that patrols them sees you, he'll make very quick work of you with his pistol!
The health and vitality meters worked out perfectly... there are no health restoring items, just food, which you eat to keep your vitality up.  This not only prevents you from starving to death (which never happened to me), but the higher your vitality, the more quickly your health regenerates while you hide in the shadows licking your wounds.  If you take enough damage, you start to bleed health fairly quickly, and MUST take cover to apply a bandage, even while being fired upon, otherwise you will surely die!
The learning curve of the game is fairly difficult, as you'd expect from a procedurally generated game, but there are infrequent save points that make dying more pallatable; I think the difficulty along with infrequent saving perfectly balanced each other out so that you couldn't be very reckless, as you'd lose a significant amount of progress, while not forcing you to play so conservatively as to completely avoid risks (Nethack, I'm looking at you!).  Currently, there's not a huge amount of replay value; the different classes are nearly identical, and all their starting equipment is easily found.  I think if they added more classes/items/monsters/weapons/biomes, and made them unlockable by reaching objectives, it would greatly add to the replay value... currently, I can see playing through this game 1-2 times before being completely satisfied with it.  Being able to craft some items from the myriads of junk, as well as adding helpful NPCs would also go a long ways.
All in all, I definitely got my $20 worth of fun out of this game; don't hesitate to buy it if it goes on sale!  I'm excited for expanded content to come out; more enemies, weapons, unique items, biomes, and player mods could easily take this game from a B/B+ to an A-, maybe even an A!

Well, This game is a survivalist, first person horror game. Oh, yeah it is. Play as journalist Miles Upshur and explore Mount Massive Asylum. Some whistleblower contacts you and convinces you its pretty messed up and needs to be investigated. So you go in. With only a camcorder (learning batteries are life to see in the dark around this scary spooky place) you adventure through. Adventure? well. Survive as their are good inmates/patients and there are those that want to kill you. With bodies and blood and darkness everywhere you got to collect documents, record notes and figure out what is going on at Mount Massive Asylum. Puzzle through floors and the maze like asylum. Those that do want to kill you? yeah, your a defense-less babe in the woods and can only hide and run. Lockers, under beds, under desks, anywhere so they dont stab, bludgeon, beat, and throw you to death. The game investigative wise, if you read all the stuff is rather a great story. There are many interesting and involved characters you run into during your time. Some are good, some bad and some are just great fiction story that you watch....and freak out about. There is alot going on then just so called ''dream therepy'' or some demon called ''Wallrider'', You have to figure out what really is going on and survive it.  The lighting and darkness is key to keeping your tension up with a soundtrack that for sure is keeping you on your toes too. Make sure you listen for other footsteps, or chains or talking of the killers locked up in there with you. Like I said a really horror story,  tension game, good mechanics of run and hide ( and find dem batteries) the atmosphere is great. Play through cause the ending is worth it. SURVIVE. Oh, and you liked the game? There is the DLC of a shorter game where you play as the whistleblower....What made him turn on his workers? What did he see when it all began? How did he reach the outside to Miles?

Made by professional individuals from
, Elven Legacy is the definition of a classical turn-based strategy wargame that has a minor amount of RPG elements added into it. Essentially being a standalone expansion for
, Elven Legacy portrays the world of Illis from the viewpoint of a "Higher Race" - Ancient Elves whom players are tasked to command in the single-player campaign. Originally released in 2007, Elven Legacy, along with its predecessor, is a title that possesses both quality and an addictive, albeit somewhat straightforward game mechanic. However, by no means does this simple gameplay make Elven Legacy less engaging or challenging, and experienced wargamers will find the difficulty level of this title much to their liking.
Most of the gameplay process concentrates on turn-based battles set in a high-fantasy world of Illis, a magical world where Elves, Men, Dwarves and Orcs have waged war upon one another for countless ages. Each of these races bear their own army with a wide variety of different units, spells and abilities. Combat takes place on maps that consist of hexagonal cells, with armies being limited in troop size and in terms of economy. Gold is the main resource and can be acquired throughout missions by means of scavenging and capturing (units are able to capture towns and scavenge ruins or other places of interest for gold, items and artifacts). Additional reinforcements can be hired for gold and are then deployed in cities which the player has under his control. Units are divided into several separate types - Infantry, Archers, Cavalry, Sky Hunters, Bombers and War Machines. Heroes are also present in this game, and are often crucial for the achievement of victory. All units in Elven Legacy, including the mentioned heroes, are able to gain experience throughout battles. Experience plays a critical role in the improvement of the player's army during both the campaign and skirmish missions. Upon gaining a level, units will be able to obtain various skills, will acquire better stats, and will ultimately have the possibility for an upgrade to a better unit. Spells, although present in the game, are nonetheless a relatively rare occurrence, for they are limited in charges, and the power of spellcasters is thus meant to be used wisely. All armies, along with their units, have their own strategies. Elves, for an example, are a mobile striking force that relies on archers, with their melee units being more of either a first line defense, either a distraction for the enemy. Human armies, on the other hand, use heavily armored cavalry while possessing weaker ranged units. As a conclusion, it can be added, that all races in the world of Illis have their own means to wage war, and when the player chooses his own army, it is going to take him some time before he gets used to leading it into battle with success. Terrain, as one would guess, plays a major role in this wargame. Throughout the entire campaign of Elven Legacy, players are going to use the cover of forests to their advantage whilst commanding the elven army, for as it should be, elven units get a bonus to their protection while fighting amongst the trees (and additional bonuses to their other stats as well, depending whether a unit had certain skills chosen prior to using the woods as cover). In Elven Legacy, different types of environment can either provide your troops with an advantage over the enemy, or quite to the contrary, might actually worsen their defensive capabilities by exposing them on open ground. Certain types of terrain can also hinder troop movement, and all of these factors add gameplay depth and realism when it comes to playing the missions, forcing the player to rely on tactical decision making while managing the actions of his forces. In a nutshell, Elven Legacy is a classical turn-based wargame, and all of the elements which are present in the game necessitate the player to think strategically, calculating his each step with attention and thoroughness.
The single-player campaign which is present in Elven Legacy can be described as both difficult and short. Composed of 10 missions, Elven Legacy will have the player saving and reloading quite often, especially on the "Hard" difficulty setting, where running out of turns equals to failure of a mission. As a sidenote, it should be taken into consideration, that all games that were developed by Ino-Co (Majesty 2 and Star Wolves are a great example of this. The latter was developed by a different company, but most of its team members later formed Ino-Co) are very difficult to beat. The campaign, even though only 10 missions long, is still very time consuming. Elven Legacy is not really a game for a casual player, a person who would like to simply enjoy the graphics or spend a tranquil few hours relaxing and clicking the mouse while managing his army in battle. Instead, Elven Legacy is a game that requires a lot of attention and patience, and to a certain degree, even stubbornness. During most, if not all of the missions, the player's army is going to be outnumbered, but if the player wishes to finish the game, he must nonetheless keep the casualties of his army to a minimum, otherwise he will find the game impossible to finish. This is because the gold that the player gets for the completion of missions will not compensate for high casualties, and the player is therefore bound to take great care of his own warriors. The plotline that is present in Elven Legacy during the campaign is unclear and vague, and the translation from the original Russian language to English is not the reason behind this, because the translation was done relatively well. Rather, this is because the story has no clear sense as such. During all 10 missions of the campaign, a much respected Elven general by the name of Saggitel, along with his magically gifted assistant Gylven, is going to hunt down a runaway renegade wizard that stole a dangerous spell. This turn of events, gradually, will lead to Gylven going rogue as well, with her seemingly benevolent attempt trying to restore a great elven tree, the giver of all life. In short, the storyline isn't particularly bad, rather it's average, but many things are mentioned quickly or are simply left unexplained, and this leaves a negative impression, that the entire plot was written over the course of an hour by one of the game developers instead of professional story writer. The overall setting of Elven Legacy, just like Fantasy Wars, was developed with both attention to detail and skill, but is still somewhere within the boundary of your average game. When playing Elven Legacy, you can not leave unnoticed an impression, that even though Elven Legacy was developed by talented people, the game was still made within a small budget. This game (and the entire franchise for that matter) had all the potential to become something much more acknowledged and popular, but unfortunately, never did.
Multiplayer is also implemented, and, as one can only assume, it would really make Elven Legacy shine, if this game would have ever become more well known to a bigger amount of people. The possibilities with all the strategic battles between players in this game seem to be very great, if not endless, and there are over a dozen multiplayer maps available to choose from. Unfortunately, playing Elven Legacy over the Internet appears to be impossible, and if players wish to test their skills against one another on the field of online battle, they will need Local Area Network emulating software such as Tunngle or Hamachi.
Elven Legacy is definitely a worthy game, worthy of being played and liked. It could have been designed to look better and more polished, but i still recommend it to all

Overall I like this game, the only downside being that the difficulty level is slightly too high, and even turning the difficulty setting to 'easy' makes no difference to this. The early missions aren’t too bad, but the very late ones are incredibly hard – and never allow you to deploy your full army at once.
Elven Legacy is basically a Fantasy General style game, but with better graphics and with more choices for which upgrades you want for which unit, with different unit types getting different choices.
For the expansions for Elven Legacy – Siege in particular though – the difficulty level is insane on many missions. When playing the expansions be prepared to reload a lot and try different ways of doing a mission. I find i have to save the game at the start of each turn and at the end of each turn (before the computer takes its turn), as there is a lot of luck involved, and reloading can lead to very different results from an identical situation.
Fantasy Wars, the game that came before Elven Legacy, was also too hard and limited you to to few units that could be deployed at once, but it wasn't quite as insanely difficult as some of the Elven Legacy expansions.
There are some of the missions in the Siege expansion that i could only complete by using cheats - and that let me manage to complete them in the "bronze" number of turns rating. Completing  almost any mission in it in gold is simply not possible. If the difficulty had been a bit more sensible on the later missions in the main game, and many of those in the expansions, this would probably have been a much more popular game.
Still worth trying though, especially at the minimal price it now sells for.

2.5 hours just flew by.  To make a long story short:  I love it.
It's a beautiful world.  There are enough structures in the world to explore and loot, but you will have to go out to get them.  I suggest being as mobile as possible, take everything you need for a campfire and don't eat uncooked meat.
The survival aspect is believable and keeps a somewhat sleepy world interesting.  You are always going to be looking for fuel for fires and food for your belly.
My only complaint is that there is no tutorial mode.  It would be really helpful to know to hold down the light a lantern button until it finishes lighting for instance.  Or how you are able to melt snow.  There are some aspects of the game that are not intuitive, so I would suggest reading up on other how-to guides to familiarize yourself.
Actually one more complaint:  The cursor is insanely small.  I get it that they love the art of their world (it is stunning afterall) but the cursor is only a few pixels and it can be hard to target things like sticks and cat tails. You are targeting a very small target with a very small cursor.  It's a bit of a pain.  But overall, this is a super fun game.  Enjoying it a lot.

"A Turd in the Sandbox" or "How not to do a sequel" -- RF:G was a great game with a large sandbox and a simple but fun mechanic of driving around and breaking stuff.  So, what better way to follow that up than with something one step above a 1990s rail-shooter.  The game is beautiful, using all the DX11 goodies it can find, and the characters are well to the right of the Uncanny Valley. But the gameplay is just so... bleh.  You just pass from zone to zone, blow up critters that jump around everywhere, then move on to the next obvious place to be attacked by another wave of uninspired enemies.  The game adds a literal rail-shooter section from time to time, or an unconvincing vehicle segment, just to remind you how much fun you aren't having.  In short, this game is agonizing to complete, and so terribly disappointing.  Do not buy.

Definitely in the upper crust of early-access survival games, The Long Dark has a ton of content already, and feels fairly complete despite still being currently in early-access. It has a much more realistic focus on survival - there are no zombies, no bandits, no friendlies in Cherno, and no way to magically craft armour, an assault rifle and a snowmobile from random metal scraps and sticks. It's kind of refreshing to see a purely survival-focused game where the primary struggle is between you and Mother Nature.
And boy, can it be a struggle. Your first concern will always be the cold - it'll easily kill you if you spend too long out there, and finding shelter is your first priority. Then it's starting a fire. Then finding wood. Then food - hunting, fishing, or foraging. Then...it's time to wander the Great Canadian North, take in the beautiful wilderness, avoid wolves, and search for survivors. Surely, someone else is out there, right? What's that? Other people and a singleplayer campaign aren't implemented yet? Well, that's fine. There's still more than enough to justify Long Dark's current sale price of 11 Canadian Beaver Pelts.

LIMBO is a grim platformer in which you journey through an eerie world full of darkened enemies to reunite with your sister. In terms of a story, that's about all you get. Rather, the strength of this game is its atmopshere, puzzles, and some aspects of exploration.
You're given no real context about who or where you are, creating a mysterious tone that endures throughout the game. The art direction complements this perfectly. At no point do you have to wait through loading screens; the world is designed very fluidly, with each area leading smoothly into the next. While the levels are mostly linear, you are expected to backtrack in several; the game encourages exploration, with side paths often leading to hidden rewards.
The controls are extremely simple, relying only on the arrow keys and Ctrl by default. The puzzles start out relatively straightforward, but progressively increase in both difficulty and complexity as you continue. With every successive level, you are introduced to a new mechanic or aspect of level design that enhances the traps. While the overall theme of the game is relatively somber, the more exciting areas require quick thinking and precise movements. Many of the later puzzles involve quite a bit of trial and error, but I never became overly frustrated with any of them.
The only issues I have with the game are that it is locked to 60fps in fullscreen mode, and that the controls cannot be changed from the in-game menu. However, these things are not especially problematic. All things considered, the atmosphere and puzzles are fascinating. It's well worth a playthrough, especially if you can get it on sale.

This game takes a simple idea and runs with it. You are stuck on an island where several groups of hunting robots trying to kill you. Your job is to recover bits of an experimental device and return home.
Initially it looks like this will be a walkover, the hunting robots are easy to evade or out run and food and materials are abundant in abandoned homes all over the island. However, as time passes the pursuit heats up. Swift hunting dogs join the patrols, sheriffs start to guard the towns and strange ambushers set leg traps in the best hiding spots. The early strategy of out running the patrols works at first, but very soon you will need to think carefully to avoid running being hemed in. The environment is the real star of this game, flocks of birds will break cover and reveal your location to your pursuers; Robot patrols will sometimes start shooting at each other when the meet and lighting a fire to cook food will attract every robot for miles to your location, useful as a tactic when you need to lure them away from a bit of the device.
The game is not perfect, it is simple to a fault and while the stealth parts are very good they are pretty much all there is. Combat is not the focus of the game and is not rewarding either in terms of loot or risk. Often you need to kill a robot to proceed, but if you can avoid this you should. The houses have mostly junk and there is no crafting or real story to this game. To me this is an advantage as it allows the player to focus on the job at hand without distraction. To some other people this game may appear shallow, watch some videos to get the feel of it if you are not sure.

LYNE is an abstract, challenging puzzle game. Connect different shapes from start to finish in order to complete a level.
The design of the game is kept simplistic, basic shapes and a background. Overall the visuals are appealing for a puzzle game, kept basic on intention, because a puzzle game does not really need good graphics.
Animations feel fitting and even help you out in some cases (see "gameplay" for more info).
LYNE is controlled by mouse. The game gives your an understandable introduction tutorial on how to complete the puzzles.
A soundtrack does not actually exist. It is more like a shallow and eerie electronic synth playing some notes in the background. The soundeffects are nice, but could get repetitive if you play this game for too long. The option to turn the sounds off is available.
Simply put, LYNE is a game consisting of 27 sets á 25 puzzles waiting to be completed. While you start fairly easy, it will get very difficult in later sets. The goal for every puzzle is the same: Connect both of the same shapes with each other by drawing a line between them. You drag the shapes in order to draw the connection. But it is not that easy: Later on, you will need to connect additional shapes with the same line or even multiple shapes at the same time. Another rule is that the connecting lines cannot cross each other. A little animation will hint you, if you try to make that mistake.
Besides the alphabetical sets, there is a daily rotation of random puzzles. The rotation starts on easy on mondays and will get progressively higher in difficulty throughout the week. The weekend will use mixed difficulties.
An option to change the colors of the game is available, if you gather enough triangles scores for solving sets or daily puzzle sets.
While LYNE has an actual learning curve, some of the puzzles seem really hard, sometimes trail-and-error was the last resort for me. I rather enjoy games that can be completely solved either through process of elimination or through finding creative solutions, hence I had some times where I put the game down for some time.
Also, be aware that this is a puzzle game and thus does not have much additional content. After you completed the main sets, there isn't much left to do besides fulfilling the daily tasks.
There only exist certain color schemes, a complete color modification would be much nicer in my opinion.
Also, while playing this on different machines, I noticed that your progress and score is saved locally, meaning if you have a laptop and download this game on said laptop while you already played LYNE on your home PC, then your score and progress in the alphabetical sets will NOT transfer.
LYNE is a little but nice, time consuming, challenging but fair puzzle game. The visuals are intentionally kept basic, in order to conform with the gameplay, which is clearly in the foreground here. While the game can look boring and bland, do not let yourself get fooled, this game is one of the teeth-gnashingly types. I can safely recommend this game for yours truly puzzle solver out there. Happy solving!

- NA servers are really empty, but EU servers are doing well (especially Requiem)
- A little bit of guild drama
- It's difficult to get the gear to go to raids, a lot of grinding
- Certain events impact the in-game economy massively making some items completely worthless in a matter of days

However, that all being said, season 3 is set to come out at some point this year.
