So what is Dungeon of the Endless? A combination of rogue-like elements, RPG, tower-defense and some anger management (comes with the roguelike package).
You crash with your ship, and you have to escape by going down floors in this dungeon until you find your exit ticket. You start with 2 heroes from a list (in the beginning you only have two heroes until you unlock more) and go at it. While you explore, you can find other heroes that can join you, to a maximum of four. You move them by selecting them (tip: ~ selects all) and right clicking on a room.
Combat is simple, if enemies are in the same room of your heroe, they fight. Skills are activated manually, each with their own effect. Some enemies don't care about you, they just want to destroy your core. You don't want that. But sometimes, you need to get crafty. See, enemies spawn in unpowered rooms. You most likely will not have enough resources to power up every room. Sometimes, you'll be way below the curve and have rooms on different routes unpowered. How do you fight this? With the Tower Defense elements.
Rooms have a number of minor module slots, and some even include a major nodule slot. Of course, stuff you build only works in powered rooms. You use major modules to either get more resources: Industry (used to build stuff), Science (used to research or upgrade new modules) or Food (used to level up your heroes and heal them in combat). And minor nodules can be support, offensive, or an assortment of other effects. The final resource is Dust, you use this to power up rooms. And if your core gets hit, you start losing Dust. The other three resources carry over from floor to floor. Dust doesn't. So don't think you can stockpile this.
Therefore, there's some form of micro management involved. You can pause the game at any time and survey the situation, and while looking around you remember you found the exit of this floor, what now? You have to go and grab your core and bring it there. While you do this, that hero will be moving slowly, rooms will start to automatically depower (you just did remove the energy source) and enemies will start coming from every unpowered room. Once you take the core to the exit, next floor. Rinse and repeat.
It's a great game, it's simple to learn, but in true rogue-like fashion, it will still kick your♥♥♥♥♥when you least want it too.

I picked up this game when it was back in Early Alpha, and at the time it felt a bit feature-scant. However, they have since gone into Beta, and I can safely say that this is worth every cent.
DotE is best summarized as a mix between a roguelike, turn-based strategy game, and a sort of tower defense. Your goal is to open doors in the dungeon so that you can find the exit and then you have to carry your power source (a crystal) to that exit without it getting destroyed by the various monsters that inhabit the dungeon. The learning curve is a bit steep at first, but once you figure out how everything works, this game becomes incredibly fun.
There are some drawbacks, such as the technical glitches, occasional crashes (at least for me), and some balance issues, but the devs are highly involved in the community and are taking steps to actively address these issues - more than I can say for other Early Access games.
You can find yourself sinking a lot of time into this game if you take the time to enjoy it. I highly recommend it.

A useful cautionary tale on curiosity and the value of journalistic integrity.
Within the first ten minutes of playtime, your character, an investigative journalist, has broken into a secure medical facility and seen, and recorded, enough evidence of maltreatment and poor management to bring it down. The government isn't actually omnipotent, you know- leak that footage and the story will spread. The authorities will go into lockdown, and maybe they'll try and deny it, but no matter how angry they might be with you, the damage has been done- silencing you now would be petty vengeance. Mission complete. Time to head home.
It's at around this point that our protagonist finds one of the unguarded doors he came into the facility through has just been locked. It's a simple wooden interior hospital/office door, from the administrative side of the asylum- it's not reinforced or tamper-proof, and you know that there are no security cameras watching it from the other side. Trapped in a kitchen as night falls, you now have several options available to you.
1. Attempt to break down the door. This is entirely achievable, although there's some risk of hurting yourself, and it might be loud enough to draw the attention of the guards.
2. Attempt to pick the lock. It's not a very secure-looking door, and there should be utensils of some sort in this kitchen you can use- given it's not a secure external lock, your credit card might even be enough to jiggle the door open. It's still hard work, though, and it's not impossible that you might fail.
3. Hide in the vent until someone opens the door again. This is the safest option available to you. You're not in any particular hurry at the moment. Just wait for an opportunity to escape.
4. Crawl through the vent into the main body of the asylum, the securest part of a facility specifically designed for people to not escape from, where you know people are dying and being tortured and eaten and stuff, because hey, maybe there's another way out down there, right?

Outlast is a first-person survival horror video game developed and published by Red Barrels. The game revolves around a freelance investigative journalist, Miles Upshur, who decides to investigate a remote psychiatric hospital named Mount Massive Asylum, located deep in the mountains of Lake County, Colorado. The downloadable content, Outlast: Whistleblower, centers on Waylon Park, the man who led Miles there in the first place.
In Outlast, the player assumes the role of investigative journalist Miles Upshur, as he navigates a dilapidated psychiatric hospital overrun by homicidal patients. The game is played from a first-person perspective and features some stealth gameplay mechanics. The player can walk, run, crouch, jump, and climb over objects. Unlike most games however, the player is unable to attack enemies, and instead must rely on stealth tactics such as hiding in lockers, sneak past enemies, hide behind crates and barrels, or hide under beds and tables in order to survive. Alternatively, the player can attempt to outrun their pursuer. If the player dies, the game will reset to the most recent checkpoint.
Most of the hospital is unlit, and the only way for the player to see while in the dark is through the lens of a camcorder equipped with night vision. Using the night vision mode will slowly consume batteries, forcing the player to scavenge for additional batteries found throughout the building. Outlast makes heavy use of traditional jump scares and audio cues, which alert the player if an enemy has seen them. If the player records specific events with their camcorder, Miles will write a note about it, providing further insight into his thoughts. Documents can be collected, which offer backstory and other supplementary information about the hospital.

LYNE is an abstract, challenging puzzle game. Connect different shapes from start to finish in order to complete a level.
The design of the game is kept simplistic, basic shapes and a background. Overall the visuals are appealing for a puzzle game, kept basic on intention, because a puzzle game does not really need good graphics.
Animations feel fitting and even help you out in some cases (see "gameplay" for more info).
LYNE is controlled by mouse. The game gives your an understandable introduction tutorial on how to complete the puzzles.
A soundtrack does not actually exist. It is more like a shallow and eerie electronic synth playing some notes in the background. The soundeffects are nice, but could get repetitive if you play this game for too long. The option to turn the sounds off is available.
Simply put, LYNE is a game consisting of 27 sets á 25 puzzles waiting to be completed. While you start fairly easy, it will get very difficult in later sets. The goal for every puzzle is the same: Connect both of the same shapes with each other by drawing a line between them. You drag the shapes in order to draw the connection. But it is not that easy: Later on, you will need to connect additional shapes with the same line or even multiple shapes at the same time. Another rule is that the connecting lines cannot cross each other. A little animation will hint you, if you try to make that mistake.
Besides the alphabetical sets, there is a daily rotation of random puzzles. The rotation starts on easy on mondays and will get progressively higher in difficulty throughout the week. The weekend will use mixed difficulties.
An option to change the colors of the game is available, if you gather enough triangles scores for solving sets or daily puzzle sets.
While LYNE has an actual learning curve, some of the puzzles seem really hard, sometimes trail-and-error was the last resort for me. I rather enjoy games that can be completely solved either through process of elimination or through finding creative solutions, hence I had some times where I put the game down for some time.
Also, be aware that this is a puzzle game and thus does not have much additional content. After you completed the main sets, there isn't much left to do besides fulfilling the daily tasks.
There only exist certain color schemes, a complete color modification would be much nicer in my opinion.
Also, while playing this on different machines, I noticed that your progress and score is saved locally, meaning if you have a laptop and download this game on said laptop while you already played LYNE on your home PC, then your score and progress in the alphabetical sets will NOT transfer.
LYNE is a little but nice, time consuming, challenging but fair puzzle game. The visuals are intentionally kept basic, in order to conform with the gameplay, which is clearly in the foreground here. While the game can look boring and bland, do not let yourself get fooled, this game is one of the teeth-gnashingly types. I can safely recommend this game for yours truly puzzle solver out there. Happy solving!

A beautiful ,addictive, and hyper realistic shooter that puts games like Rainbow Six Seige to shame. Red Orchestra 2 achieves a new level of realism while maintaining the fun, addicting gameplay found in other shooters. The game has a subtle resembelance of battlefield, with 64 player battles, an occasional vehicle, and many classes. One thing unique about the class system of this game is the  asymmetricality between the classes. Classes like the machine gunner and the sniper are far more powerful than the rifleman or smg class. Do not worry, this is balanced as there is a cap on the more powerful classes. There is also a lot of tactical gameplay here, with squad leaders being able to give numerous orders to their squads and commanders who can call in artillery, order in reconnaissance planes, and order squad leaders to attack certain objectives. The gunplay is also phenomenal, weilding a gun is very satisfying and feels very realistic and the weapons look and feel authentic. The way the gun reacts to your movements is so well polished. This game immerses you into the battlefield like no other with great sound, incredible action and fairly decent graphics. One con imo is the lack of leveling up, the only unlocks you really have to look forward to are the bayonets the stg, and the mg42.
There is a lot more to this game however I can't cover it all.
Overall this game is very fun and still holds its own in 2016. The 20$ price tag is also a steal. If you are on edge, then watch some gameplay videos and if you like watch you see, definitely pick this game up. I assure you, you will not regret it.

You can't build Zombie-"Proof" bases, only Zombie-Resistant because they will eventually destroy walls, plastered walls, and even the giant-log walls ( with ease ) and they typically target the walls or anything "bangable" ( look in the code, that's a thing ). I'd like to see them fix this because zombies can't go through solid logs ( maybe if a horde is moving through, if the wall isn't reinforced then it could knock it over )..
When using hardcore reload mode, if you right click another mag before reloading is done, the reload counter resets to 0 on the first mag. This is a huge issue, especially when ammo is scarce.
Fire unrealistically burns concrete without a fuel source ( and burns across multi-lane highways even from a small campfire ) and without wind. This is an issue when your base is surrounded by concrete ( more than a screen worth ) and a fire comes waltzing through..
Accidentally pressing USE next to a broken window makes you climb through it instead of removing broken glass ( because pressing USE opens / closes the window and HOLDING USE is meant to be for climbing through [ which it does do when the window is intact ] ) and you can get scratched by broken plate-glass windows. This is an issue with the key system which should be resolved... Never allow non-held use button-press to go through the window unless there is a floor on the other side and all glass is removed and no sheet / curtain is in front would be the ideal rule to complement their current system...
Pressing USE next to a solid store-window / display-window makes your character try to open it ( when they don't open ) like a window that opens upwards.
The lighting system is broken ( despite trying all of the options for lighting update-frequency ) in the sense that when you're fully awake / alert, and you're running, you still end up with a full-black-fog-of-war screen in your view-direction until you stop for a few seconds. Changing the FPS lock, or unlocking it, does nothing either.
Other lighting issues ( and rendering issues ):
2 ) When you're going through a building, you can't see through a door-way or in a room with an open door until you go into that room ( and run into zombies ).
3 ) When in a room that is on the same floor as another but visually below you on the monitor, if that room has objects it'll render blocking you from seeing anything in the room you're in ( bookshelves, stacked crates, etc.. ) and you run into zombies.
And more that I can't recall at the moment.

This is a genuine gem of a tactical game whose positives for the most part outweigh its flaws.
Pros:
The basics of the game are simple to pick up but deceptively deep.
Varied scenarios with genuinely optional objectives.
Soldier / Hero leveling system works well, many viable options.
I actually really liked the story, seems generic to start with but surprised me with the route it took.
Persistent army, could be a con if you struggle on earlier missions as it can be hard to catch up if you lose too many veterans but it does make your soldiers more valuable, which is good. Also the whole rpg side of the game wouldn't work without it.
The difficulty, works well with the campaign structure, its hard enough that soldiers can be lost permanently but not so hard you can't avoid most of them.
Cons:
Occasional oddly placed difficulty spikes.
One or two missions which feel like they have limited options if you want to win.
A few of the units seem either under or over powered, though nothing completely gamebreaking.
Overall while it doesn't do much new it does do a lot well and its worth a look to fans of the genre.

SW: Empire at War + Forces of Corruption is basically the real time Total War version of Star Wars RTSs, boasting a feather-weight empire management overworld, where you will construct buildings that produce your Ships/troops on your planets, and send heroes/agents around to assassinate bothersome enemy heroes and play wack-a-mole with Zann Consortium corruption, before getting into space and ground combat to wrestle control of a planet from the AI's grubby mits.
The Space Combat is where the game shines, even though the game has some annoying AI problems for their units, most of them can be ignored as they are minor and can be solved by just telling the ship to stop with the stop button on the command bar, or by just droping the SSD ontop of the enemy base before you bring in the rest of the fleet. And if/when you get mad, just start bringing the Death Star, an Interdictor and tie scouts with your "blob of death" and blow up their space station and have them commit suicide by attacking your wall of Star Destroyers and Ties head on.
The ground combat while servicable is nothing spectacular and you can often spend minutes chasing that last remaining unit of rebel soldiers, and that is when you aren't getting constantly attacked by Jedi heroes and a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t mobile fortress hero that all can infiltrate your planets with enough firepower to single-handedly beat off the Empire at Hoth. But very little can beat the coolness of commanding Veers and  a pack of AT-ATS, supported by airstrikes and planetary bombardment as they smash their way through an fortified rebel planet where even the natives wants to fight you.
Now, the multiplayer is dead out of the box for the game, but if you can stand gameranger and can get it to work properly, then you might even get a couple of good MP games out of it too, just be prepared to get stomped by someone who has probably played the game since it came out back in the Bronze age.
It is worth mentioning that the game still has a quite good, active and helpfull modding community that has produced everything from simple rebalance mods to humongus mods that are bigger than the base game.
If you want purely a good Star Wars ground RTS go and buy Battlegrounds Saga, if you want a more comprehensive Empire management Star Wars game, go buy rebellion. If you however want the best(and possibly only) game where you control the Empire/Rebels on a galactic scale, while also controlling the space and ground battles yourself, then this is the game for you.

Dungeon of the Endless is part of the "Endless Universe" games, along with Endless Space and Endless Legend (the second being in early access too). As such, all their games follow a few key rules. All are turn based, all use FIDS (Food, Industry, Dust, Science) and all are interconnected in their races/themes and such.
DotE though is not a 4X games like the other two. It is a isometeric view dungeon crawler/tower defense style game. You play as a crashed hero/prisoner on a planet. You land in a dungeon and must escape by climbing 10 floors. You start off with a crystal and some generators you can plant in some rooms. Each room is a turn, the act of opening the door to a room giving you more FIDS/advancing a turn. You can power rooms for the cost of 10 dust, which means money literally is power. Food levels your heroes, Industry builds things and Science can be spent at artifacts to learn more turrets or upgrade old ones. So far, it must sound complex and at first it will do till you learn the tricks. The key to this game are the heroes/prisoners.
Each hero has their own style of play. Some are defenders that boost towers by standing in the same room, some are solo runners who do better alone, some are tanks. It's almost DOTA like and really helps you find interesting ways to play. You find heroes on floors and unlock them for use (so you can start with them when you die) by needing to keep them for 3 floors or finish the game with them, which ever comes first. It's a really fun way to make it more interesting and i often find myself trying to unlock people more then stay alive.
At typing, Multiplayer is not in the game but it is the part i am most interested in seeing. I want to know how this will work because....simply put, this seems like a fantastic multiplayer game.
This really is worth the price. Get the upgrade too if you own Endless Space, you get a new race for that game too. The Vaulter.

A thrilling FPS experience which provides plenty of action, challenging gameplay and growing suspense as you progress.
You Sir (Or Madam), begin your adventure by spawning next to the standing stones. Unsure of what's happened, A voice explains to you that you need to collect some stones and return them back to where you are currently standing.
The problem facing the player is that these stones have been scattered randomly across the world and they are all well guarded by some deadly robot hunters. There isn't much explanation on why or how the robots got here, but one thing players learn very quickly when playing this game is that these robots only want you dead.
A world is made up of five islands: the centre is where you begin and has islands connected north, south, east and west. While the world is randomly generated at the start of the game, you can choose to have each island stick to a theme or bio dome and there are a few different bio domes to select from.
Some bio domes available are simple rural areas which provide plenty of long grass, bushes and some villages. Old Crumbling castles, Stone work and Tall Churches and my favourite The Industrial Bio Dome. Gloomy skies, Brick Mills and Huge abandoned factories.
The enviroments are well detailed, you wont see any bright and happy skies as the usual weather forecase is often overcast and cloudly. Accompanied by dark surroundings that constrast with a world of no electricty. However the coloured clouds by the sunset or sunrise in the mornings can often leave some incredible wallpaper worthy like pictures but they also enhance the feeling of being alone in the wilderness.
And while you may feel alone, There's always something out there to remind you that you're not.
The Robots have many different forms. Your average hunter robot smokes a pipe, carrys a rifle and looks left and right, while patroling his area. They will talk to other robots in their strange robotic voice, sometimes you can work out what they're saying too and its funny.
Early on the robots are found walking through the area, and you can always expect them to be near some fragements of the stones you are trying to collect. If you manage to snatch one  of them and return it back to the standing stones where you spawned, You'll be a step closer to winning the game, but more advanced robots appear...
should you set one of these bots off They'll aim to chase you and find a good range to shoot you. Be aware, It will not take them long to take you down. The early robots may appear to be dumb for a while but 3 or 4 shots and you're dead.
It's also worth noting that taking damage you risk a chance to bleed, if you dont treat the wound asap you could possibly bleed out and eventually die very quickly. The sense of panic while trying to apply a bandage as well as having a robot chase you for a better shot is fun in its own way
Bleeding? Bandages? You'll need to carry some for a lot of 'just in case' scenarios so players will need to plunder houses, buildings and anything else that may contain loot. Because while you're looking for ammo for guns, tools to distract the robots or first aid. You'll need to look after you're vitality meter too. Fortunately this isn't too hard to look after, Simply keep this meter high up and you'll heal  and have energy to run and jump. you'll start by eating dead rats, old eggs and maybe even cat food but over time you'll find more healthier things to maintain good vitality.
By the way, Try the mushrooms...
The best part of this game is the sense of flight or fight.
Sure you might have loads of ammo and you're good shot with your gun, but opening fire may alert robots near by and draw them closer. The other idea is using traps and devices to distract robots so you can walk past, loot a certain building or even take one of those special rocks to win the game. Ammo doesn't show up very often, so you will need to find alternatives to deal with robots if they stand in your way without drawing attention to yourself or resorting to violence.
Sir, you are being hunted provides many great moments where you will enjoy outwitting the robots for your own gain and frantic moments running like a fugitive and never looking behind you because it means death. The Vitality system makes the player remember the on going need for surivial but it isn't too difficult or complex and the variety of enemy robots deliver different types of AI and behaviour, they can be hilarious at times but in the right scenarios can be intimidating and sometimes even scary.
I'd recommend it to anyone who enjoys FPS and enjoys the whole stealth approach and having their brains tested, Also use headphones with surround sound for the best experince.

You're running through what remians of Stalingrad, trudging through mud and snow to attack an objective, simply because the enemy is occupying it. As you catch your breath in a makeshift trench, you see your comrades fall to the ground, clutching their wounds and begging for their mother. The look over to you, and outstretch their hand, only to fall limp seconds later.
Your commander orders you to attack a building, you charge forward along with your comrades, and you crush the enemy inside. It's quiet for a moment, but you hear the screech, the sound that will engrain itself into your mind for the rest of your life - artillery fire.
You duck for cover, and see your friends bodies fly through the air - in pieces or not. Your vision is blurred, your ears are ringing.
The artillery ceases. You stand up, and look around to see what is left of your platoon. It's quiet. Too quiet. You are ordered to defend the objective, and you hunker down, only to hear the scariest sound a German can hear.
In the distant fog, you see them. Russians. Rats. They have their bayonet's affixed, their pistols raised, and their grenades ready. You can barely see them, but you can hear them as if they're right next to you.
"OOOOOORAAAAAAH!"
Sounds of machine gun fire rip through the air, and you see the Russians fall to the ground. They keep coming. The Russian hydra is charging forth, for every one that falls, two more take his place. What seemed like a cozy trench is now filled with Russians, beating your comrades to death with binoculars, the butts of their rifles, and their own fists.
You get shot, right in the gut. You try to spam ctrl to bandage, but it's futile. Your vision is darkened, blurred, and your hearing is muffled. All you can hear is yourself muttering, "Nein! Nein! Bitte!"
You fall to the ground shortly after, left in the snow to rot.
You peek at the killfeed.

This is going to be a honest review and will list all pros and cons.
It's an survey like type of game where the best answers win, The house will try to trick you, picking those answers do have negative point deductions, but sometimes you're convinced to choose them, or it could be strategic instead of rewarding other players. The game is really fun when it's not competitive, but just pure humour, putting clever answers to win the audience is the key to win.
Pros:
~Only 1 person needs to purchase the game ($15.00-$20.00 bucks depending on where you purchase) - Up to 6 people can play, 1 hosts, 5 more join the game for free! All players will require to use a browser to type in joining code and to vote/type answers.
~There is a choice to have a new person enter the game either as a new name or mask themselves as the previous person.
~If you're not sure of what to choose as the answer, the house can create an answer for you, which if other's choose THAT answer, you get rewarded AND they get deducted points. If you choose a house answer that was just the house fake answer alone, You lose points.
~Game is perfect for large groups of people, and also fun to play on skype, If you play on Twitch, remember usually there is a delay of 15 seconds (average) so players in the live game should be patient.
Cons:
~Currently there is no kick or vote kick button for this game, If someone drops, the host can clear the person from the game, and thus removing all their accumulated points, however that person can consistently re-join the game. This can be a nuiscience if you're a streamer and you allow people in the open public to join you. Best to play privately for majority case scenarios.
~This being game that started on Kickstarter, at this moment, you may still come across some "repeater" questions, content may be limited if you play multiple times, I still find it enjoyable, but how far this game expanded to other companies, I'm still impressed. (Sony, Nintendo, Microsoft, Steam, Roku, etc)
~Timers cannot be customized at this time.
~If relying on a host, all must be able to see the screen, may not be perfect when all on skype and the host/may disconnect, If the host disconnects, should be a warning or an opportunity for another player in the game to take over as host.
Overall: I'm impressed and satisifed with this purchase. It is an excellent icebreaker for new friends and even better for close ones whether face to face or on any voice chat program;skype/discord/twitch/steam.
I rate it: 9 out of 10!
Would play again anytime, Only deduction is in hopes there will be future updates for additional content and settings. FYI: Steam may indicate I played little time, but only due to myself not hosting the game, rather joined an existing one, If you want a cheap game, this is a great way to break the silence and kill time!

Though it isn't perfect, Elven Legacy is, in my opinion, probably the best tactics game on Steam.
It is also one of the few that lets you build your army to a nice size, fielding a good dozen units or so on the field of battle.
These large armies are absolutely necessary to capture the essence of what makes for a good tactics game:
-Allowing the ability to concentrate forces,
-the ability to divide and spread to different objectives,
and the endless flexibility and mixing and matching that operating any army should be about.
Battles are very well balanced, with perhaps the exception of when (usually the AI) gets UNlimited range magic. Those few times, the entire battle experience is ruined. But most battles don't include this at all. The units are done right and everything is predictable enough to concentrate on the theory and practice of the economy of battle.
Stories normally get in my way especially for tactics & strat games, but EL's plot moves along nicely, giving you skippable events that drive you to the next fight. A few forks in the road allow you to choose different paths which adds to the replayability of the campaigns.
RPG elements like magic artifacts and hero units are useful without making the other units useless. Your units get experience that carries over for the entire campaign and may upgrade to a stronger unit type. This is one of the reasons why I mostly play campaign, because it is fun to have pride in your units and try your best to preserve them. But the game also offers scenarios as one-fight deallys, and a scenario editor, and multiplayer, all which I havent even gotten into due to being all about campaign/ story mode.
To my dismay, the game adds out of the way objectives that break up my 'exercises in maneouvre," but the game does a surprisingly excellent job in making them a tough challenge, without wanting to bash your head in. Usually. There will be some frustration if you want to get Perfect missions / all objectives but, hey, it's supposed to be tough, right..  Overall very well done.
Other thoughts
-runs your gpu a bit hard for the level of graphics
-you can save and load at will in sp, which I very much prefer, and I don't care about peoplw who whine about 'save scumming'
-full voiceovers for the story parts, not too bad at all
If you want a tactics game that offers a lot more possibilities than a 5 man game can offer, your best bet that I know of is Elven Legacy, and the earlier game done by the same guys, Fantasy Wars, of which everything in this review also applies.

Back in April Paradox Interactive released Elven Legacy, the follow-up to Fantasy Wars. In my review, I praised the turn-based battle system and story, but criticized the difficulty and creeping sense of sameness, and eventually concluded by advising gamers to ‘Try It’ for the main game. Since then I have replayed it a bit here and there, and my fondness for the game has grown – it is still difficult, still not as good as King’s Bounty: The Legend, and I would still rate it as a ‘Try It’. After its release, Paradox Interactive announced that they would expand Elven Legacy with a trilogy of $9.99 DLC modules rather than a single huge expansion. It is an interesting concept, and I’ve enjoyed the first two, so let’s see how they did with the last add-on, Magic!
A comment about the reviews for these add-ons: because they are specialized and limited DLC that pertains directly to the main Elven Legacy game, I will not spend too much time rehashing the core game in terms of how it works and plays and what it looks like. If you are interested in those things head back to my original review of the game. What I will do is address the changes the add-on makes to the core game, and also the elements of the add-on itself.
As the last add-on, Magic naturally deals with the final chapters in the story. The end of the Siege expansion opened up a wave of demonic energy that is sweeping the land and having a terrible impact on the world and is driving the Arcane Masters insane. The Holy Inquisition intervenes in order to stop the spread of darkness and madness.
Elven Legacy: Magic features a single campaign with 15 missions focused around a single hero class: the mage. The focus is around a single new hero: the Archmage supreme Alfred Brennock. There are also two returning heroes, so that you once again have three playable heroes. But the real story here is Brennock, who gets armed with some powerful new skills, spells and runes.
The game really caters to those who love playing a mage – the game introduces powerful new spells and summons that are also nicely complemented with stunning visual effects that are truly massive in scope. The scope of the world is every bit as huge as in Siege, as you are trying to save the entire world from sweeping forces of darkness.
Elven Legacy: Magic unsurprisingly continues the trend of not having any voice acting. At this point it is no big deal, and remains a fair trade-off to get such a large expansion with such a breadth of content for such a great price. The graphics and controls remain largely untouched from Siege. Once again, this add-on depicts some truly epic battles that nearly stress the engine to its breaking point, but again I found that it was more satisfying than frustrating.
The difficulty level of Siege was punishing, and with Magic we see that the lull in difficulty in Ranger was a momentary lapse, never to be seen again. If you haven’t discovered it by now, it is really important to do as well as possible in missions, which typically means repeating them for better results. However, for many folks (certainly for someone like me who likes strategy games but is no grognard!) it often means repeating missions just to survive and THEN repeating more to get the Gold victory!
More than ever, getting those Gold victories will reward you in the end. The completist in me just wanted every possible mission, but what I got in the end was a bonus mission that tied together everything from the series going all the way back to Fantasy Wars! What a great way to end the series!
That said, Elven Legacy: Magic changes nothing about the things that will make you love or hate the series. It is a great value, but really depends on you having played the original game and both add-ons, and benefits even more if you also played Fantasy Wars. Like the previous expansions, if you already enjoy the original game you’ll love this third and final add-on too!
Pros:
+ Solid turn-based combat system
+ Great value for the price
+ Decreased difficulty
+ Decent story
+ Solid graphics
+ Possibility to win … but still lose
Cons:
- No voice acting
- Poor translations cause occasional confusion
- Time limits can STILL be frustrating

Do you want PTSD lite?
If the answer is yes, then this game is for you!  This game is somewhere on the realism spectrum between a generic shooter, and an Arma game (And it leans closer to the Arma side).  The game has a very short time to kill, usually one or two bullets will finish the job pretty well, although if you can disengage,  minor injuries can sometimes be bandaged before you bleed out (and you can bleed out).  The real delight of the game is its scale and visuals.  it's best played on 64 player servers, with as many players as possible, which can make the game fairly chaotic.  Visually, the game is not the most beautiful, although it is by no means ugly, but it does a good job at portraying sone of the more horrible aspects of war, limbs can come off, although blood is not overdone, like in some games, and the game is filled with lots of little thing that catch your eye.
Anyway, I think I will end with a story from my time in game:
I was in the gunnery seat of a panzer IV, when a T-34 roles onto the street directly ahead.  I sight the gun to my estimated range and fire.  The shell shattered on impact, dealing little to no damage.  I hear a pinging noise on the right side of the tank, probably machine gun fire, I think to myself.  I  adjust my sights and wait for my loader to finish loading the shell.  After waiting some time for confirmation that the shell is loaded, I try firing anyway.  Click.  There's no shell in the barrel.  The T-34 fires, their shell bounces off the side of the tank.  I take the momentary break to take a look at the crew compartment of my Panzer IV.  Everyone in the tank is dead, and there are several holes on the right side that appear to have come from anti tank rifles.  Only my loader is still alive, and he's missing both his legs, cradling a shell and crying for his mother.  There's nothing left for me in this tank, and I evacuate out of the Hatch on the left side. Right as I have just exited, the anti tank rifles start peppering the sides again, as I'm climbing down from the tank a round penetrates and impacts the ammunition racks.  The tank explodes violently and I'm cast several feet from the vehicle, slowly bleeding out on the ground.

LYNE is a puzzle game which was ported from the tablet to the PC. The game is played on a tiled board. There are one to three colors of tiles, including two special “starting tiles” for each color. In addition, there are tiles which correspond to none of the three tiles, but instead have 2-4 holes in them.
The purpose of the game is to draw a continuous line from the starting tile of each color to the other starting tile of that same color, while, between all three colors, running through every single tile on the board, and filling up every single hole on the board. Every colored tile can only be run through once, while the tiles with holes in them may be run through a number of times equal to the number of holes in them.
The game is played on a square grid, so each tile adjoins to up to eight other tiles. Every level has a unique setup, and the game has an enormous number of them – 650 levels in the main game, plus 1-3 daily puzzles which are released on a daily basis, and which are of variable difficulty.
Some people become really enthusiastic about this game, and there is some sort of secret cipher/puzzle hidden beneath the various daily puzzles, but I never really got into that aspect of the game. Instead, I simply solved the puzzles. The puzzles are, on the whole, fairly decent, but the game is basically one of those “standard puzzle games” – the puzzles are mechanically interesting enough, but they’re not so interesting that they’ll fascinate most people. Some people get really into them, just like some people get into crosswords, but for most people this is just something they’ll periodically sit down and beat a set of puzzles on, and then leave alone for a while.
At that, it is decent, and you’re likely to spend 20 hours or so solving all the puzzles. After that point, you’ll likely have had your fill of the game, but if you haven’t, you can keep playing various daily puzzles pretty much indefinitely.
It is what it is, and it is decent at what it is. If you’re into simplistic but potentially quite challenging puzzle games, this might be up your alley. If that sort of thing isn’t your thing, though, you can really skip this and not be missing anything.

Beautiful, fun, simple. I'm a hardcore fan of strategy games so this is right up my alley. If you generally enjoy tower defense games or other strategy, you'll probably like this too. The game is set in a beautifully designed dark dungeon, with quite charming pixel animations and effects. At the time of this review, the game is in Early Access, and while the UI is bland I suspect this will improve by the time release. It's nonetheless no harm to the current game, which is very fun.
You basically try to find the exit for each level while planning your escape as you discover rooms. The amount of levels are endless as the game's name suggests, so you just solve as many as you can. While you're playing, however, you can find phat loot, upgrade your technology and gear and level your character. The mechancis are deep but extremely simple. The most difficult thing to master are the keybinds really, and those just take some getting used to really.
All in all, very fun, worth every penny and the Early Access plays like a beta (missing just a few features, needs more polish, but completely playable without game-breaking bugs). This should be a success when it goes green. Thanks for the great game, Amplitude!

SYABH has the parts of DayZ Arma2 mod that I really enjoyed; sneaking around a dangerous landscape, scavenging for supplies, limited prowess through firearms, and made a nice little game out of it.
It's not very deep, but it's still fun.  There's some really funny moments, but the focus is more on running around, scared, and hoping a Robot doesn't spot you before you find another hiding spot.
Maybe a little too easy once you get the hang of it.  And it's no doubt the game would've benefited from a month or 2 more of development.  Such as:
- Greater variety of robots.  There's a handful of different ones, and they are all very different, but it seems like there is room for more.
- Crafting would've given this game another layer of complexity.  There's many throwaway items you find in the various houses you loot.  Why not give everything in the game a use?  Put spices on rabbit before cooking it to gain a boost.  Or even weapon customization.  Would've loved to have a silenced or even scoped pistol, providing that I gathered up the supplies needed to craft one.
- Explorable interiors
- Better textures.  Although I loved the atmosphere and the open landscape feel of most of the game, I sometimes feel like they didn't put enough time into making the world look nice.  I'm not a stickler for graphics, but there could've been more done in that sense.
All in all, I really like this game.  It's fun and that's what counts the most.  I just feel that where other developers would've spent some extra time to polish this game, this one was sent out the door a little too early.

I will preface this by saying I played this game a good year before most people did, as I played it at a convention as a guest early last year, so I've seen it go through varying versions of development.

You're running through what remians of Stalingrad, trudging through mud and snow to attack an objective, simply because the enemy is occupying it. As you catch your breath in a makeshift trench, you see your comrades fall to the ground, clutching their wounds and begging for their mother. The look over to you, and outstretch their hand, only to fall limp seconds later.
Your commander orders you to attack a building, you charge forward along with your comrades, and you crush the enemy inside. It's quiet for a moment, but you hear the screech, the sound that will engrain itself into your mind for the rest of your life - artillery fire.
You duck for cover, and see your friends bodies fly through the air - in pieces or not. Your vision is blurred, your ears are ringing.
The artillery ceases. You stand up, and look around to see what is left of your platoon. It's quiet. Too quiet. You are ordered to defend the objective, and you hunker down, only to hear the scariest sound a German can hear.
In the distant fog, you see them. Russians. Rats. They have their bayonet's affixed, their pistols raised, and their grenades ready. You can barely see them, but you can hear them as if they're right next to you.
"OOOOOORAAAAAAH!"
Sounds of machine gun fire rip through the air, and you see the Russians fall to the ground. They keep coming. The Russian hydra is charging forth, for every one that falls, two more take his place. What seemed like a cozy trench is now filled with Russians, beating your comrades to death with binoculars, the butts of their rifles, and their own fists.
You get shot, right in the gut. You try to spam ctrl to bandage, but it's futile. Your vision is darkened, blurred, and your hearing is muffled. All you can hear is yourself muttering, "Nein! Nein! Bitte!"
You fall to the ground shortly after, left in the snow to rot.
You peek at the killfeed.

Do you want PTSD lite?
If the answer is yes, then this game is for you!  This game is somewhere on the realism spectrum between a generic shooter, and an Arma game (And it leans closer to the Arma side).  The game has a very short time to kill, usually one or two bullets will finish the job pretty well, although if you can disengage,  minor injuries can sometimes be bandaged before you bleed out (and you can bleed out).  The real delight of the game is its scale and visuals.  it's best played on 64 player servers, with as many players as possible, which can make the game fairly chaotic.  Visually, the game is not the most beautiful, although it is by no means ugly, but it does a good job at portraying sone of the more horrible aspects of war, limbs can come off, although blood is not overdone, like in some games, and the game is filled with lots of little thing that catch your eye.
Anyway, I think I will end with a story from my time in game:
I was in the gunnery seat of a panzer IV, when a T-34 roles onto the street directly ahead.  I sight the gun to my estimated range and fire.  The shell shattered on impact, dealing little to no damage.  I hear a pinging noise on the right side of the tank, probably machine gun fire, I think to myself.  I  adjust my sights and wait for my loader to finish loading the shell.  After waiting some time for confirmation that the shell is loaded, I try firing anyway.  Click.  There's no shell in the barrel.  The T-34 fires, their shell bounces off the side of the tank.  I take the momentary break to take a look at the crew compartment of my Panzer IV.  Everyone in the tank is dead, and there are several holes on the right side that appear to have come from anti tank rifles.  Only my loader is still alive, and he's missing both his legs, cradling a shell and crying for his mother.  There's nothing left for me in this tank, and I evacuate out of the Hatch on the left side. Right as I have just exited, the anti tank rifles start peppering the sides again, as I'm climbing down from the tank a round penetrates and impacts the ammunition racks.  The tank explodes violently and I'm cast several feet from the vehicle, slowly bleeding out on the ground.

Cuphead is the demonstration of both excellent difficulty and excellent accessibility that I've been wanting for a long time.
There was definitely something appealling about 8-bit run-and-guns of old; the feeling of survival and tension as you survive each of the varied attacks of a boss that seem utterly undodgable. But what most people don't touch on is the number of big issues those games had. The boss's movements would often be very unclear, or could be read in several different ways. "Oh, he's about to punch? OH - oh, no, he dashed across the whole room past me. And now I'm dead." The games had lives systems that limited how much you could learn about a boss in a single Continue, and leave many people walled off even if they were willing to commit more time to trying.
Cuphead is a hard game with none of those problems. The animation style not only sweetens the deal, giving you a visual treat during your many deaths, but evokes many clear and broadcasted attacks that players can almost always understand relatively quickly. There are exceptions, and times when an attack might kill you anyway, but the game is also designed for infinite lives and relatively fast boss times - so even these pain points don't amount to much.
This is definitely not a game for everyone - no one should think less of themselves for playing more story-based or reflex-light games, but I do think it's more nuanced and well-designed than the "ULTRA HARD GAME" the internet likes to make it out to be. I died hundreds of times to certain bosses, but I continued because I was enjoying myself, not because of a need to prove anything. And the bosses are definitely designed for replay - there's plenty of variety in their attacks, and some of them are designed such that if you beat them on the first try, you wouldn't get to see all of their possibilities (Example: The boss of "Candyland" has a total of 5 different henchmen bosses, but only sends a total of 3 out per try).
Once you've finished the game, an Expert mode can grant you some more enjoyment out of it - and while some bosses simply use this to tweak some numbers and add some projectiles, some make some very inventive changes to their formula to enhance the challenge (for instance, rather than performing two attacks in turns, doing both attacks at once).
If you're on the fence about whether it's too hard for you, feel free to look at videos of novices attempting some of the bosses. They'll die - a lot, but I've often been surprised at how quickly some seemingly inept players can get used to the game. Also remember that Porkrind's upgrades can make many bosses easier! Some shots work well for certain bosses, while some may make a boss much more frustrating.

Here's my elevator pitch for Dungeon of Endless:
"It's a rogue-like, tower defense game with Left 4 Dead finales thrown in."
And it truly is an amagame of these things. It's like an rogue-like RPG in that you're exploring a randomly-generated dungeon and dealing with the enemies and other things you encounter there.
The tower-defense element pulls heavily from real-time strategy and role-playing elements. There's a pretty meaty three-resource system that you engage. You build machines to generate more of the resources then use those resources to build all kinds of offensive and defensive weapons or to level up your heroes (each with their own unqiue attributes, powers and weapons to equip).
Every time you open a door in the dungeon your machines produce the goods. There's also a chance of enemy waves spawning -- that's where the tower defense comes in. You need to build defenses to prevent them from running roughshod over your stuff (and eventually destroying your precious energy crystal). Smart, strategic exploration plays a big role here, creating choke points and making sure that enemies don't swarm you all at once is key to survival.
Once you find the exit to the dungeon floor there's a final event where you must manually carry your power crystal from the start of the dungeon to the exit -- all the while fending off enemy's. That's where the Left 4 Dead allusion comes into play. These final runs can go horribly if you haven't powered and defended the path.
Since I've been playing there's been constant adjustment to the economy and difficulty of the game -- this is the kind of fine tuning you want from a game that's in Alpha. But throughout I've had fun playing the game. Even when the tuning made the game insanely hard. Even when the game is broken Dungeon of Endless is fun.

This game is a well-designed permadeath roguelike with one shocking design flaw: It doesn't have (even an optional mode that enables) permadeath!
Both the people who cite the game's enjoyable systems and the people who claim these systems fall flat are, in my opinion, correct, since the ability to respawn with minimal lost progress after every death both destroys the otherwise well-created tension in the game, and makes the optimal strategy a tedious and repetivie sucide dash for the machine pieces scattered across the islands. However, once I realised the ability to respawn was the source of these problems, I switched to playing the game in a self-enforced permadeath (delete world manually on death) fashion, and the game almost magically became the tense, engaging stealth and survival game it had always promised to be!
In conclusion, I'd wholeheartedly recommend this game, but only when played in the permadeath fashion it feels like it was designed for (though the devs never even mentioned it!). Devs, if you're reading this, for goodness sake, ADD A PERMADEATH MODE! (Also I'm sure we'd all appreciate the promised multiplayer).

I don’t feel like drawing any conclusion from some lengthy paragraphs, just my personal experience for those considering investing time in this game. I will focus on the flaws, to hear about how amazing this game is, please click 'Positive'. This review contains minor spoilers about some gameplay mechanics, but I will try to keep the story intact.
Atmosphere: Yes, Rapture has its own charm at the very first glance but think about this: the game is about 12 to 24 hours long depending on your playstyle, and to me the excitement quickly wore off. I was able to explore in different levels but it felt more like being confined in an abandoned submarine and my only freedom was to wander around from chambers to chambers since the levels all look so similar, I found many rooms pretty much interchangable, same timber floors and doors, bookshelves that are 2 metres high, same interior decoration, even the bathrooms are complete duplicates of each other......and as I made my way towards the end there’s almost no friendly NPCs, no safety zones and everyone speaks in a mocking tone that disturbed me quite a lot. There was nothing too scary really, just uneasy.

Story: If you want to make a checklist Bioshock’s got everything you’ll need: background, character development, climax, moral choices(yay!) that lead to different endings. The whole story is fragmented to small pieces in the form of diaries, the drawback of this is, if you happen to be a completionist like me then make sure to check every corner ……I sometimes got paranoid worrying that I might have missed some important ones.
Gameplay: Collecting loot literally became a chore. I had to check every closet, or drawer, or trash bin, or ashtray, or corpse, and took photos of enemy corpses for research bonus. It’s actually not fun when I began to mechanically press E. The game also became ridiculously easy when I had almost all weapons upgraded, taking down Big Daddies was a pain when I started but with proper plasmids and incendiary crossbow bolts it hardly took more than 10 seconds each.

This game.  Oh, this game.  Where do I even begin to describe the fun and introspective experience it gives you?
Story:  9/10  The story of Bioshock is usually the selling point of the game.  The story is linear, but the game encourages you to explore the environment.  By doing so, you can find recordings of a plethora of characters.  Each recording brings a new bit of perspective to the story.  Also, the plot twist of all plot twists towards the end of the story.  I wasn't a huge fan of the ending, of which there are three small variations based on your actions in-game, but it's all about the journey to get there.
Gameplay:  7/10  Anyone who has played the game will tell you that the gameplay of Bioshock left something to be desired.  The game did a good job of providing a variety of weapons and plasmids so you can approach the combat in different ways (running in guns abalze, setting up traps, etc.). The interface was clunky, though, and in the middle of combat it was pretty annoying to try and hit the right button to switch to the desired gun.  It was that, or interupt the flow of the game to open the weapon wheel.  The weapon upgrade system was also incomplete, in my opinion.  Each weapon has two regular upgrades and one final upgrade that you can only get after you get the other two, but I don't think there is a way to get every weapon fully upgraded.  Also, the darn hacking mini-game was beyond frustrating.
Setting:  10/10  I don't give out a 10 lightly.  But by god, this game deserves it.  Rapture is such a creative setting for the game to play out in, and really adds to the gameplay and the story both.  You venture through the dystopian city of Raputire in a linear fashion, but around every bend is another hallway begging you to explore it, only to ambush you with enemies.  The setting of the game is where it gets its intellectual value, as well, as it challenges your morals and ideas of what a perfect society should be.  The game does a great job of establishing the dark atmosphere of the city with the music and voice acting you find in the recordings scattered across Rapture.
I love this game.  It's the kind of love that is hard to explain to someone in a short review.  If you have never played Bioshock, I can only tell you that you're missing out on a fantastic game.  The game has an interesting replay value, as well, because the second time you play through the story I guarentee you will find places you glanced by the first time you played it.
I would highly recommend this game, especially with the remastered version coming out later this year.

For people experiencing sound stuttering issues and cannot enable EAX (WINDOWS 10 USERS) , here's a possible quick solution:
1.) Download "openal" (google "openal download") and install it.
2.) Go to windows/system32 map and copy "wrap_oal.dll" to game executable location (E.g.: C:/steam/steamapps/common/bioshock) .
3.) Rename "wrap_oal" to "openal32". After that you can enable EAX in audio options and hopefully that'll fix sound issues for you.

In the beginning, lack of supplies is your enemy. The longer you survive, overconfidence becomes your enemy. Every decision has a risk. Every ounce of supplies is a burden and relief. The Long Dark will charm you, flatter you, seduce you, fill you with hope and awe... then break your heart, crush your body, and haunt you as your life slips away in futile gasps. You'll want more.

Disclaimer: I backed this game on Kickstarter.
Use Your Words has an interesting selection of prompt types, but several factors leave it in a state I just can't recommend.
For starters, the game is paced awfully. EVERYTHING is slow and seemingly designed in a way to take as much of your party's time as possible. We don't need to be introduced to every game every time we get it, we know what Blank-O-Matic is from last time we played it this round. We REALLY don't need to see the entire Subtitled Clip up to 16 times (Twice as the prompt, once for each answer, and once again for each answer that scored points. It could really use that part cut out). So much time is spent on all these aspects, it feels like you play a 10 minute game over the course of half an hour.
Next are the House Answers, an answer for every question put in by the game itself. Instead of just voting for your favorite answer, you have to consider if that answer is actually a House Answer, which will make you lose points! I'm curious how that idea even got added to the game with the sheer amount of harm it puts on the choice section. It almost feels like it was included just to be different from that OTHER set of party games you play with your cell phones and vote on answers. House Answers also feed into the molasses pacing by adding another prompt every round.
Finally, and this one's a admittedly bit nitpicky, but the announcer has almost no personality and is just really boring. I get that it's going for some sort of throwback game show announcer, but it just doesn't do it for us.
In my opinion, if you want a good party game like this, go for the Jackbox Party Packs instead, especially 3. They're overall better games. I host a Game Night every weekend where we play all manner of games and the Jackbox Games get requests, while I had to drag everyone through a second round of this just to see if the first one being not great was a fluke.
It's got a lot of good ideas behind it, and the cellphone party game genre is still wide open for more, but without major improvements, I cannot recommend getting Use Your Words, especially with such great games you could buy in the same genre.

Then, things get a bit more complicated. Sometimes you'll make a decision that will cause some of these 4 aspects to rise or fall at a slow but steady rate, forcing you to make decisions quickly to try and preventing any of them from completely filling or emptying. There are special objectives, such as uncovering the conspiracy, or recruiting the minstrel, some of which will unlock new cards which means new possible scenarios.

This game is a kind of in-between simulator and shooter like COD or Battlefield. The brutatlity and carnage of the fights, coupled with some great mechanics make the game just enough like a simulator to love, but easy enought to pick up so that you don't spend the first 30 hours learning to play. Hopping from trench to trench or building to building in a manic run, hoping to god that you live through the dash, and then arriving and securing your immediate area is one of the biggest thrills this game offers. That and shooting people. This game captures the feeling that the next room may be your last for this life, that the next trench could be full of enemies, that the windows are full of snipers or the alleyways covered by machinegunners. This isn't a hardcore sim, but neither is it a simple twitch shooter. It toes the line just well enough to be interesting and fun. The player base is a bit small, so matches without bots are rare, but the game shines through in providing a good WWII fps that isn't too arcade-y or sim-y. Red Orchestra 2: Heroes of Stalingrad with Rising Storm is a first person shooter that puts players into a number of battlefields across Eastern Europe and the Pacific.
Many fans of traditional first person shooters find RO2 hard to grip as bolt action rifles take precedence over sub machine guns in this game, but I for one like the long range combat found on most maps. Soldiers have a very limited pool of health, with a single well placed shot being the most common cause of death for players. Regardless of map, strategy and positioning are crucial to victory. Cooperation with your squad and your overall team is also a must have, but verbal communication is not necessary. While the eastern front maps have more or less similar armies facing off against each other, in the Pacific an interesting dynamic takes place between the Japanese and Americans. The Japanese are able to banzai charge the enemy to suppress them, have light mortars, and receive no penalties for committing suicide if they kill an American along with themselves. The Americans have flamethrowers and are equipped with more machine guns and semiautomatic rifles. It is surprisingly more balanced that it would appear at first glance.
I would highly recommend purchasing this game, especially if it is on sale.
Pros:
1. Emphasis on objectives rather than kills
2. Deaths not shown on scoreboard
3. Uniquely centered on bolt action rifles
4. Unique faction mechanics on Rising Storm maps
5. Long range combat
Cons:
1. Long range combat
2. Stalemates form on occasion
Overall, I rate this game

That said... it is P2W, in a lot of ways. You can buy cash items with gold, from P2W folks who get things they don't want or have excess of, so you're not totally screwed if you don't want to put real money into this game. It is something to be aware of. The other thing is...even with cash, to do things like enhance gems (they give you stats on your gear), you can buy safeguards to prevent gems from breaking when you try to combine them. They don't guarantee success. You want to unlock stats on your runic tablet (level 60+), you buy inks...which resets all your stats on your tablet - yes, they could (and often do) make your tablet worse. Pouches for your equipment stats...well, you get the idea. You spend money (or time to get gold and find cash players) for a chance at getting better things, but most often, you just make your stats worse.

So I do definetly recommend this game, it is a great game and a lovely bit of anti-objectivist commentary; there is a lot to love about this... BUT it has got a few flaws that I feel keep it from being /perfect/ so this may be pretty nitpicky but here are some of them!
-Violence: Why am I killing all these splicers. WAIT! before you freak out and think I am anti-violence or too artsy lemme elaborate! Now I wanna note that this game is much better with the violence than Bioshock Infinite, in infinite it makes no sense why ever single person in Colombia wants my bum dead, and it just acts as filler. In Bioshock Proper the violence fits much much better, since it makes since that all these splicers wanna splice me so they can splice more. That's all well and good, but what about the /deeper themes/ *put's on beret* of the game?
Every inch of bioshock is against Ayn Randian Objectivism, with a free market everything in this game costs money, from bathroom stalls to turning off the security; the audio logs all relate to how each person deals with this society and how the working man is screwed over. Every bit of design in this game is about this theme..... except the combat: what does shooting people in the face tell us about objectivism? I mean the ammo conservation relates to it but after the first hour you will be pretty set on ammo. As I said this is really nitpicky but I do still find this a concern and one of the reasons this game isn't my /favorite/.
-Audio Logs: Okay this one is really nitpicky and already complained about by a lot of others, but audio logs are lazy. It's a cheap way to pick up exposition. The acting is nice and all other environmental storytelling in this game is great but these logs just feel silly to be perfectly placed next to whatever they are discussing; I really don't know how the game could have incorperated them better but it is a issue nontheless
-Everything after The Spoiler happens: If you've played this then you probably know what I'm talking about, after X gets whacked the game just turns into a build up to a boss fight that did not need to be in the game at all and doesn't help the pacing, gameplay, or story themes whatsoever. Note that I really love Olympus Heights for showing the life of the average schmuck in Rapture but this area could have been placed before The Spoiler and the rest of the game just ditched.
-Ethics: The Little Sisters are a really blatant and poorly included moral choice. there are enough resources in the game that the player will never /need/ the little sister rescources, so each player is more likely to simply decide from the start whether or not to kill or save all of them. Also I mean I guess it fits into the whole objectivism thing cause it's letting you decide whether or not the adam you gain is worth killing a kid and I guess that fits into the whole, "if there is a free market then everything is bad" vibe this game has but it really is just placed in so so poorly and black and white.

BioShock is often lauded as one of the pinnacles of FPS/RPGs as well as one of the finest video-game narratives. Although the game is essentially a spiritual successor to the System Shock series, the consensus from journalists and consumers alike is that it's a classic.
However, with all that being said, it's interesting how both its narrative and gameplay has not aged as well after a decade, and how fans probably have misremembered its flaws.
Don't misunderstand this as some hipster review; BS is a good game. Rapture is one of the most well-polished atmospheres ever made, the level design is very good in spite of its linearity, and its core gameplay is tolerable at best.
The problem is none of these qualities elevates the game into greatness nor to ignore its many flaws. Even worse, these problems that plague the first game are only dwelled upon in later games when they originated here.
Before we talk about the game, I do want to mention the PC version. This port is rather terrible; however, it can be fixed. Mostly.
What I don't think can be fixed is any nausea you may feel if you turn up the mouse-sensitivity. I don't know whether it's the art-style, the FOV (I doubt it as I play the game with 90) or some mouse acceleration but I cannot play at anything higher than four (out of ten.)
Unfortunately, while some of these issuesed are addressed, the Remastered does not fix everything:
BioShock suffers from two major faults: It lacks the dual-wielding system where you have Plasmids in one-hand and your gun in the other. The other mistake is the unnecessary fluff that takes away from the survival horror experience.
The former can be excused for being the first in the series; however, the latter is something that cannot be easily overlooked, namely the crafting system and camera "research" system. Both of these inclusions are utterly worthless except when you get less ammo and tougher enemies.
However, if you use the camera ASAP you can play two-thirds of the game without it. A better idea would be to throw away the camera and opted for better resource management and fixed enemy damage values. The game would be a better FPS for it, and it would be more honest.
Although this question is more often one of semantics, I think it'll illustrate a point: In what way is BS an RPG other than streamlining the RPG-mechanics from its predecessor?
SS2 focused on specializing builds around weapon types, PSI-onic abilities and/or attributes in other skills. You had the ability to shape your character from the introduction, and throughout the game you could change it to suit your playstyle.
BS strips all the complexities away with its plasmids and gene-modifications. You will get all the weapons every single playthrough, and the gene-mods are in specialized categories that discourage any freeform experimentation. You're a Jack of all trades; master of all, specialist of none.
The system itself is not bad but it is a clear sign of streamlining. With that being said, is BS's system truly an RPG or is it something more along the lines of the Far Cry's perks system?
Content is still gated by placing plasmids and mods in specific locations, but the same result is the same stilted growth of your capabilities. It's one of many instances where I have to wonder how influential BS has been on modern games (for better and for worse).
BS's role in influencing games is undeniable, but what is more interesting is what has been forgotten as to why these aspects are so enrapturing.
For starters, the usage of audio-logs. Recorded messages are now the butt-of-the-joke, but their inclusion here was to keep the horror elements without littering NPCs or to bore the player from the lack of interactions. More importantly, they told the player of what cannot be gleamed from the environments as they provide a contrast to what the player finds. They provided something for your imagination to use.
Another aspect that holds up is its environmental storytelling. For example, if you were to compare this game to Fallout 3/NV the biggest difference is how BioShock conveys more with less clutter. The developers were able to focus more so on the visual input, and let the finer details (visual or the audio) fill in the rest. And without the simple distractions like a constant UI notification for junk, the player focuses more on the surroundings.
Now are these aspects perfect? God no. BS (and SS) is the originator of the trope of hiding key-codes and/or recording information at the worst times like a Lovecraft protagonist. And compared to F3/NV, BS has tighter and more sensible level-design that lends itself to having the time to add more details.
However, it's the purpose and execution behind these storytelling methods that I think is forgotten about why they work so well, and when you dwell further on what the game set out to do you find more of its flaws more obvious now than back then.
In spite of wanting to keep spoilers to a minimum, I do want to criticize the narrative because that is what everyone remembers BS most fondly of.
No matter how many times I replay this game I can't tell you what the game is really about. BS tries its damnedest to provide an objective, apolitical story about a free-market city freed from conventions of morals and politics. The only problem is that it never commits to the idea of, "Unrestrained societies are possibly bad!", and instead gets jumbled up in its "family" nonsense and blatantly good/evil choice which comes across as being pretentious. (Sound familiar?)
It could be argued that Andrew Ryan was right all along—the city fell to parasites like Fontaine—and he was the more upstanding character as he valued merits alone. However, in contrast, the characters like Dr. Steinman and Cohen show that merit is not satisfying enough. Usually I'd be fine with this vagueness of a message, but with the forced good/bad-ending to the game it hampers any middle-ground to be found.
It also doesn't help that gameplay can clash with the narrative. For example, why can you leave money on security devices to "hack" machines? (How does that work?) Why does Andrew Ryan let his enemies buy bullets to fight him? Is he that committed to his free-market values?
Or, for less pedantic questions, why is the WYK effect on Jack inconsistent? He doesn't appear to remember being "activated" (if he didn't forget it after the plane-crash), and he doesn't respond to the command the same way (ex. when you are told to get the radio and when you are forced to lower your weapon). If it was a simple mental suggestion, then why (when he obviously knows) does he not react with speaking like how he talks at the beginning? (Why is he mute anyway?)
The obvious answer to these questions is that the developers were too busy making a good game, and that's perfectly fine. BioShock is a great game for what it tried to do, but it's by no means a masterpiece of storytelling or gameplay.
I'm under no dellusion that the remaster will address all these narrative issues. I expect the gunplay to be better and for a better performance like Infinite.
What I wanted to share is when you return to Rapture to relive the glory days under the sea it won't be same as what you remembered. Games have come a long way from BioShock in both gameplay and narrative, and the only way we get better is to learn where the mistakes were made behind us.

I remember reading about "Sir" back when it was still in the process of funding, at the time I didn't have a suitable computer to play mostly anything, and had completely forgotten about it by the time I got myself a new laptop. I was reminded of the game thanks to Jim Sterling's Squirty-play of it, and instantly threw it on my wishlist to be bought later, 24 hours go by and it went on sale for $4 and I jumped at the chance. Ever since then I can say with confidence the purchase was well worth, though I do agree with the general consensus that it could use some tweaking/optimization, and there's plenty of room for additions both in the robots, items/usage of items, and environments departments.

What "Sir" brings together is plenty of experiences that I've had with other games into one package: Paranoia, fear, excitement, all fuel your actions as you strive to escape the islands and the gently-but-lethal mechanized foes that are hunting you. The eerie and contextual music adds a layer of tension, and ambiance that draws me back to playing older PC games like Myst for the atmosphere, though the subtly oppressive one in this game has a flavor all it's own, a very british one at that with a thin layer of dry dark comedy. The art style, robot designs, and music compliment one another, and fit snugly. The game-play is tense to the point I found in some moments hiding in the tall grass from a pack of hunters passing through, holding my breath in real life as if it would matter in my attempts to go unnoticed, as well as outwardly panicking when the bullets started to fly. Sneaking about takes time, though the gun-play is an alternative, bullets are scarce, the Enemy-AI is a sharp as their aim is fine, and will notice when things are amiss, ensuring you have to be alert and considerate of your actions, or your cranium will be their new trophy. The game has tons of potential it can strive towards, and I would recommend it to anyone who wants a refreshing take on the survival genre, challenging, unique, and more British than the queen of England herself, where else are you going to snack on Fish&chips while reloading a pistol and hiding in the bushes from top-hat wearing killer robots?
