There are two types of reviews this game is going to get.
The first type will call this game good, great, or even revolutionary, with varied classes and characters within classes to keep gameplay fresh, so on and so forth.
The second type will call this game bad due to repetitiveness of gameplay, cliche and unimaginative roles for characters, lack of story, and of course the dlc (Looking at you Angry Joe).
This review will be of the first variety.
The first thing I want to say about Evolve is that it is exactly as advertised.  One of the biggest complaints about games these days is how developers and producers "fluff up" the gameplay/graphics in trailers leading up to release.  That didn't happen here, everything in the game is exactly how it was advertised to us over the long development period, which included gameplay trailers AND a whole tournament with prizes played by fans at E3.  Not even the graphics are any less than advertised, unless I missed some minute details while playing (the game looks really good even if I did, no complaints here.)
The unlock system is also very noteworthy.  There are multiple characters in each class at release that are not available at first, along with a multitude of skins for the monster and hunter's weapons.  However, you only unlock new characters as you improve your skills with the starting characters in each class.  Once you have performed with enough skill as a tier 1 assault class, you get the tier 2 one, and so on.  This requires you to play multiple roles to get the full potential out of the game, making you prove your worth and also giving you a chance to find a character who has a skill set that works with you.  The only things you have to pay any real money for are the skins, the fluff.  It's not like some other particular fps's where half the game has to be bought after you've paid for the game upfront.  Non-essential fluff is all the dlc this game has, which is pretty much all dlc should be, and the developers get it.
Gameplay itself is very different from your average multiplayer fps, which should be obvious from the get-go.  This isn't a run-and-gun shooter to get instant action on just by turning on your console.  In this game you have to play smart, especially if you're the monster.  You have to keep track of your enemy's movements and where they might go to either avoid them, or catch up, and once a fight erupts it is all-out chaos!  On either side, you also have to be warry of your environment on top of your player adversaries, as there are plenty of npc animals and plant traps just waiting to catch careless players by surprise, which can absolutely turn the tide of a whole match.  The difference in multiplayer between this game and, say, Call of Duty is pretty much the same as the Hunger Games vs. Twilight: one is for those who like to think, and the other is for those who just want something dropped in their laps.  That may be an over-exageration but I think it translates my point well enough.
The only thing I can think to say negativly about this game is that you will ultimately get stuck playing a role you don't like/aren't familiar with.  This will happen eventually, and it can suck.  In my experience though, it doesn't happen often, and even if it did, you're robbing yourself of part of your purchase if you stick with only one or two roles/characters anyway.  Who knows?  You could be dropped into a game where you are stuck as the monster, and end up liking it more than hunters.
I really enjoy this game, I fully recommend it to people looking for something new, and I'm sure given time it will go on sale if the price is intimidating.

It's a strange hybrid of roguelike and tower defense, where you open doors to reveal unpowered rooms (and sometimes merchants, chests, caches of resources, new heroes, or monsters). You can power the rooms up, allowing modules (essentially towers and resource generators) to be built inside of them, and preventing monsters from spawning inside of them. Every time a door is opened, you receive your allotment of resources per door opened (depending on your generators) and there is a chance that waves of monsters will spawn from the unpowered rooms, who will attempt to attack your core.
Upon finding the exit to the next floor, you must have a hero carry the core to the exit, each room you pass through losing power as it is disconnected from the core, with monsters spawning non-stop from unpowered rooms.
It's a pretty unique game, and despite balance issues (hopefully due to the game's incomplete beta state), is quite fun. 4-player co-op is up soon on their roadmap, so it'll be interesting to see how that works, or if it'll be a hot mess with people accidentally opening multiple doors at once due to poor coordination and getting everyone killed.
Also, it's worth noting that the developer has handled this game's early access in an extremely professional manner, and that development has sped along at a steady clip.

PZ is a really nicely fleshed-out and atmospheric zombie survival game. I wouldn't recommend it for anyone who's looking for a fast-paced shoot-em-up, but this game really manages to stand out among a sea of zombie drivel. The RPG elements add an interesting dimension to an otherwise stale and tired genre, and the ability to add both positive and negative traits to characters at the start allows you to really work out just how well you or a character would survive in the zombie apocalypse. Unlike most games, your character isn't a hardened badass, and you'll get panicked when you try fighting zombies. This and many other status conditions can really change your gameplay experience, like when you're being chased back to your house by a horde of zombies because you accidentally triggered an alarm, but the rain has soaked you so much that you can barely manage to run. All in all, worthwhile for someone who wants a more straightforward and realistic approach to the zombie survival genre.

Pillar is an interesting game.  It's primarily a puzzle game, but it's also a pretty emotional game, since the puzzles are conveyed via a personality, with personality flaws being a major aspect.  For example, the "Distant" personality puzzle is to advance through areas while trying to avoid human interaction.  You're given tools to accomplish that, but part of the fun is figuring those out so I won't explain anything.  When Distant experiences human interaction, the game definitely conveys that it's agony, at least, that was my interpretation.  You don't necessarily "lose" if you fail, but if you want to collect all the notes you should try everything.
But again, the core is the puzzles.  Some of them are REALLY hard, and once again, you're free to skip right past them, but you won't 100% the game then.  Some of the puzzles I spent 30+ min on and still didn't solve, and had to try again another day.  A lot of the puzzles are pretty genius from a design perspective.
One more thing, the music is outstanding.  I enjoyed Pillar overall.

Can you count to six?
That is basically the question this game will answer. Now there is more to it as you have to imagine a dice pushed into a 2 dimensional shape that you have to redesign in your head each time, but that´s really not that hard as... well you know, a dice only has 6 sides and once you get the hang of it, the game offers nothing new.
Nearly all level feel the same, as you do the same thing over and over. Sure, they introduce spaced out shapes which you have to put together before being able to reconstruct the dice in your head and that brings some fresh wind into the game, but it comes half way through and quickly loses it´s charm through repitition (again).
The way the game is designed, it´s just far too easy. EVERY number has a counterpart, meaning you don´t have to think about anything. Just pick a number and start filling in the tiles. Repeat until you´re done...
Instead of introducing moving shapes, more sided dices or blacked out tiles so not every number has a counterpart they just repeat the same concept for each level which for me was too little and only left me wishing for more.

I've been asked by enough friends how the game is. This is what I think about Evolve currently.
I recommend Evolve but it's not for everyone. I've been playing since the first closed Alpha. ~80 hours so far. I'd give it a 7.5 out of 10 if I had to, but please read on.
PROS
+ Has some of that L4D feel.
+ Asymmetry done right. It's a fresh concept.
+ Evolving tactics and playstyles (like L4D).
+ Very well balanced at higher levels (not perfect though and tweaks are coming "soon").
+ Controls very well (except for a couple jetpack vs. terrain glitches).
+ An absolute blast with friends. Working together, benefitting from eachothers strengths, is an amazing feeling.
+ Being the Monster at Stage 1 and even 2 (before armor) is scary. Truly an adrenaline pumping experience.
+ Everyone gets new maps if they release any.
+ Day 1 DLC is just skins. Purely cosmetic. And they usually make the monster far easier to see.
+ Other creatures in the map are a lot of fun. They can be used as traps.
+ Buffs and perks work well to fit individual playstyles.
+ The strike system to the hunter's health is well done.
CONS
- Not worth $60 or $80 or $100. You find it for under $40-you buy it.
- Glitchy with Steam Overlay on release.
- As of 3/7/15, still no patches. No tweaks or bug fixes. This is inexcusable for a AAA title.
- Get an incompetent team member and you're dead. Not everyone needs to be an expert at their class, but it can all fall apart pretty fast.
- A good monster can cheese some mechanics during combat. Ex. At Stage 3, where the monster clearly has the advantage, he or she has to either kill all hunters or destroy the relay before they respawn. The round usually isn't even close to being over as far as the time limit goes. So, whenever the Monster is close to dying, he or she can just run away, feed, and gain the armor necessary to fight again. There are ways to combat this, but I've had a monster just sit and laugh at my face while blasting it with all I've got.
- Walking simulator if you choose Abe (Trapper without a way to keep track or find the monster/more reliant on sounds and circling birds) and are never alerted to the monster presence in a large, monster balanced map.
- Hard to run away or defend yourself if your other teammates die. The monster can sniff you from a distance through walls and can also follow your glowing footprints. There's no way to hide prints like the monster (can't crouch/sneak) can even with temporary invisibility.
- Matchmaking has an awful queue system and playing the 5-day Evacuation mode is a pain because people leave and the game crashes half way through, therefore you miss out on the XP boost.
- Leveling up characters to stage 2 or 3 is a chore and sometimes counterproductive to the team game. It forces some players to focus on a specific mundane task that can cause them to ignore the game's objectives and focus on their own agenda.
- New monsters aren't free.
- New hunters aren't free.
- Both are separate DLC packs at this time.
- People aren't playing the game much because there's no patches or tweaks to fix the crashes and imbalances. The game could die because of this. Not smart 2K/TRS.

Played it for about a week now and I do like the game very much.  A fresh of breath air when it comes to the online multiplayer shooter genre.  I recommend the game, however there are some high points and low points, some of which may be a deal breaker for some people.  Here's a breakdown of top 5 pros and cons.
PROs:
1) Great asymmetrical 4v1 gameplay
2) Good graphics, sound and character design
3) Varied selection of skills and weapony
4) Good selection of characters and monsters to play and master
5) This game is really fun when the CONs below aren't bothering you too much...
CONs:
1) Too easy to find the monster - tracks, tags, dust, sounds, etc.  Thus the game always is the same at the start... run and hide and eat.  *yawn*
2) Character and monster progression is tedious...  you will always lose to whomever  you play at level 1, sometimes at level 2 and finally at level 3 things even out
3) Multiplayer character/monster selection is broken.  And getting dropped into an already existing (and half-lost) game as a random player's character sucks. It's like Russian Roulette - you either get a good character, or you're dead.  This will steal the enjoyment out of your games.  Who wants to play a character they don't want to play?  Me neither...
4) It may be fun, but it's repetitive.  You will likely not be playing this game more than a month from now anymore...
5) The extra DLC and Game editions are not worth it and ruin the character progression.  Sure, pay to win if you want all characters unlocked at level 3, but you're going to ruin half the game for yourself.
For $60, it was a fair purchase.  Anything more than that and you will feel ripped off.  Anything less is likely a bargain!

But, seriously, since
Halloween is coming up, I decided to give Outlast a second playthrough to see if it was as good as I remembered it. And for the most part it is, although I did notice a few flaws. Here's what I got out of this playthrough:
+Outlast has some great atmosphere, which is held up by the fantastic sound design, unique characters, and disorienting location. Somewhat similar to Silent Hill, you'll be in a large area full doors, but nearly all of them are locked, which creates a combination of agoraphobia and claustrophobia.
+The graphics are also decent. Of course, when you can barely see anything because it's so dark, it's hard to mess up graphics. But not much will beat turning on the infrared camera and seeing eyes glowing in the dark for the first time.
+The controls are pretty smooth; running from enemies, jumping over obstacles, and looking over your shoulder all feel very natural. It's easy to get immersed with the level of control given to you. It's kind of like a very simplified version of Mirror's Edge.
+And I personally love when you can collect notes to learn about the backstory in a horror game, which Outlast definitely provides, so that's a pretty big plus in my book.
-The enemy AI is both predictable and easy to manipulate. Once you realize that a stalker will check all hiding spots
the one you're currently in (unless you're an idiot who decided to hide while he's looking at you), hiding changes from you being scared of being found to you being annoyed that he hasn't left the room yet.
-Some of the jumpscares are kind of weak. I don't mind jumpscares, but in a video game I don't think they're effective when they're part of a cutscene. Basically, instead of thinking "oh no, I need to run," you think "oh no, I need to watch something happen." Don't get me wrong, there are some jumpscares that aren't a part of a cutscene, but there aren't many.
-But here's probably my biggest complaint: no combat. Now, I'm not some nutcase who picks up a game of Tetris and yells "WHERE IS THE COMBAT," but in a horror game I feel some level of combat is necessary to keep the player scared.
Here's my
theory on it: I think fear is strongest in the middle of a fight-or-flight moment. The harder it is to choose between the two, the more stressful and scary the situation is. Without any fighting, there's no real fight-or-flight moment, because the default choice is always to run away. Because of this, it's probably not much scarier to play the game than it is to watch someone else play.
But don't take these complaints too harshly; the game is still very well put together, and worth a playthrough. I'd give it about a 7.5/10.

Actually, to be honest, it's is entirely story-based with 4 person Coop Invasion and Destruction missions as a bonus.
After one playthrough the fun begins on your 'New Game +' where you unlock two new weapons, an assault rifle that homes in on enemies and Mr. Toots the rainbow farting rainbow unicorn created by YouTube user Freddiew. You are also able to unlock cheats and weapons torn off of vehicles with salvage for even more destruction and killing fun. I personally use the L.E.O. Triple Homing Rocket Launcher.
All in all, a fun addition to the Red Faction series.

My recommendation is based on a player playing this game for the first time mid 2016 onwards and not having played a Bioshock game before. I am being harsh on this game on the basis that is has not aged well, and to be blunt, does not hold up to standards. The tipping point for my recommendation is being able to purchase it while on sale only.
For reference, I got this game on sale for SIGNIFICANTLY less than the current price, in the triple pack: it came to $2.71USD.
Even though I chose to recommend this game, a more accurate appraisal would be “Neutral”. I don’t regret buying the title (since I got it dirt cheap), and I still enjoyed playing it, but it is definitely not without flaws, and should not be purchased wihtout a discount.
Honestly, the positive comments about this game being a masterpiece must be more than a little bit exaggerated. There is almost nothing about this game that is a “masterpiece”, I find it difficult to believe that people genuinely think this...
realise that I completely appreciate how great this game could have been during release. It has all the hall-marks and potential, but by 2016 I found that the glaring issues weigh on its freshness, atmosphere and charming characters. It simply falls short of potentially being a masterpiece. Some things, such as the feel of the gunplay for example, are just so poor, that even in 2007 I would have had my reservations, let alone today.
It’s not a big positives list. What you should take from it is that you’ll have an enjoyable time. A great deal of effort has gone into this game and it really does show (in most areas). The environments, textures, lightning and audio all still hold up and ar great.
Most of the failings, I found, were in gameplay and some design choices as well as what ultimately ended up being a bit of a weak ending. Could it be more anti-climactic?!
Towards the end of the game, I kind of wanted to just get it over with. After the plot reveal (which was nice by the way), the story took a sudden pace change and you immediately got that ‘rushed’ feeling. Which proved correct once you beat the final boss and saw the cutscene.
Although the atmosphere and visuals were nice, I couldn’t enjoy the combat because the weapons were so stiff and dull, and the plasmids just weren’t viable enough.
Then when I saw the ending, or lack there-of, I had no urge to go into NG+. What was I going to do? I had already explored enough since you can travel between levels. Not to mention… there are no achievements to do anyway.
Ultimately I did enjoy it. I never.. forced, myself to play it. Was it a masterpiece? NO. Not even _CLOSE_. Do I regret buying it? No, I got it cheap on a sale and almost 13 hours of entertainment -you can’t argue with that value.
If I had paid 20$ for it, then it would have been an instant NO Recommendation and probably a regretted purchase.
Ultimately, it's just my opinion. I personally found the issues listed to be glaring. I’m more than capable of overlooking age and minor issues (Deus Ex, Oblivion, Diablo 2, NWN, MGS1, etc), but unfortunately in Bioshock they stuck out a little too much, to the point where they did get in the way.
If the weapons and gunplay FELT better, and the plasmids were far more viable for the sake of variety in combat, then I think, despite the story’s weakness (at the end), it would have been an easy $20 USD recommendation.

The first time I played this was, i think, about 8 years ago, and I quit after my second Big Daddy fight. It's not that I intentionally stopped playing the game, I just ended my first session there and never felt the need to get back in it.
After playing the incredible Bioshock Infinite, I thought maybe I should give this another chance. So, eventually, I did.
I'm going to recommend this game, but just barely. The story is nice, the city of Rapture is extremely appealing and the concept is great but I have so many issues with this game that damage the fun. Here are some:
- The combat system is not very good. Having to switch between plasmids and weapons all the time is tedious and eventually i just gave up on using plasmids in a fight. The weapons are just not that fun to use and there's not much strategy to the combat - just hit everything as fast as u can and spam first aid kits when you get low on health. It's not like they're hard to come by.
Eventually, I actually gave up on weapons and used only my wrench. It actually made the game easier.
- Fighting Big Daddies and collecting little sisters was fun at first, but eventually became a chore. I kept fighting them because I wanted the Adam, but every time I started a new level I just couldn't wait to get it over with.
- There isn't any in-game use of the fact Rapture is an underwater city. No one ever tries to flood you, you never go outside into the ocean or anything like that. It felt like a bit of waste of this great concept.
- Your only interactions with other characters (other than the ones you kill on sight) is through a communicator that they use to talk at you. They're just voices that tell you what to do next. It's pretty hard to care about any of them, and when you don't care about the people you're supposed to help or kill, the game loses some of it's immersion.
But, as you can see, I still DO recommend this game. While it does have many flaws, it has very important redeeming features:
- The atmosphere is great, and you'll find yourself intrigued to learn the hitsory of Rapture and it's downfall.
- The story is clever and very philosophical. It's all about choice, or lack thereof. The story is mostly praised for the major plot twist, but to be honest I found it kinda predictable. Even so, the reveal of it was extremely well done.
- It's the first one. It's your gateway to the triolgy, and it really should be played before the way-more-polished Bioshock 2 (which fixed pretty much every issue I had with the original). You have to play this if you want to get the whole story, and trust me - you do.

It's sort of like the logic of sudoku, but instead of playing on a square grid, you play on a collection of overlapping unfolded dice (and filling in digits 1-6 instead of 1-9).
You can fill in the squares either by clicking repeatedly to cycle through digits or by typing the number on the keyboard.
You rely less on process of elimination and more on the knowledge that opposing faces of a six-sided die always add up to 7. You may find yourself imagining the cubes in 3D space, or you might learn how the opposing faces are distributed across the various possible flattened nets.
Technical suggestion: While it's great that you can type the digit you want when the cursor is hovering over the square, it would be nice if the player could navigate the board with WASD or arrow keys. I'm not bad at 10key, but trying to 10key left-handed while my right moves the mouse is quite awkward. I ended up playing the majority of the game by clicking.
Colorblind folks might have a tougher time with this one. Because so many of the die nets overlap in so many places, they're marked with little color tags. Unfortunately, some of the more complicated levels have so many nets involved that some of the colors look a bit similar. In these cases, the similar colors are usually kept fairly far apart to avoid confusion, but some of the later-game twists also affect spatial relationships and you might find yourself double- or triple-checking to make sure you aren't connecting the wrong colors.
It would also be nice to get some music added in. It wouldn't need much for how short it is. 1 or 2 ambient-sounding tracks would be really appropriate and welcome for this type of puzzle game. The existing background hum is better than nothing, but it gets a little unsettling and it's kind of ominous.
I hope that additional levels are added as DLC, I'd love to play more of this.

Crystal Picnic is a colorful role-playing game brimming with witty, humorous dialogue and charming music and visuals that takes you on a journey to find crystals that were stolen by a legion of ants.
In your pursuit to hunt down the ants for the purloined crystals, you take on the role of several anthropomorphic animals. The game begins with two characters, Egbert the duck and Frogbert the frog, but others join you later on in the adventure. Each character has unique personalities, aspirations, and reasons for helping out. The character dialogue and writing are very well executed, and each character has a unique group of soundbites that plays during conversations. Conversations between characters are almost always very witty and humorous, which keeps things interesting. You definitely will not be bored by the colorful cast of characters.
Crystal Picnic plays in a traditional top-down perspective during exploration and character encounters, but switches to a unique action platformer perspective during battle sequences. During exploration sequences, you roam through villages, castles, forests, and different countryside vistas. You can chat, trade, and play games with the many characters that dot the landscapes during exploration, as well as interact with environmental objects, like bushes. During battles, you use sticks, stinky socks, and other so-called weapons to fend off against wolves, ants, pooping birds, and other enemies, all the while performing platforming feats. The battle sequences are unlike those I have experienced in other games, and always pose a challenge.
I love the game's art style. I had recently come off the high of finishing the original Paper Mario a couple of years ago when I first stumbled upon a trailer for this game. The art style reminded me a lot of Paper Mario's, which was very attractive to me at the time, and is what ultimately lead me to getting the game. The art is just so colorful and lighthearted. I love it!
The game has a pretty nice soundtrack. Each piece is appropriate and well-suited to its perspective area. I especially like the title screen music. The sound effects are satisfying, what with some items' "swoosh" sounds, and the menus' "swish" sounds; the sound effects fit nicely and add to the experience, but they aren't anything to write home about.
One of my personal favorite parts of the game are the various boss battles. Bosses range from giant, nearly Bane-like ants, to crazed royals, to sentient trees. There is a creative variety in the types of bosses, as well as how they play. No two boss battles play out the same way, so you always have to be on your toes if you do not want to die. Beyond fun bosses, there are recurring enemies, like pooping birds, different kinds of ants, wolves, and more. Each enemy has its own set of attacks and movement patterns. Learning how each enemy behaves can be tricky, but definitely helps in the long run.
Crystal Picnic is a casual role-playing game, and a bit of a short one at that. My first play-through took about 4 hours, which is short compared to Nooskewl's other RPG (Monster RPG 2), where I spent 8 hours. Even so, I thoroughly enjoyed every moment of my time playing. If you are a fan of more lighthearted and sarcastic role-playing games, like the Mario & Luigi series, but want something that plays more like the old-school stuff, this game is for you. It is definitely worth the price tag, and is fun to go back to every now and again.

Crystal Picnic is a nice little RPG tribute to the classic ages of gaming. The game is fairly well-done except for some problems currently existing. I will add a TL;DR at the end.

Crystal Picnic is an RPG designed with colourful creatures and interesting characters. You start off as Egbert a kind-hearted and pure Duck who has been trying to join the Royal Guard for quite some time now unsuccessfully, and he is with his good friend Frogbert, a common gardener who helps his friend. You are near the castle when all of a sudden ants dig out and walk right on by with crystals from the castle, which begins the main plot of the storyline.
Control-wise the game is fairly simple, however do note that the controls are not actually introduced to you at first. This makes it so that depending on how you play (Controller/Keyboard) you will have to do a bit of a guessing game. The combat portion of the game is not like most RPG games with a turn-based mechanic, but rather has a real-time combat situation where you and your computer controlled companions will fight against whatever you come across. The combat is not bad at all, however the programming of your companions is another story. What would usually happen is that I would fight and my companion would end up running into the enemies usually getting themselves injured or killed. It became a tad bit frustrating and I would prefer it there was an option to not include them in combat (You would fight independently and if you fall you can come back as your companion to help minimize the mistakes a CPU is capable of making). The game also has a nice mini-game of whack-a-skunk and overall is a very playful and nice environment. The maps however can get a tad bit large and annoying to traverse especially with the ability I can always slip over a banana and get attacked by one group, then another, and one more just in case. Once you are able to grasp the controls nicely this becomes quite a relaxing and enjoyable experience for the more casual gamers, and the story is just a tad silly.

For an pixelated RPG the graphics are rather impressive and overall polished for the characters and level design. Very reminiscent of the older days of gaming when it all started to develop. The music in this game is superb and I honestly loved it, it was perfect for the game and was able to make a very relaxing experience and improve the game's overall quality. The only problem is I'd like an option to disable all other sounds except the music at some points so I can just listen while playing.


+ Very polished Graphically
+ Fun style of combat
+ Good relationship between Egbert and Forgbert making an authentic feeling of friendship between the two
+ Music is beautifully relaxing
+ Not hard

- No introduction to controls
- Random combats can become annoying when you get caught in a loop of more than one battle with no time to even move
- No sort of map system or assistance with objectives
- Problem where to consume the potion/item you want you have to first use whatever item is first then you can select the item you want
- No options menu

These are suggestion that I feel should be added to the game to polish it and make it more enjoyable
- Quick introduction to controls at the begging or an options menu where you can see the controls
- Option to fight independently in combat so you don't have to worry about your companion
- An objective assister or local map which can help guide you

Crystal Picnic has overall done a good job expect for the problems which have already been listed. I was able to enjoy my time playing this even with the little snips that gave me a bit of rage. The music always helped me to relax into this game and I honestly love Egbert and Frogbert's relationship, truly enjoyable there. The storyline was quite silly in my opinion, but I was a duck trying for the royal guard and whose best friends was a frog. Overall yeah I'd say this game was worth my time and be for a more casual gamer who simply want's to relax and enjoy something silly (I especially love the "The Accused" achievement showing the developers have a sense of humor).

Although an enjoyable experience, Crystal Picnic has its fair share of issues. The most annoying being that there is no introduction to the controls. The game succeeds in its goal of feeling like a classic RPG from the simpler time of the gaming industry. The soundtracks helps to fully immerse you into the game and overall is one of the things I was able to love about this game. Crystal Picnic is definitely enjoyable for those who like the genre and are not too picky,
so I would recommend this to more casual gamers who are able to look at the work and effort seen in this title, because once you figure out the controls (whether it be controller or keyboard) it's actually a pretty fun title.

I finally beat it...24 hours playing this game and I finally beat it. I can say without a doubt, Cuphead is an absolute masterpiece. If I got hit, died, or restarted (frequently), I never felt like the game was unfair...it was because I sucked. Though it's through failing, that you build an understanding of attack patterns, and which weapons and skills work for that particular boss or level.
Each time you die, you get a simple breakdown of what stage of the fight or level you made it to, and how far away from finishing it you were. With each attempt you see yourself improve, which pushes you to try one more time. As frustratingly difficult as some levels or bosses can be, you always feel like it's possible, and this small bit of feedback at the end is a big part of that.
Each fight seems simple enough, the attack patterns themselves aren't overly complicated, but the somewhat random nature of them coupled with several of them being used at the same time makes each fight a challenge, no matter how many times you play it.
The rest of the package is just as polished as the core mechanics - but the real star of the game is the art and music. No matter how many times I'd die, I still enjoyed every bit of art and sound this game threw at me (I think my favorite is the start of the dragon fight, that animation and music made me smile everytime I seen it...and I seen it a lot). The hand drawn animation and jazz score might be some of the best visuals and audio I've ever seen in a video game. The care and love that went into each drawing, each animation, each song - just, wow.
Is it difficult? Yes. Is it impossible? No. Should you buy it? Without question, this is a game not to be missed. If I had to score it, it's a 10\10 for me. Do not miss out on this game!!

Don't let my Steam playtime fool you, I've played this game for approximately 80 hours in total, with 2 x lvl 70 toons. Leveling is quick and easy on this game. The quests are varied and don't feel too grindy even though they are the usual 'Run here and fetch this' or 'Kill 5 mobs for drops' but because you're never asked to kill too many mobs per quest, it feels varied and like you're constantly moving on to discover new areas.
However, once you hit lvl 70 the game becomes a huge grindfest. You have to grind solo dungeons 30 times a week to get a chance at purple gear. If dungeons aren't your thing, you have the pleasure of killing 150 normal mobs and 50 elite mobs per day to get Chrome tokens to exchange for gear. It gets old really fast.
It's ironic that this game is called Echo of Soul because it lacks so much soul and personality. You tab and click/button mash through your skills all the while feeling slightly disconnected from your toon.
The only good thing I will say about EOS is that they have done a great job with dungeon bosses. You have to pay attention to mechanics and dodge attacks, making each boss kill feel rewarding in end.
I'd only recommend this game for beginner MMO players because it is so easy to pick up and learn to play, but after that, move on to something with more depth that you will truly enjoy.

But, seriously, since
Halloween is coming up, I decided to give Outlast a second playthrough to see if it was as good as I remembered it. And for the most part it is, although I did notice a few flaws. Here's what I got out of this playthrough:
+Outlast has some great atmosphere, which is held up by the fantastic sound design, unique characters, and disorienting location. Somewhat similar to Silent Hill, you'll be in a large area full doors, but nearly all of them are locked, which creates a combination of agoraphobia and claustrophobia.
+The graphics are also decent. Of course, when you can barely see anything because it's so dark, it's hard to mess up graphics. But not much will beat turning on the infrared camera and seeing eyes glowing in the dark for the first time.
+The controls are pretty smooth; running from enemies, jumping over obstacles, and looking over your shoulder all feel very natural. It's easy to get immersed with the level of control given to you. It's kind of like a very simplified version of Mirror's Edge.
+And I personally love when you can collect notes to learn about the backstory in a horror game, which Outlast definitely provides, so that's a pretty big plus in my book.
-The enemy AI is both predictable and easy to manipulate. Once you realize that a stalker will check all hiding spots
the one you're currently in (unless you're an idiot who decided to hide while he's looking at you), hiding changes from you being scared of being found to you being annoyed that he hasn't left the room yet.
-Some of the jumpscares are kind of weak. I don't mind jumpscares, but in a video game I don't think they're effective when they're part of a cutscene. Basically, instead of thinking "oh no, I need to run," you think "oh no, I need to watch something happen." Don't get me wrong, there are some jumpscares that aren't a part of a cutscene, but there aren't many.
-But here's probably my biggest complaint: no combat. Now, I'm not some nutcase who picks up a game of Tetris and yells "WHERE IS THE COMBAT," but in a horror game I feel some level of combat is necessary to keep the player scared.
Here's my
theory on it: I think fear is strongest in the middle of a fight-or-flight moment. The harder it is to choose between the two, the more stressful and scary the situation is. Without any fighting, there's no real fight-or-flight moment, because the default choice is always to run away. Because of this, it's probably not much scarier to play the game than it is to watch someone else play.
But don't take these complaints too harshly; the game is still very well put together, and worth a playthrough. I'd give it about a 7.5/10.

This game is an amazing way to see how well you can keep your cool in situations this game puts you through. Never have I been so stressed, scared, and felt so helpless as of what to do when your on the roof of a building, running out of ammo, bleeding and bruised, fighting off a zombie hoard about to no doubt rip you up. Then after they have gotten you, watch your reanimated body stand back up and become one of "them". This game is the perfect mix of badass survival, and sadness that you would normally feel in "The Last of Us" or "The Walking Dead". Walking through a house and finding a kid's room filled with stuffed animals and toys, right after you had killed a zombie, and made a huge mess. I would keep playing this game becuase of the fact of how hard it is to actually survive and keep a stable safehouse secure, and search and scavenge for supplies in changing weather. 'Too hot to go out today, will go at night', 'too cold to go out, I'll need to find warmer clothes', 'It's raining, but my safehouse is a long run away, I'll catch a cold if I try'. Just all the needs that you have to fulfill in this game makes it such a fun and fresh playthrough whenever you load up again after dying of infection, zombies, hunger, sickness, or getting shot by your buddy while walking into the front door of a house.

With out a doubt one of the best games that I purchased this year.  It's a rogue-like and it can be hard and unforgiving at time but that makes it all the more sadistically fun.  The RPG elements including character leveling, equipment, and individual abilities unique to each hero, mesh well and ensures multiple playthroughs which can be very unique depending on which heros the player is using.  As your heros open doors of the dungeon they accumulate resouces which are used to build offencive and defensive turrets in rooms,  power rooms and constructed turrets or generators in rooms,  to level characters and to purchase turret and character upgrades and equipment.   The combination of managing all these elements might first sound complex  but the game does a great job at intragating all the features togather well in a way that makes sense and also makes you think tactically the further you get in the dungeon.
Though the game is stll in development  it  has been updated regularly in the six or so months that I have owned it and alot of new content has been added.  At my last playthrough there were eight levels to the dungeon implemented and over ten heros (though I have only unlocked 5 or so) with more being planned as the game is updated and gets closer to offical release.

Ok, I'll tell you how you start out.
You wake up (spawn) in your workspace or home, you read the toturial, and move along. You loot your house and walk outside. at first, it seems harmless, just 3 or 2 zombies. "I'll kill them with my knife.". You stab the zombie(s) rapidly until they fall onto the the ground, only to realise that your bleeding, you make some sheets and bandage yourself. "Ok, i'll build myself a base in a store". 1/4 of your way to a secure base you feel sick. "I'll take some medicine!". Medicine doesn't help, you get sicker and sicker. Until you realise, your bitten. You barricade yourself in a room, but the hammering bring in a horde. you try to remain calm, until a metal/wooden crunching sounds fill your ear. You're Panicing, screaming, actracting more zombies. You try to escape but with no luck.
1. If your in a resturaunt, goto A.
2. If your inside a house, goto B.
3. If your inside a base, goto C.
A. You turn on the oven while the zombies are trying to break through, you push on the door, hoping you have strentgh to keep the zombies at bay, your character gets hot, and hotter, you look behind you, a fire. You burn the place, the zombies, and yourself to death. You're dead.
B. You run to the closet and baricade that with everything you got. A couple hours have passed and as the zombies bust through the closet door, there's nothing but a rotting corpse. You're dead.
C. Inside your base (or someone elses), you get the nearest weapon. "Fight me! You'll never take this base!". The zombies bust in through the door. You run to the other door on the other side of the base. It's locked! You try to open it with your keys but you drop them (cliche). Zombies rip you apart from limb to limb. You're dead.
So... How will you die?

Bioshock is an excellent first-person shooter game that perfectly combines both the horror and action genre. The game takes place in an underwater city named rapture that is in turmoil and it is up to you to solve it's mysteries and to escape. The horror element in this game does wear off after a while, but the true nightmare of this game is how little supplies are. as you play through, you do not get hundreds of bullets like you would in any other shooter. Instead, the ammunition supply is low and you will be desperate for bullets and check every little crack for anything. The lack of ammunition adds to the horror element by adding a sense of desperation to the game and a fear of not being prepared.
Much of the game comprises of other tasks that are helpful, but not entirely necessary. The game uses a mechanic called "hacking" to lower prices on in-game items like bullets or First-Aid kits. The "hacking' is a little difficult, but it gradually gets easier to understand as you progress. The biggest problem with "hacking" might have to be hearing those vending machines use their pre-recorded sounds over and over again. The most problematic vending machine might have to be the "Circus of Values" vending machine as it constantly usses a clown and clown voice for it's mascot.
The weapon variation is really impressive, however, switching between them was a little difficult. I could not find a way to switch the controls anyway I pleased, so for the entire game, the weapons were swapped using the mouse's scrolling key. The plasmids (in game abilities that allow you to shock your enemies, burn them, enrage them, etc.) are swapped for the weapons by pressing the right mouse button. I got confused a multitude of times over this, but it did not have an overall impact on my gameplay experience.
The graphics and attention to detail are exceptional. The developers added a multitude of in-game artwork that is easily missable, but once found, it adds a sense of being in the 1950's. The underwater environment is fleshed out and even has sea life swimming in it. The enemy designs are mostly the same, but it does not take away from the breath-taking atmosphere of the game.
All in all, Bioshock is a wonderfully made game that tells a beautiful story that engages you and allows you to explore an underwater city full of steampunk enemies and gadgets. If you are a fan of first-person games and 1950's memorabilia, you will love this game. Even if you are not, this game is still worth the money.

Эта игра пришла со смартфонов и отличается крайней упрощённостью во всём.
Под руководством игрока королю нужно удержать власть и сохранить собственную жизнь, поддерживая хорошие отношения с народом, церковью и армией, а также следить за капиталом. События представлены в виде перемешанных карт, которые сменяются, как только дашь один из заранее установленных ответов. Раз за разом в государстве возникают проблемы, решение которых будет иметь последствия в виде увеличения или уменьшения значений этих четырёх шкал. Допустим, монах говорит, что солдаты учинили беспорядки в церкви: легко догадаться, какие шкалы задействованы в этом скандале и как они изменятся, если принять одну из сторон конфликта. Всё очень просто и достаточно интересно, пока не повторяется в десятый раз. Жаль, что в игре помечены шкалы, которых коснётся очередное решение короля – уж это можно было бы оставить додумывать игроку.
Ещё один минус – воспитание у игрока прагматичного отношения к проблемным ситуациям. Сейчас твоему королю не хватает расположения церкви – значит, надо проигнорировать просьбу местной доброй ведьмы прекратить убивать невинных девушек и позволить церкви продолжать их сжигать. Как будто, если жить и править по совести, ты обречён на провал. Но ведь это не так, просто в данной игре вот такой примитивный механизм, а в другой можно было бы, например, переубедить главу церкви, или нанять тайный отряд по освобождению пленных девушек, или устроить нечто, что отвлечёт всеобщее внимание от этой темы, и девушки останутся целы и невредимы. Это так, навскидку. Здесь же демонстрируется и навязывается очень узкое мышление, а в роль такого глупого и поверхностного короля невозможно вжиться, его как будто вообще нет: мы просто переворачиваем карты и решаем теоретические тесты про несуществующую страну.
Думаю, многих в Reigns привлекает её весёлая придурковатость. Посреди обсуждения важных политических вопросов может прийти шут и поинтересоваться, каким животным хотел бы стать король. Ты только что решал судьбу захваченных в плен варваров, вынужден был сжечь заражённые запасы пшена, обрекая подданных на голодную зиму, и застал жену в постели с генералом, а тебя вдруг спрашивают, не хотел бы ты стать скорпионом. Что-то потешное в этом есть.
Ещё раз пройти эту игру вас может заставить разве что желание получить достижения, всё-таки один «забег» длится около полутора тысяч игровых лет, а карты частенько повторяются. Чтобы добраться до хорошей концовки, нужно проделать довольно замысловатую цепочку действий, требующую не то чтобы смекалки, но внимательности – точно, здесь такое происходит редко и потому смотрится любопытно. Вот только карты попадаются случайным образом, и дождаться какого-то события в нужный момент бывает мучительно сложно. Иногда необходимая карта выбирает такое неудачное время для появления, что ты вынужден ответить неправильно, иначе на следующем ходу тебя ждёт проигрыш в результате нарушения баланса.
Сказать по правде, вы почти ничего не упустите, если вместо личного знакомства с игрой посмотрите чужое прохождение.

Cuphead is the demonstration of both excellent difficulty and excellent accessibility that I've been wanting for a long time.
There was definitely something appealling about 8-bit run-and-guns of old; the feeling of survival and tension as you survive each of the varied attacks of a boss that seem utterly undodgable. But what most people don't touch on is the number of big issues those games had. The boss's movements would often be very unclear, or could be read in several different ways. "Oh, he's about to punch? OH - oh, no, he dashed across the whole room past me. And now I'm dead." The games had lives systems that limited how much you could learn about a boss in a single Continue, and leave many people walled off even if they were willing to commit more time to trying.
Cuphead is a hard game with none of those problems. The animation style not only sweetens the deal, giving you a visual treat during your many deaths, but evokes many clear and broadcasted attacks that players can almost always understand relatively quickly. There are exceptions, and times when an attack might kill you anyway, but the game is also designed for infinite lives and relatively fast boss times - so even these pain points don't amount to much.
This is definitely not a game for everyone - no one should think less of themselves for playing more story-based or reflex-light games, but I do think it's more nuanced and well-designed than the "ULTRA HARD GAME" the internet likes to make it out to be. I died hundreds of times to certain bosses, but I continued because I was enjoying myself, not because of a need to prove anything. And the bosses are definitely designed for replay - there's plenty of variety in their attacks, and some of them are designed such that if you beat them on the first try, you wouldn't get to see all of their possibilities (Example: The boss of "Candyland" has a total of 5 different henchmen bosses, but only sends a total of 3 out per try).
Once you've finished the game, an Expert mode can grant you some more enjoyment out of it - and while some bosses simply use this to tweak some numbers and add some projectiles, some make some very inventive changes to their formula to enhance the challenge (for instance, rather than performing two attacks in turns, doing both attacks at once).
If you're on the fence about whether it's too hard for you, feel free to look at videos of novices attempting some of the bosses. They'll die - a lot, but I've often been surprised at how quickly some seemingly inept players can get used to the game. Also remember that Porkrind's upgrades can make many bosses easier! Some shots work well for certain bosses, while some may make a boss much more frustrating.

This DLC continues on pretty much directly from
and follows exactly the same blueprint; a single screen filled with puzzles to solve that reward you with items which you'll have to figure out how to use in order to unlock the next puzzle - repeat until end. They probably could have gotten away with calling it a sequel, since it's about the same size as the previous entry, is filled with entirely new puzzles and takes place in a new setting. But given that there's no real innovation or any new ideas here built upon the main title, I'm glad it's being sold as DLC instead. I think they'd need to shake things up drastically before they could slap a number on the end of it.
They're both short, pleasant little titles that should satisfy most puzzle lovers and feature an array of different puzzle types, too. It shares more or less all the same pluses and minuses of the base game, but with an additional issue of a sudden difficulty spike with a couple of brain-teasers. It seems that it's not uncommon for some players to spend maybe half an hour making good progress through the majority of the game, only to come to a complete stop and spend multiple hours trying to find one solution before either skipping it, looking for help, or just giving up entirely. Reading up on it in discussion boards and such, I think I can speak on behalf of the majority of the Hare in the Hat community when I say the Hungarian Rings can just straight-up go f*ck themselves. Like, proper, full-on f*ck themselves hard... with the wrong end of a rusty claw hammer...up the *ss... then go bounce around on a space hopper for a few hours. I don't think anyone seems to like it, and personally I'd be very happy to never see it in another game again.
It's usually incredibly lazy critique or reviewing to say something is "more of the same", or even worse, the greatest sin of all, to qualify anything as "good if you like that sort of thing". Anything is good if you like that sort of thing. Being kicked in the balls is good if you like that sort of thing, that doesn't mean it should ever be recommended to anyone. But here, I really do feel like it deserves to be described as more of the same and worth getting if you liked its last outing, so similar is it to its parent title.
85% fun, 15% "f*ck you!", Hare in the Hat: The Abyss is a largely welcome addition that offers a nice, mostly enjoyable, occasionally taxing slice of entertainment at a more than reasonable price and comes well recommended... if you like that sort of thing.

This is one of the best stradegy games I own. Right up there with Total War: Rome 2 and Age of Empires 3. Why? Because:
1. I am a big Star Wars fan. I have seen all of the Star Wars movies atleast 3 times.
2. It has everything you need and want from a scifi stradegy game: It has space action, land action, different troops that are good for different situations. It actually tells you what the units do. Like in Total War: Rome 2 the game tells you "Yeah, this is a spear unit. Guess what it's good for." Obviously it's good against horses, thats obvious but what about the other units? I don't know what is the best counter for an elephant from 2 000 years ago. But this game, it tells you EXACLY what it's good for. Like saying: "Here, dumbass, look, bomber is good against slow moving targets like this this and this. Also, these things counter it." It tells you 3 units that it's good against and 3 units it's not good against.
3. A great storyline. Sure, it feels rushed at times and forced but the quality voice acting combined with the "I am the most powerful person in the galaxy. Now hold and drag this unit here.", makes it a great experience. It is a both a tutorial and a great story at the same time. Feels like Sly 2 on PS2. Oh the good DLC-free no-microtransactions times...
4. It screams Star Wars. It has rancors, Darh Vader, fitting music, Admiral Ackbar and the Death Star. It has everything you wished from a Star Wars game. (you can also blow up planets with the Death Star! CAN YOU BELIVE IT!?)
5. Okay a few complaints now: The Death Star is the second Death Star, I understand that it looks good, but why isn't it finished? It looks just like the one from Return of the Jedi. But in RoTJ it was not finished. Now I am attacking with an unfinished Death Star and throwing it around the entire galaxy? Come on man, build it first. Also, there is a bug when you destroy a planet that has Han Solo and Chewbacca, the game crashes. The makers, Petroglyph Games still exists so why haven't they fixed this HUGE bug? Come on, the last update was in 2009. Come on. Fix your game before saying good bye.
But overall it is a satisfying experience to any Star Wars fan. If you don't like Star Wars, you can skip this one. There is nothing much to offer to people who don't like Star Wars or scifi.

The game, alike its brethren endless space, has stunning graphics however it is styled in 8-16 bit, i.e. the game keeps style with the old bit-like games but does not look completely like an old cartridge game. The game play is surprisingly smooth and easy to understand but the game gives quite the challenge regardless what character you have or how skilled you are. Every level and play through you will have to think strategically and place defences so, you also have to keep a constant watch on your hero's life as well make sure that your producers are all equal or close in production or focus mostly on one type. As you traverse through the seeming less endless floors, every item that you get holds a big value even if it is a stray jacket.
There are a few glitches left in the game but all are being fixed quite constantly by a very active dev team which are probably the most friendly dev team you will ever come across and the community, even friendlier.
The music is done by FlyByNo, the musician for the well known endless space, has again created more masterpieces. The music in this game is very well thought out as the music does not make you have to battle with it in order to think of strategies rather it helps you, while setting the mood and vibe very well. The calm music, slow paced and thought inventiveness is what makes the entire game so relaxing most of the time yet so frantic at others.
The multiplayer, however, is still having difficulties but has only recently been released so is technically in beta still. The multiplayer, regardless of your upload speeds/download speeds, has a big lag problem which is getting much better slowly over time as it isn't amplitudes forte but they have worked with multiplayer on turn a based game before.
At first glance the game looks entirely turn based, D.o.t.E. is part turn based, part strategy and part real time, the turn based comes from the doors and the material obtaining being that each 'turn' is counted in doors. The strategy is obvious, planning where you will go and where certain things go along with the difficult choice of weather "should I have all defence in here or make it a place for my hero's to heal...or both?" will be asked about in every room that becomes available to you to place defences an the such. There is more strategy in the characters as well, as you will have to plan who gets what and who should have what role which becomes even larger and harder to do in multiplayer (more on that later), in fact you even have to plan your escape. Finally the real time comes down to doing all of the above whilst being attacked, placing defences, watching your health, equipping items, you name it, you can do it in real time when the waves of monsters are out.
multiplayer doesn't only have problems with lag or randomly disconnecting but also somewhat in communication and majorly in sharing items. When there is an item no one knows what the chest holds so no one knows what the item is until they pick it up, once the item is picked up, instead of the item going into the global inventory it goes into the personal inventory which if you cant equip the said item for any reason, you cant drop it nor trade it in any way. This makes the game more difficult as loot gives more bonuses and traits than levelling meaning your entire team is more likely to die unless you all get lucky.
Next problem is communication, due to the lag building things and claiming a room becomes more difficult as more than one person may try building/claiming at once. The only way around this currently is to let the host of the server to build/claim, meaning your entire team will depend on you if you are the host.
All up the game is well balanced, not pain numbingly boring, even after a few plays, and looks very good for its chosen style.

Even after I bought this game, and invested a few hours into it, these previews inspire me to want to play it even more.
So if I had to sum up this review into 3 words, it would be this:  Buy this game.
Luckily, I don't, so I won't!.... Maybe I shoulda saved that for the tl;dr.  And yes, there is a tl;dr, so scroll down if you hate words.
So after like a 30 second little intro, which you can totally skip, you get thrown straight into the game.  Which is nice because when you die, restarting takes like 0(thats a zero) time at all.  And oh yes, there will be much death.
Now normally, when you play a game, and you die a lot, you aren't usually having a lot of fun.  Well thats totally not the case in this game.  Although the game is still in early access, that means it might be 30% completed if we're lucky, it still manages to entertain.
When you die, you start over, and you take what you learned and apply it to the new run.  In all honesty, I have only made it past the 5th floor once.  And... the 4th floor once....  And the 3rd floor twice... on the easiest game setting.   XD
When you start the game you pick two heroes you want to take with you, considering right now you only have 3 to choose from, it's not that hard of a choice.  As you progress through the game you'll meet other heroes that can you hire with food, so try to keep a surplus at all times because you don't want to miss out on adding a massochistic marine, or a crazy short guy with a sword twice his size to your team.  I've only managed to unlock two characters so far personally.
Other things you will run across are artifacts which for research points, you can add new modules to your list of goodies, or even upgrade existing ones.  Really awesome, hope to find these early on in a level.  In rare cases, you can even find two in the same level, which when that happens, is like winning the god damned lotto.
And without further ado, lets get down to the nitty gritty of this review.
:  This is the most awesome sci-fi rogue-like turret defensesque RPG squad based retro dungeon crawl game I have ever played.
:  This is the only sci-fi rogue-like turret defensesque RPG squad based retro dungeon crawl game I have ever played.
:  It is not a *multiplayer* sci-fi rogue-like turret defensesque RPG squad based retro dungeon crawl game.(yet)
:  There is no multiplayer, there is no story, there is no tech tree, and thus is no substance.
:  Mulstiplayer is grayed out, the tech tree is grayed out, the story has not been added, the substance does not exist yet.
:  There
be multi-player, there
be a story and quests, there
be a tech tree like thingy; and what does this add to this already awesome sci-fi rogue-like turret defensesque RPG squad based retro dungeon crawl game?  The most badass thing I have bought in years, duh!
All in all, even if you don't like sci-fi rogue-like turret defensesque RPG squad based retro dungeon crawl games(You sick of me saying this yet?  I'm not!), you'll still probably like this one.
Oh, and incase you are wondering why I didn't review things like music, graphics, gameplay, or anything else like that, that normal people review, well lemme sum it up for you.
:  It's pixelated.  What more do you expect?
:  It's very ambiant, changes when things happen, all in all, not the best or the worst, though not sure how it could be better.
:  It's in Early Access, gameplay is subject to change.  Duh.
So to sum it all up, for those of you who hate words, I present:

The most immersive entrancing survival game I've ever played. The gorgeous visuals - outright stunning at times - in combination with the varying weather conditions and active local flora will leave you in awe of both the beauty and harshness that mother nature has to offer.
I never thought I could find my self so focused on whether or not I could light a fire out of a desperate need to warm up, whether I could survive working a fresh kill without freezing or starving to death, or simply trying find wood fuel to stay alive in a white-out blizzard.
It's hard to put the game down at times: there's always that constant want to explore over that next ridge, or finish crafting that new bow or animal skin coat, or securing your next few meal(s).
And that's just the sandbox alpha. There's further updates to come including a storymode with full release. There's also already Challenge scenarios and a(n as of now simple) feat/perk system.
My only real area of concern is the ability to keep replayability up given the mostly static maps. (Of which there are already plenty, which are fairly varied. As of the time of this writing, there are six full maps/regions and a number of small transition and interior maps)

Five Nights at Freddy's is a point and click horror game developed and published by Scott Cawthon.
The game has you as a security guard for a fictional Chuck E. Cheese-like restaurant called Freddy Fazbear's Pizza. You work the night shift for 7 in-game hours for 5 in-game work shifts. Two unlockable modes, 6th Night and Custom Night are unlocked by completing certain elements of the game. You need to use your security camera and doors to prevent the 4 (technically 5) animatronics: Freddy, Bonnie, Chica, Foxy, and technically Golden Freddy from getting into your office. You have limited power, so you need to close the doors and use your camera only if absolutely necessary. You are guided by a man on the phone dubbed by fans as the "Phone Guy" in further detail as to why they can't come into your office.
Overall, Five Nights at Freddy's is a good experience whether you know what you're doing or not. In the early part of the game, it keeps up the action by scaring you, and by the later part of the game, you should be significantly less scared of the game and keeps up the action with a very noticable difficulty curve.
With the fanbase out of the picture, I give this game a solid 8/10

With an intensity that rivals The Walking Dead, Sir, You Are Being Hunted is a fantastic example of the survival horror genre. Unlike much of the rest of the genre, you are not constantly overwhelmed by enemies, but are absorbed in to the empty, lonely world of the British Countryside. The most intense moments, are not when you are being attacked, but when you see the enemy, and are working your mind as fast as possible to figure out how to escape. The collection mechanic isn't original in any of the sense of the word, but is given new life through the danger of finding a highly visible artifact. Finally, the game has been carefully crafted to always give the player the sense that they are being followed. This unsettling feeling drives this game to be the best it can be, and very soon, sir, you will be being hunted.

If you have a reliable group of friends to play the game with,  it can actually be a lot of fun.  Outside of that though, it's a crapshoot.
The single player AI is maddening in that if you're playing the Monster, the Hunters are relentless BMFs.  If you're playing as the Hunters though, it's like they're all rejects from the Keystone Cops and if you're taking that monster down, it's basically all up to you.  The Monster AI is also aggravatingly canny at determining which hunter YOU are playing, and pounding on you EXCLUSIVELY until there's nothing left but a red jelly smashed into the dirt.
You can mitigate the AI ineptitude somewhat by customizing the settings, but that kind of feels like cheating to me for some reason, and thus any victories earned that way seem hollow.
The maps I've played so far have been interesting to play on, though as the monster I wish there were more places to hide/lurk for an ambush.
I also wish there was a way to move into a 1st-person view as the monster because all-too-often in tighter terrain the camera goes completely wonky and you can't see anything but your own backside, making it impossible to target the hunters with attacks.  I know the 3rd person view gives a better sense of scale to the monster, but when I'm getting shot up and the camera blinds me, it's frustrating to the point of just wanting to quit the game.
So overall I'm giving this game a "No" vote, but with the proviso that if you play with friends (not just random people who won't coordinate), it can actually be a good time.

A seemingly straightforward and deceptively difficult game. Not that the choices themselves are particularly hard, but rather it's deceptively difficult to remain both alive and in power for very long. Despite it's simplistic interface the game is actually rather long. Not in terms of actual gameplay time, but that in truth after awhile the game starts to feel like one long slog through the motions. Its components are great! The choices diverse, interesting, and occasionally whacky, combined with a simplistic artwork that adds charm to the game. The only real problem is that after your 10th or so death, while waiting for the "only choices that really matter" with regards to the ending, the game becomes a repetitive grind.
That said, the game is enjoyably silly and worth at least one playthrough. Its certainly worth the price you pay (even more so the rare time it's on sale.).

Cuphead is the demonstration of both excellent difficulty and excellent accessibility that I've been wanting for a long time.
There was definitely something appealling about 8-bit run-and-guns of old; the feeling of survival and tension as you survive each of the varied attacks of a boss that seem utterly undodgable. But what most people don't touch on is the number of big issues those games had. The boss's movements would often be very unclear, or could be read in several different ways. "Oh, he's about to punch? OH - oh, no, he dashed across the whole room past me. And now I'm dead." The games had lives systems that limited how much you could learn about a boss in a single Continue, and leave many people walled off even if they were willing to commit more time to trying.
Cuphead is a hard game with none of those problems. The animation style not only sweetens the deal, giving you a visual treat during your many deaths, but evokes many clear and broadcasted attacks that players can almost always understand relatively quickly. There are exceptions, and times when an attack might kill you anyway, but the game is also designed for infinite lives and relatively fast boss times - so even these pain points don't amount to much.
This is definitely not a game for everyone - no one should think less of themselves for playing more story-based or reflex-light games, but I do think it's more nuanced and well-designed than the "ULTRA HARD GAME" the internet likes to make it out to be. I died hundreds of times to certain bosses, but I continued because I was enjoying myself, not because of a need to prove anything. And the bosses are definitely designed for replay - there's plenty of variety in their attacks, and some of them are designed such that if you beat them on the first try, you wouldn't get to see all of their possibilities (Example: The boss of "Candyland" has a total of 5 different henchmen bosses, but only sends a total of 3 out per try).
Once you've finished the game, an Expert mode can grant you some more enjoyment out of it - and while some bosses simply use this to tweak some numbers and add some projectiles, some make some very inventive changes to their formula to enhance the challenge (for instance, rather than performing two attacks in turns, doing both attacks at once).
If you're on the fence about whether it's too hard for you, feel free to look at videos of novices attempting some of the bosses. They'll die - a lot, but I've often been surprised at how quickly some seemingly inept players can get used to the game. Also remember that Porkrind's upgrades can make many bosses easier! Some shots work well for certain bosses, while some may make a boss much more frustrating.

So when I learned this game supports splitscreen co-op, I ran out to gamestop and grabbed 3 usb controllers for my brother, my girlfriend and I to play this over the weekend. Here's how that went.
We spend the first 30 minutes figuring out how the controls work. Zombies everywhere in custom difficulty. Brother and I run, girlfriend somehow gets bit. We bunker down overnight and the bite wound kills her. She raises as a zombie and I have to put her down.
We try a few more custom difficulties until we decide to just go with the first bite. We spawn in a decent house with a white picket fence and a grill in back. Not too many zombies in sight. Until we see the horde down the road. Girlfriend thinks it's like left 4 dead and goes in swinging her bat, gets bitten again. We don't change the bandage out often enough and it kills her. She raises again as a zombie and I have to put her down again.
Her THIRD character gets a small scratch from a zombie. By now, I have it down on how to treat the wound. I fully heal her. Then I notice her status goes to Zombified and I sigh, taking her out back with my spiked baseball bat and await the inevitable. I put her down for the third time.
Her fourth character does better, though now she avoids any zombie. My brother, our scavenger, accidentally jumps from a second story building and fractures his leg. He waddles back to base and my girlfriend treats him, since she's supposed to be the medic while I'm the carpenter. It took an in-game week for his leg to heal enough for him to run with the splint on. It heals while he's out...and he accidentally falls out a second story window, breaking his leg again. I talk him out of drinking bleach while I gather corpses in the middle of the street to burn. I start the campfire and my pants leg catches on fire. I panic, running about and then into a building to grab water to throw on it. I die and my burning pants set the building on fire, making me glad I didn't walk into our base.

Like most documentaries on sub-cultures, you're likely coming into this with minimal knowledge of the subject matter and, at the very least, the curiosity of what it's all about.
Branching Paths focuses on the Japanese independent game developer scene and aims to answer the question "Why does no one talk about indie games in Japan?"
As an avid gamer and aspiring game developer myself, I found this film infinitely inspiring. To see others grow, connect and find success in a very challenging and demanding career is all I could hope for.
After removing my rose-tinted glasses however, and weighing it amongst other high-profile documentaries (like Indie Game: The Movie or King of Kong), I noticed one crucial difference: Branching Paths lacks the human interest underdog tale that would really drive home the passion of these indie game devs to an audience unfamiliar with them.
The film is filled with mostly snippets of interviews and convention footage and really only shows one success story, though it is rather disjointed and arrives much too late into the runtime.
If you have an appreciation for all things gaming related, it's a must watch. For those with just an inkling of curiosity for Japan's indie game scene, it's a good way to kill an hour and a half.

Absolutely zero gameplay effects and absolutely zero reason to talk about it. Want the skins? Cool, buy them. Don't want the skins? Cool, don't buy them.
With that out of the way, this is a really really fun game. I'm a sucker for asymmetrical multiplayer, and this just pulls it off so enjoyably. There are 4 classes of hunter, each with (as of the time of this writing) 3 characters to unlock for a total of 12 hunters. Each is very unique - even within the same class - but yet they all remain balanced, and all are essential to the team's success.
As of now, there are three monsters. I haven't played as all of them so I can't speak too in depth about their effectiveness, but as someone who has played against them all a handful of times, I can say that they seem balanced. I do know that playing as the monster is great fun, especially early when fight or flight is a huge deal. The tension and excitement are something that I've been missing in games recently, and its nice to have one that can really deliver it.
The only major bug that has yet to be patched out is the occasional persistent cursor glitch where your mouse pointer stays on the screen while playing, moving around as you move the camera. It is annoying at first but you eventually stop seeing it. I'm not excusing it by any means (seriously turtle rock, cmon. It's been like 2 weeks, hide the damn cursor already) but the game is not nearly as buggy as some people make it out to be.
All in all, I definitely reccommend this game for purchase. Should you wait for a sale or at least another patch? Ehh...maybe. I can however tell you that I spent 80 bucks on this game and the season pass, then another 20 from csgo skin trades on the skin packs and don't regret a single cent.

Just like many other things about the video game industry, this documentary will be discussed and debated by a lot of different people from a lot of different perspectives.
That said, I enjoyed it, and do recommend it. I think perhaps the greatest strength is that is does span a good amount of time, so there's some depth to some of the experiences covered - which I feel is important.
Personally, while I think the attempts to draw parallels to Indie Game are valid and it was somewhat surprising to see western developers featured prominently, there are interesting insights to ponder. Several times people mentioned the cultural expectation to get a 'proper job', so making the decision to be an indie has that extra baggage on top of the usual and more known pressures.
Another reviewer pointed out that there are some interesting timing issues surrounding the choice of titles covered - specifically with Mighty No. 9 - but I think that's inevitable when covering projects still in development and doesn't detract from the film.
Overall, I'm more compelled to re-watch this than I was Indie Game, as I think there's more content and food for thought to be uncovered.
