I have actually played Patrician IV for many hundreds of hours since 2010 that were not logged on the Steam application (as I played them on the CD).
Patrician IV is an overhauling upgrade to Patrician III; so if you have not played the previous games in the Patrician series, starting with IV is really all you need.  Also, the game of Patrician is very straightforward and addicting, so playing previous versions won't offer you anything unseen in Patrician IV.
The game plays upon a fundamental capitalistic principle: "buy low, sell high."  Patrician IV colors this principle in a video game set in the 14th Century North Sea and Baltic Sea.  (Sure, this concept could have been done in any setting: 17th Century Carribean; 4th Century BC Mediterranean; or something after the Panama and Suez canals were both in full operation.  But those have all been done already; who ever took the time to learn about the Hanseatic League...?  Rich history there.)
There are three phases of Patrician IV: (1) auto-trade, build ships, and make (more) money; (2) build businesses, expand into other cities, and build more businesses; and finally, (3) perform city management as a mayor, Hanseatic League management as the Alderman, and optimizing your production/selling operation (to include manual "expeditions" down in the Mediterranean Sea, which is more of a "side quest").
As with everything, there are things that I like and dislike about Patrician IV.  What I like are the music; the ability to build my own economic empire, learning from my mistakes; and the addicting genre of constantly trying to think my way through the most optimal uses of my growing economic empire.  What I dislike are three: (A) you can't expedition out to the New World, like in Patrician III; (B) the voice acting of your competitors is some of the worst you will ever hear in all of video gaming history; and (C) the game has been developed/published by Kalypso Media (Gaming Minds Studios), a German company, whom I think do a poor job in supporting their games and respecting their customer base.  (Most non-American studios or publishers seem to be clueless on how to treat people, in general, such as UbiSoft and Paradox.  Of course, EA - an American company - at least learned from their mistakes.)  On that last point, there are a few glaringly obvious bugs that they have openly stated that they will "fix in Patrician V."  (Meaning, they are aware of them in P4, but will not fix them.)  These bugs are things like: disabling the terrible voice actors - you can't, even with the button saying you can; clicking on a convoy on the Convoy List - you sometimes can't without a work-around; and the inability to sell all your cargo during Expeditions, thus coming back with amounts of what you are trying to get rid of!  (The developers think this has to do with overall population in the Hanseatic League during your game, but they are unwilling to explore this further and correct it.  I relay this information to you based on the responses to my bug reports on their game forums.)
The Rise of a Dynasty (RoaD) expansion to Patrician IV made the game better.  There is more to do than in the original, including developing inland cities and establishing overland trade routes.  And heck... having 8 more cities on the map is just better (totalling 40 possible).  Of course, the whole paradigm of "withhold content intentionally so that we can charge extra for an expansion pack" has everything to do with RoaD.  But like I said, it made the game better.  Would it have been nice to be offered in the base version?  You bet.  But you know how developers/publishers are nowadays, as well as undisciplined gamers, too.
The other thing that I dislike about the RoaD expansion, specifically, are the overland trade routes and the wagons used for transport.  While I like that they added 8 more cities to the map, the trade routes to them must be unlocked - there is no way around this.  This might sound like "something interesting to do," but the way to unlock them is to please all the hegemons (princes and dukes and whatnot) of the European regions by way of doing them favors: give them a lot of money; give them goods tributes; and/or sabotage others (whom you are trying to keep happy, as well).  The problem with that is that the opportunities to please them are not easy to come by when you need them the most, thus extending the time frame to do so almost completely stupid.  But then, once you unlock all the European overland trade routes, you must then build Wagons to transport the goods.  Now, you can build ships that hold tens of thousands of goods (10,000+) that can be carted all over the sea to coastal towns.  The wagons, on the other hand, only hold 100 goods each.  So if you want to carry 1,000 goods from an inland town to somewhere else, you are building ten wagons.  But 1,000 goods is dinky by that stage of the game!  So you'll have wagon trains of 71 wagons just so you can carry 7,100 goods (which is similar to 3 Hulks and 3 Caravels, which carry a total of 7,110 goods).  That is just asinine.  But even worse is what happens to your game's performance with that many wagons in a train - get ready for crashes.
The last thing that I dislike about Patrician IV is the multiplayer offering within it.  Basically, it is only cooperative (a.k.a. "co-op").  You cannot have your friend log in to his game, and you into yours, and then start developing the Hanse in competition with each other - which is really the only friggin' way to play multiplayer on this type of game!  Instead, you both own the same business; so you basically only compete against the computer opponents.  I guess it could be fun having each other develop their own cities; but pulling from a common pool of money and essentially trying to ignore what the other one is doing (so as not to step on each other's toes) is quite lame.  The fact that this is the only way to play Patrician IV multiplayer is also asinine.
In all, the very nature of the gameplay is why I recommend Patrician IV: it is addicting and makes you think, think, think - learning from mistakes and pondering how to make things better.  (Yes, you will think about this game while you are not even playing it.  You might even create your own spreadsheet, like I did, in an attempt to optimize your operation.)  There will be times where you will actually turn off the game and feel like you accomplished something worthy and important, as if you are smart or something.  It's kinda funny to look at yourself in retrospect, ha ha.  But I also recommend Patrician IV because modifying it is not too terribly hard (if you have the RoaD expansion pack - you cannot modify it otherwise).  You can figure out how to set up each city's resources for trade, which ones pop up with the corresponding research, and a few other things about the towns and computer players.  I really like customization, so that is a step in the right direction.
To close, I would say that Patrician IV (with the Rise of a Dynasty expansion pack) should be bought for $7.49 or less.

Surviving out the zombie apocalipse world was never had so many features.
Hunting, foraging, maradeuring, crafting, building, medical treatmenting, fighting, shooting, thinking of future strategy...
In this game you can build a house far away and live on foraging, farming, hunting.
Or you can fortificate one of the many houses in the world (but be better to have a few), and looting houses, searching for food and weapons.
Character RPG system is nice, really nice.
You can upgrade self on the way you live: if you shooting - you can be better on what. If you cooking a meals instead of eating raw - you can upgrade cooking. In any case you get bunuses: more accurate and deathly shooting, better meals, better crops, better fish catch, and so on...
Inventory system is good too!
You have some main inventory, its have their limits: in weight. But you can find a bags for equipping in hands and for equipping in back (backpacks provide instant access to second inventory without need to be equipped in hands).
It makes searching more efficient!
Crafting system lets you live easier!
Craft weapons, or tools for surviving.
Building system is easy, but to build strong fort you need to upgrade building by build structures.
You also can craft fences or some furniture, like beds, shelves, storage crates, rain collectors, tables, chair and so on.
If you find brush and can of paint - you can leave some marks on the walls, like arrows, skull, etc.
Barricades strenght depends on building skill too!
You will see as builded objects getting better (looks better) when you upgrade building skill. Its also meand objects getting more strong!
Weather, day|night & season system is good!
In winter you must wear warm cloths, in summer - light. Otherwise you can catch cold or warm yourself to bad condition (maybe to death, have not tested :3 ).
In rain you get wet, so you need a towels to dry self, alsewere you can catch cold.
By passing the time world getting conquered by the nature.
Epic picture of city, what slowly destroyed, tall grass everywhere, and zombies. Oh yeah!
In the game you can fing clock and calendar.
In nigh will be colder... Well... And darker :3
Whole world will be look different on spring, summer, autumn and winter! But changes was not going fast, whorld slowly comes to current season, makes game look really great!
Stats system very nice.
Eating rotting food or raw meat/eggs leads to food poisoning.
Catching cold make the character lauder (by couthing).
Be bitten by zombie can make your zharacter a zombie (funny thing is: when you after die restart in the world - you can find previous character zombie with all things they carry! But be aware! If zombie character was a good sprinter and melee fighter - it can be end bad, when you get catched!).
Getting bites leads to wounds, falling from high - to legs bones brakes.
Many medical supplyes can help heal the wounds, but it take time and require peace and be well fed.
Meeting much zombies can shock, long sleepless to fall in sleep.
Many dangers awaits survivalists in the world, no matter - maradeurs, builders, soldiers, farmers, hunter or big grammas.
About optimization & mods:
Game uses LUA, it designed good, mods makes easy, works fine, no lags or bugs founded.
Whole game have sprite graphics, mean low pressure on video/CPU. And its great!
Well, game runs fine, gameplay very interesting and re-playeble, looks good, leaves much of positive :)

Each time a room is oppened there is a chance that either you find some monsters, loot crate, party memeber, vender or a few different objects. You also collect Dust which is the primary resource used to power rooms and used as currency, a lot of the time rooms will allow you to build a major module which will give you a certain amount of a resource each time you open a door and you can alos build minor modules to defend the room. Offcoursee you're doing all this while exploring, upgrading characters and trying to find the exit.

Uriel's Chasm is a confusing game to say the least. It contains of 4 stages of different gameplay.
1st Stage - Asteroid type game. You're in a spaceship and have to destroy meteors to find bible pages. You have to keep an eye on your fuel and ammo while avoiding a giant spinning monster roaming around aimlessly. Every time you get a page of the bible you'll get half a screen of text that you have no real time to read so I just left it there.
2nd Stage - A sidescrolling bullethell shooter. The most confusing part about this was the hitboxes, sometimes it seems the  player's head is the hitbox, sometimes it's the entire body (when touching the ground). This part of the game was actually kind of fun since it was somewhat challenging.
3rd Stage - 2D platforming, item collecting. So this time you're walking around, jumping from platform to platform, trying to find the crucified Jesus to hear some nonsensical text. On top of the lack of any real gameplay the screen is constantly spinning around, disorienting the player.
4th Stage - Bullethell boss battle. You're fighting a boss who keeps shooting black and white circles at you. On a black background. So good luck dodging the bullets. Fortunatelly when you die the stage just resets so there's no waiting involved. After defeating the boss you get a screen saying "The End" and as far as I know that's the end of the game.
Pros:
+ 2nd and 4th stage are challenging and somewhat fun
+ Controlls are actually pretty okay
Cons:
- Unskippable cutscenes that last around 90 seconds
- Gameplay is all over the place. Some of the stages are challenging and fun while others are dull and boring
- Repetitive music
- Poor or no sound effects
- No continuing after exiting the game
If you have any patience you can complete this game but it's not really worth it other than the trading cards.

Hmmm, what to say, what to say.
I want to like this game, I really do. I'm British and no longer living in the UK so this game does a good job of making me feel at home. It is very quirky, has a tinge of black comedy about it and is very British, however...
This is one of those games where you have to spend alot of time playing it... dying repeatedly, starting again, rinse and repeat trying to do a little better each time. While alot of players are into this, I am not one of them and instead favor games with progression.
I will say that it's very hard because your character needs to eat every 10 minutes and the amount of food in any given game won't be able to fill a saucer, let alone your belly. Not only do you have hunger to contend with but also robots with insanely good aim which all seem to huddle around the objects that you need to collect to progress. Killing them really isn't an option as there are usually so many around at any given time and distracting them works for only a few seconds and they WILL spot you before you are able to grab the object and hide.
I dunno just feels like it could do with some more work maybe some tweaking. The general gameplay as is right now, is basically: Start game, find one fragment (the objectives) get hungry, spend ages trying to look for food before going for another fragment which is heavily guarded. Try to kill/distract them, fail and end up sprinting away while getting shot at as if you were caught with the farmers daughter. If you survive, hand the fragment in and then eventually end up starving to death or running out of bandages/ammo/distractions very quickly.
I know alot of people are into this masochistic kind of gameplay but I like to relax and enjoy a game. If you are like me then you should avoid this game, if you like the sound of what I described or you like to play RPGs on "hardcore mode" you'll probably love it.
Oh and despite the bragging there is neither tea nor biscuits. I know that your "servant" narrator promises them but I am dubious about anything he says.

The docu is about the Japanese indie scene, created by a French woman. Unfortunately, half of the developers who got screen time were Westerners that for some reason live in Japan. Near the end it gets a bit better with some focus on the future but overal it was a bit fuzzy. I really like "Sir, you are being hunted" and I think it's a very special game that deserves your attention, but there are things in this game that stings me in a very uncomfortable way and that may scare away players.
- First time I jumped into the game I had no idea where to go. North? West? East? South? Stay in Central? In that specific moment of time, I felt the game was drenching me with choices and oppertunities. I like those moments very much and they get rarer each time I play.

- This is a part of the game I also enjoyed. When you start a new game you'll have the option to change what biome the islands will have (Except for the center island. It's always rural.) and the amount of enemies you'll face.
- Since this is a game about stealth, it will punish you for not being stealthy enough and it does so by letting the robots run after you and try to kill you if you've been spotted. Robots will also alert other robots nearby of your presence, which makes the game alot tougher. I have gotten myself hunted and killed a number of times and sometimes a special type of robot will hide in thick patches of forest and wait until you get close enough to them.
- After about 27 hours of running around on islands looking for fragments I have noticed certain graphical errors such as bricks you're able to see through and houses that looks like tall buildings that just sank into the ground until they hit something.
The textures makes me cringe a little, especially one of the ground textures that reminds me of Call of Duty's digital camouflage but with fitting colours instead of the traditional black, white and grey. Another example of my despise towards some of the textures is in the castle biome. I enjoy walking up in castletowers and looking down on robots with my binoculars but I always notice that the inside of the towers have the exact same texture as the outside which I find to be a little annoying.
- Collect 17 pieces from the islands. Bring them back to spawn. Win the game. This entire process is quite boring and it prevents me from continuing to play due to all of the motivation that was drained when acquiring just a few of these fragments.
An example of my train-of-thought when returning fragments:
"Alright! Returned 3 in a go and I have ... 9 fragments left?!? *sigh*"
"Screw it! I'll deal with this later."
- I have to admit that the firearms and weapons lacks authenticity in both sound, look and feeling. The guns have a very basic design and the reload animations are basically non-existent. The revolver's cylinder doesn't pop out of its place so new bullets can get in and double-barreled hunting shotguns doesn't break in the middle. It just tilts itself in a way that makes me think that a hole opens and new shells glide in without me seeing it.
The game compensates this by making ammunition so rare that it is nearly impossible to really observe and analyze how a certain weapon looks and feels like.
- Survival in games is generally a value that the player has. The player needs to find objects that reduces this value from reaching zero. Survival in this game is exactly what I just described. You walk around and look inside buildings in order to find something to "eat". No sound is played to amplify the feeling of eating. You just "use" the item, it disappears and your hunger has a slightly higher value.
- Houses and buildings is a common sight in "Sir, you are being hunted". It can get people pretty excited when they can imagine themselfs walking into an uninhabited shelter, desperately looking ammunition, food or tools. Or just seeking refuge. That doesn't apply to this game. Houses in "Sir, you are being hunted" have the same function as a chest or a crate.
You open it up, take what you need then leave. This will make houses in this game useless if you ever need to take cover in them. I personally wish I could get inside houses when I'm being chased. Getting cornered when hiding behind a giant rektangle is one of the worst ways to die, I imagine.
However, this doesn't apply to the aforementioned castletowers.
I like this game. You might not like it. Buy it on a sale. Preferably 75% off. That's what I did.

Branching Paths is the best documentary on indie game development, and game development in general, that I've ever seen.
It focuses on the Japanese indie game development scene, and it doesn't just focus on the big players, like other documentaries do. Sure, it shows ZUN of Tohou fame, and Nigoro of La Mulana fame, but it also focuses on smaller indies, including ones that do it for fun, or those who have only started for a few months.
It takes place over the course of a few years, showing the progress in several indies, most notable Ojiro Fumoto (also known as Moppin) and his game Downwell. It also shows a large variety of opinions on any one matter - For example, the topic of whether indies should be developing in their spare time with a job as security, or if they should be spending all their time on game development.
I not only found out about many quirky games and things I did not know previously (There's an indie game dev cafe started by the Pico-8 creator!) but I also was extremely moved by a lot of the raw passion that the developers had for creating games.
There were some awkward aspects, though, namely Keiji Inafune (the footage was filmed before Mighty Number 9 was released) complaining about how the general public do not place faith in the developer's skills, but rather only in the final product. Uh, yeah.
But overall, I felt that it was an extremely good documentary. It was well shot, with lots of tiny details (I especially like how it showed some shots of the developer's bookshelves or rooms) and extremely comfy. It's inspiring in a way I can't exactly put into words, but I highly recommend it to anyone who has an interest in the indie gamedev scene in Japan, especially the weirder side.

I just finished watching this doc and my feelings are mixed. It feels very western-oriented: many western developers living in Japan are shown, there's a big segment about Bit.Summit, other big segments about various meetups organized by westerners, and well can you do a documentary about the Japanese indie scene without mentioning the Comiket even once? Apparently you can! lol.
Well maybe it was mentioned in the first half of the movie and I don't remember it because I saw it in two parts (gotta sleep sometimes), but what I strongly feel is that what we see in this documentary is the "whitewashed" version of Japanese indies, and at some point there's even an explanation about how indie developers are different from doujin developers. It boils down to "indie developers want to make money with it, doujin devs don't".
All in all it's not a terrible way to spend about 80 minutes, and it's always refreshing to see Japanese people with all their naivete and their eyes full of hopes, as opposed to the western indie scene with all its drama.
But if I had to take an insight from this documentary is that the West wants to impose its view of indie gaming to Japan, and this movie is kind of the propaganda of that idea.
Still I'm gonna recommend it since there are virtually no other such productions around so, still better than nothing I guess! Oh and about "still better than nothing" the movie eminently features Keiji Inafune, as it's set in 2014 and 2015, before the Mighty No. 9 crash'n'burn, a bit funny to see in hindsight.
EDIT:
Also if this documentary can be viewed as a peek on Japan by a westerner, I think that for a Japanese person it can really be a thing like "hey kid, forget doujin! did you know that indie games from the West are cool and that now they're coming to Japan too? why don't you make them too! don't think about the money, think about your dreams, and while you're at it publish your stuff abroad and on Steam, because that's where the real money is!" ok maybe not like it but I feel it can be highly "inspirational" for Japanese devs, a bit like Indie Game: The Movie was inspirational for western ones.
But my guess is that Indie Game: The Movie produced many unemployed starving gaming developers, and I hope this movie doesn't do the same back there in Japan.

If you're a MotoGP fan and you've never played a MotoGP game before, this is the one to get. The newer versions; like most sports games (FIFA, Madden etc.) add next to nothing and MotoGP 2015 is the best balance of features and price.
If you're a GP fan you'll love it.
If you're a casual racer, it's as good as the niche amrket of motorcyle racing games gets.
If you already have a previous installement however, there's no real need to buy.
As a HUGE MotoGP fan (Staying up well past midnight and getting up real early to watch every race because I'm Australian and timezones are a minge of a thing) this is bliss. Being able to race for actual GP teams against the actual racers on real world circuits is a dream come true.
The bikes feel great, physics are well balanced and realistic but still enjoyable. it does benefit from a good controller; I'm using a crappy 360 controller from ebay and it's rubbish. You really need to be able to apply finite amounts of lean angle and throttle at precise monents to be really quick.
There's a distinct feeling of satisfaction when you nail three apexes in a row, get your lean angle perfect and get great drive out of the corner, leaving everyone else in your dust. It's also controller smash inducing when you brake too hard, lean in and lowsie into the gravel. I'd say it recreates the excitement of racing fairly well.
There are downsides obviously, as you'd expect with a less than AAA sports game. While the visuals are fine on what matters, everything that isn't a bike or an apex looks pretty meh. Not awful, just meh. And while you're usually not worrying about it when you're flying past at 300kph, it would be nice for some of the awesome locations like Aragon and Phillip Island to feel a bit livlier.
All in all though, as far as recreating the experience of ripping around Doohan corner at 200pkh on a YZR-M1, this is pretty hard to hate. If you like MotoGP, you'll likely love this.
But maybe wait for a sale.

(Let me preface this by saying that I've completed two full letter sets and half of a third one, plus several daily sets.)
I'm a big fan of minimalist/indie puzzle games, but this one leaves me cold. I've not invested the time that other reviewers have, but I can imagine from what I've seen that the mechanics of this game don't get any more complex as you progress. Each level set does become more difficult between its beginning and its end, but because there are so many level sets, it feels like playing the same game over and over again.
There is no ambient soundtrack, which is for me an essential part of a minimalist puzzle game (although on the flip side, you can listen to your own music over it instead).
There is no real logic to be applied to the solution process -- yes, there is a little bit of reasoning involved (this node has this number of empty slots, so this many paths will go through it; that color tile can only be accessed that way), but nothing engaging or stimulating. Any given puzzle often has multiple solutions, which is . . . nice, I guess, and uninteresting.
There is, basically, nothing to DO. And with 26 sets of 25 levels each, plus new daily sets, there's a whole lot of nothing to do. I take another crack at this game every other evening to see if I just wasn't in the right frame of mind last time I played it, and every time I close it after a level or two, more bored than when I started. If it's on sale for less than $1, sure, buy it, get some achievements to make a funny message in your showcase. But if you're looking for a puzzle game that makes you really feel the blood flowing in your brain, play Hexcells.
Really, play Hexcells anyway. It's a fantastic game.

TL;DR Great game, devoted devs, buy now if you want to shape the game and experience the development.
As of 0.6.1 i am enjoying this game thoroughly. There are enough characters and since adding 8 levels an indepth clear is currently around 3 hours of play. Though i have read aot of complaints and they fall into two categories too hard or no diversity.
In respect to difficulty there are currently two options, easy and too easy. As their name suggests  neither option is very difficult. However if you play this game and do not consider that is a combinations of many game types and aproach it as one you will lose fairly quickly. Also, aproaching each level with no forethought or strategy will cause a loss aswell. It is of course a strategy game so those who lack it will not suceed. Furthermore, the learning curve is fairly easy and once you get the hang of it is a blast.
In respect to a lack of diversity you have to remember this game is still in alpha. if you are buying a early access game looking for a full game experience then you will be dissapointed. The devs are pushing out consistent updates, much faster than alot of the other early access games on steam. They fix bugs very quickly and if a patch is game breaking they pull it so you can still play while they work on it. By buying the game now you can shape development by voting on their website.
The game itself is quite simple. There are currently 3 resources industry, science and food. Industry is for building modules and major modules help produce those three resources. Minor modules are turrets support turrets and defensive turrets. Science allows you to resource upgrades for your modules and new modules themselves. food allows you to recruit new heroes after your starting heroes, level up your heores(current max lvl 8 due to 8 Floors) and heal them during fights.
You use these resources to build a defense network so that when the exit of the lvl is found you can safely bring your crystal(the object that allows you to power rooms so you can build in them) to the next lvl. Each level gets increasingly difficult with new enemies and more rooms.
Heroes: Heroes come in all shapes in sizes and currently there are four stats, and five weapons types(currently 0.6.1). Stats are health,speed,damage and wit. Weapon types are sword, spear, pistol, machine gun, unarmed. health is how much life you start with and how much life you get every time you level up. Speed is movement speed. Wit is comparable to an intelligence stat but is mostly used for heroes you can operate major modules(Operating is to give a bonus to their production rate or bonus it gives) by increasing the operator bonus. Damage is the amount of damage you do. All of these stats scale when you level the heroe and different heroes are more proficient in different stats.There is no heroe that is useless all of them serve a specific purpose and you can win by using any combination of them.Also, there are armors and support items, most with comical names or premises.
Finally a great amount of thought has gone into this game from the item descriptions and the heroe backgrounds to the strategies that are available and to the details in each room. This ia a great product and i am highly anticipating the finished version.

Dungeon of the Endless is an interesting new title by Amplitude Studios currently in Alpha development which spans several popular genres.
For my full featured review with pictures and videos coming soon please visit
You begin Dungeon of the Endless with two hero characters and a crystal in a small escape pod. The basic premise of the game is to explore each dungeon and find the exit. Each dungeon is comprised of interconnected randomly generated rooms. Many of these rooms contain mobs of monsters that attempt to end your game by either killing your heroes or your crystal. As you explore the dungeon's rooms you acquire resources and have the ability use these resources to deploy defenses. Game play is actually a hybrid of real time and turn based strategy in that you have the ability to pause live game play and issue commands if you so desire. The game can also be played in real time mode exclusively. Once the exit is located, your job is to transport the crystal safely there. If you make it you win the round and move on to the next level. If your heroes die, you lose. If your crystal’s dust level (essentially health, power and currency all in one) falls to zero, you lose. Piece of cake right? WRONG.
Dungeon of the Endless has a lot of things going on. At its heart, it is a rouge like (hate that term) dungeon crawler. You explore a procedurally generated environment with a small group of  playable heroes. What that means is this: the dungeons and encounters are never exactly the same. Sure you’ll see similarities, but by and large the environments will never be exactly alike. Additionally, your band of motley heroes isn’t invincible. Once they die, they’re dead… FOREVER. Kiss all that experience and loot goodbye! Rogue like game play; check.
So what else does the game offer? How about some resource management? In Dungeon of the Endless your success or failure is largely linked to your resource acquisition and management. There are four main resources to worry about: Dust (no you can't snort it), Industry, Food and Science. Every time you open a room you receive an amount of each resource except dust. Additionally, you can deploy resource modules in powered rooms (more on that later) that add a modifier to the amount of a particular resources obtained when subsequent doors are opened. For example, an Industry module will provide additional industry every time you open a new door. Heroes with the required skill can even operate the module and provide an additional, additional bonus to the resources. Phew, that sounds complicated. Of note here is that extra resources, except dust, are carried over to the next dungeon.
Dungeon of the Endless also has Role Playing and Character Progression aspects. Even though the game features permadeath you have the ability to level up your hero's and outfit them with gear discovered in dungeons. Your heroes have stats which increase as their levels increase. In addition, as you level up your heroes they gain access to special combat skills.
But wait, there's more...
Dungeon of the Endless also offers tower defense like game play. As you explore each dungeon level you "open up" additional parts of the map. Each new room traversed is dark, which means it is currently not powered. These darkened rooms serve as spawn points for mobs of monsters which attack in waves and make a beeline toward your crystal. How do you stop these waves of monsters you ask? Well, you power some of these dark rooms with part of your limited supply of dust. Once powered, you then use your Industry resource to build defenses. As waves of enemies appear, your smartly placed defenses and heroes take them out. Sounds kinda tower defense like huh.
One of Amplitude Studios goals is community involvement. Amplitude wants the players to take an active part in the game's development and it is facilitating this by utilizing a system called GAMES2GETHER . One of the biggest reasons to play an early access game is to participate in the evolution of a game. Plenty of Steam early access games claim to use player feedback to help shape the final product into what the community wants... and then promptly don't. Amplitude appears to actually be following through with it. By utilizing it's G2G Votes system, the community has the ability to vote on art and game design decisions. For example, the current vote is for creating a new playable character. There is also a standard forum where players can follow the games development and post their questions and comments. The jury is still out on how much the community will drive development however so we'll have to monitor the process and see how it goes.
Like every other game out there, Dungeon of the Endless is not perfect. I'll cover what I feel are weak points for the game first. The game needs a lot more explanation. This is a reasonably complex game and the current tutorial slides just don't cut it. I found myself with more questions than answers after the tutorial and had to stumble into them myself. A proper tutorial level guiding the player through the games nuisances would help to acclimate players better. As this is just the alpha stage, i'm sure the developers will address this in the near future. The graphics are basic. Again, this is by design but worth noting anyway.
Another issue is repetitiveness. Although the levels are procedurally generated they all look and feel essentially the same. This in addition to the fact that the basic game play remains the same can make the game feel a bit tedious after a while.  Is there an end to the game or is it truly endless? I don't actually know the answer to that question. But if the game had milestones or varied locations to make you feel like your progressing it might help. Its worth noting that in general I usually don't play rogue like games specifically for this reason. As an old school RPG and MMORPG player, I tend to become attached to my characters and devote a good amount of time carefully picking their skills and equipment. The permadeath aspect of these games is a turn off for me. I like to feel that i'm making progress towards a larger goal and I just didn't feel it with this game.
All that being said, I still really like the game. Dungeon of the Endless is a fun and reasonably deep game. What's most impressive is the games complexity despite its current Alpha state. There's enough depth and strategy here already to keep you playing the game and checking back to see how it evolves. Also, at this point in my life, I tend to be gravitating towards games that i can play in small chunks. Dungeon of the Endless gives players the ability to save and pause games at any time. If your a new parent like me, trying to juggle work, parenthood, and everything else life throws at you, this is HUGE. For the price of entry, Dungeon of the Endless is definitely forth a look.

Honestly... it's Bioshock.  It's 8 years old now (seriously??? Where does the time go...), and it'd strain belief that someone using Steam has not at least heard of it before... and if you've heard of it before, chances are you've heard how damned GOOD it is.  It's the spiritual successor to the System Shock games (which are themselves now available on Steam), which means it's a shooter with RPG elements.  Unlike the System Shock games, you don't need to invest 6 points into a skill to be able to effectively beat people over the head with a jagged piece of rock - you're decently effective with all weapons.  Instead, character specialization is largely accomplished via the use of tonics and plasmids, which the game will do just fine at explaining to you.  You run around in expansive, largely nonlinear levels while blasting all sorts of different baddies and zapping them with sufficiently-advanced-technology to stun them with bolts of electricity, ignite them, freeze them, and even mind-control them.
Rest assured, it's still aged quite well and while you might need to fiddle with some .ini files or settings, it still works just fine on Windows 7, Windows 8, and Windows 10.  There are multiple guides on Steam, all with different methods, so if you're like me and didn't have any in-game sound, try em until one of em works.  I've got a Realtek audio chip on my motherboard, and it appears that Bioshock just plain doesn't like Realtek in W10.  I solved it by enabling the "Stereo Mix" device in my Sound panel, located under Recording Devices.  Others recommend .ini edits or running the game in Windows XP SP3 compatibility mode.
Regardless, if you run into any bugs or issues running it on modern OSes, chances are people have found a workaround for it.  If that was what was keeping you on the fence, keeping you from playing this absolute masterpiece of a game, don't worry about - get it and play it.

Seeing the description of the game and the overwhelming amount of negative reviews, I initially thought that Uriel's Chasm ticked off a bunch of edgy atheist teens who freak out at the mere mention of anything religious. Thankfully, the negativity had little to do with this, but I still was not satisfied with the actual reasons motivating the bad reviews. Upon reading a review which spoke highly of its religious themes, controls and similarity to games of the full motion video era, I decided to buy Uriel's Chasm at the price point of $0.49.
After the first level, it became clear to me that Uriel's Chasm uses the fact that it's a game to create an experience unlike any I have ever had. The gameplay here is incredibly simple and easy to learn. Four out of the five keys used are for directional controls. The sole complication this game provides to the player is the fact that each level plays differently than the last. Any curveballs beyond this would interfere with what this game ultimately achieves.
A menacing atmosphere inundates Uriel's Chasm and it intensifies with each level. I cannot wait to reach its conclusion. I never would have imagined that a tandem of the 2006 YouTube and 32-bit 2D game aesthetics could be used to such frightening effect. Play alone at night for the full experience.
With all of this in mind, this is not a game upon which you are going to spend 100 hours. In fact, it shouldn't take you any more than 2 hours to complete. However, a movie ticket costs $10, and this is a far superior experience compared to anything that's currently showing in the multiplex. A fantastic documentary covering the curious case of the Japanese indie game scene. Branching Paths paints a picture of an indie scene that is trying to find its place in both Japan and abroad.
The easiest comparison to make is with the 2012 documentary Indie Game: The Movie. However, Branching Paths sets itself apart in how much variety is showcased, rather than focusing on a handful of developers.
From three-letter giants like ZUN and IGA to up-and-comers like Moppin (creator of Downwell) and Lucas Pope (creator of Papers, Please). From giant conventions like BitSummit and Comiket to more intimate local gatherings like Picotachi and Tokyo Indies. The variety of games and people shown cannot be understated.
There's an idea repeated a couple times throughout the documentary. The idea that you should do something only
can do, make something only
can make. It's a really "romantic" notion, perhaps one unique to Japan, that I think sums up this documentary rather well.
You play as Logan Paul on an adventure into Suicide forest in Japan, where people go to hang themselves.

I really wanted to like this game, and at times I have a great deal. Sadly over-all I can't recommend the frustration I've experienced from this game to anyone else.
This is not going to be one of those reviews that bashes the game because of it's dlc policy. Abusive or not we're here to talk about the game as is and frankly there is plenty of diverse content to enjoy in this game. There are four character classes; Assault , Medic , Trapper, and Support and there's also the Monster class. Each of those classes have three different characters to enjoy it with. There's a medic who uses a TF 2 med gun to heal you but then there's also Lazerus who's best time to heal a character is actually after they are already down or dead. There are assault characters who are best up close and personal and assaulters who do their best damage at a distance. There are 15 characters in all to unlock and each one plays utterly different than the other. I can actually applaud the variety
I can also praise matches that go perfectly. There are times where you are the exact class you want for an entire Evacuation match (which is really 5 mini-matches rolled into one big instance) with a great team against a skilled monster. When it comes together Evolve is a lot of fun.
BUT Evolve doesn't come together all that often. The only way to start playing is to just enlist into a massive pool of random players and hope the game puts you into a match of your preference. You rate the classes on a scale of 1-5 which measures how much you want to play a give class. When you pick you preferences the game even promises to try and give you your top picks as often as possible. Total and utter bold faced lie:
I usually have the monster rated 5th in last. He or she (yes there are female monsters) plays just fine and is balanced enough as long as you're pretty crafty. After a long day at work where I have customers ganging up on me day and night I don't want to play a game in which a group of 4 does their best to gang up on me. That is my number one preference and I have felt it ignored at every chance it could. I've spent ten straight minutes joining and rejoining matches in the hopes that I wouldn't be thrown into a monster roll or a dead hunter and have quit without even playing a match. There is no way to indicate that you want to start on Day 1 and that you are willing to wait for a party as long as you get the position you want. Yes it's annoying watching impatient players come and go, but I'd rather do that than join a match as a level 1 Wraith already domed and down to half health.
There's a way to play Evolve strictly Co-op (the monster is AI controlled at all times) and this has sadly become my only option. The monster AI is good but also lacking in everything you want it to have. You want the monster to be like a Predator from the movies; giving you a mighty good chase only to lead you into a tunnel where you are BBQed by the crafty monster as he chargers threw your party like a bowling ball (I won once using this strategy). Sadly the AI doesn't have that resourcefulness and most matches are just you following the monster from feed sight to feed sight getting in a shot here or there till it reaches level 3.
What brought this review on was a repeating glitch I've been suffering from in Co-Op where I've finally said enough is enough. As stated before Evacuation matches go on for 5 days and saves the best XP and accolades for the end of the 5th day. I've been suffering from a glitch that for some reason ejects me from matches stating "I am not signed into a profile so I'm not allowed to play" despite the fact that I'm on Day 3 already. I am thusly ejected from the match and miss out on the XP I deserve and since there is utterly no way to have any say about which match you join you've practically just wasted your time.
These problems can easily be fixed with a few patches and I am genuinely intrigued as to how this game will grow. Depending on who wins a day (the monster of the hunters) the game will introduce a pro-winner perk that'll change the game. The hunters can get AI buddies to follow you around or portals to transport you around the level while the monster will get increased wild life, more aggresive wildlife toward humans, ecetera. The perks sadly go away at the end of the match; I can't help but feel the loss of depth. Imagine if they carried over through-out the campaign? There could be massive amounts of angry wildlife, which are bombarded with a space laser that the humans saved. They need to expand Evacuation, possibly into an intergalatic monster war (there is a terraformed moon revolving around the planet so I'm assuming we'll get up there at some point.
I'm sorry for the massive length I only wanted to get every thought out and I thank you for reading if for some reason you did. I do like this game and I had some fun with it but in it's current state or at it's current price I can't recommend this game

Most of the negative reviews have little to do with the experience of this game.
It is a trading/economy sim, at it's core, and it's a pretty serious simulation, taking into account the production and transport of goods throughout most of northern Europe.   The political simulation element does feel a little tacked on, but it does serve as a sort of tangible demonstration of your achievements.
It's largely a sandbox simulation--nobody is there to hold your hand and tell you what to do next, and there isn't going to be very much help in game telling you where to buy and sell your goods.
It is a slower-paced game; about strategy and planning.   It rewards you for long-term planning.
For those familiar with the series, it is a very faithful recreation of PIII, with numerous interface tweaks and some additional content.
It's not for everyone.  But for a trading economy simulation, it is the finest of its kind, and you'll enjoy it.

Echo of Soul is one of those games you pick up when you're bored and want to play some anime styled free2play MMO but have already played the well known games like Mabinogi, Maplestory, Aura Kingdom, Elsword, and the like. It's your typical, run of the mill tab target MMO that doesn't require much thinking. And for that it's great, but man the game does get boring rather quickly.
Graphics: They're good; not 10/10, but unless you're a big name developer your game isn't going to have 10/10 graphics anyway, and this is the case of Echo of Soul. Character models look alright, though I wish the archer elf model didn't have such huge ears. This is one of my gripes with MMOs anyway that feature elves; why must they always have huge pointy ears? I blame LOTR and other franchises, but that's neither here nor there. As for the game environment, it's alright. Standard MMO fare, nicely modeled but still a bit rough around the edges, but that's to be expected. I will give props to the user interface and the control system though. The UI is very intuitive and easy to understand while the control system is very familiar; plus, the drop system actually makes sense and doesn't act funky when dealing with multiple mobs (unlike Aion, which is incredibly finicky and bulky).
Gameplay: As I have said (and so have others), it's a tab-targeting system. Playing as an elf huntress was rather easy; just click and spam skills at enemies, no need to memorize rotation or worry about cooldown times; just click away. I confess though I am not at end game, so maybe this changes when you reach level 60. That said, gameplay is very, very, very basic at this point and I can see why some people might get turned off and not reach end game. It's just pick up quests from one area->kill the monsters/pick up drops->turn into respective NPC->repeat process. Heck, even the map layounts don't change much and are easy to memorize. It turns into one large area with four small areas connected to the side; complete all the side areas, move onto the next, and you're done. Combine that with the questing process and the combat system and you have yourself a game that is so brainless you can play it half asleep - hell, I've done it.
Sound: Nothing fancy; moving on. Music is pretty average for this game as well, but I wasn't expecting anything else.
Ultimately the game's averageness is its own undoing. Boring combat, repetitive quests and predictable area mapping makes for a painfully mediocre game. I can't think of a game that is just more "there" than this. I also find it hard to recommend. One one hand, not recommending it is not being fair; the game isn't terrible, but recommending it would give it too much credit. Maybe the game is there to sate our hunger for average MMOs, but there are better MMOs out there. But if you played all those MMOs already, there is this.

The warden just had to see Auriga.  After arriving in the system, his pleasure yacht of a prison ship was intercepted by an alien fleet and cut it to pieces.  The ship is in chaos as the damage has caused the security force fields to fail.  Prisoners, guards, and crew members all scrambling and fighting to get to the few remaining life pods.  Fate smiles upon you as find a pod bay still open.  You rush for the door thinking that, if its Autamatons then this may only buy you a few more hours of life.  After all, those machines won't leave until their ledgers check out.  If it is Cravers then it may be even shorter.
Strapping in, you lock eyes for a moment with your new partner.  You break the contact realizing that the real danger may be here in the pod with you.
The pods launch.  The port display shows a shower of pods blasting away on their dust drives away from your doomed ship.  As you steady against the accelleration, you notice all the pods change course towards Auriga.  Whomever is at the helm of the prison ship must have thought they would have better luck on the Endless grave planet.
Craver fighters scream past your pod.  You brace for inevitable firey death.  Your partner prays to the Virtual.  The outside of the pod burns as you hit what remains of the Auriga atmosphere.
The pod jostles, spins, and vibrates as the dust drive battles against the Auriga sky.  Weightlessness leaves you as you are embraced by her gravity well.  The pod settles out and your display shows that the blackness of space has been replaced with Auriga's alien horizon.  You can see that several pods have made it through.  Honeycombed ruins can be seen mottled against Auriga's ruined surface.
The view lasts for moments before the pod roars to land.  The pod lands roughly causing sparks to fly out from the manual control console.  Your partner shouts fire as you both unbuckle.  You are lurched and twisted as the pod breaks the surface.  The hull creaks and sheers as the ancient roof collapses under the pod's weight.  For a moment, you are weightless again.
You wake with your face on the floor. The cabin reaks of atmosphere and smoke.  Your partner helps you up with one hand, a depleted extinguisher in the other.  You shrug them off, coughing, and stagger to the environmental display by the escape hatch.  The display details what you have already guessed.  The cabin's air has become toxic.  The next part surprises you.  "Breathable?  How?"  Your partner shrugs and hits the pod's door release.
Outside of the ship lies an ancient hallway.  You can only guess that you've crashed through the surface of Auriga and into the fabled catacombs of an Endless city.
After a couple hours you figure out a way to connect your dust drive to the hallways power jack.    This is not surprising as most of your civilization advances came from discovering the secrets of these ancients.  In minutes, the lights are on and the air seems a bit less musty.
In the middle of the hallway lays a terminal.  Interfacing with it brings up three easy to understand options:  food, resources, or knowledge.  To the Endless, these were the three pillars of their civilization.
While debating which to choose, you stumble upon a smaller terminal.  In fact, several of them are found scattered about the hallway.  You pick up the terminal.  The display shows an option for a defense gun.  Why would you need this?  Auriga has been abandoned for centuries and remains inhospitable on the surface.  Could there still be life on Auriga?
You and your partner debate the possiblities but are interrupted by what may only be described as a howl.  At the end of the hallway, a deep baritone that rumbles through the closed door.
This isn't an abandoned city.  The terminal, these options...a mythical dungeon of the Endless.  You remember from your history classes that guilt, innocence...these concepts did not matter to the Endless.  Their alien legal system was the dungeon.  For a race whose gravest crime was ineffectiveness, these dungeons were both trial and sentence.
"We are in an Endless dungeon."
"So, this is where they torture people?"
"No.  It is a form of judgement, those who make it through were allowed back."
"How does that help us?"
"A dungeon this big may have been shared between multiple systems..."
"...and you are thinking there is a way back?  An Endless ship?"
"Or what passes as one.  We also need to get away from this wreck before the Cravers find it."
"True 'nuff."
"Hit the door."

Firstly, a tl;dr review:
Get it, and play it. Your first couple of runs might not feel very fun or make much sense, and you may feel this game is lacking content. But keep playing, and you'll understand what this game is all about. If you're one of those people who can't appreciate a good soundtrack, an immersive experience, and patient gameplay, stick to your H1Z1/CoD.
9/10 overall. Brilliant, not overpriced, with active developers, mod support, and there's even local/online multiplayer. Can't go wrong with this. It's just sheer good-ness.
Anyway. Onto a REAL review.
Project Zomboid is one of the few games that actually makes me feel on edge whilst I'm playing. The game expresses how you ARE going to die, no matter what. And it's true. You WILL die. One scratch from a zombie can get infected, killing you irreversibly.
'Surely that's too powerful', you may be thinking, but no. This game stresses for you to skillfully outmanouver and sneak past zombies instead of killing them just because you can, or for some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥tty 'XP'. Weapons are effective, and zombies are easy to kill, true... but one misclick is all it takes for your life to be over.
And you know why it's not even frustrating when you die? Because the game told you that you were going to die. You knew this moment would come. I like to randomly generate a character, and 'live their story' if you like, trying to guide them through this unforgiving world as long as you can.
When it comes to crafting, it takes effort to get the knowledge to actually craft things. As it should be. The building systems in other Early Access games are fun, aye, but they don't make much sense. Let's take 7 Days to Die, for example. 7dtd is a brilliant game, don't get me wrong - but Project Zomboid is more fun in terms of IMMERSION and REALISM.
And there's one small feature in the game that I really love. In one of the soundtrack songs, there's the sound of a clock ticking in the background. That clock ticking signifies your time left to live before you die. Such a simple feature keeps you on edge, and keeps you as alert as a meerkat as you stroll around with your trusty butter knife.
The only gripe I have is that I'd like to see some more/better animations on the player model. The combat system could be a little better too, as I often find myself 'charging' attacks, but I'm not even sure if charging my attacks matters or not most of the time.
Regardless of those, this game is brilliance, created by innovative, clever, and active developers. It's fun, engaging, and a wonderful way to pass a few hours by. Mods are awesome with it, too.

This is a game about stalking for 3 days, and I've always wanted a game about stalking for 3 days, but it's not what I really had in mind.  It's a good game, but it's too compacted down.  The day/night cycles are a little short and the maps are a little claustrophibic.  You have to eat every 20 minutes, which is not what I would want to do if I was stalking for 3 days irl.  I'd probably only want to eat once in a 3 day period irl, but in this game, if you don't eat within 20 minutes, you will die!
Also, even though this game is about stalking for 3 days, it's also about being stalked for 3 days, which is fine, except the robots are everywhere and pretty tightly packed (because of the claustrophobic maps).  The gameplay is fine though, and it's a good game, but it's not a game about wandering the wilderness for several days, perhaps not seeing another person the entire time.
What I really hope for is a survival game where you can't see another person or hostile entity for a long time.  You cover your tracks and travel light, taking only what you need and surviving hardcore mode.  When you see another person, you stalk them for 3 days, because there is great risk involved in getting close!  That is the game I want, but this is not that game.  It gives a small taste of what that game might be though and so I will recommend this game.

Evolve is team vs solo player Left 4 Dead style shooter. One players plays as the monster while the other team of 4 are tasked to bring it down. The concept is unique and fun. The weapons for each hunter are interesting and result in a variety of play styles - enough to keep interesting but simple enough to not be overwhelming. You will find three types of monsters. They fall into the main archetypes - warrior (Goliath), mage (Kraken) and rogue (Wraith).
Mechanically, this game is a console to PC port. It still plays well, there have been no issues with online play, and there are a variety of available resolutions. Just don't expect this game to justify a PC upgrade or anything.
The game currenlty suffers from severe balance issues that were not really present during the open beta. Why the devs decided to change so much in the wrong direction is an interesting question. Many of the hunters offer no advantage to the more popular picks, some of poor to the point where they will set your team at a severe disadvantage. Decent monster players are capable of killing your entire team at level 2 in one go without great difficulty, which they really shouldn't be.
This game would be great but the above issues really hold it back. Hopefully a patch or new DLC may bring this game back to the hype that it should have had.
If the game were 30.00 dollars versus 60.00 then we would have a good buy. But considering the balance issues and lack of content currently I would recommend a pass. However, it is good enough that if you have already purchased it, or have a group of friends to play with, it is still worth your time. Future patches or expansions may make this game from a average game to a great game.

I copied a good portion of this review from my review of the base game. I'll be adding on some stuff for this DLC towards the end. Also, for the people thinking of buying this game and is just checking out the DLC too, I recommend getting the DLC with the base game. Rise of a Dynasty adds a lot: Land based trade routes, treasure hunting(by collecting map pieces), Online/LAN Co-op, and lots of Graphical improvements, among other things. So it's definitely worth getting both.
Patrician is a great nautical trading game. You buy low, travel to another city, and sell high. As you gain more money, you buy more ships so you can carry more goods. Then you can start a second Convoy(a team of ships basically), and assign it a route. A route tells the ships which cities to go to and what order to do it. You can tell them what they should buy and what they should sell in that particular city. And they'll do all that without any more input from you, and they'll be earning you money in no time.
You can even start producing goods yourself, and have dedicated ships to deliver it to another city either to sell high, or give it to another goods producer you own so they can make more complicated, and therefore more valuable goods to sell. You gain favor in a city by selling them goods that they are low on, which makes them like you more. Once they're happy enough with you, you can start buying buildings in their city, and producing goods unique to them.
You can also take up Contracts/Missions/Whatever at the Pub. This ranges from delivering a certain amount of a specific good, or even hunting down a specific pirate or rival.
One thing it's starts losing quality on is sea based combat. Most of the time, you'll just want to let the fighting resolve automatically rather than take control yourself, since it's rather boring. Once you start getting more well known in the game, your ships will be attacked by pirates more often, and sometimes not even towards you specifically. Sometimes they'll park their boats outside a cities port, attacking anyone who comes or goes. Most of the time, if you lose, they'll just take a large amount of your goods, and sometimes a ship, and let your convoy go. To counter this, you can assign specialized boats with armor and weapons to fight, protect, and even scare off pirates on occasion. You can even put cannons on your merchant boats, however, this subtracts from overall storage space, but it's worth it if a specific convoy gets attacked a lot. Sometimes though, they're just a pain in the ♥♥♥, and you'll have to send your own specialized combat convoy to take them out permanently, since no one else will do it.
There's a lot of trading to do in this game, and the DLC will add quite a bit more. I'll need to write up a review for 'Rise of a Dynasty' too, but later.

One little problem, don't lend money to Princes, because they do not pay you back.

Fighting pirates/: If you have a crayer, upgrade to 2nd level and add 70 sailors.  Try to lead the pirate vessel/s and turn toward the fastest point, cripple the fastest pirate by firing at the sails, do this to the next fastest until all pirate sails have been destroyed, now change to round shot and destroy the fastest.  If ithe last or only one is a cog or crayer make sure you reduce the sailors to nil before reducing it to about 10% when it should surrender.
Eventually you research the hulk which is a faster vessel and carries more cannon.
Happy hunting.

I highly recommend this game. It is a fun rogue-like dungeon crawler that has tower defense like strategy and resource management. When you start the game you are giving 2 random heroes to venture out into the unknown (random) Dungeon. Your heroes level up and can find/equip weapons and armor to help hold off the hordes of creatures that are for some reason attracted to you and your ship. As you leave your starting point on the map you will progress by opening doors to rooms and corridors that will hopefully lead you to the exit. Once, you found the exit you have to make your way back to your starting point and transport your power source to the exit as well. Be aware that the waves of enemies do not stop once you find the exit. They just get progressively more difficult.
Dungeon of the Endless sports an old school feel with its' retro style pixel art and tilted camera. I almost want to say Isometric, but it isn't at such an angle. So, don't look at this games simple design and expect an easy game.

This game is great. It has a way of being particularly immersive, especially when extreme conditions force you into crazy situations. To illustrate, here's what just happened to me.
I had run out of food on my current map because I messed around long without accomplishing much. Instead of starting over I decide it's time to move on to the next map to see how far I can take it. I set off with my few supplies to try to find another loot-rich area. During my trek, I:
-First, I quickly began starving
-Then I ran out of wood and ended up on the cusp of hypothermia
-I found my way to an abandonned mine, and made my way through the darkness holding single matches along the way
-when I exited at the other end, there be a most violent snow storm. I really couldn't see where I was going.
-I then took shelter in an abandonned car and ate a mouldy granola bar. It gave me a poopy butt.
-Realising that I couldn't just await a slow death in the car, I head back into the storm and stumble along all exhausted.
-I got hopelessly lost in the woods then set upon from behind by a wolf. My one rifle shot was not enough.
-I was able to defend myself with my knife and followed the blood trail to the wolf's corpse, whereupon i immedately feasted upon its raw hot flesh.
-once I was done eating the storm lifted enough for me to spy a cluster of glorious loot-filled  cabins. With its dying breath that wolf had lead me to salvation.

Short summary:
To start of with, I'd like to point out that this game is very unique in the fact you can play as a monster and that it has a very high replayability because of many unlocks (be it badges, charactermasteries or perks). The game also has a lot of characters avaible to play.
(Vanilla version on official release has 12 hunters and 3 monsters)
The game is basically 4 hunters matched agains't one monster.
You have many different gamemodes and a lot of characters with a lot of unlocks that emphasise replayability. Matches normally wont be linear, they'll vary a lot aswell which is also a good bonus to this game.
The game itself however needs to be approached carefully.
If you're interested in the hunters's end I recommend you play this with friends or play this with premade players. Hunters rely on good communication and teamwork to make their games even more fun.
If you seek out to play as the monster. My advice to you would be to get used to them vs AI or friends.
For pvping it is kind of mandatory to have good perks and some character masteries if you want to have fair matches.
In-depth description/info/summary
The game modes:
Hunt, is currently the most played one (competitively at least). This mode is pretty straightforward Monster tries to survive the hunt until he becomes strong enough (by feasting on corpses and evolving) to become the hunter and kill the hunters. At stage 3 you also have a 3rd objective which makes the game mode a bit more intense.  There's also a limited time that forces the match to be somewhat fast paced.
This mode is pretty balanced, depending on the map, some maps are better for hunters some are better for the monster.
Nest, the hunters have to kill the eggs or the alpha monster (the player) before the timer runs out the monster has to keep at least one egg or minion alive or kill the hunters.
This mode usually favors the monster despite putting some pressure on the monsterplayer.
Rescue, The survivors have to evacuate 5 survivors, the monster has to kill 5 of them. First party to do so or to kill the other party wins.
This mode is rather equal through it can heavily favor the hunters.
Defend: The monster has to kill 2 generators and a fueltank to win. The hunters have to defend until the timer runs out. There are 2 stage 1 goliaths that spawn at a fix interval for the monster to relieve pressure.
--
You have singleplayer, multiplayer co-op and multiplayer pvp.
You can create custom games with your own rules and play Evacuation
Evacuation is a 5 day campaign where all players vote for the next mode out of 2 random generated modes, first mode beeing Hunt. Last mission beeing defend. Every time a party wins the other party will become stronger (get more hitpoints and higher damage output). This one is the best for farming experience because you get a huge bonus to your experience at the end of a campaign depending on how well your party performed during that campaign.

Okay, let me expand on that.  First, as in the base game, you start with a small business and a ship.  Primarily thru trade do you grow your wealth, although you also can set up your own supply lines throughout the Hanse.  The businesses that you need for that need workers, which need food, which need etc. etc. to maintain production. In conclusion, this is a really good sim.  Fairly simple and focussed on trading and growing cities organically.

Patrician IV, henceforth known as "Patty IV's" is in something of a niche genre, in that it is a Renaissance trading simulator set around the Hanseatic League in Northern Europe. Patty IV's behaves something akin to a sandbox, and the main campaign introduces you to the core concepts in a really intelligent way rather than simply throwing a standard tutorial at you, whereupon you start with modest resources as a simple hemp smuggler operating out of Lubeck aspiring to grow his empire until you control all the booze and kush in Denmark.
The difficulties in the true sandbox mode work pretty well too, they basically make more bad things happen the higher difficulty you select, like pirates stealing your♥♥♥♥♥♥or bad winters freezing ports over as well as ramping up the costs of production, so that in order to maintain a decent profit margin you actually have to spread your goods out intelligently. Because of this, on the higher difficulties you truly end up as a wicked beer baron, having to ship your product all over Europe to find enough people keen for your booze and bud (Stockholm can't get enough hemp for some reason).
Once you've gotten enough dosh behind you from your 'legitimate businesses' you can move into the world of protection, racketeering and exploitation. You can create fleets of pirate vessels or hunt the pirates that menace your trade. You can be 'elected' in charge of a town and pay off the local authorities to leave you in peace. Its a good game all in all. I haven't played it an exorbtitant amount, but I have had quite a bit of fun with the time I have had. So far the only 2 complaints I have are as follows:
1) The sheer number of foreign language speakers on The NA server. Its not that I am against foreign language, but its far past the point where they should have made servers specifically for these other groups, because they aren't exactly a minority group. Its actually starting to cause problems when grouping with other people for dungeons.
2) I actually find this one a tad amusing: The censorship system. It censors any words that are specified inappropriate, maybe a little TOO well. Even if the letters are in seperate words, like Four's Excellence, its censors the letters xD
As for the pro's to the game, there are quite a few, so I will confine it to 5.
1) The music, Oh good grief the music! It is AMAZING, it fits very well, and right off the bat on opening the title menu my first day I felt at home
2) The graphics. Now some of you may think "ok, its got good graphics, so what?" but I'm not saying, jacking it up all the way to ultra, even at minimum, which I found to be just as manageable as other MMORPG's, the graphics are stellar. So if you are looking to focus on game performance over graphics quality, you aren't sacrificing a whole lot by running minimum.
3) The player base seems to be quite friendly thus far. Although not a whole lot of questions have been answered for me, there are still plent of friendly people I have run into. Dont take that to mean this game has no trolls, every mmo does to some extent, but the people who are friendly go above and beyond ^_^
4) The skill paths for classes are quite simple, but it still requires a bit of careful planning to get a suitable combination.
5) The main hub for the first large zone has ALOT to do, and is quite large. I didn't do a whole lot of exploring, but there were quite a few vendors.
I hope this has helped to some degree, and if you have any questions that this review failed to answer, please feel free to ask in the comments below ^_^

Updated review:
Still a great game but am waiting on additional features (which are coming soon). Don't get me wrong...this is a complete game and could have been released a year ago. You will have loads of fun (there are tons of videos that show gameplay). The devs provide a clear roadmap and share their progress and set-backs in weekly updates. This is clearly a labor of love for them. They have promised loads of features coming up in the next build which I am excited for (this explains my lack of recent play time), but I've invested over a hundred hours already which backs my claim that there is already tons of entertainment to be had in its current state.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Don't be fooled by the graphics. In a sea of survival games, this one is one of the best titles I've played. Great solo experience but even better multiplayer experience. Only one copy of the game but have a spare controller? You can play local split-screen with a friend. Oh, you died and your buddy is still alive? Don't worry, you can respawn back at your make-shift shelter with your buddy. And speaking of controllers...if you can't grasp the keyboard/mouse style of play, the controller plays really smoothly and is intuitve. Although, you can always rebind the keys on the keyboard to suit you. Either way, you'll find a confort zone to best play this game.
There are deep crafting systems and survival mechanics at play in PZ. You can level-up your characters over time as you adapt to the end of the world as we know it. Build a shelter (or multiple shelters). Grow your own food. Fight off hordes. Survive.
And the music and sound...freaking fantastic.
With the ever-growing modding community with full develeoper backing, this title is simply amazing. And yep, it's still in early access. Lot's of videos and blogs out there to get you started, but they also include a simple tutorial, beginner mode, and hints and tricks in-game to help you out. I'm happy to pay 20 bucks for this title, but if you can get it on sale, consider it a steal. 10/10.
