This game CAN be played multiplayer, through GameRanger or some other external service.
As for the game itself... well. Empire at War, I would say, stands as my favorite Star Wars game, since it combines an infamous franchise with a beloved genre, and their child is beautiful and healthy. That child is Empire at War.
EaW and Forces of Corruption (FoC) are both rather uniform in regards to gameplay. In EaW, you can play as the Rebels or the Empire; same goes for FoC with the addition of a third party of pirates and criminals. The basic premise of the game is in conquering the entire galaxy by force alone; to do so consists of two separate stages: a space assault with fully customizable fleets, and a ground assault on terrestrial defenses. Once both have been met with success, the planet is yours, along with whatever bonuses it provides. Another "hidden" bonus with capturing certain planets is that you can cut off hyperspace lines, or to simplify it, place roadblocks that would prevent your enemy with combining his forces, since he can't pass through planets unless they're either neutral or allied. For races, I suppose, counting Forces of Corruption; you have three different choices that have their own benefits and quirks, but can ultimately be played the same way, or however you'd want them to.
First up is the Galactic Empire (or just "the Empire"), and no different from the rest of its appearances in Star Wars, the Empire has a fetishistic love for firepower and big guns. The Empire has a VERY strong Navy and Army that deliver a serious wallop at the tradeoff of a considerable cost. Most of their best weaponry is unlocked in the fourth and fifth/final tech tiers, which gives the Rebels and the Zann Consortium plenty of time to strike at leisure.
The Rebel Alliance (or just "the Rebels") don't match the Empire in terms of raw strength, and their tech tier development is dependent on that of the Empire, but what the Rebels offer in exchange is more flexibility and diversity. For example, the Empire's Star Destroyers have automated hangars that automatically deploy TIE fighters/bombers as the battle goes on (unless the hangar is destroyed), but their shield generators are exposed to enemy fire. The Rebels' cruisers have internal shield generators that can't be destroyed (but the shield can still be knocked out), but no hangars - to compensate, you can specifically build whatever bombers and fighters you need, and how many you need; also, you can deploy them whenever and wherever you'd like, as opposed to the Imperials, where you're caught in a waiting game for what could potentially be what you are or are not in need of.
Added in the expansion, the Zann Consortium is what I can only describe as "parasitic", in that the bulk of their strength comes from that of their enemies; allow me to explain. The Zann Consortium has a tech tier that, for the most part, is based on stealing technologies and credits from the Empire and the Rebels, and in certain cases can actually acquire units from those two factions. One of my favorite features of the Zann Consortium is their ability to enslave races on certain planets, meaning you can get Ewok suicide bomber units, where a guy with a whip forces Ewoks out of a burlap sack and they charge at an enemy with a bomb strapped to them. It's extremely easy to play as the Zann Consortium, and they are brutally overpowered (their method of destroying the Death Star whenever it shows up is what can only be described as "cheap and effortless"), though it does take a bit of a learning curve.
As far as game modes go; both Empire at War and Forces of Corruption share the same modes, of a singleplayer campaign; a single-or-multiplayer Galactic Conquest mode which is the main course of this excellent game; or basic "skirmish" battles that can take place on land or in space, and better units are issued as time goes on. Empire at War contains singleplayer campaigns for the Empire and the Rebels; Forces of Corruption only contains a campaign for the Zann Consortium.
Empire at War caught my attention before I even knew of its existence, and I bought it as soon as I saw it. It was a perfect buy, and it was in the will of the Force.

In simple, The Shock game for the simple modern man.
I have played through this game about 3 times now on Easy, Medium, and Hard on my original disc version when it first came out. I got my steam copy through a promotional deal for Bioshock Infinite.
While not as mechanically deep as System Shock 2; Bioshock holds strong to the core of what tonally makes a "Shock" game. Right from the get go you are flung unknowingly into hostile territory with the only semblance of a friend being a voice on the other side of a radio giving you directions to try and remedy your situation.
Its dark, its scary, and its tense.
On harder difficulties you will need to be aware of your surroundings and scrounge for resources constantly to keep yourself ahead of the game.
There isn't much in the way of creating a "build" as there is in System Shock 2, but in a way, from how you spend your weapon upgrades and ADAM for plasmids and tonics, you can mold your own game experience to your preference.
The story of the game (for the main plot), is probably one of my favorite parts about the game, but the reason as to why is a gigantic spoiler.
The only real downfall of the game is the choices you make with the little sisters; its pretty much more beneficial to the player to spare them for the bonuses you gain later on at regular intervals over the course of the game. (Namely one of them being an exclusive plasmid that, to my knowledge, you can only get by sparing little sisters)

Can I recommend Sir, You are Being Hunted?
The answer, in it's current state, is no.
While the game has a lot of potential, it doesn't seem to know what it wants to do. The art style is dark and gloomy and there's some suspense to be had in hiding, but it also tries to be funny which takes any of the suspense that was there away. Don't get me wrong, I applaud the devlopers for trying to be unique, but it isn't very well executed.
The game is focused on replayability and when you are generating the world, you can choose the biome types of the five islands. However, there's really no difference in each of these biomes and they're merely for looks(No new threats per island). There's really nothing new or any reason to replay the game.
Also, for a game that cites itself as survival, I've found it harder to die than to live. Food is relativly easy to find and you likely won't starve and the robot who are supposed to be hunting you seem to clump up at the shards you're supposed to be getting, so you can pretty much run everywhere without worrying about being spotted.
I would love to be able to recommend this game, and I understand it's still in development, but I simply can't.

You have many different gamemodes and a lot of characters with a lot of unlocks that emphasise replayability. Matches normally wont be linear, they'll vary a lot aswell which is also a good bonus to this game.
The game itself however needs to be approached carefully.
If you're interested in the hunters's end I recommend you play this with friends or play this with premade players. Hunters rely on good communication and teamwork to make their games even more fun.
If you seek out to play as the monster. My advice to you would be to get used to them vs AI or friends.
For pvping it is kind of mandatory to have good perks and some character masteries if you want to have fair matches.
In-depth description/info/summary
The game modes:
Hunt, is currently the most played one (competitively at least). This mode is pretty straightforward Monster tries to survive the hunt until he becomes strong enough (by feasting on corpses and evolving) to become the hunter and kill the hunters. At stage 3 you also have a 3rd objective which makes the game mode a bit more intense.  There's also a limited time that forces the match to be somewhat fast paced.
This mode is pretty balanced, depending on the map, some maps are better for hunters some are better for the monster.
Nest, the hunters have to kill the eggs or the alpha monster (the player) before the timer runs out the monster has to keep at least one egg or minion alive or kill the hunters.
This mode usually favors the monster despite putting some pressure on the monsterplayer.
Rescue, The survivors have to evacuate 5 survivors, the monster has to kill 5 of them. First party to do so or to kill the other party wins.
This mode is rather equal through it can heavily favor the hunters.
Defend: The monster has to kill 2 generators and a fueltank to win. The hunters have to defend until the timer runs out. There are 2 stage 1 goliaths that spawn at a fix interval for the monster to relieve pressure.
--
You have singleplayer, multiplayer co-op and multiplayer pvp.
You can create custom games with your own rules and play Evacuation
Evacuation is a 5 day campaign where all players vote for the next mode out of 2 random generated modes, first mode beeing Hunt. Last mission beeing defend. Every time a party wins the other party will become stronger (get more hitpoints and higher damage output). This one is the best for farming experience because you get a huge bonus to your experience at the end of a campaign depending on how well your party performed during that campaign.

The last patch for this title, as of this writing, was 0.5.2, so things may have changed as you read this review.
Even if things have changed however, this is still a very solid recommendation. I had this game on my wishlist from the first time I saw it, and struggled with whether to get it or not as I have been burned by other Early Access titles before. But this game blends several genres together beautifully; roguelike (or roguelite, depending on how picky you are at naming it) along with tower defense and turned based role-playing.
The story is pretty barebones at this point; you're on a prison ship, and it gets shut down and overrun by monsters, and thus you have to escape. For some reason that isn't explained, you need to take a crystal (presumably a power source?) with you. The crystal serves as your "base" hit points, along with a power source and currency. You start with two heroes out of three to start with, and as you progress you can unlock additional heroes by means of first finding them at random and surviving three straight floors with them in your party.
Each 'turn' is the opening of a door. In between you can build modules to provide one of three resources (food, science, industry) or specific modules to attack incoming enemies, increase attack power, defense, or even debuff enemies. This is where the tower defense element comes in because you have to manage the resources you have to make sure the crystal is properly defended, and your resources aren't unlimited. Once you run out of rooms to open on the current floor, you're out of resources.
The roleplaying elements come from finding equippable items, and using your food resource to level your heroes. Combat isn't involved, as your hero and the enemies take turns swinging, and while you can heal them mid-battle with food, that's about as involved as the combat gets.
The roguelike/roguelite elements come from the fact that each floor is randomly generated, so you don't know what enemies you'll find, where the exit is, where any additional heroes are (f any), etc. Also the fact if you lose, that's it. If you meet the criteria to unlock a hero they will be available upon starting a new game but that's it. I should also point out that the only thing that carries over between levels of the dungeon is the hero's equipment and levels.
It sounds complicated, but it's easy to figure out after spending some time with it. The music and sound is fitting, not really exceptional, but the graphics are very pleasing to the eye. But in this case it's the gameplay that sells the same. It's very good right now and should only get better from this point.

Been playing this game off and on for well over a year.
I've seen MANY updates, mostly good.
The Devs really do care about the game, as it's updated at least once a month (with a running timer on the start menu of the game), if not more, with hotfixes if need-be.
It's got a story to it (still a bit developing but I feel mostly complete) that is satisfactory; but you can completely ignore it if you want, which a lot of people do.
There is a single player mode, and a multi-player mode. Of which you can invite either Steam friends only or open it up to the public (with larger servers based on how well your computer runs lol).
There are also different degrees of difficulty; peaceful (mobs don't hurt you), normal, hard, and survival (very difficult with food/water/damage penalties). Once you complete the story mode of the game you can unlock creative.
It is a bit on the scary side, but not in the realm of horror game. It keeps the game pace up as you search for building items and food and work on the story line.
My only major complaint currently is the building system. Although you can build a lot of different things, it's pretty creative in that aspect, some of the placing is wonky. It gives you a ghost of the item about to be placed but it's at a set distance from you, and you can't move your head/view by itself. So you end up placing something incorrectly or in the wrong spot a lot. Because of this someone who likes intricate disigns or for things to line up perfectly won't be too happy.
A minor complaint is the online multi-player system. You can't multi-player by yourself (say, while waiting for your friend to get online) without having the server open to at least one other person. So if someone who is on your friends list decides they want to come into your game, they can. Sure, you could kick or ban them (if they won't listen and leave), but that just seems way too mean. I'd like an option to play multi-player with an invite only option.
Over all I'd recommend this game to anyone who likes survival games. 9/10.

Short version: Game of the Year material not because you will play it for hundreds of hours, but for the combination of old school hard games like Contra and the new achievement in development to create the feel of a classic cartoon to make something unique out of all the games being released this year. Note: Do not buy if you rage too easily.
Long version: This game was worth the wait. While the animation makes it something to marvel in itself, the game has solid content that makes you want to progress to the end, if you can handle the difficulty. This is a game where you will likely die more times in a single boss fight than in most AAA games you played in the past years combined. And this on top of computer controls that you can map yourself to make it easier to fire a weapon (the only time someone will tell you this game is truly easy).
It is nice that the game allows you to explore the hubmap to choose which levels/ fights you want to do first, which is nice since the dogfight bosses are ones I hated more than the devil himself. Each boss has it's own interesting looks, soundtracks, and multi-phase stages with varying lengths.
I do have two minor negatives to this game. The first is the bugs in this game. I was facing one of the bosses, died, and it continued playing as if I had a buddy playing with me. The second is that the different "weapons" are pretty useless compared to your starting shots. The only purchased ones I used were the homing shots and the multi-shots, everything else I didn't see a point to.
But you know what? This is one of the games in a recent time where I bought a game at full price, and I felt it was worth every penny. Buy it at full price, buy it during a sale, buy it when it's on humble bundle, make a deal with the devil to get the game for free, whatever it takes, this is something that should be in your library as long as you are a patient gamer who can handle seeing the Continue? screen over and over again.

MotoGP 15 review:
Just what I wanted from a MotoGP game.
I've played a few in the past on PS3, and SBK09 on PC.
I don't know about realism and hardcore sims when it comes to MOTOGP style games.
Steering wheels work well with car games, but for a motorbike game, I'm not sure what would be 'required for realism'.
So, my expectations for 'realism' in a motorbike game aren't very high - as long as the physics seem good and it runs smooth, with decent AI, I'm happy.
That said, my Xbox controller works a treat for what it is.
I can enjoy this game with full traction control on for an 'arcadey' experience, or ramp it up a bit for a more hardcore challenge.
My first review of this game was negative (see below) because I had terrible jerking and stuttering graphics.
I'm not sure how, but I redownloaded the game and it runs smoothly now.
So now I can have fun like I used to on SBK09, but with a more up to date game.
So it's all good.

Empire at War is not your typical strategy game and definatley not your typical 4X sins of a solar empire/ star ruler etc brand of space strategy either. And despite that Empire at war really isnt anything special even back when it cam out  over a decade ago EAW Was not that innovative or edgy, or even orgional..this game uses a tried and true method that the total war series took up and perfected upon, Like total war it Empire at war sports a simple enough turn-based campaign map along with an equally simple easy to use Real-time battle map.
Now, even with all that Empire at war is unique for that fact that you can not really find anything equivalent that does not require hours upon hours upon hours to complete Or is so superficaly put together or badly designed that enjoyment tends to be losst after a meere few hours of play.
Empire at war is a rather thin game without all that much depth..or width but whats contained within the admitedly narrow scope of this game makes up  for it all tenfold.
Personally i have rarely seen such a well put together bug free game with amazingly designed graphics that can still hold relevance today ((although that point is probably more opinion based, still point dersrves to be made)) along with the fact that this games devs put the time and effort into going over every single inch of this game making sure that pretty much everything is polished and finished. this is probably one of the most well made games you could run across..its just old.
To sum this up simply put, imagine total war rome in space minus the minor social management and diplomatic features boil it down to war and you have Empire at war.

When presented with multiple different foods while scavenging houses, I found many options. Canned vegetables, steaks, even bacon! But when I was given a dead rat in a cupboard-I got an idea! I butchered it, sliced some bread, made it into a sandwich, added pickles and lettuce, a dash of pepper, and renamed the sandwich "Mystery Meat Sandwich Surprise!". With local and online co-op now added, I can feed it to friends and/or complete strangers too!
Not only can you eat rats, but you can eat rats creatively. Eating the rat straight raw or cooked will make you unhappy but when you turn it into a sandwich, burger, or even stir fry, you'll be fine! As a matter of fact, eating Mystery Meat Sandwich Surprise made me HAPPIER because of the toppings! Oh, and you can customize your sandbox to not have zombies. Great fun for everyone! (But not for vegetarians. Steer clear, vegetarians.)
TLDR: Turned a dead rat into a sandwich with pickles and lettuce and didn't lose happiness eating it.
EDIT: Turns out you can also turn a rat into a rat pie, rat salad, rat stew, rat soup, or rat vegetable roast. All you need to do is grab a kitchen/hunting knife and Butcher Small Animal in the Cooking section of the crafting menu.

Almost exactly one year ago I wrote a review of this game praising it for its uniqueness and realism. I then stopped playing for a long time. About 3 days ago I came back and have been playing non stop but I have found a lot of issues I never noticed a year ago. Today I come back with an updated review. I'm not gonna dive into what the game is about, I know you can figure that out for yourself. So instead what im going to do is dive right into the pros an cons about this game.
Pros: 8
>Great artstyle and atmosphere.
>Hardcore and challenging. (Especially on Interloper difficulty).
>Fairly realistic. (More than most others of the genre).
>Extremely unique. *This game takes its own path and doesn't try to clone other games*.
>Lots to explore and many Items.
>Skills and journal logs.
>Lots of in depth aspects such as hunting, fishing, repairing, crafting, curing, cooking, smithing, looting, researching, and more.
>Extreme Weather.
Cons: 10
>You get hungry, tired, and thirsty way too fast. Unrealistically fast.
>Food and Items decay too fast. A jar of peanut butter spoils in like a week. Seriously? And axes go dull way too fast. I used to split wood for work. We sharpened our mauls maybe once every 3 months. And the sharpening stones lose 5% each use. Like really? Those things last years. And just a lot of other items in general have the same problem.
>Wolves KOS. And there are SO many of them. IRL you would never even see them. I'm not saying to get rid of them. But maybe slim their population down to about 1/3 and make it a much less chance they agro on you. Right now if they spot you they will attack you no matter what unless you can counter them. maybe make it so its a 50% chance they will run away upon seeing you.
>You walk way too slow and you lose stamina from sprinting way too fast. Even with an empty backpack. Your character must weigh 400 pounds.
>Starting fires is bullsh*t. It would either be impossible to do in your location/situation IRL and you can still do it somehow. Or you fail to light a fire in a pot belly stove with an 80% chance 4 times in a row. There is no in between.
>Story mode STILL has not been finished. They have had nearly 3 years to work on it.
>Boring challenges. But at least they are there to be considered as "extra content".
>You can't wear multiple layers of the same clothing. Super unrealistic and if it was in the game it would be very helpful.
>You can't break down stuff without tools. Really? If I was freezing I would just throw the whole thing on the fire if I couldn't break anything down for wood.
>Rifle mechanics. The rifle mechanics in the game are just really bad. Bullets don't go where you're aiming and you have to wait 2 seconds to fire again after loading another round into the chamber making rapid fire impossible. Which can mean the difference between life and death against bears. Just really clunky all together.
Anyways. It may seem that I hate this game from all the negatives but I really do love this game a lot and it has come a long way since 2015 even though it may not have been as much as we had hoped. I do still recommend this game and if they ever fix the issues above it will be the best survival game on the market. Not that it isn't already.
Quick note. I have a lot more playtime than my hours say on Steam. I had a non Steam copy long before.
My overall score: 8.5/10

Having played games in the real world such as paintball and having hunted wild boars with a double barrelled shotgun, this game gravely recreates the stress, adrenaline and aesthetics of those experiences. The stealth is insanely realistic and you are forced to stay hidden in shadows, vegetation and below topographical features. The sound of a robot is distressing and you need to turn on your hyper perception to see and hear them before they see you. Sometimes, a gun fight is unavoidable, the best cover with fast thinking and reactions are needed when a robot lifts his gun in your direction. Stressful decisions must be made all the time; fight or flight, stealth or rush, stop bleeding or keep running, rush or stealth. There are many different types of robots after you and jump scares should be expected frequently. On top of the action and stealth, there is breathe taking scenery, 5 very different biomes and the world is always changing weather and time of day.
I personally find this game hard to play due to all the stress it gives me but it's certainly rewarding. I have yet to play this game properly due to lost progress in previous updates. The developers have not added more content in a long time due to some networking issues of a multiplayer update. They are planning to release the multiplayer update early next year and I'm highly anticipating coop with friends. As a result, the game is still a bit barren like a beta but it should get more content and details in the future. Even though a great deal of improvement of a great game can be expected in the future give some thought about getting this game now to support the great indie developers.

In this game the cold, starvation and predatory animals are your enemies. That means you have to find shelter, food and clothing. You have to find things to make a fire so you´re able to cook the rabbit you caught or heat up a can of tomato soup you found. You can skin animals to make new pieces of clothing so you will have better protection against the wind, snow and animal attacks. And of course a wolf coat is just simply warmer than and an old ragged shirt.

WHat is there to say about DotE?
Its good.! Its a Roguelike, its a Tower Defense, It uses Exploration as a limited resource. Only other game I have seen pulling this of was desktop dungeons, and that was allways a tense fight there.
The graphics - Lovely. Its all Pixel graphics, but they still look so Good. I mean, It is Pixels, but then again they actually look like something other than blocks.
Gameplay : It takes a little getting used to, but a lot can be found out in a few sessions of trial and error. still think this needs a Tutorial and/or First Time Tutorial floor, but you can only deliver what you have and since not all systems are 100% done and are subject to change, building an extensive tutorial wuld be a bit in vain. But the system at all is simple
you build stuff, you open a door, you see whats inside - Monsters, Relics, Survivors, Loot - and you gain resources from your built stuff
I also love how they got an EXP-less Levelling system. Thats what one of the resources is for. You give them enough food, and they Level up. But the limited building space, the limited Dust to activate rooms to build stuff in them and the fact that you have 3 resources you have to take care of make this game a really hot decision sometimes.
Sound - The music is Gorgeous. Need I say more? I love me some good music in games
Overall - for an early access game it is quite good and delivers a lot of content already. a good bunch of loveable heroes, a hard make-you-thing management system and most of all, tons of Rougelike Try againsy fun, since the game may end up playing the "Diablo 2 Wheel of Skills" with you and your building/resource decision
(To explain the reference, Diablo 2 was a Clicky RPG with a multitude of classes and different skills. However, most builds that bring you through the game just fall short at the final boss. Means you could breeze through the game with a necromancer summoning skelettons wreaking havoc, but on the final boss they will be killed of way before they reach him. Not to forget that he one hits you as average necromancer.
That boss was the "Is your Skillset viable?" moment. And no, the only way to respec was to use a trainer/Savegame editor. If you didnt want this, its start the game from scratch )

In depth review, do notice that large parts of this review are sarcastic because I can't take this serious:
- Graphics: Cheap, sure the engine is great, but there are no textures except white and grey. Character design is really very well done; people have no faces, no clothes, and if I remember correct, not even fingers. Best graphics ever?! I think so! This is how every game should be, just imagine it: running in white wilderniss, through white-tiled rooms, who needs textures when you can have 50 shades of grey? This game runs at a solid 60+ fps, simply because there's nothing to load for my graphics card. Why do Modding communities even try to revamp textures, when you can have the vanilla-est of the vanilla, and not even like real vanilla pudding, but the whitest of whites?! Yeah, why vanilla when you can get milk with vanilla extract!
- Story: So much background, so much depth, I've never seen anything like it. Spoiler alert! You're a hacker, hacking away in a command prompt together with some other hacker dude. The story has so much development, I really feel connected to the main character. You see emotions develop, betrayal, a story of lost love and returning to your roots only to find yourself. Wow! This game taught me a lot about myself. The story keeps you locked to your computer for at least a whopping 2,5 hours. And if that's not enough, there's always some extra content to be found. Or isn't it?
- Concept: Who doesn't want to be a hacker in an open world, hacking away to save your fellow citizens, trying to beat the systematic suppression and influencing of people through big data and AI systems.. Oh wait, that was Watch Dogs.. Right.. This game doesn't have any of that. It's more of a proof of concept for a new Max Payne mini-game. But this time, it's nothing more than a proof of concept; there are no textures, remember? You're a hacker, hacking by just playing a FPS game. How does that even work? Do firewalls actually work that way?! I never knew!
- Gameplay: Like any FPS game, but with slo-mo. So, like Max Payne, but this time it's so different! Wow! There's so much stuff I havent seen before in other games that this game really deserves all the awards. This game is so ground breaking, because it has all the things from other mini-games-inside-games, combined. Except for a long, good story, textures, well designed models, good music, character development, a likeable main character, and everything I usually like about games. But back to gameplay: you just have to walk around, pick up things, and shoot people, it's a FPS, what else is there to say about it?
- Overall: I can't understand why people love this game so much, and why they are willing to defend it to the death. The game isn't bad, but it's too short, it's a fun gimmick and nothing more. There's no story, there are no textures, even the characters that do move don't move in a natural fashion. Steam recommended me this game, I watched the trailer and decided to buy it. I don't like watching gameplay but I should have done that. That's my bad. However, the reviews say this game is outstanding, which convinced me to actually click 'confirm'. Thanks for going along with the hype. I'll never trust you again, Steam community.

I haven't played previous MotoGP titles. So, I am highly impressed and recommend this game "IF" you like to play in first person view with no riding aids. There are always room for improvements, specially on the visual quality. But despite all the critisism Milestone developers get, they are indeed the masters of simulating motorcycle racing successfully. As they are the handful of guys creating such games, I am thankful to that :)
PROS-
- Handling is near perfect and refined. Physics feels really good as you progress from lower classes to higher ones. Handling is challanging but still fun.
- Visually not that demanding and looks decent at fluid 60fps.
- The game has high replay value. I find mastering corners and improving time in time attack mode quite satisfying. After nearly 80hrs, I am still about to start in moto2 from moto3 in career mode on simulation difficulty.
- AI is quite good and competitive to play offline. Online community is quite challanging as well.
- motogp madness experience...visually :) Loved the included multimedia videos as well
CONS (so to say)-
- It feels as if the PC version is not a priority and has been ported from ps4 version. Visually it can be more refined.
- Online latency can be an issue sometimes. Also lobby rules and structure can be improved. Things like showing time left for qualifying sessions, ability to join qualifying in progress, skipping session and host transfer can be very helpful.
- Inaccurate leaderboards. Times way lower than real records takes away the sim factor :P
Both "Ride" and "motogp" are good games. I play these games with xbox controller and have my G27 eating dust since I bought these. VR might change that. So I hope Milesone are also working on next version of their games with driveclub quality graphics and VR support.

Project Zomboid is fun game that's come a long way since I first played it years ago. Each new build gets more refined and more interesting.
The game's premise is pretty depressing and pretty blunt during the loading phase of the same and ends with "...this is how you died."
To reflect that; the same is brutal in that if you don't die of starvation, third, cuts and scrapes, the cold, disease you will probably die from one bad decision in the face of several zombies. Perma death is a ♥♥♥♥♥...especially when you've spent all that time leveling up--yep you'll be regretting taking that risk after you watch your character become zombie chow.
However to counter that you get quit a huge number of parameters to change your starting world in Sandbox. You can make zombies silly weak and rare or crazy smart, fast and so numerous you probably won't leave your starting house alive. You can also tweak how far along after the zombie apacolypse starts as well as when things like electricty and water stop working. Lots of settings or just go with the defaults--it's up to you.
Character classes and traits round out the intitial setup with lots of things to help or hinder your ability to fight or flee zombies and make all kinds of stuff.
Once in game its really up to you what you want to do. Go off in the woods and live off the land? Make a fortress in the middle of town? Build your own house or fortify an existing one. Looting is a huge thing in the game. Will this house have that saw you need to make lumber? Will that daycare have that shotgun you need? (Yes, the game isn't polished enough so you'll find weird stuff in odd places. Maybe Daycare children are really dangerous in Kentucky?)
The game, at the time of this review of course isn't finished. There are bugs that might crash your game (although now that's rare) and its more about weird quirks. My favorite quirk is bottled water. You can't drink from it no matter what you do. All your character can do is pour it on the ground. Apparently people during a zombie appocolypse don't know how to drink from water bottles and drinking from toilets are all the rage. Eventually they'll fix that--or you can and the context menu for it is not obvious.
Overall the game is lots of fun; I've certainly had my money's worth of the game several times over. So if you enjoy crafting, zombie smashing with an sprinkling of survivalism (is that a word? dunno) and don't mind putting money on a not-yet-finished game then buy this one.

The game is now out of Alpha, which means the developers are considering it more or less finished. In the past I made it clear how disappointed I was with how the game was turning out, and now I'd like to step back and review the game, the developers, and the history of both in their entirety.
The game taken completely by itself, with no consideration of the developers or the Alpha development phase, I feel is a decent but flawed stealth shooter. There's some fun to be had in sneaking around in the tall grass, but nearly every other aspect of the game has something wrong with it.
Exploring is flawed in that there are far too many "dead zones" with nothing interactive in them.
Looting is flawed in that nearly all loot is gotten from largely non-interactive buildings, as enemies rarely have valuable things to offer when defeated. This is also a flaw of combat, since the lack of valuable items means there is very little reward for winning a gunfight.
Combat is also not exceptionally fun because it doesn't have much gravity. Bleeding can be cured with a single button, health regenerates, and most enemies are weak and easily evaded or defeated.
Music doesn't appear to play a large role in the game. I recall hearing an opening theme, which was interesting, but not memorable.
Graphically, the game has a lot of heart, which I appreciate, but at the same time it's got a very dated, rushed look. Most objects have bland, flat textures and barely react graphically to light. Even the guns looks like they're made of matte plastic, not wood and steel.
The rushed look is present in other elements of the game as well, such as the user interface, which lacks key features like a quick option to discard something (there's no discard button, there's no dragging the item off the inventory screen, there's no icon to drag over, just a context menu opened with M2) or the ability to stack similar items (bullets cannot be stacked once separated, be careful with your rifle ammo).
Animations look sped up and choppy, though this may be on purpose for the robots. There are no reload animations, instead the character lowers his guns offscreen and reload sounds are played.
And finally, the AI is not exceptionally good at tracking you. Even the searchlight, which can see you even when you're perfectly hidden, will forget where you are if you're near a building.
Overall, I'd say it's worth a play if you could pick it up on sale, but it's certainly not worth $20, not for this level of roughness around the edges.
Now, taking into consideration this game had an alpha stage in which quite a bit of money was raised for its complete development, and that there are multiple developers who have had years to fine-tune and polish the game, the overall image becomes considerably less positive. Instead of appearing to be due to time delays or personal problems, the lacking aspects appear to be due to developer inexperience or possibly even laziness.
It has been made clear to me that the developers are a team of ten or so people with decent but not exceptional talent in making games. It has also been made clear that funding was a large concern for them during development. However, a similarly sized team with inconsistent funding and only two experienced game designers was responsible for the creation of GoldenEye 64, which was lauded as one of the greatest first-person shooter games of all time and maintains that status even now (96 on Metacritic, compared to this game's 63). If a team with similar resources and worse technology can make something so memorable, the only thing keeping the developers of SYABH from doing the same is the developers themselves.
It's an unpleasant but well-known fact that game developers who are paid for their work ahead of time can be known to cut corners or even abandon projects at a whim. KickStarter and IndieGogo are rife with such half-finished and abandoned projects. This game, while at the very least playable and somewhat enjoyable, is certainly not finished, and definitely should not have been released from alpha in its current state.
And this doesn't even take into account the fact that many of the lacking features were requested by the community, but outright ignored by the developers during the alpha phase. One of the most requested features was interactive buildings, even something as simple as a 3d door that opened when interacted with. All of these were labeled "too difficult to implement" by the developers and ignored.
This reveals much of their mentality during development. Even during the alpha stage, they'd already decided what the scope of game would be like. Implying that the community had any say in the matter was at best misleading and at worst outright lying. Furthermore, since they already had the finshed project in mind, releasing the game from alpha stage is a sign that they consider that pre-defined scope nearly reached. The fact that they're currently working on additions that do not expand gameplay, such as bugfixes for already implemented features and controller support, seems to enforce this conclusion.
I bought this game when it was on sale during its alpha phase and followed the development for quite some time before it became apparent to me that these developers were not going to produce a finished game. It appears instead they've opted to produce the bare minimum according to their own standards and not the community's. I'll say again, this game has heart, but it just doesn't have enough life in it currently for me to recommend it
And unfortunately, it looks like it never will.

I went into this game blind. I had no idea any of the story, setting, gameplay... nothing. All I knew was that people are flipping out over how "amazing" and "perfect" this game is. Now I know never to make that mistake again.
The first moments of the game, I was pretty into it. The underwater city is pretty awesome looking and I like the art deco style it's built in. It's very unique, as I've not seen any kind of environment like Rapture before. I was creeped out by the first splicer you encounter, and I love the moment you first see a Little Sister and Big Daddy. I was looking forward to the rest of the game, but alas, my emotional attachment was later shattered and I began to feel annoyed and irrated.
The gameplay is downright awful. It's repetitive and bland. Every single time the story is advanced in some little way, or whevener you get a new plasmid, here comes a handful of splicers, yelling their insanity. At first, I was a bit on edge, but then it just became ridculous. Ugh, more enemies to fight. More annoying turrets and cameras. Moving around the levels is a chore. Dying has no penalty, it's just another annoyance. I got so freaking sick of listening to the splicers screaming and I wasn't even halfway through the game yet. (And the fact that enemies respawn made it 10x worse!) Then when you do get halfway through, the enemeis become even tougher for no reason. I ended up changing the difficulty to easy because I was not about to waste my time fighting and dying repeatedly. Any possible emotional attachement to the story was destroyed by how dreadful it was navigating and fighting through the levels. I reached a point where I couldn't wait to finish the game and uninstall it forever.
The story is ok, but it's nothing special. Altering genetics and losing humanity is an interesting subject, but I thought it took way to long to get to anything remotely interesting, and there was just a bunch of filler that was unnecessary. Go kill these random nobodies and take their picture for this mural, go save these trees that were killed for no reason other than to make the game longer. Maybe I wouldn't be so critical of this game if I hadn't gone in expecting something truely amazing, I don't know. All I know is this game is horrificly overrated and I have no desire to ever play it again or any of the sequels.
I suppose one could say I like the "concept" of this game, but the actual thing is very disappointing. If you're going to buy this game, would you kindly lower your expectations and get it on sale when it's only a couple dollars.

These are the words that you will hear all throughout your playthrough of the game. The game's not long, but it's certainly
than any game you've ever played. It's certainly not your average FPS DOOM-like game. This doesn't mean that you can't feel like an action movie hero - the game even let's you edit and upload your sick plays at the end of each level.
One of the core mechanics of the game is that time only moves when you move, which allows you to carefully think through your strategy. Yes, strategy is important, because when an enemy hits you
, you are done and have to repeat the level. Once you finish the 2-3 hour long main story, you can still put countless hours in the Endless Mode and all the 14 challenges.
SUPERHOT has very simple, minimalist art style and no music at all, just the sound of your glass-like enemies dying, guns shooting and katanas slicing.
The game is perfect with keyboard and mouse, but it's ofcourse also playable with the xbox and PS controllers and the Steam Controller.
If you have the chance to do it, buy this game in VR. Because of the more-advanced gameplay (you can crouch - which you cannot do on PC) and the nature of the story, it makes the game even better.
I also haven't noticed any bugs, glitches or FPS drops (GTX 960).
The story is complicated (at first), disturbing and even scary. Don't rush through it, though, because there are several secrets that unlock hidden features or add something to the story itself.
The story is being told through messages on the screen at the begining of levels and through a chat room, and it is often breaking the fourth wall - speaking directly to the player. It seems promising and it kinda sucks you in at first but it leaves you hanging a bit towards the end. Not that the ending is bad, I just feel like the Polish developers could have pushed it even further.

General synopsis of the game:
This game is actually surprisingly deep once you figure it out.  It tricks you into thinking its just a roguelike dungeon crawler.  And if thats how you treat it, you will not last past the first floor.  It centers around exploring each level room by room, and once you locate the exit to the level, moving your power source to the exit.  You have to place your heroes tactically (at choke points basically), and build defenses around those heroes to harden their key positions around your power source.  This usually leaves only one hero remaining to explore.  Enemies spawn in random unpowered rooms you have discovered.  So, sometimes one of your heroes may get overwhelmed, and you will have to take advantage of the handy pause feature to make sure one of that hero is not getting totally butt-r***ed.  And, if he is, then you need to figure out which hero you can send to reinforce him.  Or, you can activate one of his, unique to each hero, cooldown skills.  Which will give him a temporary boost in combat.  Or, you could order him to run away.  Fleeing is always a viable option in this game.  The in-game currency revolves around entering new rooms.  For each new door you open you get a set amount of resources and/or currency which allows you to build extra defenses, hire another hero, level up your existing heroes, research better defenses, heal your heroes in combat, power new rooms (to set up new defenses), or buy new gear for your heroes.  Once you have opened a door, you cannot close it.  So, you have to be careful not to expose a flank route to your power source by brainlessly opening doors.
Thats kind of it in a nutshell.  I obviously recommend it, even in its alpha stage.  It has not crashed once for me, and is pretty content rich.  I can't wait for the game to be content complete.

What is Ninjahtic? Ninjahtic is a fun platformer , that requires more and more skill the further you go. It also requires good space awareness. See, the game is kind of like an open world metroidvania , except you don't get new skills or stuff , you just need keycards to proceed in the different areas , some time the keycard you need will be in an area that you need a different keycard to enter , and so on. So if you , like me , play the game with long breaks (I'm talking 2 days between play sessions) you can get easily confused as to where you have already been , and where you needed to go. But that is what makes this so much fun, that is what made me feel like a kid playing on my knockoff nintendo way back. The graphics sure helped too . Well , I haven't played a game that made me stop for a moment and take notes or draw a map , in a long time. Combat is pretty fun as well , with some rooms requiring you to kill a specific enemy in a certain spot with a certain attack (you basically have 2 attacks , depending on which direction you are pressing the analogue stick in , while you are mashing X) in order for their dead body to press a pressure plate located somewhere in the room. Every now and again you will meet a boss , and on later stages even two at once , which add a whole new level of challenge , seeing how everything insta kills you and every time you die enemies respawn with full health. Oh , almost forgot to mention , different types of enemies have different HP and mostly require multiple hits to die. They also have different attacks , like , melee , lasers , and electric shock waves, which adds some tactical element to combat.

I really wanted to enjoy Cuphead. It has some of the best graphics ive ever seen in a video game, and I generally enjoy boss battles in games, but there are some problems with it that sadly ruin the expierence for me.
1. Now, I get that the entire point of the game is difficulty. And I enjoy a good challenge in games, but this is hard for all the wrong reasons. You will usually have to play a boss multiple times, not because of a mistake you made, but because the RNG decided to spawn in bullets in a way thats impossible to avoid, or the boss using an attack you never saw before, killing you before you know what to do. However, the game still sometimes has a fair challenge based on your skill
2. I hate how much this game is based on luck. Take Baroness Von Bon Bon for example, there is 4 phases to her fight, the 4th and final phase is against her, and the first 3 are against 3 of 5 randomly selected enemies. A few were easy to avoid, and then there was some that felt almost impossible to not lose health against. The entire boss felt like praying the game decides to give you the easier ones and not the hard ones.
3. I hated how repetitive and how relient on trial and error the bosses were. The game felt like I was going: Start Boss. Get hit by attack multiple times. Die. Restart boss. Repeat. This quickly becomes unfun and just frustrating and annoying
4. My final complaint is about the platforming challenges. Obviously the bosses were the main focus and I get these challenges were a last minute addition, but I still want to talk about them. These were never as fun as the boss fights and often relied too much on cheap tricks, even moreso than the bosses themselves. For example, in the tree level in world 1, there are bugs with leaves on them, your first reaction would be to use them as a platform, right? Well, you have no way to know the second you jump on them that they are destroyed unless you watched a video on youtube or already died from it.
Now, if you only care about visuals in a game, like cheap and repetitive challenges, or dont care about doing the same thing in a game the entire time, this game would be amazing. However, I dont feel like they put enough time into making the game fun, and spent most of the time on the amazing visuals.

Over all review:
Oh my god! Its wall jump, screen based tomb raider!
Lol, seriously, its not tomb raider, but if you squint and try to forget that the game description calls "ninja" a guy, you could convince yourself that you're playing a tomb raider de-make. and I'm not even being disingenuous; before I read the description, i seriously thought that the main character was a woman, with the tomb raider comparisons, metroidvania ish gameplay, and character with long flowy hair.
Just to recap, we've had ronin, dag, imp/fiend and now some guy who literally goes by the name "ninja", and ninja is an archaeologist, with there being so much cross over in the world of feudal wars and ancient grave robbery. The story starts out in some ancient Mayan refuge that's been taken over by red robots and security drones, and your job is to get some treasures from the site. But after venturing around, you'll find that the treasures are actually keys for opening locked doors, and then the key hunting puzzles are on.
The metroidvania elements make a return, but ninja isn't ronin or impfiend by any means. There's no double jumps or air dashing in this game, instead the jumping is like mario meets later megaman. So theres wall jump and slide, but you can jump higher and faster if you're moving faster.
The game is still solid, and i like the art style of this one.. its another screen based wall jump platformer, but its trying to be more action adventure than wall glider simulator. Once again it is impressive, if frustrating, but i have 3 Major gripes about the game, none of which are game breaking, but something the developer might want to keep in mind at any rate.
(1) DO NOT PUT TWO SCREENS IN THE SAME AREA THAT ARE NEARLY IDENTICAL!!! Identical screens/areas back to back can be used in horror games to instill a feeling of fear or confusion (and later on,the similar room area can be used as a point of navigation). and a series of repeated screens from a long forgotten part of the game can be used to bring the character back and hint that your character is going back in order to discover some secret. BUT IN THIS GAME near the end of the last level, i kept getting turned around because 2 of the "forks in the road" looked incredibly similar, and since i had completed both dead ends on one fork, i was now neglecting the other.
Once again there's no map, but the game locks you out of completed areas  and levels aren't a confusing mish mash like they were in "... pixelated fist", so it doesn't really need one, it just requires the player to think, which is actually a welcome change of pace, as long as trick identical screens dont turn you around
(2)KEY CARD FRACTALLING IS ANNOYING! I'm grateful that this is mostly left up to near the end game, once,  but making a HUGE journey through the level to get other keys just so you can get another key to the main puzzle is really easy to get wrong. Done right it can feel like a quest within a quest, or a stand out in the adventure. here there's really nothing telling you that this is what you're doing and it FEELS long and arduous to do so (EVEN IF ITS NOT). SO by the end of the pathway that i was following it feels like a slap in the face as my reward is a key card to another door that gives me... a key card. either make the fractal journey a test of the some new skill that we HAVEN'T BEEN USING or make it feel special to the player in some other way like a new means of getting around or the reward can be a fun freebee level or SOMETHING. The way it's done here feels like i was just getting key cards for one other key card. AND I'M NOT TALKING ABOUT THE MID GAME WHERE THE PUZZLE IS FINDING WHAT DOOR TO GO THROUGH FIRST, that specific section is well done and its just the right length accounting for distance and "key card layers". And the night level, getting the card FOR THE DAY SECTION is in itself a good example of this, so why fractal within the night level to get keys for keys sake? ITS ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥!
(3) DON'T CHANGE THE RULES OF THE GAME FOR THE FINAL BOSS FIGHT. the final boss can only be attacked for .5 seconds right after it attacks, and for the FIRST TIME IN THE ENTIRE GAME: GOOMBA STOMPING IT DOES 0 DAMAGE. through the game, your opponents don't have a rhythm of attack and counter, and head stomping always works. So getting used to this for a very hard to get to level was its own pain in the neck.
I would like to suggest a final cut scene where ninja is going back home with the alien tech, given the nature of the subsequent games.
Still is it good, yes, it is. but i cant help but feel that blaze epic is falling into bad habits. If all of his games had been one form or another of the first samurai jazz; that is, a top down hack and slash game like a cross between the legend of Zelda and kingsfield, i'd have been worried then too. I'm begging to think that blaze is losing faith in his ability to design new games, not only from the atmosphere of each game fluctuating between feeling immersive and feeling like a pretty background picture but seriously some of the platforming tropes and puzzles are starting to feel very familiar... and as I've played all 3 ninjahtic games already, i can say (with certainty) that feeling isn't going to go away.

If you are buying this game looking to complete the hardest challenges, and to try to perfect every boss, turn away now. As good as the game might appear visually, the design is so lacking that it turns what should be a fun and hard-as-nails platformer into an unfair slog. Let me explain. To perfect a boss, you need to a) beat it in under 2 minutes, b) parry 3 things (which means pressing a button right before getting hit by specific pink objects), c) not get hit, and d) use your special move 6 times. You also have to do these three things in the same run. Here is the issue with this.
Most bosses only produce parry-able objects during certain stages of their fight. This means that you often has to do less damage deliberately just to wait for the RNG gods to bless you with those pink objects, which in turn means that even if you'd normally be able to beat the boss under two minutes easy, this becomes more of a challenge as you spend precious seconds just waiting for the boss to give you stuff to parry.
There is also problems with the special move requirement. In a certain stage, even if you use 6 specials, it won't count unless you used them in a specific spot during the fight. Again imposing random (and unforeseeable) constraints that don't test skill, but luck and how good you are at finangling a boss to do certain things at certain times.
It's truly a shame. Some of the bosses are excellent, and if not for these silly constraints necessary to do well on a boss, it would be a gem of a game. As it is, this game spits in the face of people who want to do well in it, and after 30 hours and reaching the end of the last world...I'm done. I'm not gonna put up with this abhorrent design mess anymore. Maybe a patch can fix the special move problem, but the way they implement the parry system in the ranking requirements are just...game-ruining for me.
This isn't something that is going to affect everyone, but please, don't buy this game looking for a fair challenge. It's not.

Really wanted to like this game. Around 50% of deaths felt like they were the fault of loose or inconsistent controls. Many puzzles just required annoyingly perfect timing instead of dexterity or creative problem solving. The game slows down and gets worse as it goes on. The brain worm things take a game with already crap controls and make things even more frustrating. Your reward for getting through several of these annoying sections is more tedious block-pushing. I think I might uninstall this "short" game without ever finishing it, and go play something fun instead.

The good:
-Survival experience focused on actual survival, instead of fighting off hordes of zombies/cannibals/hounds/whatever while you craft things for a base. There is some fighting(against wild animals) and crafting(survival objects), but it's more realistic and never overshadows the need to manage food/water/temperature.
-Gorgeous graphics. It refreshing to have an actual art style instead of the all-too-common hyperrealism(which has its place, but is a bit overdone). That's not to say this game is unrealistic, but everything has a painterly feel instead of a photographic feel.
-Has some of the best early-access devs I've seen. Regular updates(complete with a roadmap of what players can expect in the future), ability to say 'no' to the fanbase(meaning TLD has stayed a coherent product), and prompt bugfixes(usually - more about that later). They set realistic expectations for the game, instead of overpromising and underdelivering.
-Currently has 5 maps to explore, all connected by transition zones. Completely exploring everything will take quite a while, even for a well-prepared player. Each map has different benefits and challenges to keep things interesting - one might have good weather and supplies but lots of wolves, another will have terrible weather and little shelter, but easily avoided wolves.
-Has a range of difficulty levels, ranging from the relatively casual(animals won't attack unless you attack first, abundant supplies) to the hardcore(few items, small starting inventory, extra-dangerous wildlife). Unfortunately there's currently no way to fine-tune difficulty so you could, say, have minimal resources but normal wildlife.
-They've recently added challenges, which give you a goal to work towards under specific conditions. Good if you're getting bored of the regular sandbox.
-Teaches you the correct way to pronounce "touque".
The neutral:
-There's zero hand-holding. Figuring out how to survive is entirely up to you. Whether or not this is a good thing depends on the player(I personally like it).
-Many objects decay, but which decay fastest can be counterintuitive. For instance, canned food slightly degrades faster than other prepackaged foods you scavenge. And clothing decays simply from existing, although it's much slower than the decay from wearing it. In both cases it's minor enough not to matter unless you're going for a very long survival streak, but people doing that transition to hunting their own food and crafting their own clothes anyway.
-A few odd mechanics in the name of game balance. You can't tear up a cardboard box for tinder while it's dark, many things that should be flammable can't be broken down for fuel, you can't chop down trees for wood, etc.
The bad:
-There's always going to be a 'best' strategy in any survival game, but the best strategy here is pretty silly and overpowered - starve yourself all day, then eat enough to regain whatever health you lost while you sleep. Consuming a fraction of the food you're (presumably) intended to eat with no long-term consequences is just a little unbalanced and counterintuitive.
-For the past month or so, there's been a common bug where objects(especially trees) will rapidly flicker, which is incredibly distracting and can even crash the game if it gets bad enough. It can be 'solved' by forcing DX9 in the launch options, but then you get neon pink trees.

I went into this game blind. I had no idea any of the story, setting, gameplay... nothing. All I knew was that people are flipping out over how "amazing" and "perfect" this game is. Now I know never to make that mistake again.
The first moments of the game, I was pretty into it. The underwater city is pretty awesome looking and I like the art deco style it's built in. It's very unique, as I've not seen any kind of environment like Rapture before. I was creeped out by the first splicer you encounter, and I love the moment you first see a Little Sister and Big Daddy. I was looking forward to the rest of the game, but alas, my emotional attachment was later shattered and I began to feel annoyed and irrated.
The gameplay is downright awful. It's repetitive and bland. Every single time the story is advanced in some little way, or whevener you get a new plasmid, here comes a handful of splicers, yelling their insanity. At first, I was a bit on edge, but then it just became ridculous. Ugh, more enemies to fight. More annoying turrets and cameras. Moving around the levels is a chore. Dying has no penalty, it's just another annoyance. I got so freaking sick of listening to the splicers screaming and I wasn't even halfway through the game yet. (And the fact that enemies respawn made it 10x worse!) Then when you do get halfway through, the enemeis become even tougher for no reason. I ended up changing the difficulty to easy because I was not about to waste my time fighting and dying repeatedly. Any possible emotional attachement to the story was destroyed by how dreadful it was navigating and fighting through the levels. I reached a point where I couldn't wait to finish the game and uninstall it forever.
The story is ok, but it's nothing special. Altering genetics and losing humanity is an interesting subject, but I thought it took way to long to get to anything remotely interesting, and there was just a bunch of filler that was unnecessary. Go kill these random nobodies and take their picture for this mural, go save these trees that were killed for no reason other than to make the game longer. Maybe I wouldn't be so critical of this game if I hadn't gone in expecting something truely amazing, I don't know. All I know is this game is horrificly overrated and I have no desire to ever play it again or any of the sequels.
I suppose one could say I like the "concept" of this game, but the actual thing is very disappointing. If you're going to buy this game, would you kindly lower your expectations and get it on sale when it's only a couple dollars.

I purchased this on sale for a little over a dollar. I figured I found a cheap game that would provide me with some hours of fun. Unfortunately, I was wrong. This game wasn't worth the $1 I paid. It most certainly isn't worth the $5 is usually priced at.
Let's roll over the most glaring of negatives here:
- The A.I. is the worst I have experienced in any game. There are games that came out 20 years ago that have better A.I. The enemies are designed to run a set path, every time. They will spawn in the same exact spot, beyond the horizon of which you cannot approach without dying, and will run the same route. If you put yourself smack in the middle of their warpath, they will walk past you to continue on their merry way.
-Many shooters already suffer from a boring plight of uniformity in gameplay. This indie game commits this crime and takes it step further. Each mission has small variations, but you can expect the exact same experience every time. Enemies spawn from afar, you kill them with some headshots, you wait for the next wave. I have more fun chopping wood. Seriously.
-There are a variety of weapons, but only a few that are actually usable. Some accomplish the same thing a more "powerful" and expensive weapons does, but with higher ammo reserves and less hassle. Do you love shotguns? Me too, but you won't want to use the one in this game as it does next to nothing without being obscenely close to the enemy, all the while being chewed up by the enemy you are approaching. There are very few CQC encounters in this game, making this weapon, and others, useless.
The two positive things I have to say about this game:
+It has low hardware requirements. I purchased this to play on my toaster of a laptop. Ran well with only a couple snags.
+There is one level where a giant chicken will fall gracelessly out of the sky when you murder all the regular chickens. Among these regular chickens, there a couple doing the dirty deed. At least, it appears that way. The giant chicken shoots eggs out of its♥♥♥♥♥and has twin gatling guns under each wing. This is fun the first time, but will quickly get old.

Gameplay is very fun when you have a competent team, but that's the problem.  The matchmaking is absolutely awful.  I'm not talking 'my team is bad' awful, I'm talking, 'it's 2 hunters + 2 AI vs the monster for the last 2 matches and everyone is bored but every game I join is the same' awful.  If I play during 'prime time' I am more likely to have fun, but that is a load of♥♥♥♥♥♥for a 60$ game.  Not to mention the servers crap out about 10% of the games I play.  Tonight I spent the last 50 minutes trying to get 1 last game in.  The first game I joined and it was right at the end of the game, we lost.  It was me and another hunter vs the monster.  No one joined all lobby.  I left at the lobby load, waited my minute, and joined another game.  It put me in the SAME game in progress.  The monster realized no one was joining and just trolled us with 2 strikes, looking at the last hunter alive and dancing until the dropship came, then did it again.  We had to kill ourselves by wildlife.  I guess you could make the argument that that sort of gameplay is 'innovative', and it damn well is when there is nothing in the game discouraging it.  Why not simply grief your opponents for 20 minutes when there is no way to report people who are purposefully trying to ruin the game?  Not tonight, but last week I had a game where our medic was mad and continually ran away from the group to die to wildlife, rinse repeat.  He wouldn't leave the game and was intent on ruining it for everyone.  WHY IS THERE NO VOTE KICK SYSTEM?
Triple A my♥♥♥♥♥ I really wanted to be able to recommend this game because I want my friends to buy it, because it would be fun to play it with them.  But I can't recommend people to buy this game and support this sort of design when the product is ultimately not finished.  The environments are beautiful and everything feels smooth/natural, but that doesn't justify a 60$ gametag.  It's just a nice shiny polish to a broken foundation.  It really pains me to write this because when I play with 5 friends I have a ton of fun for hours, but the community is already (3 weeks in) so small that it's literally not possible to play with anyone else.  I can't recommend someone spend 60 dollars to participate in this, especially when the only way people can have fun is with a balanced game.  The only way you can balance a game this ambitious is with a giant playerbase, and time.  I thought they  had the right approach with the open alpha and beta time, but it's not nearly done.  And the fact that everyone is no longer playing proves that.  If you don't have a lazarus, you lose.  If you don't have a good hank, you probably lose.  It took me 5 hours of gameplay (I hadn't even unlocked lazarus yet) to realize that, how did it go over the developers heads?  What's more likely is that they realized it, and didn't care, because the average consumer just likes shiny, not balanced.. Hearthstone is a shiny and polished product with a solid BALANCED foundation that is making money hand over fist because they didn't try to release something too ambitious, before it was 100% done.  Those tiny errors, like my mouse not showing up in the menu or falling through the floor in a game, cause one more person to quit forever each time it happens.  I can guarantee you that.  Imagine if you released the game for 20 dollars and actually did some creative DLC, huh?  Pay 5 bucks and you get to unlock an interface and design the colors and pattern on your trappers dome.  How about 4 hunter classes period (since 2 of them are already forced to be lazarus and hank) and then you can customize your 4 personal hunters with cosmetic items you purchase if you want, but that drop randomly?  You already don't have a campaign in the game, I guess you could say we're missing out on the 'personality' of the hunters you made but by not including a story in your game it's obvious you don't actually give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about their personalities either.  You could have done this soooooo welllll.....
Hopefully they patch everything (don't get me started on the broken wraith) and drop the game to 20$ in a big sale event so the community isn't completely ruined.  But seeing as how we're talking about the same studio that allowed this to happen in the first place, I wouldn't hold your breath.

At its most base level, this four-vs-one co-op shooter acts as a hunting sim. Either you and three chums/AI bots form a crack hit squad looking to kill the other player's monster, or you take control of a beastie that makes the thing out of Cloverfield look utterly dreamy. Its chief objectives? Survive and gorge... oh, and make basically every other species on the planet Shear extinct. Survival of the fattest, baby.When you play as a Hunter its your job to track, trap and ultimately settle your differences with the monster through a combination of reasoned discourse and biscuits. No wait... through brutal electrocution and air strikes.
I always get those mixed up. As the monster, you must first simply eat any local wildlife in sight; the ultimate goal to evolve into your most powerful, 'level three' form, thereby either wiping out your puny human foes or destroying a power relay. It's a nice dynamic. Both the Kraken and Wraith must first be unlocked by reaching level one on all the Goliath's skill trees - buffed up by say, throwing boulders 20 times or doing 20,000 points of damage with its leap attack. It's an unwanted grind in an otherwise sensible progression system, and something you'll have to endure to unlock all available 12 Hunters, too.
It’s worth noting that Evolve supports bots, an all-too-uncommon feature, and while the AI reveals its imperfections as time goes on, it’s strong enough to make playing offline matches rewarding on its own terms, and bots will fill in for disconnected teammates, or will leap into action should you not be able to find a friend to take that particular role. As with Turtle Rock’s Left 4 Dead, Evolve is best when you play with buddies; getting matched with a novice can lead to ghastly results if your newfound friend constantly seeks out the nonexistent “I” in “team.” It doesn’t take long to whip a newcomer into shape, at least, meaning you can usually focus on Evolve’s unique brand of greatness: the suspense of the hunt, the exhilaration of battle, and the drive to dominate Shear. Even Sasquatch would shiver at the dangers.

played to the end, so it's good...but it's not great.  worth it for the price, nice game to run through if you want a quick somewhat challenging retro style action platformer with adventure elements.  i used to rent a couple of NES games every weekend and ploy through them - this really reminded me of that, which is cool.  And this game is cheaper than a rental, which is essentially what it is - not exactly short, but not worth more than a couple days, and no replay value unless you want to speedrun the whole thing.
good albeit simple gameplay mechanics (jump/slash).  the big specialty here is the parkour-style grabbing ledges, wall-jumping/sliding, and running up walls a little.  despite the platforming strengths, the challenge is more timing-based - enemies and turrets that can quickly insta-kill you.  luckily you have infinite lives and only have to restart whatever screen you are on (there is no scrolling in this game at all).  but it seems like if the platforming was the best part, why not get more tricky with the ... platforms?  there are no moving platforms.
also the presentation is very lackluster.  this goes beyond NES retro.  It feels like a freeware DOS game - you return instantly to the start screen after finishing the game - not even credits!
pixel art is good, and there is decent variety for the length of the game, but some areas can become quickly confusing since their screens start to get real familiar looking.  the gating is done by key cards and switches - problem is there doesn't seem to be a way to know which ones you've gotten other than remembering, so you can do a lot of backtracking, and with the screen art having no distinctive visual cues, it can get a little frustrating.
pros:
- parkour platforming
- good challenge, and ramps up throughout
- pixel art
- good bang for the buck
cons:
- lackluster presentation
- gets repetitive
- confusing maps/repetitive level art
- enemies sometimes feel random, too easy for enemies to kill you in a cheap manner
- i can't see any replay value here
verdict: definitely buy this if you like pixel art, retro (simple) gameplay, challenge, and don't care much about presentation, length, or replay value.  It's cheap and enjoyable, but not going to stick out as one of your favorite games.

Review Info:
-Game: Outlast
