Miles Upshur, is a freelance journalist who one day receives an email from an anonymous source known only as "The Whistleblower," about a psychiatric hospital owned and operated by the Murkoff Corporation. Upon arriving, the place looks completely deserted and deserted, however SWAT cars are at the entrance of the asylum and Upshur with his curious instinct of journalist goes to investigation. After finding a way to enter the asylum, he is faced with bodies of people scattered around the corridors (some mutilated and even shattered), and the patients who escaped, known as "The Variants" roam the place. Progressing through the upper dorms, he encounters a SWAT officer impaled, who in his final moments tells the reporter to leave the premises while still able, unlocking the doors of the main entrance into the control room. Leaving the dorms, Upshur is attacked by an inmate named Chris Walker, who throws him through a window, falling into the lobby. Still recovering consciousness, the protagonist comes face-to-face with "Father Martin", a patient who believes he is a priest. Martin says Upshur was sent by God to be a witness of his worship, which must remain in the place and only then can leave.
Upshur begins his attempt to find a way out of the building, avoiding attacks by Walker and other patients. However, as he tries to unlock the main doors in the control room, he is ambushed and sedated by Martin, who again states that he must remain in the asylum and witness the events occurring there. Martin shows him footage of the site's security forces being massacred by a mysterious, seemingly supernatural entity known as "Walrider," before bringing unconscious Upshur to a cell.
Waking up, Upshur is forced to find a way through the sewers after finding two prisoners, "The Twins", who express a sadistic desire to kill and eat him. However, the duo did not attack at that time, as Martin asked them not to harm the journalist. Upshur makes his way through the sewers, avoiding attacks by Walker and other hostile prisoners, before finally arriving in the showers.
During the attempt to escape by the showers, he is attacked again by Walker, and escapes through the openings. Progressing further through the building, Upshur is soon pursued by several inmates at once but escapes through a mini elevator, however he is surprisingly attacked and captured by one of the hospice doctors - now psychotic - Dr. Richard "Rick" Trager, which collects parts of patients' bodies and practices unconventional surgeries. Trager imprisons Upshur, trapping him to a wheelchair. After a brief walk through his surgical ward, Trager cuts off two Upshur fingers using a large pair of scissors. Upshur manages to escape and a chase is initiated. When Upshur is about to escape, Trager unlocks the elevator door with the key and starts a fight with Upshur, resulting in Trager's death crushed between floors by the elevator.
The journalist meets Martin again, instructing him to meet him outside. Upshur walks out onto the grounds outside the asylum but is chased back in by Walker and Walrider, which has turned out to be a kind of ghost or spirit that Upshur can only see when using the night vision of his camera. He is forced to use a ruined staircase to access different floors of the building, following a trail of blood that Martin left for him. Upshur manages to reach a floor not yet explored, where everywhere there are altars with candles and patients praying, as if something of great importance were to happen. Finally, with the presence of several patients, including The Twins, Upshur meets Martin in the asylum chapel, which is attached to a crucifix telling Upshur to witness his death and that his freedom would be near, handing him the elevator key and later being burned on the cross. Before taking the main elevator, Upshur is pursued by Walker again. Upshur manages to get to the elevator, but it does not work, because instead of taking him to the exit, the elevator takes him to an undercover military facility under the madhouse. While searching for a way out, Upshur is attacked and disabled Walker, however, before killing the journalist, Walrider appears and brutally attacks Walker, killing him. Upshur proceeds through the facility and finds in a "Dr. Wernickie" room (which they originally believed to be dead), the scientist responsible for the entire experiment known as the "Walrider Project".
Wernickie explains that Walrider is the result of nanotechnology experiments conducted on a patient named "Billy Hope", and that Walrider is controlled by Billy. Wernicke asks Upshur to find Billy in the lab and kill him, shutting down his life support system, So, therefore, killing Walrider, before enacting Billy's death, Upshur is repeatedly pursued by Walrider, who will try to do away with the journalist's plans at any cost. After performing the task given by Wernickie, Upshur is repeatedly beaten by Walrider. Completely weakened and limping toward the exit, Upshur is confronted by Wernickie accompanied by several armed guards who end up firing several shots at Upshur. Upshur falls to the ground, dying, the screen turns black and a phrase is heard in Wernicke's voice: "You have become the host." In his last fight with Walrider, Upshur is possessed by him, since only a person who has experienced great psychological pain can sustain possession. Before the credits, shots and shouts are heard, certainly Upshur, now owned by Walrider, killing the guards and Wernicke.

First, I'm gonna start with the pros:

- You could always try a quick skirmish battle from the home screen if you're short on time.

- Very little lag.
- Very few glitches.
- You actually look at what your/the enemy's troops are good/weak against and use that information to win the battle instead of just aimlsessy making them all charge like hooligans.
- ADAPT, ADAPT, ADAPT!
- Snowspeeders are fun.
- AT-ATs are even more fun.
Now for the cons:
- It's not fun  going against a snowspeeder or AT-AT when you don't have the opposite.
- Not the best graphics, for those who care about it.
- Units may sometimes be unresponsive, especially in space.
- Special abilities don't always work.
- It's sometimes hard to go from right click for move/attack to left click for the special ability.
- Money is very rarely a challenge.
- WHAT?! 4 SHOTS FOR A BLOOMIN' KILL FOR ONE PERSON, WHAT IS THIS?!
- Some beginners may find easy mode feeling medium or hard (EDIT: The first few missions are normally quite hard, the rest rather easy).
- Auto resolve is pretty harsh and unbalanced.
- Most of the times that I tried out the Death Star it crashed (luckily it works for the campaign).
Overall, it's a very good game with its cons being rather minor. The content has kept me up for days  yet I'm still going. It is very addictive and it's hard to just leave among all your other ditched games. It also is probably one of the very few games that is actually tactical, making you adapt to certain situations. 9/10.

Easily the best survival zombie game out. This game makes you scared of zombies in a video game. You can be easily moving from house to house gather supplies, and that can all change in an instant if you get ambushed by a zombie or two events happen (either a nearby gun shot or helicopters flying overm so zombies in the surrounding area will flood into the zone you are in). This has a really good line of sight system to where zombies won't be able to see behind and most of their side, as well as you. If you don't watch around you, you will eventually get ambushed and may leave you in a world of hurt. This is always in "hardcore mode" to where if you die, your person that you have been leveling up for days or even months is dead forever, and there is no getting him/her back. You can create a character with many different professions, traits, and drawbacks. While in the game, you can level up various different skills, from fishing to farming, and blade weapons to blunt weapons. This game is also a sandbox, to where you can customize almost everything about the game, to how fast the zombies move (from slow to sprinters), and how the world is.
You can also not be alone, you can create your own server and bring your friends along for the zombie apocalypse, and it isn't hard to do, all you have to do is google it and you will be able to get a server up and running in less than 10 minutes. There is also mods you can put onto the server and there is a few good ones that I saw, like different maps and craftable items. This game is really well done with few bugs from what I have found.
If I would rate this game, it would easily be a 10/10. Best survival game imo, and it actually give the atmosphere of being in a zombie apocalypse (unlike most zombie survival games).

This game is very unforgiving and has a sharp learning curve. The tutorial is a brief 4 pages and leaves one a bit confused as to what exactly you should be doing, but the game can be summarised as:
Open doors -> Power new rooms (middle mouse) -> Build supporting machines in new rooms -> Build defences (Think tower defence) -> Open more doors (Discovering new loot/Monsters/NPCs)
Rinse and repeat, All the while looking for the elevator down.
Note: Monsters can only spawn in "dark/Unpowered" rooms, even ones you've previously explored.
Once you've found the elevator, if you're happy you're done with the floor you can pick up the power crystal from your ship and head down to the next level (This generally spawns a few monsters to oppose your hero as they try move the power source)
The game uses various resources to research/upgrade your heroes and build defences/upgrades for rooms
There are a few features I eagerly await, including a more in depth research system.
All in all, a good investment if you want a quick repeatable little game with a strong theme in a consistent loreverse

The controls feel fairly unresponsive, the music is repetitive as hell, and the movement and combat - the central tenets of these retro platformer style games - just feel off, like they don't quite flow as eloquently as, say, the movement in Super Meat Boy.
So why is this review positive, then?
In spite of these glaring issues, for some strange reason I found myself very much having an enjoyable time with this game. The open feel of the Metroidvania world is very endearing indeed, and the world is rather endearing and easy to get lost in, and I find that the mystery behind the lost civilization is more than enough motivation to keep going even in the more frustrating levels.
The second aspect of this game that was incredibly enjoyable was the level design. Though it seems bare-bones and simplistic initially, very soon you realize that the arrangement of the admittedly very generic obstacles leads to a very interesting almost puzzle solving aspect of the game, one which surprisingly never begins to feel even a little bit repetitive.
Overall, I would have to tell anyone looking for a precise platforming experience with tight controls and an innovative (or even very enjoyable) combat system to find a different game to play. But for anyone looking for an intriguing experience to get lost in and some interesting puzzles to solve, this game is a must have.

There are some very special things about Red Orchestra 2 and Rising Storm. It seems like they just don't make games like this anymore. I'll try to touch on the reasons that I and many other people continue to play this game 5 years after release.
-The game has a raw, terrifying feel to it. Especially as a new player, I felt the stress of battle when I would play. This game actually made my heart race. There was nothing like finding myself scrambling for cover as artillery lands around you and your comrades, or as you watch machine gun fire whizz by your face. Or the burst of adrenaline you get when you obey an order from your commander to charge into a smokescreen, not knowing what lies on the other side...
-That's another thing. Never before have I played a game where effective leadership mattered so much. A skilled team leader will mean the difference between victory and defeat. It's not just the ability to call artillery...teammates under your command will follow your orders and rush into combat, even if the order is wrong. I've seen games lost because a TL acted on bad information and ordered an attack at the wrong time. The sense of responsibility that you have to do your part, whether a TL or rifleman, brings the team together.
-The people who play this game are top dudes. If you like military history and appreciate guys who play seriously but know how to crack a WWII joke between matches, this is for you. There is a humor and fun competitiveness in this game that I haven't found anywhere else.
-The game is very well balanced. Each side can win if they play to their strengths to coordinate an effective strategy. Get on the mic and work together. You'll win.
-The game does not determine the winner of a firefight by who has the better weapon unlock. Unlike battlefield or call of duty, there's no point in grinding for weapon unlocks. Your class determines your gun, and that's it. Sure, you can unlock some minor upgrades (like a bayonet), but if you're a rifleman, you will always carry a rifle. The same one your teammates carry. Winning a firefight will require tactical positioning and coordinating covering fire.
-The maps are well laid out and conducive to team play, but some of them will give you a sort of PTSD. Don't believe me? Check back in after your first match spent trying to get across the river on Bridges. Perhaps you chose to crouch low and follow the Panzer across the bridge. Then the plan went to hell when the tank lost a tread and you had nowhere to go.
There is a learning curve to this game. If you're used to sprinting, jumping, quickscoping, etc, you will struggle. Take it slow. Every shot that you take counts, and every incoming bullet could be the one that takes your life. Stick with your squadmates and follow instructions when someone gives an order. Pick up a position of responsibility now and then and play your role. Maybe be an engineer and make it your mission to destroy tank traps so that the Panzer can move forward. This game can be a meat grinder sometimes, and it will always feel like one if you try to play too fast.
But overall, everyone who plays this game is acutely aware that this experience does not exist anywhere else. Six years after release, there are still full 64-player servers. There will still be full servers for years to come.

I got this game from an indie bundle and I was quite keen on it before installing it. That Lego-style TPS caught my attention and got a good feeling about it.
What a fool I was.
This is surely one of the worst indie games I've ever played. Everything makes me feel now that I've been scammed, betrayed. I absolutely approve the indie game generation (and actually I'm more into them than into triple-A games) but this is a paradigmatical way of "let's make something, it might give us money". And sure, you can say "hey, don't be so bad to them, they're probably a very little company", but this becomes senseless when you see that games such as Braid, Hotline Miami, VVVVVV, Super Meat Boy, FEZ and many others have been made by 1-2 people each and they're absolutely astonishing. So this is not an excuse.
I was running this game on the maximum settings (it doesn't have any high requirements anyway) and oh my god, the number of mistakes is so huge you should see it for yourself. ALL shadows were going crazy, in EVERY single map. Almost all textlines somehow got crazy too and were IMPOSSIBLE to read, like in a super low resolution. So actually I had to guess what every option did by pressing it. If you don't believe it I do not have any inconvinient in uploading screenshots.
The soundtrack was... what could I say? There's only 1 track. Or maybe not. I don't know. If there's more than one, then all of them feels the same. The same boring. Even on the menus. And even though I've listened the same music all way through my total gameplay, I've already forgotten how it sounds.
The AI. Oh my damn God, this is one of the most ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ AI's I've faced in a very long time. It can be fooled the SAME WAY on Easy than on Extreme difficulty. ALL enemies follow some patterns that after 1-2 waves will be absolutely predictible. Jesus, there was one time where an enemy was facing me but without shooting a single bullet. I stared at him for ten minutes. TEN MINUTES. He didn't do a thing. Again, you won't even image how sad the enemies react until you test it.
The game is also astonishingly short. Yet it felt long, because of how boring it was. All chapters were wave-based, and since this game is 1 player-only (together with a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ AI), guess how similar everything looked like. The only stage I actually enjoyed was the chicken massacre one.
This was one of those VERY FEW games I ended up playing only for achievements, which were surprisingly rewarding. Yet some of them were unfairly grind-based, condemning you to stay more hours than you wanted to. Since I like achievements and hate to leave things undone, this was quite a pain even if it only took me about 4h to unlock all of them.
Overall, do yourself a favour and DO NOT buy or play this garbage. I've been critically disappointed and I'm sure you have plenty of better games in your library. Which isn't hard at all. Only play this game if you wanna check my words and see how bad this game is.

Bioshock is a first-person, sci-fi, fictional shooter where you take the role of Jack, a normal person at the beginning of the game soon to become one of the most iconic figures in both this game and the entire Bioshock series. You must traverse the underwater so-called "paradise" of Rapture, where those who dwell in it are free from religious criticism against their own ideas, free from the restraints of government, and are free to pursue their own ideals, to take down the rebellious tyrant Frank Fontaine.
I have to admit, when I first started playing this game back in 2010, I had my doubts. Why? Because for me, violent videogames wasn't so much my cup of tea, in fact, back then I never really played violent videogames; I usually played Mario. But after playing this game
, TWICE, both on PC in 2014 and PS3 of 2010, this game has made me a huge fan of the Bioshock series because the story is insanely rich, dark, driven, and deeply fulfilling, packed with violence, betrayal, and revolution. And the entire setting in general: an underwater city, who ever thought of that? You can think of Atlantis, but heck, not this one!
To start off, the start of the game where you're in the plane seems to bring about curiosity as to what this game really is about, because you can look at the front cover of the game and say, "Hey. It's a man in a diving outfit, and he's with a little girl. Well that's pretty cool." However, I usually say that covers can be illusions to what lies behind, and for Bioshock, this is 100% correct. Already do you crash land in an ocean somewhere off the North Atlantic ocean, near Iceland, swim to some very imposing and unknown, yet beautiful and intricate, building, enter inside, go into a bathysphere (a ship-thingy), and already you're in Rapture. What better way to already jump into the dark, underwater "paradise" then crash-land, swim, then witness the city first-hand through a metal sphere?
Now, aside from that, Bioshock
a first-person shooter, and it does that well. However, what makes this game unique in it's POV is that you fight with genetic weapons called Plasmids, made from a genetic resource known as ADAM, which serve as your primary utility throughout the game. Rather than say, "Okay, this guy's got magic for some reason," you can say "The guy's a severely altered, genetic freak, so kick your heels and run!" It's interesting to see a game where the magic is the result of genetic mutations and self-splicing alterations rather than some natural, innate gift because it really brings about that gruesome background of the game... and teaches kids why you shouldn't use drugs.
Anyways, the story, damn! I played this game four times and not once did I get bored with the story. It is huge, and while repetitive, it is great, and it never dries up, it never goes dull, and it always stays alive. The whole foundation of the game itself is heavily dependent on its story because it is the story that sets the game in a momentous rhythm that will leave you wanting more. From how Rapture fell during the Civil War of 1959, to the remains and its genetically-altered denizens and future impact is so well woven and produced that I could not imagine a better game story that can compete against this one.
The enemies in this game that you fight against are very creative, different, genuine, and, of course, unique. Big Daddies,   altered humans in diving suits who have been heavily spliced and grafted
their suits are a true challenge to face, but enjoyable to fight against. Splicers, possessing different types of abilities through the overdose of ADAM and Plasmids, makes the game more intense as you have to come up with different ways to fight them off or run away.
Truly, the best thing about this game is the entire environment and setting itself. When I saw Rapture through my own TV screen for the first time, I thought that this was perhaps the most amazing creation in a videogame I've ever witnessed. An underwater city that isn't a utopia, has a different name, and can no way be related to Atlantis really brings about the unique quality of Rapture and makes it stand preeminent amongst all other underwater myths. While shocked, I was also awestruck by Rapture's own beliefs and ideals set forth by its philosophical leader Andrew Ryan, because normally, people would just create a history for a city, but this is a whole new level of "history," filled with insanity and dark athmospheres.
Overall, all I can say about this game is:
🐅Snowy's Scorey🐅:
9: Truly brilliant, recommended at its best
8: Okay, will recommend
7: Decent, will recommend, but within certain limitations
6: Average, probably not worth recommending, but at least looking at
5: Meh, some things are right, some wrong, but not complete
4. Um.., not sure if this game is up for grabs
3. Not worth buying
2. Not worth looking at
1. Quarantine yourself from this game
Although the graphics are not exactly perfect, who freaking cares? The game itself is a masterpiece, with a heavily-driven story, cool combat mechanics and environment, and the lavish and beautiful setting of underwater Rapture. Buy this game when HD Remastered comes out in September because I can guarantee you this game will be amazing. The game is definitely worth the price, and it is entertaining all around.

Okay, I only made it part way through the second level, and my retro gaming skills are not everything that they used to be, so I died a lot. Not sure if I'll ever get through it.
But it's not the terrible game that so many reviews make it out to be.
The first level is easy. Z to shoot. Arrow keys to move. It's Asteroids-esque with resource management. You have fuel, "ammunition" for you mining laser, and faith. It also shows you the faith in The Garden. You goal is to get your faith higher than that in The Garden. Taking damage lowers your faith. If you faith becomes 0, you lose. If your fuel becomes 0, you lose. You gain faith by mining asteroids, and additionally, by picking up the bibles that come out of said asteroids. You can also pick up DMT drops from asteroids, which fuel your mining laser. Kill enemy ships and collect the orbs they drop to get more fuel. Avoid the strange, gigantic creature that roams around aimlessly. He will ♥♥♥♥ your faith. Once you have more faith than the Garden (which starts at 1000), proceed to level 2.
Level 2 is a classic scrolling shooter. Hold Z to spam lasers. Dodge enemy shots. Be better at this than I am.
I like the voice acting. It's weird. The game is weird. It works.
Art style is pretty much what you'd expect from a retro arcade style game. Which is neither good nor bad; just depends on your preference.
This game is challenging. It doesn't hold your hand. But it's not bad (at least, for as far as I could get in it, given said difficulty.) It's certainly a lot better than other games I've played recently. The mechanics are infinitely better than Type:Rider, which I just finished. It's just difficult. If you like challenging games, go for it. If you don't, don't.

After 16 hours I'm still not even half way through the achievements. This sounds like a good thing; like there's a lot of content, but unfortunately its just a dice roll for new encounters. The past three hours have just been repeats of what I've done before. Despite trying to do the opposite thing in a scenario I've done before I still don't really make progress.
The game itself is fun, for the price I wouldn't say to stay away, just don't expect too much.

Slow-motion at its finest. This is a game where the time only really flows when the player is moving.
Simple controls: run, grab/throw objects (you can grab the guns from your shot opponents, the game provides very limited ammunitions so you have to switch weapons regularly), fire (or punch/melee). You can also jump but that was rarely useful to me. There is not much more to it, not much interaction generally speaking. The levels are usually small, baddies spawn from portals (that the player can watch a bit too closely imho, but that wasn't game-breaking at all for me). Kill them all, go to the next level - or, if the game requires it, advance the story a little bit using the game built-in console.
The story feels a bit like déjà-vu, but the fact the whole games is about VR (the characters absolutely look like vintage 3D/VR games) makes it more fun. Expect some fourth-wall jokes or allusions.
This game lacks a bit of depth imho (there is no denying level design could have served the main concept -which is slow motion- better, or that the game could have used a few more features). Some of the not-so-obvious-but-cool things you can do are playing with the bullets and try to dodge them (barely !) or even shoot/cut them.
Anyway, it should be pretty fun for you while it last. Pretty short game but the devs included alternative modes.

I bought this game on sale today, and was not disappointed.
Pros:
+Beautiful artwork
+Tight controls
+Very atmospheric
+Not too short, not too long
+Simple and effective gameplay
Cons:
-Some puzzles are not very intuitive
-Low replay value
This game is more a work of art, an experience, than it is a game. Not that the gameplay is bad by any means, in fact it's really great and puts other more gameplay oriented games to shame. What i mean, is that the gameplay seems like more of a way to help immerse you in the world rather than being the focal point. For example, a game like The Binding of Isaac is similar with its simple gameplay premise, however it is far more replayable because of how hard it is to master, as well as the variety of the gameplay via different items and strategies in which to utilize them. Limbo uses its gameplay as more of a means to an end, albeit very effectively. I would have liked to see the gameplay a little more fleshed out with more levels testing your platforming merit, as well as a few more "bosses" (if you could call the spider that) or similar challenges along the way. I would attribute this game somewhat to The Last of Us, in the sense that it's more about the experience of being in that world and the journey through it as opposed to being a highly replayable, fun game to play.
<Gravity Puzzle Rant>
Another thing to note, is that now that i'm all old and stuff, i don't like wasting too much time on puzzles in games once i get stumped. There was one puzzle in particular that, although with more time and effort i could have solved on my own, i ended up looking at a walkthrough for the solution. The reason i'm mentioning it here, is because it really kind of stalled the experience of an otherwise fun game. Not only that, but i feel like puzzles should be somewhat intuitive. Meaning that the answer shouldn't be something that has never been fully introduced as an idea or mechanic in the game before that point. Granted the puzzle in question is a variation of a concept that is shown and used in the game before that point, but it's used in combination with another idea or function in the game that is never really utilized (to my memory) up until that point. Every other puzzle in the game is pretty straight forward, and the solution to them is something that you have been presented with before, but for some reason the one puzzle came out of nowhere and didn't make sense to me until i looked it up.
</Gravity Puzzle Rant>
The last thing i would like to highlight is the atmosphere in the game. In my opinion, this game is highly immersive with the sound effects and artwork. This is something that is highly subject to opinion though, as i read a review not long ago about how the game's atmosphere was lacking because there wasn't any music or dialogue. I feel the opposite though, as the lack of music and the focus on creepy sound effects and eerie artwork is very immersive. It's nice to play a game that respects quiet moments and allows you to take in the scenery.
I recommend this game to people who aren't afraid to try out indie games, and also enjoy great platforming alongside fun puzzles and a dark, gritty, but awe inspiring world.
P.S. Also, because i'm old and stuff, i have a hard time spending a ton of money on games anymore to the point where $10 can be a little steep for me. This game is EASILY worth $2, but i honestly would have a hard time paying full price for it knowing what is in store.

Was excited to play this game, only to be let down :(
This is an old school retro platformer. While the controls feel solid a majority of the time, they can also be finnicky. The wallrun doesnt work half the time, and sometimes you will want to pull up onto a ledge and it will have you jump off instead. Combat isn't great as guys take many kills and you die in one hit. All of the levels look the same and the environments are boring, blocking, and look copy and pasted with just a few color/background changes. There is no story. There is like 3 enemies total. You do the same thing in each environment. You hunt down keys, go into a building, and unlock a door. It gets super repetitive. Then there's the biggest problem, the map design. Each level has a few branching paths, and then some of those have branching paths. But since there is no map whatsoever and all the ways look the same it is hard to remember which way you came or you need to go. There are no markers or directions at all. The other biggest problem with the design is you will go super far one path, having beaten a bunch of hard parts, then you find at the end you need a key. So you have to run all the way back. There's nothing you can do, since no markers or map you have to trial and error hoping you found the right way. Even if you do, you will find a key, but you have to go all the way back again to use it in another area. This is just artificially inflating game length and is lazy design that makes the game boring. I would then get back and since it is hard to tell where you've been I would go back one of the paths I had come, but theres no way of knowing till you get back to start, then you have to retrace your steps again. So much of my time in the game was wasted retracing steps, going wrong way, etc. This saps all the fun from the game and makes it a chore. Finally I took a day off and was at a part with 3 paths, went 1 way, didn't have a key, had no idea which way I had come from the day before, went back one way, and finally decided it wasn't worth it and gave up.
The sad thing is, even with the finnicky control and combat, the game could be fun. But the terrible map design, lack of direction, forced backtracking and trial and error on paths, and repetitiveness of each area, just make this game an amateur effort. I just think of what could have been......

is one of those games that you look at and go "Ehhh maybe it could be fun, but I don't know if it's worth picking up..." and then a Steam sale comes along so you get the game at a cheap price. You forget you have it in your library, see it a few months later and think "Oh yeah, I forgot I bought that," install it, then get REALLY FREAKING ADDICTED to it.
Seriously, I think I played this game for hours on end and never got tired of it. It's surprisingly addictive.
puts you in the role of a king managing his kingdom. The "cards" are the various advisors of your kingdom asking you to make binary decisions for all of their problems. The decisions you make impact the four meters you are attempting to keep balanced. The four meter bars that are constantly in flux are: Religion, People, Army, and Money. The goal is to keep these meters from hitting 100 or 0; if they hit 100 or 0, you will die. And then you get to play as another king! Over and over and over again! Yaaaay! Also, the Devil has put a curse on you, and you will lose the game after a couple thosand years have gone by if you are unable to "trick" him (which gives a few alternate endings). The game is meant to be replayed over and over to experience all the deaths, all the storylines, all the cards (and accumulating all the different advisors and people you can interact with), all the "fights" (easy and silly little combat games with a few characters), and the alternate endings.
The game is played using your arrow keys and only your arrow keys. All you have to do is "swipe left" or "swipe right." I believe the game was originally designed for tablets/phones, thus the "swiping" mechanic, but it works fine for PCs as well. The controls are super simple and intuitive.
The art of the game is kind of pixel-ish? Very blocky edges. But that doesn't mean I don't like the art style! I find the art to be endearing and appropriate to the game.
If you're looking for a relatively quick game (maybe less than 8 hours to see all the content?) that can be picked up cheap in a Steam sale, this is a game worth considering!

In conception, this game sounds decent.
In execution, NOOOOOO.
Both on a control level and a design level, this is a disaster.
The movement is stiff. When you land from a jump you're stuck in place for a moment. The wall running mechanic that is super important sometimes doesn't work, arbitrarily. Climbing onto ledges only sometimes works. Sprites don't always line up with hitboxes - poles especially, but sometimes the edge of a ledge seems too close and you fall off without jumping.
But the design is worse. There are five boss fights in the game, but surprise, actually only three. The third boss is both the first and second bosses at once, the fourth is two of the first boss. Okay, so it's a little repetitive there. And also everywhere else, too. The game tries to be "exploration-based" but aside from one branching path point in the first zone, it's entirely and wholly linear, so you can end up going down a path only to reach a dead end because you don't have the right key. And the third zone is atrocious with this, requiring you to go all the way to the end of the zone, back to near the start, then pretty deep in and work your way back to the start, with where all the key locations are. It's FILLER, plain and simple. The second zone has a bit of this design too, and it's just a huge time waster.
The enemies in the game can shoot bullets at random intervals and without any sort of warning, so getting past them in some spots really just comes down to luck. The combat isn't very satisfying and in the second zone onward most things take too long to kill. All the bosses are way too tanky, too, they all only have one attack so it's just a tedious slog.
The dungeons are all designed so that you end up having to go all the way to the end and back in most every dungeon that doesn't end in a boss, which is just, again, filler. Such a waste of time.
I'm prepared to say, at this point, that the developer behind these games really needs to take up some game design lessons or just outright quit, even aside from the horrible controls there's not even any potential in this game, it's badly design, not very fun, and the only reason I played to the bitter end was mostly to say I did, I hate giving up but I considered it with this one.
Avoid at all costs, avoid the developer's games at all cost. I still have two more of these to play but I don't know if I can take another game like this...

I heard lots of great things about this game, so I decided to buy it at a discount along with INSIDE. The first hour was unlike anything I've ever played before. The pitch-black landscape and undisclosed identity of the main character wrap the game in a shroud of mystery, and I immediately wanted to find out more. Even after completion, the game doesn't reveal much. LIMBO succeeds in this respect, because it leaves much of the story up for interpretation and forces you to actually think(something not many games do at all). Similarly to how rich writing creates a certain vagueness, LIMBO's setting is what makes it so enigmatic.
Another aspect of the game I enjoyed was how smoothly the different areas blended together. You begin in a forest, run into some natives, and before you know it, you are inside a factory. Though there is a rigid dichotomy between nature and industry, LIMBO blends these elements seamlessly, without any obnoxious loading screens.
Why do I not recommend this game? It begins to feel empty and boring very quickly. In the beginning, the puzzles involved ripping the legs off a giant spider, bringing an unprecedented sense of satisfaction. After this thrilling section of the game, the puzzles turned into mind-numbing block-pushing, button-pressing, and lever-activating. The fearsome giant spider was replaced by an annoying little maggot that burrows in your character's skull, causing him to move in one direction until you reach the spot where the game changes your direction for you. Though the idea is interesting, I always dreaded the moment when I would contract a brainworm and lose control of my character.
The unfortunate truth is that the segment with bad puzzles constitutes the majority of the game experience. Even when LIMBO introduces a cool new gravity changing mechanic, the damn block-pushing puzzles are still there, and everything begins to feel like one big chore. I actually wanted the game to end. Luckily, it did, because the game is quite short.
Since LIMBO relies on a very simple control scheme, it would make sense for the puzzles to be based solely on interactions with the environment. However, the developers definitely could have came up with something better than pushing blocks next to ledges, or timing button activations. In my opinion, this is what ruins the experience the most.
I plan on playing INSIDE very soon, and I hope Playdead will be able to deliver a stunning experience from start to finish.

Take a game with no color, no dialogue, no 3D, and a musical score so subtle it might as well be ambient noise. In most cases that sounds like a terrible game, but Limbo pulls it off incredibly well. This indie release has received much deserved praise for its simplicity, yet very effective gameplay. I think this game masters one aspect incredibly well, and that is the sound of the environment. Heavy footsteps, loud electrical crackles, and scurrying spider steps all are done to perfection to a point where no background noise is necessary at all. 2-D sidescrollers have been done to death, but Limbo feels almost entirely original because of how it is presented. The plot is very simple and almost doesn't need to exist for this game to work. It is more about the tension, and players will be on edge the first time they play this game. The platforming, with some exceptions, is satisfactory. The game is a bit short, but much like Portal, this game is better because it is shorter, not overstaying its welcome. I did have a few gripes about some of the ludicrous amount of precision required for certain platforming sections, and some false paths will lead you to nowhere except certain death, but all in all it is a unique little platformer that I am glad is in my collection.

Right from the bat, I knew this game was going to be a polarizing one. To begin, classes are gender-specific. If you want to play a female rogue, well tough luck. There isn't a lot of customization in character creation, so you'll find several copies of your character once you're out on the field. The graphics are nice, but it's nothing special.
It's fairly easy to level up quickly, but it's also very boring. Quests are the generic "kill this many creatures," "gather this many items," or "kill creatures to gather this many items that may or may not drop." The skill tree is not extensive. This might be good for first-time MMORPG players who can better understand the simplified rundown of skillsets. But again, this brings back the con of lack of customization. A serious flaw with this game (in my opinion) is how difficult it is to earn money. This makes professions useless and expensive in the earlier levels.
Like many F2P games, there is a cash shop. While the game doesn't shove the fact in your face as much as others, the fact that there are actually quests in the game that requires you to purchase an item from the cash shop just irks me. Also like many F2P games, PVP is horribly unbalanced. Some classes far outlast others in the battleground. Archers are the devil.
This is just your average MMORPG. It will keep you entertained for a few hours before you get tired of the redundancy.

I will catalog this review the best I can to get straight to the point in each topic I feel a person should know before they play this game. Overall I want to focus less on my experience on other MMO's I have played and tell you why I continue to play this one.
1)Leveling-So as I said in my very brief Intro, I am going to get straight to the point and not fluff anything. Somethings about this game could be better, but most things work very well as are, and "If its not broken dont fix it". Leveling in this game is hands down my least fave part of playing. I have 3 level 60 characters(Max Level) and I havn't enjoyed leveling a single one. I still love this game and heres why. This games content is tailored to level 60 characters, and leveling is a very repetative yet still fairly easy process if you just quest. Quest over and over. Doing battlefields will give you experience to level but only will make you level faster than questing if you have close to a 70% win rate. I say rush to max level as fast as you can.
2)Guilds-Many players have a different opinion on who to make friends with (or not make friends with) and why. For many players they join a guild because it's mainly there nationality(Brazil Im talking to you). There are many guilds to choose from, and many guilds choose to fight monsters while many choose to fight players. I prefer to fight players so I picked a pvp guild and I still get to do just as many raids or dungeons as I would have had I not picked a pvp guild. Choose one early in the game to ask questions and make friends. Being in a guild is very rewarding and often helps you learn things the easy way rather than playing the game "in the dark".
3)Gold becomes a thing of desire once you hit level 60. Gold is not needed in any way before level 60 if its your first character. If its your second character or later it can help you to get better gems which make leveling faster, but the game drops enough of them naturally you wont need to worry about it your first run through. Gold is your vehicle to get what you desire. EVERYTHING in this game that effects combat can be purchased with gold. You will have the fastest access to making gold in level 60 raids and dungeons. Or buy and sell goods on the market place if you study it before hand.
4)Gems-Gems are extra items that attach to a players gear to make a player stronger(extra stats). They are a very important part of the game, but often highly over glorified. As a player with 3 level 60's I often play in pvp "gemless" and still compete just fine for MVP. This game isn't that hard if you always are trying to learn what you can do better in a given situation. Gems are luxury!!! Now dont ignore them 100%, they can be a great way to make gold, and a great investment into becoming a stronger player. Far too many players blame their gems as the reason they are losing, when more importantly people with very good gems MOST of the time have better gems because they are better players, although I have beaten many players in flat 1v1 situations having worse gems. I have average gems because i refuse to spend money on this game. Hear that? Never spent a single penny.
5)Dungeons-Dungeons before level 60 are very important and let me tell you what to do and what not to do. Before level 60 do the dungeons just to learn the in game mechanics on bosses, becuase the dungeons you see before level 60(or the bosses) you WILL see again. Focus more on improving as a player in dungeons, than the gear. Going through the same dungeon before level 60 is a flat waste of time once you learn the mechanics. Yes it will give you good gear, but I argue your gear would be better if you spend that same time questing into higher levels over farming a dungeon. NOW AT LEVEL 60, the dungeons are good for gear, and will start to bring a lot of gold. They drop gems and become a true test to your understanding of the game. Do not be upset if people lose their tempers with you in a level 60 dungeon. A lot of players are so used to the dungeons you may be new too, that they dont understand why you are still learning the bosses. My best peice of advise, let good friends or guild members take you to your first lv 60 dungeons to help you grow.
6)Events-Now this game like many MMO's has holiday events. The events in this game so far are more community builders than actual content events, although some events still bring exciting content into view. I argue this is something that Echo of Soul needs more focus on(Maybe through studying World of Warcraft events) But the EOS team has shown willingness to make this a larger part of the game, and i think much more is to come.
7)Reward Drops-Hands Down my least fave part of this game. Most items in this game are worth 1 silver to sell to a vendor. Yes, 1 silver.... Now, I will not focus on that, as much as what Im about to tell you. There is no world rare drop system as in other very fun MMO's. This is something I hope very dearly will enter this game. We need to be able to go into a raid with our friends or guild hoping to get a SPECIAL MOUNT or special item that is ONLY available in that spot. Just by creating a system where some high value items drop very rarely, it creates a passion for players and a great enjoyment. A strong rare drop system allows people to actually feel rewarded for their time OUTSIDE of the personal satisfaction of completing a challenge. I love being challenged as much as the next person, but when you already know you are smart enough to figure them out eventually, a rare drop system keeps it very entertaining and exciting.
8)Battleground-I have covered this a small amount already. Overall its just another way to test yourself. If you find yourself blaming your gems because you die, or your weak gear, it has partial truth. As a player who has been in a new players shoes, I still owned the noobs. Some people can mentally handle the learning curve that will come your way, and many run to excuses. Do the best you can and have fun! Try to learn and enjoy. There is 2 battlefields(3rd if you count Valhalla aka-guild war). Dont make excuses, if you arnt doing well ask others how they play your class in pvp.
9)PAY TO WIN?-FLAT ANSWER NO! This game is 100% NOT PAY TO WIN. You may ask me why I feel that way, well heres point number 1, I have spent not a single amount of any type of real life currency on this game. I still can get beat, but as an experienced player of this game, I find when i get beat it was a result of my own failure of knowledge. Some players are going to be stronger than you, maybe their class "counters" your class. Yes crazy idea I know. When you see a situation like this in battle its best to not fight the 1v1 you think you will lose. I know many good players who wont win a lot of 1v1's. They are viewed as good players because they know when they do and dont have the advantage, and sometimes having your team with greater numbers is what it takes. Dont listen to anyone who says this game is Pay to Win, its a scapegoat and quite frankly, very poor excuse. This game can make your growth faster if you choose to pay, but with that still comes a lot of risk. I know a lot of people who have spent money and not gotten any stronger for it. Think outside of the box and learn the game and the answers will come to you.
10)Last Thought-I find this game to be the closest video game to a much loved anime called SAO. Now that has nothing to do with my love of this game. I personally enjoy testing myself, which this game helps me do. And i love the vast majority of the community. Players here can be mean just like anywhere else, but I have made friendships and I enjoy the time I spend playing. This game far surpasses the time I could spend watching TV or playing another video game.

Bioshock is a first-person, sci-fi, fictional shooter where you take the role of Jack, a normal person at the beginning of the game soon to become one of the most iconic figures in both this game and the entire Bioshock series. You must traverse the underwater so-called "paradise" of Rapture, where those who dwell in it are free from religious criticism against their own ideas, free from the restraints of government, and are free to pursue their own ideals, to take down the rebellious tyrant Frank Fontaine.
I have to admit, when I first started playing this game back in 2010, I had my doubts. Why? Because for me, violent videogames wasn't so much my cup of tea, in fact, back then I never really played violent videogames; I usually played Mario. But after playing this game
, TWICE, both on PC in 2014 and PS3 of 2010, this game has made me a huge fan of the Bioshock series because the story is insanely rich, dark, driven, and deeply fulfilling, packed with violence, betrayal, and revolution. And the entire setting in general: an underwater city, who ever thought of that? You can think of Atlantis, but heck, not this one!
To start off, the start of the game where you're in the plane seems to bring about curiosity as to what this game really is about, because you can look at the front cover of the game and say, "Hey. It's a man in a diving outfit, and he's with a little girl. Well that's pretty cool." However, I usually say that covers can be illusions to what lies behind, and for Bioshock, this is 100% correct. Already do you crash land in an ocean somewhere off the North Atlantic ocean, near Iceland, swim to some very imposing and unknown, yet beautiful and intricate, building, enter inside, go into a bathysphere (a ship-thingy), and already you're in Rapture. What better way to already jump into the dark, underwater "paradise" then crash-land, swim, then witness the city first-hand through a metal sphere?
Now, aside from that, Bioshock
a first-person shooter, and it does that well. However, what makes this game unique in it's POV is that you fight with genetic weapons called Plasmids, made from a genetic resource known as ADAM, which serve as your primary utility throughout the game. Rather than say, "Okay, this guy's got magic for some reason," you can say "The guy's a severely altered, genetic freak, so kick your heels and run!" It's interesting to see a game where the magic is the result of genetic mutations and self-splicing alterations rather than some natural, innate gift because it really brings about that gruesome background of the game... and teaches kids why you shouldn't use drugs.
Anyways, the story, damn! I played this game four times and not once did I get bored with the story. It is huge, and while repetitive, it is great, and it never dries up, it never goes dull, and it always stays alive. The whole foundation of the game itself is heavily dependent on its story because it is the story that sets the game in a momentous rhythm that will leave you wanting more. From how Rapture fell during the Civil War of 1959, to the remains and its genetically-altered denizens and future impact is so well woven and produced that I could not imagine a better game story that can compete against this one.
The enemies in this game that you fight against are very creative, different, genuine, and, of course, unique. Big Daddies,   altered humans in diving suits who have been heavily spliced and grafted
their suits are a true challenge to face, but enjoyable to fight against. Splicers, possessing different types of abilities through the overdose of ADAM and Plasmids, makes the game more intense as you have to come up with different ways to fight them off or run away.
Truly, the best thing about this game is the entire environment and setting itself. When I saw Rapture through my own TV screen for the first time, I thought that this was perhaps the most amazing creation in a videogame I've ever witnessed. An underwater city that isn't a utopia, has a different name, and can no way be related to Atlantis really brings about the unique quality of Rapture and makes it stand preeminent amongst all other underwater myths. While shocked, I was also awestruck by Rapture's own beliefs and ideals set forth by its philosophical leader Andrew Ryan, because normally, people would just create a history for a city, but this is a whole new level of "history," filled with insanity and dark athmospheres.
Overall, all I can say about this game is:

Here are just a few of the things that make
such an amusing title:
The Developers - I realize that this point is not a core component while playing the game itself, but I feel as though I must give recognition to the development team of
. I personally have never witnessed such a respectful cast of individuals when it comes to interacting with players and the game itself. As a primary mention, these individuals send notifications to subscribers consistently every Monday, termed Mondoid Monday by the Indie Stone, which provides readers with updates as to what ideas are to be implemented, answering questions from contributors, and informing players of the current build’s status. Though the game is currently in Early Access at the time of this review’s writing, these constant updates presented by the developers have the potential to comfort players such as myself as to the condition of the completed product.
may be considered by some to be concluded as it stands; this is much more satisfying in strict comparison to other Early Access titles that stereotype the build and tend to break promises.
Pre-Game Setup - In the general disarray that encompasses the world regarding defeating and surviving against an endless undead hoard, there are certainties in the abundance of pre-game editing that tailor the experience as one that is unique to the individual player.
I would first like to speak about the initial world composition, which allows simple attributes while playing through modes such as Sandbox to be altered. With these features, the player creates how the apocalypse occurs by selecting a premade map, modifying certain functions such as how long a typical in-game day lasts-ranging from five minutes to a realistic twenty-four hours out of game-, and the period of time in which electricity and water will remain operational throughout the selected world. These attributes can be set to be more random while in Sandbox mode, but add so much to customization that they should not be overlooked; of course, the game was updated many times since my last online play-time so I may be missing out on some features as it stands.
Character creation appears to be very simplistic but its intricate nature is revealed while the players flesh out their individual during play. The player selects a basic set of clothing as well as a profession, traits, and look; a character’s profession outline starting equipment and statistics while the character’s appearance is merely cosmetic. Character traits are where the game excels, though, as these allow the player to outline how they will possibly play. For example, a character with claustrophobia will be plagued with fear while indoors, but may have a trait which counteracts this. As players select possible traits, negatives must also be selected to even things out, so there is decent balance to this system.
Undead Artificial Intelligence (AI) - The enemy AI react to players as you would expect them to: merciless, in a one-directional path with the intent of slaughtering the player’s created character to produce the end-game indication. As simple as this may sound, the undead AI in
is actually quite brilliant, as they can track your movements only if you are in a presented location-such as on the other side of an open window; a hoard crowds a character if a gunshot is heard. Interaction with these enemies intensifies the atmosphere of lay, and has likely been improved with more recent updates. Though neutral non-player characters are not yet present in
in the time of this review’s writing, tests by the developers suggest a promising finished product.
Gameplay and Mechanics - Your character has much more depth in-game then what is in their biography and statistics sheet. There are multiple conditions which must be monitored by the player-including thirst, hunger, fear, mood, and physical strain. Given status effects may afflict the player such as fatigue, and determine the player’s tactics, with enough openness to allow the use of multiple approaches; with a world infested by the undead this is highly necessary as the game’s open-world style should permit such an approach. Unlike other top-down zombie survival titles,
features an impression of realism few others can accomplish: line of sight is paramount for your character, which enhances the survival aspect perfectly; be sure to watch your back! Apart from the conditions and base statistics associated with your character, they can also learn new skills such as farming, carpentry, and cooking to perform unique and useful tasks by taking time in-game to read related books. This system permits the player to specialize in specific skills that may enhance play.
TL:DR - I regretfully can say that there are some features such as the Steam Workshop and Creative mode that I have not yet experienced, however the base game is so fantastic that I would like to vouch for it being worthy of its current retail price of fifteen dollars. If you enjoy more realistic survival games and combatting or running from hordes of undead while scavenging a rather large world, then this game is most definitely for you. This title is also recommended for players who enjoy roleplaying as characters in an open-world adventure; I prefer to write journals for my characters to enhance this aspect. Please give this game a go even in its current Early Access state. Thanks for reading.

Bioshock is an amazing game.  It deserves all the praise it gets.  "Why is BioShock such a big deal?" I hear you ask.  (If not, meh :P)  Let me explain why BioShock is one of the best games of the 2000s and of all time!  If your not aware of an FPS-RPG, it's a first-person shooter with RPG elements.  The genre is always cool (Fallout, Deus Ex and this!) and BioShock does it great.  The game allows you to mix shooting with plasmids (basically magic) to deal more damage or inflict status ailments on your foes.  I admit combat was done better in BioShock 2 and perfected in Infinite, but I can still look back at this one and enjoy it!
But BioShock's real attraction is the narrative which covers mature themes like "Corruption", "Isolation", "Betrayal" and more.  You end up in Rapture, a city under the ocean created to reject society's rules.  Obviously this goes wrong and Rapture becomes a ruined atlantis.  It's your job to get out of this mess, with the help from your pal Atlas.  While the game features linear levels and no replayability story-wise, it's always nice to return to Rapture and try out different plasmids and vary your playstyle.
All in all, BioShock is a classic FPS that has you explore the unknown, face fear and question morality in the best ways possible.  I highly recommend this title!

They don't do any of the genres well, needless to say, but it's interesting! There are some good ideas here, but they're all butchered by awful design details.
I'll break this part into each level, as they're pretty short and simple to review.
In this, you have a space-ship, and 4 "attributes". Fuel, Ammo, Faith, and a Garden (?). The level is just a big square, with asteroids and a huge rotating creature that is invincible. Don't ask questions.
Your objective is to destroy asteroids. They can drop: a bible, ammo, or an enemy -- if you destroy the enemy, you get fuel. When you destroy a big asteroid, it's broken in more, smaller asteroids, and those are the ones that drop something.
Basically, you collect to bible to increase your faith. Your objective is to get your faith up to the Garden number. After you collect a bible, your faith is also increased every second, or so. You lose if you run out of fuel, or ammo.
You can basically get one bible, and then just avoid things, being mostly quiet, not to waste resources.
Getting hit decreases your faith (and maybe increases the Garden level, although I'm not sure).
The brilliant idea to make your Faith be increased after you collect your first bible is this: Each bible gives you a citation, that appears at the bottom of the screen. Reading it, of course, is stupid. You in the middle of a video game, you can't read and shoot at the same time! So, in order for you to read it, they increase your Faith. That way, you can mostly be quiet, and able to read.
...
Let that sink in. That makes absolutely no sense to me. I mean, it's a freaking piece of text, IN THE GAME SCREEN. Why...? N-no. Don't do that, come on. It seems completely out of context as well. Again, remember the NES ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t Bible games and you can probably understand! Oh well.
This is more of a Gradius-like shooter, with a bit of a bullet-hell element.
Your character looks like a small super-hero, with a big tin on your back. I repeat, don't ask questions.
Your hit-box is really small, in the form of a red cross. However, they never explain it, and your character is huge.
The enemies shoot lots of bullets, here, and you'll probably die a lot. It's just a memorization exercise. Once you know the level, you know where the enemies will spawn, and you can play accordingly. You can take 6 hits, but here's the issue:
Yep. I honestly don't understand why that it, but I also didn't take LSD before playing this.
The playing field is also pretty narrow, and the edges hurt you... It's awful. There a bullethell-ish boss fight at the end, but he only has 1 phase, and it's pretty easy to beat.
It sounds mostly really bad so far, right? Well, it is. But the enemies have interesting patterns! I think the level design was pretty good, honestly. Each enemy guided you in a certain way, and it felt satisfying when you beat it. But then, there are all the other issues.
This level is just a 2D platformer. You can walk sideways, and jump. That's all.
...AH! You should never think that with this game. Actually, the level flashes with different colors, and is slowly rotating. Also, your object is to collect "trees" -- as in, crucified Jesuses that give you yet another biblical passage out of nowhere. Here applies the problem with the time to read it being either too short, or too long.
It's easy, though.
I don't want to spoil this. I'm assuming you fight Satan, although I'll never know for sure.
This is another epilepsy-inducing fight, with flashing eye-bullets, and a rotating background. It's a bullet-hell, with a bit hitbox... Don't... ask.
It requires attention, and I died a lot, but it's fairly short, and it didn't get too frustrating, to me.
I don't know what to feel. I mean, the game is clearly awful, despite having a few nice ideas. It's all over the place...
Do NOT buy it. Seriously, it's not worth it, if you're looking for a game to play.
If, however, you've gotten it for free, or you are intentionally looking for one of the weirdest and cheesiest games to play, then sure, give this one a go. It's amusing.

With the very little hours I have in this game, I feel like I still have the right to speak about it. With that being said, let's get into it.
The Forest is a survival horror game that for me is a unique and extremely immersive experience. This game is currently in Alpha and yet doesn't fail to please me at all. While some features are a bit buggy in certain events and the NPC cannibals aren't exactly currently the best AI I've ever seen in a game, with these features improved and fixed upon, the game will have fully immersed me in this world. Maybe if the NPCs acted a bit smarter and more tactical and in a bit more of a scarier way than they currently do, to really make the player feel threatened and scared instead of just mowing down things that are in the way of their objective. With that being said, I'll reinstate that this is alpha and all of this can change in the future, which is what makes the game in it's current state so impressive. Every other feature of the game is highly immersive and when playing I feel engulfed in its world due to all of the open possibilities I have and the sheer interaction possibilities with everything else in the game world. A solid example is the mechanic of having to return to your base to save your game in order to keep your new items collected on your journey, bringing a true sense of accomplishment at the end of every single journey you go on and a nice reminder of the beautiful world the developers have crafted outside of the endless, dark and lonely cave systems filled with cannibals which also contain a wide variety of atmospheric effects to truly make you believe where you are. The graphics are impecable, especially for something on the Unity engine which tends to be underestimated. This combined with good optimisation really sets a good tone for the game and makes it to run extremely well.
There's nothing better with sailing in your raft with the sun settled on the ocean after a long gruesome night of aimlessly wondering through cave systems to find what you were searching for.
I highly recommend buying this title, it truly breaks the "cliche" behind survival horror games these days and brings a true unique sense to it.

Take a game with no color, no dialogue, no 3D, and a musical score so subtle it might as well be ambient noise. In most cases that sounds like a terrible game, but Limbo pulls it off incredibly well. This indie release has received much deserved praise for its simplicity, yet very effective gameplay. I think this game masters one aspect incredibly well, and that is the sound of the environment. Heavy footsteps, loud electrical crackles, and scurrying spider steps all are done to perfection to a point where no background noise is necessary at all. 2-D sidescrollers have been done to death, but Limbo feels almost entirely original because of how it is presented. The plot is very simple and almost doesn't need to exist for this game to work. It is more about the tension, and players will be on edge the first time they play this game. The platforming, with some exceptions, is satisfactory. The game is a bit short, but much like Portal, this game is better because it is shorter, not overstaying its welcome. I did have a few gripes about some of the ludicrous amount of precision required for certain platforming sections, and some false paths will lead you to nowhere except certain death, but all in all it is a unique little platformer that I am glad is in my collection.

Rogue Like Dungeon crawler.
You end up on this planet after "your" (aka the ship you were on as staff or prisoner) prison ship got attacked and destroyed. Dont worry you managed to launch a escape pod and escape death... for now.
Your only option once landed with 2 survivors is to open the door out the unknown... with a minor hope of a ticket somewhere away from this dangerous place.
Economy is split between Four things.
Food to level and heal your heroes.
Science to remove cooldown on abilites or research new modules that will make your journey easier (to make it possible that you might survive without good luck or being veteran to the game)
building material (dont recall correct term) That you build modules that increases one of these three or many minor one with offensive defensive or boosts to the room you build them in.
And finally we have Dust... Your best friend. Without this materia darkness will consume the entire level. Also the merchants love Dust since it is also the currency in this game.
So will you spend some dust to buy a new weapon or armor? Or will you light another room so unknown lurkers cant spawn there to attack you that might occur when you open up yet another door into the unknown? The option is yours, but know this; To many dark rooms will for certain mean a bigger fight once they come... And they will come for either your blood or powercrystal (your dungeonheart where dust is stored).
There is currently a bunch of diffrent unique heroes(more being added all the time), you start with a few ones, all being unique. But during your journey you will run into outsiders, good and twisted characters, all ready to join you up to a party of max 4. Keep them alive for 3 levels and your permantly unlock them for your next round... which open up the game depth even more. The levels is randomized, however the number of doors isnt. (currently)
This game currently in beta, the devs got a very clear structure of what they want to do and they have frequently updates for the game.  You shouldnt be to worried about this game not being finished or ending up as a mess.
Currently the game is fun enough and with more content being added it refreshes the replay value of the game.
I highly doubt you gonna regret getting this game. But if your in doubt, do more research or wait until complete.
Personally I recommend this game.

After crashing on an unknown planet, Nurse Deena Ratchet and genetically engineered warrior Hikensha began working their way through the ship to hope for an escape. Along the way they recruited a young burglar named Golgy Phurtiver who, incidentally, thinks she's a spider of some sort.
Things were going relatively well - Nurse Ratchet discovered a woman in stasis, who was revealed to be a bounty hunter named Sara Numas. They did not know that they were effectively recruiting Hikensha's replacement, however, who died tried to defend another survivor from the alien natives.
The party marched upwards, exploring for every resource they could. Another survivor was revived from stasis, but the mercenary (who dubbed himself "Butcher") was eviscerated by what can only presumed to be giant mutant slugs when making casual conversation with a merchant.
The three survivors, Deena, Golgy and Sara saved the merchant from the rampaging aliens, and quickly cleaned him out of his wares in exchange for the Dust they were using to power their various defenses, just before they moved on up to a new level of what was beginning to feel like a dungeon.
For real though, Dungeon of the Endless does a lot of things right for a... roguelike, resource management 4X, RPG, platypus of a game. And as they're apparently working on multiplayer, I could see this becoming a Thing.

DO NOT PAY FULL PRICE FOR THIS GAME! Wait until you can get a good deal. We all know a solid 33% or 50% steam sale will happen soon enough or, if you're impatient and want the game right now, go to one of the many online VERIFIED Steam retailers that offer the game at a discounted price. I know of one where you can get the game right now for 25% off. This game is not worth paying full price for, especially when you simply don't have to.
That being said, this game is FUN! Don't listen to the people giving this game bad reviews just because they were impatient or too stupid to find a deal and paid full price. That does not a bad game make. Why pay full price when you don't have to?
Now, the people giving this game bad reviews for other reasons, they have their points. There's not a ton of content to this game atm. The number of monsters is limited, the number of playable characters is limited, the number of maps....limited. You get the idea. After you've played the game for a few hours, you'll have experienced most of what there is to experience.
The true value of this game however is the replayability. It's simply fun to play as a giant monster and kill your friends, or to play with your friends to bring down a giant monster. Take turns on which roles to play, cycle out who plays as the monster and have fun with it. When you get tired of playing after a few hours, take a break or play something else. When you and your friends are in the mood again, break out Evolve and kill each other for a few hours of solid entertainment. This brings me to my second point.
This game is BETTER WITH FRIENDS! If you don't have any friends willing to pick up the game and play with you, then purchase at your own risk. Online play with strangers can be fun for a time but it's just SOOOOOO much better playing with your buddies.
TLDR: If you have friends to play with, BUY THIS GAME! Just don't pay full price for it.

However, despite the levels and puzzles being interesting, there is nothing that is keeping me interested in the game at all. There isn't anything that actually motivates you to keep going forward. In Inside, when you see all of those people moving like zombies in the streets, you get interested and want to keep exploring to find out more. However, in this game there is absolutey nothing to interest you. Sure, the world itself looks nice, but there isn't anything actually hapenning in the game that you want to know more about.
There is basically no atmosphere in this game. There is not music, which there doesn't really need to be, but I would think that this game would benefit from it considering that the only other things contributing to building the atmosphere is sound effects from in game objects, like water or saws and the background. Nothing really makes you feel like you're there.
I understand that a game doesn't need all of this stuff that I have said the game was lacking to be enjoyable, but I feel that with this game's gameplay, the lack of atmosphere and interest makes it not worth playing. There is nothing to back up that good gameplay that is in this game.
If you only care about the gameplay in games and absolutely nothing else, then go ahead and buy this game. However, if you actually want the games you play to actually have any substanance to it, then I would refrain from buying this unless there is a very good sale on it.
I honestly wish these Steam reviews had a middle button, like a "meh" option I could choose. Me deciding to say I don't recommend it might make it seem like I'm saying that this game is bad. It's not by any means BAD, I would rate this game a 6/10. I just think it's average.

Game starts up in fullscreen, no video options on menu. Just start, continue, exit.
Edit : I've since come back and spent more time with the game. I'm going to say that it's worth the 2 or so dollars it is right now, but i'm still not compelled to beat it.
Effectively the game is Knytt, but with some really janky combat and much...stickier controls.
The way the auto-wallrun / grab and ascend ledge was done feels incredibly stiff. In fact, just about everything in the game feel stiff.
Like knytt, the game has no camera movement. You move from screen to screen, find rather unobvious keys and put them into a door to open up more paths.  There's an incredible amount of backtracking throughout all the areas i've been in, and all the enemies seem to take random amounts of damage to kill. sometimes it's one kick, sometimes it's seven. I don't get how it works.
There's also this really annoying quirk, where if you're sliding down a wall and reach the bottom, he flings himself away from the wall and down. There are quite a few spikes around to kill you for this, and it just seems like a control quirk designed to be  annoying.
On the whole i've seen 3 tilesets that all look very similar, maybe 2 similar floating enemies, 3 similar walking enemies, and some timed instant death hazards.
And one 'boss'. It never attacked me, and took about 20 hits to kill. It opened up the next area, full of  moving turrets that shoot when you're in their line of sight.
The audio is real weak. The sound effects are, from what i can tell, all sfxr fare you've heard 1000 times before, and has no personality. The music is modern synth, with pads and such doing a very
well, Knytt-like thing. None of it stands out to me, and on the whole it's pretty forgettable.
The visual design is cluttered. No one seems to have told the dev how important it is to clearly lable collidable surfaces versus the background. Numerous foreground elements are colored with the exact same textures as walls you can interact with. Grabbable ledges along the background are colored exactly like walkable platforms. Enemy bullets are red, even in rooms made of red metal.
It's pretty disappointing overall, but hey, it's 2 bucks.
I'd recommend it, if you really, really like games like knytt i guess.

The game is also a bit old, I mean, 2007 is a long time ago, so using it on Windows 10 is a bit of a pain, since you need to edit properties and run it in windowed mode to function properly. And the sound likes to cut out whenever there's multiple things at the same time making sounds.

Quite possibly the best game you can spend $15 on and arguably the best game on Steam. And in my honest opinion it is the best zombie survival game in existence. But let me get this out of the way. If your ideal zombie game was Left 4 Dead or Killing Floor, then this might not be the game for you. (although I'm not saying those are bad games) The sheer realism and rogue-like elements will keep your full attention even when performing a repetitive task (which will not happen often, depending on how you play) The game is still in Alpha stages, so there are a few bugs here and there but they are hardly transparent or noticable and the game has felt complete since the day I bought it. Remember one thing: death is real in this game. If you get bitten, you are infected. There is no cure. Unless you adjusted the zombies in the custom sandbox. (wuss) There is no saving. Once you are dead, the most you can do is create a new character in that world. Whom will also die eventually. Until then, just focus on scavenging, building, crafting, and fighting off the undead. I noticed that a few of the survival mechanics could use some tweaking, and the game can be a bit overwhelming to get started in but this definitely isn't a game that you will need to wait until it's full release to actually enjoy. I can't wait to see what's to come!
