Back before the turn of the century, I had access to free roaming satellite television stations, the kind you could only watch by using one of the old ten-foot diameter dish setups.  On one of the far ends of the dial there was a station called "Network 1".  In the evenings it would show little more than bad B movies, randomly placed 90's music videos, and terribly dubbed 80's anime.  Plus, nearly all the commercials were advertizements for phone chat 1-900 numbers.  It was badly done and amateurish, but it was one of the most fun stations I've ever watched.  It felt raw and unregulated, like I was watching something made from an underground entertainment industry, never intended to be seen by the general public.  The kind of place where cult classics are born.  I couldn't help but enjoy it, simply because it felt so unrepentantly wild.  There is freedom in witnessing something that is not bound by the constraints of normal behavior, even if you aren't a part of it.
Uriel's Chasm reminded me very much of Network 1.  It's strange in a way that a VAST majority of the people who play it will not enjoy.  However, if you're able to appreciate the fact that this game includes a space nun who strapped a giant tank full of DMT to her back in order to rocket into another plane of reality, possibly even into the mind of God, then I would encourage you to play it.

One of the things that you would have to say, first off, is that the game is not yet complete - which is actually not a bad thing. There is a certain charm in having to witness a game being developed and you having the chance to contribute to the end product. The developers set up a really good system for early access players to vote, comment and suggest elements to the game the might make it a better experience.
The game, in it's incompleteness, already boasts a lot of promise. The concept is a tight weaving of several game elements into one neat package. It's a Rogue-Like Dungeon Crawler, with a dash of role-playing customization and turn-based, strategic tower defense gameplay. You get to play with two to four randomly thrown-in heroes who must make their way through the a randomly generated dungeon, in hopes of moving a precious cargo onto the next level. The progress is segmented by several doors that you choose to open or leave alone depending on your conceived strategy.
You manage four resources such as Food, Industry, Science, and Dust to make your way to find the exit. These are basically the things that you need to upgrade your heroes, build and upgrade defense.
Turns are based on the opening of doors - they serve us passages to the next area and the indication of the passage of time. (Skill cool down is based on it) Doors are basically the whole gamble of the game as they open to both treasures and threats (and ultimately the level's exit.) The more doors and rooms unlocked the more areas where mobs of monsters can come crawling from. Do you cut through one specific path or open several in all directions? The journey is always different as your heroes are always different and the layouts are always unique.
The game is packaged neatly into a very simplistic art style - who would have thought that pixels could be very sexy? Soundtrack is very subtle, giving the game an eerie and gloomy feel to it. It's topped off with simple click ( and hotkey) controls and user interface. The game is really focused on your management of resource, ultimately leading to the survival of our small band quirky heroes.
Set as a prequel to the Endless Game series, I can't really say much about the story or lore. But the character profiles, skills, and even weapons are written with much wit -- that a piece of clothing or weaponry is a laugh on its own.
If you're looking for a game which has multiple layers of strategy and decision-making involved, with enough randomness to keep you trying and playing, then this title is for you. Get the game now, and get involved, and play.

First Impression Review
So I have a couple of hours under my belt in this new instalment and figured it's time to give you guys some feedback. I will update this later after a couple of full seasons.
Is this game fun? Yeah I would say so. If you like Motogp then it does what it needs to (just).
Is it much of an upgrade to Motogp 14? Nope, not really. Cosmetics and small tweaks only (so far).
Should the die-hard Motogp fans buy it? Absolutely, it has a nice feel to it and obviously it is updated with this seasons riders and such. It is still very much lacking in features that other driving sims have, hell even other sport games. But for the motogp series, it is slowly getting better...very slowly though.
Should casual players buy it? That depends on if they have any previous instalments of the game. If they have 2014 I would say no, wait for next year. It is another of those games that only get small adjustments each year so just buy every other one or grab it on a 50% sale later in the year. I do not honestly think It is worth shelling out all that cash each year for a casual player on a game that always seems much like it could just be a DLC to the previous year.
Pro's
The bikes seem to be a little bit more responsive this year in cornering(motogp at least), it is fun to leave some black lines out of corners and pull wheelies on the  moto3 bikes. Nothing you would really notice unless you have played motogp 14 within the last couple of days but it is there.
Slight wind wobble on the camera at high speeds, that seems to have been updated for this year and gives it a more realistic feel.
Custom bikes in career mode. It's not all singing and all dancing but it's about time we got this feature.
Seeing dry lines appear towards the end of a drying out qualifying session is nice. Yeah it may be 2015 and this should not be a surprise in this day and age but it still gave me a little lip curl.
Con's
The AI seem to fall off very easily if you bump them. I have noticed this while giving the game a try on medium AI so I will update this a little more when I try out the pro settings a little later.
It really isn't the best racing sim out there, it's more aimed at giving the motogp gearheads their fix for the year and making milestone some money. The same company also make Ride and the MXGP games and they are all pretty poor bike sims so dont get your hopes up for an amazing game.
My rider looks way too shiny in the wet. Graphics wise this game is still pretty poor, I don't see much of a difference on last years edition and some tracks look pretty empty.
Some strange sound effects... like crashing for instance, it just doesnt sound like it should.
--
All in all, Milestone need a good kick in the butt. Motogp still doesn't have a brilliant game like it should. If you like Motogp you will enjoy playing this game. It is not total crap like some would say but it is not much of an improvement on last year, just as last year was not much better than 2013. For me, it feeds my need for bike racing and as I said before, if you are a casual player, just buy it on a sale or every other year.
For what this game is, i would say 8/10 this year. Milestone need to try harder next year though.

I generally avoid horror games as I am not really into scary games but this point & click style survival horror game kept me coming back. In the game you are a security guard tasked with overseeing several animatronics out to get you, and using methods such as looking at cameras and closing doors the player must survive from 12-6AM for 5 days. The game becomes progressively harder as the nights go on and the intensity increases exponentially. Although most jump scares are a cheap way to terrorize the player and occur randomely FNaF uses them in a unique way. The jump scares do not occur randomely and only happen if the player has failed in maintaining an eye on the animatronics and allowed them to sneak up on him/her. The game may seem unfair at times however with a chance of dying randomely and no way of preventing that in the alter nights. Aside from being unfair at time the game maintains a spooky atmosphere while also being fun to play. The game has replay value with a bonus night and custom nights. Overall

I played through a few hours of mild disappointment, thinking I would just beat it and be done.  I had cleared 3 of 5 islands at this point, and had quickly come to expect nothing but more of the same monotonous slog of gameplay from beginning to end.
So I go to the West island and... my boat dock procedurally generated right into a sheer cliff's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.  No matter, I shrug it off, as I just finished the mountain island and learned you can jump up about any embankment.  At the top of this one was one of the Mysterious Fragments, and some robuts wandering about.  HOWEVER, I must have been wearing a stovepipe tophat I was unaware of, as one of them saw me, behind some thick grass hanging off the edge of a cliff.  After I use my last marshmellow ammo on them, I sigh and reload.  Walking up the dock to bang my head against this, not the first nor last samey, mind-numbing obstacle in this game, a bundle of those robot arms that sprout from water shoot up THROUGH THE DOCK. This game becomes repetitive really quickly and doesn't have enough content in it to make it worthwhile the amount of time it'd take to finish it. You have to find pieces scattered around generated islands and bring them back to the starting position to do 'something' (What that something is I don't know, I never finished it). As you progress new enemies will appear that will ramp up the difficulty. The way I see it this game has 3 main elements, combat, stealth and exploration.
The exploration aspect of the game is extremely lacking as there is rarely anything interesting to find. Just more and more houses to scavenge for supplies and the occasional 'something' piece. You can find diaries and stuff that help you understand the setting but they are rare'ish loot and without them there is barely any kind of narrative. It's just not fun to explore because there is nothing worth finding. Just more random houses that does nothing.
The combat in the game is boring, I understand that it is not meant to be a combat oriented game and that you need to preserve your resources in order to survive long-term, but whenever combat 'does' happen it is extremely clunky. I ended up just sitting behind a wall and then waiting for a robot to pop around the corner so I could blow the head off and that's it. There are traps you can use (which are especially useful for the robot dogs) but the enemies might not walk into a trap and then you might be♥♥♥♥♥♥out of luck.
And finally, the stealth, in order to not attract attention you need to sneak around sometimes but when you progress far enough into the game it becomes a necessity to stealth in order to avoid being cluster♥♥♥♥ed by dogs. The problem? It's a sandbox world where you have to travel large distances. It isn't fun to move the speed of a slug when all you want to is to just get another damn 'something' piece. The stealth works well enough on its own merits but the problem is the amount of distance you need to travel 'and' the necessity to use stealth. It becomes tedious real fast.
The setting is really interesting, the enemies are well designed, the concept behind stealthing around and using resources is great. But the gameplay is boring, repetitive and tedious.
What the game needs is a stronger narrative, it needs to ditch the generated islands in favor for consistent set-pieces, it needs to polish the resources system, the healing system and the combat system. It needs to have something more worthwhile to find while exploring, like unique mini-bosses, NPC's, locations, puzzles and traps. And it needs to ditch the extremely repetitive "Fetch 24 'something' pieces" for a more clear and focused story.
If a sequel does what I just suggested then I'm definitely getting it. But 'this' game? It ain't worth it. Even on sale.

Very solid game thus far. It has a strange mixture of serenity and suspense, making you appreciate the scenery one minute and feel complete and utter desperation the next. It is still in Early Access and it's clear many features and mechanics need refurbishing or fine-tuning, and the story mode hasn't been completed yet either. However, this game is already a blast to play. I enjoy the crafting system, the exploration, tracking animals, the good feeling when I recognize a place. I also like how I, perhaps implicitly, make certain choices which later turn out to affect me negatively. For example, packing light for a trip can go wrong when the player isn't successful in fending off a wolf attack. Good luck fixing torn clothing without cloth or a sewing kit. I also like that however I plan my day, the game can always find a way to make me have to reconsider my plans by throwing a gale or heavy fog in my face. It's deliciously frustrating and extremely rewarding at the same time. The soundtrack in the game is an added bonus. It is beautiful.
Pros:
- immersive experience
- realistic feeling
- unpredictable how each day will progress (especially early on when you lack clothing and tools)
- several difficulty levels (it is not easy!)
- crafting system (making a bow for hunting purposes is awesome)
- strangely beautiful even though the graphics are not high-end
- no map or HUD
- replayability value
- beautiful music
- (Jennifer Hale)
Cons:
- still contains many graphical glitches and bugs
- items could be more diverse
- graphics could be better (fe. showing hands when you're holding a gun)

Please do read my review before purchasing this game, as this will guide you through what wonder Uriel's Chasm is.
You might be quick to toss this game aside as "just another cheap prodigy" of no real use, but I must admit that this game is one of the most unique in it's genre. Not only is it made very professionally and with care, this makes about any game from the publishers Electronic Arts look like rubbish. What you're about to purchase is a true masterpiece, I'm just going to go through the wonders of this game with a short list:
* The Intro
As you're opening the game, you'll encounter this very well animated 3D video that gives you an almost 6D experience of two girls discussing the state of the world in a very exciting yet academic manner that makes you want to play this game immediately. You're met with a lot of dialogue that is crafted intelligently which in result makes you eager to continue playing this game. As your hands are shaking, let me go further into my review.
* The graphics
Now this is a wonder to itself. Don't you think some games are just too sharp and it's a little boring how you can identify every lamp from a donut? Well this game fixes this problem. As you're going through the mindblowing and visually stunning experience in this game, you're met with various times where you're simply asking yourself "So was that a space ship, or just a huge floating undefined pixel I just went by right there?" and there's more. When you reach the point a couple times in the game when you're dying there will be an explosion. Animations? Overrated. A yellow splur of pixel is enough to indicate what's going on and this game gets it! Who needs welldefined animations to explain what we already know?
* The storyline
This game is actionpacked so much that I'ma have to write a novel on this. At first playthrough I was shedding a small tear as I was getting hit by a huge donut. Or well, an asteroid but as I wrote in the graphics part it's kinda hard to differ which makes this game so unique. You have to achieve faith before the garden erases you. Faith in what you might ask? Well, that's another part where this game is very ambigious in a mysterious and sexy way that is exactly enough to not make it seem pretentious and fake. Exactly where you're destined to, and what happens when you finally achieve more faith than the garden is a wonderful mystery too, as your spaceship will probably turn into a huge splur of yellow pixels before you reach the goal of this game, and the best part is that you will have no clue what happened as the donut, asteroid, and background fades into the background which in turn creates this wonderful visual masterpiece I already went through in the graphics section.
* The music
Ah, my favourite part. This makes Mozart and Beethoven crumble in shame as the sounds are vastly comparable to the highlights of the four seasons but just a tad better than that. You'll find yourself in a personal peaceful space as you open the game and listen to the wonderful melodies that neither The Legend of Zelda or Super Mario's tunes in any sense can compare with.
10/10 would buy again 3 times along with 7 copies for my friends. You will never regret this purchase.

A very cutesy 3D puzzle platformer with some barebones hack and slash combat. The game is rather short and can be beaten in an afternoon, and while I don't think it gives a lasting impression it had a nice story and some interesting puzzles.
It didn't hold any real challenge for me outside of some of the later puzzles and the combat felt a little wonky and repetitive, however that also makes it easy to pick up and play and more accessable to casual players. Due to the cute art direction, the story that could have been taken straight out of a fairy-tail and the very child-like voice acting, I believe this game could be very appealing to younger audiences.
I recommend this game to anyone looking for a gift for a younger family member, perhaps as something a parent could play with their child and help them with some of the more difficult puzzles. It does have some minor cartoon violence but delivers a good message and I think it could be good for improving problem-solving skills. Outside of that though, I'd say pick this up only if you're looking for a short puzzle game with a cute asthetic.

If I could give sort of a mixed opinion about this game, I would. It's one thing to say this game is bad, but it's not that great either.
For the most part, Echo of Soul plays out like your average tab-target MMO where you go around questing, leveling, etc. What separates this game from its other competitors is its focus on its endgame content, which happens at level 60. The entry barrier for getting to 60 is pretty low and you'll find the path to leveling is pretty simple. However, the moment you hit 60, you'll feel like you're starting at level 1 again. You have to grind your way up the gear ladder just to be able to run party dungeons efficiently, and PVP is not exactly a good option entering level 60 due to a number of powerful players.
This is all due to the game's inherent jewel system. The idea of jewels was pretty neat when you're introduced to it around level 15. These jewels enhance your stats and can be combined to form stronger jewels, which can be inserted into sockets on your equipment. While the jewels had a chance to break after a certain point, the game gave you a decent amount of jewels as you leveled, so there was always a steady form of progression in the form of jewels and gear. However, this was all thrown out the window and slows to a halt at level 60, mainly due to the game's separation of jewels into two tiers: dull (used from levels 1-59) and lucid (used at level 60). A fresh player will enter level 60 feeling much weaker than before, as the enemies' power suddenly spikes up as you're forced to trudge through this initial stage of endgame and progression slows down considerably.
The biggest problem here is time. As you play, you WILL get everything you need, but that depends on how much time you're willing to invest. Without friends or a nice guild helping you out, you're pretty much stuck grinding some boring dungeons until you can get more these lucid jewels for upgrading your character. The cash shop has a few time-savers that more serious players would consider investing into, from safeguards to prevent jewels from breaking when upgrading and pets that can loot items for you. I do recommend trying to play without spending on these premium items, as they're pretty unnecessary if you can play smart and try to be as self-sufficient as possible.
Other than my personal gripe with lucid jewels and the beginning of level 60, the PVE gameplay is pretty good. Questing from 1-59 was a breeze for me and once I managed to gather up some gear at level 60, the party dungeons have been fun to run through thanks to the dungeon mechanics keeping players in check. PVP from 1-59 can be pretty fun and has normalized stats to keep it in check, but I suggest staying away from level 60 PVP unless you manage to gather a lot of lucid jewels.
If you're looking for a decent F2P MMO like WoW, EoS might be a good game to check out, but I wouldn't recommend it to everyone.

So, you've always asked yourself ''how long would I survive in a zombie apocalypse?'' and you've at some point had that conversation with your friends. Well this game is the ultimate Zombi Apocalypse Survival Simulator. With new content being added on a regular basis and things being teased (NPC's, Cars, new areas) you can't help but want to keep playing.
It's a hard game to get used to, and the beginners mode is definetely a great thing to start with on your first real run through yet juming straight to the real experience...It's definetely a challenge. I can't even survive the night no matter what defenses I try to build, amount of food I have or weapons I can scavenge.
With awesome mechanics like crafting, combining, cooking, gardening and a skill levelling system (e.g Blunt Accuracy, Sprinting, Foraging etc.) you always feel like you're going to get stronger the next day. Before you even consider starting the apocalypse, a trait system is there after you create your survivor to spice things up a bit.
Trying to push yourself to survive that extra night is always a challenge, because you will die and its going to happen a lot.
The fact you can get panicked, nervous, bored, tired, hungry, thirsty and more, is just amazing. If you've ever thought how you think you'd do solo in a zombie apocalypse, definetely buy this game. Don't let the graphics fool you, because you don't give a damn how the game looks once you're into it.
Only negative is when you find items you know you can use to build stuff with and the game doesnt allow it because it hasn't been put in the game yet. It is rather frustrating but if you thought of it, I'm pretty sure the developers have too.

Red Orchestra 2 is a game created by Tripwire that was released in 2011 on UE3. The game is set in WW2 on the eastern front, hence the name Red Orchestra.
To put it simply, it's a hardcore version of Battlefield. It's possible to kill anyone with a shot to the head or torso. Other than that the game is 32v32, features a ticket system from battlefield and most maps have a "rush" like game mode. That said, the games are very different, and that's mostly due to the fact how easy it is to die in Red Orchestra. This game forces you to think differently.
In this game, you never run in the open in full height for example. You always go from cover to cover, preferably crouched. When you find a shooting position, you should try to have as much of your body behind cover. Really, in a lot of ways the game makes you feel as if you are in a real war, cause everybody will be acting as if they are in one.
I suppose your first question is whether it is fun? It is in it's own right. It's quite a unique experience.
Usually most maps are played with Attacker/Defender style. Defenders are given a few points on the map at a time, and must hold them. If they lose them, they get pushed back, and would have to defend a new set of points. Sort of like rush, except that you have flags instead.
Unlike battlefield, the capture points are very big. Let's say the attackers need to take point, which happens to be a house - the capture point is the whole house. Why am i bringing it up? Cause i want to talk about camping. It's a tactic that will be commonly seen among defenders, but it's not your typical camping. You do not just sit in the corner. You have to correctly disperse your forces to fend off the attackers, and usually you are also given 2 points to defend at once.
Attackers have it much harder on them, since they actually have to advance to win, but they also get more tickets.
The game also has a very minimal UI. It's practically only your eyes and ears - no minimaps, no names over targets. In fact, friendly fire is turned on all servers, so one of the first things a beginner must do, is learn the difference between russians/germans and americans/japanese (their uniform).
RO2 does some things much better than Battlefield, for example classes. Each team has 1 commander, and multiple squads made of 10 players. A squad has squad leader and he acts as a mobile spawn point to his squad mates. Usually a team is given 4 squads. Yes, that's 40+ slots for 32 players - it was done on purpose. A team gets 1 team leader, 4 squad leaders, 4 machine gunners, 6 assault (automatic weapons), 1 sniper, a few more elite assault and elite riflemen, and the rest are normal riflemen. You cannot make everyone in your game medics, engineers, snipers etc. Instead there are roles, that increase in complexity.
Normal riflemen have bolt action rifles, which are inferior to everything else in the game due to their fire rate, and pretty much 75% of the players will be playing as them.
Elite riflemen have semi-auto weapons. Assault and elite assault have automatics. Each has their own role in the game that they must fulfill. These guys are there to fight in close quarters on the objective.
Machine gunners are another class with automatic weapons, but they cannot aim with their machine gun until they station it - making them very inaccurate for close quarters, but good for defense. Their greatest strength is that they can shoot 50-200 rounds before having to reload.
Usually a team gets 1-4 snipers max (depends on the map), and these are used to take out important roles such as team leaders, squad leaders and machine gunners. Unlike other roles, they can't spawn on the squad leader, so if they die, they will have to make it all the way from the base to the frontline.
Squad leaders are a mobile spawn point for the 9 players in his team. It's very important for them to survive. Other than that they are the only role that has smoke grenades, which are commonly used in this game to block vision for the enemy and allow your men to charge in. They also have binoculars, which they can use to mark points on the map for artillery.
Team leader is the one that is calling in artillery basically. He actually has the same gear as the squad leader - a sub machine gun, smoke grenades, he can mark with his binoculars as well, but he requires to be next to radios to do his job, like for calling artillery. The radios themselves are located on certain point on the map, and usually they are not where the action is.
Some maps also feature tanks, and with them they bring engineers and AT gunners. Engineers are basically allowed to choose the gear that elite riflemen or assault use, and they get anti tank grenades. But their main job is to destroy obstructions, like tank barriers. AT gunners on other hand get a big anti material rifle, but just like machine gunners they have to station it.
Like i said, it also gives you great immersion, but it's more than what i described. There are a lot of things in the game that improve immersion even more. Stuff like this for example.
They modeled the whole interior of the tank, and even added animations for the crew members.
A bit about tanks themselves. This is no battlefield - the tank can fit 2-4 crew members depending on the tank. Unlike battlefield again, the driver only does the driving for example. He has a very limited view by the way, as you can see over here.
Usually there is a tank commander, a turret gunner and an MG gunner. There is also a loader who is played by AI, but you can replace him if he dies. Not all tanks are the same though. They are like 4 currently - Panzer IV and T-34 were available on release, but Panzer III and a 2 seated T-70 were added later on.
That said, unlike red orchestra 1, there is a lack of tank battles. There are only 3 maps for huge tank battles. Most of the time the tank is used to support the infantry.
UI is very minimal as well. There is no indicators of how much ammo you have in your rifle for example. But you can check that by holding R, and your character will physically unbolt the rifle and check it. Little things like that make it very immersive.
In 2013, Rising Storm was released - an expansion to RO2. It's set in the pacific and features american and japanese. It's basically the same game, except without tanks and it's asymmetric. Meaning one side is better than the other - americans get auto and semi auto weapons, while most of the japanese roles have bolt action rifles. Americans also get flamethrowers.
It's a nice challenge for more experienced players and it's a great place to start learning the game. You also don't have to own the expansion to join the servers - the game allows people to play as a normal rifleman if they don't own it.

DO NOT PAY FULL PRICE FOR THIS GAME! Wait until you can get a good deal. We all know a solid 33% or 50% steam sale will happen soon enough or, if you're impatient and want the game right now, go to one of the many online VERIFIED Steam retailers that offer the game at a discounted price. I know of one where you can get the game right now for 25% off. This game is not worth paying full price for, especially when you simply don't have to.
That being said, this game is FUN! Don't listen to the people giving this game bad reviews just because they were impatient or too stupid to find a deal and paid full price. That does not a bad game make. Why pay full price when you don't have to?
Now, the people giving this game bad reviews for other reasons, they have their points. There's not a ton of content to this game atm. The number of monsters is limited, the number of playable characters is limited, the number of maps....limited. You get the idea. After you've played the game for a few hours, you'll have experienced most of what there is to experience.
The true value of this game however is the replayability. It's simply fun to play as a giant monster and kill your friends, or to play with your friends to bring down a giant monster. Take turns on which roles to play, cycle out who plays as the monster and have fun with it. When you get tired of playing after a few hours, take a break or play something else. When you and your friends are in the mood again, break out Evolve and kill each other for a few hours of solid entertainment. This brings me to my second point.
This game is BETTER WITH FRIENDS! If you don't have any friends willing to pick up the game and play with you, then purchase at your own risk. Online play with strangers can be fun for a time but it's just SOOOOOO much better playing with your buddies.
TLDR: If you have friends to play with, BUY THIS GAME! Just don't pay full price for it.

Very solid game thus far. It has a strange mixture of serenity and suspense, making you appreciate the scenery one minute and feel complete and utter desperation the next. It is still in Early Access and it's clear many features and mechanics need refurbishing or fine-tuning, and the story mode hasn't been completed yet either. However, this game is already a blast to play. I enjoy the crafting system, the exploration, tracking animals, the good feeling when I recognize a place. I also like how I, perhaps implicitly, make certain choices which later turn out to affect me negatively. For example, packing light for a trip can go wrong when the player isn't successful in fending off a wolf attack. Good luck fixing torn clothing without cloth or a sewing kit. I also like that however I plan my day, the game can always find a way to make me have to reconsider my plans by throwing a gale or heavy fog in my face. It's deliciously frustrating and extremely rewarding at the same time. The soundtrack in the game is an added bonus. It is beautiful.
Pros:
- immersive experience
- realistic feeling
- unpredictable how each day will progress (especially early on when you lack clothing and tools)
- several difficulty levels (it is not easy!)
- crafting system (making a bow for hunting purposes is awesome)
- strangely beautiful even though the graphics are not high-end
- no map or HUD
- replayability value
- beautiful music
- (Jennifer Hale)
Cons:
- still contains many graphical glitches and bugs
- items could be more diverse
- graphics could be better (fe. showing hands when you're holding a gun)

Not recommending this game makes me sad.  SUPERHOT is a really unique premise that's let down by way too high a price for how little content there is.  This was my first time playing through the main "campaign" if you can call it that and I beat it in 1 hour and 50 minutes with 10 mins or so of that time probably being just me sitting on the menu chatting with a friend on steam.  So it's not like I went into this being a pro or anything; if I could beat this in less than 2 hours on a first run (and this is with me messing around every few level) I can't even imagine how short this game would be if I tried to speedrun/replay it.
If this game goes on sale for $5-$10; absolutely buy it.  But for $25 or even $15 honestly less than 2 hours of gameplay is pretty bad.
My only somewhat strong complaint on the "gameplay" side of things are the collisions.  Bullets and melee attacks very often can just clip right through walls podiums etc leading to some pretty cheap and lame deaths, I even exploited this once just by sitting behind a podium and punching the enemies through the concrete on the other side as they lined up for me.  Sometimes when you throw an object at an enemy (this is supposed to stun them briefly) the object will just bounce off instead of breaking against them and stunning them which was pretty frustrating every time it happened to me.  My only other minor gripes are that about 3/4 of the way though SUPERHOT gives you an ability that honestly just makes the game way too easy and that about halfway through the story just kinda starts to write itself into a corner and I can't help but feel as though it isn't as smart as it thinks it is.  Again though these are all minor gripes and in no way influnce me not recommending the game.
If price isn't an issue for you I would say you should buy it but personally for me unless the developer adds some free DLC or updates that expand the game in a meaningul way I would prefer to spend my cash on something I could get more mileage out of.

As of this review, I've only got one hour in gameplay. However, after having completed that hour, I am quite sure that one hour is all that is required to get the full understanding of this game, or at least enough to leave a review.
You play as a King and have to keep in balance the Church, the People, the Military, and the Coffers. Reaching 0 or 100 of any of these four will result in the death of the King. The goal is to complete certain short-term objectives but ultimately to simply reach the high score by reigning as long as possible. Your reign conists of certain persons approaching you with a question, a problem, or an offer, and so on, and you have to "swipe right" or "swipe left", simply choosing between the two options.
PROS:
+Simple, but good-quality entertainment
+Funny
+Dark af
+Good writing, if simple
+Enough to keep your attention
CONS:
-Perhaps too simple
-Eventually will get repetative
- It can sometimes be hard to follow and keep up with everyone and everything

The Expendabros is a strange little curiosity.
Developed to promote the action film
, Devolver Digital's tie-in game puts you in the shoes of the "Expendabros" as you tromp through jungles, destroying everything in your path as you try to stop your former mentor Conrad Stonebanks from taking over the world.
Just another day in the life of a Bro.
Based off both the film and its parent game,
, this is a short little campaign that introduces new characters and some remixed levels. You play through two "stages" from the main game as the characters from the film, who play almost identically to the original Bros.
is an interesting game, in that it functions as a movie tie-in, a standalone expansion and teaser for both the film and game. There's a self-contained plot that utilizes short cutscenes, a couple of contextual prompts and some slightly remixed level elements to create an experience that is worth checking out at least once.
If you're interested in trying out
(or even if you have the game), it's worth giving this a spin. It's free, short (my playthrough took only half-an-hour) and has a decent amount of fun.
Well worth a look.

Cuphead is a aesthetic platformer that focuses on bosses, while there is a few platforming stages, the bosses are the meat of the game and what people remember from it.
The game is visually amazing, the setting and environments all are based on the "golden age of animation" from the 1930s. While nothing is a direct rip off of any existing real character, they are so well done they could totally pass for real characters from that time. It pretty much never leaves this style either, no power or effect used contrasts this style so it flows seamlessly, Its absolutely gorgeous.
As far as the controls to the game go it all feels fairly responsive and it all works, you have a decently wide range of shot types and powers so you can go at a boss with a different style if one is not working, and there are multiple charms to make use of that also can completely change how you go at bosses, be it aggressively or defensively. You do need to make use of these styles as well because one style wont work on some bosses at least to the most effective level. Lastly the game uses what it calls a "parry" system, which more accurately is a guard absorb, any shots or attacks that are pink can be parried to destroy the object and gain special meter, learning and mastering this is required in this game.
The Game boasts 19 bosses, each with their own styles of attack and themes, all the bosses attacks lend to their designs, some of their specials you see if playing on regular or expert get a little weird (A queen bee turning into a "buzzbomber" GET IT!?) but it still is enjoyable to fight all of it. Some bosses you have to fight in a 2d shooter mode as an airplane which were my least favorite parts of the game simply because there wasn't any variation to how you can configure your character going in, so they are only fought one way. Still I say "least" but they were still enjoyable, just the weakest part of the fun.
Cuphead is a game that has a reputation. People compare it to being the "Souls" of platforming. I more compare it to being the "Mirror's Edge" of platforming. The patterns are simplistic enough that anyone can eventually beat the game, but you'll always lament that stupid hit you took. So much like mirrors edge it makes you compelled to have the perfect run with flow unbroken. That might be the biggest secret to the game design, the patterns seem extremely overwhelming at first but then you slowly realize just how simple they are, much like the animation of the time.
Overall the game is very fun and I reccommend it, but even when I say the patterns are simplistic there is some skill demand in this game and I don't recommend it if you struggle at platformers on the whole. Overall though you can't really go wrong with this game, its a fun ride and with simplistic mode to learn the patterns and the heart upgrades anyone can at least beat the game.

"Hello, hello, hello? Uh, hey, welcome to your new job at Freddy Fazbear's Pizza, where kids and grown-ups alike, where fantasy and fun come to life. Fazbear entertainement is not responsible for death or disembarressment in the workplace..."
Five Nights at Freddy's is an indie horror game by Scott Cawthon, where you assume the role of a night watchman at Freddy Fazbear's Pizza, the Chuck E. Cheese's out of hell.
You work from 12-6AM, watching cameras and defending yourself from the animatronic characters is means necassary.
Oh yeah, I didn't mention that...
The animatronics here are possessed by the souls of dead kids who were murdered at Freddy's in 1985. The killer hid thier bodies in th animatronic suits, and they were possessed.
The four chacracters are:
Freddy Fazbear
Bonnie the Bunny
Chica the Chicken
Foxy the Pirate Fox (One of the most unique names I've encontered in awhile...)
Anyway, the animatronics (kids) work hard in the day, and want to be left alone at night. However, your distrubing thier rest, and they want you OUTTA THERE! So, they roam the halls of the resturant during the night, hunting down anyone whom dare disturb thier "Happiest Day".
To defend yourself from meeting a painful death, you must watch the cameras to see where the robots are, check the lights ooutside your office to see if thier about to come in and attack, and if they are, shut the security doors. You must do this whilst not using up all the resturants power. Thier on budget cuts, so they cant spend a fourtune on electircity. Using the cameras, lights and doors will use your power up, aswell as a fan which you cant turn off...(grr, I hate that fan) This gameplay mechanic makes the game extrememley difficult in the later nights, as the robots will show up at your doors more often, using up the power. So, its mostly stratergy, but I cant help but feel that its also partially down to luck in the later nights.
But, I would now like to point out the part where Five Nights at Freddy's really shines through...
Lore.
This game has one of the biggest, most complex storylines I've ever seen. This is expanded upon in the various sequels.  a novel adaptation was also made and a movie is in the works by Warner Bros. If you like big lores, secrets and YouTube theroising, Five Nights at Freddy's is perfect for you!
Overall, Five Nights at Freddy's is a fun, enjoyable little game with a big, BIG backstory. There is a massive community and the game went viral very quickly and stayed that way for over a year. There is now:
3 sequels with another one in development for release in Fall 2016
A cutesy JRPG spin-off
An offical 464 page novel written by the developer
A bunch of merchendise
Massive community
Movie adaptation in the works by Warner Bros.
One more thing...

I have no idea why this has such a bad metacritic score. Maybe im fanboying here, but this game is awesome if you play it the right way.

I have to mention, I don't use the save-function. I play 'hardcore' which adds some more of the survival instinct and makes me overthink my actions. As the maps are all random generated, it makes sense to start over from a whole new map.

This game is brilliant. You really, really should try it if you like the thrill of survival and discovering the mysterious unknown.

Red Orchestra 2 is a game created by Tripwire that was released in 2011 on UE3. The game is set in WW2 on the eastern front, hence the name Red Orchestra.
To put it simply, it's a hardcore version of Battlefield. It's possible to kill anyone with a shot to the head or torso. Other than that the game is 32v32, features a ticket system from battlefield and most maps have a "rush" like game mode. That said, the games are very different, and that's mostly due to the fact how easy it is to die in Red Orchestra. This game forces you to think differently.
In this game, you never run in the open in full height for example. You always go from cover to cover, preferably crouched. When you find a shooting position, you should try to have as much of your body behind cover. Really, in a lot of ways the game makes you feel as if you are in a real war, cause everybody will be acting as if they are in one.
I suppose your first question is whether it is fun? It is in it's own right. It's quite a unique experience.
Usually most maps are played with Attacker/Defender style. Defenders are given a few points on the map at a time, and must hold them. If they lose them, they get pushed back, and would have to defend a new set of points. Sort of like rush, except that you have flags instead.
Unlike battlefield, the capture points are very big. Let's say the attackers need to take point, which happens to be a house - the capture point is the whole house. Why am i bringing it up? Cause i want to talk about camping. It's a tactic that will be commonly seen among defenders, but it's not your typical camping. You do not just sit in the corner. You have to correctly disperse your forces to fend off the attackers, and usually you are also given 2 points to defend at once.
Attackers have it much harder on them, since they actually have to advance to win, but they also get more tickets.
The game also has a very minimal UI. It's practically only your eyes and ears - no minimaps, no names over targets. In fact, friendly fire is turned on all servers, so one of the first things a beginner must do, is learn the difference between russians/germans and americans/japanese (their uniform).
RO2 does some things much better than Battlefield, for example classes. Each team has 1 commander, and multiple squads made of 10 players. A squad has squad leader and he acts as a mobile spawn point to his squad mates. Usually a team is given 4 squads. Yes, that's 40+ slots for 32 players - it was done on purpose. A team gets 1 team leader, 4 squad leaders, 4 machine gunners, 6 assault (automatic weapons), 1 sniper, a few more elite assault and elite riflemen, and the rest are normal riflemen. You cannot make everyone in your game medics, engineers, snipers etc. Instead there are roles, that increase in complexity.
Normal riflemen have bolt action rifles, which are inferior to everything else in the game due to their fire rate, and pretty much 75% of the players will be playing as them.
Elite riflemen have semi-auto weapons. Assault and elite assault have automatics. Each has their own role in the game that they must fulfill. These guys are there to fight in close quarters on the objective.
Machine gunners are another class with automatic weapons, but they cannot aim with their machine gun until they station it - making them very inaccurate for close quarters, but good for defense. Their greatest strength is that they can shoot 50-200 rounds before having to reload.
Usually a team gets 1-4 snipers max (depends on the map), and these are used to take out important roles such as team leaders, squad leaders and machine gunners. Unlike other roles, they can't spawn on the squad leader, so if they die, they will have to make it all the way from the base to the frontline.
Squad leaders are a mobile spawn point for the 9 players in his team. It's very important for them to survive. Other than that they are the only role that has smoke grenades, which are commonly used in this game to block vision for the enemy and allow your men to charge in. They also have binoculars, which they can use to mark points on the map for artillery.
Team leader is the one that is calling in artillery basically. He actually has the same gear as the squad leader - a sub machine gun, smoke grenades, he can mark with his binoculars as well, but he requires to be next to radios to do his job, like for calling artillery. The radios themselves are located on certain point on the map, and usually they are not where the action is.
Some maps also feature tanks, and with them they bring engineers and AT gunners. Engineers are basically allowed to choose the gear that elite riflemen or assault use, and they get anti tank grenades. But their main job is to destroy obstructions, like tank barriers. AT gunners on other hand get a big anti material rifle, but just like machine gunners they have to station it.
Like i said, it also gives you great immersion, but it's more than what i described. There are a lot of things in the game that improve immersion even more. Stuff like this for example.
They modeled the whole interior of the tank, and even added animations for the crew members.
A bit about tanks themselves. This is no battlefield - the tank can fit 2-4 crew members depending on the tank. Unlike battlefield again, the driver only does the driving for example. He has a very limited view by the way, as you can see over here.
Usually there is a tank commander, a turret gunner and an MG gunner. There is also a loader who is played by AI, but you can replace him if he dies. Not all tanks are the same though. They are like 4 currently - Panzer IV and T-34 were available on release, but Panzer III and a 2 seated T-70 were added later on.
That said, unlike red orchestra 1, there is a lack of tank battles. There are only 3 maps for huge tank battles. Most of the time the tank is used to support the infantry.
UI is very minimal as well. There is no indicators of how much ammo you have in your rifle for example. But you can check that by holding R, and your character will physically unbolt the rifle and check it. Little things like that make it very immersive.
In 2013, Rising Storm was released - an expansion to RO2. It's set in the pacific and features american and japanese. It's basically the same game, except without tanks and it's asymmetric. Meaning one side is better than the other - americans get auto and semi auto weapons, while most of the japanese roles have bolt action rifles. Americans also get flamethrowers.
It's a nice challenge for more experienced players and it's a great place to start learning the game. You also don't have to own the expansion to join the servers - the game allows people to play as a normal rifleman if they don't own it.

My name is John Le'borsho, Im from Lake Charles, Louisiana. I was drafted, like my friends and brothers, into a war that had to be fought. I was 19....just had my birthday, when our ship got the news, we were headin to a island named Iwo Jima. Since me and my squad hadn't seen a fight, we waited to land on the second wave. They told us about this place, how they burned it to flat earth, yet the tojo still hid somehow, I aint gonna lie, I was scared. I sat there, ready to load into the landing craft, reading my Bible, when our Navy Corpsman, Justin Landry, walked up and tapped me on the helmet. "Its time to go son." he said quietly. Grabbing my Garand, I got ready to load up at our Captains command....I dont really remember the ride, it was quiet on the boat, the faint sound of gunshots started to grow however. Suddenly, the vessel shook violently, throwing me down. As I climbed to my feet, I looked to my right, to see a boy, Pvt.Rick Barson, slumped in the corner, blood pouring out his neck from shrapnel. "Oh my God." is all I could breath out, before the landing boat suddenly slammed to a stop, the gate falling open....but I just kept staring at the body. "UNLESS YOU WANNA END UP LIKE HIM, GET YOUR♥♥♥♥♥MOVING!" The Corpsman yelled at me, throwing me off the boat and into the inch deep water washing the sand.
Quickly I grabbed my rifle and started running, bodies laid on the beach, craters filled the rocky sand, blood soaked the ground. I saw a squad of Marines on the top of the crest of the beach, handing out ammo and supplies. "Whats the situation Corporal?" our 2ndLT yelled out. "This is the 3rd ♥♥♥♥ing day sir, and the tojo are hanging on the that damn mountain with their lives. We are pushing, but not quickly. They keep trying to flank left from the mountain, we are barely keeping them back, with all spares moving up the mountain!" the Cpl shouted over planes, tanks and cannon fire. "Then we are going to back up Sgt.Nickle's squad boys!" Our 2nd LT yelled to us, and we quickly nodded.
Running through the woods, we couldnt get past the smell of burning flesh, and flies everywhere, till we finally came to a small dip in the rocks, to see a half dead squad of Marines, fending off about 200 japanese imperial soldiers. "Pvt.Daniel, Corporal.Youngblood, get up on that rock and set up the 30.cal Browning, Lance Corporal and PFC on me, PFC.John and Justin, go help those Marines on the right of those barricades, NOW GO!"
As I ran past whizzing bullets and dead bodies, I saw the Marines we were assisting. One was holding a patch on his side, blood oozing out as he fired from his side with his 45. , the other was young, but firing frantically with his Browning Auto Rifle, and the third, was carefully picking shots with a 30.caliber carbine. I then realized this was the Sargent, so I ran to his side and dropped down as Justin landed beside the wounded Marine. "Sargent, are you ok!?" I asked. "SHUT UP AND SHOOT!" was his response.
As I leaned up, a sudden blast of dirty hit me in the face and a round landed 5 inches from me, quickly making me drop back down. I regained my senses and gripped my 30-06 tightly, leaning back out to pick a target....but I couldn't, cause just as zebras confuse lions, there where to many to count, or focus on.....so I waited till one ran infront of my sights and......bang...miss. I was starled, I was an expert marksman, so I took another bead and....bang.. I watched the japanese soldier run a few more feet before stumbling, and suddenly slumping to the ground.....I had killed a man.I stared for a moment as the world stood still, only to come back and fire again, and again, and again and again till *Ping*. Looking down at my open chamber, I went to reach for another enbloc clip, when suddenly the BAR Marine yelled "LOOK OUT, MOVE!"
I glanced up just in time to see a slow, light mortar land 7 feet from me. Then I just laid there....I had been thrown, I chunk of my leg was missing from the side, the wounded Marine had a shoulder and arm missing, the BAR Marine was laying on his back, firing until a round hit his heart, Justin was going hand to hand with a Tojo officer, the Sargent was trying to get his Colt out, and the Tojo had just brought friends. I saw the 2nd LT try to get to us, on for a hell of rounds hit the cover he was behind. So I just laid there, a load ring was all I could hear, my vision tunneling. I watched as Justin overpowered the officers, stealing his short sword and killing stabbing him with it, before drawning the officers nambo from his holster and firing at Japs heading to me. A wave of gun fire hit the officer, and Justin as they both fell over, and a Tojo ran up to me, sticking a bayonet to my chest.
As I tried to reach up and grab his arm, he laughed and pushed down. I groaned, and grabbed his arm, trying to push back and use my other hand to grab his grenade. However, suddenly a round smashed into his chest, throwing him off of me, and about 20 Marines ran out the trees, some shooting, others charging the Tojo. I watched as the officer's body somehow rolled off Justin, only to watch the Corpsman push off the dead body and get up, holding his side and firing a type 100. I looked up as another Corpsman lifted me up to a sitting position. I heard a young Marine yell out, "LOOK, ON TOP OF THE HILL!" and I glanced to see what he was worked up about.
And among the hell and chaos, I saw a poll, with a small American flag on it, get slammed into the face of that mountian, claiming in for the U.S.A., I watched it wave in the wind as Justin and the 2nd LT ran over.....then I passed out.....and was calm

I really wanted to like this game. Everything aesthetic is beautiful, and the concepts are really interresting. Unfortunately, the gameplay is beyond unfair. The core challenge in this game comes being able to survive an onslaught of attacks for long enough to beat each level, and the controls do not lend themselves to being able to dodge or attack enemies. This is not a satisfying challenge; it is a frustrating endurance run.  The controls feel loose and the vast majority of the input involves simply spamming the X button. After spending half an hour on the first level, the feeling of beating it was not a sense of legitimate satisfaction; it was a feeling of "Oh my god, finally!" That is not a good feeling to have in a game, A game should feel as though it was set up with the appropraite challenges for the player to accomplish it. Cuphead feels like a custom level made by a child who diecided to put the maximum number of sprites in the smallest space possible, then spend the next hour getting mad at their own creation. It had a massive amount of potential, but it was squandered on the idea that a game's value comes from the amount of time needed to be invested to be competent at it.

I give this game thumbs up because I appreciate the idea of it, and want to support developers trying to do something different. Yet, it was a mixed experience overall. My biggest issues were;
1)The trailer is quite misleading. The game has pretty gloomy and dark atmosphere, not comical as the trailer was. So my initial feeling was disappointment, because game was nothing that the trailer made it look to be. But eventually, the atmosphere of the game stands on its own. Just be prepared that the game is not as funny as the trailer.
2)I didnt feel that the procedural system adds anything to the game. The environments are made randomly for each playthrough, but there is not enough variery in the landscape patterns to make any worthwhile differences via procedural system. Its the same barren lands, and having the same trees in little different places doesnt really enchant the gameplay. The game is not a roguelike either. When you die (and you die very easily), you dont start the game from a 0, but just load a checkpoint. This imho kills the point of randomly generated world, since you dont need to really adapt into new world every time you play it, like you would do in Binding of Isaac, Rogue Legacy, Spelunky, etc. In this game, I kept thinking that it would be much better, if the open world was well planned solid world full of unique situations, instead of a procedural world.
3)Sneaking is too hard, and too punishing. The distances in the game are very very long, and most of the gametime you will be running from point A to B, without really sneaking. But when you reach a point where you "must" sneak, often its better just to shoot the enemy who is in your way, and run away as fast as you can. Doing proper sneaking can take a lot, lot of time, and getting spotted by enemy when too near to them is almost 100% death to you, which will mean a lot and lot of time wasted due to rare checkpoints. If you run and gun instead, you will lose only a 1-2 minutes of your time (most spent on running), instead of 10-20 minutes you would spend trying to sneak properly.
Overall I was somewhat disappointed with the game, but liked the idea and style of it enough, that I wish the developers move into a new interesting and unique projects soon. Apparently this game is getting a multiplayer someday, but IMHO its waste of time of the devs, and they should just make a new game instead. For time being, I can still recommend this game to the people who are fascinated by the idea, even though it has its share of problems.

Hands down one of the best games of the past decade, unsurprisingly made by the developer of two of the most legendary games of all time - System Shock. And it's getting a free remaster for owners, to boot.
BioShock is the spiritual successor to System Shock 2, also directed by Ken Levine, and plays almost identically to Shodan's last space romp. While System was a first person RPG with shooter mechanics that offered many playstyles through its different class selections, psionics abilities, weapons and nanite upgrades, BioShock is more of a first person shooter with soft RPG mechanics where the only things determining your playstyle are the plasmids equipped and the way you upgrade, though guns and ammo types play a huge part just like in the previous game.
It can't be stressed enough how nearly identical the games are. You wake up, are thrust into a situation you don't understand - both involving an exploding or exploded air/spacecraft, and have to embark upon exploring the area and figuring out how to escape alive. Both are linear games with a world that offers limited exploration and re-visiting of previous areas. In both games you use research in order to learn more about enemies and better deal with them.
Specifically, you gain powers through the use of plasmids, allowing you to light things on fire, electrocute, freeze, use telekinesis, and many other standard "magic" abilities. There are also plasmids which let you bypass security or turrets. As for the hacking, System Shock 2's basic minesweeper-ish hacking minigame has been replaced by the game Pipes, where you have to direct water from one spot to another. Really the only new thing in BS is that you can choose to - or choose not to - kill Big Daddies and their Little Sisters (or rescue them) in order to harvest the material needed to become more powerful. Ultimately at the end these choices don't amount to anything significant, but you get a slightly different ending and slightly different boss encounter.
The "shock" concept comes from what is a relatively creative twist in the main storyline after a certain point of progress into the game, and at least in SS2's case - it was a fresh idea that hadn't been done before in video games. Even so, 17 or 9 years later, the writing in the stories of these games is still refreshing.
Rapture is a meticulously crafted objectivist's wet dream (pun not intended) of essentially unfettered free market economics. The environment, the dialogue, the NPCs, everything has been designed to reflect that. This is a dystopian society - naturally - where scientists were encouraged to pursue their endeavors for the interest of everyone, which in addition to the inevitable realities of capitalism leads to the collapse of the city after these forces send Rapture into utter anarchy.
If you liked System Shock 2, you may find BioShock a more "casual" game that drops "hardcore" mechanics like jammed guns, weapons breaking, chemical research, stat building, sneaking, and a managable inventory system. However, the game more than makes up for it in narrative pacing and presentation. Not to mention, being an Unreal 2 engine game, it is far more pleasant on the eye than Dark engine, and can still hold its own against modern graphics despite the huge advancements.
The art deco style of the city is straight from the 50s and downright gorgeous. Even from the ruins of this city, where everything is dark and dank and frequently flooded or grown over with sea life because of water. Even if you hate the game, it more than deserves praise for the art direction alone and the effort that was put in to make this city look good. Admittedly, if you compare Rapture in the original game to Rapture in Burial at Sea, it loses some of its authenticity - after all it is a huge city and it doesn't actually feel like any sane human beings still live there. I think the game can get a pass for that, though, based on its age and the fact that it was never meant to be an open world RPG.
Even with those criticisms, BioShock is simply one of the most unforgettable games produced in the history of gaming, and stands out even among the many other games that can claim that accolade.

I've owned this game on disc for a long time and have easily sunk hundreds hours more into it than what I have on Steam.  As a kid the battles of Star Wars were mind blowing.  So, the chance to play an RTS that lets you command all the inconic units of the original trilogy was a dream come true.  This package also includes the Forces of Corruption expansion.  This added the criminal empire of Tyber Zann as a third faction, and added additional units and heroes to the Rebel and Empire factions.  When launching this game, steam will ask you whether you want to launch the original or expansion, so you can pick whichever you prefer at any time.
For anyone who hasn't played this game, it is primarily a singleplayer game.  The main mode is galactic conquest.  In this mode you control either the Empire, Rebellion or Zann Consortium and are battling for dominance on a galactic map.  Each time fleets clash on the map or a planet is invaded by ground troops you get to fight the battle in real time.
There are story campaigns for the Rebels and Imperials in the base game, and for Zann in the expansion.  These are basically galactic conquest maps that feature special missions and maps, as well as some basic story in the form of voice acted conversations.
There's also a skirmish mode that features single battles either on the ground or in space.  In my opinion the skirmish mode is the weakest part of the game, but there may be many who disagree with me.
Experienced RTS players will probably find this game a bit easy, especially playing as the Zann Consortium.  A patient player with a few units on the ground can sometimes sneak past a max level space station and destroy armies of units on a well entrenched planet, occupying the planet and automatically destroying the space station in orbit.  As the Zann Consortium, I can't tell you how many times I've just sent my five heroes  to occupy planets single handedly.  It's amazing how 5 people can so effectively hold an entire planet.
But even so, it's undeniable how satisfying it is when you do get those classic Star Wars battles.   Dozens of Imperial Star Destroyers squaring off against Mon Calamari Cruisers over Coruscant.  AT-ATs mulching inferior rebel T2 - B light tanks, only to get tripped by Airspeeders.  Zann or the Rebels bringing a massive fleets only to find themselves locked in battle with a Super Star Destroyer and the Death Star.   NOW WITNESS THE FULL POWER OF THIS FULLY OPERATIONAL...  *ahem*  You can get the idea.
And keep in mind all that I've said here is just about the base game.  This game is many years old now, and there are truly incredible total conversion mods out there that are even better than the base game.  You owe to yourself, whether you're a noble Rebel leader, an ironfisted Imperial general , or a cutthroat Consortium goon to try this game.
BUY IT!

The other positive reviews will tell you what I also thought was interesting about this game... at first.
The first thirty minutes are interesting as the developer's story (via narration and game art) begins and you as the player wonder what will come next.
Unfortunately, by the end of the game you realize you wasted your time in a walking simulator, and the developer is apologizing for himself, making any part of the initially quirky story fall to pieces.
As the player you come to the realization that you're still trudging through yet another dark, poorly lit mini level that mimics the Source engine style. You still don't have the ability to dash or sprint. You also rarely, if ever interact with the environment, so you also realize that you are playing a narrated walking simulator. Also, the narrator is actually wailing regrets in your ear.
"What went wrong?" the narrator asks, as you the player climb yet another flight of stairs in slo-mo.
The game also crashed in the menus, requiring a restart.
If you really, really, want to see what the positive reviews talk about, I guess you could get this game on sale for 50% off or more.

The gameplay is interesting in how you have time to plan out some wicked cool moves. The story isn't really there. It never tells you why you are doing it, and I think that's meant to be the hook to keep going. But in that case, once you finish, that's a part of the game that never needs to be revisited. I found many of the levels felt more like a slog that a challenge. Enemies will seem to spawn right behind you, or close in quickly, and later levels were essentially dumping a pile of reinforcements in your lap. Once you alert one enemy, they all know where you are so there's no stealth involved. As far as I could find looking at the empty Controls and Readme menus, there isn't a crouch/duck/slide move so no sliding under the shotgun blasts.
The game has 32 levels, though some are just unskippable cutscenes with you sort of participating, and finishing unlocks Endless Mode which I assume is battling until you get hit. There are some minigames in your terminal (menus), and extra tidbits to read & watch, so it has a retro nostalga feel to it.
It took me 4.9 hours from start to finish. I replayed some of the levels to get a nice replay clip during that run. Give it a go while it's on sale, but add it to the Wishlist when it's not. If Steam used Stars for ratings, I'd give it 3 or 3.5(4), but as I don't see myself coming back to it soon, I'll have to decline.

Dungeon of the Endless has been one of the most pleasant gaming surprises I have had in the last months. I usually don't trust early access games, and honestly, I am not too fond of pixelated graphics, but after reading the different positive reviews from other gamers, I decided to give this game a try.
And what a nice surprise it was, up to the point that I have decided to make my first review in Steam to support these developers and their game. As you might have read, this game is a mix between roguelike and tower defense games. Though they are two very different genres, the gameplay is so smooth that they blend together seamlessly.
The difficulty is hard, but fair. You are going to die a lot, but you will learn something new from each run. Everytime you play, you will perform better and better (or at least learn new tactics or approaches).
The randomization of the levels and heroes makes this game replayable many, many times. However, this randomness can also provoke that some of the levels are more difficult (or easier) on every run. Overall, I really love this approach, as makes every game very different from the previous ones.
In spite of being an Alpha, the game is very playable, and in about 6-9 hours you will be able to finish the 5 levels that are currently developed. However, you will probably come back for more runs.
Pros:
- The gameplay is a blast, even in this Alpha stage.
- Excellent blend of tower defense and rogue-like games.
- A game that makes you think and choose wisely your actions. One mistake can doom your run.
- Very nice art style.
- Randomness makes this game very replayable.
- Distinct and interesting heroes.
- Nice difficulty level which makes every advancement very rewarding.
Cons:
- Pixelated graphics. It is something personal, but I don't like them very much. However, as I priorize gameplay over them (and the art style is very nice), it is a minor complaint.
- Randomization can make a level very easy, or very difficult (it is a good thing, but also a bad one). For me, it is also a minor complaint, as I love surprises...
As you have seen, I don't think that the difficulty level is a Con. I prefer the game being difficult (or at least having that level adjustable), because I think that games should not be a walk in the park.
Very nice game, and definitely recommended! Thumbs up for the devs, and I am eager to see the new surprises you have in development for us in the following patches!

Sir is a game I really want to like, and have enjoyed parts of it, as it has a number of great ideas going for it: the wacky and creepy setting, the committed focus on stealth survival, the great variety of items, environmental biomes, & enemies, and of course, the ambitious randomly generated world. There's a lot to like on paper with Sir, and even once you are in the game some of that potential shines through gloriously.
However, of this never quite comes together in a cohesive whole. The game feels incomplete, and seems to lack some more substance and depth, in terms of gameplay, goals, and story. The AI of the robots ruthlessly hunting you down is actually quite good, but the process of evasion, distriction, fleeing, and/or fighting them quickly becomes tedious and uninteresting; and this interaction is supposed to be the focus of the gameplay! Often times the best strategy is to just sprint around grabbing your objectives and ignoring the thoughful stealthy approach, which should not really be possible, and essentially breaks the way the game is clearly designed to be played. Also, after the initial cutscene, there is next to no story or world development, which is a somewhat bizarre decision, as the setting is one of the most compelling aspects of the game. Where the hell am I, and what is the backstory of these tweed clad robo-gentlemen? Who is my character, and who is this myserious Butler who speaks at the game's beginning? Why are all these houses abandoned? None of your questions will ever even be acknowledged by the game, let aloned answered, which is a major cop-out for an incrediblely unique and interesting set-up. Additionally, the random world generation, while ambitious and great in theory, doesn't always work out well, and leads to really weird and hard to navigate terrain and towns at times, which also helps to undermine alternative playstyles and the believability of these strange islands actually being a real place.
Much of this seems to stem from the sudden jump in development from late Alpha to full release earlier this year; as someone who was supporting the game from almost day one, it seemed somewhat inconsistent with the planned development of the game, and the final product is proof of that. I feel that development dragged on internally, and once a workable build without significant bugs was finished, with enough development bullet points technically checked off, and a decent existing player base, the developers pushed the game out, without actually confirming if the game actually worked like they had intended it to. I hesitate to say it, but I would argue it does not.
If there are any more large updates for Sir to bring some fullness to the package (such as the often promised, but as of yet undelivered exciting competitive/cooperative multiplayer mode), this may still become realized as a great game. And I hope it does because many of the pieces are here, and I would be lying if I said I didn't have good fun with it at times. However I cannot recommend the game in its current and sadly, final state (if the developers are to be believed), and have taken Sir as a lesson in the dangers of supporting overly ambitious early access games, even if the developers are genuine in their intentions.

Great concept.
But that's it.
I'd expect this to be a beta or even an alpha or be sold for $5.
A short synopsis: (don't worry about spoilers because there's little to no plot to spoil)
You pick a character, generate a group of five islands, and then begin. With a smug sounding narrator telling you some basic information every so often, you quickly pick up the basics of gameplay of movement, looting, and stealth.
And then thats it.
You just wander around an island searching for rocks to put in a bigger rock while avoiding robots that are hunting you.
Sure there are letters and little tea sets you can look at but they serve no purpose. After a certain point the narrator even says that he'll be gone and you're on your own for the rest of the game. No crafting, no special items or gamemodes that can only be obtained with certain actions. The only real difficulty in this game is the lack of inventory space. Robots can be easily avoided by walking in a large circle around them with the use of some alarm clocks.
I'd love to see a crafting system or more variety in the game, being able to pick what type of island each one is and what starting items you recieve is hardly variety. Seriously, just look at Don't Starve for ideas to expand gameplay.
I'd rate this a 2/5: this is either an alpha or overpriced

UPDATE:
Does not look like its being worked on at all anymore, so dont bother. When the Dev works on it more, then I'll update this. Not until then though.
Early Access Review:
Rough around the edges with work that needs to be done, but keep in mind this is early access, so that is to be expected. In general, YES, I would recommend this to others IF YOU ARE WILLING TO GIVE FEEDBACK.
If you are looking for a fully created game, then come back in a few months. It does a lot of cool things and hints at even cooler stuff, so if you want to have a say in what you want this game to look like, then buy it now.
Pros:
-Involved Developer:
This is a developer that genuinely wants to make a good game. They actively seek responses from their audience and are very engaging. Based on my interactiong with them, I have a great deal of hope they will make good on their promises.
-Unique Management system:
I have never seen something anything like the game building mechanics before and it is really exciting to figure out. You build each little element of the game you are developing: genre, music, subplots, character, monsters, and more. Being able to name each element also gets your imagination working. I got attatched to the itty bitty tiny platformer that was my first game. A little confusing at first, but I will give it a passing grade based on how unique it is. There is a tutorial in the works that will hopefully clear up some of the confusion. There is still a lot of work to be done, but the developer has stated that fact.
-Cute Art:
Maybe a little basic, but it's cute and the girls ARE NOT bad walking sterotypes.
Cons:
-Unfinished:
What do you expect from an early access game?
-Blandish story:
So far it hints at a fascinating larger story arc and something I would love to explore, but as of right now its mostly a managment game with a few lines of dialogue here and there, which is fine, but in a VN like format, they need to give us a story to care about.
-Character development:
They are cute and hint at having really interesting personalities, but all seem a little bland because of how little you interact with them. Also... all of the team are girls and you are a guy. This is not a bad thing, but if they aren't careful then they could be dealing with a bad harem trope style game.
-Lunch Time and Shopping:
Unless you have played it at the state the game is in now, you wont really understand just how underwhelming this is. This is something that needs a lot of work, I want to be able to buy cool things and software and gifts and visit with my friends/dev team, but I can't really. I WANT THIS SO BADLY!!!
Play it.
Stealth, shooting, humour, and HOLY♥♥♥♥♥♥WTF IS THAT?! moments make this an awesome game, totally worth buying.
