I quickly discovered something important about Project Zomboid - I'm not very good.  Spinning to face a zombie, I recalled my son's reaction when I beat a guy one-on-one in a shootout in WolfET.  He looked at my dead opponent and said "thank you for sucking".
I bring this up because I can set Sandbox Mode to ease me into harder and harder levels.  Nobody's gona watch me on YouTube if I'd been recording my playthroughs (I haven't been)(you're welcome), but poor little Joey Fatone has a pretty good base set up, and his much tougher brother Fred Fatone is working on his own.  I'm learning the system, and having a ball.
Most guys will play PZ like it's Dwarf Fortress ("Losing is Fun!") which is great, but it's your call.  There's a deep and satisfying skill system, but that's poorly suited to die-in-a-week scenarios.  So you make an important choice when you start the game, entirely apart from which Fatone brother to play and what skills he has.  Sandbox can be adjusted to encourage learning a lot,
Survival, well, not so much unless you're adept.  I've seen enough playthroughs to convince me that very, very few guys, and I don't mean old ones like me, will bother much with most skills if they know that living a month is unlikely.   The game has not yet reached a point, however, where an effective base will be fun for very long, at least not your second or third one.  If you make yourself safe and reasonably self-sustaining, you've won, and it's probably time for a new Fatone.

Sadly, as much as I wanted to enjoy this, I cannot recommend The Beginner's guide.
Many people point to this game as similar to the Stanley Parable. I thought The Stanley Parable was amazing, and I thoroughly enjoyed it. It had multiple different endings, the motif of authority and a person's longing for freedom. It also had a deeper meaning about defiling somebody's art. The Stanley Parable was funny at times, had a few secrets (like a broom closet), and made me think. I was even compelled to read literary analysis on the Stanley Parable. I replayed it once to put it all together in my mind, and considered all of the contradictions. The narrator made it almost feel like portal (I guess it was made on source). I wanted to escape but I knew there was no actual way.
The beginners guide does not meet the Stanley Parable's standards. I cannot tell if this is actually a true story or not. The narrator is not funny, and just made this game to pity himself and his friend Coda. Usually, I consider games to be good depending on if I spend more hours than dollars spent on a game. I bought the stanley parable on sale, bought it for 4 dollars, and have about 5 hours on it. I bought half life 1 for 99 cents and played it for about 20 hours. (Great game by the way.) I bought minecraft for 30 bucks and have about 4500 hours in it. Hence the reason minecraft is my favorite game. Even if I do not spend a lot of time in a game, I still think I got my money's worth if I REALLY ENJOY every bit of time I put into it.
I did not enjoy the beginner's guide. I was intrigued for a little while, but for the most part, I was bored out of my mind. And a played it for 90 minutes. (They did warn me that it does take about 90 minutes to complete). I spent 10 dollars on the beginner's guide, and I didn't even enjoy it. It looks lazy, and should have been only for personal use. Others could argue that this game is a piece of art, and it is. Its just not art that I actually cared enough about, and I did not think it was worth 10 dollars.
There are no secrets, no other endings, and the narrator actually tells you his interperitation WHILE you are playing it. This makes it so that you do not even think about it, or come up with your own interperitation. You don't come to a conclusion by yourself, the narrator just tells you. The narrator isn't even actually funny like in the stanley parable. In the stanley parable, you need to figure out how to interperate all of the events. It had depth. The beginner's guide feels like a shallow piece of art that could be good if it was free, or 99 cents.
What they could have done: Maybe they could have thrown in a few puzzles into the games to make them feel less pointless (NOT INCLUDING THE ONE PUZZLE THAT YOU REPEAT OVER AND OVER). Maybe they could have allowed the player to explore one of the worlds/levels, allowed them to discover for themselves the psychology and feelings of Coda. Maybe they could have created puzzles that show a deeper meaning into the thoughts of coda, putting one in each of the levels, so that you would feel that you have accomplished something. Maybe they could make it a little more open ended. The Stanley parable was not very interactive, but at least you had choices (and no choices).

"SUPERHOT is the most innovative shooter I've played in years!". Kind of true, it's involving, original and fun to play, but let's get to the details.
You are a guy, some kind of hacker, mostly a gamer, through a chat you get to know and try a new innovative shooter called SUPERHOT. Truth is SUPERHOT is not a simple shooter, it's something more, but your will to know the truth will cost you a lot.
That sound like an involving intro but the retro aspect of the interface and the minimalistic graphic and gameplay should be enough to resize your expectations for the game. Menu is something for experienced gamers old enough to have lived in the dos era when Norton Commander was the thing, as it has all its looks, including the blinking cursor moving from block to block. Every portion of the story you're being told is revealed with a chat... That looks like a DOS command line. Otherwise there are some short ingame messages that flash for 1 or 2 seconds on the entire screen. Ingame there are no textures at all, just white/light grey walls and the red polygonal guys to kill with black polygonal guns.
Minimalistic is the appropriate word for the approach adopted by the developers. Yet it works damn well, who needs fancy menus, this retro feel is simply appropriate considering the atmosphere. And the white/red/black contrast is simply perfect. Makes easier to focus on the action. It isn't pleasant to see (except for menus, but I'm a nostalgic). But it works damn well. Everything developed smoothly in Unity.
No soundtrack. Which is ridiculous, the game and the gameplay itself could give greater emotions with some badass soundtrack. Dear developers, Does it cost too much to make your own soundtrack? Give players the opportunity to throw some mp3s in a default folder to play randomly. Considering the slowmotions it might be fun to hear some music that slows down or speed up according to the game's speed. Or maybe not, some plain music could have been fine at all.
Gameplay is VERY simple. According to the description AND the very first message flashed ingame "Time moves only when you move". Which sounds cool but is half true. Time moves 1:1 when you move, and slows down a lot when you're still. Which makes things more fair and not too easy. There will be weapons around which can be carried and used. No additional ammos, only shots in the clip, once you're out you can throw them on the red guys' heads (I'm dead serious) and if they carry a weapon they'll immediately lose it throwing it on the air. And if you're close enough you can grab it and use it. Just to add some irony to the game with style. After the Story campaign the game will unlock the challenges and the endless mode (I guess it's not necessary to explain this one) to add some life to the game.
All in all the gameplay is the real core of the game itself, which is simple yet extremely effective. Standing still while avoiding a bullet and watching it slowly fly next to you is pure style. I bet this game must be simply awesome with VR, but I will know it only in a not so near future.
"Story mode" is short. 2 Hours. Literally. On the bright side the story is quite involving, almost breaking the fourth wall, with some meta moments and some rare/original ideas. The problem is the campaign is extremely short and themes are quite superficial. I've realized on my second gameplay that there are some secret terminals, once you find them the "protagonist" will ask "the game" ONE question. The first questions have very interesting answers that makes you think the plot thickens and gives you doubt on how deep this "conspiracy" can go. Then all answers suddenly become generic, evasive and disappointing at the very least. It's a waste of potential. They had a working general line, they had the right style to work on it but it looks like a stub.
The game itself is fun and all, and if the story is not enough for you there are challenges. Too bad that they take place in the exact same maps. No new maps for challenges, except for endless mode, so you will find yourself always playing in the same areas. Just with different conditions. So if the story is short, these challenges won't add too much life, not because they're not enough to entertain, but because they don't entertain enough. That's when a game fails.
Harsh words, yet I still advice playing because I paid a misery for this (not from steam's official store, of course) and because I played as long as it was fun for me. One thing that helped were the many easter eggs hidden inside the menu. Folders are not there for mere aesthetics, but if you dig enough you can find some real retro pixel art, hidden minigames, a "fake" chat room which has been a great fun to read. It seems like a bottled version of a reddit forum, or whatever.
And once again, I will definitely try the VR version to see how much the headset can improve the awesome gameplay and which problems it might bring.

+ Even if you saw it on YouTube when it first came out (which I had), it's still being updated and there are probably a few jokes and events that you haven't seen yet.
+Quite funny and immersive if you slow down and read the cards - play it like an RPG, not a resource management game
+ Simple concept that is easy to grasp and perfect
- It doesn't take too long to finish, even if you are shooting for near 100% completion - about 10 hours for me. Fine for the price, I suppose, but still feels a little sparse, especially given that some events are harder to access than others.
- Loses replay value after a while. There are (at the time of writing) ~850 cards in the game, 29 deaths, and ~40 characters and objectives. In one run - assuming you don't just play infinitely without taking an ending or resetting AND you are paying attention - you can probably see half the cards, meet almost all the characters, do 2/3s of the objectives, and get about half the deaths. Bear in mind, one run takes about two hours at a slow pace. After three, you are probably short twenty cards and have seen and done everything else. At a certain point, the immersion and humor stops carrying the game, and you are left with what amounts to resource management Tinder.
Overall, I'd recommend it if you want a funny, immersive, casual experience or if you are a completionist looking for an interesting challenge. Just don't expect the world, and you certainly won't be disappointed.

+ The game doesn't take itself too seriously. Amidst all the Battlefields and CODs and other sickeningly serious war games, its refreshing to see an FPS that was made for the purpose of fun, not money.
+ The artstyle is very appealing. The environments and enemies are very cool and nice to look at. It's all very colorful and interesting.
+ The soundtrack is good. I don't know if all of it is original, but all of it is good. I mean, it's no Castlevania SOTN, and I wouldn't just listen to it for kicks, but while playing, it's very nice and never gets stale.
Stuff I don't like:
- It's too damn hard. Now, inb4 people start yelling at me that I suck, no, I don't. I don't suck, I'm just normal. I'm a normal person who plays video games sometimes, and I don't want to have to pour days into trying a level over and over again to get it just perfect so I can squeeze in a win with 1 second left on the clock. That's not fun, it's frustrating, especially when I know the next level is going to be just as much of a pain.
- Some of the enemies are stupid and irritating. They sneak up on me, they don't make any discernable sounds, and they can be really frustrating.
Ultimately, I really do like this game. It's flaws never really deterred me from playing or enjoying it, and though there have been some times where I got too mad to keep playing, I still kept coming back.

I love puzzle games, and adorable characters. This puzzler has the cutest knite princess main charcter with a giant sword. The sword is used for fighting obviously, so there's that too. The game is short, but so pleasent. Also, the final fight did feel quite rewarding. This game has a relaxing feel and peacful soundtrack. Plus every level has 100 gems to collect via statures to break or skelotons to re-kill. You have to find secret arias to get them all including solving puzzle to find them, though it is optional as you can beat the game without getting them all.

The gameplay is pretty much as you see it: any movement you make accelerates time, kill the red guys.  In this fashion it is like a puzzle in some ways, where the need for reaction time is diminished and the need for planning is enhanced.  It is still very much an action game though, and it can be very satisfying to pull everything off.  What surprised me is the bizarrely engaging meta-narrative that frames the seemingly disparate levels into a cohesive story of sorts.  While I would argue that the game plays better in VR, the VR edition's framing is not nearly as compelling; it is for this reason that I would recommend buying both (assuming you have VR, naturally).
In terms of negatives, the hit detection is occasionally questionable, and it is not a long game.  To that second point, you will probably find yourself disappointed if you're the type to demand "one dollar for every hour of gameplay" or some such price-to-time metric.  I would encourage you to relax said requirement, but in the absence of markedly changing your point of view over a two paragraph user review on Steam, you will probably want to wait for a decent discount.
All that said, it's the most innovative shooter I've played in years.

In this particular gem, you play as an Englishman who's been transported to a quintet of dreary islands by a machine. Robots of every social class roam the isles and are busy hunting you as their own little fox so they can kill you. In order to survive, you have to hunt wild game, rummage through the various (thoroughly de-human-fied and therefore abandoned) buildings, and track down pieces of the machine that sent you to the robot-ruled hell. Lower class, upper class, it doesn't matter which they're from, each and every breed of robot has its own unique method of coursing you. This is not a game where you blast through hordes of enemies and stand tall with a crass cigar between your teeth. You have to take careful stock of each and every potential encounter and perform a cost-benefit analysis, as even two or three robots can annihilate you with a single volley of their shotguns and rifles. Combine this with a limited inventory space, and you have a pleasant challenge. The islands are also randomly generated, which makes each playthrough unique. You can modify the generator to a wonderful degree, producing a ton of island variations. If you want to be both scared and amused, I would suggest getting this game right away.

When I first started this game, I was truly draw in by the aesthetic of the first area, the Forest. In the second area, the Wasteland, as you travel you, begin to see more and more vestiges of a ruined civilization. By the third area, the Caves, the aesthetic started losing their appear as a more industrial setting began to take over. The last two areas, The Hotel & the Industrial Mill, compeletly lose the aesthetic charms of the beautiful, though disturbing naturalish landscape, for the sterile and boring.
The puzzles fall in the three standard puzzles types: (1) The obvious solution; (2) The better get the timing right; & (3) The guess what the developer was thinking. The number of times you'll die to each puzzle grows exponentially based upon which type it is. In addition, while the rotating building and messing with gravity puzzles were decently designed... they felt extremely out of place with the rest of the game. Maybe if there had been some sort of context, which itself would not have meshed with the rest of the game, I could have appreciated them more. But from my perspective, they belonged in an entirely different game.
I can clearly see why there are a large number of individuals who would praise this game. I even know several friends I wouldn't mind bring this game to their attention, but based upon my own prefrences I cannot recommend it to strangers.

Having recently finished a ritual slog through the rebooted ‘Thief’ (How I forced myself to play through the entirety of that dross I can only attribute to some kind of rabid frothing loyalty to the genius of the original) anyone could be forgiven that thinking that stealth – and I mean real stealth (Forgetteth not Original Thief, Hitman: Blood Money, System Shock etc.) was surely dead. Perhaps the harsh unforgiving landscape of the original hard-core PC genre is simply too much for the AAA studios of today to stomach - given how most of their output has become about as creatively impotent as Michael Bay directing the latest Transformers snore-fest. Well it turns out not all is lost as once again an indie darling swoops in to save the genre with the excellent (if not perfect) Sir, you are being hunted.
But steady on now dear boy! What’s it all about?
Starting with a wonky hand drawn cutscene (Though narrated by an excellently plummy butler voice-over) the simple premise is presented: Being stranded on a series of very British Isles you are tasked with recovering a series of scattered mystical stone artefacts to activate a kind of magical Stonehenge endgame – a simple but effective plot device not only permitting but encouraging the open ended ramble you embark on. Oh - and all the while avoiding the murderous but delightfully polite gentlemen robots who, if you didn't quite catch it already, are out to hunt you.
Go on then, spill the beans! Is it any good?
Endeavouring to avoid the very British habit of meandering around the point I should start by stating the most important thing you need to know: The stealth works. And golly is it a thrilling chase! Sir, makes use of its gloriously procedural open(ish) world and enemy placement to generate a genuinely compelling rhythm of long eerie walks, interrupted by tense moments of avoidance as you slip by patrolling hunters and the occasional run in with live fire in response to which you mostly run for the hills (But often rather the safe bosom of stealth-friendly shrubs and long grass).
Details man, I need the details!
While a shocking amount of AAA games still continue to pile on such migraine inducing modern videogame tropes as overzealous tutorials, quick time events and general (Console era) hand holding, Sir, plays like a greatest hits of all the classic stealth and RPG mechanics of 90s with a dash of the modern survival genre throw in there for good measure. You will manage a classic grid style inventory system. Your enemies will not patronise you with obnoxious alert level visual indicators. You will bleed out in seconds unless you brought bandages with you (And can apply them fast enough). You will not be guided by point defeating objective markers. You will shoot, cook and eat pheasant if you want any chance of surviving your time in the country. In short – jolly good times ahead!
With its short but well-structured runtime Sir, can also evoke some very special moments of player agency. Its clever reinterpretation of the classic scaling challenge/empowerment mechanic, invite new opportunities for emergent character development: Building resources and confidence you can eventually embolden yourself to take on the hunters - the cathartic fantasy of transformation from prey to predator or Garret the Master Thief to Gordon Freeman if you like. However with stealth and avoidance mechanics as enjoyable as they are you’d certainly not be missing out to ghost you way through the entire experience given your ruthlessly oppressive and increasingly thorough adversaries.
Oh, and did I mention it’s quite funny? Yes indeed. It seems no one is better at capitalising on the pastoral, fox and hound theme than mocker-in-chief (And game designer) Jim Rossignol – a Brit himself. I’m not sure the quintessentially British sense of humour will tickle everyone’s fancy but if the image of homicidal robots drinking tea is enough to muster a chuckle you’ll probably be ok.
So, you’re saying it’s rather good then?
Sir you are being Hunted is an inspired stealth gem not to mention a legitimate vision for the genre’s future. Despite its modest graphics chops, Sir, evokes a mythical version of the British countryside we almost forgot existed. The pervasive sense of danger, juxtaposed against that ancient, almost ethereal beauty conjures a unique sense of place that will linger long in the memory after your short adventure/ordeal ends.

This review will contain light concept spoilers, but given the nature of this game I recommend you read it before playing anyway, as in my opinion this game is shovel-ware hiding behind the "Well, it's short and cheap, so don't spoil it for yourself and just buy it!" idea.
I just want to say that I generally like puzzle games, narrative-driven games, "walking simulators", and I adored the Stanley Parable.  This game is none of those things.
The game is basically an exposition where the developer creates a fictional character to discuss and lament in order to express his inner frustrations over how difficult or directionless game development can be.  While I generally love story-driven games, there's really no story here.  You just walk around small snippets of areas with virtually nothing to do while the narrator says what he has to say.  I understand there is some grey area out there, and one man's walking simulator is another man's adventure, but this game is just too far beyond the line, and shouldn't be compared to games like The Stanley Parable, What Remains of Edith Finch, The Vanishing of Ethan Carter, or Life is Strange.  Those games actually have a world and a story, whereas this game feels more like a DVD extras commentary that could have been bundled with another game.
I was so thrilled when I originally found The Stanley Parable because it gave me some hope there are plenty of hidden gems out there.  Unfortunately, it seems the same dev is responsible for this piece of software and is just contributing to the problem of shovel-ware on the store.  I'm not saying the feelings he expressed aren't genuine, but trying to make a buck off of something that isn't worth a buck is tough to watch.
For those that do want to play it, also bear in mind that many of us get it to boot once and then get an error of a missing language file on the second boot.  It took a fair amount of searching to come up with a workable solution (add "-langauge" to the set launch option section of the game).  Part of me wonders if the dev couldn't be bothered to fix that or if maybe that was part of the game, as a lack of game progression is one of the themes he discusses.  The other part of me doesn't really care why this problem exists.  Since I did end up finishing it I'll act in good faith and not ask for a refund, but I hope others learn from my mistake.  I hope this dev can turn things around in the future, but I will be applying a higher level of scrutiny before buying more work from them.  Ultimately, this game is boring and is at a Brian Griffin-level of faux cleverness.

(This Review may contain Spoilers)
Uriel's Chasm is a very weird shoot-em-up/side-scrolling shooter/platformer, the shooting sections are "Bullet Hell", term considered for games with a lot of bullets in the screen while having you to dodge.
- First things first -
This game is religious and really disturbing. Let's make some notes before actually starting on the game.
1- The game is always in fullscreen and you can't change it to windowed (F2 is usually a common hotkey to toggle fullscreen in games made in Gamemaker and other engines);
2- You also can't bind your own controls, and the game does not provide you instructions, it just throws you on the level without explaining anything;
3- The game has no pause function, and if you press "Esc" by thinking you're going to pause, you're going to go all way back to the main menu and then first level of the game;
4- The beginning of the game starts with a camera-recorded scene with two women, called by themselves as "Shovelware Queens", I didn't really listened to that, but along the progress of the game, you may hear and watch more of these parts (including a guy later on). The quality is abysmal and there is no subtitles either. I didn't wanted to actually turn up my volume because it could be a prank (as if the game wasn't already).
- Story and Levels -
The story of the game, by all honesty, I don't know. It's a religious story that follows really weird by each level (I couldn't follow the story due it's bizarreness).
The first stage of the game is a shooter like the game Asteroids, from the Arcade. Your mission is to get enough "Faith" to proceed to the Garden. You can shoot with Z and move your ship with the Arrow Keys. You have a Life energy and Fuel energy. Moving it too much will consume fuel, and losing health by touching the Asteroids will also drain your health. There is also a big spinning jaw on the level (seen also on the Story cutscenes), that drain your health almost instantly.
The second stage is a side-scrolling shooter, you have 3 hearts (each hit takes a half of a heart) and you have to reach to the end by destroying baddies.
The third stage is a platformer that you need to rescue some people that will give you some descriptions after each one is free. Find all ten and proceed to the weirdest part of the game.
The fourth stage, by all honest, I haven't beat. The game had a huge difficulty spike (the difficult increased greatly between the first three levels to the fourth). You have to kill a boss on a Shoot-n-up style that you can only go Left and Right, and again, you only got 3 hearts. The boss shoots really fast projectiles that I can't even dodge so well. The design of the boss and the stage is really disturbing, which is also another reason why I didn't want to beat this level and this game.
I don't know if there are other stages, but I read this game is relatively short.
- Game art -
Uriel's Chasm art is not pretty. It attempts to make it retro, but there's also too much stuff on the screen (like the big spinning jaw). The graphics tries to be somewhere between 8-bit and 16-bit, but it fails miserably. The music, is bad, some levels have cool musics, but the rest may be very generic musics with no tension for that level. There is no fourth level music, you only get a lot of people screams.
- Conclusions -
I don't recommend this game for being really short, bad art (Music, graphics and story), being way too expensive (even though I got this for free, I do not like it) and really disturbing. If you get this game for free like me, and you wanted it only because the Steam Trading Cards, please do not play it, keep it on the Main Menu and Mute your computer's volume, and after you're done with, uninstall and never touch it again.
3/10

I sincerely doubt that many other people will like TBG, hence the "Not Recommended" rating.  After the first half hour, I was thinking to Myself: "This is time I can never get back.  I should quit now and play something actually fun."    I kept thinking that for quite a while.  Near the end, I think that I understood what was going on, and I saw what the creator was trying to do, and I did actually LOL at the whole thing,  but at that point it was a bit late.  This may have worked better as an actual short story in Asimov's or something.
There are some technical glitches, particularly with the text dialogue sets.  (I'm running Ubuntu on a laptop, so might just be My machine.)  First time around though, after the first area, the controls froze and the mouse disappeared ENTIRELY.  I had to bring up a terminal (command line) and kill the process manually.  Restarting, I continued without incident.  The loading between scenes was a bit long sometimes as well, so I wasn't sure if the game was stuck, but it did EVENTUALLY get going.
I'll note also that in the credits at the end he thanks Jack Parsons.  I'm not sure if it's a reference to *the* Jack Parsons or simply someone else with the same name though.  If the former, it does explain quite a bit about the creator. ;)

The Forest is a rare standout in the bogged down genre of Early Access Survival games. Despite its rough edges The Forest is a compelling game with enemies that keep you always scared and on your toes. There are no overpowered strats, and even basic survival will be a true trial and error test. My friends and I originally tried to build a walled in compound with around a small pond as a food and water resource, eventually we were swarmed by too many cannibals to handle who tore down our walls. When we tried to live out of a houseboat and rafts we realized that it was hard to actually accomplish anything on land, and when we tried to build a treehouse village the trees were knocked down. Nowhere is safe. Some of the most fun I've had in co-op and the games ending will send you for a ringer. The endgame is legit and the game is only in alpha. Great for multiplayer, still recommended for single player.

It's a fun and unique game but the presentation feels so unnecessary. Before reading this, please take time to realize that I don't really have any problems with the gameplay. It works well and poses a good challenge that feels satisfying to overcome. The stuff you gotta sit through just to get from level to level is what's draining.
I'm probably in the minority here, but I find the game is obnoxious to the point of not even wanting to finish it. If I find the presentation that bad, then I don't see how I can recommend it. Every time you complete a level, the game feels the need to chant SUPER HOT repeatedly and flash the words over 80% of your screen. It's as though it needs to constantly remind you what you're playing.
The developers of
reached a good level of style with the colour contrast and smooth modelling. Somewhere along the way, that wasn't good enough for someone. And now it has gone too far: past the acceptable and enjoyable levels of style and into a realm of redundant "story".
As a player, these fourth wall breaking approaches feel kind of insulting. In my opinion, the fourth wall should only be broken for comedic effect. The second most writers try to do something serious with it I roll my eyes. I play games to get in the role of something I'm not, not to be told that I'm a dude at a computer and that I'm being controlled to kill people or whatever.
Not all games need a plot. I don't see any of the positive reviews clamoring about how gripping it was, so it's obviously not a big reason people liked
. Spend less time making these unintuitive menus and more time designing levels. Why bother adding filler? It's not the kind of game that needs a story to tie it all together. It could literally have a menu that shows the available levels where you click one to play it and I would have been more satisfied.

Back in 2010, when LIMBO came out, I didn't consider myself a gamer. Well, I still wouldn't now, but I've certainly worked on my gamer know-how. I was reading a couple of gaming magazines back then and all they reported about were AAA-titles.  OK, occasionally there was a new-ish, kind of retro-ish game that they would call "Geheimtipp" or "insider tip" (as I think it ought to be called in english), but the majority were games that continued to work on external values such as graphics etc. I wouldn't say people actually wished for a change, but that was kind of the case in 2010.
Suddenly Indie became a legit genre and ventured into the mainstream with games like LIMBO or Super Meat Boy. External values weren't as important as they had been and thus the ground was opened for developers that aimed for a rather minimalistic approach in graphics and concentrated on gameplay instead. And nowadays both approaches begin to mold as we see in games like The Witcher series. It seems to get harder for developers to make a both critically and publically acclaimed game if they don't put enough effort in both internal and external values.
So far, enough on the boring part. Good games stay good regardless how "important" they might be "historically". And LIMBO really is a good one. I'd say it has remained an "insider tip" over the years even though most casual gamers probably have at least heard the name once. Even more so with INSIDE that came out last year.
No idea. Figure out for yourself. Watch some videos on YouTube or read some articles on Wikipedia. It doesn't change the experience much. "Story" as in the common meaning of the word doesn't exist in LIMBO. It's more of a collection of symbols that make up for a dark, surreal and often times dream-like atmosphere. But sadly (at least in my opinion) gameplay is way more important. The "story" picks up some leads and leaves them out in the open without even resolving them. And the "ending" doesn't give anything of a closure. It uses the infamous "Möbius strip", which means that the game ends exactly where it begins.
Some might see the lack of "story" as a disadvantage, some might see it as cool as it evokes a kind of mystery that is rather uncommon in video games. I think that it really isn't that important as we're dealing with a "puzzle" game in the first place. As such, LIMBO is really interesting, frustrating at times, but often times also extremely repetitive.
At the start of the game you really just have to walk on, figure out the controls until the "puzzles" gradually start to increase in quantity and difficulty. Over the course of the game you encounter various new elements, like magnets, turrets, elevators, saw blades etc. You have to master all of them properly so you can (most of the time) get a box to a certain place in the screen so you can climb up a platform you couldn't have reached normally. Death is inevitable. In my first and until now only playthrough I died exactly 180 times. That's because LIMBO isn't about "puzzles". It's about timing. Kind of like in the Raymond-series, but more gritty and brutal.
I'm not really a fan of games that need you to have good reflexes and timing instead of having to actually use your brain. Gameplay in LIMBO didn't surprise me. But neither did it disappoint me. In fact, it just frustrated me most of the time. I just wanted to go on and look for a possible answer to the mysteries of the "story". But then I kept dying and dying and...
I was impressed. Every time I died the animation was completely different. I think it's amazing how fluently the ragdoll system seems to work in LIMBO. Take that [insert random video game with bad ragdoll physics here] ! Sometimes screens were too dark though so I could barely see anything- even with lamps in the particular screens. Sound design was OK, it managed to enhance the atmosphere.
LIMBO is more than just the sum of it's parts. As a whole, it's an experience worth your time. If you liked the Rayman-series you'll probably like LIMBO as well. But if you're looking for a gritty adventure game with difficult puzzles that rely solely on brain power, you've definitely come to the wrong place. Also, if you think that the 13 achievements are easy to get, think about it again, you overconfident prick.
Jokes aside, you should get LIMBO whenever you can. Although it's hardly a game in my opinion, I think you should get it. Decide for yourself whatever amount of money you want to spend on it. Gladly, I got it last year when it was completely free. I'll probably never play it again, but it has deserved it's place in my library. It was once an "insider tip" but it always will be a gem for your library.

Until this game is finished, I don't recommend playing it unless you can get it for DIRT CHEAP. I'm not saying it's impossible to win, it's not... it's actually incredibly easy to finish a game (which is currently locked at I think 5 stages) but my problem is that it's too damn easy, there just aren't enough variables on both sides to provide a compelling and replayable game without using the same or similar builds you previously used that worked.
So far it's barely worth a 2/5 and I would even go as low as 1/5 except it works well enough to allow you to get an idea of what they were invisioning, their goal is certainly not 'ambitious' regardless of what bs the company might be playing up for marketing purposes but it has potential to carve up a nice niche genre slice all of it's own.
Combat is a solid 2/5 and IF it ever gets finished and continues at it's current pace will probably manage a 4/5.
Exploration is a sad 1/5 as since an entire ♥♥♥♥ing mechanic (research tree) is missing, you have to rely on random drops to learn new tech which can be a significant burden on resources leading to a no win situation.
Role Play is unfortunately a 1/5 as well since it seems that most if not almost all of the features they have yet to actually implement have been thought of for the current balancing and so there are times where you are either TOO powerful and just steam roll everything or you are pathetically weak and can't go any further without some serious resource spending (if you have any to spare/spend).

The paranoia of just knowing that Foxy could charge your door at any given moment, or that Freddy may be lurking just around the corner. I would 100% recommend this game to somebody who wants something different in a horror game. Great concept, decent execution.

I spawned in a trailer park, ran from some zombies, found a gun in a trailer, found some ammo in another. I made a run for it to a grocery store, there I met some other survivors we looted the store, lots of food was taken, I took 5 cans of tuna. As we were leaving I fired at a zombie (big mistake). Zombies from miles around were on us in minutes, they were attracted by the sound of my 9mm. It got chaotic some died, the rest were separated, I made a dash for the woods. I was lost for what seemed like forever with no shelter and the scratch on my arm from the earlier chaos was beginning to fester with infection. I tore up my shirt and made some bandages, good to stop the bleeding, but no help for the infection. Now without my shirt I was cold and it was pitch black midnight. I would come across a straggler zombie here and there, but they were easy to avoid by hiding in the trees. I dared not shoot this gun again it was a curse disguised as a blessing. Around day break I found some railroad tracks and decided to follow them. The tracks led me to a bridge that I crossed and soon I found myself at an old drag racing strip, finally! I found shelter in one of the garages and a fork to replace my all too loud pistol was found in a near-by trailer. I was in rough shape though as my infection was getting worse and I had no food, since I had no can opener to open the tuna. I did find a rotten tomato in the fridge of the trailer and against my better judgement ate it. I was now sick, with an infection, shirtless, cold and my bandage was dirty. I was going to die... I followed the tracks further and they finally lead me to a bar where some other survivors were holed up, they were friendly, greeted me and invited me in. One of them was a fellow I had met earlier at the grocery store. We pooled our resources,I got a can opener for my tuna, I changed my bandage and got some first aid. I was still very sick, but now I had hope. I went to bed that night with a full belly of tuna and cola, my last meal. I died in my sleep and my animated corpse attacked the group I hope they survived...they probably didn't....neither will you...

It seems to me that there's been an influx of Apocalyptic Zombie-Survival games recently, and for good reason.
It's an interesting and exciting genre that does deserve to be explored.
Sadly, no one has gotten it right though.
At least, not until Project Zomboid came along.
Project Zomboid is one of those indie gems that comes along once in awhile. I'm sure people will shrug it off because of the graphics, but I don't mind them personally. But let's talk a little about the synopsis.
In this game you play as a customized character of your choosing with the ability to pick a starting proffession and a few traits. You have a certain number of "trait points" that you can spend on your character. Interestingly enough, you can choose "negative traits" to give you more points for "positive traits". These negative traits can range anywhere from Obese to Deaf. You then move on to pick which town in Kentucky you should spawn in, Muldraugh (small urban setting) or West Point (big city). It is up to you at this point on how you will survive the zombie apocalypse. The crafting system is simple enough to understand, yet advanced enough to add variety. Warning though: You will die.
Overall, this is an excellent game and definitely worth the $15.
For me, Project Zomboid get's an 8/10.

When it comes to survival games, this one is my very favourite. Here's why:
- More realistic mechanics than other games.
- You're not just fighting enemies (which can even be turned off), you're also trying to survive in the environment. Blizzards can kill you quickly if you're not careful and there's no fighting back against them.
- Fantastic atmosphere, very immersive despite the beautiful stylized graphics.
- The crafting is great. I wish there were more things to make but I always wish that no matter the game.
- Tends towards a slower pace, which can be relaxing if you enjoy that.
- Doesn't feel like a regular game with food and water bars tacked onto it.
I wish more survival games were like The Long Dark. If they add in building (which I believe it planned), transportation (also planned), and co-op (pretty please?), and it would be absolutely perfect.

First-Hour Impressions:
Menus:
System menues are cryptic and (sometimes) buggy. Had to exit game once because settings menu caused permanent grey overlay, disabling any further input.
Controls:
-Game lacks deadzone for analog stick and character movement is stuck in 8-direction.
-Menu navigation with controller is difficult and non-intuitive.
In short, game was developed more for keyboard/mouse than controllers.
-If you don't jump, character falls like a lead weight instead of accelerating downward.
-Mouse isn't bound to the window of the game (even in fullscreen). This can lead to clicking outside the window instead of attacking.
-Can teleport onto top of platform if jumping high enough next to it.
-Attacking needs polish: Button clicks are queued such that if you double click, your character will attack twice. However, if the second click is done toward the end of the previous strike, the second strike won't happen until the next time you click to attack, upon which the character will attack twice despite clicking only once the second time. This can make your character fall off the sides of the map if you're unlucky.
-Holding down backflip button will cause character to continually backflip rather than backflipping once.
Can be an issue since character backflips rather far and may lead to accidentally falling off the map.
Additionally, since shift button is backflip, the character backflips when opening/closing steam overlay menu. Combine these two issues and you'll find yourself backflipping off of the map quite often.
Presentation:
-Graphics are pleasantly cel-shaded.
-Levels are geometrically simple and easily navigable.
-Puzzles and platforming!
-Voice acting isn't great but isn't terrible.
-Dialogue tends to interrupt or overlap itself.
-Falling off the map simply brings you to the general area you were in, so only seconds of play need to be redone.
-Losing all your health makes you redo the entire level over. This wouldn't be as much of an issue if the battle controls were better.
The game looks nice so far though it could use some polish.

My god this game was boring. So, so boring. Its only positive it that it was also short, so just when I kind of wanted to die I realized I was 80% done.
There was honestly nothing about this game I liked, although there was at least nothing I absolutely hated. The puzzles were frustrating and unintuitive, and even when I could figure them out they were often these awful timing things that you had to do over and over and over to get just right (that ♥♥♥♥ing minecart). The game was also bad at making it clear which objects were interactable and which were part of the scenery, and by didn’t make clear I mean it didn’t try at all. There was no way to know, for example, which rope was climbable and which wasn’t, until you tried to jump for it. Often, things that looked like ledges were actually moveable. I got in the habit of just holding down the interact button as I ran because the odds of missing something I could use were so damn high.
On the other hand, the game tried to trade on atmosphere, but I found the atmosphere to be bizarrely muddled. It was part psuedo-intellectual-art-film, part 12-year-olds-playing-war-gore, and the result was a tonal conflict that the game could never resolve. I couldn’t tell what the dev was going for or what I was supposed to be feeling. Was it muted horror and hopelessness? Was it “lol mutilated children”? Was it supposed to be both? Those aren’t two tones that work together, and as a result I just ended up not caring about either one. I also found it really… squicky? uncomfortable? how excited the game seemed to be about over-the-top violence directed toward a little boy. Was it expecting me to be like, excited by that? Did it think it was edgy? I don’t know what the game thought or what it was trying to do.
All of this is made worse by the fact that there’s literally no story. I’ve played several games in this Sale Roundup that manged to tell stories without any words, written or otherwise, and let me tell you, it’s entirely possible to have a meaningful narrative that propels you forward without any linguistic input from the game. This game didn’t have that — “You turned this on and you know how platformers work, so you might as well just go,” seemed to be its thesis, and I’m not sure if this was some stupid attempt at metacommentary or just the work of people who don’t know how to tell a wordless story, but this was a game with awful gameplay, no plot, and an incomprehensible tone that I would have quit 15 minutes in if I didn’t feel the need to finish it for the review. There was nothing here that gave me any reason to keep going.
And then at the end it rewards you with the requisite woman (well, girl), as though that has any meaning at all. I was just glad it was over.

Querky and Fun.
But... A bit of a hit and miss. I'd still recommend the game any day, but you may want to pay close attention to many of the other reviews before purchasing the game (and/or reading the rest of this review).
Don't mind the number of hours - I've easily put in about 10-15 hours, most of it played offline on my laptop on bus journeys.
I'd rate it about 6/10. I got it on sale, if I recall correctly, so it was rather cheap; and for the price I purchased it at (a few pounds), it proved to be a decent casual game I could pick up and play at just about any time - be it on my desktop, or my outdated laptop, which more often than not struggles to run anything.
So what brought me to this arbitrary rating?
-> The game is rather easy. Actually, it is almost ridiculously so at some points due to the ease of evading enemies. It may be a stealth game, but more often than not you'll find yourself running out of the way or taking a different route rather than sneaking past those pesky robots. Why? Because it is easier, faster and generally more simple to do so.
Robots
somewhat dangerous if you're new to the game - they hit hard and you will probably die pretty fast. But after you've thought up a few tactics to combat them, you'll find that early difficulty gone.
Robots are also fairly easily to spot out. They produce alot of noise, so if you miss them because they're deep in some shrubbery, you're sure to hear them fairly quickly and thus avoid them. Or you'll see their glowing red eyes, and take a different route.
Hunger on the otherhand can catch you out if you're not careful. They've got a decent hunger system, which can keep you on your toes if you're not careful. But then again, after going through a village or two, you'll find yourself loaded with plenty of food (unless you arm yourself up).
Guns. You're not really meant to use them, being the way the game is set up - but you can anyway. They hit hard, and given enough bullets you can drop the whole evasive and stealth part of the game and go on a bit of a turkey shootout. They're pretty easy to kill, and if you use a bit of cover and run enough, you should have no issues at all.
-> Highly subjective, but I'd rate the graphics quite high - many others would probably rate them much lower, but you should be able to make your own mind up from the screenshots alone. I think they look rather pretty and give off a nice atmosphere, despite being potentially 'dated' or at the least, far from AAA graphics.
A big plus concerning the simplistic graphics is... Well, I'd put it down to the specs. It isn't intensive, and you can run it easily on old systems.
-> I believe I got it on sale, as mentioned earlier, so I'm giving it a 7 out of 10. This is largely due to the fact that I do not regret spending cash on it, nor do I feel cheated out of pocket. I've spent cash on AAA games and felt cheated or that I've wasted cash, such as CoD, but in the case of 'Sir, You Are Being Hunted', I don't.
But, then again the price is really down to how much money you have to spare. For me a few pounds was cheap, but for others you may find buying something else to be more value for money.
-> I'd actually rate the UI rather high. It is relatively unique and rather simplistic, and has a nice feel. That, and the inventory system is the sort I like too, on top of it (Diablo/Two Worlds Style - a limited number of squares within the window in which items can be placed, and some items use up more squares than others).
-> Beyond looking pretty, I sometimes feel a lot of space is wasted in this game. You can find yourself wandering through plains and fields, and then the odd forest - actually, you will likely find yourself spending most of your time doing this and the wilderness doesn't really feel threatening, which is a downside for a game where you, the player, are being hunted.
Another minor issue would be that despite the worlds being random, they do often feel and look rather similar. A little more diversity in world generation would be wonderful, such as large hills, denser forests or bigger towns or villages.
---
I'd say the devs have done a good job on the game, but they can do plenty more to make it considerably more fun and interesting for the player. I would like to say first of all what you most likely have heard many times about this game to get it over with, its hard. Though, if you keep playing the game and keep acknowledging that this is a game meant for you to have difficulty striving as you figure out how to defeat some of the bosses and run 'n guns, you feel amazing. The game looks amazing, reminds me of a cartoom I used to watch as a kid called looney toons, it just makes it even more fun to play. All this I am sure you have heard before, so I will say my expierience. I rage at games, a lot, I broke my desk twice playing this game (I can fix it). Playing some of this game, I can not bare it, for me, it is one of the hardest games Ive ever played. Though I do not account that for how good the game is, its difficulty should absolutely not affect its rating. I finished it by myself on regular mode, so it is most definitely not impossible. Aside from my rage while playing the game, the music, the visuals, the designs, and my urge to get to the end of the game made me want to see this game to its very end. I did not expierience glitches or any wierd lag issues in this game so there is nothing that is going on there. I always found myself in a position where I cannot stop playing a boss until I have killed it. Some I have played for hours, and I did not get tired of it. This game is a game where you are not going to kill a boss first try, and if so, I will not believe you. Whenever I played a boss or a run 'n gun, I had to play it at least 10 times before I really knew what to do and where to be. Some bosses you need to be on the very edge of the screen, some bosses you need to be up close and personal to actually deal damage, some bosses you need to take it slow or you will die. This you need to learn in a series of retrys. Now, going back to what kept me going in the game and how I was able to bare sitting in one place just shooting a boss and dying over and over was just the looks, but especially the soundtrack. It fits the theme and especially the boss itself, and in general, It is just flat out good. I have a lot of the soundtracks on stand by and there have been a lot of times where I stop and just listen to it. The music in any level in the game did not get old no matter how much I played it, and it sure as hell made me keep wanting to play the game. One thing that I found amazing about the game was its effort in the creativity factor of the game. Some bosses I played and I found it how amazing its phases were so different and amazing. Some times it blows my mind how much thought went into making the idea of the progression in these bosses. One of the bosses is a bee and then turns into a plane, anoher is two frogs that turn into a slot machine, it is crazy what they come up with to make the bosses. That does it for What I think about the game and what makes me love it. Over all, I really recommend it to anyone, even if platformers are not your thing, but be preped for something that wont be easy and will make you rage.

Survival Horror FPS where you play as Sir or Madame, a human who got teleported to a series of islands inhabited by killer robots wielding guns. You have to find multiple pieces of the teleportation device that are scattered across the islands, all while trying to stay fed and healthy.
The game is randomly generated, allowing you to choose the general theme for four of the five islands you'll be trying to survive on. There are many times you'll see houses clipping inside of hills, which kind of removes some of the immersion. However, it doesn't detract much from the game since there is always the constant threat of being spotted by one of the robots.
Not gonna lie, this game is scary. The world is dreary and gray, the only person you have contact with is a gentleman that gives you advice on how to survive the islands. The world feels very cold and against you. If you stay in the water for too long, giant robot tentacles come out of the water and attack you, with little to no warning. This just adds to the tension of never knowing when something is going to attack you. Weather balloons manned by robots act as flying sentries, patrolling towns in search of you. If you they spot you, they keep a light on you while sounding an alarm to alert all nearby robots.
You tend to be weaponless, and when you do have a weapon you scarcely have any ammo. Most food you'll find is rotten, and inventory management prevents you from hogging a bunch of bandages, food, and ammo while still making progress. The scattered teleporter pieces can range from big 9x9 items that take up most of your grid inventory, or a small 3x1 item that can be placed alongside a bottle. It's very intense seeing a couple of robots by an artifact, but very rewarding when your plan to kill them and take the piece works out.
The more pieces you collect the harder the game gets. I haven't gotten very far because I always quit when a robot spots me and I'm defenseless. This game is actually up there in the list of scary games I insta-quit out of when I'm ♥♥♥♥ed. For such a silly concept presented in a funny manner, I personally think this game lives up to the survival horror name.

NOTICE: I see that my total playtime for Evolve is listed as 0.0. This is an error, I am not sure why it has occurred. I played the game for approximately 6-8 hours before I wrote this review.
Evolve is a pretty simple game, at its core. You and three other hunters team up to defeat an enormous monster controlled by a fifth player. Or, you control the monster yourself, starting off relatively weak but through eating local wildlife and staying out of the hunters’ path, you evolve to two more powerful stages. Reach the third one, and you become a nigh unstoppable killing machine. Though there are multiple game modes and each of the four hunter classes have three different characters with a unique loadout, every round of the game plays pretty much exactly the same. And that’s where the problems start to pile up. You see, Evolve is a bare bones experience to put it mildly. There are only a few maps, and all play the same. There are only two modes of play. The main mode is Hunt, which has the hunters searching for the monster which tries to evolve to a powerful enough stage so that it can kill the hunters or destroy an important building. And then there’s the “campaign” mode called Evacuation, which is five random matches loosely tied together by some well-produced but hollow and meaningless cinematics. The matches themselves are played in three different game modes - all of which are slight modifications to the Hunt-mode, all playing the same.
After some time, you’ll come to realize that you had seen the entire game already within the first few hours of play. Sure, playing with a different hunter or monster gives you other abilities, but you still do the exact same thing every match; escape and evolve as the monster, search and hunt as the hunter. And the way you do it isn’t even altered either. Every match either ends within a couple of minutes in which the monster player is trapped and killed early - and likely rage-quits as a result - or the monster eventually reaches stage three. By this point, the hunters have been running around the entire map for fifteen minutes, uneventfully sniffing at tracks and looking at birds. It might sound like some sort of intense “quiet before the storm” build-up, but it really only is exciting like that the first few rounds. After that, the distinct feeling of monotony sets in. Evolve is extremely repetitive, and the flawed progression system that’s supposed to have you coming back for more, does a♥♥♥♥♥♥poor job at doing so. It even goes so far as to force players to use ineffective methods that can lead to a match loss, just so that you can level up and unlock the next character for a class. And if you don’t have any friends who play the game - or God forbid, you live in Europe where nobody uses voice chat in public play - then you are out of luck. Playing Evolve will feel like playing the lottery. You’ll rarely find a match where people talk in a friendly manner, work together and try to enjoy the game without ruining everybody else’s day.
Evolve is, if anything, a solid backbone to what could’ve been an amazing game. Evolve would have been an amazing free-to-play shooter. The groundwork is there, and it’s solid. The controls are responsive and the mechanics are streamlined to the max. It’s a concept that is clearly thought out, and apart from a few frustrating bugs and balancing issues, the overall impression is extremely polished. But with the lackluster amount of content that you get for the asking price, the inherent monotony of the gameplay and the downright offensive DLC strategy that asks $15 - the equivalent of an overpriced map pack - just for a single new monster-character, I doubt that a couple of paid DLCs offering new monsters and hunters will be enough to keep the player count strong for more than a couple of months at best. And that is just sad because it’s evident that the developers knew what they were doing, but it seems the publisher got in their way at every junction. Cut this out, save it for later. DLC this, DLC that. When you pay this much from the get-go, and then are expected to keep paying in order to actually get a slight semblance of variety out of the damn thing, then it honestly isn’t worth it in my book. If you’re going to get Evolve, then get it cheap. Very cheap. And because there aren’t any dedicated servers, you’ll be wise to check if the game actually has an actively playing community at all when you first decide to plunk down the dough.

-Overview-
LYNE is a simplistic, minimalist puzzle game in which you must draw lines in order to conect the colored dots in each level, passing through each a defined number of time and not crossing other lines. The concept is simple, and the execution elegant and the final product represents a great casual game for the bored.
The Pros:
Loads of Levels! - There are close to 1000 levels to be completed - a set of 25 levels for each letter of the alphabet. Each set has it's theme, such as number of colors, number of nodes and the size of the matrix.
Great Design - Vectorised graphics, bright colors, ability to unlock and apply color themes, seamless transitions through levels and an intuitive menu. This game looks and feel gorgeous.
Relaxing - This is a great casual timekiller that you can pop in every now and then. The music is calming, the gameplay smooth and nobody rushes you.
Random Daily Sets! - Finished the game and feeling you need more levels? Don't worry! Every day you get a randomly generated pair of sets for you to complete!
The Price - Without discount, you can get this game for the modest price of 2,99Euros, which is great considering the ammount of levels you can get out of this thing.
Achievements - Just as a bonus, the achievements unlock as you complete sets, and are each a letter. If you have an achievement showcase, you can write words with your acomplishments and it seems to be really popular among LYNE owners.
The Cons:
Repetitive - The game runs out of new game mechanics early, as it presents them to you in the first sets, and then it's just a combination of those in the rest of the game. Which isn't a bad thing, but it means that this game is best enjoyed in small sessions, as doing many levels at once can prove to become boring.
Conclusion:
If you enjoy a good puzzle game and a casual experience that looks and feels like a quality program, don't hesitate to grab this one off the "shelf", especially considering the small price tag. A great casual experience!

Still one of the best historical FPS games ever made.
Red Orchestra 2 improves upon the realistic experience of its predecessor. It also adds a new weapons and class advancement system, updated visuals, and historically-accurate maps in the horrific Battle of Stalingrad.
Major pros:
-Realistic combat: sans cross-hairs, ammo counters, and radar. Health/damage model is made more "realistic" in that if you are hit, you must bandage yourself to survive. I personally find it hard to go back to CoD because it seems almost childish
-Tank combat, though more limited, is more realistic: if a crew member is killed, you can't just jump instantly from spot to spot
-Graphics are excellent for 2012 standards, and are still not bad in 2016; the ambient occlusion makes the lighting and world have volume and feel life-like
-Each map is unique, and requires different tactics to win
-The new campaign system gives more "purpose" to the multiplayer experience
Cons:
-Tank combat is more limited than RO1; however, some of the newer custom maps like Arad2 and Barashka have added more tanks (though still limited to Pz III and IV and T34)
-You can't use every weapon when you start out. You have to level-up to use guns such as the MG42 and MKB 42; however, this does give a sense of purpose as well: the more you play, the more weapons you unlock
Overall, the cons are not a big deal and this game is very immersive, gritty and fun. But, be prepared to die A LOT if you are a noob, and spend a lot of time waiting to respawn.

Highly recommended for those seeking something at a different pace.

Even early into it's beta, DotE has been a pretty enjoyable mish-mash of tower defense of roguelike RPG bits for me. The premise is simple: Take control of larger and larger swaths of the dungeon and fortify that territory against an increasingly persistant enemy until you feel comfortable enough making a mad dash with your crystal to the next level and start building up again.
The pleasure and the challenge of the game comes from the very complex and meaningful choices you have to make at every turn. Every resources has multiple uses that are critical to your run. Food, for instance, can be used to heal in battle, permanently level up your hero, or purchase new ones. Dust is used to power rooms so you can build there, but also to purchase key items to keep your heroes alive. Even gathering these resources is a tough choice: You only generate income when you open doors, exposing yourself to new risk. Any room you open but can't afford to power could be an alien spawning point.
This tightrope provides for a great spot of strategic fun as you constantly balance all these equally important needs. On the other hand, the tactics of the actual hero combat is rather mundane.  While they've recently added active abilities to keep things a little fresher, your best offense is still returning to whatever chokepoint you've created and let your turrets do most of the talking. This moment-to-moment combat may be further improved when they implement research and tech trees.
Monster variety is aesthetically rather boring at the moment, though they do everything they ought to in that several of them have unique targetting priorities, even if it means completely ignoring you to bee line for critical systems. Keeps you on your toes.
In the end, keep an eye on it if it's the sort of genre that appeals to you. There's the foundation for a very good game here, and their roadmap indicates they've got a lot of ideas for interesting content as they approach release.

Forward to the Sky is short action-platformer that I'm not entirely sure how I picked up.
You guide your generic moeblob through six levels of generic platforming challenges, and throw out your two combos (press one button five times or press the other button four) against the four generic enemy types - Skeleton Mage, Skeleton Archer, Skeleton Warrior, and Mr. Bones.
So this is fine, so far. It has the good sense to be short in the face of not having any depth, and there's always room for games that don't waste your time but do what they do well.
The trouble is that it's not any good.
The environments and characters themselves are fine, the cell-shaded look certainly pays off despite the lack of asset variety. The OST fits, the designs are okay (even if the enemies are a bit F2P mobile game-ish), the lighting actually works, the problems don't start there. They start with the mechanics.
Movement is mapped to eight cardinal directions that operate independantly of the camera. This means that you can be right next to an enemy and still miss with the lunge combo. And often will.
A fair few of those enemy types get larger versions that ignore hitstun and are otherwise unstaggerable. This is combined with the Skeleton Warrior having a few attacks with no startup or telegraphing. Or the Mage stunlocking you with its wonky hitboxes. Or the Archer constantly running away. So double the unfun to fight.
Mr. Bones is alright though.
Most of the platforming challenges are trite timing or physics puzzles, and combined with the locked movement directions they're not much fun either.
None of these remotely break the game. You've always got plenty of time of correct your falls (along with falling just meaning a return to the last checkpoint) and more than enough health to sleep your way through levels. It's just annoying. The whole game is just short and annoying, without even mentioning the characters.
The two lead characters repeat themselves more often than a broken record, cry at the drop of a hat, and sound like 30 year olds sucking on helium.
Plot is that bullied moeblob cries a lot until spunky young moeblob comes along and repeats how much she wants to banish the bullied moeblob. Then it turns out that it was all a big misunderstanding and then they shag or something I don't care.
Forward to the Sky is pet peeve of a game. It is a short, annoying roadbump in your existence.
It demands little and delivers nothing. Don't even bother.

This is quite a strange game. In my opinion, it's pretty genre-bending experience. I'll just sum up what the plot is: You are an English gentlemen who has mysteriously teleported and anbandoned on an archipelago of 5 islands, which are inhabited by several different types of robots, who, like you, are English gentlemen. These robots range from Hot Air Ballon pilots to just normal humanoid robots with rifles and hounds. Their mission is to hunt you down and kill you, before you are able to acquire a certain amount of crystals, which in return transport you back to your home, where your butler awaits.
I'll tell you first hand, that this game is TERRIFYING when you start playing it. When you see a Hot Air Balloon, you'll run for the forests to hide. When you see a group of hunters moving towards you from a distance, you WILL panic. Not only is this game scary in some ways, but it is also very depressing. Somehow the abandoned and destroyed setting and constant rain somehow brings it all down to a quite sad and almost nerve-wrecking experience.
But nevertheless, all of that depression is replenished with the spirit of scavenging and hunting your hunters! Although this seemingly a stealth game, you have all the wits and will to fight back. Eventually, you may find an axe. Or a rifle. Or even a grenade, Which all can be found through this game's scavenging system. Food, gadgets, and gizmos can be found all across the 5 islands in houses, destroyed robots, and more.
I would strongly recommend this game to anyone who likes a nice amount of stealth and a strong sence of fear.
WARNING! You need a pretty beefy computer, as mine cannot handle some of the detailed textures, and often lags when looking at, say, a forest. But even if you don't have a good computer, still try getting it! It's really worth it!

GOKEN:
~~~~~~

Every 5,000 years a celebration is organized to honor the gods! The latest one wasn’t the most memorable for you, Wielder of the Fives Swords. Honestly, God himself forged five swords for you to keep this world at peace, but what were you thinking when you challenged all the gods outside the small village of Cardina? You knew one of them would get super . . . cranky! And yes, you were sealed in rocks for a few millennium!  Now, after all this time, you are finally free, but only with one of your five swords. Tell us, how are you going to recover them, my dear hero? Welcome to GOKEN!
GOKEN is a 2D action / role playing game where you play the Wielder of the Five Swords. Your goal is to recover all of your swords - well, that’s one part of it; you’ll find out the rest when you play the game!
As you start a new, you‘ll go through a short introduction of the story. From there, a girl who goes by the name of Chao will free you by finding your sword next to your eternal prison and you’ll go through a small tutorial which will show you how to fight and what you have to look for within the world.
The world consist of three islands. Two of them are fairly large and the other one is small. In this game, you’ll basically be led to your next destination where you’ll not only find important information about your lost swords, but you’ll also revitalize yourself at the Inn, buy items at the merchant shop, or even get ink at the tattooist to enhance your abilities.
As you go through this gorgeous world (artwork), you’ll come across numerous enemies, the likes of the unicorn fox, goblins, feral rabbits with swords, cyclops and stingers, to mention a few – there are many more. As you find your swords, you’ll be able to select one of them for your attacks. Now bear in mind, you have two attack buttons and up to five swords (if you get them all) to choose from. Right now, I have three of the swords and I had to swap them around to get through some of the levels. Every time you kill an enemy, he will drop coins, experience points and ink. However, ink is rare. Just hover over to collect them. With the coins, you’ll be able to purchase items from the merchant, the experience points will get your character new levels and ink will give you the opportunity to buy extra abilities. You also have a speed dash (that’s what I call it) where you can avoid being hit during battle, and which can also be useful to move faster within the world. However, you must be careful how you use it, as it will deplete your stamina gauge every time you activate it. The good news is that the gauge refills itself quickly.
You’ll fight bosses here and there, but I must admit that I would like to have these battles a little bit harder; don’t get me wrong, they are still a lot of fun!
I really enjoy the artwork as it feels somehow unique, and the animations are pretty good, too. The soundtrack is well done and the controls are responsive, whether you use the keyboard or gamepad. I did have a few freezes here and there –mostly when I was reading wooden signs within the game. Apart from that, the game was running well.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Nice Artwork
-	Good animations
-	Varied and plenty of enemies to dispatch
-	Good story
-	Achievements and trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Need to save your progression
-	Battles need to be a bit harder
Goken is a well-designed game and beautiful to look at – it just needed to be a little bit more challenging!
7/10

Sir, You Are Being Hunted, (SYABH), is a proceedurally generated game that is a little unlike most games I have seen.  It is a rather plesent blending of alot of little game ideas that seem to pay off.
You play as a inferorior human, and some strange monolyth like marchine has exploded.  It is up to you to put it back together.   However while playing across some Britich Archapellago, you are being hunted by a colorful veriaty of robots who seem to find you fitting spot.

You need to eat to stay strong, you need rags to bandage yourself up, you need all kinda noise makers to distract robots, and if you lay your hands on a weapon you really need to wonder, is it safe to shot the robot, or is there another way. The worlds are pleasent and procedurally generated from game to game, you do have some control over it. An awesome game that so many have overlooked, if you like stealth and hide and seek this game is most certianly for you.

This is everything I want from a stealth game. Frequently I find stealth games are somewhat elementary. You can sneak but you're just as good fighting it out with all the guards. The only real penalty for not being stealthy is usually a rank at the end of the mission or game. This is little better than a wagging finger.
Sir, You are Being Hunted turns this on its head. You are vulnerable. You drop in unarmed. The clock is ticking. You have to scavenge supplies. Being spotted starts a mad dash for cover. You have little way to fight until you get lucky enough to find a weapon. Even then, killing a robot is difficult and you often stand to expend more ammunition taking one down than you will gain from having killed it. Stealth and patience are key.
My only complaint is that I wish the robots had posh British accents.

I bought this game, expecting something similar to the Stanley Parable.
I got something different.
In some ways, it is a very similar game. Walking and Jumping while a disembodied voice tells you a story. But at the same time, it is completely the oppisite due to the lack of any freedom of choice. The core of every game is interactivity; it's what makes this medium special. I played and saw a lot of games that heavily focus on a story they want to tell. However, the Beginner's Guide is the first game I played that focuses so hard that I would not call it a game anymore.
Maybe I should give probs to it for trying something new, which it really did. But I won't. I didn't like this game at all. I enjoyed the first third of the game quite a bit, I giggled here and there. But then I got bored. This game does not offer you anything but the single one story it wants to tell. You remain absolutely unrewarded for any exploration or out-of-the-box-thinking-stuff you do (at least after the first three or four levels are over) and you just have to walk through a seemingly endless amount of corridors or voids to reach the next void.
I felt more and more unhappy the longer I played it. I went on and kept thinking "when is it over?" but knew, that when it was, there would be nothing I could proudly look upon and think "well, that was worth the struggle to get here". Maybe it's the point of the game to give you this unrewarding feeling, this feeling of impuissance (just discovered this word via translator, sound nice). If that was the idea behind this game, then this game is absolutely bombastic. But I don't play a game to feel these things. I want to engage, to discover, to try, to achieve. But I couldn't.
