Project Zomboid is, in a way, what games like DayZ and H1Z1 want to be but seemingly will never become. It's a survival game where survival actually matters to players. As you level up your skills and begin being able to build nicer quality things for your base, or you can run longer, or even get stronger and can carry more, your need to survive only increases. Having to start over and redo your work means that the game's goal, survival, only becomes that much more important. The zombies also pose a very real threat, because one bite is almost guaranteed to kill you, and to a lesser extent a scratch. The hordes are massive, and if you want even more of a challenge you can make them sprinters. Good luck if you do.
With the challenge of the zed, and the need to survive in mind, many players in multiplayer opt not to just be kos bandits, and instead attempt to work together to survive. There are still kos bandits, but unlike Dayz not every single person is one. Finding other players on servers can lead to growing communities with thriving bases as you all attempt to survive the dead, the winter, and the bandits. Overally it's just a very enjoyable experience in which the bandits add to the suspense and the difficulty in a way that is fun and expected for the setting, and yet not game breaking. This could of course depend on the server you join, but there are a bunch of public ones to choose from, the official SpiffoSpace servers, and if you check the Indie Stone forums you can find lots of private servers with varying rule types to apply for.
As for the dev team, they seem to get some flak on still being in Early Access, and how long the game is taking to develop. Well in my opinion the devs for this game are really good. They aren't a massive team with AAA budget, and yet they still manage to provide weekly updates about upcoming content, and consistently provide new content that expands onto the game world at I believe monthly or so intervals. The direction they are going is clear cut, we know they are working on it, we know what they will be changing, fixing, or adding, and we also know that because of this the game is ever expanding.
As for the Early Access model, the devs of PZ are a beacon of hope, true paragons of the system. The model is supposed to allow players to play the game as it expands, acting as testers to find flaws, suggest content, etc, and that is exactly how it goes with PZ. The game will of course at times have bugs or glitches, but you know that the devs will eventually get to it, and that is more than I can say for most other Early Access survival games.

My First Impressions on LYNE:
LYNE seemed to be an appearantly simple puzzle game when I looked at the video. It made things look easy. However, In set C, things start to get puzzling. The first 50 levels (i. e. Sets A & B) can be finished in under a minute each, but set C (the set which I'm in as of writing this first impression) requires me to spend much more time. I wish there was continous background music, but I found out that only sound effects existed.
When the levels seem to get too hard, leaving and resting for about half an hour and going back seems to be one of the best solutions for me. Also, when you finish the 650 levels in the game, you can continue to play the computer-generated daily sets too (they are unlocked with set B).
Overall, I give it my recommendation.
Buying Info:
I've noticed many reviewers stating that they bought this game for spelling something in the achievement showcase (usually the name of the player), but I bought it for it was interesting and I had enough "free money (i.e. Trading Card Sales Proceeds)" to buy this game on the sale (for about ₹ 50). Also, as of the writing of this first impression, I'm level 6 and don't have an achievement showcase.

is a sad addition to the already-replete ranks of bad religious games; its intended satirical nature cannot save itself from its own dysfunctional gameplay, lazy execution and general misapplication of its religious themes.
It's maddeningly difficult to give a synopsis of this game, as the game never tells its own story properly. New players are introduced to one Sister Tabitha, who both monologues about being asleep for years yet inexplicably also knows about events that trouble the world. Players are then immediately dropped into a space setting, in a spaceship, with text explaining that they must collect Bible verses via mining asteroids. The game also launches a HUD that has four different values on it, including "Faith" and "Fuel", and before even processing what the controls are, the ship is crushed by some massive unknown object and the level is reset. This madness encapsulates the experience of
well.
This game is ravenously difficult, and little of it comes from fair, legitimate sources. The game's interface provides no indication for new players on how to play the game. Naturally, players will discover on their own that the arrow keys move the ship, but no other keys seem to do anything. Only after stumbling about on the keyboard will one find that the Z key fires the weapon. The shots fired from the weapon often phase through smaller asteroids, making it unreliable at best. The lack of collision sound effects for when the ship takes damage or when asteroids are destroyed makes it even easier for those not paying attention to spontaneously die. Perhaps the greatest injustice this game offers is that it has no pause menu, meaning that gamers that naively assume some level of competence by the developers and press "Escape" during a level to pause will find themselves back at the beginning video sequence...which is unskippable. It's always unskippable. The unremovable Bible tracts that appear on the bottom of the screen during the first level in putrid green hues rounds out this spectrum of awefulness. The game's length is quite pathetically short at only four levels, though no player of sound mind will make it past the first. Perhaps it is merciful that this mess cannot last for long.
This game tries to save face by marketing itself as a satire of early religious videogames, with its lackluster interface and tough-as-nails difficulty serving as callbacks for nostalgia's sake. However, the protection that satire provides, despite being quite overarching, is not enough to save this title. What differentiates good game satire from
is that good game satire must convey that it has the potential to be good, but is intentionally made badly in attempt to pay homage to bad source material. Without the implementation of basic functions or a good system for the game to run on, the satire fails to parody its source and instead just becomes what it tries to mock. See
and
for examples of satire done right. The former parodied old-school platformers with brutal difficulty and the latter parodied modern microtransactions by making everything in-game DLC. However, both of these games have basic functionality and don't turn off players with awful aesthetics and unfair mechanics. If those two were designed the way
was made, then
wouldn't have a jump button and
would make players pay actual money for the fake in-game DLC. Because the developers do not understand how to effectively render satire in videogames, this game fails on all levels: as an actual game and, most importantly, as a parody.
Good games and religious games are not mutually exculsive in theory, but this game does nothing to prove this theory correct. Adequate functionality in controlling the character does little to forestall the mass of horrible elements that this game forces players to endure, from the lack of simple components like a pause menu to no explanations of backstory to such an out-of-place shoehorning of Biblical passages in a game that otherwise has nothing to do with Christianity, that this game can only be described as
. Avoid this like the plague.

I really wanted to like this game. Everything aesthetic is beautiful, and the concepts are really interresting. Unfortunately, the gameplay is beyond unfair. The core challenge in this game comes being able to survive an onslaught of attacks for long enough to beat each level, and the controls do not lend themselves to being able to dodge or attack enemies. This is not a satisfying challenge; it is a frustrating endurance run.  The controls feel loose and the vast majority of the input involves simply spamming the X button. After spending half an hour on the first level, the feeling of beating it was not a sense of legitimate satisfaction; it was a feeling of "Oh my god, finally!" That is not a good feeling to have in a game, A game should feel as though it was set up with the appropraite challenges for the player to accomplish it. Cuphead feels like a custom level made by a child who diecided to put the maximum number of sprites in the smallest space possible, then spend the next hour getting mad at their own creation. It had a massive amount of potential, but it was squandered on the idea that a game's value comes from the amount of time needed to be invested to be competent at it.

I love the ambiguity and wonder this game produces. I haven't quite looked into much on the robots themselves, but I find that the immersion comes from wondering just what the robots are and observing their behaviors. Trying to stay hidden can be somewhat of a chore, but I find that it takes some amount of practice to be able to successfully sneak or confront robots and remain alive. Building your inventory is less "what if" and more "this is what I need right now". Some weapons and items are outright useless (I've had no luck using bear traps at all. I was able to set one off, but it just sat floating in the air). The weapon mechanics take getting used to, especially with the hatchet, but they are entirely usable, such as the shotgun and revolver. I enjoy the pseudo-sandbox aspect, wherein you can change your class to increase or decrease the difficulty and change what and when different robots appear throughout the game. Bottom line, Sir requires a bit of immersion on the player's end, which can be tough for some people who are used to better stealth games, but this game gives me chills and a racing heart. I have no idea what most of the robots are there for, but I really don't want to find out.

The game's mechanics are a good start, but they lack depth.  The only really good way to survive is to completely avoid the robots.  If you try to attack the bots, you'll most likely get killed and will definitely run out of ammo.  If you try to ambush a bot with an axe, you'll get shot and bleed to death before even landing a hit.  The robots have nearly unlimited ammo, but if you kill them, you'll rarely be able to scavenge any.  Trying to avoid the bots takes forever, so you starve to death.  Getting an objective without alerting the guard bots is pretty much impossible.  The guard bots get alerted, and even if you survive them, bots for half a mile will come running to kill you.  This game had potential, but wasted it.

NOTICE: I see that my total playtime for Evolve is listed as 0.0. This is an error, I am not sure why it has occurred. I played the game for approximately 6-8 hours before I wrote this review.
Evolve is a pretty simple game, at its core. You and three other hunters team up to defeat an enormous monster controlled by a fifth player. Or, you control the monster yourself, starting off relatively weak but through eating local wildlife and staying out of the hunters’ path, you evolve to two more powerful stages. Reach the third one, and you become a nigh unstoppable killing machine. Though there are multiple game modes and each of the four hunter classes have three different characters with a unique loadout, every round of the game plays pretty much exactly the same. And that’s where the problems start to pile up. You see, Evolve is a bare bones experience to put it mildly. There are only a few maps, and all play the same. There are only two modes of play. The main mode is Hunt, which has the hunters searching for the monster which tries to evolve to a powerful enough stage so that it can kill the hunters or destroy an important building. And then there’s the “campaign” mode called Evacuation, which is five random matches loosely tied together by some well-produced but hollow and meaningless cinematics. The matches themselves are played in three different game modes - all of which are slight modifications to the Hunt-mode, all playing the same.
After some time, you’ll come to realize that you had seen the entire game already within the first few hours of play. Sure, playing with a different hunter or monster gives you other abilities, but you still do the exact same thing every match; escape and evolve as the monster, search and hunt as the hunter. And the way you do it isn’t even altered either. Every match either ends within a couple of minutes in which the monster player is trapped and killed early - and likely rage-quits as a result - or the monster eventually reaches stage three. By this point, the hunters have been running around the entire map for fifteen minutes, uneventfully sniffing at tracks and looking at birds. It might sound like some sort of intense “quiet before the storm” build-up, but it really only is exciting like that the first few rounds. After that, the distinct feeling of monotony sets in. Evolve is extremely repetitive, and the flawed progression system that’s supposed to have you coming back for more, does a♥♥♥♥♥♥poor job at doing so. It even goes so far as to force players to use ineffective methods that can lead to a match loss, just so that you can level up and unlock the next character for a class. And if you don’t have any friends who play the game - or God forbid, you live in Europe where nobody uses voice chat in public play - then you are out of luck. Playing Evolve will feel like playing the lottery. You’ll rarely find a match where people talk in a friendly manner, work together and try to enjoy the game without ruining everybody else’s day.
Evolve is, if anything, a solid backbone to what could’ve been an amazing game. Evolve would have been an amazing free-to-play shooter. The groundwork is there, and it’s solid. The controls are responsive and the mechanics are streamlined to the max. It’s a concept that is clearly thought out, and apart from a few frustrating bugs and balancing issues, the overall impression is extremely polished. But with the lackluster amount of content that you get for the asking price, the inherent monotony of the gameplay and the downright offensive DLC strategy that asks $15 - the equivalent of an overpriced map pack - just for a single new monster-character, I doubt that a couple of paid DLCs offering new monsters and hunters will be enough to keep the player count strong for more than a couple of months at best. And that is just sad because it’s evident that the developers knew what they were doing, but it seems the publisher got in their way at every junction. Cut this out, save it for later. DLC this, DLC that. When you pay this much from the get-go, and then are expected to keep paying in order to actually get a slight semblance of variety out of the damn thing, then it honestly isn’t worth it in my book. If you’re going to get Evolve, then get it cheap. Very cheap. And because there aren’t any dedicated servers, you’ll be wise to check if the game actually has an actively playing community at all when you first decide to plunk down the dough.

In short, the monster puppets are creative and this would be a fun smartphone game to kill time with but as a pc game, if one can get it on sale for a dollar or two I'd recommend getting it just for a few moments of fun but in a world where most games have a open world where you can go all over the place, jack cars, do quests, etc, and so on, this game feels out of place.

Drunken Robot Pornography is a weird game. I did like it, but it sort of left me underwhelmed. The combat is very stimulating, everything is bright and colorful, and I enjoyed it for the most part, but it's far from the best shooter I've ever played.
The controls are floaty and imprecise. You really have to work your keyboard to land where you want to. Even when you are running it's hard to control. The jetpack also takes some time to get used to, as it is unable to overcome gravity when you're falling past a certain speed, making it difficult to know when you can no longer feather your jetpack to cover long jumps.
The time limits seem very arbitrary as some levels you can pass within seconds and some you can barely finish in time. These time limits also mean that a complete playthrough is very short. Even after failing a few levels multiple times, I was able to complete the game in just over four hours.
I'm no expert on "bullet hell" games, but I found the bosses unchallenging even on hard difficulty. The only real difficulty seems to come from the level designs themselves. Level 13 took me a few tries to pass, mostly from timeouts, as it was simply quite difficult to move around in.
The drone enemies seemingly never stop spawning on some levels, constantly interrupting boss battles. I died more from drone damage during boss battles than I died from the bosses themselves.
The pickups are definitely helpful. The weapon pickups stack, so you can combine them for more damage to take down bosses faster, but I have difficulties telling the difference between split fire and triple shot. I could detect no significant difference between them. The decoy, nuke, and invulnerability pickups are all pretty self explanatory and useful. The health pickups were very rare, and unfortunately, tended to be on levels were health was not an issue for me. The extra time pickup appears on only one level, and was not worth the time I wasted to get it, as it only gives five extra seconds. The orbital friendship cannon appears on only two levels, but is useful on both. Unfortunately, no in game prompts let you know how the cannon functions. That would have been something useful Suit could have told you, instead of yammering away telling you nothing. Something I found weird about the pickups is the audio cues. Why does Suit tell you when a pickup appears on the map, but there is no sound when you get it? A few times I missed a pickup, but in the frantic action I didn't notice, and had to go back for it.
The plot feels largely extraneous, the audio logs don't really add anything to the story, and the humor falls flat for me. The sound effects are adequate, and the music is ok, but like the rest of the game, it's a little off. It's mostly dubstep and synthesizer tunes, with a few levels featuring some music that catches you off guard. The best song in the game might actually be its theme tune which plays at the main menu whenever you start up the game, complete with karaoke lyrics.
For the price it is, DRP has more entertainment value than a feature-length movie. If you like frenetic action and bouncing around blasting away giant robots, you'll probably get a few hours of fun out of it. I know I did, even if it did make go, "Wha?" more than once. The challenge mode might extend your play time, but as for me, I get the feeling I've seen all that DRP has to offer. It's a fun little distraction.

Goken is an early access title from developers Gianty that attempts to “bring back everything that was right about gaming in an action packed open world environment in the form of the good old Action RPG genre and have the old school gamers tremble in nostalgia.” That is quite the bold statement, but besides a few balance and pacing problems Gianty developed a solid action JRPG with good looks and some pretty funny humor.
Combat is simple, consisting of 3 hit attacks with a chance of performing a super attack on the 3rd hit. While this makes the beginning hour of the game drag on due to only having one weapon, it does get better once you obtain your second sword. You will be able to equip a main and secondary weapon and are able to swap between the attacks with the 3 hit combo. It’s by no means a complex system, but there’s enough variety in situations that will be requiring you to swap for certain enemy encounters. Each weapon has their own unique style and some will even give you access to secret areas or you will have to use them to proceed in the game.
The upgrade system is pretty creative, however. While experience upgrades give you the standard HP, stamina and damage upgrades, it also gives you ink. Ink can then be used at a tattoo artist to further upgrade you weapons and stats. The weapons offer a mostly set list of upgrades, but there are also “free ink slots” where you will be able to use found ink that offer different stat boosts. As you unlock these upgrades a new piece of the tattoo is unlocked and while that is a cool gimmick, it sort of loses its uniqueness since you can’t actually see the tattoos on the swordsman’s body.
The graphic design is very nice, offering a very stylized hand drawn look and, while there are no graphical settings, the appearance is sharp and good looking and performed flawlessly during my playthrough. Each area of the world has a very distinct look with bright colors and is detailed well with some interactive elements. Goken, features your typical RPG areas: snowy mountains, lava filled volcanoes, lush woods, but they also have a few unique areas that were nice to see. The sound design is decent, not all of the sound effects are great or the highest quality, but the music is fantastic. Each area and town all have their own unique tune, each boss fight has its own battle music. My only complaint is that every step, no matter the surface, your feet make the same sound which does get a little irritating, but you quickly block it out after a while.

Holy Crap on a Cracker, this game is awesome! Where can I begin?
Firstly, the entire setting is wonderful. An archipelago of islands filled with deserted towns and houses, being watched over by Tweed-Donning robots with a taste for tea and murder. Exploring the islands is great fun, as you must always be on the lookout for roaming hunters and their dogs, hot air balloons lighting up your position or the Landowner, a fearsome robot with a cane that is well accustomed to crushing various bones and organs. Some variation in setting between islands whilst keeping the same British-Grey colour palette allows each area to be individual but memorable. The Castle biome has many ruined walls and turrets of old fortifications, while the Industrial Biome has larger towns with great chimneys and drilling platforms. Finding landmarks in the terrain that are often guarded by the posh automatons makes exploring no walk in the park, and adds to the tension and sense of adventure this game can create.
The enemies are very well designed, with types varying from the standard Winchester-wielding Hunters to the turbo-charged  robo-horses that are ridden by jockeys determined to run you over. The big cheese of all the robots is the Landowner who, as mentioned before, is a formidable opponent that must be avoided or outwitted in order to survive his metallic glare. Enemy variation doesn't stop there, and the combinations these types of robots can be found in can make taking certain Pieces a challenge.
The Main Object of the game is to retrieve each Piece of the "Device" that was destroyed in the "Experiment" (some backstory here wouldn't go amiss) and return them to the standing stones on the centre island. Each piece is guarded by at least two or more robots and can vary in size from tiny pieces that barely take up any room to giant parts of the device that need prior planning and inventory space to take back to the standing stones. Once all of the pieces have been collected the game ends. As time passes and pieces are returned, more robots appear, in greater numbers and variety, making each piece harder and harder to collect.
The Inventory system is tile based, so that certain items take up more room than others. A Flask of Luke Warm Tea only takes up 2 tiles but the Largest Piece of the Device takes up 16 tiles all together. Looting houses, fallen enemies and occasionally bins and phoneboxes mean that your inventory will stack up with all kinds of good loot, making you consider whether you want those extra shotgun shells or that canned pie that might be needed later.
All in All, I enjoy this game immensely and hope that Big Robot continue to add fresh content to this already wonderful concoction of a game.
EDIT: Props to the Devs for allowing you to play as a Madam!

GOKEN follows the story of Edge - The master of the 5 blades. Edge has spent the last 5,000 years sealed away at the top of Swords Peak by the god O-Zone after an unsuccessful challenge on his life. Woken up one day by a small child, Edge must travel the world in search of his lost blades. Only then can he finally have his revenge on the gods!
GOKEN is an Action-JRPG, not dissimilar to classic JRPG's such as The Secret of Mana, A Link to the Past and Alundra.
The first hour or so of GOKEN is a real slog, you only have access to one weapon so combat consists of spamming your choice of X or Y, you lack any real stamina, so you won't be going anywhere fast and the omission of a mini map means you may feel a little disorientated at first.
Don't let the slow start put you off, before long you will be reunited with your second weapon. A giant great sword, at this point the game starts to pick-up and its unique combat system really starts to shine.
You can have any two of your potential 5 weapons equipped at any one time. By tapping either attack button you can perform a 3-hit combo, at the point of the 3rd hit you have a chance to generate a special move. The special move generated will depend on what weapon you have equipped.
Enemies are strong and varied in GOKEN, there's at least 20 - 30 different enemy types and maybe 5 or more variations of each type. Each enemy has their own attack pattern and weapon weakness, you'll need to learn these if you don't want frequent visits to the Game Over screen.
The game will automatically save your progress at points, but this is far too infrequent for my liking. Luckily you're able to save your progress at any time from the pause menu.
The progression system in GOKEN is separated into two parts, character upgrades and weapon upgrades.
The character upgrade system is really quite cool. When you level up, you are rewarded with ink points, collect enough of these points and you can take them to your local tattoo parlour and apply them to your character. Applying tattoos will reward you with standard stat increases on top of what you receive for levelling up.
You can also unlock empty slots, in these empty slots you are able to place special ink which you will find during your travels. These special ink's are much more powerful than the standard upgrades. They're able to infuse the protagonist with special offensive and defensive powers, they can even increase the amount of gold or experience acquired,
The weapon upgrade system is more standard fare and pretty typical of most RPG's. On occasions, defeated enemies will drop crafting items, you can take these items to blacksmiths located in each town. Assuming you have acquired enough weapon experience, you can use these items to improve each weapon and make it even stronger.
Don't expect a massive array of graphical options in GOKEN, after booting up the game and navigating to the options menu I was greeted by 2 very lonely options. Resolution and window type. There's actually no graphical fidelity options of any kind and at this point the game doesn't support native borderless window mode either. With that being said, I was able to Alt & Tab back to the desktop on multiple occasions and the game didn't crash once.
To my surprise, the graphics in GOKEN are beautiful. Bright, colourful, detailed, there isn't even a hint of aliasing. The world is separated into large and very distinct areas, each one brimming with secrets to discover. And being an open world game, you're free to travel to each area at your leisure.
At first I had a few performance issues with GOKEN, nothing major, but there was some very obvious frame skipping during screen transitions. After some investigating, it was clear that my GPU was dropping down to idle clocks during gameplay. I switched my GPU to max performance mode and that seemed to do the trick, from then on it was smooth sailing.
I have absolutely nothing bad to say about the audio. Sound effects are synced well with actions and the music is high quality. There's plenty of varied audio tracks and it always felt appropriate to what was happening on-screen at the time.
My time with GOKEN was spent exclusively using an Xbox One controller. Controller support works well straight out of the box and the game features two separate Controller schemes.
GOKEN is a great throwback to classic JRPG's of yesteryear. The story is interesting and for the most part very well written. Combat is tight and has a nice layer of strategy.
The game is large but not massive, my first playthrough clocked in at just over 15 hours, this was literally an A - B playthrough, there's plenty more for me to see and do in GOKEN. After beating the final boss you also have the opportunity to load your completed save and carry on. I haven't had the opportunity to play this content yet, but I'd be very surprised if GOKEN didn't have more secrets to uncover.

I found a fix.
1. Get microsoft dxgi error hotfix:
2. Go into GeForce Experience (or download it), find evolve game, click "optimize" then click the "wrench" icon.
3. Move the cursor for graphics settings from "optimized" to "performance" (towards left) 1 or 2 ticks. You won't notice any lack in graphics, you will notice MASSIVE increases in performance.
Explanation: Microsoft has a lag timeout with the graphics card. The hotfix increases this lag wait time, while dropping graphics settings allows your graphics card to process the game faster, avoiding the lag issue. The two together should hopefully eliminate the problem.

So, "Sir, You Are Being Hunted" is a relatively neat concept of a game that you a in fact being hunted, with a twist of some british humour. I like the concept of being hunted, but the execution is rather disappointed.
I expected the rush of being the target of a manhunt, but got a scavenger hunt with a heavy emphasis on inventory management. Like, the main goal of the game is to find some "mysterious objects" which tend to differ in size like some can be relatively small and other, very big. So how can this be a problem? Well, you gotta manage your inventory all the time since it is not intuitive. You have to scavenge for food all the time since your vitality keeps going down and well, you gotta keep some space for guns and ammo. However, from the guns I tried, they were weak and the robots took a few shots before being brought down... and more than half the times, their scavangeable goods are trashed. So, guns are weak and ammo are more than scarce. So you're better of just avoid the robots huh? NOPE! They'll find you anyways since in each strategic places you have to go, there's not only one but a few robots patrolling. And talking about places, you keep trying to figure out WHERE THE FRAK YOU HAVE TO GO, since the map isn't working... or maybe I haven't found it on the character I've picked? Bah whatever!
The game do look nice and the procedurally generated world is well made, but are often repetitive and mostly empty. Playing around with your grid-based inventory can be time consuming enough to break immersion. Having limited inventory for a game like this is great, but having to reorganize a grid-based inventory to pick up an item when enough space is availabe is annoying (so you're hunted and you gotta play Tetris at same time!). Also, you can't enter buildings since they act like chests.
So overall, sneak around robots, scavenge for goods and ammo, manage your inventory "Tetris style" while being Hunted, look around and find the plot items "mysterious objects" FIFTEEN TIMES without knowing where they are. Fun? NOPE!
PROS:
+Procedural world setting is decent.
+Atmosphere and setting of being hunted get's creepy.
+Audio atmosphere is gloomy.
CONS:
-Poor inventory management.
-Game world looks pretty much the same everwhere.
-No maps to help your navigation around (maybe you do get one from another character build?).
-Way too scarce ammo.
-Fetch quest is the main goal of this game... finding those mysterious objects FIFTEEN times gets tedious for nothing.
-Story is simply not interesting.
RECOMMENDATION:
I DO NOT RECOMMEND THIS GAME. Unfortunately, Sir, You Are Being Hunted fails to either impress me and make me feel like I am being hunted and breaks immersion too often to maintain my interest.  Basically, "Sir, You Are Being Hunted" is not good enough to justify spending X amount of hours just to finish the game. I haven't finished this game nor I am willing to spend more time on this below-average game when I got lots of better titles around.

I bought this game expecting something cool and suspenseful and replayable, but what I got was a half-baked product that was so low-quality that I couldn't believe that the developers would release something so unfinished under the tag of 'Early-development'.
The first thing you'll notice in this game is the complete lack of challenge. The bots are completely easy to avoid, and hunger isn't really ever a struggle or challenge for the player because you can find food everywhere in the towns. The only part of the game that comes close to difficult is when the air-balloons fly around and spot you with their spotlight.
Second, there's absolutely nothing to do in this game. Every game has some sort of direction it wants players to go in. Even DayZ has the loosely defined goal of 'getting tons of cool stuff, making a helicopter, and killing other players'. But in
, there is nothing that the player needs to accomplish. The developers /knew/ this would be a problem in an open-world, single-player game like this, but do you know how they tried to fix it? They added a goal where players need to follow these little shiny 'wisp' looking things to crystal shards so that they can go to another island.
As a player, I'm left thinking, 'why do I want to even do that'? What's my motivation to collect the shards? The next island is gonna look pretty much the same, and it isn't going to be any harder to clear than the last. The game itself is a chore. A chore I paid like $15 for, and not even a fun one like pulling lint out of an AC filter.
Don't buy this game. I bought it a year ago expecting the money to help the developers work even faster on the game and make a great final product, but now the game is pretty much the same as it was when I bought it.
Oh, and one final note. The voice-work in this game is pathetic. It's some guy with a painfully-fake British accent talking into a headphone microphone. You can even hear it 'pop' when he says 'p' syllables because they didn't even have a professional microphone with a pop guard. It makes me angry to think where the 'early-development' money PLUS the kickstarter money went.

LYNE is a fun, simple, and good-looking puzzle game. I'm normally not a huge fan of straight-up, narrative-less puzzle games, but there was something about LYNE that hooked me from the first time I started it up. It's really smooth, responsive and snappy, and it has a really satisfying set of feedbacks; it seems like it was initially designed for mobile phones, so even with the mouse the interactions feel really tactile. The game is surprisingly challenging. During my average play session I was usually able to clear 6-7 puzzles before I got stuck and had to take a break. It was satisfying to get stuck on a puzzle and then come back to it the next day and solve it immediately. Like most video games, LYNE gets more difficult as it goes on, and the final set of boards is a real challenge. I usually played in the morning, listening to podcasts instead of the game sound. It was a good way to wake up my brain in the morning. I recommend LYNE if you have any interest in puzzle games. Even if you don't normally play puzzle games, you might like this one.

Anyway, besides that one complaint this game is awesome. Beautiful colors firing all over the place, genuinely amusing characters/dialogue, imaginative (and super fun) boss battles, competently executed platforming, and a real sense of chaos. You can't stand still in this game - you will die. You can't cheese in this game - you don't have enough time. You can't pick off this game's minions - they respawn too quickly. An experience you will never forget.
I own this game on three consoles just so I could support the developers. I have never felt more lonely and depressed than when I play this game. The simplistic beauty of the art, the sound and overall level design come together to create an atmospheric experience of a lifetime.
Granted, Playdead's newest game INSIDE is definitely better. However don't let that discourage you from getting this. LIMBO is truely a masterpiece that stands on its own.
LIMBO puts you into a world that you will never be able to comprehend nor were you meant to. This world doesn't exist for any reason. It just does, and you are a poor lost soul who happens to be there trying to find the one thing that can bring you comfort even if you aren't quite sure it's even there. The further you go, the crazier it gets and the moment you begin to think about what's going on is when the true hollow feeling of loneliness and hopelessness kicks in.
You will not find escape nor answers in this game. The only thing you're given is that somewhere out there in this crazy world, there might be something that can comfort you for the rest of your poor meaningless life trapped in Limbo.

I found this game rather enjoyable given I bought it on sale.  Definitely feels like a "my first game" attempt, but it's rather enjoyable.  If you're bored, this might be a solution for the afternoon.
Pros:
-Bought it on sale and got some enjoyment out of it (if I had fun, that's a good thing)

Some occasional graphical artifacts when looking at walls from a distance.  This seemed to be regardless of the graphics settings and resolution.

I've got a thing or two to say about this game.
Pros:
Visuals look amazing, 1930's hand drawn style catched my eye, this is one of my favorite times for cartoons, and the rubber hose animation looks fantastic.
Music is great. The up-tempo songs that progress across which stage in a boss battle you are, just fit perfectly, you can tell that a lot of effort has been put into this jazzy funky ost.
Great revival of one of my favorite genres, 2D platformers, and i must say this one did an amazing job. If Studio MDHR had just smacked a standard Mario background on here, i would've lost my mind in the fights i was stuck in, like Cagney Carnation and Fiery Frolic. This one stands as one of my favorites in the genre.
Gameplay. Repetitive boss fights with same patterns and attacks is not something you see in this game. Though they have something in common, the fights typically have 3 or more stages to them. (bug causing devil to only be in one stage) It's based around boss fights to collect soul contracts, and Run & Gun levels, which you just run through, with a weak boss fight at the end.
Strategy. Theres a lot of strategy in this game, even if it's not layed out like in strategy games. You can buy weapons and accesories to clear enemies faster, or give you perks. Example: I was buying Spread, (weapon) and an extra heart, for 7 gold coins (coins obtainable in Run & Gun levels, or from NPC) in Porkrind's Emporium, i then also proceeded to accesorize. Then when confronting Baroness Von Bon Bon (Inkwell Isle Two, Sugarland Shimmy) i was missing something, my Spread was damaging enough in early stages, but then it turned long range, i found my Peashooter horrible, so i went to some Run & Gun levels. There i got coins, and bought Chaser (weapon), and immediatly found myself hearing "knockout".
This game isn't the Dark Souls of 2D Platformers. It's hard if you're new to this genre. But idk maybe you just roll through all the levels and fight in like 2 hours.
I don't think speedrunners strats should be applied to a casual player. Speedrunners use the fastest method not always the smartest, but they've practiced many times. This is a Pro cause i just wanted to get it out there.

So I played several hundred hours of Left 4 Dead back in the day and thus I was confident in Turtle Rocks ability to bring something fun to the multiplayer-stage. When I played the Alpha I got very dissapointed because I felt that there was something that was missing. I didn't enjoy the Alpha of this game and had after that totally written it off.
When the Beta came around I thought that I should give the game a second chance which I did but again I was dissappointed...at first. After a couple of hours it dawned on me that I was severly underestimating the gameplay of the game. Even though I recognised that there were classes I didn't completely play as my class sort of speak. When I realized that I had to do it and that the game, contrary to first impression, is very cerebral and tactical. On paper the gameplay seems to consist of: Chase the monster, kill the monster OR run from the hunters, eat, evolve, kill the hunters and while that is certainly true to an extent there is a lot more to it than that.
So what I mean by that is that there are 12 hunters split between 4 classes and the hunters within the class play completely different compared to the other hunters. For example, you have 3 different assault characters which all play completely different to each other. Markov is kind of a medium distance guy, Hyde is close quarters guy and Parnell is long distance guy. Depending on which of the ones you pick you have to adjust your strategy. Same goes for all the other classes which consists of Medic, Trapper and Support. All the characters have 4 different abilites. The classes share 1 ability but the other 3 is tied to that particular character.
The same goes for the monsters. There are 3 monsters in the Retail-version of the game: Goliath, Kraken and Wraith. Goliath is the first monster which is a kind of brute force close quarters monster. You run in and tries to smash the hunters to bits. Kraken can fly and is a monster that is equipped with long range abilites and thus best suited for attacking the hunters from a far. The Wraith is more of a stealthy hit and run character where you swoosh in to combat, deal damage and swoosh out again.
All of this combined makes the gameplay for both Monsters and Hunters very deep in my opinion. As the monster you have to at the start of the match quickly check which characters the hunter-players have picked and adjust your strategy accordingly. As both Hunter/Monster you have to try and outsmart the opponent. As a Hunter you have to predict where the monster is going and cut it off and the Monster have to shake the hunters off it's tail so you can eat and evolve in relatively peace.
This game has gotten a lot of negative press for different reasons. Some of which is earnt and some isn't. This game certainly isn't for everyone and if you enjoy Call Of Duty-esque run and gun then this game isn't for you. To succed as the Hunters you have to use teamwork and preferbly mics or you are most likely gonna lose if you encounter a somewhat decent monster-player.
There are a total of 4 gamemodes (Hunt, Rescue, Nest and Defend) plus a gamemode which is a combination of the former called Evacutation. Evacuation is the closest Evolve has to a Campaign and consist of 5 matches where the Monster and Hunters duke it out. The first match is always Hunt and the last match is always Defend. Depending on whom wins a single match the side that wins will get an advantage in the upcoming match. For instance, if the monster wins then in the next match there are perhaps more carnivourus plants that the Hunters can run in to and be damaged by. If the Hunters win then there maybe are med-stations littered around the map where they can heal up and remove health strikes. What buff the winning side will have next map is random and determined by the map they played. The losing side will get an "autobalance"-buff. What this exactley consists of is unknown so far to my knowledge but it probably gives the losing side a damage-buff or something like it.
Personally I like Evacuation and the outcome of the match since it means there are a bit more consequences even though they might be slim in some cases. Regarding the different game modes Rescue tasks the hunters with finding and reviving survivors and bringing them to a dropship or kill the monster. The monster tries to kill said survivors or kill the hunters. In Nest the Monster is tasked with protecting 6 eggs and kill the Hunters. The hunters win by killing the eggs or the monster. The monster can hatch one minion from the eggs to aid him in killing the hunters.
In Defend the Hunters have to protect a ship that is refueling by hindering the monster from destroying a couple of generators. The monster have minions that spawn regurarely to help him (like a MOBA) as well as being fully Evolved from the beginning of the match. As in every other game mode The Hunters win by killing the Monster and the Monster win by destroying the generators.
Regarding the DLC-controversy I agree that 2K messaged it completely wrong and that have most likely hurt the game unfourtunately. As it stands all the DLC available at the time of this writing are cosmetic and thus not essential. In the future we will get more hunters and monsters where the hunters will go for about $7,5 a piece and a monster for $15. Now this is a bit pricey but even if you don't buy the Hunters/Monsters you can still play with/against the ones whom buy it. You can even face them in solo-mode as I have understood it. So what you essentially pay for when buying the DLC is the ability to play the Hunters/Monster yourself.
Turtle Rock has also said that future Game Modes and Maps will be free for all which to me is the better route to take instead of doing it like Battlefield or Call of Duty where they sell you a Map Pack which consists of 4 maps, new weapons,  new vehicles, achievements and so on and effectively splitting up the playerbase.
With Turtle Rocks approach the playerbase won't be split up which I consider to be a huge plus and the lesser of two evils when it comes to DLC. Because DLCs will always be included in games now a days wether you like it or not.
I am sure I have missed a lot of information but I hope you have a rough idea of the game.
TL;DR: I recommend the game to people whom like to play teamwork-heavy games. The game is most enjoyable with friends but can be fun with randoms. And you can always play the monster with randoms. I think the game is really fun and I intend to play it for the forseable future.

At first glance, this game seems really interesting, and a real switch up for the gaming formula.
Four hunters chasing down a lone monster in an epic fight to the death.
Unfortunately this game ultimately just turns into a very long game of tag.
A decent monster will evade a group of hunters easily until Stage 3, after which it will be nigh on impossible to fight the monster, even with good players. The monster is rewarded slightly too much for playing cat and mouse, and to avoid conflict.
Hunters in the mean time simple follow along at a slow pace constantly needing to recharge their jets, due to the overwhelming number of cliffs that require traversing, slowly dying to all the wildlife they encounter along the way.
Unlike the 'Left 4 Dead' series, which dealt overall minor damage to most players except when utilized properly by the infected, which took skill and patience to put into practice, these NPC monsters get annoying quick. Too often you'll find yourself getting insta-killed by a plant or crock, and can only be saved by another teammate, and sometimes not even then.
The actual gameplay is fantastic. The monster moves fluidly and the animations roll into each other with fluidity and finance. The gun play is also solid from the hunters. The guns feel relatively week against the monsters, even they might be doing major damage. The "pea shooter"'esche gun sounds don't help either. Sometimes you'll feel like you stepped out of a game of Halo 2, (without the fun).
Really, this seems to be a case of mistaking the worth of your product.
The overall conclusion on this game seems to be that the gameplay is a great, but the main draw of the game gets old quick, and really just feels like a free add on extra for another, bigger game. I would issue a cautious recommendation, [ONLY WHEN] at a time when it go's on a major discount. The game is pretty fun with friends, but wont hold your attention for long.
This huge little controversy is about as contrived and annoying as the H1Z1 debable, and seems to be a case of the community getting crazy over something that isn't really important, TO A POINT.
First off, I approve of the dev's decision to keep the game whole in terms of the future maps, as all will be released for free later down the line.
The cosmetic stuff for hunters, monsters, and general aesthetics are crazy expensive, and really are just too expensive to warrant a purchase, even for die hard fans. This was obviously the way the dev's wanted you to pay a little extra.
While I feel they are WAYYY overpriced, this stuff is only aesthetic, and doesn't effect the gameplay in any meaningful way. I give them a pass on this one.
The bundles of DLC are however, unacceptable. There is wayyy to many versions, all of which look similar in every way, except for the price hike. The 'digital deluxe' edition nets you the base game, and the season pass which gets you the aesthetics and random other pointless stuff, while the 'pc monster race' edition, gets you even more pointless stuff, plus the 'Hunting season pass' which will have the extra hunters. Also other hunters are thrown in. All these bundles are grossly mis priced and don't offer any decent value for any customer.

Generally disappointing. I think It lacks depth and variety.
Your first and only objective is to find pieces of the mysterious machine that can take you home if fixed. That’s what you’ll be doing for the rest of the game.
So, you approach a piece and see that it’s guarded by a couple of robots with guns. You can throw an empty bottle or a rock to the side, the robots will leave to investigate the noise, you safely grab the piece and leg it. It doesn’t matter if they see you: they can’t run nearly as fast as you or shoot straight. Even if they hit you, it still doesn’t matter—your health regenerates over time and their guns don’t do much damage from a distance. The old bottle trick will help you get the first fragments, but, the thing is, it’ll work just as perfectly for the very last fragment on the last island. There are other tools you can use to distract or fight the enemy, but why bother if bottle throwing works every time? At later stages of the game some tougher enemies will appear. They never seem to approach the fragment sites. You have no reason to disturb or confront them, so I’m not sure how tough most of them really are.
You need food to regenerate health, but it is abundant. I only ran out once, and that was at the very end of the game when I already had all the fragments. Sure, it’s neat that you can hunt and cook the game you’ve just shot, but you can easily get by with whatever you find laying around.
The intro is intriguing. How did you get there? Who built the device and what does it really do? What was the experiment all about? How did it go wrong? Who’s the man helping you? Why do the robots hunt you, and why do they seem to control the area? Where did all the humans go? What’s with the will-o’-the-wisp things and what do they have to do with the device? Sadly, I didn’t get closer to finding answers to any of these questions when I got to the end. Even the ending cutscene just shows the machine starting and then cuts to credits.
All in all, I guess it was interesting enough for one playthrough (took me roughly 4.5 hours), but I don’t think I’ll be getting back to it unless there’s a patch that makes survival harder or expands the story greatly.
Many thanks to AvantGuard for gifting me this game.

Superhot is a unique and creative game that is unlike any other first person shooter out there. The idea is simple, but effective and makes for interesting challenges. The slow motion gameplay advertised is all there, but digging into the game brings up a lot of ugliness.
The phrase "the most innovative shooter I've played in years" that you see copied and pasted on most positive reviews is a bit of an inside joke, as this is how the game refers to itself at the end of the campaign, but there is some truth to this statement. Superhot is definitely unlike any other FPS I've played and, in this oversaturated market of FPS games, the game design is a breath of fresh air. Superhot plays more like a puzzle game than a run-and-gun shooting game, which is great.
I'm sure you've already noticed my play time and you might be thinking that I haven't played long enough to be writing a review, but I've already completed the game. I have 2.2 hours of play time, which includes leaving the game running while I use the bathroom and do other life activities, watching cutscenes, and replaying levels after I fail them. If you buy this game, I really hope you're not good at it, because the game can be beat in half an hour if you're good enough. Even for someone like me who feels that they replayed levels way too many times, the whopping two hours I was able to squeeze out of the game is disappointing for the price of $25.
Simply put, this game has an attitude problem. From beginning to end, you will see the game tell you in plain text that it's amazing. As you saw in the last section, the game calls itself "the most innovative shooter [you've] played in years". When you boot up the game, an unnamed character sends a message to your in-game character saying that Superhot is a "sick shooter" and that they've never seen anything like it. Throughout the story, if you can call it that, the game constantly complements itself, insults the player (the game literally calls you a dog several times), and claims that it controls you. I understand that might be hard to believe, but look at any playthrough, check out screenshots, or ask any other person, it's 100% true. I appreciate games that have their own personality, even if the game is cocky, but for TWO HOURS of gameplay for $24.99, this holier-than-thou attitude is uncalled for. Superhot is the girl that musicians are talking about in songs about girls with rotten personalities. Maybe the game has a point, maybe I really am its ♥♥♥♥♥ and the game controls me, because I just paid $12 an hour for it to tell me that.

Drunken Robot Pornography is a 3D FPS Bullet Hell Precision Platformer. Not only is the name a mouthful, but so is the genre.
According to the Steam description:
“You're Reuben Matsumoto. You used to own a bar.  You gave your robot bartender, Tim, sentience. He went nuts, stole your other 12 bots, and burned down your bar. He's attacking Boston with 20,000 drones, 40 Titans, and his lieutenants, the 12 Drunken Robot Centerfolds.”
Oddly, the Robot centerfolds thing isn’t quite accurate; the in-game descriptions of them suggest that most of them were random robots which did things around the bar, with only a few of them being “exotic dancers”.
The game comes complete with a rap video in the menu screen, which is hilarious, well executed, and surprisingly catchy. That isn’t the only song in the game, either; there’s also a parody of the Kingston Trio’s M.T.A. (this one set on the MSTA – the Metropolitan Sky Transit Authority). The soundtrack in general is decent, but the two songs really stand out, and, given that every time a video game has actually done something like that I have felt impressed, it really makes me wonder why more video games don’t use songs in games.
In any case, the game’s plotline is light but funny. Reuben Matsumoto is a gritty-voiced sociopath. His sentient, living starfish suit – sadly never seen on-screen – is quirky and provides amusing commentary. You get some random voicemails throughout the game from a reporter, your uncle, your friend who helped you with the robots, and your nemesis, Tim.
All of this is fun.
The actual gameplay is more questionable, though.
The core of the gameplay for most of the levels is running/flying around the level on your jetpack (which has limited fuel per jump). You can gather up to four gun upgrades in each level (though many have fewer), which make you shoot faster/better/more powerfully/more spread shots (with limited ammo). There are a few powerups that a few levels have, most notably invincibility, a bomb, and a an orbital friendship rainbow cannon (which definitely isn’t a MLP reference, no sir).
The way the game works is that the player runs around shooting at one or more titans who spawn in the level. The goal is to kill all the titans. You do so by blasting them to bits, shooting off the outermost portions of them at first, and working your way inwards. You must shoot everything off of the core of the titan (or at least, ALMOST everything) in order to kill it. The net result of this is running around a 3D titan while blasting bits off of it.
As a bullet hell game, the game throws a bunch of independent enemies at the player, along with having the titan itself often unleash a hail of gunfire/bombs/ect. at the player. You have limited health, and standing still can often result in your death in a matter of seconds in some levels – or even in just a moment if you’re in the wrong place at the wrong time in a few places.
It starts off easy enough – almost too easy, really, but the idea is to get you used to the idea of how the game works. The first eight levels or so are all quite simple, and you’d think “Oh, this isn’t going to be so bad.”
Things then start going to hell.
The first real nasty level I ran into was around level 19. But the game has a very odd difficulty curve. And this is where we get into the flaw of this game.
Sometimes, people complain about games being badly designed when they really mean they’re badly programmed. Drunken Robot Pornography is a well-programmed, poorly-designed game.
The problem comes from the mix of genres I noted above. A 3D FPS bullet hell game suffers from a problem – you have a restricted field of view. This means if attacks are coming from above, below, or the sides, you can’t see them coming. Worse, some of the attacks clip through the scenery, meaning that if you’re behind a blocking wall, they can still hit you even though you can’t shoot back at them (or see them coming, in some cases).
Likewise, as many, many people know, precision platforming and the first-person perspective mix extremely poorly. The problem is that you can’t see where your feet are, and if you need to be looking in another direction when you jump (and you almost invariably do in this game), you can’t tell where you’re going to land. This is especially bad when you’re floating around through the air on your jetpack and need to land on a small launchpad to do so again. This is not helped by the game’s often-frantic pacing, and the fact that you need to continually move while fighting to avoid being destroyed by a hail of enemies and gunfire.
Finally, a few of the levels (most notably Tightrope, a late-game level) have extremely, extremely tight time limits.
The net result of this is that, even more than two years after its launch, according to the final level’s scoreboard, only 303 people had beaten the game. Glancing at the achievements, 78.5% of the people who played this game beat the first level. 2% of people beat the final boss. That suggests only about 1 in 40 people who start this game see it through.
And it isn’t that the game is all that long, either – it took me about 9 hours to beat the game and get 10 of the 11 achievements.
No, it is that some levels are incredibly, incredibly frustrating because the intrinsic design of the game fails to deal with the limitations its own genre sets for it.
The thing is, it isn’t that the levels get uniformly harder – the levels DO get harder as the game goes on, and there’s a difficulty curve to it. But superimposed on that are a few random difficulty spikes, levels which are extraordinarily more difficult than anything else in the game, usually because of some combination of a tight timer, enemies spawning behind the player or in such a configuration that it is difficult to strafe away from them all at the same time, and, most frequently, precision platforming.
The net result is that there are a few brick wall levels which are utterly miserable to beat, followed by a number of levels that the player is likely to beat on their first try. There is little rhyme or reason to this, and the robot boss levels – while often bearing snazzy music – are generally not appreciably more difficult than the others, though they generally do feel a bit snazzier in terms of design.
These difficulty spikes make the game difficult to recommend. The game’s levels, when they’re good, are generally reasonable enough, while the extremely difficult levels are often extremely frustrating. It isn’t that they’re unbeatable, it is that they are just extraordinarily difficult. I probably spent 75% of my playtime on about half a dozen of the most difficult levels, including the final level, a very neat level wherein you stand on the boss while you blow it to bits which pretty much exhibits all of the design flaws of the game.
The game is interesting, but I don’t know if it is good. Most people wouldn’t like it, and would get frustrated with it and give up. If being interesting is more important than being good, maybe this is worth a try, but if you have anything other than a very high threshold for frustration, it is best to steer clear.

... I... I don't really know how to explain this game to you. No, it doesn't have anything to do with pornography. Yes, it does have something to do with drunken robots. Or at least I think so.
Drunken Robot Pornography is a FPS-arcade-bullet-hell. And that's pretty much it. There's not much else going on with the game besides a pretty absurd and nonexistent plot. Don't get me wrong. The plot is fun but it's only a shell around the game. It doesn't enhance the experience by any means but gives you a couple of good laughs throughout the game. The gameplay is the thing in this game.
The gameplay of Drunken Robot Pornography is fun, original and tight. Even though the key gameplay elements are simple the hyperactive tempo of the gameplay and amount of things you need to keep track of you soon realize the controls are fine as they are. It's the eye coordination you need to get going.
But truthfully it's not the gameplay, nor the interesting title, but the transition between FPS game and a bullet-hell game. Drunekn Robot Pornography is the first proper FPS-bullet-hell game to be released and that's the main selling point of this game. Drunken Robot Pornography has it's flaws but because of how well they managed to create a FPS-bullet-hell game is amazing. If you've ever enjoued playing games like Touhou or eXceed and are looking for a bit different kind of experience you should buy this immmediatly.

I was sitting alone in a house overlooking a train yard with my PPsh clutched in my hands. I heard MP40 shots go off behind me and a comrade scream in agony. I waited patiently in the house until I saw the bratwurst eating culprit whiz past the frame of the door I was covering, and watched him take position overlooking the train station. I seized my chance, came up behind him and put about 4 or 5 rounds in him.
Thing is, I didn't kill him though. He lay on the ground and let out a blood curling scream of absolute terror and suffering as he slowly bled to death on the dirt. There was no time to survey his wounds though, as immediately, 2 foot soldiers overheard the commotion and advanced on me from 12 oclock. Getting into a prone position right next to the bleeding, writhing enemy I had just shot, I quickly dispatched the two with a couple more short bursts of gunfire as his deafening last screams pounded at my right eardrum.
TL;DR: ♥♥♥♥ed up a German, laid in his blood next to him, popped two more of his buddies as he quite loudly let me know what horrible pain I had inflicted upon him.

I have recently purchased the Forest, and I am actually surprised how this game has become one of my favorite survival games. The game isn't perfect, but people often forget the price tag that also goes with it. This game delivers a lot for it's price, and it's unique in it's genre.
I really love how you can decide to just play the "survival"aspect of the game, but what adds a plus for me is the story part of the game. Most survival games have no endings, plots, quests, and this is what makes the forest different. I love the creepy part of it, the story, the team play and just the overall experience. A lot of people have been saying to keep at it, and I will say the same. Much more can be done, being a dev myself, but I already love and enjoy what I see here.
Some things to consider :
- Some of the sounds really need to be balanced. In many areas, such as the boss fight, waterfalls, etc, you can't hear anything at all. Really hard to hear teamates ..unless lowering the game sounds. Really important to balance the audio, since it's part of the experience.
- The rope glitches...  this one was our least favorite. Often it keeps bringing players back up... or people just ending up falling to their deaths.
- And collisons. Often people can fallt through the map (Probably due to the lag issues of the game)
But I really recommend this game to all survival fans out there. The forest is different and unique in it's genre.

A very, very neat idea for a game ruined by a few poor choices.
The basic gameplay is very fun - shooting the bosses apart is fun, trying to manage the pickups is fun, trying to keep the spawned enemies at bay is fun, trying to dodge the lasers is fun, the levels look fun, the music is fun, the ability to make custom bosses is fun. There's an awful lot to like.
But there are two big problems that really bring things down.
1. The first is the questionable choice to include levels without bosses. The bosses are the point of the game. The developer knows that - that's why they're in the videos. They're why people are playing the game. They're the best part. The game already has a ton of variety in bosses. And yet the game is filled with seemingly random levels that you have to play through where your only goal is achieving a certain score or collecting a number of items. Even some of the bosses require you to kill the spawns and grab the point pickups to achieve a certain score before the boss will spawn for some completely inexplicable reason (all while the timer is running down).
These levels and sections feel like padding. I think the idea was to inject some variety, but it doesn't end up being the good sort of variety. It just feels like mindless dreck you have to go through to get to what the game is really about. And the game has so many levels that it would be a perfectly acceptable length without these even if no more boss levels were added.
And while most of these levels are mercifully short and relatively easy, a random few will serve as towering difficulty walls. And it isn't fun when you're stuck replaying a level that doesn't interest you. It isn't fun to replay a level that isn't playing to the core idea and strengths of the game a dozen times in order to get to one that is,
2. Which gets to the second point: the difficulty. There's nothing uniformly wrong with the difficulty. The game gets hard and it's mostly a good kind of hard. Learning to multitask and move around and aim with the different powerups and dismantle the bosses and navigate the levels is all, on the whole, satisfying. The problem is that the difficulty is incredibly uneven in places. You'll breeze through ten levels in a row on your first try without breaking a sweat only to encounter a level that suddenly takes you two dozen tries only to finish it and then breeze through the next ten. It isn't that these levels are necessarily unfair either - the difficulty is still of a tolerable kind - they just seem profoundly out of order. This happens repeatedly throughout the campaign. In a few particularly egregious cases, it's impossible not to wonder how a few minutes' testing didn't reveal these problems.
Ultimately, Drunken Robot Pornography is a great game with some faults that eventually become too hard to overlook. It's a game that's easy to fall in love with, but that you're likely to ultimately have to break up with. In this case, I think it might be better to have never loved at all.

Liked:

-You can be farely close to a mob without aggroing it, making it easy to travel from location to location

-In big quest hub/major city there is a quest guy who will send you to your next questing location via a map teleport, if you're ever lost.

-The Cash Shop doesn't really have a whole lot in it, no dangly carrot to make me WANT to spend money...just two quests kind of introducing the Cash Shop (If you're interested in doing them, you need to drop cash or you can easily ignore the two quests)

-Incredibly tiny player base.

I found a fix.
1. Get microsoft dxgi error hotfix:
2. Go into GeForce Experience (or download it), find evolve game, click "optimize" then click the "wrench" icon.
3. Move the cursor for graphics settings from "optimized" to "performance" (towards left) 1 or 2 ticks. You won't notice any lack in graphics, you will notice MASSIVE increases in performance.
Explanation: Microsoft has a lag timeout with the graphics card. The hotfix increases this lag wait time, while dropping graphics settings allows your graphics card to process the game faster, avoiding the lag issue. The two together should hopefully eliminate the problem.

There isn't much that hasn't already been said about this game. It really is as good as it sounds. And it is amazingly addictive; be prepared to find yourself sucked in for hours at a time if you're a fan of tower defense or strategy games in general. I've never been big on the tower defense formula for its own sake, but DotE sold me on the idea that tower defense can be fun. Of course, DotE offers much more than just tower defense; it introduces an economy-like system--if you've ever played a 4x strategy game, the system will look pretty familiar--that ties in with the tower defense setup (among other things) and at the same time rewards you for exploration and taking calculated risks, which is what the game is really about. On top of that, the game gives you a specific resource that can be used to power unlocked rooms and the defenses and production modules you've built in them but also doubles as currency; deciding to use it for currency instead of power always has consequences. If you like a challenge--the kind that requires a brain--Dungeon of the Endless will hook you pretty fast.
The RPG elements add a surprising amount of depth to gameplay. You may not fall in love with any of the characters that make up your party, but you WILL be dismayed when you lose one, especially if you've spent any amount of time getting them kitted up--aside from the sinking realization that you now have one less defender. With different skillsets and weapon types, recruiting and keeping characters alive is an investment in your team-building strategy as different characters can complement each other in different ways (melee with ranged, for instance) and can also be put to work boosting specific segments of your economy to differing degrees depending on a proficiency statistic. Future releases promise even more layers to team-building, as inter-character relationship balancing (guards vs. inmates) and personalities will also play a role in pursuing (or avoiding) character combinations. Granted, the alpha is very short and misses out on giving you the chance to bring any long-term team-building strategies into play, and especially early-on you'll find yourself taking any character you come across just to keep your team's collective head above water. Having a really good team fall into place is more a matter of luck than planning. Hopefully later versions will realize the potential there.
New players should be aware of just how short the game currently is. Dungeon of the *Endless* isn't really (endless, that is). Not yet. At only three levels it's a bit of a tease, one that lasts about an hour and a half even with obsessive exploration of every nook and cranny. I can hardly fault the developers though. They've told us what we'll find going in. The randomization of the levels (and recruitable character encounters) and the way the game still manages to throw curve-balls and stay challenging keeps me playing and giddily anticipating the masterpiece that this game will be if the developers deliver. The alpha is already amazing. I doubt we'll be disappointed.

.
Excerpt:
If you’re less confused about the Drunken Robot Pornography part of this review and more confused about the “bullet hell style shoot ‘em up” part, this simply means that it’s one of those frustratingly difficult and potentially seizure-inducing games where you dance around trying to avoid enemy fire as much as trying to shoot back. And good it may be, let’s be honest: half the fun of the game is telling people you’re playing Drunken Robot Pornography and watching their reactions to the title.
You find yourself filling the shoes of Reuben Matsumoto, the previous owner of a robot-run bar in a shiny, near-future version of Boston. In order to better serve your fine establishment’s patrons, you decided to give your robo-bartender, Tim, sentience. This is all well and good – that is, until Tim finally snaps under the pressure listening everyone’s problems. Instead, he destroyed the bar, took off with your 12 dancing robot employees and together, begun an assault on the city.
...
While Drunken Robot Pornography certainly has its moments of overly frustrating difficulty, it is a very fun game to pick up for short bursts. Each level is generally limited to a couple minutes at most making it a great choice to start up while dinner is cooking. The small amount of time for each level is not a representation for the length of the game itself. There are tons of levels to be played as you try to save Boston from the mechanical attackers as well as the option to build your own levels and play those made by community members.
The $15 price tag is not bad when considering the fun the game brings and it usability as a non-time consuming experience. Personally I would look for a sale on it as it can come down pretty far in price (I got it for only $3.75) making it even more worth the investment. This game is not for the faint at heart, well, at least not for those prone to epilepsy, but it is a good game for players of all skill levels to pick up and learn.
If you like well put together and detailed survival games that focus on atmosphere and environment you really ought to try this game.  If you want to mow down hordes of enemies skip it though.

Tomorrow:  I'll cut and store wood and water
Next day:  I'll fish at the ice hut and set some snares
Next day:  I'll explore the cabins on the other side of the lake
Should I move locations or establish 'this' as my camp?
what am I going to do when this clothes wear out?

"Forward to the Sky" is an adorable puzzle/platformer. As a princess, you try to unlock the mystery behind a witch and her odd relationship with crystals that aren't your standard gems. Although not particularly difficult, some of the puzzles can be a little bit challenging. Each of the areas are relatively small, and everything is simple logic and platforming. The music is very light and appropriate to the game style, and the art direction is simple yet elegant in its own way. The story is not much, but it does keep you wondering. Voice acting is ... there. It's not incredible, but it's by no means bad.
I finished the game to 100% completion (all achievements) in about 2 1/2 hours, but that's with a lot of pauses while I had to take care of something else. If you don't go for all achievements you can probably have it done in less than an hour. It's a good way to play in short bursts, such as one or two levels at a time, but it's also short enough that it doesn't feel padded.
Overall, it's a simple yet very enjoyable way to spend an hour or two.
