Now anyone who sees this game would easily say that this is a watered-down version of FF14,
, I beg to differ.
Echo of Soul (EOS) is a game that targets to make its own take on things. Beautiful worlds, great mechanics/ animations, and hours of addicting fun. The game is quite difficult proving that there are no healing roles whatsoever, so keeping a watch on your health bar is an absolute must. This game isn't so hard in the leveling process, as grinding is not really required. You don't rake up xp as much as you do grinding helpless creeps for hours but rather doing quests in a timely manner. This was done in order to make the player feel rewarded for their quests and accomplished for doing something to progress the game.

This game doesnt require pay to win at all. It was setup so that the player gets often rewarded for leveling up, questing, earning achievements,a nd also winning in pvp matches and gamemodes. The store only offers "outfits" that are costumes for your characters and you can wear on them. These outfits have no effect but change only the outer appearance of what your character is wearing. All the armor can be found in game :)
The roles/classes each have their own unique abilities and feel to playing that you can easily tell each other apart. However, each class has 2 specific paths in which you can take in order to level your skills, giving the player the freedom to play how they want when they want.
Speaking of which, there are jewels that players can "inlay" into their equipment that give mighty buffs. Combining these jewels, if you have more than one, will boost the effects given to that jewel if it will be laid into the  specific piece of equipment.
sad i know.
This has a great dungeon and pvp aspect in the game that give both high risk and reward. If in any case you may die in a dungeon or in the world you would face a durability loss on equipment and would have to repair. PVP is different however in which you can die however many times you want and get either a consolation prize or a victory prize after the match. This has smart matching so you can do wahetevr you want while you wait.
I cant stress this enough but just enjoy all the game for what it is. For easy levling do the daily quests for the pvp. You need to play 2 games (win or loss) and there. You get basically a level and lots of money. Money is a bit difficult to aqcuire in the game, but is super easy to buy and sell as everything, and i mean EVERYTHING is 1 silver. (excluding all the rare stuff).
From completing the pvp you get either a consoloation jewelery box or a victory jewelery box depending if you lost or won. After open and i suggest you save those jewels to create greater ranking jewels. Selling a +5 dull ruby on the marketplace you can make an easy 75 gold.
I think those are good odds considering that 1,000 silver make 1 gold LOL
All in all, a great game worth playing. Enjoy!

So I played several hundred hours of Left 4 Dead back in the day and thus I was confident in Turtle Rocks ability to bring something fun to the multiplayer-stage. When I played the Alpha I got very dissapointed because I felt that there was something that was missing. I didn't enjoy the Alpha of this game and had after that totally written it off.
When the Beta came around I thought that I should give the game a second chance which I did but again I was dissappointed...at first. After a couple of hours it dawned on me that I was severly underestimating the gameplay of the game. Even though I recognised that there were classes I didn't completely play as my class sort of speak. When I realized that I had to do it and that the game, contrary to first impression, is very cerebral and tactical. On paper the gameplay seems to consist of: Chase the monster, kill the monster OR run from the hunters, eat, evolve, kill the hunters and while that is certainly true to an extent there is a lot more to it than that.
So what I mean by that is that there are 12 hunters split between 4 classes and the hunters within the class play completely different compared to the other hunters. For example, you have 3 different assault characters which all play completely different to each other. Markov is kind of a medium distance guy, Hyde is close quarters guy and Parnell is long distance guy. Depending on which of the ones you pick you have to adjust your strategy. Same goes for all the other classes which consists of Medic, Trapper and Support. All the characters have 4 different abilites. The classes share 1 ability but the other 3 is tied to that particular character.
The same goes for the monsters. There are 3 monsters in the Retail-version of the game: Goliath, Kraken and Wraith. Goliath is the first monster which is a kind of brute force close quarters monster. You run in and tries to smash the hunters to bits. Kraken can fly and is a monster that is equipped with long range abilites and thus best suited for attacking the hunters from a far. The Wraith is more of a stealthy hit and run character where you swoosh in to combat, deal damage and swoosh out again.
All of this combined makes the gameplay for both Monsters and Hunters very deep in my opinion. As the monster you have to at the start of the match quickly check which characters the hunter-players have picked and adjust your strategy accordingly. As both Hunter/Monster you have to try and outsmart the opponent. As a Hunter you have to predict where the monster is going and cut it off and the Monster have to shake the hunters off it's tail so you can eat and evolve in relatively peace.
This game has gotten a lot of negative press for different reasons. Some of which is earnt and some isn't. This game certainly isn't for everyone and if you enjoy Call Of Duty-esque run and gun then this game isn't for you. To succed as the Hunters you have to use teamwork and preferbly mics or you are most likely gonna lose if you encounter a somewhat decent monster-player.
There are a total of 4 gamemodes (Hunt, Rescue, Nest and Defend) plus a gamemode which is a combination of the former called Evacutation. Evacuation is the closest Evolve has to a Campaign and consist of 5 matches where the Monster and Hunters duke it out. The first match is always Hunt and the last match is always Defend. Depending on whom wins a single match the side that wins will get an advantage in the upcoming match. For instance, if the monster wins then in the next match there are perhaps more carnivourus plants that the Hunters can run in to and be damaged by. If the Hunters win then there maybe are med-stations littered around the map where they can heal up and remove health strikes. What buff the winning side will have next map is random and determined by the map they played. The losing side will get an "autobalance"-buff. What this exactley consists of is unknown so far to my knowledge but it probably gives the losing side a damage-buff or something like it.
Personally I like Evacuation and the outcome of the match since it means there are a bit more consequences even though they might be slim in some cases. Regarding the different game modes Rescue tasks the hunters with finding and reviving survivors and bringing them to a dropship or kill the monster. The monster tries to kill said survivors or kill the hunters. In Nest the Monster is tasked with protecting 6 eggs and kill the Hunters. The hunters win by killing the eggs or the monster. The monster can hatch one minion from the eggs to aid him in killing the hunters.
In Defend the Hunters have to protect a ship that is refueling by hindering the monster from destroying a couple of generators. The monster have minions that spawn regurarely to help him (like a MOBA) as well as being fully Evolved from the beginning of the match. As in every other game mode The Hunters win by killing the Monster and the Monster win by destroying the generators.
Regarding the DLC-controversy I agree that 2K messaged it completely wrong and that have most likely hurt the game unfourtunately. As it stands all the DLC available at the time of this writing are cosmetic and thus not essential. In the future we will get more hunters and monsters where the hunters will go for about $7,5 a piece and a monster for $15. Now this is a bit pricey but even if you don't buy the Hunters/Monsters you can still play with/against the ones whom buy it. You can even face them in solo-mode as I have understood it. So what you essentially pay for when buying the DLC is the ability to play the Hunters/Monster yourself.
Turtle Rock has also said that future Game Modes and Maps will be free for all which to me is the better route to take instead of doing it like Battlefield or Call of Duty where they sell you a Map Pack which consists of 4 maps, new weapons,  new vehicles, achievements and so on and effectively splitting up the playerbase.
With Turtle Rocks approach the playerbase won't be split up which I consider to be a huge plus and the lesser of two evils when it comes to DLC. Because DLCs will always be included in games now a days wether you like it or not.
I am sure I have missed a lot of information but I hope you have a rough idea of the game.
TL;DR: I recommend the game to people whom like to play teamwork-heavy games. The game is most enjoyable with friends but can be fun with randoms. And you can always play the monster with randoms. I think the game is really fun and I intend to play it for the forseable future.

At first glance, this game seems really interesting, and a real switch up for the gaming formula.
Four hunters chasing down a lone monster in an epic fight to the death.
Unfortunately this game ultimately just turns into a very long game of tag.
A decent monster will evade a group of hunters easily until Stage 3, after which it will be nigh on impossible to fight the monster, even with good players. The monster is rewarded slightly too much for playing cat and mouse, and to avoid conflict.
Hunters in the mean time simple follow along at a slow pace constantly needing to recharge their jets, due to the overwhelming number of cliffs that require traversing, slowly dying to all the wildlife they encounter along the way.
Unlike the 'Left 4 Dead' series, which dealt overall minor damage to most players except when utilized properly by the infected, which took skill and patience to put into practice, these NPC monsters get annoying quick. Too often you'll find yourself getting insta-killed by a plant or crock, and can only be saved by another teammate, and sometimes not even then.
The actual gameplay is fantastic. The monster moves fluidly and the animations roll into each other with fluidity and finance. The gun play is also solid from the hunters. The guns feel relatively week against the monsters, even they might be doing major damage. The "pea shooter"'esche gun sounds don't help either. Sometimes you'll feel like you stepped out of a game of Halo 2, (without the fun).
Really, this seems to be a case of mistaking the worth of your product.
The overall conclusion on this game seems to be that the gameplay is a great, but the main draw of the game gets old quick, and really just feels like a free add on extra for another, bigger game. I would issue a cautious recommendation, [ONLY WHEN] at a time when it go's on a major discount. The game is pretty fun with friends, but wont hold your attention for long.
This huge little controversy is about as contrived and annoying as the H1Z1 debable, and seems to be a case of the community getting crazy over something that isn't really important, TO A POINT.

The cosmetic stuff for hunters, monsters, and general aesthetics are crazy expensive, and really are just too expensive to warrant a purchase, even for die hard fans. This was obviously the way the dev's wanted you to pay a little extra.
While I feel they are WAYYY overpriced, this stuff is only aesthetic, and doesn't effect the gameplay in any meaningful way. I give them a pass on this one.
The bundles of DLC are however, unacceptable. There is wayyy to many versions, all of which look similar in every way, except for the price hike. The 'digital deluxe' edition nets you the base game, and the season pass which gets you the aesthetics and random other pointless stuff, while the 'pc monster race' edition, gets you even more pointless stuff, plus the 'Hunting season pass' which will have the extra hunters. Also other hunters are thrown in. All these bundles are grossly mis priced and don't offer any decent value for any customer.

In 2013, a small group of friends put out a scrappy little game made for web browsers. Three years, a full team and a gallon of shoe polish later, the game has been remade as a downloadable title for console and PC.
SUPERHOT is a fast-paced FPS where time only moves when you move. This simple premise can be manipulated in so many ways, allowing for a short but sweet ~20 level campaign, ~20 level challenges, and an infinite shootout mode with ~5 challenges and arenas. Simple and clean graphics clash with the hardcore, dirty action SUPERHOT delivers in a hypnotizing way.
The first level starts in a L-shaped hallway. Turning the corner reveals an armed enemy on the other end of the hallway. Once you stop, you have (literally) all the time in the world to make your shot. Lead the bullet for a headshot, or shoot where you can already see your target. It adds the RTS feeling of strategy to a genre where immediately taking action is a core mechanic, but both aspects of both genres mesh smoothly and naturally.
The game introduces more weapons as it goes on. You start with a pistol, but then you start using shotguns, semi-automatic rifles, katanas, and even your own fists. Throwing a weapon will stun your enemies (except for the katana, which is an instant kill if thrown), and causes whatever weapon they’re holding to fly straight towards you, allowing you to grab it out of mid-air and use it against them. Despite that mechanic being used a lot, it’s so awesome to see and play that it never gets old.
When enemies shoot their weapons, the bullets are tailed by a thick, red line to easily see where they go. You can simply get out of the way, you can slowly watch it barely skim your head, and (my personal favorite) you can slice the incoming bullet in half with the katana.
Beating the level rewards you with a replay of your performance, but the whole video plays in real time, so all the moments you took to stand still and carefully aim appear as knee jerk reactions made at breakneck speeds. It’s more satisfying than any achievement or trophy could ever be, because it makes you feel cool. In quick paced action games that encourage you to be creative with your objective and switch weapons on the fly, being fluid, quick and perfect on every hit is the ultimate self-goal, so seeing your gameplay portrayed as a flawlessly executed takedown of every enemy achieves that goal tenfold.
The menu imitates old operating systems from the early 80’s, providing a stark contrast with the modern, sleek look of the actual game. Buildings, vehicles and background objects are pure white, with very light tones of blue in shadows and dark areas. This allows both the bright red enemies and pure black interactables to be easily distinguished, making the whole world look very clean and crisp.
Both the enemies and weapons have textures that look like perpetually moving tessellations. Triangles and polygons construct the bodies and weapons, so seeing these shapes crumble and explode makes the kills all the more satisfying. Gunshots cause the polygons of the body to explode in a million shattered red and orange shapes, while cutting with the katana slices enemies clean in half, revealing an inner light source. When game developers take simple, polygonal designs and add beautiful color, art direction, and a crapton of polish, they’re crafting a style that will withstand the test of time.
When you’re booted into the aforementioned operating system, a chat log starts. The stranger on the end of the chat tells you that there’s a new game being passed around on the internet called “superhot.exe”, and that you should totally play it. You download the file, and start playing.
Throughout each level, little tidbits of story appear in quick slideshows of text. They start out extremely vague, discussing something about a broken deal, but as the game goes on, things start to get stranger and stranger, more and more ominous; superhot.exe is more than a game.
Obviously I won’t spoil much but it’s a neat piece of meta-storytelling that can easily be completed in one sitting. You can tell that the developers put more focus on the sandbox aspect of this game, rather than making a linear action game with some bonus modes on the side.
Sound is a large factor in shaping the atmosphere and tone of SUPERHOT; just about as much as the visuals. While the visuals definitely pack a punch with exploding tessellations, the sounds are where the satisfaction of a hit comes from. You can hear crunching when striking an enemy with a bat; sounds of glass shattering when a bullet hits; metal slicing the air when you cut a bullet in two.
The lack of music helps because it gives all your attention to the fighting. Normally in an action film, there’s a heavy symphonic or electro soundtrack behind the epic scenes. SUPERHOT gives you no fanfare whatsoever, and it just makes the sounds of violence even louder. It’s all about the hardcore, brutal, violent matchups between you and your computer generated foes.

Project Zomboid can be a ball ache and hard to get into but once you get going this is by far one of the best survival games in the genre. The thing is this game is actually a survival game where you need to learn how to grow food, find weapons and build a settlement not just go around ganking newbies. It's a hardcore game and for the first 5-10 hours while you learn it you'll spend a lot of time looking up tips online, dying loads and just viewing the game map to get your head around things. I put over 30-40 hours in before it went onto Steam so my played time isn't accurate. If you want to run around killing other players then this isn't a game for you but if you want a tactical survival game that requires a lot of thought and management of your resources then buy it.
It doesn't suffer from the newbie farming or spawn die syndrome that many games in this genre have problems with, there's more team play and focus required on living than other games. This isn't your typical hunt stuff, kill stuff, build stuff and repeat. The game devs have gone in a more hardcore survival direction. You will actually need to think about food, water and where the heck am I going to build my settlement. Sometimes the game will even♥♥♥♥♥kick you and force you to abandon your base because someone made the mistake of leaving a door open or attracting hundreds of zombies that you get over run by. This is like the Walking Dead where you actually need to find food, build the correct things and think about all those little extras like supply runs, having the right skills in your group and actually choosing a good place to settle. You will learn to trust no one be it NPC or player if you choose to go the randoms route with online servers.
You can play online and still kill other people like in DayZ etc but this game works best played in a private group and treated as an actual how the hell am I going to live through this day type game. I'd recommend playing private mode with a group of mates.
The game starts somewhere during a zombie out break and you spawn in a random building. You must survive for as long as possible but ultimately you'll all die eventually be it eaten by zombies, running out of supplies or just being isolated you go mad. Hardcore and experienced players will become self sufficient but I'd imagine you'll need hundreds of hours to master enough skills to do this.
Project Zomboid has all those realistic extras like the power eventually running out, water sources drying up apart from rain water and actually having to become a self sustainable group by making things, storing things and not being greedy and using all the supplies up quickly. You'll need to collect and purify water, grow food from scratch and actually harvest wood to make tools and build things. Shops and houses do not respawn items either!
Whilst you do all of the above you'll need to protect your settlement from zombies, illness and pillaging. You won't always see a lot of action but when you do be prepared to fight hordes or run for your life. Just make sure you have a decent first aider and decent guns for hire type character in your team.
Hours can pass and you don't achieve much and then you find that abandoned warehouse full of supplies and finally get to finish building that water collector or massive barrier!
Just be warned this isn't a fast paced game and will punish your for mistakes HARD!
The sound, graphics and stability are all very good for what it is, this is no frostbite/unreal engine based game it's 2D top down with a slightly cartoon feel. It doesn't need a beast of PC but the engine and way it plays does the job nicely. Character customisation could do with a few more skins and looks but  skill wise you select positive and negative skills for your character so you could be super fit, strong and able to carry alot but at the same time have a poor temper or bad vision just like in real life! Over time you'll learn which traits you play best with. I would really recommend playing this on a private server of your own on voice comms with your mates you don't need other "random" players for this game to be good just a few friends. More players brings more problems though like increased risk of mistakes or the need for more food and drink to keep the bigger population healthy.
My final thought is.... You'll always remember the first time you found a loaded shotgun and fire it off in the middle of a deserted street in the middle of the night :-D

There isn't much can be said about the game's visuals asides from that they're minimalistic. Pretty much the same thing can be said about the game's audio.
There is no difficulty mode option that's assigned. But each of the puzzles has their own difficult.
The objective of this game is rather simple. Is figuring out on how to connect point "A" to point "B." The lines can't interesect with each other and where as shapes can't intercept each other. However, there's some exception where they can intersect each other.
There are two different kinds of sets: Alphabet sets and Daily sets.
The alphabet sets has twenty-six sets with twenty-five levels each and it totals out to six hundred fifty levels.
The daily sets plays a different than the alphabet sets. Each day there'll be one to three different sets of twenty-five levels to solve. This unique set can be unlocked only after the second set of alphabet is completed. Playing the daily sets unlocks more of the alphabet sets.
There's no time limit in this game. Allowing the individual take as much time that they want to solve each of the puzzles.
There's a option for color pallet customization section but it's only available after completing the first daily sets. There are plenty of color pallets to chose from but they needed to be unlock first.
There thirty-three achievement for this game. Each of these achievements has certain requirements before they can be unlocked.
There are total of five different trading cards. You only get the three of those cards from the game. There are several ways to get the rest of the trading card: Purchased from Steam's Market; Trade with friends; Booster Packs and it's Booster Pack Creator.
Final thoughts, it's an great game to play and enjoy. As for the game's replay value it's low. I would recommend this game but not at the full price.

Project Zomboid can be a ball ache and hard to get into but once you get going this is by far one of the best survival games in the genre. The thing is this game is actually a survival game where you need to learn how to grow food, find weapons and build a settlement not just go around ganking newbies. It's a hardcore game and for the first 5-10 hours while you learn it you'll spend a lot of time looking up tips online, dying loads and just viewing the game map to get your head around things. I put over 30-40 hours in before it went onto Steam so my played time isn't accurate. If you want to run around killing other players then this isn't a game for you but if you want a tactical survival game that requires a lot of thought and management of your resources then buy it.
It doesn't suffer from the newbie farming or spawn die syndrome that many games in this genre have problems with, there's more team play and focus required on living than other games. This isn't your typical hunt stuff, kill stuff, build stuff and repeat. The game devs have gone in a more hardcore survival direction. You will actually need to think about food, water and where the heck am I going to build my settlement. Sometimes the game will even♥♥♥♥♥kick you and force you to abandon your base because someone made the mistake of leaving a door open or attracting hundreds of zombies that you get over run by. This is like the Walking Dead where you actually need to find food, build the correct things and think about all those little extras like supply runs, having the right skills in your group and actually choosing a good place to settle. You will learn to trust no one be it NPC or player if you choose to go the randoms route with online servers.
You can play online and still kill other people like in DayZ etc but this game works best played in a private group and treated as an actual how the hell am I going to live through this day type game. I'd recommend playing private mode with a group of mates.
The game starts somewhere during a zombie out break and you spawn in a random building. You must survive for as long as possible but ultimately you'll all die eventually be it eaten by zombies, running out of supplies or just being isolated you go mad. Hardcore and experienced players will become self sufficient but I'd imagine you'll need hundreds of hours to master enough skills to do this.
Project Zomboid has all those realistic extras like the power eventually running out, water sources drying up apart from rain water and actually having to become a self sustainable group by making things, storing things and not being greedy and using all the supplies up quickly. You'll need to collect and purify water, grow food from scratch and actually harvest wood to make tools and build things. Shops and houses do not respawn items either!
Whilst you do all of the above you'll need to protect your settlement from zombies, illness and pillaging. You won't always see a lot of action but when you do be prepared to fight hordes or run for your life. Just make sure you have a decent first aider and decent guns for hire type character in your team.
Hours can pass and you don't achieve much and then you find that abandoned warehouse full of supplies and finally get to finish building that water collector or massive barrier!
Just be warned this isn't a fast paced game and will punish your for mistakes HARD!
The sound, graphics and stability are all very good for what it is, this is no frostbite/unreal engine based game it's 2D top down with a slightly cartoon feel. It doesn't need a beast of PC but the engine and way it plays does the job nicely. Character customisation could do with a few more skins and looks but  skill wise you select positive and negative skills for your character so you could be super fit, strong and able to carry alot but at the same time have a poor temper or bad vision just like in real life! Over time you'll learn which traits you play best with. I would really recommend playing this on a private server of your own on voice comms with your mates you don't need other "random" players for this game to be good just a few friends. More players brings more problems though like increased risk of mistakes or the need for more food and drink to keep the bigger population healthy.
My final thought is.... You'll always remember the first time you found a loaded shotgun and fire it off in the middle of a deserted street in the middle of the night :-D

This is one of the greatest games available so I'll share how I fixed the crashing and sound issues. My method to fix the game is quite simple and works perfectly. I did this on Windows 7 64 bit, although it could work on 32.
First, set the game to run in compatibility mode for Vista. I don't know if it works with particular packages or not, I just used Vista. It does NOT need to run as admin. Now when you start the game it wont crash, and you can change settings like resolution and sound. How ever there may no longer be sound when you get past the plan crash.
To fix the sound issue go to Sound inside of the control panel. Make sure you have the correct device selected. If you hear sound when you hit Test you should be fine. Disable the other unused devices.
Next right click on the sound icon in the toolbar, and select Recording Devices. Right click and enable Show Disabled Devices. Now enable Stereo Mixer.
Open Steam and right click Bioshock and click Properties. Click Set Launch Options, and type -nointro. (without the period). This part is important! I don't know why but skipping the intro credit videos makes all the difference. Otherwise it'll still crash.

An excellent game plagued with a poor cosmetic DLC system and highly priced future characters.
However, all maps and gamemodes released in the future will be free for everyone, which doesnt split the playerbase the way paid maps and gamemodes would. All skins and the future characters obviously are optional to buy, and in my opinion are not necessary if you don't want to/have the money to buy them, as the currently playable characters (12 hunters and 3 monsters, all of which are included in the base game) allow for many different strategies and playstyles.
Graphics are quite good, and the game is very well optimized.
(I get a consistent 60 FPS with everything on max (except particles, which I turned down out of preference) at 1080p with an i5 4670k 3.40GHz CPU and a gtx770 2 GB GPU).
There are two main search queues, with the option of solo play and custom games not counted. The first is Skirmish, which is just repeated games of Hunt. The other is Evacuation, which is a 5 game mini campaign in which there are 4 available gametypes (Hunt, Nest, Rescue, and Defend). On the fifth game Defend is played, the other games are voted between the three other gametypes.
Maps are well designed for the gameplay. there are currently 12 maps available with the game, and 4 additional maps that are only available in the Defend gametype. They are very large and allow for the monster to roam around and eat at his leisure, but are also just small enough that the hunters can fairly easily find the monster if they know what they are doing (ie. cut off the monster vs. mindlessly chase it).
Currently there are some balancing issues, mostly regarding the third playable monster, the Wraith. It is very easy to escape with and very easy to do lots of damage with, but it will be patched in an update I assume. Her escapability makes games boring since the hunters just chase the wraith all game (other monsters can make this happen but it is much more difficult).
There are also a few minor annoyances and bugs, such as the mouse cursor showing on screen when it should, and disappearing when it shouldn't, but Turtle Rock Studios has acknowledged this so it should be fixed soon. All of the major/noticeable/found bugs have been acknowledged by TRS iirc, so they should all be gone soon.
Despite the many ill-informed people (such as the articles that claimed Evolve had $136 of day one DLC, when they counted bundles and the individual items together, instead of just one or the other), many of whom have reviewed the game without even acknowledging gameplay, this game is one of the most entertaining games I have ever played.
I highly suggest it.
P.S. If you want the game but are turned off by the high price for what some have called lack of content" (which I wholeheartedly disagree with) then just wait for a Steam Sale (I hope I just stated the obvious for you). You won't regret your purchase.

First of all, I do recommend this game.
Lets start with its problems. Day one DLC is one big problem that I think TRS should fire its entire marketing department for. Much of it was poorly worded, and gave the wrong impression to  gamers. The skins that are avaliable generally don't change the look of the characters that much, although given the complexity of the character models I'm not surprised, just disappointed. However, TRS does intend to keep supporting this game, and I will back them on that.
Balance problems. Wraith is a balance problem. TRS has stated they will release a balance patch, and given that the rest of the game's balance is almost perfect, I trust that they'll do well with the balancing act.
Complexity. This is a mixed bag. The monsters and hunters are all easy to learn, hard to master completely. To an inexperienced eye, the maps can feel the same, but the veteran can pick out engagement locations, suitable arenas that favor hunter or monster, common feeding locations, and places to find buffs for an advantage. This is not going to be a casual gamer's game. To win as the Hunters, one requires adequate knowledge of not just their own role, but the roles of their partners, and to coordinate with them. To win as the Monster, one requires knowledge of the limits of their creature, and the ability to outthink not one, but four enemies.
Story. Evolve does not have a traditional campaign, but the banter between the characters hints at a rich lore and universe behind the game. The casual player or team who picks the same characters over and over again may be bored by the repetitive banter they come across, but if you branch out just a little bit, you can find ancedotes, tales, and tidbits of story that flesh out each character beautifully and tantalizingly. I fully expect the story to grow and expand, and I look forward to it.
Yes, Evolve has its problems. It may not be worth its 60 dollar price tag, it may be the same repetitive crap over and over again in a game (in the opinions of some), but let me ask you this. Have you really thought about it? How much money has the common gamer spent on "free to play" games like League of Legends, Planetside 2, Warframe, Mechwarrior Online? Aren't the activities in those games just as repetitive (and don't get me started on one of the most-played FPS games of all time, Counterstrike, and its maps de_dust and de_dust2).
Ultimately, Evolve is uniquely in a category all of its own. TRS has created one of the best assymetrical battle systems ever in a game. Like any uniquely new game, it will have growing pains, but from what I've seen, I look forward to its growth.

Forward to the Sky...to summarize, it's a bit of a platformer, with some puzzle and action elements. There's a modicum of backstory, but even without 100% completion (which is required to get all the details), you can probably fill in the gist of it yourself. Which doesn't speak too highly about it, but anyways...
The combat in this game is, shall we say, subpar. There're only two possible attack moves (which I can't figure out the difference between, practically speaking), and a seemingly useless dodge mechanic. Enemies are either worthless or insanely annoying, and with no way to recover health, the game becomes a bit of an endurance test - can you make it to the end of the level before you run out of health? Not the most compelling gameplay.
The saving grace of this game - and the only reason you should consider looking at it - are the puzzles. Each level introduces an interesting mechanic for you to learn and use, and with only one personal exception, the puzzles have always seemed to be of appropriate difficulty - giving you the satisfaction of solving a problem without much frustration. It would've been nice to see levels combine these mechanics, but considering the other issues with the game, its short length is probably a boon rather than a liability.
For its normal asking cost, I wouldn't, but if you find it on sale and want to spend a couple of hours on some nice puzzles, then why not?

I've spent all day today in The Long Dark, on my first play, and 25 days in found myself facing an almost incessant howling white-out blizzard trying to dress my first bear. This game is as punishing as it is rewarding, it's slow to progress but not grueling, and you almost always find just what you need while right on the brink of death. Almost.
This is a game about solitude and isolation in the frozen tundras of Canada, where you fully immerse yourself in a truly hostile atmosphere which works to strip the breath from your lungs the minute you walk out the door. You begin by choosing from a handful of pregen maps, or by letting the game randomly drop you into one of its choosing (I do hope procedurally generated maps will be in this game's future). Like most survival games, you start with scant resources and face the most steep and difficult climb during the first 8 hours or so. But, it's hard to ever get truly comfortable. Your clothing and tools degrade, you get attacked by stalking wolves and charging bears, your wounds (and bad choices in food) lead to infection and illness, you're constantly trying to find the ideal balance of gathering food and... Well, doing other things. And, just when you start to let your guard drop your hatchet breaks because you haven't yet found a replacement whetstone, sending you back to the dark ages of burning sticks to stay warm.
Having come from 7 Days to Die and Minecraft and Osiris, I can safely say this is a well-done game. Don't let the lack of photorealistic graphics dissuade you, the weather and atmospherics suck you in from day 1 and never let go. Despite being Early Access I didn't encounter a single bug or crash, and the game is incredibly fleshed-out compared to other EA titles. The only frustration comes in getting stuck in a cycle of spending all your time harvesting resources just to stay alive. Especially early-on, you can easily blow an entire day fishing, boiling snow down into potable water, cooking your fish, eating, returning home and going to sleep. With a 3,000 calorie "fullness" meter, I put down 4-5 rainbow trout in a single day! You get hungry a lot, you get thirsty a lot, and almost to the point where you can do nothing but eat and drink. The carry limit is also pretty harsh, forcing you to do a whole lot of back-and-forth trips. Remember to save time to strike out and explore, because only through exploration will you discover tools and resources that break you out of the primal "survival trap".
If you're a survival fan and you don't mind playing alone (very alone), give this one a go. Especially if you have surround sound. The howling of the winds and creaking of the cabin walls in the pitch black of night is seriously eerie.

I'm not clear on why this game has such mixed reviews - I think it's great, and a bargain at the price.  It's not the smoothest, best looking or the most stable gaming experience I've ever had, but it's 10 years old.  Given its age, I actually think it's a fantastic looking game.  It's fun, challenging and involving.  It makes you think.  It's highly engaging.  It's difficult without being unforgiving.
You'll be put in command of a US submarine just after Pearl Harbour and will get sent on patrols in the Pacific.  You'll manage your crew roster, recruiting new men and installing new equipment with the renown you win from sinking enemy shipping.  You will upgrade your crewmembers as they become more experienced.  Most patrols will be to go somwhere deep in Japanese waters and sink enemy merchant shipping, but there are also missions to do more covert stuff like getting US spies ashore in enemy territory, or photo reconnaissance of enemy harbours.
The game has a variety of difficulty settings, from full-noob mode to ultra-sim mode.  I would thoroughly recommend it at the asking price, on sale it would be a steal.
+ Realistic
+ Thoughtful
+ Detailed
+ Long campaign
+ Great price
+ Many difficulty / realism options
+ Full world map - ♥♥♥♥ off to Sri Lanka or Argentina if you get bored
+ >8000x time acceleration (this is a serious + given the map size)

There is no reason to not recommend playing this game. LIMBO offers a spectacular immersive environment that reveals itself piece by piece. LIMBO communicates through the meaning of actions instead of through words. Though words only can describe so far the experience that LIMBO brings, I dare not try to fully deduce the elaborate ideas that are touched upon but would much rather encourage you to discover them for yourself.
Even after all these years, LIMBO is still one of the greatest indie games to play. It's hard to classify it: it's a platformer (which doesn't require spot-on timing), a puzzle game (which slowly progresses to harder puzzles), and a horror game (without blood and jump scares).
The graphics are very simple, but very elegantly produced. It's a 2D side-scroller, offering a beautifully crafted black and white tone environment. The use of light and grain effects really create a spooky atmosphere, which a lot of games try to produce but fail to capture as well as LIMBO.
LIMBO has a very open ended story; the main plot is you are trying to find your lost little sister. I don't want to spoil the ending too much, as there is a bit of questioning that takes place after finishing it.
There is next to no audio in the game, and no music. All of the sound effects are very minimalist, this fits in well with the spooky atmosphere which is being created. The effects allow for a truer scare instead of using sound cues to heighten the tension inappropriately.
A couple of puzzles in LIMBO had me scratching my head quite a bit before I was finally able to figure out what to do. I would warn you - there is a lot of jumping style puzzles and platforming events to get through. The game does offer a very good respawn/checkpoint system though. If you die, you won't end up miles and miles behind where you just were, you'll normally spawn right before you messed up to let you try again - this made the trial and error mechanic work so much better as you don't have to replay content.
The minimalist theme keeps you on track the whole time, and you have little chance to explore off the track, simply because there is nothing to explore. Essentially, you need to get from A to B, and you cannot come off the path that is laid out. That's not necessarily a bad thing; games these days are often too much of an "open world" style, and often overwhelm the player with too much to see. I liked how LIMBO kept me focused on the puzzles and progressing through the dark world I was in to survive.
I see little reason to play through it more than once. It's 100% linear, and you will always end up with the same outcome. Even, the puzzles don't have multiple ways to complete them, so unless you want to go achievement hunting, there is no reason to replay LIMBO for the main storyline. (Bonus content is achieved by obtaining all of the eggs from in-game which adds a new dynamic. I don't want to spoil any of it for those that want to achieve full completion.)
LIMBO is certainly a highly popular game and is so for good reason. LIMBO showcases just how an indie game should be developed and published, because of the beauty that is created with few mistakes. For the price of $10, it is well worth the enjoyment that is created.

This is one of the greatest games available so I'll share how I fixed the crashing and sound issues. My method to fix the game is quite simple and works perfectly. I did this on Windows 7 64 bit, although it could work on 32.
First, set the game to run in compatibility mode for Vista. I don't know if it works with particular packages or not, I just used Vista. It does NOT need to run as admin. Now when you start the game it wont crash, and you can change settings like resolution and sound. How ever there may no longer be sound when you get past the plan crash.
To fix the sound issue go to Sound inside of the control panel. Make sure you have the correct device selected. If you hear sound when you hit Test you should be fine. Disable the other unused devices.
Next right click on the sound icon in the toolbar, and select Recording Devices. Right click and enable Show Disabled Devices. Now enable Stereo Mixer.
Open Steam and right click Bioshock and click Properties. Click Set Launch Options, and type -nointro. (without the period). This part is important! I don't know why but skipping the intro credit videos makes all the difference. Otherwise it'll still crash.

The Beginner's Guide is far less of a game with goals/directions and far more of an interactive experiences where you see a developer go from an experimental stage in game development to a comfort level with a particular type of stage, and then is pushed further and further by his fans and community until he loses the drive of developing all together.  It's a story that projects the troubles with needy/demanding fans coupled with a potential undertone towards modding and game altering and how it effects the artistic style that a developer put into his game to begin with.
Overall, the atmosphere of this game starts off whimsical and interesting, but quickly turns dark and depressing as you uncover more of the truth about what's actually happening behind the scenes of the story being told.

So... this is my first review ever written, and I'll try to keep it short but still in-depth enough. And if you find any spelling mistakes, feel free to keep them, english is my second language.
So, what is Evolve? In short, evolve is a 4v1 Multiplayer FPS. 4 Hunters hunt down 1 monster. 1 Monster eats and tries to evolve, then kill the hunters. If you need to know more, go ahead, google is your friend. Coming to the main parts.
Gameplay:
-Lots of fun as the monster, but takes time to learn
-Hunters are fun with friends or if your team communicates well
-A con is the unlock-system, but it doesn't take too long which is good
Graphics
-Pretty amazing
-Playable on older machines with lower graphics, though still looking amazing
Teamplay
-As the monster it's basically non-existent
-For the hunters there is voice chat, which is very rarely abused. The community seems great so far.
The biggest flaws may be the lack of game moder, but the developers already promised that new will come, and the lack of customisability for the monsters. You can basically only buy skins to customize them.
Now to the main complaint of a lot of people. The pricing/DLC.
Now, 60 bucks may seem much, but it's pretty much the same price you pay for every modern game, and it has less bugs on release and is more fun than most other games on release. Of course yit is a lot, and I agree that it's too much, but that's not a flaw of the game itself, but a flaw of all games that are released nowadays. Games are too expensive period.
Then there's DLC. DLC is another problem of modern games, that annoys a big part of the community. BUT (and this is a very big but(pun intended)) this game does it better than CoD/Battlefield/almost any modern AAA title. The so called "day one DLC" in this game is ALL SKINS. Yes, they are not nescessary, but there is no reason to buy them. They give you 0 in game benefit. As of now, any content in the game right now, aside from cosmetics, can be unlocked by playing. And it doesn't take too long either, which is good.
The main reason for the cosmetics DLC being released with the game release is that the last months of game developement are just fine-tuning, and so the arts team has nothing better to do than to make these skins.
But what about map and game mode DLC's? Well, they will come, BUT according to the developer NONE of them will cost anything. All new maps will be free. The community won't be split by DLC's, you will be able to play with anyone no matter how much money you spent on the game.
And the monster/hunter DLC's? Okay, this is a flaw, I have to admit that. You can buy new hunters and monsters, whcih will be added later on in the game, and they are too expensive. I see why people are bothered by that, and I am too. But it's another thing that all game developers do. It's not good, not at all, but it's not exclusive to this game, and I don't think you should give a negative rating for that reason.
As a conclusion, the game has it's flaws, though mainly in pricing. It is still a lot of fun. The main problem of the game is the DLC and the premium editions. Actually, the main problem is the lack of communication between the developers and the players. It is a great game nevertheless. if you want more information on the pricing of the game, and an even better review, watch these two videos by the YouTuber Totalbiscuit:

side note: modern bow needs nerf. It is WAYYY too op. headshoting any type of cannibal (starving, pale walker, ect.) kills them instantly. Its a little unfair to be completly honest.

I really like this game. The campaigns are fun and serve as a good introduction to the rest of the game. After you beat the campaigns, you should be able to play the Galactic war scenerios with ease. Speaking of these scenerios, they are varied and place the different factions in different situations. One, for example, puts the Empire on the brink of collapse while another has them about to crush the remnents of the rebel alliance. This increases replayability as I want to play the different scenerios and see how I do. The expansion increases this by adding in a third faction and a corruption system. The actual gameplay is a mixed bag. The space battles are fun. Most space battles will revolve around the attackers trying to destory a space station while the defenders try to repel them. The station can only be defeated by attacking weak points that house key features in the station (such as a hanger or shield generator). Larger ships also can only be attacked in this manner.  The land battles on the otherhand... they are pretty bad. I'm not even sure how to explain why they are bad. You really have to play them to understand what is wrong with them. I find myself just building an overwhelming force and auto-resolving land battles instead of a more balanced force and trying to win through strategy.  Overall, it is a good game and a worthy edition to the library of any Star Wars fan. If the premise intrigues you, I recommend buying it.

I've spent all day today in The Long Dark, on my first play, and 25 days in found myself facing an almost incessant howling white-out blizzard trying to dress my first bear. This game is as punishing as it is rewarding, it's slow to progress but not grueling, and you almost always find just what you need while right on the brink of death. Almost.
This is a game about solitude and isolation in the frozen tundras of Canada, where you fully immerse yourself in a truly hostile atmosphere which works to strip the breath from your lungs the minute you walk out the door. You begin by choosing from a handful of pregen maps, or by letting the game randomly drop you into one of its choosing (I do hope procedurally generated maps will be in this game's future). Like most survival games, you start with scant resources and face the most steep and difficult climb during the first 8 hours or so. But, it's hard to ever get truly comfortable. Your clothing and tools degrade, you get attacked by stalking wolves and charging bears, your wounds (and bad choices in food) lead to infection and illness, you're constantly trying to find the ideal balance of gathering food and... Well, doing other things. And, just when you start to let your guard drop your hatchet breaks because you haven't yet found a replacement whetstone, sending you back to the dark ages of burning sticks to stay warm.
Having come from 7 Days to Die and Minecraft and Osiris, I can safely say this is a well-done game. Don't let the lack of photorealistic graphics dissuade you, the weather and atmospherics suck you in from day 1 and never let go. Despite being Early Access I didn't encounter a single bug or crash, and the game is incredibly fleshed-out compared to other EA titles. The only frustration comes in getting stuck in a cycle of spending all your time harvesting resources just to stay alive. Especially early-on, you can easily blow an entire day fishing, boiling snow down into potable water, cooking your fish, eating, returning home and going to sleep. With a 3,000 calorie "fullness" meter, I put down 4-5 rainbow trout in a single day! You get hungry a lot, you get thirsty a lot, and almost to the point where you can do nothing but eat and drink. The carry limit is also pretty harsh, forcing you to do a whole lot of back-and-forth trips. Remember to save time to strike out and explore, because only through exploration will you discover tools and resources that break you out of the primal "survival trap".
If you're a survival fan and you don't mind playing alone (very alone), give this one a go. Especially if you have surround sound. The howling of the winds and creaking of the cabin walls in the pitch black of night is seriously eerie.

This game is... Just so hard to review...
First off I'd like to say this game is 100% clean.
No porn.
No alcohol glorification.
No violence.
It's basically a kids game with a really obcene title. (that doesn't mean it's not challenging or creative, mind you.)
Drunken robot pornography (or DRP for short) is a flashy, fast-paced, intense, and deeply challenging game.
It's also the most rage inducing game I've ever played.
So do I reccomend this game?
Well, you don't have to be a genius to see that I reccomended it at the top.
Why though?
Because it's fun as hell!
Flying around shooting robots is some of the most fun I've had in quite some time.
It makes you feel like a kid again, jumping around going "pew pew pew!" With your little gun taking down enourmous robots and watching as everything explodes.
But this fun comes at a price.
A hefty price at that.
When you get into the game for the first time, you'll notice it's really easy.
Trust me, it doesn't stay that way for long.
You know how those "unfair" games are pretty rage inducing, because they're... Well, unfair?
This game is worse.
Why?
Because it's all your fault.
That's right, if you ♥♥♥♥ up, it's on you.
While in other rage games, you can pretty much blame your failure on something else.
For example, in "unfair" games you can blame it on the fact that the game is literally rigged against you.
But theres some games where you can't blame it on things, like hotline miami for example.
So why isn't hotline miami as rage-inducing as this game?
It's simple. "press R to restart."
In games like hotline miami and super meat boy, you can't blame the game, you have to blame yourself.
But it doesn't matter, since you can just hit R and restart.
And since each level takes roughly 30 seconds - 1 minute to complete (depending on if you take it slow or not) you aren't losing anything real.
What does this have to do with this game?
First off, you can't blame the game,
Second, each level takes AT LEAST 1 minute, sometimes up to 5 minutes to complete a level.
And since it's really easy to die in this game (health packs = as rare as winning the lottery)
You have to restart time.
"So what?" I hear you saying.
"3 minutes isn't an eternity."
There's this one level called "fling yourself." Where you have to take out 4 titans within the alloted time.
I spent so long trying to beat this level and I recently finished it, but I spent nearly an hour on it. Thats nearly 30 times I killed the same old 4 bosses in the same old arena FOR A ♥♥♥♥ING HOUR!
By the end when I finally beat the level, I felt not like I had beaten a major accomplishment, but that I had survived a holocaust.
It also does this weird thing which I'm not sure is innovative or quirky, where sometimes it'll introduce a new concept like collecting alcohol without a gun trying to avoid attacks, or standing at capture points for small lengths of time, and then it never uses them ever again and goes back to the normal shoot bosses/get points sort of thing. It's really weird, and since the level are manditory it fells like they threw a bunch of stuff at the wall hoping it'd stick but none of it did.
So should you get this game?
Well, if you rage quit easily, stay the HELL away from it.
If you like action-packed fast paced games focused on fun over all else, then this is definetly the game for you.
Just don't play it if you get mad over games. I really wanted to punch my computer.
TLDR: It's a really fun and fast paced action game that can be really rage inducing
A must have.

Waoo! A cute and clever platformer with very nice art style, fresh ideas in every level and only a few hiccups here and there.
This game is full of ideas and each level has something new to offer. New monsters, puzzle types, ways of moving around... it really makes you think this had to be developed with love. There's no such thing as repetition and lazy level design here.
The combat isn't the biggest part, yet it's done pretty well too. You have two attack types with advanced combo moves, there are walls and pillars that you can use for cover or you can smash them apart and hit enemies on the other side with falling chunks of rock.
Main downside is the length of the game, especially since it makes you want to play some more. Other problems are rather typical for smaller games - like sometimes a bit unpredictable collision detection, few unimportant graphical glitches and rather oversensitive controls for my taste, especially mid-air.
Tl;dr: You will probably finish this game in a single run, but it will be a very enjoyable one if you like the genre.

A truly engaging addition to the franchise which encourages, and rewards, creativity and guts. I had the luxury of not playing the game until I'd already played Silent Hunter III and V and I would actually recommend that strategy to others. Playing III beforehand gives you an appreciation for the streamlined management system in place in Wolves of the Pacific. Now, watches are organised for you, orders are easier to issue, and the crew aren't dropping dead of exhaustion all the time.
However it does lack the emotional investment of Silent Hunter V, in which you can walk the boat and get to know the characters which make up your crew, so if that is the experience you really want from a WWII submarine sim, go with V rather than IV (if you don't mind putting up with the Ubisoft launcher's BS)
Overall it's terrific, a welcome addition to the genre for it's historical content, upgraded and streamlined features and additional DLCs.

Five Nights at Freddy's is the summer job from hell.  Work from 12 to 6 in a graveyard shift with fo- three animatronics, all created to please the kids and sell the pizza!
...during the day.
But when those doors close for the night, they are allowed to roam.  You'll wish you'd taken the day shift, because now you have to spend five nights at Freddy Fazbear's Pizza.
Couldn't go wrong, could it? Just six hours in a dark pizzeria surrounded by robotic animals?
No.
Terror will shine through as they begin to move, slipping from camera to camera, inching closer to you. Closer, closer. Uncover the secrets of Freddy and friends, hidden behind the thick curtain of childlike wonder and delight.
Check the cameras. Close the doors. Watch your power, or else it's game over.
Not everything is what it seems here.  A friendly poster shifts into something horrific. A inviting smile becomes a terrifying glare.
Welcome to your new job.  After all, it's only Five Nights at Freddy's.

This is certainly a unique and quirky little game. Aside from the slight British humor that saturates the game, I found the robots themselves to be a bit comical (In a murderous, creepy, sort of way). It's an easy game to get into, but I must admit it had me checking the Wiki every so often, especially when a little creepy voice kept whispering "Behind you!".
As a fleet of enemies, these robots can be both heart-stopping and childish. One loan hunter is no problem at all if you have a rifle or a man trap, but 5 hunters in a party with dogs becomes a force to avoid. Thankfully I never had the misfortune of alerting the landowner, but his thunderous steps were intimidating from the distance I kept between us. Each class of robot has their own strengths and weaknesses, but virtually all of them can be lost by just running in a straight line and ducking behind some cover. So long as your visibility is low they will almost never find you. I found it very interesting that the robots will eventually attack each other. I noticed that groups of hunters will often attack each other, riders, squires, and scarecrows. Although a little confusing, it sometiems works to your advantage when a group of 5 hunters shoot themselves down to 1 and have taken out 2 riders and a trapper.
The narrator is a gem, but a little more could be done with him. His ability to talk to you is never explained nor his in-depth knowledge of the alternate universe you've been accidentally flung into. Nonetheless, more of him would have only added to the charm of the game. I was a little dissapointed by the backstory and ending; they could have been a lot more indepth and provide an atmosphere that better explains and better allows for this alternate universe. There are books spread across the islands with little tidbits of story, but I found those few and far inbetween.
Starting from the easy setting, it took me about 7 hours to make it through the game. After finding all the parts on the center island I would collect all 3 items on each adjacent island and run them back to the center. Each island was a different landscape with a different theme, but as I collected more pieces there were more robots.
All in all this was a cute game that I enjoyed playing, well worth the $5 I paid for it when it went on sale. It has some decent replayability to test out harder settings, but i look forward to any future updattes the game might see. Since the story and ending will be the same every time, it may be a while before I choose to play again.
Exploitables (Possible Cons):
-Saving the game does not save the robots. Saving at either the center rock or a boat and then immediately loading the last save point will erase all the robots and reset their spawn allowing the player to make a mad dash to find the next piece.
-If a machine piece is surrounded by enemies, just find a cozy spot with 0 visibility and wait for another group of hunter to come through and shoot up the place. Normally they do a good job defeating the other classes (squires and riders hardly fight back at all) and leaves the player to take out the 1 or 2 survivors who are at lowered health.
-Hiding is too easy. A patch of grass can hide you completely and have a squad of hunters walk directly in front of you without ever being alerted. The only exception is the rider who will see you from his vantage point attop his robot horse and run you over repeatedly until you sprint away. You think the fastest robot in the game would be able to chase you, but they don't. At least not very far.
-Robots need an invitation to shoot you. When a robot spots you it will make a little beep and take aim. Hide or croutch, lowering your visibility, and it forgets it ever saw you. You can juggle a hunter by doing this, letting him see you, hide, let him see you, hide, and so on. This works especially well to pick off the last person in a line of hunters by having the others continue on while your target can't decide what to do.

Sequels to great games carry the weight on their shoulders to creators that has some noticeable impact. Reputation of success or of a certain style can either be a blessing for marketing or an overhanging shadow of the past that casts furthermore over a departure from it. Whether it’s directly associated or loosely together, comparisons are made through association of the creator. In many ways, Davey Wreden, the creator and the protagonist of The Beginner’s Guide, can best be described as the J.D. Salinger of video-games. The Beginner’s Guide appears to take these ideas quite metaphorically, yet it’s self-aware enough to be a trap for critics who make this game into some autobiographical piece on The Stanley Parable’s fame.
In short, this “game”—if an interactive piece of assets made by made-up characters given a narrative behind why they are a collage of incomplete ideas can be thought of a game—is an experiment. Sometimes it feels like a creator’s self-reflection piece; sometimes it may feel like a hidden moral told to pass on to other similar people; and sometimes, The Beginner’s Guide feels like an open mockery of itself and everyone who praises it.
This question is asked with genuine honesty because it remains an elusive riddle towards making sense of The Beginner’s Guide: Who/What is The Beginner’s Guide intended for? Or asked in a more blunt manner: What is it a beginner’s guide for?
At first, the game does appear to be an autobiographical narrative about Davey and an unnamed developer named Coda who may or may not exist. Given the amount of real-world similarities as well as documented pressure under fame after the success of The Stanley Parable, TBG feels like a sobering lesson about reflection. Instead of a good versus evil narrative, the actual story behind TBG explores how far can a creator become a byproduct of their own creations and their own fame that they begin to impose meanings on to something that had no meaning there to begin with. It may feel at times like TBG is more so a lesson to pass-on to future indie developers of a warning of their own fame.
However, the role of Wreden in this experience is less about being the creator of something and more so about the pitfalls of being a critic. His greatest mistake is to impose meaning on someone else’s work where there was nothing to begin with; as a result, the critic tarnishes the creator’s original intention. This aspect promotes a view that critics are manipulators by their own drive to push their own ego that they tarnish the honesty behind an original work, and the fact that I am criticizing this criticism as a critic of another critic puts me on the spotlight. This is why TBG feels like the critics’ trap as trying to make sense of it as well as explaining why it works makes them as guilty as Wreden. Is this then what The Beginner’s Guide is intended for—a warning towards critics from creators to think about how they view other’s creations and how they have a domino effect towards their audience?
Or, as another possibility, is The Beginner’s Guide addressing the audience itself in a meta-commentary like The Stanley Parable? Is it addressing the actual individual audience or the collective audience that watches it (streamers, viewers, etc.)? What lesson then would it promote? We could continue with hundreds of other interpretations behind answering the initial question of asking who as well as what The Beginner’s Guide is addressing. The point behind all of these semantics is that the value or the take-away message of The Beginner’s Guide depends largely on what merits you see in its ramblings, and it greatly challenges your suspension of disbelief if it’s based on true events or a fiction of its own.
Here’s the problem when dozens of critics evaluate this game as an autobiographical piece or reference this game as a response to The Stanley Parable: You have to believe Davey Wreden is not self-aware of making this product on Steam.
It’s immediately apparent from the product description that The Beginner’s Guide knows it’s a critic’s trap, “The Beginner's Guide is a narrative video game from Davey Wreden, the creator of The Stanley Parable. It lasts about an hour and a half and has no traditional mechanics, no goals or objectives.
” Right there on the Steam page it boils down all the emotional baggage of the game into a concise set-up for critics to think it’s all about Davey when it’s really not. Especially after experiencing the more emotional moments of the storyline, it would be hard to be believed this last statement could be said when it reaches the height of its hysterics. It would also be hypocritical of Davey to share this game online after hinting at the lesson he learns.
You also have to stretch how much this interactive experience warrants being a game. The Stanley Parable warranted actually playing it because it was an Easter-egg hunt to test how much agency you truly have in games. TBG only is a game by the fact that it is about an unnamed game creator and what kind of story you can get from wandering around in his unfinished levels. Recommending it for anything other of its weirdness and its narrative is pointless because it has less purpose behind playing it than simply experiencing its strangeness. When the only justification to the question of “Is this really a game?” is that it takes place inside of game files, then I think you are stretching how that definition can cover.
People don’t often like art without purpose as it is a wandering experience that is difficult to judge its merits; however, I believe the greater concern is when art is aimless like a blindfolded person with a gun shouting at their targets. Despite this issue, The Beginner’s Guide succeeds like its predecessor in that it is something different and interesting to think and talk about, only this time it overrides the incentive to play it rather than discuss it. There are some merits behind it like its more interesting set-ups, its environments and its other small scenery details that give nice metaphorical qualities to its minimalistic style. It’s ultimately an experience that is difficult to describe in words why it is so appealing rather than letting you experience it for yourself, and the only way I could recommend it is if you purchase it with The Stanley Parable bundle.
What lingers in my mind about TBG as time goes by is that lingering quote by J.D. Salinger that I believe speaks more to the narrative of The Beginner’s Guide. It makes me wonder if the real narrative or the real Coda is something to lament about in the availability of The Beginner’s Guide or if The Beginner’s Guide itself embodies that statement about the price of fame.

Evolve is not a game for casual play. It has a (sometimes frustratingly) high learning curve and punishes you and your team if you mess up. However, that depth is what makes it such a satisfying experience.
A note before we begin: Be careful when reading/watching reviews on this game (even this one), because Evolve is often and easily misrepresented.
Evolve is like a pool with nothing but deep ends. As a hunter, your goal is to track down and kill a player controlled monster. As the monster, your job is to roam around the map, eating wildlife and gaining strength to evolve into a bigger and badder monster. However, as a hunter, you must be extremely aware of your surroundings. There are obvious environmental cues to indicate the position of the monster which occur when the monster startles birds or walks through a sound spike, giving away it's position. However, there are also subtle cues like the sound of its footsteps (which often get louder as it grows bigger) or falling trees, huts and other debris as the monster stomps around the map. A clever hunter is rewarded for recognizing those cues, but therein, as they say, lies the rub. You are not alone.
If you recognize the cues and rush off towards the monster, leaving some of your more oblivious teammates behind, you'll find yourself engaged with the monster with no backup. Alternatively, if you are left behind by teammates who are faster than you are, you run the risk of being eaten by a plant or wildlife that instantly incaps you, with no one around to save you. While frustrating, learning to navigate these hazards feels extremely satisfying, and tracking a fleeing monster across the map is an exciting and robust experience.
Because the game practically requires all 4 members of your hunter team to do well in order to succeed, one loose cannon often causes you to lose what may have otherwise felt like a successful hunt. Because of this, Evolve is a hard game to drop into casually. However, with experience and a group of players, this game is extremely deep. If you don't have friends that play the game, you can always play as the monster where you are on your own team against the four hunters. Also, between games you stay with the same group of players so finding and friending players to group with is easy.
A note on some negative aspects of the game: There are some balance passes needed for some of the hunters/monsters, and while none feel "OP", some are much more fun to play as/against than others. There are also a host of bugs which result in poor performance, game crashes, or strange cosmetic functionality (like a mouse cursor that doesn't go away), however, these bugs do not happen enough (or are not serious enough) to be game breaking, and I trust that they will be fixed soon.
Also, because of the asymetric nature of the game (4v1), it's hard to get a feel for where the "correct" balance is. For example, new players often find that the monster is extremely difficult to beat or even to find (if the monster is sneaking). However, at later levels, as players become more experienced, it almost feels like the monster is too easy to keep pace with.  This is one aspect of the game that will be interesting to watch as time goes on and as the player base continues to grow.
If you're interested in a game that requires fast paced reflexes but also requires strategy and superior tactics in order to be successful, I would highly consider picking up Evolve.

STAR WARS™ Empire at War - Gold Pack is an enjoyable RTS based in the Star Wars universe. Including the expansion, there are three factions. These factions are called the Empire, the Rebels (or Rebellion), and lastly the Zann Consortium. Each of these three factions has a nice variety of ships and land units to choose from for upcoming battles. Each faction also has their own type of research which gives the game more variety.
The Rebellion has to send one of their hero units to an enemy faction to steal technology. Usually this tech that the Rebellion steals is a unit or building. The Empire must have a research base on the planet that they want to research tech levels which gives them a new tier of buildings and units. The Zann consortium cannot steal tech, but they can send hero units to planets with a black market to get unit upgrades.
Now on to the maps: By default there aren't many maps to choose from unless you mod it. Each map has a set number of planets that your faction can control. You can build up to 8 buildings on any planet you control, although you won't be getting 8 slots on most planets. You may also build a space station above that planet, which can be upgraded up to 5, but depends on the planet. Land combat is quite dull in many peoples' opinions but space combat is quite good.
There are also many mods to choose from that give the game much more replayability which I would suggest getting after a couple playthroughs. I've personally played Republic at War and I enjoyed it, a nice change from the base game. I did experience a few crashes and a bug, but that's expected from a mod. This game does feature a campaign for all three factions, which I think you should play through as well because they aren't bad. Lastly, I believe I'm right in saying the Zann Consortium is overpowered if you play them. You can fix this by modding or not playing them. If you don't believe me, you probably will when you play them. Just spam out the hovertanks.
I'd give this game a 9/10 because it's pretty amazing. Some people might think it gets repetitive, but not me.

Your player character is adorable, and that's why I bought this game, but sadly that's where the good things end :\
As soon as I loaded the game up I wondered if there was a bug with drawing text on the screen, but no, the menu system really just is a clunky icon-only thing that's a game in itself of figuring out what does what. Kinda like those wordless instructions that come with all sorts of things these days so they don't have to bother to translate it into a hundred different languages.
But that's just the menus, surely the gameplay is ok, right? No, not really. Moving and attacking are mutually exclusive, you can't interrupt your attacks to dodge and you can't attack while in the air, which makes combat frustrating. It isn't very clear what counts as an enemy attack either. There's also no sense of "flow" between one bit of the level and the next - there's a bunch of typical platformer segments in there, moving spike puzzles, moving platforms, lever puzzles, box-pushing puzzles oh and bits of combat - but it's like they were put in willy-nilly rather than creating any sense of progression or building on earlier elements.
Oh, and when you run out of HP? There's no game over animation or anything to tell you you died, you just go to one of those wordless menus that looks more like a pause screen than a game over screen.
All in all the whole game feels like a 3D version of what a bored 14 year old might make in Game Maker. It's just not fun to play.

LIMBO by Playdead is the pinnacle of atmospheric puzzle platformers. You control a young boy wandering a desolate, deadly landscape in search of his sister. This can take you about 3-5 hours, depending on how quickly you can solve the puzzles. Even after your journey is over, you can return many times to discover the game's plethora of hidden secrets, and the ultimate challenge: a one-sitting run of the game with a maximum of 5 deaths (not easy: you will die a lot. Very brutally).
The key to LIMBO's success is it's aesthetic. Many puzzle platformers exist, and there are many that have more difficult (Braid) or more unique (Life Goes On) puzzles. However, what those games lack is the deceptive simplicity of LIMBO's look. The entire game is monochrome: all black and white and gray. Simple enough, but this aesthetic adds so much to the atmosphere of the game. It gives the world a very bleak look, despite the many different environments contained within it, which increases the dread that fills the player as he traverses it. It causes you to examine everything very closely, it makes you worry that any little thing might kill you (and it often can),  it makes you wonder what kind of a world it is, and it makes you wonder whether you can even succeed in your goal at all...
Can you? The only way to find out is to face the darkness, and enter the harrowing depths of LIMBO...
