I've read a bit of the other reviews for Sir, You are Being Hunted and as far as I can see, they are pretty spot on. The good reviews show the good sides of the game while the bad reviews show the bad sides of the game. Most importantly, many of them are incredibly truthful, althought this game gave me a fun challenge for a few hours, I'm going to have to give it a negative rating.
Lets start off with the good things about this game!
First of all, the game runs and looks as it was advertised, with all the features the store says it features, but do not expect anything more from this game.
First-person stealth and survival.     Check.
Procedurally-generated British landscape.        Check.
Five biomes to explore: castle, industrial, rural, mountainous, and fenland.            Check.
Powerful, brutal AI that becomes tougher as you play.          Check.
Tea and biscuits.             Check.
Foliage-based stealth system.            Check.
Scavenge to survive.          Check.
Play as Sir or Madam.          Check.
Relentless Britishness.         Check.
HOWEVER.....
Infinite replayability in a sandbox world.
Now this is where my review gets a little bit on the negative side. The game is infinitely replayable, IF you like playing the exact same game, but a slightly different generated world. Sure the landscape will not be the same, but everything seems the get more and more repetative the more you play the game. Villages become bland and overdone and you see them quite often without much variation besides the occasional big village or small village. Of course the AI acting differently must add some kind of extra replayability right!!??? No. Yes, they have different hunting patterns, but if you play long enough, they dont just become easier to predict the more you watch them, but they become easier to avoid. As said, "The AI becomes harder as you play," is a pretty acurate statement by the devs, except the the fact they don't really get harder, there are just more of the tweed jacket wearing hunters. Max I give the game a few hours of playability before it gets bland and overdone, maximum would be maybe 48 hours of gameplay.
THE NUMBER ONE THING THAT MAKES ME HORRIBLY DISSATISFIED WITH THIS GAME was that it was released with low resolution textures. I mean the textures were REALLY low resolution. They look like alpha placeholder textures that devs put in before-hand to make sure everything runs and looks as it should. The textures have not gotten any updates to clean them up or make them neater and prettier, the game looks nice and all, but everything looks as though it was painted by a four year old with water color paints. ALSO, with all these horrible textures, the game runs like absolute♥♥♥♥♥♥ Although it does not run as bad as another MAJORLY disappointing game, Starforge, it runs worse than Skyrim, which is saying something because Skyrim is a pretty intensive game to run even with it's high resolution textures. Sure they might try to pass it off as the games artstyle, but at least try to make that excuse convincing and make some good artistic textures.
All in all, Sir, You are Being Hunted is a fantastic game, besides its extremely limited playability and horrible textures. If I had the choice to either by this game or not, having played it, I would choose not to pay $20 for a game that looks and runs badly, that can only be played once or twice. I hope my review helped anyone on edge about buying this game.

Hands down the best zombie survival game i have ever seen.
The map is still under progress, but it's already huge with two major towns , and many factories / hidden places.
The zombies are really well coded, and everything is taken into account : the noise you make, if you are visible through a window, if they see light inside a building, ect...
Also, your character can only see what's in front of him, you thought you'd have a nice, aerial view of every danger around ? Nope.
The variety of items that can be found is huge, it makes the game very realistic, and scavenging all the more interesting.
The weapon system is made in a way that you can't kill many zombies easily, so it's vital to establish strategies like catching the attention of zombies to get them away from your shelter, and loose them by running between trees.
The graphics are great, the game is light and will run on most computers.
This game is everything DayZ (and many other similar games) should have been, and it keeps getting better with every update, thanks to the awesome Devs.

This originally seemed like a game where you would be frozen in time to plan your next move. In this way you'd be able to handle incredibly dangerous situations in movie-style action sequences. It is not that game.
Looking around is treated as movement and this makes the time-freeze mechanic completely backfire. The problem is that you can't look around your surroundings to plan without taking a bullet to the head as time moves on without you. It's still possible to get those amazing action sequences but they will require you dying multiple times until you know the spawn locations of all the enemies and you can plan from there. But really now, if I'm going to memorise spawn locations you could give 'I wanna be the guy' the same title.
If you could look around without time moving then as the game is it might be too easy. However my response would be that this would then give you room to increase the difficulty of the rooms and that would make the spectacle even cooler when you nail it. Right now I find myself dying in levels until I know all the enemy spawn points and then executing the level with as little mouse movement as possible because I don't want to needlessly move time.
Maybe I'm just terrible at this game, it's definitely not what I was expecting though.

This game certainly seems to polarise opinion (what game doesn't?(Civ maybe?)), so I write my review based on the fact that you may have similar tastes to mine.  This game has a bucket load of atmosphere, the sound and music particularly are superb and the recent addition of 5.1 surround is tactically important.  Combat is short and brutal.  I still jump when the bots fire their first volley at me.  It's a superb sound.  Not booming hollywood gunshots, more the snap of a 18th century musket.  And being shot in SYABH is a genuinely unpleasent thing to happen.  It absolutly cains your health and unless you find cover quick you will not last long; the screen shakes and rocks, things start to go grey when health is low and your heart becomes audible.  All standard gaming tropes but effective nonetheless.
I found that the stealth is satisfying.  It isn't hardcore stealth.  It's easy to figure out and get right, but it feels fair and believable and it requires a fair amount of patience and observation.  I think the most important thing about this game is that, like Mario, the game never feels broken.  You never get spotted, or killed and think "screw this, that shouldn't have happened, this games broken".  It's ALWAYS your fault.  Or you got unlucky.  Either way it feels fair, and in this kind of game (indeed any game but particularly this kind), that is important.  The hunger/health mechanic works well, and I like the plethora of objects to loot.  There is a loose backstory, however I have yet to find all the letters and books scattered about.
For me, the most important thing about this game is the setting, theming and atmosphere.  In this regards, this game is an absolute winner.  The gameplay might not be for everyone, but I thoroughly enjoy being hunted by those loveable, ruthless robots.  It's only going to get better once mod support and co-op is introduced (if this happens, and I have heard that it might).  So put the kettle on, grab a packet of Hob Nobs, slip into your smoking jacket and get ready for the most British sneaking experience you are likely to enjoy this year.

I can't save that I've been this eager to write a review before.
The Beginner's Guide is the story of Davey Wreden's understanding and explanation of another person addressed simply as "Coda."  In merely 90 minutes, the concepts of misjudgement, comprehension, familiarity, happiness, depression, ambition, human relations, self-image, regret, and forgiveness are merged into a single game.  I've read reviews labelling The Beginner's Guide as art, or even a masterpiece, and I don't believe that claim to be so farfetched.  I find it tremendously ironic that something as mechanical as video games could potentially build bridges among humans and burn them just as easily.
Video games center around the player, and it really doesn't matter who that person is.  He or she is the player.  The game is created with the purpose of giving the player the optimal experience.  That is not the case for this game.  The entire game is really just a final attempt at one person's contact with another.  All the player is in this game is a witness to Davey's tribute to Coda.
Many complain that this game is nothing like The Stanley Parable, and I think you simply have to view it as its own creation.  Sure, Davey Wreden created both these games, but the expectations for The Beginner's Guide should be much more broad.  If you enjoyed The Stanley Parable, there's a chance you may find similar enjoyment in this.  Maybe enjoyment isn't the right word.  I believe that in providing thoughts for the player, the game has done what it can for you.  The Beginner's Guide is like a book.  It tells a story, plain and simple.  Yet, there's the aspect of interaction and the viewing of games that can't be experienced in the same way as a book.  The humane voice of Davey and his flaws allow the player to feel involved in his emotions and thoughts.

Dungeon of the Endless is a fantastic mash up of the Rouge like and Tower Defence genres.
This is not a practice I will commit to often, reviewing a title prior to its release.  The only reason I'm doing this is to sway the uncertain, and I'm sure theres a good few out there that are probably a little on the fence.  Its a spin off to a 4X title that isnt that is 'okay' as far as 4X titles, its a participant in a wave of Rouge likes, and follows another 4X title spin off put out by Sword of the Stars.  Let me tell you this, unlike Sword of the Stars Spin off Rouge like The PIt, Dungeon of the endless is an unusual, and very compelling little adventure.
I'll preface further commentary with the clear qualifier that I am by no means a fan of this genre, Rouge likes, for me, are at best a neat little idea over there in the corner with all the other games that I'm terrible at.  I respect them, but do not love them.  I do however, adore Dungeon of the Endless, because it goes beyond a traditional Rouge like game.  First of all its really only Rouge like in that you're delving into a mysterious dungeon, with charachters that level, death is permanent, and the goal is to get as deep as you can, unlock mysteries and score some serious loot.  Dungeon of the Endless is really a tower defence game mashed with a Rouge like, they share quite a few similar elements, namely in a mixture leveling, and nail biting will this next move ruin my adventure sensation.
You'll progress through your dungeon, open doors, set up defenses, and fend off waves of enemies while seeking the exit of the dungeon.  When you find that you then have to get your crystal, which you've been fighting to defend, to the exit while the monster waves go all out to stop you.  All of this is managed with 1 to 4 man team of diferently skilled warriors at your disposal, and this is the real fun, finding the combo you like of people (Provided your a lucky devil) whom all have different skills, like repairing your turrets and equipment (So far as its in beta this is the only skill, but they're clearly promising more so I'm excited.).
The usual rules for a Rouge like apply, loot is found by exploring, explorings dangerous, if all your guy's die, or your crystal is destroyed you gotta start from square one again.  The fact that it employs more strategy than skill is probably what draws me to this over the other more traditional Rouge likes, I'm not very skilled, so when Strategy is the focus, the only one to blame for my failure is me, for approaching the problem wrong.  The levels are random so you cant just plan ahead you have to think on your toes when laying out turrets, and structures.
Overall its a little difficult to concisely describe this game, if you're still on the fence, look up a video.  This game is a very fun title, and I reccomend it to anyone, doubly so if you love endless space and its lore.

So... this is my first review ever written, and I'll try to keep it short but still in-depth enough. And if you find any spelling mistakes, feel free to keep them, english is my second language.
So, what is Evolve? In short, evolve is a 4v1 Multiplayer FPS. 4 Hunters hunt down 1 monster. 1 Monster eats and tries to evolve, then kill the hunters. If you need to know more, go ahead, google is your friend. Coming to the main parts.
Gameplay:
-Lots of fun as the monster, but takes time to learn
-Hunters are fun with friends or if your team communicates well
-A con is the unlock-system, but it doesn't take too long which is good
Graphics
-Pretty amazing
-Playable on older machines with lower graphics, though still looking amazing
Teamplay
-As the monster it's basically non-existent
-For the hunters there is voice chat, which is very rarely abused. The community seems great so far.
The biggest flaws may be the lack of game moder, but the developers already promised that new will come, and the lack of customisability for the monsters. You can basically only buy skins to customize them.
Now to the main complaint of a lot of people. The pricing/DLC.
Now, 60 bucks may seem much, but it's pretty much the same price you pay for every modern game, and it has less bugs on release and is more fun than most other games on release. Of course yit is a lot, and I agree that it's too much, but that's not a flaw of the game itself, but a flaw of all games that are released nowadays. Games are too expensive period.
Then there's DLC. DLC is another problem of modern games, that annoys a big part of the community. BUT (and this is a very big but(pun intended)) this game does it better than CoD/Battlefield/almost any modern AAA title. The so called "day one DLC" in this game is ALL SKINS. Yes, they are not nescessary, but there is no reason to buy them. They give you 0 in game benefit. As of now, any content in the game right now, aside from cosmetics, can be unlocked by playing. And it doesn't take too long either, which is good.
The main reason for the cosmetics DLC being released with the game release is that the last months of game developement are just fine-tuning, and so the arts team has nothing better to do than to make these skins.
But what about map and game mode DLC's? Well, they will come, BUT according to the developer NONE of them will cost anything. All new maps will be free. The community won't be split by DLC's, you will be able to play with anyone no matter how much money you spent on the game.
And the monster/hunter DLC's? Okay, this is a flaw, I have to admit that. You can buy new hunters and monsters, whcih will be added later on in the game, and they are too expensive. I see why people are bothered by that, and I am too. But it's another thing that all game developers do. It's not good, not at all, but it's not exclusive to this game, and I don't think you should give a negative rating for that reason.
As a conclusion, the game has it's flaws, though mainly in pricing. It is still a lot of fun. The main problem of the game is the DLC and the premium editions. Actually, the main problem is the lack of communication between the developers and the players. It is a great game nevertheless. if you want more information on the pricing of the game, and an even better review, watch these two videos by the YouTuber Totalbiscuit:

I've spent all day today in The Long Dark, on my first play, and 25 days in found myself facing an almost incessant howling white-out blizzard trying to dress my first bear. This game is as punishing as it is rewarding, it's slow to progress but not grueling, and you almost always find just what you need while right on the brink of death. Almost.
This is a game about solitude and isolation in the frozen tundras of Canada, where you fully immerse yourself in a truly hostile atmosphere which works to strip the breath from your lungs the minute you walk out the door. You begin by choosing from a handful of pregen maps, or by letting the game randomly drop you into one of its choosing (I do hope procedurally generated maps will be in this game's future). Like most survival games, you start with scant resources and face the most steep and difficult climb during the first 8 hours or so. But, it's hard to ever get truly comfortable. Your clothing and tools degrade, you get attacked by stalking wolves and charging bears, your wounds (and bad choices in food) lead to infection and illness, you're constantly trying to find the ideal balance of gathering food and... Well, doing other things. And, just when you start to let your guard drop your hatchet breaks because you haven't yet found a replacement whetstone, sending you back to the dark ages of burning sticks to stay warm.
Having come from 7 Days to Die and Minecraft and Osiris, I can safely say this is a well-done game. Don't let the lack of photorealistic graphics dissuade you, the weather and atmospherics suck you in from day 1 and never let go. Despite being Early Access I didn't encounter a single bug or crash, and the game is incredibly fleshed-out compared to other EA titles. The only frustration comes in getting stuck in a cycle of spending all your time harvesting resources just to stay alive. Especially early-on, you can easily blow an entire day fishing, boiling snow down into potable water, cooking your fish, eating, returning home and going to sleep. With a 3,000 calorie "fullness" meter, I put down 4-5 rainbow trout in a single day! You get hungry a lot, you get thirsty a lot, and almost to the point where you can do nothing but eat and drink. The carry limit is also pretty harsh, forcing you to do a whole lot of back-and-forth trips. Remember to save time to strike out and explore, because only through exploration will you discover tools and resources that break you out of the primal "survival trap".
If you're a survival fan and you don't mind playing alone (very alone), give this one a go. Especially if you have surround sound. The howling of the winds and creaking of the cabin walls in the pitch black of night is seriously eerie.

I haven't found a way to swap between team members on the fly, but maybe that was intentional. Most of the game is somewhat easy, but there are a couple of challenging boss fights in the late stages.
The game is kind of short (took me less than a couple of hours to complete), but it's packed with fun and is free to play. In addition to the top notch combat, you also have a cool narrator voice, some high pitched enemy screams, and at times some epic music.

What is comes down to is that this game isn't fun to play. On your first playthrough you may find your self enjoying the game somewhat but if you were to step back for a second to take a more objective look at the game you would see that it's rather bad.
The combat in Forward to the Sky could be completly thrown away and nothing would be lost expect for a couple of sales because they wouldn't be able to feature it in promotional images and videos. It's awful, pointless and adds nothing to the experience other then frustration at how little range and "AOE" you have in your attacks.
The platforming is trash and only has one mechanic to it... the jump key and movement keys... you get no double jump, sprinting varying height nothing. You can jump and move that's it for a platformer these mechanics are far too simplistic.
The puzzles are ok however with that said this isn't a puzzle game it's a 3D collectathon puzzle platformer with combat elements. The collectathon part of this game is pointless and is only there to make sure that you kill all enemies and solve the "optional" puzzles. Honestly though if you skipped the collectathon part of this game you could probably beat this in under 30 minutes.
Forward to the Sky feels like a foundation for a better game as it has ok ideas it's just that they're executed poorly. TL; DR Version:
Recommended for jump-scare-junkies or body horror/torcher-porn people. NOT recommended for horror story lovers and/or atmospheric horror fans.
I consider myself a lover of the horror genre, I own shelves of Stephen King novels, I’ve been hunting for H.P. Lovecraft books, and I love all the old cheesy horror movies... Anyway, after a while I’ve started to think the “cheap scares” became over used as an easy way to cover up bad writing and, well, this game is a good example of that.
I want to start off talking about the game as just a game.
-Every time the game is started you have to set the brightness and visual settings, saving user settings is a basic, A BASIC, in any video game. The weirdest thing, however, is for some reason the game now starts up in Italian, no idea why but I’m thankful it’s not Japanese.
-Moving on, this was the first game in a really long time that ended up giving me a headache. Between the screeching high pitched tones that have become a horror staple (and make up the entirety of the games sound track) and the really bad visuals of the in game camcorder (which is used a lot in the worst night vision mode imaginable), I couldn’t stand to play the game in long stretches.
-The lighting system is also one of the worst I’ve ever seen in any video game. Lights provide very little illumination even on the highest brightness setting, and the developers apparently have no idea that the human eye can adjust to accommodate for low light levels. (but one could also assume that the in game character had is eyes swapped out for ones that can always see clearly in darkness, but only in a three foot radius.)
-Game play is also repetitive in the form of 1.) Find key, 2.) Hide from bad guy in the small map, 3.) Run the stretches to next map, 4.) Repeat.
-Gore is another thing that is used poorly, the first sighting is shocking and works well, but then everything else is nothing but blood and guts, so it eventually losses any horror value at all.
-As for the nudity and sexual content, it’s a farce to get certain people’s attention. All game characters are male, so the nudity is more to provide small levels of discomfort and the sex is a guy feeling up a dead body. So the "graphic sexual content" is just bait.
-OH NO, A BARRICADE MADE OF A CHAIR!!! I’M TRAPPED!
-Most jump scares are predictable.
Now let’s talk story-
You play a silent (faceless), hardcore investigative reporter, who has no idea what self-defense is, (or how to punch for that matter). You set off to investigate an asylum that is ran by a greedy corporation that always has ulterior motives, and now you’re trapped. (Which is debatable in my opinion.)
-It seems like the developers couldn’t make up their mind on whether or not this asylum should have been an abandoned building to cover something more, or a working asylum use to cover up something more, as some parts do look like a functioning medical facility and others look like a long burned out and rotting condemned building. (A simple KEEP OUT, WING UNSAFE UNTILL FURTHER NOTICE sign could have fixed this.)
-As you work your way around you find documents and take personal notes, these are the only background you ever get and it is bare minimum. (But this game wasn’t made with story in mind. Jump scares, gore, and no pants: Now that’s good horror! That’s this games motto.)
-In terms of story there is just so much wrong, so much that is too basic in the horror genre, and so many questionable decisions. I really believe that the developers were so concentrated on the visual aspect that they gave no thought to story.
This game is cheap horror, but most people like it because it scared them and that’s what they wanted. They don’t buy these games for stories, they buy them because of the same reason people go into haunted house attractions and ride roller coasters, it’s the lure of controlled terror, people want to be scared and say the thing is good because it scared them. I thought I would knuckle under and say yes, but that's not my style I DO NOT RECOMMEND THIS GAME, so do your worst fan boys.

I don’t actually know how to preface this one. Drunken Robot Pornography is an indie, FPS bullet hell game from Dejobaan Games, LLC. Let’s get rocking.
The Good
I went in with no expectations and I was pleasantly surprised.
You’ve got one gun to use against teeming hordes of drunken robots and drones. Luckily, there are power-ups scattered across each map that cause your gun to fire in different ways. You can get Split Fire and your bullets will go in two directions. You can get Rapid Fire and vastly increase your fire rate. You can get Triple Shot and fire three bullets at once. The best part? These all stack on top of one another. You can be shooting three bullets in every possible direction as fast as you can.
The color scheme is oddly pleasing.
It is weirdly fun to fire endless amounts of bullets at giant, laser firing robots.
The Bad
I could never find where my health was located on the HUD (and it’s entirely possible that it wasn’t present). When taking damage, you’ll be verbally alerted to what percentage your health is at and it will flash on the screen, but there is no way to consistently monitor it. This led to several careless deaths.
The Meh
The horizontal axis is really, really sensitive.
Verdict: Yea
If you’re bored of what you’ve got and are looking for something different, DRP is a pretty good option. If you see it go on sale, you may as well pick it up and give it a shot. As always, thanks for reading.

Despite the mixed reviews I saw for this game, I still went ahead and bought it because of its promise of a free-form, British survival experience.  It turned out to be better than I expected!  The atmosphere is fantastic and it really does feel like Britain especially on a dark drizzly night, crouching in the woods with the moon shining down above you.
While it's definitely not Amnesia (and doesn't try to be), the robots can be genuinely scary, especially when you hear the slow thud of the Landowner bearing down on you.  Which brings me to maybe the best bit about this game - the sound.  It really evokes a dark, 'tweedpunk' future filled with menace.  The first you'll know of the robots is when you suddenly hear their whirring and clanking from behind a hill.  They also come out with some humorous phrases ("I blame the foreigners").
The AI seems pretty good, and the robots will sometimes erupt into firefights amongst themselves, giving you even more ways to outwit them.
This is a game you need to use your mind for as the sandbox environment (and 'British Countryside Generator') provide a pretty much infinite number of situations you can find yourself in.  If you like sandbox games and sneaking games, this is definitely for you.
While this game is very nicely designed from an artistic point of view, the textures can look very plain close up.  I was surprised to learn that the engine used in this game is the same as the one used in The Forest.  However, this really does not detract from gameplay at all, and I especially love the effect of the sun's rays shining through woodland at sunrise and sunset.  It also means that the game is well optimised for slower systems.
Downsides?  If you want a comprehensive survival experience this isn't it.  You can hunt for food and cook it and so forth, but it's not worth it.  You can keep your 'Vitality' topped up by munching on blackberries and drinking tea every now and then and that's really all there is to it.  There's no system of shelter, sleeping or crafting so it's nothing like as deep as other 'survival' games out there such as Rust and The Forest.  It's a 'shallow' survival game, which to be honest is all it professes to be.
Approach this game with an open mind as there is really nothing else like it out there.  It is still being patched currently and I think multiplayer support is still to be added.  It's certainly well worth the asking price and I look forward to seeing what Big Robot can make next.

I went in with low expectations based on all the criticisms I heard about the game, yet still left disappointed. I'll try to go into more detail on why I think this game fundamentally doesn't work, as I think there is more to it than just "you like RNG or you don't".
The RNG is totally fine, for the most part. I really don't mind RNG when it's put to good use- board games like Galaxy Trucker can massacre you in a small few turns with no control, but still manage to be fun. The problem with the RNG in Reigns is how it's used. Each RNG value feels like it's own special "box" that doesn't interact with other "boxes" next to it. What you get is an unfeeling series of immediate action -> immediate response with a few small exceptions. You can unlock new characters and "abilities" to aid your kingdom, but once you learn that these things carry over all you end up doing is always picking "yes" whenever you are asked if you want to sacrifice a ridiculous amount to buy them. There are also a few "questlines" that have long term actions, but other than these two small features that only take up a small portion of the game there is very little that has lasting impact. What you are mainly doing is looking at the top bars to avoid anything reaching maximum or minimum, and reading the text occasionally to spot any cards that say "I'm going to kill you now" -> "Yes - No". Other than that, it's just guessing on what cards will give you what immediate resource.
The new card unlocks are fun, I like the progression the game has with gradually seeing new content as your empire grows over time, but due to the disconnected feeling nature of each card I didn't really have fun with it. On sale for like a dollar or so it's worth it just to see if you'll like it, but I can't really recommend it even for the price of 3 dollars.

Played the first two nights without much mishap, except power going out on the second night right as I got 6 AM.
Now, onto a review:
The game controls are rediculously simple: point and click.  That's it, really.  However, the game mechanics are slightly more advanced than simply pointing and clicking.  Just slightly, though.  Pay attention to the animatronics' patterns and paths, keep an eye on Foxy sometimes (start doing this when night two starts), watch your power consumption (it goes out really fast, so use lights and doors sparingly since they seem to drain the most power), and make sure you make it to 6 AM with power left to spare, because that final hour feels like forever.  Oh, and one more thing: the game is luck based, meaning no two playthroughs are the same.  Pretty much a new experience each time you play.
The lore, however, if not paid attention to, will seem like just background noise that's just there as filler which is fine, really.  You can take this game at face value: a simple horror point and click to just kill time.  But, if you listen to the calls and pay attention, you'll learn that things don't seem very hunky dory concerning Freddy Fazbear's Pizzeria.  I won't get into details, but some interesting and depressing things have happened.
Now, onto my opinion: the game is very good, but far from great.
CONS-
Since it's luck based, sometimes the night will be impossible to complete, while the next time around it'll be an ice cream cakewalk.  It's virtually a grab bag of possibilities.  The graphics aren't super fantastic, but certainly better than most flash games/movies you find on Newgrounds.  Prerendered environments, rather than full 3D.  Gif style animations and jumpscares.
PROs-
The game is easy to pick up and play.  It'll make a good and fun few hours on a Friday night.  Good atmosphear and soundtrack.  The sounds can genuinely be creepy sometimes.  The jumpscares are good at making you jump, but can get tedious after long.

Project Zomboid is absolutely not your typical run and gun Zombie game that often plagues the market. This is in fact more of a Zombie Survival Simulator. Your goal is to survive as long as you can against impossible odds, as not only are the Zeds out for your flesh, but the water and electricity shut off after a certain amount of time. You will have to battle with fatigue, hunger, depression, and so many other factors that would play into a real Zombie Apocalypse. This is a Zombie game that not only sets itself apart from the rest, but stands victoriously above them all. If you're a fan of slower paced, tactical games then this one is for you. Make no mistake however, just because the game may seem slow at times, doesn't mean you won't find yourself fighting off hordes and running for your life like a typical action game. At present the game is still in early access and with the astonishing features planned in upcomming versions, the fun will never stop. Truly the only complaint I have is the controls take a tiny bit to get used to. Once you quickly master them however, you will be stock piling food, barricading safe houses, and trying desperately to survive. This is not the tale of how you lived, this is the tale of how you died. Buy Project Zomboid and you will not be disappointed, especially if you play with others online in order to survive as a group. The early access is certainly worth the price and I wouldn't be surprised if the price jumped once the game is fully completed (if they don't keep adding more content over time afterwards which I'm sure they will), so do yourself a favor and pick up a copy now. There are Zeds to be slain. Don't forget to watch your back, you never know what will be lurking behind you with a vicious appetite.

Firts of all. Lets get one thing out of the way before I start the actual review. In my own opinion all the hate that this game gets because of the amount of DLC in the game is getting out of hand and I personally think that people are over reacting. Nearly all the DLC except the Season Pass are all cosmetic stuff like weapon skins and monster skins witch to me is perfectly fine and they are giving us all the upcoming maps for free witch is a very good thing. Now on to the review.
Evolve is a tactical team based shooter. The matches are played in 4 vs 1. The four players take control of hunters ( as of writing there are total of 12 hunters avaible and 4 more coming later ) Assault witch damages the monster, Support who buffs the hunters, Trapper who tracks down and traps the monster and finally Medic who heals and revives team mates. Eeach class has ( again at the time of writing ) three unique hunters, each with their own weapons and skills. The remaining player takes control of a huge badass monster ( at the time of writing there are 3 different monsters and 2 more coming later ) witch include Goliath who can take a lot of damage from the hunters, Kraken who specialise in long range attack and finally Wraith who is a sneaky little ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. In the matches themselves you will find dangerous wildlife among the monster witch can be dangerous if you are not carefull. Thease monsters have a chance to have a buff to you witch can have effect like jetpack recharge speed, damage increase and so on witch can be a good tactical gain for you.
There are 4 game modes in the game.
- Hunt witch is the basic mode in the game. Hunters need to find the monster asap before the monster can evolve to up to stage 3 and kill the hunters OR destroy the power generator.
- Nest: In this game mode the hunters need to find 6 monster eggs or minions around the map and the monster needs to kill the hunters before the hunters can destroy all of the eggs. The monster however can hatch thease eggs for a powerfull minion to fight beside the monster at the cost of a egg.
- Rescue: In this mode the hunters have to find downed survivors around the map, help them up and escort them to the marked area for rescue. The monster again has to kill the hunters to win the match, while the hunters have a certain number of survivors they need to rescue to win.
- Defend: In this mode the hunters need to defend up to 3 power generators from the monster. The monster here starts at stage 3 automaticly and also those more powerfull minions from Nest mode come to help the monster. The hunters have to defend a certain amount of time to win while the monster has to destroy all three of the power generators to win.
NOTE: There is a so called mini campaing in the game called Evacuation witch is a 5 round game where the game modes mentioned above are cycled around. The key part in Evacuation is that depending on who wins the next map may have some surprises :)
I should also note that all of the modes are playable offline and there are custom modes where you can set the rules yourself ( like more corpses for the monster to feed and so on and so son ). The game also relies heavily on TEAMWORK. So communication is the key among the hunters. And if you que up together with a group of friends the monster class is disabled. I will also say a little bit about the games unlock system. As you continue to use weapons and gadgets with hunters and abilities on monster you gain points for them and they will upgrade the more you use them. Note that later on the upgrading becomes harder.
I will conclude this review in classic pros and cons
Pros
+ The idea and execution is amazing.
+ The hunters and monsters have good variety.
+ Maps look beutifull and are well done.
+ Surprisingly deep strategy in the matches
Cons
- Matchmaking issues.
- No solid campaing or story.
Final Score
8/10

The developers should take a leaf out of the building systems from other EA titles, eg '7 Days to Die', 'Subnautica', 'Rising World', 'Subsistence', all of which have superior implementations with regard to building placement.
Time is usually precious In survival games and having to fight against the interface on these two counts puts a serious dent in my enjoyment of the game. Hopefully these issues will be addressed in later versions, I can't recommend the game until they are sorted out.

I've never had so much fun losing at a game. This game combines aspects of the MOBA genre with a genre from the roots of MOBA, tower defense. Maybe I'm overexplaining it. This game is a tower defense game that requires your to manage 3 different resources, a team of heroes, and base construction/map exploration. It allows (and forces you) to build structures to increase your resources and defend your buildings, and a hyper-important power crystal. Resources are throttled tight, forcing the player to be proficient at economy, construction, and hero manipulation. The game features a rogue-like model of character growth and map randomization. This is the first game I've ever played that can be considered primarily rogue-like, and it is a blast. It's really hard, but it's still fulfilling when I get overzealous and open too many doors (Opening another door typically activates a wave of combat. It's a simultaneous unstap step/entering attack phase) in an effort to replenish enough resources to upgrade in time for the first wave.

While this game falls into the generic "sandbox crafting survival" niche everyone is so fond of looking down on, it - thanksfully - doesn't strictly conform to most criteria. It's not about the vicious cycle of mine-shoot-kill-loot-craft, rinse and repeat. The Early Access plaque it's been having for a couple of years is mostly related to the Story Mode which it still lacks, whereas the game's been here all this time along in the form of the Sandbox mode. If you want the original story, wait for it. If you want your own little experience, try this out.
One might argue that this one is a "Dead Souls of a crafting survival genre" in that you'll gonna be dying the first N tries, N being a two-digit number. Don't let that put you down. Don't google all those user-created maps for game locations, because ultimately game content is a limiting factor on replayability for some, and part of the game is about getting familiar with your immediate surroundings and doing proper orienteering - without ingame maps or compasses or whatever, mind you. This is exploration game, after all, with usually no end goal set in stone. Well, apart from not dying.
Have good headphones of you. Audio gives you so much spatial awareness here, and ambient sound quality is so good, you'll be recalling the game for the next couple years of yours when you're in your bed bed trying to sleep and you hear wind howling behind your window. I'd say the latter alone a clear and definite indication that this game is worth it.
PS: don't look up the name Fluffy if you don't want to spoil your pants-crapping experience at some point. If you're easily scared, though, go for it, though Fluffy will not be pleased.

I would like to say first of all what you most likely have heard many times about this game to get it over with, its hard. Though, if you keep playing the game and keep acknowledging that this is a game meant for you to have difficulty striving as you figure out how to defeat some of the bosses and run 'n guns, you feel amazing. The game looks amazing, reminds me of a cartoom I used to watch as a kid called looney toons, it just makes it even more fun to play. All this I am sure you have heard before, so I will say my expierience. I rage at games, a lot, I broke my desk twice playing this game (I can fix it). Playing some of this game, I can not bare it, for me, it is one of the hardest games Ive ever played. Though I do not account that for how good the game is, its difficulty should absolutely not affect its rating. I finished it by myself on regular mode, so it is most definitely not impossible. Aside from my rage while playing the game, the music, the visuals, the designs, and my urge to get to the end of the game made me want to see this game to its very end. I did not expierience glitches or any wierd lag issues in this game so there is nothing that is going on there. I always found myself in a position where I cannot stop playing a boss until I have killed it. Some I have played for hours, and I did not get tired of it. This game is a game where you are not going to kill a boss first try, and if so, I will not believe you. Whenever I played a boss or a run 'n gun, I had to play it at least 10 times before I really knew what to do and where to be. Some bosses you need to be on the very edge of the screen, some bosses you need to be up close and personal to actually deal damage, some bosses you need to take it slow or you will die. This you need to learn in a series of retrys. Now, going back to what kept me going in the game and how I was able to bare sitting in one place just shooting a boss and dying over and over was just the looks, but especially the soundtrack. It fits the theme and especially the boss itself, and in general, It is just flat out good. I have a lot of the soundtracks on stand by and there have been a lot of times where I stop and just listen to it. The music in any level in the game did not get old no matter how much I played it, and it sure as hell made me keep wanting to play the game. One thing that I found amazing about the game was its effort in the creativity factor of the game. Some bosses I played and I found it how amazing its phases were so different and amazing. Some times it blows my mind how much thought went into making the idea of the progression in these bosses. One of the bosses is a bee and then turns into a plane, anoher is two frogs that turn into a slot machine, it is crazy what they come up with to make the bosses. That does it for What I think about the game and what makes me love it. Over all, I really recommend it to anyone, even if platformers are not your thing, but be preped for something that wont be easy and will make you rage.

I picked this game up for $5.
It's not worth it.
But not for the reasons one may think! The game is a very simple game, with procedurally generated maps and loot 'chests' (the doors of buildings are basically all loot stashes, and you just loot them instead of going into the building), and some good AI for the robots that are always trying to kill you.
On the one hand, I often found myself bored as I trudged through empty fields, seeing nothing and becoming lost all the time.
On the other hand, when I was finally able to defend myself, figuring out ways to combat the often overwhelming bot force became very fun and action packed. So much so that when I was inevitably killed, I felt like playing again (after a bit of a cool down, thanks to my temper lol).
Normally, I'd say this easily merits the $5 tag I picked it up for... but for one word: Glitches.
Did these developers test their damn game before releasing it?! I have CONSTANTLY been running into three specific glitches that make the game unplayable.
Glitch 1: My inventory mysteriously vanishes- yet I cannot place items into it, or remove items from it (or try to use any of the few items that do show up).
Glitch 2: The boats in between islands mysteriously dissapear, thus stranding me on the island I am currently on.
Glitch 3: My most hated of all glitches- randomly (though it likes to do it more when I get shot), the entire game will vanish, leaving behind nothing but a colored blur that you can tell is the layer behind the clouds above. I still have access to my hud, and can even open my inventory (but not use items), but everything else is gone. no buildings, no weapon in hand, no clouds, and no ground. It's just blank. I can hear when i use my weapon, and even still take bleed damage (but cannot be shot or hurt otherwise), but anything else (including enemies) just dissapear, and never come back.
After the 5th or 6th time of this occurence, I have decided to give up on this game. Please try harder next time, devs.

Alright, so.  Having already acquired half of the Stones, (of which are 18 BTW,) I think I should be able to write a decent review on this title.  Let me start by saying this:
Unique.  Yup.  I've played a lot of games, and nothing is quite like this one.  YOU are being the one hunted, and boy are you ever; those robots are EVERYWHERE.
The robots, being CPUs, have really good AI.  They aren't just idiots who, when seeing you run behind a corner, completely forget about you and walk off.  No.  They will search wherever you were last, and then some.  An interesting mechanic is that you can use trains, rocks, clocks, and glasses to distract said robots.  Using this technique, you can even trap them.
At first, getting a gun can be hard work.  Then you have bullets... Sometimes, there will be a small village with around six mags of bullets, each of which includes 6 bullets.  And then other times, you won't be able to find any bullets for an hour or more.  So don't expect this to be a war zone with guns blazing... well, not YOUR guns blazing, anyway.
After that, you have to remember to watch your "Vitality" bar, or hunger bar.  This does not deplete fast, but the more it's filled, the faster you regain health.
So, overall, what do I think of this game?
Very unique, with a pleasant art style and decent game mechanics.  Robot AI is quite smart, and there is a wide array of different kinds of robots.  Being a survival game, there are lots of survival mechanics and good stealth mechanics as well.  I HIGHLY recammend this, though for the $20 price, It's steep, but with a replay value, worth it.

Still looking good graphically but suffering on repeatedly emulated gameplay. The game that popularised the one-two punch in video-games and reformatted the first person shooter has crept it's way into pop-culture. Steampunk sees a resurgence in popularity, good story-telling becomes a standard; the gaming world is a better place because BioShock existed.
When it comes to viewing BioShock for what it is, a shooter, it is now, it's safe to say, an item of historical interest rather than a game that demands a playthrough by everyone.
BioShock inherited the throne left by its parent series System Shock, which delivered two games in 1994 and 1999 that each redefined what the tired FPS genre meant and could achieve. Using those same techniques and a few new tricks, BioShock swept in on a tidal wave in 2007 and again acted as catalyst to reinvent a dying genre. Losing a lot of it's predecessor's RPG elements, BioShock retained a level of customisation that made the game interesting and personal to the player each time.
That storyline, my goodness. If there's one thing about this game that will not dwindle with time in the face of bigger, better and more advanced games, it is that unflinching, brutal, utterly disturbing story of a man named Jack and a city below the sea where the lights are on ... but nobody's home.
If you decide to open the doors to Rapture for the first time, be aware that it will suck you in and still hold you there under the waves even after all this time.

While this game falls into the generic "sandbox crafting survival" niche everyone is so fond of looking down on, it - thanksfully - doesn't strictly conform to most criteria. It's not about the vicious cycle of mine-shoot-kill-loot-craft, rinse and repeat. The Early Access plaque it's been having for a couple of years is mostly related to the Story Mode which it still lacks, whereas the game's been here all this time along in the form of the Sandbox mode. If you want the original story, wait for it. If you want your own little experience, try this out.
One might argue that this one is a "Dead Souls of a crafting survival genre" in that you'll gonna be dying the first N tries, N being a two-digit number. Don't let that put you down. Don't google all those user-created maps for game locations, because ultimately game content is a limiting factor on replayability for some, and part of the game is about getting familiar with your immediate surroundings and doing proper orienteering - without ingame maps or compasses or whatever, mind you. This is exploration game, after all, with usually no end goal set in stone. Well, apart from not dying.
Have good headphones of you. Audio gives you so much spatial awareness here, and ambient sound quality is so good, you'll be recalling the game for the next couple years of yours when you're in your bed bed trying to sleep and you hear wind howling behind your window. I'd say the latter alone a clear and definite indication that this game is worth it.
PS: don't look up the name Fluffy if you don't want to spoil your pants-crapping experience at some point. If you're easily scared, though, go for it, though Fluffy will not be pleased.

This game is awesome. It's a short (~1.5 hours) light-hearted puzzle platformer game.
Every level has its own theme and implements specific gameplay mechanic, which keeps the game fresh until the end. The story is presented both in-game through conversation as you progress through the levels  (they do not interrupt the gameplay) and through short picture/text presentation at the end of each levels.
You can complete each level simply by reaching the balloon at the end but you really should try to get the 100 crystals hidden in every level (25 from monsters, 75 from 3 statues). You're rewarded with additional story bits when you do so.
At first It seemed like this game was too simple and kind of lackluster but as I cleared each level, my opinion changed completely. I just kept going forward compelled to hear more audio interactions between the princess and the witch and to discover and toy with the new mechanics of each level. Overall, the pace turned out to be just right, no mechanic felt overused, every levels brought something new and there was always a surprise around the corner.
I recommend this game!

Oi, I wanted to love this game I really did.  Ok First things first.  Yes it's a big galaxy strategy game of Star wars, you can build fleets and armies, have land and space battles, build star destroyers etc, it's all there.
BUT: When I'm playing it I'm thinking, for every thing the game does well, there's two things that crop up that make me think, 'rebellion did this better six years earlier'.
1)You get limited 'command points' so that the biggest battle you get is about 5 star destroyers... if you have 20, fine, they come in one at a time as reinforcements.
2) Ships repair automatically, so if you cripple a ship in a hit and fade mission, eg, you play as rebels, fly in blast a big star destroyer, fly out then your main fleet comes in just after, literally 1 second can transpire, which represents maybe 1/12 of a galactic day, and that ship will be completely fixed.  So anything you don't destroy is immediately repaired.  That seems like basic logic has gone WAY out the window.
3) You can not sabotage anything, you can only steal technology as the rebels, so usig spec forces or whatever doesn't come into it all.
4) Ground battles are  alittle repetitive, and if for eg, you take over a planet, you can't build defences on the ground level until a battle starts... WHAT THE HELL! So eg you can build BIG things like Ion cannons or shields for the planet, but little 'build pads' for local defences to help you shoot down AT-AT's or whatever can't be built until an invading army arrives... what was my army doing for the six months I held that planet, just standing there? Then they go.. 'oh right, the enemy is landing, maybe we shouldn't have been just giving each other piggy back rides this whole time...'
These might sound niggly as problems, and  they are, but they and a few more I wont mention REALLy pile up to hold the game back from being great.
The story is paper thin, leads up to the destruction of the 1st death star in star wars 1977.
THE EXPANSION PACK:
In short, it fixes about three little problems, much improved story campaign, you can now sabotage and do things like that BUT ONLY WITH THE NEW TEAM, but the issues above are still largely present.
And when you play games with all 3 teams (ie NOT the campaign) You can see how balance was not an issue for the developers.
The new team, the pirates are SO overpowered and will absolutely cripple the rebs and imps, so play as them or get angry, that's your choices.
So overall, yes I do recommend it, you can see by my hours played that I still gave it a go, and the expansion definitely improves the game enough to give it some reply value. ( I got a MOD with some maps, so I could play the expansion on old maps WITHOUT the new pirate team, thus it wasn't so unabalanced, but could play with the new features, ships etc)
Flying into battle with the Death Star II and Vader's super star destroyer with another 4/5 star destroyers is still very enjoyable. So worth a play, but beware its drawbacks.

In the days that followed, my dreams consisted entirely of connecting shapes together and solving puzzles.
I started to become frustrated with everyday life.  Why couldn't I connect shapes together in real life?  Why didn't connecting shapes together in my head solve my real world problems?
That was a month and a half ago.  I have since picked the game up again, but I'm using a guide this time.  It's a compromise between having no fun and the shape-infested hell I was living in when I first started playing.  There are also randomly generated puzzles that are just as good as the normal ones, so if I start seeing shapes again, I can always just cheat all of the achievements and play the random levels afterward.
Let it be known that I beat sets A-F and got partway through G before losing my mind.  I urge that if you want to play this game legitimately...at least pace yourself.  Otherwise, you could end up like me.
Edit:  Today, scared of returning to shape-infested hell, I cheated the achievements.

This game right here, five nights at Freddy's, has really changed my life and helped me through some tough some tough times. Everything about this game is incredible. The lore, the characters, the gameplay itself, it's amazing. My favorite thing about this game is the characters probably. There are a wide variety of them to know and love. My favorite is Freddy fazbear and he always will be. :3  Ok, now that Got that out of the way, I'm going to talk about the gameplay.
The gameplay is really creative, unlike any other game I have played. In Five Nights at Freddy's 1, you have to try and defend yourself from the animatronics by checking the cameras, and the door lights, and you must close your doors only when it is needed due to the fact that you need to conserve power. Or else ;)
You have to check pirate's cove from time to time, which is VERY important. XD
If you do beat the game, you can then do custom night and change the animatronics' AI levels. the higher the AI, the crazier and more dangerous they will become. There is my review for this game. So i might as well talk about the other four games while im at it. (because reasons)

In Five nights at freddy's 2, you have a TON of things to watch after. Now you thought lights, doors, and Foxy was a bad thing, well, get ready for a music box, a long hallway, vents, and many other coincidental things that are perfect for animatronics to crawl through. XD In this game, freddy fazbear's pizzeria reopens its doors. "The grand reopening."
You must check the vents, and the hall for any of the characters. If they happen to get into the room or the vents, there is a Freddy Fazbear mask sitting there for you to use to ward them off. (This does not work on foxy, the puppet, or BB)
To keep the puppet from getting to you, you have to go and wind the music box (rev up that music box m8 XD)
It keeps him in the box. Also, there are minigames that help explain some of the lore which is really cool! :D
You also get custom night if you beat this game.
In Five nights at Freddy's 3, you are the new security guard that works at Fazbear's fright. Now, the old animatronics that you knew of in the other two games are used for "spooky props" for the pizzeria. Now you have only one real one to deal with. Springtrap. In this game, you have to play audio in a room to lure Springtrap there. (I think he is attracted to BB's voice. ;) ) You want to keep him out of the vents, and far away from the office as possible. If he gets into a vent, you can now seal them (which would have been helpful in fnaf 2 at the time) You also have maintenance panel to reboot things such as the ventilation, the audio, and the cameras which WILL go down during gameplay to make it more difficult. Also, hallucinations of Freddy, Chica, Foxy, Puppet, Mangle, and BB can cause you to have to reboot things. When you beat this game, you are greeted with an extras menu, and Nightmare mode. So fun! :3
In five nights at freddy's 4, the terror follows you home. You must play as a child and defend yourself against your own "nightmares." You have only a flashlight and doors to protect you from the animatronics. You must check the closet in front of you, the bed behind you, and the doors that are on both sides of you. When checking the doors, you must listen for breathing (which can be hard to hear sometimes) If you hear breathing, the worst thing that you can do is to try and shine your light down the hallway. IT WILL NOT WORK. Instead, you will rudely shine it right into the face of Nightmare Bonnie or Nightmare Chica. You must keep things such as fredlings (fredles) off of the bed, or else you will NOT be ready 4 Freddy. XD Now, the closet acts as pirates cove, so once foxy is in there, you will need to keep an eye on him. If you survive the night (song reference) you get to play a minigame, and do something called "fun with plushtrap" You need to use the flashlight and try to stop him on the "X" which will advance you 2 hours into the next night. When you beat the game, you also  get to see an extras menu, and nightmare mode. :3 There is also a halloween edition for this game that is EPIC. XD

You must find out whats wrong on the flipside, and save the day. there are multiple endings, and many characters and attacks to use. It is really fun. There is an update 2 coming someday! XD
So there is my review on the entire fnaf series. Scott is also working on some kind of a fnaf sister location thing too which I can't wait to see. anyways, Scott, if you are reading this, thank you for everything. You are amazing! :)

This is a horror game which is meant to be simplistic and creepy at the same time. What makes it so creepy is that this game, despite it's limitations is able to throw in alot of scares, mostly due to making you paranoid because of the animatronics which can get you at any given time. Also, the fact that you have limited power is put into consideration. If you power runs out, you're done. Freddy, the main antagonist will slowly come to get you and if it's not 5AM, there's a high chance that this is game over for you. There is also another problem which is Foxy the Fox, which if you don't check him periodical, he will most likely come to rip you apart aswell, or as the game shows, give you a heart attack. By the way, if you see him in the camera running towards you, lock your left door. Him hitting the door will drain your power, but will save you from dying. Then there's Bonnie and Chica. They're the ones who will regularly occupy you as Freddy stays in place for most of the time, and because they are the most active ones. They ways to counter them are far more simpler, just close the door when you see them in the hallways outside of your room (Which you check if they're there by using the lights. Look out for their shadows since that's how you can see them in the windows since the doors being closed don't let you see them.) and wait for them to leave. And you have to survive this 5 times, or 5 nights, rather. There's also some extras but you have to beat the 5 nights first to unlock them. And that's the game in a tl;dr format. But yeah, thanks for reading and i hope this review was useful to you. This is my longest review yet and i had quite some fun writing it. Hope you guys enjoy the game!

I love this game, there's so much about it that makes you cringe, freak out, and get an adrenaline rush from. It's one of the few games where when a zombie pops out from behind a door and the music cues, I jump in my chair. You panick so easily from things like zombies banging on your doors and windows smashing while you hide in your basement.
Here's just one moment I had:
I'm playing as a hard working man who found a home in the suburbs and reinforced it, with plenty of ammunition, guns, and food to last me for days if things went sour. Eventually, I run into a massive horde while looting, and sprint back to my home where I barricade the doors, eat a can of spaghetti and then go to sleep. I wake up at 1:30 AM to the sound of my windows smashing, and panic. I barricade my upstairs door and lock myself in the bathroom, and wait with a shotgun and pistol ready. After almost a day of the zombies hammering away and me drinking from the sink to stay hydrated, the door finally breaks. Zombies flood my room. I can hear them scratching at my bathroom door, and I do the only thing I can think of to end it all
I drank a gallon of bleach.
I ended up dying of poisoning before the creatures could eat me, and I had survived for almost a month.
That is just one of the likely scenarios that can happen in this game.

If you liked FTL but wished it had more depth and choice this game is going to be for you. The concept is simple. Every time you open a door you're given resources. You use those resources to power rooms (preventing monsters from spawning in them) and place machinery to gather more resources and act as defensive/offensive turrets. Of course it's not all that easy, each room has a chance to contain monsters, useful items, blueprints for more machinery and additional people that you can hire.
The goal, get your power crystal at the start room to the exit, when you find it. Each play is randomised so you're never sure what's going to be behind that next door!
Of course there are lots of other elements in there beyond this. Each member of your team has their own stats and abilities which you can level up at the cost of food. Placing them in a room with a machine increases its efficiency but of course this means spreading your team out. If a machine is destroyed so is the building platform making the room much less useful. It goes on and on.
Regarding the Alpha. Game length seems limited right now, you get three dungeon runs before you win but of course each run is different so the limit really is more to do with leveling your team than actual play time. This really is a state whereby the mechanics are being tested rather than the content. The developer is keen to engage with players and encourages feedback and voting on features. And the future feature list is quite extensive.
As I said at the start. If you like FTL then this should suit you down to the ground, it's Alpha but it's very much playable and will be fun to see it grow into a full release.

If you're considering buying this game but are unsure how it compares to other survival games this is the review for you.  I'm a fan of the survival and thrive type games and The Forest didn't disappoint.
Essentially your thrust onto a beautiful Pennisula that mostly covered with a fairly thick forest.  It's full of wildlife to hunt, and resource to use in crafting. You can build anywhere on the map, and finding a good location is key to surviving. Base building is very easy, intuitive and offers a nice range of things to build from structures to live in, things that provide fresh water or dry meat, or defensive walls or traps.
Which brings me to the neighbors....meet the Cannibals. These creatures are one of my favorite thing about the game. They don't act like typical enemies, that will see you and just attack. Sometimes they will stand off in the distance and just watch you. Sometimes they'll run away and get more buddies. I've had them kneel in fear when I killed other cannibals and I've seen cannibals lose their minds in rage when you kill their mate and they charge you with no regard to their self preservation. When they run they tend to run almost like they are on all fours, looks very creepy.
Definitely a creep factor to this game. Besides the cannibals or dark caves filled with cannibals to explore. There's a dark storyline and hints of a very dark history to the area. Evidence of people are all over the island but no people besides cannibals who seem to have eaten most of the people. Even the wind blowing through the trees when you're deep in the forest has a slight creep factor. I typically don't find many games scary, but this one had me jumping a few times.
I've talked up the game but here's some of the things that could be considered a negative.
The game is also early access and they seem to update the game on a monthly basis. But besides somewhat lacking content it seems like a fully fleshed out game. The storyline isn't much, and it's not the typical game that will have you traveling all over the map doing quests to save the day. It's a game that puts you into large map filled with things for you to hunt or things that hunt you. The storyline is revealed as you explore the map.  You could easily never focus on the storyline and still have a very enjoyable game.
I played single player, although this would be a great game for co-op.  And probably less creepy.
The game more or less lacks music. You can find music tapes on the map that provide some music but it's not very convenient.
Combat-you have attack and block.  You have access to some basic ranged weapons but combat isn't anything special.

While this game falls into the generic "sandbox crafting survival" niche everyone is so fond of looking down on, it - thanksfully - doesn't strictly conform to most criteria. It's not about the vicious cycle of mine-shoot-kill-loot-craft, rinse and repeat. The Early Access plaque it's been having for a couple of years is mostly related to the Story Mode which it still lacks, whereas the game's been here all this time along in the form of the Sandbox mode. If you want the original story, wait for it. If you want your own little experience, try this out.
One might argue that this one is a "Dead Souls of a crafting survival genre" in that you'll gonna be dying the first N tries, N being a two-digit number. Don't let that put you down. Don't google all those user-created maps for game locations, because ultimately game content is a limiting factor on replayability for some, and part of the game is about getting familiar with your immediate surroundings and doing proper orienteering - without ingame maps or compasses or whatever, mind you. This is exploration game, after all, with usually no end goal set in stone. Well, apart from not dying.
Have good headphones of you. Audio gives you so much spatial awareness here, and ambient sound quality is so good, you'll be recalling the game for the next couple years of yours when you're in your bed bed trying to sleep and you hear wind howling behind your window. I'd say the latter alone a clear and definite indication that this game is worth it.
PS: don't look up the name Fluffy if you don't want to spoil your pants-crapping experience at some point. If you're easily scared, though, go for it, though Fluffy will not be pleased.

Do you like stealth games? Do you like robots? Do you like -punk universes? If at least 2/3 of your answers are yes, you should get this game! I've been playing it since it was early access and feel like the devs have managed to balance every item and robot type very well, and you can tweak stuff in the options to suit your tastes.
Some initial reviews say that you don't really feel as hunted as the name suggests, and at the time that was true. The robots spent much of their time with the teleporter fragments you're gathering, largely allowing you to set the terms of the confrontation. In the full release, however, the devs have upped the number of robot patrols and depending on how your island generated, you really can't get too far without having to duck in the grass, the bushes, the woods or behind a structure. There's gentleman robots looking for you all around. There's trappers in the woods / bushes. There's bots ready to stalk you on the fields. Every environment (but not every island type) has its own special hunters, and some hunters look for you all around. Lucky for you, some of the bots don't get along and will fight when they encounter each other, allowing you a chance to escape or get some loot when things die down. There will usually be some at the fragments too, since the bots know you will be coming to get them sooner or later.
With the variety of enemy types and starting equipment, beautiful environments that are randomly regenerated each time you start a new game, different options to customize your game (even removing all the enemies if you just like to walk around) Sir is an excellent choice for the stealth enthusiast. The graphics aren't to everyone's tastes, and the open world environment with its own stealth mechanics might rub some of the fans of the genre the wrong way. Personally, I adore the look and the mechanics, but these are the gripes others have repeatedly expressed and which seem to be dragging the metascore down.
TL;DR: Stealth is cool, robots are cool, tweedpunk is cool - Sir, You Are Being Hunted is cool. Buy and enjoy.

Reigns is an interesting thing that falls somewhere between a visual novel, a sim, and a card game. You guide the monarch of a kingdom through their rule by choosing one of two options given a randomized set of story cards. Each time your king dies, you progress forward in time to the next king, and you have 2,000 years of rule to try to complete the overarching story that loosely follows all your rulers. The game has a good sense of humor, oddly likable pixel graphics, and a unique setup. It was so simple, but one of those game where you look up and you’ve somehow been doing it for two hours.

I don't quite remember what drove me to the Sient Hunter series. I think I saw them on Steam one day and thought to myself "hey cool, submarines!". Before that moment I had very little interest in the subject and even less knowlege. To my understanding: a submarine was just a boat that traveled over and under water with a periscope for looking around. I know now that they are so much more than that.
A submarine is a complicated piece of machinery that is designed to stealthily ambush enemy merchant ships. They are no match for destroyers and dive bombers are a constant nightmare. Above water, in daylight, they are sitting ducks. Underwater they are blind as bats, with only sound to guide their eyes. Most of your torpedoes will be duds, and if enemy war ships become aware of your presence your only hope is to submerge and leave the area quickly; and pray that the depth charges don't sink your boat.
There is a reason why German u-boats were called "iron coffins". It's because they had the highest casualty rate during WW2.
In Silent Hunter 4 (wolves of the pacific) you get to play on the American side as a submariner in the pacific theater of the war. With the U-boat Missions addon you can play the German side in the same theater. That expansion updates the game to 1.5, so it is required in order to use a lot of the mods for the game. There is one mod in particular that expands the default German campaign into the Atlantic and North Sea areas; definitely a must if you prefer that side of the conflict. Or just get Silent Hunter 2, 3, or 5 (all u-boat games). Silent Hunter 4 is unique because it's the first game since Silent Hunter 1 that lets players command American subs. Unfortunately Japanese subs are not playable, which would have been a huge bonus.
I think the general consensus of this game is: you will either love it or hate it. I've seen people putting the game down either for some annoying bugs (and they are annoying) or simply because they don't prefer the submarine warfare in the Pacific theater. Personally, I like it. The American subs are unique in their own way, but not completely different from the German u-boats. The threat is still there, but the Pacific Ocean is a vast place. You may find yourself traveling around for what seems an eternity before engaging in any type of action. To me, this is the only drawback of the game. Most of the bugs and failings of the game can be improved with mods, however; and there are plenty of them online.
The entire Silent Hunter series is great, and every game in the list is a good submarine sim. If you are just looking for an arcade experience and want to jump right into the action, then you can do that. However, if you want an ultra-realistic simulator then turn up the realism settings and dive into the plethora of game-changing mods that are available online. This game is a great entry for anyone even remotely interested in the subject. You won't learn everything about submarine life, but you will walk away with a new found appreciation for it!

Game is great and gameplay is awesome but I feel the scope of the game is far too large. The zombies are a consistent threat at all times and the smallest mistake will make you run for the hills! The skill system is good as it provides milestones for a player to level up a skill. However requiring the player to read books to increase the speed of skill development feels like an intentional wall to prevent players from getting a skill up too quickly. Since skill books are loot and are RNG it could mean that you could never find a specific book, which as happend to me during play-throughs. Gainging exeprience is not the greatest thing about the skill system since most gains are gotten one point at a time and there is no way to really grind exprience with out putting your character at risk. As experience gains, from my experience, are only gotten from slaying and sneaking around the undead. Meaning that you either have to slaughter most of the undead on the map to gain enough skill points to put into skills or have to farm sneak like in skyrim. I also feel the developers aren't prioritizing features that the community actually wants. As I am writing this review the developers are currently working on maps that lead to survivor caches. Ironically there are no other survivors (NPCs) in the game world. The developers have showed off their animations in previous mondoids and mondoids after say they have made progress on them with out showing that they have. It would be nice to be able to test such features within the options menu in the IWBUMS branch.
Conclusion:
While Project Zomboid is a very fun game to play it does leave a lot to be desired.
Developers actevly ignoring community requested features is dissapointing.
Scope of the game is simply too large for a small team of developers to handle and as such the game has suffered from it.
Developers developing features that could be considered "Non essential" instead of "Essential" features. EX: Maps > Animation

I need to clarify something right here, right now. This is a game you either like or dislike, that is obvious.
I am not a horror fan, I hate being jumpscared, I have actually played very little of any of the games in this extremely popular series. Yet I am a big fan of the series because like most fans like me, appreciate the lore of the games and how far the games have come.
I mean this is a series created by a single near unknown developer and within 1 1/2 years has become so popular that there is now: 4 games, a spin-off title, a novel and a movie in the works. Along with billions of views on Youtube, a line of Merchandise and about a thousand knockoff titles.
This is exactly what happened with Minecraft! And that gets roughly the same about of criticism thrown at it.
I agree that the fanbase is..... bad. But there is a large amount of it that are brilliant like the Theorists, Song writers, Youtubers, animators and artists.
I know that i am going to get a lot of s*** from this review. But I dont really care, all I ask is for people to show a little respect for the little game that has changed not only the horror genre but gaming and gamers as a whole.
OK with that clarified, Im going to start the review.
It's doesnt have the best graphics nor the best gameplay. But it is the story that keeps some players coming back for more.
It does have that initial scare factor, but it will wear off after an hour or 2 once you have learned the patterns. But it is a refreshing take on the traditional horror game, rather than a walking down a dark hall simulator, you are unable to move and the tension comes from know that something is coming but you don't know when and what is coming.
Horror fans will as i said either love it or hate it.
It is a good game, it's innovative, but it wont appeal to everyone. That is just how the industry works...
