This is a total rewrite of my review. Its still a no, but Im going to correct some things I was wrong about in the original.
I say this is a no for the most part, or at least currently. The game is fun, its a good time. Its interesting and very compelling. But, the way DLC is handled, the amount of it, and some of the chore game isnt very fun.
DLC: There is no DLC on the market that changes the game. There are no new monsters available, no new hunters available. I was totally wrong about that in the original post.
The DLC that is currently available is all weapon skins and asthaetics for characters. Does this change anything? I dont think so. There are only a few skins available with the base game. All of these skins i think should be in the game for free. If your going to make a skin option for characters and weapons, you have to give the base game at least a decent selection of skins to unlock for free. I have no problem with them adding new skins in the future, but there shouldnt be day 1 DLC of something as simple as a skin. Those could have just been thrown in with the day 1 update for free. Then they could have made more skins to release as DLC in a few months.
The other DLC. All DLC that changes the game is not released yet. No new monsters or hunters yet. However, the way you can obtain this DLC, or I should say these DLC's is really bad. Each monster costs 15 dollars. just 1 monster. Thats completly over priced. But you would think that the season pass solves this. Well kinda. There isnt just one season pass, theres 2. One gives you all the Monsters, and the other gives you all of the Hunters. So instead of paying for 1 season pass to get all the DLC, you have to pay for 2. And both of them are full priced DLC season passes. So not only is there a ton of overpriced asthaetic stuff already on the market, you have to pay $45+ dollars to get the total amount of DLC that actually does change the game. You will still have to pay over $100 just to get the full content of this game. For some people that might be alright, and for some thats unreasonable. I think its unreasonable. If it was one season pass, thats fine. But if your splitting your DLC up into two passes, your kind of just a money pinching ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
Gameplay: Im going to agree with TotalBiscuit on this. The game is really good when things go right but its super boring when things dont. If you have a crapy teammate on hunters, you lose. You just lose. Especially if its a really core character like Trapper. If the skill gap between the hunters and the monster is too large the game length is almost random. If the monster if way better, than the hunters are playing hide and seek for 10 minutes and never find the hider until hes stage three and destroying you. If the hunters are way better than the monster just gets cuaght at stage one and dies instantly. The game is super boring for the hunters, since it ended in 2 minutes and 1 dome, while the monster is just♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥that he never even had a chance. If you are a monster who is way better, you cant really have any fun either because you just spend the whole game eating wildlife with no threat of getting killed, and after 10 minutes of feeding you win.
When the games are even between hunters and monster, and the hunters are competent, the game is amazing. It plays well, its exciting, and each role is unique. Its not perfect, but its still really fun.
If you are fine with paying way to much for content, then you will probably love the game. But if your not trying to shell out cash, wait until a game of the year edition comes out, or be content with only 3 monsters and 9 hunters.
My review will change to a yes when the DLC nonsense if fixed. You cant charge the cost of an entire game just for the DLC of a few monsters and hunters. Thats so little content for so much money its comparable to the prices of illegal narcotics.

Interesting idea, classic "indie" mistakes. The levels are all short enough that mistakes have no long-term consequences, meaning that the game can be essentially bruteforced --- that is, one can repeat a level over and over again until it is beaten by a coincidence of sorts, developing little to no skill along the way. The aesthetics are quite frankly disgusting, with all the levels being totally indistinct "futuristic" sets of platforms and all the robots ("titans," as the game calls them) being totally indistinct messes of semi-random pieces. I cannot remember exactly what a single one looks like, but I have a very clear image of what they all look like --- and that is what one calls bad aesthetics. The whole thing is compounded by terrible in-jokes abound and a sense of humor that could only be inbred in the indie scene. This alone would be typically enough to damn a game, but Drunken Robot Pornography takes it a step further.
The bullet hell genre is interesting not because of its sea of bullets, but because there is always a pattern to the sea of bullets --- a casual observer may call it chaos, but any experienced savant of the genre knows that bullet hell has nothing at all to do with chaos. Recognizing and reacting to these patterns is an essential part of playing any bullet hell game. In Drunken Robot Pornography, bullets are often sprayed in random directions, or wherever the player happens to be going. There is barely any rhythm to get into, and in the rare occasions when there is one, it is pitifully simple, and the enemies that just happen to follow the player quickly become the bigger threat. This would be a huge annoyance if the game wasn't so easy (and yes, I played on the hardest difficulty level) --- essentialy, the best strategy is always to grab a few power-ups, find a place where the robot isn't shooting, and spray bullets directly at for a few seconds. I have no doubt that impressive powerplays are possible, but the game does not make them particularly desirable: in Ketsui, to complete the game on one credit at all, one must develop a robust, powerplay-like strategy. Play ten minutes of that game and then all of this one and say which one you remember better.
While merging bullet hell concepts with modern shooter mechanics is a good idea, this game fails to pull it off, and fails miserably. Those interested in what a decent developer might do with the concept should play Vanquish.

I wanted to like this game, it's pretty, I liked the art style... unfortunately I just can't.
The controls are bad, especially if you are using a keyboard and mouse. The camera is INCREDIBLY twitchy if using a mouse. If you play this you are going to want a controller or you're going to have to slow mouse movement to a literal crawl manually.
I understand this is more a puzzle game than a fighting game but the combat system is horrible. You can't swap between light (swing) and strong (thrust) attacks mid combo. You're locked into the animation until it finishes... which is not an issue for the basic trash mobs but very bad for the "boss" mobs. The puzzles are simplistic, you're not going to get stuck on any of them. The timing of the traps are odd, and while they should not kill you they are going to hit you a lot.
The voice acting is cringe worthy. The characters sound like little kids playing pretend. The main character is assumably at least a teenager, and the witch should be an adult but they sound, and act, much younger than they should be. You can tell the story is supposed to sound semi-serious but the writing itself sounds juvenile to the point of it could be badly written fanfiction... or again, little kids playing pretend.
The game IS pretty, very pretty. The music is not bad either. I like the look of it, I like the sound of it (minus the voice acting)... I just can't stand playing it.

Peering towards the horizon to see distant red mechanical eyes pierce the moorland mist fills one with both dread and excitement.
It's certainly not for everyone, but in my opinion the unique steampunk design and atmosphere, along with the replayability offered by procedurally generated environments, makes for a refreshing stealth-survival experience.

This is a game that you either love or hate, and that's kinda what I've gathered from peoples' reactions to it.
The general flow of things is you are security guard Mike Schimdt, who gets a job working for the now run-down and defunct "Freddy Fazbear's Pizza". You're informed by a fellow on the phone that the animatronics try to get into your office, and if they do they'll think you're an endoskeleton without its suit on, and stuff you into an animatronic suit full of metal compartments that will skewer and crush you to death. So how do you do this? By keeping track of the animatronics via cameras, of course! You also have doors you can shut to keep them out, as well as lights on each side that will let you light up a blind spot in the cameras. The only catch? You have limited power, and must last from 12am - 6am. Run out of power, and Freddy Fazbear himself will come for you.
Each animatronic also has their own behavior that you have to counter or keep a look out for in some way. Bonnie, at least for me, tends to be the more aggressive one, and has a knack for getting around rooms quickly. Chica will sometimes stop in the kitchen to make noise to distract you, and also attacks often at times. Foxy must be kept watch of from the Pirate's Cove Camera so you can see when he'll strike but watch too much and he'll come out faster; watch too little and you'll miss his attack and find him screaming at you. Fazbear himself is excellent at hiding himself, and unless he's kept close tabs on will come for you later in the week. And then there's that golden fellow...
The game, I find, is very tense which lends itself a lot to the horror. True, the jumpscares work when you're caught off guard and don't know when they're coming, but most of the time playing I feel very much at the edge of my seat. Though I must mention that it does feel like it's part luck based and part skill based. You could be doing things all right, but because of how often Bonnie and Foxy attacked you could be down to 50% by 2am and really not looking like you're going to survive. Or get stuck in the worst scenario where Bonnie and Chica BOTH are waiting outside, which means your doors should be locked, and it's later in the week when Foxy and Freddy need to be checked constantly. But oh man, when you hear that 6am jingle it is one of the best sounds ever.
So who would like this? Well if you're a furry you might dig it, since Freddy and Friends are all dolled up like anthro animals. If you like the idea of a scary Chuck E. Cheese it'll work too. Those who take more than a derelict setting and creepy robots to get a scare out of might not find the game that scary, if frightening at all. And those who don't jump at jump scares will probably find losing to be annoying more than frightening. I'd give it an honest reccomend though.

Where do I start with this game...going into it, and playing the Alpha and Beta, I got pretty pumped for this game. Watched some gameplay videos and was like "Hell yeah, man let's do this!"
Then I actually got to play it.
Gameplay first.
I will admit, they have a really solid idea here. Not many other games come to mind with some of these mechanics. Now if only the game did better with them. After playing quite a few rounds in quite a few modes, I feel like I can comfortably say this: this game feels unbalanced as♥♥♥♥♥♥ I don't feel that it's fair to make it so that if the monster evolves just once that it spells a team wipe for the hunters. Playing against Kraken and Wraith gives the impression that they are OP and broken, even at only level 2. Level 2 should be a challenge, not prolonging the inevitable. I also feel like they should tweak the AI of the monsters so that it doesn't just gank the medic into a corner as soon as the hunters and monsters meet. Doesn't really give the player a chance to upgrade much and improve in the class if they're immediately just rushed and downed. (Also, sometimes the monsters would still hone in on me, despite being cloaked? I wanna know how THAT one works, devs)
Next, in Evacuation mode, I feel like the "Auto Balance" function is merely a placebo. Even with Auto Balance favoring me by a lot, the game didn't feel any easier for me. Hence, I feel like this is a functionality that should be taken out. Instead, perhaps they can randomize the map effects and use that to balance the game in favor of the hunters or monster.
Finally, the one everyone and their mother has been talking about: the DLC format. Now overall, I don't hate the existence/concept of DLC for games. But I feel like this game is not even trying to be subtle about ripping you off. They don't seem to know what the term "Season Pass" means, since it doesn't include the DLC due to come out in the following months after release. I feel like for the $80 price tag on the game plus season pass, that should cover it. Charging the $100 for MORE DLC that isn't included with this other DLC is a bit extreme.
In conclusion: If you don't mind the steep pricing of some of this content and are willing to lose games a LOT, then I recommend this game. If you're on the fence, I'm gonna go ahead and say don't bother. This game took some great ideas and falled utterly short of delivering fully on them. Honestly, I wish I'd done more research and NOT spent $80 on this game.
EDIT: They did make some balance changes, and getting the opportunity to play a lot more has helped. Seems this game had a steeper learning curve than I even anticipated. Dare I say, I am actually having fun in this game now. I find myself regretting taking such a huge dump on the gameplay, so I would like to take this opportunity to rescind those comments. (still ♥♥♥♥in hate their mindset on the DLC pricing, but what can ya do) I would also like to change my recommendation to "yes i do recommend this game, if you want something with a steep learning curve. something that really will challenge you and test your patience."

Pros:
* Beautiful setting.
* Great sound design.
* Interesting story.
* Audio files.
Neutral:
* The plasmids are a breath of fresh air, but it's not too well implemented.

* Points in the lore are not explained and are left to your imagination.
* Last bundle it was in was 22 months ago (as of writing), so while it's been cheap, the value has risen quite a bit over time.
Cons:
* An extremely basic shooting system. Basically you just hold the LMB and just wait for the health bar to drop down.
* Felt like it dragged on slightly.
* The "moral" system is just basically a "Gandhi or Hitler" type of thing.
* Food, drinks and substances like cigarettes can't be carried with you.
* Some pickups are just objectively bad. No real trade offs with a lot of them.
* On modern systems it can run like♥♥♥♥♥♥ so you might have to remove shadows and things like that + mess around in the config files.
Overall:
7.5/10

A legitimate classic, coming straight out of 2007, no less.
BioShock has been critically acclaimed by many, and I am
late to the party to be reviewing it, but it certainly can't hurt.
BioShock is a very different kind of shooter/horror game.  It borrows heavily from the dystopian themes of topics that Ayn Rand frequented (more specifically
).  The art style and story and in-game architecture of the world is very Art-Deco heavy.  It is dark, foreboding and occasionally frightening.
The graphics are phenomenal for it's age.  The physics, historically, were mind-boggling, and we'd take these for granted today, but back then this
modified version of Unreal Engine 2.5/3 mashup blew everyone away.  Not to mention the usage of a separate physics engine, "Havok."
The story is phenomenal, very dystopian, borrowing from idealologies presented in works like
and
If you really are interested in the driving forces behind the plot elements and the stylistic and metaphorical themes I suggest you check out the Story and Theme Development section of the Wikipedia article on the game.  The characters and story really follow suit here.
The gameplay itself, while not the smoothest in the world, is good.  The gun works pretty good, with good variation.  The enemies are well done in difficulty and AI.  The controls can seem a bit clunky at times, but overall, pretty good.
The score is phenomenal and the sound effects are great.
Overall, this game does something that many struggle to do:  It makes you feel.  It makes you think.  It makes you question things outside of the game world.  The story is elaborate and well thought out, and the gameplay is pretty smooth.  The score is great.  There really isn't much I can realistically hate on this game about, it's very solid.
One of the biggest recommendations I can give as a gamer.  If you haven't played BioShock, at the very least, get it on sale and
it.

Forward to the Sky is a cute little puzzle platformer. It follows the story of a Princess who explores the Sky Tower to learn what happened to it and reclaim the crystals. It's a nice, relaxing game with good music and pleasant, vibrant visuals. The game is 6 levels long, and will keep you occupied for about two and a half hours. The combat is very basic with a strong attack, light attack and a dodge, but that's really everything you need. The jumping is good overall but changing direction in mid-air moves Princess a bit further than you'd like to, making precision jumping difficult at times. But the game is forgiving enough that it never really becomes an issue.
The meat of the game is in the puzzle platforming, and it's pretty good at that. Every level introduces new mechanics and presents you with interesting puzzles. None of them are especially taxing though, so don't expect taking hours on finding the solution to a puzzle. The only disappointment was that the game never really put all the different mechanics together to make a truly diabolical puzzle, preferably for the final level.
Overall though, I really enjoyed this game. It's a good, relaxing game with a cute story and mechanics that don't overstay their welcome. People looking for a long or difficult game might want to look elsewhere, but those who want a fun disctraction for a few hours should definitely take a look at this game.

A unique little game, you carefully manage a team of ghosts to haunt the everloving crap out of houses.
Functionally it's a perfectly servicable small scale strategy game. You assign your pre-selected haunters to different locations and objects based on what anchors them to the real world: Poltergeists can anchor to kids and electronics, creepy-crawlies hide in specific rooms, elemental spirits have their element, etc. You set how much they can use their powers and you let them do their work. The real appeal is that the missions give you a variety of tasks so it's rarely as simple as "attach a to b, scare everyone stiff". These objective are neatly wrapped up in your favourite horror movie cliches as well: Get the campers to investigate the basement of the abandoned cabin, help the tenants discover the body of the ariel repair man in order to recruit his ghost, etc.
Since it's on sale every halloween odds are that you're only going to end up paying 39p for it and I cannot adequately express how good a deal that is. Really. There may only be a dozen missions and no modding support but the base missions are well worth the full price tag, let alone the sale one.

I've been a huge fan of this game since I first picked it up from our company store while I was working at Sierra Online.  I wasn't sure what I was getting into with it and the style of game was never my thing, but I was completely hooked after completing the first level.  It was simple to learn from that first tutorial-like level that gave you enough room to play around with things on your own, as well as including other ghosts to unlock.
I loved being able to play the game however I wanted to for the most part, although there are times when you are better off using specific ghosts and / or buying specific skills for them.  You're never really penalized for doing that, though, since you can pretty much complete all of the levels with the ghosts' base-level powers, even if you don't unlock any newer ghosts on your own.
Most of the fun was later going back and replaying the levels to earn the max scare score, unlock ghosts you missed, or try out a different mix of ghosts for practice.
This version of the game also includes the special post-ending levels that were hinted at in the original release's ending video (which is why I bought it on Steam when I still own the CDROM release).  It's too bad they never did an actual sequel.  I dust this game off of my digital shelf on Steam about once every couple of years to have a few days of fun -- and it still runs well on Win7 and Win10 machines!

Post-early access addition:
The game has come a long way from my initial review, and I am overjoyed that the game maintained the spirit of a true survival game throughout its development. The game has become rather balanced and a surprising number of options have been mad available in order to survive in the full release of the game. There is something quite satisfying about throwing rocks at rabbits and eating it raw in a last ditch effort to survive.
The introduction of the story mode brings a new element to the game, which is true purpose for your actions. The game moves beyond simply existing for as long as you can, into to truly feeling the necessity to survive through to the next day. The quests are rather simple, mostly gathering quests, but when placed in such a harsh enviornment, a gathering quests is the decision between your character starving or moving on to the next portion of the story. It becomes tempting to try and cheat the system, being lazy and avoding your needs to complete the quests as quickly as possible. This does show itself to be fruitless, however, as survival and the enviornment keep the spotlight.
The actual voice acting was decent and the story itself a bit hammy for my taste. I also was a bit jarred by the cut scenes, as they seemed to be unpolished and a bit below the level quality you can feel everywhere else in the game. The conversation system also leaves a bit to be desired, cutting between fully voiced cut scenes and static text conversations with no voice over and little animation. I got over this pretty quick, but I think for people who are on the fence with the story and the game itself, these small cut corners could be the difference between enjoying the game and deciding its not their cup of tea.
Overall, I highly recommend The Long Dark. Its peaceful, difficult, and does an amazing job of taking you out of your home and placing you in the wilderness. There is no other survival game quite like it, and I've played a lot of them!
(Furthermore, no zombies, mutants, or other supernatural beasties is a plus for me. Its all you V mother nature!)
Early access review:
------
Honestly, the best survival game overall. No other survival game brings such a depth of game play while mantaining a viseral experience. The game world feels alive and your survival feels like it depends on your wit and choices rather than purely invetory managment.
The game does have an interesting difficulty curve, in that instead of getting easier over time, it goes from difficult easy to difficult to easy to difficult until you die. The game feels pretty well balanced, you rarely will find ever survial need fulfilled at once, meaning that despite having lots of food you may be freezing slowly. Maybe you set up camp in a nice home, plenty of water and warmth, but that wolf bite from earlier the in the game has forced you to need medicine.
Something always forces you to leave you're shelter and face the cold, making you once again vunerable to elements and keeping the fear of freezing always in the forfront of the game play.
Cons: The game may feel like you've seen all there is to see after a relatively short time for a survival game. It really depends on how much you enjoy exploring. But if you are someone who enjoys the actual "game mechanics", you'll master these relatively quickly. You may want to wait until story mode is added before jumping in.
On the other hand, if you want a game where you can simply exist and survive, this is one of the best experiences available.

almost passed under my radar.  It's quirky name and decidedly tongue-in-cheek "maximum Britishness" approach made me think it was going to be too much gimmick and not enough game.  I am happy to say that was not the case.
(what an acronym) is a solid game that perfectly captures the appeal of the stealth FPS genre, but with its own unique ambiance and the added boon of high replayability thanks to random map generation.
To be more specific about the gameplay,
seems to combine a lot of elements from other stealth (or stealth-optional) shooters into one attractive result.  Combat plays out a bit like
, of all things: crouching is the key to being unobserved, enemies won't detect you if you're not in line of sight, and sometimes the best choice in combat is to simply leg it.  Inventory management is also a bit like
, certainly with the grid-based "you have X slots" system, but the use and variety of items is more reminescent of
, especially with the game's focus on looting and storage.
also comes to mind with the game's health and vitality (read: food) system, along with the possibility of bleeding from injuries and the necessity to stop said bleeding with bandages.
As for the ambiance, it's very tongue-in-cheek humorous while also retaining that real sense of danger and, dare I say it, horror at times.  Some enemies can and do strike fear into your heart if you see them under the wrong circumstances, which in this game is more often than not.  Above all though this game is very, very British.  The robots look British, say British things, and act British.  I once caught a hunting party stopping mid-field to have tea before continuing on.  It's the little touches that make this game charming, some of which I'm sure I'm missing because I'm not British myself.
Difficulty wise, I've found this game pretty decent.  Early on the game is easy for anyone experienced with stealth combat, particularly for
players.  The basic robot variant is fairly easy to take on in combat if you're sneaky, and will even reliably miss you at close range so long as you're circle-strafing.  Once more variants start showing up though, or even simply start appearing in more numbers, things definitely get more challenging.  Certain combinations and/or numbers of enemies are definite "run away only" situations no matter how much firepower you've managed to scavenge, and just sprinting across the landscape in the hopes that you won't get shot too much simply won't work anymore.  You have to think, observe, and plan in order to make it to the end of the game, picking your battles where you can.  It's a reasonable difficulty ramp, and one you can tackle more or less at your own pace, since it seems to be tied to how much of the game's central fetch quest you've completed.
Overall,
is an enjoyable game that manages to amuse in one second and induce very real tension and even a touch of fear in the next.  Anyone who likes the sort of stealthy resource-reliant looting-with-optional-combat type gameplay seen in
,
, and countless other titles will find that same part of their game brain satified by this, and the randomized and adjustable nature of the game makes it highly replayable.  If that sounds like your kind of game, then it's well worth the modest asking price.

The hype surrounding this game was/is nuts. Between the fans debating on the lore, the dozens of fan-made clones, and the disturbing fan art this game has clearly had an impact on the gaming community.
It uses simplistic controls consisting of 5 buttons (2 light, 2 door and one map) and they're very easy to learn but, like chess, the game is difficult to master.
The whole idea is stress management: keep one eye on the left side for animatronics while keeping the other eye on the right side all with a limited power supply and increasingly more aggressive AI.
If you're the kind of person who wants to finish the game 100% you're going to need both luck and insane amount of patience as the AI has a nasty habit of sporadically changing between in-your-face horror and timid-as-a-mouse shyness without any rhyme or reason.
If you have the spare money, get this game. It's no more overhyped than Call of Duty or League of Legends and there's a certain charm to the bare bones game design that makes it both frustrating to lose at but so satisfying to finish.
Get those 3 stars...if you can survive...

I also feel like they should tweak the AI of the monsters so that it doesn't just gank the medic into a corner as soon as the hunters and monsters meet. Doesn't really give the player a chance to upgrade much and improve in the class if they're immediately just rushed and downed. (Also, sometimes the monsters would still hone in on me, despite being cloaked? I wanna know how THAT one works, devs)
Next, in Evacuation mode, I feel like the "Auto Balance" function is merely a placebo. Even with Auto Balance favoring me by a lot, the game didn't feel any easier for me. Hence, I feel like this is a functionality that should be taken out. Instead, perhaps they can randomize the map effects and use that to balance the game in favor of the hunters or monster.
Finally, the one everyone and their mother has been talking about: the DLC format. Now overall, I don't hate the existence/concept of DLC for games. But I feel like this game is not even trying to be subtle about ripping you off. They don't seem to know what the term "Season Pass" means, since it doesn't include the DLC due to come out in the following months after release. I feel like for the $80 price tag on the game plus season pass, that should cover it. Charging the $100 for MORE DLC that isn't included with this other DLC is a bit extreme.
In conclusion: If you don't mind the steep pricing of some of this content and are willing to lose games a LOT, then I recommend this game. If you're on the fence, I'm gonna go ahead and say don't bother. This game took some great ideas and falled utterly short of delivering fully on them. Honestly, I wish I'd done more research and NOT spent $80 on this game.
EDIT: They did make some balance changes, and getting the opportunity to play a lot more has helped. Seems this game had a steeper learning curve than I even anticipated. Dare I say, I am actually having fun in this game now. I find myself regretting taking such a huge dump on the gameplay, so I would like to take this opportunity to rescind those comments. (still ♥♥♥♥in hate their mindset on the DLC pricing, but what can ya do) I would also like to change my recommendation to "yes i do recommend this game, if you want something with a steep learning curve. something that really will challenge you and test your patience."

First, take a second to appreciate that the developer has included a free demo for this game. It's on the store page; no review (not even my stellar, first-rate, excellent, incomparably fantastic review) can match what you'll get from the demo, so if you're on the fence go download it and try it out.
My opinion is that this is a very charming, simple game. I enjoyed the game thoroughly (with a few slight misgivings), and I hope to see more from the developer.
I'll cut right to the chase and tell you that this game is EXTREMELY short. My gameplay stats list it at an hour, but I did play the first few levels without running Steam so it's actually about twice that at 2 hours (I did go back and replay the first 3 levels in Steam to get the achievements, but at that point I remembered the layout and basically just speedran them). There are 6 levels (5 levels, really; the 6th is just a boss fight), so that puts it at right about 20 minutes per level on average. I bought it on sale so I wasn't put off by the lack of playtime, but it is something you should consider.
This game is mostly platforming, with two or three combat setpieces per level between platforming sections. I have absolutely no problem with the platforming beyond the fact that every level introduces a new gimmick, and none of these gimmicks are ever repeated, meaning that the skills you get in one stage never carry on to the next. As an example, the third level introduces wind gust tunnels that you have to navigate to get to different sections of the level, but no other stage has these tunnels. Every stage is mechanically completely different from the next. However, that's really just kind of a nitpick. If the game ever gets a sequel, I'd love to see stages that incorporate the gimmicks from previous stages. Level design does incorporate the gimmicks well, though, and overall each level is pretty fun. Thankfully, the camera is completely controllable and the princess controls great, so there's really no major gripes from me about this portion of the game.
Combat, though, is a little boring and really just amounts to a button masher. You have left-click attacks and right-click attacks, but the difference is minute enough that you can go in swinging either way and it doesn't have an impact on combat. There is also a backflip button, which acts as a dodge, and that's fairly useful late in the game against the mage enemies, but they only appear in the last two platforming stages. Earlier stages can be beaten by literally just tanking every hit and whaling away on the mouse. However, the stages are mostly focused on platforming and like I said there are at max about 3 major "battles" per level, so it's not unbearable.
During each stage you have to pick up the various crystals you find. Small enemies drop one when defeated, big enemies drop three, and statues you break apart are each worth 25 crystals for a total of 100 in each stage. Typically, the split is 25 crystals from enemies and 3 statues. For every 33 crystals you pick up, you unlock one section of that stage's story; if you only collect 33 crystals, for instance, you'll only get 1/3 of that stage's exposition. Honestly, it's kind of a non-issue. If you have absolutely ANY sense of exploration you'll easily find all of the statues (some later stages have statues hidden behind puzzles, but all of them are rather simple, and the statues have a very noticeable glow that is visible even through solid objects) and enemies are NEVER off of the beaten path so it's very rare you'll ever finish a stage without getting all 100 crystals. I don't know what happens if you don't get all crystals from each stage; there might be two different endings depending on whether you get all of them or not, but like I said, it's simple enough to get all of them.
I did have a slight problem with the voice acting. None of it is awful, but none of it is good, either. I would describe it as "endearingly mediocre." The princess and the witch, the two main voices you'll be hearing throughout the game, are both fine, but I really didn't like the third voice actress.
The story is just a setpiece, really. It's there to justify the fact that you're a cute girl jumping around in a tower in the sky. There's nothing wrong with that; the story fills its purpose, and even though it's about the simplest and most cliched story you can think of, it's amusing enough that it doesn't get on your nerves. Though I enjoyed the game and wish it had been longer, I think that if I had had to listen to either the voice acting or the story for much longer it might have started to drag the experience down. As it stands, though, the game is short enough that neither are too grating.
The characters are rendered in a cel-shaded chibi style, which fits the tone and is pretty cute. The early levels are rather plain and bland, but later on there are glowing crystals and colored fogs and other visuals to help keep things interesting. The music is enjoyable and, again, mostly fits the tone of the game.
One thing I WOULD like to complain about is the presentation of the menus. There's no text; everything is done via pictures. This isn't a terrible thing, but I did twice accidentally end the game because I couldn't tell which button was supposed to take me back into the game. I will chalk that up 90% to personal idiocy (just hit the Esc/start button again to get out of the menu, idiot), but even just a single word "Resume" or "Close" would have been helpful. The buttons for camera inversion are also a little awkward. However, this is another tiny nitpick and the game itself is not in any way negatively impacted by this.
Overall, I think this is a thoroughly enjoyable game. Bear in mind the cost when deciding if you want to buy it now or wait for a sale, and above all, since the developer was nice enough to include a demo, play that to see if you want the full product. My guess is that you'll enjoy it.

Sometimes your diet consists of wet dog food and mouldy crackers. Sometimes you'll be lording it up on venison and fine fizzy drinks. Either way, you find ways to survive.
The sound design is top-notch too; it really hammers home the feeling of exposure.
At the moment in sandbox mode there's several different "regions" to explore, each a tangent of Northern Canadian life. Some of which used to be small transition zones between regions but are now so huge they are pretty much regions themselves!

The currently in-development Story mode will be a nice cherry to finish off this snow cake!

Overall I really like the game. I bought it two years ago and it has taken so many significant steps from back then that it makes me very impressed about the whole package. I amreally looking forward to the story mode and I hope it gets out as soon as possible.

LYNE is a pure game of combinatorics, one could also place it somewhere into knot and graph theory. Up to a certain extend, it is locally decidable. Strictly speaking, the player has to pass knots with lines of different colors (up to 3 different colors appaer in one level) for a determined number of times to connect two loose ends (knots) of the same color, i.e. the player is choosing the edges (color & direction in terms of horizontal, vertical, diagonal) to complete a graph. Thereby, he may not miss out to visit a knot of a certain color with an edge of the same color and he may not undermine the number of passes of a colorless knot (Euler path variation). Up to 60 vertices occur in one level and although it is basically trial and error to arrange one line in correspondence to another one, it takes some of the players attention and asks for a certain amount of concentration.
As one can easily guess from the amount of money being spent to develop this game, the complexity is not too high. For example, the daily level challenges are merely a randomized composure of the in-game levels.
But in spite of this circumstance, the game is like a compactified idea and one could call it an inspiration.

Sluggish controls, tactical map unit caps, and a real time macrostrategic map of the galaxy make this a pain. Yes, there's a pause button on the galactic map, but you can't do anything while paused like move fleets or build units. It only works on the tactical map. Also, some of the scenario maps seem glitched on tech levels. If you go to advanced settings and reduce the starting tech level while playing on hard, then you start with reduced technology but the computer starts with regular technology. Having X Wings, Y Wings, and basic frigates doesn't really match top of the line Imperial Star Destroyers.
There's also no hold position command. You can tell units to stop, but it's very easy to lure or get lured, especially when units won't respond instantly after being lured. This creates a very annoying situation where rocket infantry wreck light tanks, anti-infantry vehicles wreck light infantry, and aircraft become pointless (although aircraft dominate easily until AA weapons are around). In space, it means fighters and bombers won't withdraw from cruisers, and larger ships that are slightly misoriented beacuse they advanced two inches too far take forever to turn around.
The game really isn't that bad, but it's like they choked it for no good reason and ruined the experience. If the units were responsive, tactical map unit caps didn't exist, the galactic map was turn based instead of real time, and the pause button let you issue orders while paused, then this would be an easy thumbs up. I have no idea why they ruined their own game with arbitrary restrictions.

I have stalked convoys for days on end, slowly whittling down their numbers. I have used daring tactics to great success, narrowly avoiding the avalanche of depth charges from the surface. A game that, mockingly but unironically, claims to be “The most innovative shooter [you’ve] played in years”.
A game where time moves only when you move.
A game that’s not an experience, nor a work of art. Just a game, in its purest form. Where you play, and you have fun, no holds barred.
SUPERHOT is honestly just a really, really fun game. Why so? Well, fundamentally it’s because it
cool,
cool, and
cool. Picture this (Which you can from the Trailer Videos and Screenshots) – A lone, stoic black crystalline figure, walking through time laid against a monochromatic background, shattering hostile Red “Dudes” in style. All while a clock slowly ticks down at the back of his mind, and sound warps around him coupled with glaring text.
In a game where time only moves when you move,
in control. Those bullet weaves you’ve always wanted to try, all that fancy swordplay, even slicing a bullet in two – All achieved with little to no practice required. This game makes you feel like a total badass while simultaneously not being a walk in the park.
There are no difficulty settings. A single bullet will kill you if it makes contact with your fragile figure, as it will to the many, many unfortunate Red Dudes that will lay in your wake. Weapons have limited ammunition in them, at least after they’re in your possession. Chambers will click empty, baseball bats will shatter and crowbars will turn obsolete. After you’ve used them to their fullest, you have no choice but to toss their empty husks away and pick up something else. If there’s nothing else around, you’ll have to rely on either jumping onto your enemies’ collarbones or punching them to death.
Hitboxes are polished to perfection. You can weave shots through any holes you spot, you can shatter blades while they’re in the hands of an enemy, you can destroy a bullet with your own, you can catch weapons in mid-air and most importantly you can dodge bullets heading towards your body by simply looking to the side. SUPERHOT is a game that knows its potential for frustration, with everything being killed in one shot and whatnot, and so it addresses it by making sure that when you die, you won’t be blaming anything apart from the decision you made in that precise moment.
About decisions. The game is about decisions. With its time mechanic, the game is less of a First-Person Shooter and more of a Turn-Based Strategy game. You’ve only got those select few options to take while time is slowed down to a crawl, and every moment and action is precious. Even looking around makes time go a little faster. It all boils down to the courses of action you take, but unlike a Turn-Based Strategy game those actions are executed not by luck, not by numbers, not purely by animations or scripted events. They’re executed by skill; The same skill that you acquire playing a First-Person Shooter.
Now, onto the content offered, which is the main gripe many have with the game.
First off, I’d just like to say that yes,
. The main campaign, consisting of 25 levels, is beaten in about
.
.
Secondly, the storyline, if you’d call it that, is extremely weak. It’s very linear and predictable. But like I said at the beginning of this review, it’s not an experience, it’s not a story, and it doesn’t try to be any of those. It knows its place, and it knows it well. It’s a game.
But that doesn’t mean that it’s a bad game. No, it’s far away from one. It’s a wonderful game, with
. I’ve spent over 100 hours on this game already, because for me it never gets old. Every time I jump in and play a level, I feel that same sense of style and polish that I did the first time I booted it up.
A good 98% of my total playtime has been spent on the real content in SUPERHOT – The Endless Mode, Challenge Mode and Secrets.
The Endless Mode is my absolute favourite part of the game. It’s a place where you can let yourself loose and go on a total rampage of Red Dudes, in style of course. What the Campaign limits with spawn times, locations and weapons, Endless Mode gives in abundance. You’ve got a plethora of arenas and timed modes to choose from, and I can assure you that they’ll last you a while if you so choose to invest yourself in them.
Challenge Mode pits you through the same 25 Levels as the Campaign does, albeit with a different 25th level and some of the “cutscenes” removed. Each Challenge has a different requirement, largely varying in difficulty. You’ll find it a fresh way to relive the thrill of the Campaign due to the consequences and layout of each level, while being presented with a real challenge that scales well after you’ve finished the Campaign.
Secrets are… To be honest, a pain. I looked for all of them without any guides and it took me forever. Do use a guide, I’d recommend it.
All in all, SUPERHOT is a beautiful game, be it on sale or not (OK fine, it’s much more attractive on sale). I’d heavily recommend you buy it and try it out, as it’s a ton of fanciful fun!

Metin 2 is lacking in any kind of enjoyable content to be considered a good game. The game mechanics are sufficient and the game generally functions how it should. The largest flaw the game has is a complete lack of any direction or story.
The menu systems are functional if not confusing at times. The ability to rearrange menu windows around the screen was nice, but certain menus didn’t work well. The large world map was too small and missing all the standard game map functions to be considered useful. The Friends menu was completely useless. Adding friends only worked a percentage of the time, saying that a user was offline even when they weren’t. Even if you were lucky enough to be able to add someone as a friend, it served no purpose, as the messaging system was broken. All received messages are blank. During the several hours I played the game, it also seemed that there was no way to join friends to complete quests together.
Any interesting story and game content the game may have seems to be hidden by high level requirements. At the outset of the game, there is no story, little direction, no real objective, and no fun game mechanics. Speaking to characters in the town shows lots of equipment and abilities that appear to add interesting mechanics to the game, but high level requirements means you have to grind through a slow and boring campaign for hours before reaching any content that is enjoyable in the slightest. It seems like a rather poor design decision to postpone any amount of the game’s interesting content to the end.
The game looks visually boring. The world itself felt empty and missing any variety in landscape and architecture to enjoy. Nothing stood out from the rest of the world. Character customization is limited, and, once again, you don’t get any kind of gear that changes your character until you pass the high level barrier. Enemies all look the same, and there is very little variety in the actual types of enemies. Enemies are also just thrown into empty areas at random to make the areas seem less empty. Enemies respawn rather quickly, meaning you can’t clear an area. By the time you kill an enemy, the last ones you killed will soon respawn. The result is an endless swarm of enemies that you can’t ever clear. It’s unsatisfying to try fighting an endless swarm like this.
The game audio falls short in the same ways the rest of the game does. It is boring and offers little variety. The sounds and music are so dull and repetitive they would easily get drowned by any normal game, however, the boring nature of the game isn’t able to drown out the sound. Instead I found that, at times, the game audio, as boring as it is, was more interesting than what was happening on screen.
The controls may be the one true redeeming quality of the game. Generally, the game controlled well, and the camera was surprisingly smooth. Movement was a little slow however, and the player often collided with objects even from a generous distance. This made navigating the towns especially difficult. Combat controls could use a little work. The player wouldn’t turn if you were continuously attacking, and required a brief pause in attacking to turn. This results in situations where you would be attacking while facing away from an enemy and doing no damage if you weren’t carful. Picking up coins requires clicking, and while not technically bad, it was tedious to pick up coins after every combat encounter. It would work a lot better if characters picked up coins when walking over them.
Considering all the mechanics and systems in place, the game could be a decently fun game if the developers put a little more effort in developing content for the game. The game runs well from a technical standpoint, sans a few minor bugs and annoyances here and there. As the game currently stands, however, I would not recommend spending your time with it.

The game requires you to find different magical stones for The Device, which I assume takes you away from this godforsaken place. Or it explodes and alerts every robot on the island to turn you into swiss cheese. EIther way, I haven't found out yet.

Robots can spot you from just looking at you so it's best to crouch when they're near and to get a rock or some other cover between you and your hunters.
Overall, this game is great and has a lot of replayabilty considering you can tweak the world generation and the amount of robots. I also think this game would be great if they had more survival features and it was a challenge to survive without the robots.

´Forward to the Sky` tells the story of a princess that, with the help of her trusty hot air balloon, seeks out to climb an enormous tower high up in the sky, in order to hunt down a witch. On her way, she has to fight her way past  enemies and solve puzzles in order to unlock the passage to the next floor of the tower as well as the "full story", with more lines getting added the more crystals you collect in every stage.
The game is quite charming both in terms of visuals and sound; both add quite a lot to the feeling of being high up an uncountable amount of feets up in the air. However, this doesn´t mean that it´s impressive from a technical point-of-view: It looks very low-res and without much detail, and the only thing that stands out a bit (outside of its style) is the destructibility of the terrain: Most pillars, bricks, stone piles and even some walls can be destroyed with your sword, even possibly hurting you in the process if you aren´t careful. Soundwise, it needs to be said that the voice acting, while not exactly terrible, feels very amateurish as well: While I personally had no problem with it, this may be a downer for others. Controls for the most part are fine, though a bit too floaty and not always as precise as they should be. Combat controls are very simplistic, with two kinds of attack and a parry move; the latter one being kind of useless though (you´re better of just jumping out of the way).
Gameplay-wise, each stage consists of platforming, hitting switches, finding specific statues and defeating enemies, neither of which is particularly difficult even if you aren´t used to platformers in general. Each stage also has one or two unique gimmicks (like boulders that you need to roll on, or lasers that you need to dodge with the right timing) that aren´t reused in other stages, as well as one or two new enemy types. You can´t fall to your death (your trusty hot air balloon will always catch you), but you can die in battle or by getting hit from obstacles; if that happens, you have to restart the stage from scratch, so keep that in mind. Even then though, you will rarely get stuck, and no stage should take you longer than 15 to 20 minutes to complete.
Concerning the length: It´s a very short game and should not take more than two hours to complete. The only kind of collectible are crystals that you need to collect in order to unlock new story passages, and they can only be found by killing enemies and destroying hidden statues. Some of those statues are fairly well hidden, but nothing you can´t find on your first try. Otherwise, there is no replay value, no hidden bonus stuff or unlockables. Having said that, I found those two hours to be quite enjoyable and entertaining. Still, its price point (8 $) may be a bit steep for it´s overall content.
Overall, I would I recommend the game. If you feel that its price is too steep, wait until a sale occurs: At a lower price, I wholeheartily recomment it.

I fully endorse this game. However, I simply must state the caveats contained therein.
-	I originally thought this was going to be a “based on reality” type of survival game. The inferences the game gives are obvious by the items one need acquire to survive. i.e. Rosehips (Are in fact 50 times higher in Vitamin C than citrus fruits) and Red Reishi mushrooms are in fact Medicinal. As stated by the developers however, this isn’t the case at all, which leaves me perplexed as to what the game actually IS about. This seems more of an excuse for scale, or laziness, most likely the latter, as they wouldn’t wish to research many plants, and alike.
-	While I’m not from the far north, (beyond the wall  ) I am from Ohio, where we have many of the same exact edible, medicinal and fibrous wilds. So my question is, what is with only guts being used as cordage? Are there no Nettles or sapling inner barks to craft cordage? Are there no wild grape vines to extract fresh water? No Pine bark to make bowls, quivers, or wood pouches?
-	Things I feel are absurd;
The wear times of the materials you do acquire are redonkulous. This includes cured skins you have left laying…they wear down…for some silly reason.
The wear times in general are way too short which includes food, bullets, arrows (I accept the food times as balance explanation, but not some of the others.)
-	Which brings me to Arrows…WTF is with you having to forge scrap metal into arrows on only one map? Are you the dumb? Did you not know you can just use a sharpened shaft? Or a stone?
It’s not as if the bow is even useful at all.
-	Bow usage is null in this game. Using a real bow is much more accurate and easily used. Survival in this game simply comes down to how many bullets you have. Period. If you are out, you can’t hunt. Processed food all gone? You’re dead.
-	Actual range for bullets are limited. It would seem to be about 50 yards or so. Beyond that, the bullet does the magic disappearing act that is oh, so common in games. It wouldn’t be a big deal except the critical role, and limited supply of bullets themselves. It is guaranteed to anger the player at more than one point.
-	That said, the game does have enough to keep you playing, and enjoying it, even with the issues that will slow boil in the back of your mind.
All said and done, it IS worth a buy, hopefully at a discount, not because it isn’t necessarily worth twenty dollars, but sort of to teach them a lesson on laziness. By far the most realistic fps, and maybe even the most realistic game, I've ever played. Unlike COD or Battlefield you feel constantly under threat, knowing that at any moment a stray bullet or hidden marksman could kill you instantly before you even realise what happened. There are next to no indications of who is friend or foe apart from the clothes you wear and what side of the battlefield you are on, with occasional hints at enemy postion on the map when recon is available. Alpha Review- I am impressed!  For me, this is definitely activating that "just one more attempt" impulse that the best of roguelike games induce.  The rpg, roguelike, resource management and defense building elements are blended together so well that they create a simple to understand but totally unforgiving game that feels totally new.
Is it a roguelike? - Well, you will die.  A lot.  The game also hinges on exploring a dungeon, collecting loot, and fighting the creatures inside.  However, it's not a traditional Roguelike, since you only control which room your characters are in the dungeon, but they automatically attack enemies in that room themselves.
It is an RPG? - A light one. Your characters each have unique stats, can level up, and carry an inventory of weapons, armor, and equipment.  There is loot to collect, and merchants to buy/sell with.  At this stage, no dialogs, quests, or set storyline.  Much more a dungeon crawler.
Tower Defense? - I'm not usually much of a tower defense player, but it seems this game gives players a little more control over the whole concept.  You can create modules to collect resources, and the spend those resources to build weapon modules, healing stations for your characters, and other static devices in explored rooms.  Each time you open a door in the dungeon, you run the risk of letting a group of creatures flood into the explored area, and strategic building of modules will allow your characters to defend against otherwise grim odds.
The art and sound are both beautiful and really produce a unique atmosphere.
In alpha state, I haven't hit any bugs yet, and the basics I described are all there.  It is the skeleton of the game, but it's a really solid framework for what I suspect will turn out to be a stellar game.  That said, It definitely is still under development and I'm looking forward to a number of features the devs have described as in progress.

Like RTS? Like Star Wars? Just like crushing your enemies with giant war machines in both space and planetary battles? If you like any combination of these then you will most likely like this game. You get to control the Rebel Alliance, Galactic Empire, and, if you have the FoC expansion, the Zann Consortium (basically underworld units). Each of these factions plays differently with the Rebels focusing on stronger armies, hit and run attacks, infantry focused armies, and guerrilla style warfare. The Empire uses numbers and brute force (Hint: check what happens when rebel infantry play chicken with your vehicles ) Finally the Zann forces use a mix of subtle corruption type debuffs and overpowered units. There are two main ways to play, skirmish and campaign. The skirmish allows you to do one off battles that are slightly different from the usual ones with resource capturing, and building up your tech in-game. The campaign allows you to play your own war between all of the factions. You manage your troop movements, production, and strategy. There are multiple set ups for how to start, each with a different number and distribution of planets. I prefer the  campaign, but sometimes its fun to just play one battle.
I highly recommend the FoC pack as it adds a new faction, new planets, and new units for everyone. Both of the game types (space and ground) are fun, with the space being my favorite. Little tip, some heroes (like Han and Boba Fett) don't just hangout on a transport if you get into a space battle with them, but take part in their own ships as well as on foot in ground fights. Also as your tech level gets higher, make sure you own at least one of the "shipyard" planets so you can build your ultimate capital ships ASAP.

Super-hot sort of feels like one huge practical joke.
I bought the game to shoot a bunch of red dudes without a care for the plot.
And that’s not what I got at all.
For starters the first thing I wanted to do was just play the endless modes. And you can’t do that unless you finish the main story.
I don’t care about the story. I wanted to just play the endless mode from the start. you know  like every other multiplayer game like call of duty lets you do.
The next problem I can across was the sounds of the game. One of the sounds it uses it make you feel more immersed is an old fax machine screech that plays for a few seconds.
I would rather It didn’t play at all but I supposed a few seconds was fine. Except I found out it plays a lot longer if quit the game at a certain point. it plays in the levels intro screen, and it feels like it drags on forever screeching at you all the while.
so while your mashing your keyboard to skip the into screen for that level the game is blasting you with fax machine noises.
You can turn them off but its through the sfx slider. That means all the in game gunshots will be silent.
oh yeah turning the Sfx slider all the way down also mutes the dude saying “Super hot!” over and over. Honestly I got so sick of him saying that, that having him muted was a bonus for me.
Then there is the story. it feels like a bad rip off for the matrix.
Without spoiling anything some dudes at first try and scare you way from what they are doing and then they do want your help.
I don’t get their logic at all.
And the music option in the sound? There is no music.  Just vague wind noises and computer beeping noises later on. In fact now that I think about it you might as well mute the entire thing and just play it silent.
As the only other thing you will be hearing is “SUPER-HOT! SUPER-HOT! SUPER-HOT!”ect over and over gain in some parts.
And then there was thing that made me rage quit the game.
Granted I came back later and finished the game but that was MONTHS later. That’s how much this game wanted to make me rip my hair out here. I’m not exaggerating here either. I really did want to rip my hair out at times.
So in the last level of the game the controller starts vibrating if you’re using one. Again to make you feel more immersed.
This is fine for some people but im someone who hates vibration and will turn it off in every game a play.
Only in super-hot I can’t turn it off. For some brain-dead  reason the devs decided that it would be a good idea to include no vibration option and make the controller vibrate full blast throughout an entire level.
this makes you want to use the mouse and keyboard more and in a game were slow precise movements are better, this is is a terrible idea.
I ended up watching a bunch of youtubers play super-hot and though “why are they always moving in and rushing so much?”
Now I know. Because keyboard keys don’t have different degree’s of pressure it’s either pressed or not pressed.
In other words Super-Hot is one of the few games were using a controller will actually make you more precise. well for moving anyway.
No matter what you are using though, if you slip up just once your back to the start and have to do the whole thing again.
And if you rush the level to stop the constant vibration you will most likely mess up a bunch making it still take about as long.
Also the way the last level was made “hard” is terrible game design. Throwing tones of enemies at you and spamming shotgun wielding enemies is not a recipe for skill. it’s a recipe for trial and error.
Because while you are killing dude A and aiming at dude B, dude C has already shot you in the back with his shotgun.  This forces you to learn the patterns of were enemies spawn so you can wait for them instead of constantly being on the move and thinking of how to counter them on the fly.
Did I mention that shotguns basically negate dogging at those ranges? And you can’t chop or punch the bullets mid-air like you can with pistols either.
Because while you are punching bullet #1 out of the air all of the other 5 or so bullets have already slammed into you and you are now dead.
this causes you to cower in a corner while you wait for enemies to funnel towards you…  IN A GAME WERE YOU ARE MEANT TO BE A BAD#SS!
The lack of a crouch feature really shows in this level as well. I get that the developers might have wanted you to feel more like a fearless assassin but that feeling is already ruined by the fact that you have to hide in a corner like I stated above.
Instead your character will stand there going “DU-DOY! I GET SHOT!!” while you stand behind a chest high wall holding control. or whatever the default crouch key is these days.

Then at the very end of the game they make it like your part of some hocus pocus matrix like system and tell you it’s your duty to spread the game to other players for story reasons.
My duty?? What duty? I bought this game to play it and that’s it. I have no duty to do anything. I get that it’s either supposed to be witty or a joke.
But it’s a bad joke and not witty at all.
that’s why im giving super-hot a thumbs down.
Sure I have unlocked the endless mode and challenge modes now, but the journey  get there devolved from 5% frustration and 95% fun  to 95% frustration and 5% fun in the end.    Not worth it.

First time writing a review here, mainly because I am a bit annoyed at all the whining and misinformation going on here. If you honestly did not like the game, whether because of some of the bugs or because you did not have friends to play with, fine. But all of the people who only played alpha (evidenced by the "early-access" tag) who come on to complain about "day-one dlc" (which is only cosmetic) are skewing the actual customer feedback on this game.
Evolve is a lot of fun, perhaps the most fun I have had in an FPS. It might be because I consistently have friends or siblings to play with, but I haven't lost interest in it yet, after almost two days of playtime, which is more than can be said for a good number of games with a $60.00 price tag. Just yesterday, me and my friends had a fun time for a few hours drinking and playing king of the hill with the monster in a 5-person custom game. There is a good variety among maps and game modes, all the monsters play differently, and same with the different characters in the classes, to a certain extent. There is a good amount of balance, with monsters and hunters winning almost completely even at around 51 and 49 percent respectively. Wraith is a bit unbalanced as of now, but I am sure that will be tweaked. They are even going to be releasing free game modes and maps in the future, which is more than can be said of most modern FPS's.
There are going to be DLC characters in the future, but I think they will probably be worth it to add diverse play-styles and hours of fun. If you don't want to buy these future dlc's that is fine, no on is forcing you. I will probably cherry-pick the ones that interest me. Complaining about dlc's on this game is ridiculous, especially since the only dlc available now adds absolutely nothing in terms of gameplay, and is simply a way for the developers to continue to support the game with future maps and game modes.
If you are on the fence about this game I will tell you, its probably not for everyone. If you have some friends to play with, or enjoy coordinating with strangers in games like L4D then you will probably like this game. If you like the idea of asymmetric multiplayer, and an intense, often heartpounding game of cat and mouse, you will probably like this game. Don't let the reviews with the "early-access" tag throw you off. They obviously only played during testing, and are, for some reason, using their time to review a game that they did not even buy, perhaps out of some "anti-dlc" vendetta.

Metin 2 seems to be either incredibly unfinished and in some kind of technical alpha to test servers, or just lazily done. From the start certain UI elements, such as text, do not fit in their containers and end up overflowing out and into the rest of things. In addition to this, lots of the buttons throughout character creation are just odd icons that only kind of hint at what the button might do. The game makes up by this by letting you hover the mouse over buttons to get descriptions but I don't believe I should have to do that for every single button.
After creating a character and logging in, the UI awfulness continues, with things just free floating across the screen upon login, a set of windows you can open that either don't show the information they talk about, or show too much and allow you to see things and place them on your hotbar regardless of whether or not you have them. The biggest map you have is a bit larger than the minimap, but it shows the entire area, which makes it incredibly hard to see anything, and the icons that ARE on the map have no key or explanation for what they are. On top of the UI, having just started I found myself on an incredibly flat surface, maybe 100 or more feet from the npc I was supposed to talk to, which would have been fine, had the game done something to visualize that I was supposed to talk that particular NPC, but it didn’t. This NPC was incredibly flat and basically just said 'You'll be here until level 10' in dialogue. After that I was sent on a few errands, which the developers had not even attempted to disguise as anything but. NPC dialogue was incredibly flat, and the only plus of it was that it was straight forward, because they just told you what you needed to do in list format, with no actual dialogue in most places. In addition to that, NPC's like teachers are all the same model, with the same synched up animations, placed in a perfect line with little to no care as to why they are there other than to click on every few levels. There is little to no dialogue when this is done, and you need to go find the things they gave you by searching through menus that have no tutorials and have icons that do not convey the meaning of the buttons or pages they represent.
On to the world, upon crossing a bridge I was met with hordes and hordes of dogs. Just for miles, the same model, with the same HP, in droves. The only kind of definition to the landscape in most places was that it was swarming with dogs. Now, this would have added an element of danger (albiet a poorly done one), but you can run right into any of these dogs and not be attacked at all. In fact, if you run for an additional five minutes, you can find wolves, and five minutes more you will find boars, and five minutes more there will be bears, that are lower level than the wolves. None of these enemies will actually attack you, which I'm not sure is on purpose or not, but either way, is poorly done. Speaking of running for five minutes, as you run through these areas with enemies, a stamina bar will drain at the bottom of your screen, even though nothing is attacking you and all you are doing is the base movement (there is not sprinting of any kind by the way) and you will eventually be forced to sit and wait as your character acts winded and sits there, before you stamina bar instantly refills itself to full. I'm not sure if that is a bug or not, but I am incredibly thankful to whatever gods there are for it, because the game was tedious and awful enough as it was, and it saved me a long time, seeing as that bar held 840 points of stamina.
With combat, the animations are probably the only nice thing about the game that I found, they were fluid and nice, but quickly became repetitive, as all of the enemies were the same, and couldn't hold out, even in hordes, against my character at level 2. I eventually found a 'metin stone' which I still don't know the purpose of, only that they were sprinkled about in completely random spots, sometimes being in places you couldn't actually get to. Upon hitting said stone I realized that it would not break, and had a lot of health, I then found out, about a minute later, that it had spawned enemies, with absolutely no clue that it had beyond that they were now standing amongst the sea of other creatures. They easily blended in as the only difference between them and the other creatures were that they were level 16. I killed two of the three, being able to drink potions with no cool down at all (and having been given one for everything other thing I had killed) until i did eventually die while the last enemy was at a sliver of health. I was then given an option to respawn off at the town, or in the exact place I died. I quickly found another UI issue as the game does not clearly tell you how much time you have left to respawn, rather leaving a small message in a tiny dialogue box in the bottom left, that is also full of a ton of other things and chat that quickly drowns out said message. After respawning I found the last enemy at the same health and killed it. There was absolutely no penalty to dying other than that I had to wait 7 seconds to kill the thing that had killed me.
After eventually wandering back to town, I found about 20 quests for me. Apparently my quest that I hadn't known about had been to level up. I was never told to go level up, and now had quests to go kill the exact same enemies I had been grinding through before. All of these quests were the same flat and empty listed goals as last time, and I completed a few before I found a quest with dialogue. This bit of dialogue was the first real dialogue I'd seen beyond the occasional sexist remark made by male NPC's at the end of their lists. It was a short, incredibly awkward, and entirely unneeded bit about how this particular NPC needed deodorant, of all things. His solution was for me to go kill more things for ingredients, because apparently wolves collect flowers and deodorant makings. It was at about this point that I stopped playing.
A wide scattering of poor design quite quickly ruins this game. As a recap, the UI, while looking decent, has horrendously designed UX. Buttons have icons with no meaning to the player, lots of the UI spill out over it's parent buttons with no real care given by the developer, and alot of UI elements are hidden behind tons of others, or are simply useless. For example, there is a gestures menu, none of which you can use, that includes things like waving, clapping, and your other standard gestures, but then goes on to include kissing, french kissing, and other completely unneeded emotes that seem to have no place in the game. On top of UI the quests are poorly done, almost all of them are the same list style 'go do these things' quests, with no dialogue explaining why beyond a quest title. All of the quest givers have names like 'Potion Dealer' and 'Weapon Smith', I believe I saw a total of four named NPC's over the course of my playtime. On top of this the world design was terrible, with wide open, flat, and entirely empty spaces left to just have swarms of enemies randomly generated in groups of three on it. All of the enemies are the same with slightly different naming conventions across levels, and no real difference between the four enemies in the area. Overall I would not recommend this game to anyone, regardless of who they were.

Metin 2 is a F2P MMO, and like other F2P games, it isn't very well put together.
Now the game does have a lot of potential, but the lack of focus in much of the game's structure causes problems for players.
Pros:
Camera's controls are intuitive and user friendly. The camera adjusts naturally as your character turns and you can move the camera around with Right Mouse Button or Q and E.
-A big problem with most MMO's is the camera controls. Metin 2 does it right.
Animations are clean and smooth. They execute quite well and feel nice when attacking enemies.
Attacking and leveling up feel swift and meaningful.
Unfortunately there aren't too many pros other than those
Cons:
The UI is a bit stretched and not immensely intuitive.
-It's displayed like similar MMO UI designs, which is convenient, however it's not explained and pretty cramped making it hard to access some important elements.
There's no clear direction.
-Now, I don't like MMO's that force the player into the story without engaging them, however Metin 2 plops you into the world with no explanation at all. No tutorial, goals, or explanations. This causes problems as I frankly had no real idea what I had to do. I just explored and killed animals for XP.
Networking has a few errors in it.
-Sending messages to other players results in them being alerted to the message, but the message is blank and the content is missed.
-Some small lag, which is expected.
Lack of content.
-Most content is in the later half of the game which requires more experience which takes more time
Overall, the negatives greatly out way the positives. The game has potential and is better than other MMO's in other regards, however, the lack of direction and content leaving the game feeling very empty.

But I trust Dejobaan, who have yet to disappoint me with a game. So i kept at it, and boy am i glad i did. What seemed like a small game with 15-20 levels, is actually chock full of robots and the difficulty rises slowly but surely. Soon, i was getting into tense fights with robots that seemingly wouldn't die despite the huge firepower i was throwing at them.
I like that there is both a platforming aspect, trying to maneuver your jetpacks where you need to, but also a tactical one. Since you're on a timer, you need to figure out the best path to maximize the damages to the Titans, while getting all the vital power-ups you need. Dwell around too much, and the clock will be the death of you.
DRP packages this challenging game into a very nice shell. First the graphisms, with grandiose, colorful arenas that are a nice changes to the usual "gritty brownish" of many games. Second the soundtrack, which is all over the place in a positive way : one arena will have dubstep, while the next will be more jazzy, and the next one will offer yet another ambiance... Very nice mix all around :). Finally, the silly-in-a-good-way Dejobaan humor ties the story and the gameplay  in a nice way.
I still find the controls a bit too floaty for my tastes, but I've mostly adapted to that, and i can't deny the adrenaline rush this game provides me. You dance around countless lasers, you tear off bits and pieces of the Titan one by one, while you keep moving to avoid the smaller enemies and seeker projectives. DRP is really EPIC BATTLES AGAINST GIANT ROBOTS.
A game that all should try out :)

By far the most realistic fps, and maybe even the most realistic game, I've ever played. Unlike COD or Battlefield you feel constantly under threat, knowing that at any moment a stray bullet or hidden marksman could kill you instantly before you even realise what happened. There are next to no indications of who is friend or foe apart from the clothes you wear and what side of the battlefield you are on, with occasional hints at enemy postion on the map when recon is available. This neverending vulnerability forces you to act carefully and calculate every move. Simply running straight at the enemy as you would in other games will inevitably result in your death. Teamwork is key and is much more important than individual success. However, when it all comes together, the satisfaction is hard to match. In short, buy this game if you're looking for something brutally realistic but rewarding.
