Drunken Robot Pornography - bringing bullet storms to the first person perspective.
You're fighting back the robot uprising, brought on by your own bartender. As far as the story is concerned, this is right up dejobaan's alley. This mixed in with the various "voicemails" makes for a humorous storyline, even if the premise of the game isnt too heavily focused on it.
Set in sky boston, and using lots of bright colours you might expect this game to be too garish to play, but I feel as if the developers got it just right.
This game played at a high framerate with mouse and keyboard gives it a really nice aesthetic. It almost seems like those multiplayer arena based shooters, except you're fighting with bullet storms rather than normal weaponry. Initially the whole bullet storm aspect threw me, as i've never come across that in 1st person mode, but in this game it works really well.
The individual level designs are, individually, very good. Each level is unique, as are the titans, and this adds a lot of variety to the game. I do have a slight complaint in that sometimes it feels as if you get a randomly difficult level placed between easier levels. I feel this kind of mucks up the difficulty progression in places.
This game has a great rap at the start, and throughout the game makes use of great royalty free music. The styles of music chosen seem to vary greatly between levels, but that doesn't bother me too much.
This game has a built in level and bot editor, with workshop integration. Mucking around with all the community creations is good as it will extend your playtime by quite a bit. Also, it's I think it's a great idea to have the weekly challenges (listed under "Robot Unicorn").
One major issue i have with this game is that the initial load time when you start the game is very long. Loading individual levels is fairly speedy, but initially it does seem quite slow.
Overall this is a very good game. Definitely worth a go if you've never tried a first person bullet storm game.

There's a lot of average and bad survival games in early access and there's The Long Dark. It's the single most immersive sandbox survival games I played. You feel in danger and near the edge of death all the times and live just another day only feel all that more rewarding.
The looting is a joy everytime that you searching everywhere for that one thing that can help you sustain a little longer. This game definitely has the potential to be something more than what it already is: Awesome. It's a thrilling game because of it's risk/reward system as well as the expanding base-defense concept. The more you open, the more technology, energy, and resources you collect for leveling, healing up, expansion and defense. But for every dark, unpowered room, you have 1 more entry point for a wave of monsters. While you can build defenses in powered-up rooms, it's impossible to defend forever. And you must move. Eventually, you will locate the exit to the next level. That's when the real thrill kicks in. You have to disable fighting ability and slow down one of your characters so you can carry your ship's core to the exit. Meanwhile, enemies will be crawling up from those rooms you left dark...

To my knowledge I never played a rogue-like game before 'The Binding of Isaac' and normaly I wouldn't consider myself the type of gamer that likes a challenge or wants to play a game to completion. TBoI really hooked me in that regard though. When I first read about 'Dungeon of the Endless' I expected something similar. But in space. Which would have been awesome! What I got was something differently awesome.
Right now DotE is still an alpha and rightly so. The aesthetic is there, the gameplay is there, but it still seems to be missing a lot of content. The alpha is enough though to give you an impression of what to expect.
DotE is not a rogue-like twitch-reaction shooter like TBoI. It plays more like aprocedurally generated turn-based RPG with Tower Defense  elements. That sounds weird, I know.
You play as one or two survivors of a spaceship crash and have to explore the dungeons surrounding the wreckage. You are able to install various machinery in the rooms you encounter, machines that generate food or technical supplies, defensive or offensive istallations, etc. Your power source is the crystal from your crashed shuttle and it can sustain only so many rooms. To expand your energy reserves, you have to explore the dungeon and defeat monsters. Everytime you open a door, time passes and new ressources are regenerated based on your installations. New rooms may contain items, blueprints, supplies, merchants, new characters to hire and of course sockets for more machinery. And monsters.
One of the main differences to TBoI is that you cannot control your characters directly. You just send them to a room and they will do what whatever can be done there. If there are monsters, they will fight. Your heroes are pretty squishy though. You have to use the defensive and offensive machinery you installed earlier for support. It's almost imperative to lure the monsters into prepared death-traps. So you have to explore, build, strategize and fight all while juggling your limited power supply, because you cannot sustain all the rooms and machines at once.
And then you have to move the crystal to get to the next level of the dungeon and all hell breaks loose!
Currently there are only 3 levels in this build, but the learning and difficulty curve keeps it interesting for a while.
I'm looking forward to what's coming!

It feels like real war— and sounds like a real war.
My buddy on steam told me to get the game. My steam buddy is not like many gamers. He admires his games, yes, and has difficulty explaining why casual gamers need a game that is so realistic. But he also hates the idea that the hardcore players can support developers that make a game so terrifying.
The death never stopped coming. The body parts disoriented me as they flew past my face. Watching my buddies getting mowed down at a steady pace made me sick. The explosions — loud like a bomb — gave me a temporary case of PTSD. For at least an hour after playing the game just a few times, I was anxious and irritable.
Even in arcade mode, it is very simple to die 100 times before you even know what has happened. In realistic mode, it doesn’t take any imagination to see dozens of bodies falling in front of your barrel.
All it takes is the will to do it.
Thousands of people can be gone in just 60 seconds.

Absolutely brilliant game.  From the gameplay to the cartoon graphics to the music, it is practically flawless (there are a few bugs here and there, but they are very rare).
Best of all though, is the difficulty.  Each boss requires an understanding of their abilities and mechanics before you will be able to beat them, so the onus is on you to 'git gud and l2p' rather than the game offering endless crutches to carry bad/lazy players.
And once you beat a boss, there is always the option to go back and do it again to get the highest score possible, so there is a great deal of replayability built into the game.  Even if you beat every boss/level with a perfect score, the game will still be challenging if you come back to it at a later date.  There is no vertical progression system that makes the game easier the more you play it, you are 100% dependent on your own gaming skills.
For the price, this is well worth getting, it is a classic.

It is stupid but I somehow keep coming back to this game.
I picked this game up because it seemed unique and it was really cheap, which is always nice. I knew going in the gameplay would be basic and repetitive, you are only selecting practically yay or nay on people's lives over and over again. I knew that there would be no world changing graphics, just simple geometrical shapes that resembled cartoony lords, ladies, minstrels, etc. I was actually shocked by the music, it is really nice and smooth, settling quietly into the background perfectly. Usually I turn off any music and turn on my own but for a select few games and this game has the privilege of that. But for some reason, despite this game not being particularly special, I keep coming back.
The main reason I keep coming back is the puzzle aspect, there are riddles littered throughout the game which I will not hint at for the sake of avoiding spoiling. As long as you do not dig around the community hub and read guides and discussions on how to solve said puzzles, you slowly start finding your way through the games. You develop an understanding of how the cards work and how to direct your king's destiny to what you want to happen, pushing yourself forward to solving the final puzzle.
The downside to this game is that the repetitiveness does wear you away. The cards are almost always the same unless you get a) lucky or b) figure out ways to nudge the life towards a specific card branch. You essentially just go through the same thing over and over again until you finally succeed, sort of like Dark Souls without the sense of accomplishment after bashing your head against a stone wall until your dizzy. I would have to wonder if there is anyone who has sat down for hours and clicked away at options, though I would doubt it. That is not to say that you can not put plenty of hours into this game, I have eleven as of writing this and going rather strong, picking up thirty minutes to an hour or so when I come back to the game, and it seems to keep me coming back somehow. I expect that until I have seen everything in the game I will keep coming back because it is in my nature to not leave any puzzle unsolved.
Thanks for reading,

Sir, You Are Being Hunted, is aa unique and fun game.  I love the game and would recommend it because it's funny, fun, and it also provides moments where things are very tense.  Getting stuck hiding in grass while there are robots, horses, and dogs sweeping the area, can be nervewracking.  The only things that I don't like about it, are how the dogs can instantly put you down, and as far as I can tell, all you can do is just sit there and do nothing.  The giant landowner is the same way, but he's supposed to be powerful.  I would suggest making the moment when a dog downs you a quicktime event where you shake the mouse.  That way, the player will feel like they're actually doing something, instead of just struggling for nothing.  Aside from that, the game is really fun, and that small problem isn't enough to stop me from loving everything else about it.

The game has a great concept and proves that modern games don't need to have flashy graphics. If you are a zombie lover, this game is for you. However, I wouldn't name your character after yourself quite yet, as you will die many times, but not in vain! You will learn from your mistakes over time and survive...
for a little while.
Pros
- Great zombie Ai. They pound on doors, chase you slowly, join packs and hide in closets. Closets are for clothes Mr. Zombie!
- Scavenging is fun! It's what you will be doing mostly, when you aren't avoiding moaners.
- Weapons! Rolling pins, butter knives, and more! Hammer plus nails plus baseball bat = excalibur!
- Get hungry, get thirsty, get sleepy, get wounded! Tear off that curtain and use as a bandage, but oh crap! Now the dead heads can see you through the window!
- The power turned off and the taps stopped giving me water. I was all like oh snap.
- I found a shack in the middle of nowhere which became my homebase for a while. Boarded up the windows and filled it with bags of stuff. If there weren't shufflers around it woulda been a man cave.
- A pistol! and nine rounds! Now I can kill nine whole Zomboids. That'll help!
Cons
- The inventory system is terrible! So confusing, I still don't think I have it down.
- Often zombies just appear behind you. The game trys to use a cone of sight system, but please, I think I would hear a shuffling moaning crap-head coming up behind me.
- The music is fitting, but quickly becomes annoying. Too much "divas singing like monks".
- The game saves itself, leaving your death permanent. Name your character after someone you don't like as you will inevitably die in a horrible way.
- After stocking up, making a fort, a garden and finally becoming kinda safe, there really isn't anything else to do but go out and finally get killed by zombies. A harsh fact of zombie survival I guess
THE BIGGEST CON:
My inventory keeps disapearing! Once, I suddenly had two of everything! And don't even think about putting a bag down that has important inventory because you may never see it again. I had two baseball bats, then suddenly I had none. It's sort of a game breaker.
I will recommend this game as I did have fun, but this is a terrible bug that needs to be squashed for a game of this stature or it will not survive it's own apocalypse.

By this point you've probably heard alot about evolve, and most likely have seen some of the bad press it's gotten recently, some of which is blown out of proportion - but alas, from my point of view - its brilliant - just flat out brilliant! We are always asking and complaining about AAA titles just being sequels because its safe to do, but Evolve took a chance, what other game is like it? Nothing, that's what.
Now it definately is a niche game, and I won't lie - half the people who play the game have no idea how to play their class, but when you and a few friends join up, land on the planet and go hunting for a two storey monster - its great! The classes are balanced and the evolution of the monster does ramp up the difficulty, so you need tactics! Do you build a team designed to find the monster fast? Do you want your team to be able to hold up a fight against a stage 3 monster? it's entirely upto you!
Playing as the monster is great too, you have to eat to evolve, and if you don't evolve, chances are you will die - and there's something ever so satisfying about taking out a team of 4 players on your own!
So if you're still on the fence about this game, go educate yourself - watch gameplay vids on youtube or twitch, check out the forums and speak to the community about whether or not you think you should get it, but this is a game that is unique, and isn't that what we've been asking for?

Pros:

Animations are clean and smooth. They execute quite well and feel nice when attacking enemies.
Attacking and leveling up feel swift and meaningful.
Unfortunately there aren't too many pros other than those
Cons:
The UI is a bit stretched and not immensely intuitive.
-It's displayed like similar MMO UI designs, which is convenient, however it's not explained and pretty cramped making it hard to access some important elements.
There's no clear direction.
-Now, I don't like MMO's that force the player into the story without engaging them, however Metin 2 plops you into the world with no explanation at all. No tutorial, goals, or explanations. This causes problems as I frankly had no real idea what I had to do. I just explored and killed animals for XP.
Networking has a few errors in it.
-Sending messages to other players results in them being alerted to the message, but the message is blank and the content is missed.
-Some small lag, which is expected.
Lack of content.
-Most content is in the later half of the game which requires more experience which takes more time
Overall, the negatives greatly out way the positives. The game has potential and is better than other MMO's in other regards, however, the lack of direction and content leaving the game feeling very empty.

is an Action J Style platformer.
Personally, the story is short, sweet, and to the point. It kept me engaged as there is not much filler, or flutter, but it felt as though I was playing through a story, and my actions were of the princess. I genuinely wanted to complete the level to find out the next part of the story. As with anything, there is room to improve.
You play a princess in a 3rd person action platformer. The controls on the keyboard are tight, and tapping keys allow for finite jumping and a great experience. I personally had issues using the gamepad from the start, so I have no opinion if it works properly or not. The goal is to complete the level, and optionally collect all of the crystals.
If you plan on being an achievement completionist, you should expect this game to last you 2-3 hours for the genuine most. For me, the puzzles were not too difficult, or too easy, and I found myself having to go back and forth in some areas a few times to completely understand some of them. When you complete the puzzle, you will feel positive for completing it and continuing on. The combat of the game is lacking; you will face a handful of different skeletons with varying abilities, all will prepare you for the final boss; but the combat is weak and leaves a lot more to desire.
When first launching the game, the menus confused me, clicking each one of them takes you to a different part of configuration or tutorial, and eventually will start the game. I would have personally liked if the menus were a bit more intuitive. Performance was fine with a full 60fps and no dips in graphics. Some of the sounds, like a whistle for the balloon when you die can get annoying; I would prefer something a bit more lax.
Recommended gameplay for a simple platformer, with cute graphics and an engaging story. Nothing to write home about, but something you will remember playing.

I do not give a flying ♥♥♥♥ about DLC - I haven't bought any and I'm still having loads of fun.
Two teams, 4 v 1. The 4 are the Hunters, they work together to track, trap and kill the 1. The 1 is a big♥♥♥♥♥super-monster that can kill an unprepared team of Hunters effortlessly.
Gameplay for the Hunters is like a cross between Left 4 Dead, Monster Hunter (google it) and Borderlands (each class has unique class-abilities). You can play as a Medic, Assault, Support or Trapper. Each role has a couple of unlockable Hunters with varying abilities, strengths and weaknesses. Everyone has jetpacks, but there is a bit of a learning curve in using them efficiently (which is a good thing). As long as one Hunter lives, the rest can respawn and dropship in again (this is on a fairly long cooldown, if you die after the dropship has launched, enjoy your wait).
Playing the Monster is also like Left 4 Dead, except that you are alone as the 'special infected' while being much much stronger. You can get around the map much faster than the Hunters, and generally mess with their heads/annihilate them if you have the right mindset and cunning.
The typical Monster game consists of things like ♥♥♥♥♥hit♥♥♥♥♥hitshitnomnonomnomOW♥♥♥♥♥hit♥♥♥♥♥hitnomnomRAAAGH! I win? weee
Currently you can pick from the firebreathing Tank/Fighter, the Teleporting/stealth Rogue, or the ranged/lightning flying tentacle-face dude.
I played the various Alpha and Beta releases and initially found the game to be too similar to Left 4 Dead (far too simple); but after playing the full release for a few days, and the Evacuation mode (multiplayer campaign), I've come to realise that the game is ridiculously well-balanced and really deep - personal experience as a player is a lot more valuable than progression experience (just like Monster Hunter), the maps are big and open enough that you can't predict exactly how the match is going to play out. There's real 'meat' to this game.

Whoever you end up playing, it's easy to pick up the basics, but difficult to master them. The tactics you employ for each match vary wildly depending on your class(es), the environment, and the Hunt type. The maps are awesomely varied (heh, acid maps), and the wildlife is a lot of fun to deal with (fun). The autobalancing is probably the best I've ever seen, even if people drop out, lose a few games in a row, etc, the game stays fun for all involved. Matchmaking is solid, and usually lets you play your favourite role (if you insist on having one) without any trouble.
I'm always impressed by how much work the devs must have put into building up the game world, giving it a unique character all it's own. The Hunter dialogues are pretty good to listen to, especially once you get a good mix of the rarer Hunters together in the dropship.
Basically this is shaping up to be one of the best Coop games I've played since Left 4 Dead. All I need now is a regular crew and some Teamspeak tactics :)
The (overpriced) skins are optional, and the addtional Hunters and Monsters are not available yet (if the devs pay the same attention to balancing as they have done with the rest of the player characters, the DLC PCs won't confer any particular advantage either).
It's easy to underestimate the effort and production values the devs have put into game balancing (it's amazing)  and cutscenes/interactions. I suspect the Season Pass (overpriced) will make more sense as players mature with unlocks and progression - new Hunters and Monsters will affect both game balance and the various cutscenes and player character dialogues, probably a lot of work involved in that.

tl;dr This game is a bit mislabeled and levels aren't quite linear in difficulty, but it plays well, had great visuals, and is ultimately very fun
I had been pretty curious about this game since I saw the trailer for Drunken Robot Battle Royale on fridays or whatever. I didn't know what it meant, but it looked cool. That's always a good start, right? Turns out the actual game is called Drunken Robot Pornography though. Weird name. Totally is in the favor of the game, because it's not something you'll easily forget after hearing it one time. I mean, really, who is going to forget a name with "pornography?"
I had read some reviews and I was a bit skeptical. Most of the negative reviews were really short one liners that complained about the difficulty, so I didn't let that scathe my desire to play.
Onto the actual review part that matters:
This game is beautiful. Sure, it doesn't quite tell you all the rules in the beginning (but what game really does?), and you start off on a very simple tutorial where I don't think you can die. Basically, the premise of the game is that, because of REASONS (I don't pay attention to story, sorry), you have to dispatch some titans. Titans are these giantass robot things that are hitting up Boston in the worst of ways. So you, with your trusty suit, rocket boots (!), and all purpose gun thing are up to DESTROLISH all of the bots.
This game is labeled as a bullet hell game, but I'd think that's pretty inaccurate. Sure, you have to dodge a ton of things, but dodging stuff in games isn't unique. Admittedly, there are, at some points, LOTS of things to dodge, but bullet hells typically rely on you being able to see the whole map at once, so you can actually dodge everything. This game only lets you see 120 degrees or so. That's not quite the same as full field of view. Then again, there's also an entity tracker thing on your HUD that lets you know vaguely where things are. I think. I'm not too sure how it works, but there are totally arrows pointing to things and they seem to move around if you flick your view in a different direction. That said, though, they aren't reliable or are proximity based or something because I've totally had entities on the map that weren't tracked.
One thing I love about first person shooters is movement. I love to rocket jump in games that allow it, and I love speed. Just being able to do fancy movement stuff is great in all games, really. It increases the skill ceiling. This game not only makes you move really fast (you can fall off edges if you hold W long enough and try to do "Air Strafing"-like things to turn; you have to actually press a or d to ensure you don't fall off a ledge during a turn). You basically handle like a car. That's pretty neat. Sure, it's not the best, but it's something to learn. Not only do you move fast, but you have ROCKET BOOTS. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥that's such a fun thing to play with. Usually with games with jetpacks, you can cheat out the duration of the jetpack by tapping the jump button and they go ahead and let you know that is a feature in this game on the loading screen. Cool! Also, there's totally jump pads that make you go flying up in the air so that you can ascend faster. Man, I love movement in this game. Why can't more games have this? :/
But what's  first person shooter without shooting, right? Sure, you can do fancy stuff with jumpin and movin, but that's not good if you're not jump n shoot man, right? Well, admittedly, the weapon variety is limited, it seems. You're stuck with one weapon for the whole game (I think, I haven't beaten the game yet). That's not necessarily a bad thing, though, because you can pick up power-ups within each map. Triple Fire will turn your pew into PEWPEWPEW, rapidfire does what you'd imagine, splinter fire does... a thing, heavy fire... also does a thing, and then there's also other power ups like Decoy and Invulnerability that you can activate by right clicking. This doesn't apply for the entire map, though. Instead, you're limited by how many shots each power up lasts for (600 on all of them, as far as I've been able to tell). There's also likely more upgrades that I've not gotten to yet. But basically, each of them alters how your gun works and lets you murderate the giantass robots fasterer.
It gets better, still, though. Sure, while you might so far think that the game is really dull and all you do is shoot things that don't have brains, you also get to stare at the pretty visuals. I mean pretty. Like, dang, these are pretty. There's so many vibrant colors and it feels so sleek. Ok, look, listen, my words can't do it justice. Words are hard. :( Just know that this game is very, very pretty. Some might be a little put off by how many colors thare are, though. Something about sensory overload or something. Whatever.
Man, it's not just the visuals that are great either. This game has a pretty solid soundtrack. I dunno, maybe I'm just a sucker for video game music. Fortunately, this game comes with a goodies folder and that gives me access to some of the music (though, tragically, not technically this') . I'd put most of it on a playlist. Sure, there's only 6 songs in the entire thing, but they're genuinely fun to listen to. It, of course, also fits pretty well with the game. It's got a pretty high bpm and that's handy because this game rewards you for going fast.
Some gripes with this game, though, are that levels seem to fluxuate heavily on difficulty. I thought that people were kidding and just bad when they were talking about this being an issue, but it's pretty apparent. I did the first 12 levels like no problem, but then I got to Alleyways and I just got #rekt hard. Something about those new guys shooting at me while I'm not able to see them and having to deal with a new boss damage attack... Yeah. That level is really good, though. It does restrict your access to a resource (Rapid Fire) sometimes with the boss covering it via his drop down cannon ball attack thing. I think entering the black circles at all is a bad thing. Dont' touch anything in this game that isn't a platform.
This game is also pretty cute with its voicing. Your suit talks to you or something (Think Iron Man and JARVIS) and lets you know things or just offers silly banter between the main character and the main character's suit. Always gotta give props to games that are intentionally silly.
Admittedly, I haven't cleared all of this game, yet, but I'd still suggest it to people looking for a new game to play. The game just plays really well and, while you basically are forced to constantly stay moving and holding down m1, it ultimately offers solid gameplay. This game also just feels like it was a testing ground for an arena shooter because good lord this game would be an INCREDIBLE arena shooter. If I had to put a number on this game I'd give it something like an 8. It's certainly not a perfect game, but it's one I'm pretty happy to have a copy of.
It's hard to suggest what other games are similar to give you an idea of how it plays. It's not like Team Fortress 2, not like Call of Duty, not like Sanctum, I guess kinda like Tribes: Ascend? What game has stuff on the floor that you can pick up, jump pads, rocket shoes, one weapon, and super fast movement? I dunno. There aren't any comparisons I can make, but that's also something worth noting. This game is somewhat novel. It also feels like this game would fit PERFECTLY in an arcade. In fact, I'd be surprised if this wasn't inspiried by some Japanese arcade game that one of the developers remembers vaguely.
Basically, pick up this game because it's kind of incredible. It's pretty, it's fun, it plays well, and the only thing wrong with it (so far; I'll update when I beat the game) is that difficulty is all over the place sometimes.

A lot to love, but it's not perfect.
Bioshock is the "spritual successor" to the System Shock games, and it certainly shows in a myriad of ways. From the audio logs left behind, to the hacking system (brillantly done), to the dark, creepy atmosphere of the setting, right down to the "twist" in the plot, this is a game that closely follows the blueprint set forth by the original System Shock.
I've read people feel this game is a bit "uneven", and I think that's an apt way to describe it. Some stuff is wonderfully done, and other parts seem as if they were put together with less care.
For starters, my biggest complaints:
1) The enemies are not varied enough, and in the dark, gloomy lighting they can be difficult to distinguish, so it can be difficult to assess the enemy and determine which weapon is best suited to kill it. Ammo and EVE can be fairly scarce, so one naturally would like to use the most effective means of killing a foe, but when they are nearly indistinguishable from each other, this becomes a chore. THe game provides you with a way to "research" your enemies for damage bonuses, but there is no way to access this information in-game. You must go to an external website somewhere to see pictures of your foes and realize their weaknesses.
2) Combat can be too simplistic, despite the myriad of tools at your disposal.
There are some interesting opportunities to shock groups of enemies standing in water with lightning, or make use of exploding canisters, but for the most part combat is fairly straight forward and boring, since there is little meaningful variation in the enemies.
Only when you need to take down a Big Daddy does the game's environment and combat reall shine. Killing a Big Daddy, especially early in the game when you are weak and underpowered, is a challenge, and requires you to position environmental objects (like canisters and exploding barrels) into makeshift traps. The ability to set traps in your evironment and wait for enemies to arrive is sadly underutilized in the game and within the story. There's a ripe opportunity to set traps once, and that's it. The game could have really benefitted from multiple opportunities to set traps and reinforce your position before a fight. The game gives you tools for this (crossbow tripwires), but sadly the opportunities are simply lacking.
3) The control system - flipping between plasmids and weapons and cycling to the correct one - is clumsy at best, and frustrating most of the time. In a quick-combat environment you'll find yourself swapping to the wrong weapon or plasmid often, and quite frequently wasting precious ammo or EVE.
4) Some of the level designs seem uninspired, which is a shame given the potential of Rapture. There are some great levels with unique designs (a hallmark of the original System Shock, as every level was very unique) and these are welcome and fun when present. But when the area design is boring/uninspired, it drags the game down a notch.
All of that said, it's still a great game. The inspiration from System Shock is apparent. Rapture is a great setting, and dealing with Big Daddy's is fun. I'd give it an 8/10. The graphics are dated a bit, but it's not enough to downgrade it. I think the issues with the game are more with the design and the lack of variety in the enemies. Stil worth getting on-sale this late in its life span.
Oh, and I have dual NVidia cards in SLI. I did not experience ANY issues playing this game that some recent Steam reviews have reported. The game played flawlessly for me. No bugs, no issues, one CTD the entire time.

Lyne is a simple, yet intuitive indie puzzle game that revolves around creating "pathways" that link matching shapes together without crossing paths of other color variants. Honestly, that is the goal of every puzzle in the game, but what I enjoyed about Lyne was the variety in which you could complete such a simple task. The game takes you through the letters of the alphabet and, as you'd probably guess, the further along you go, the harder and more complex the puzzles become. You start out with two colors and a simple solution is often identified quickly, allowing you to seamlessly glide through the first set of puzzles. As you progress, the game adds sort of "gateways" in which a set number of lines, or lynes if you will, can pass through without conflicting with one another; think of it as a sort of intersection.
As time progresses , the game adds more shapes to match and gateways to fill and it can become quite complicated, but never frustratingly so, in my opinion. What I enjoyed about the difficulty is it never really spiked; the game gradually increased the challenge as you progressed. I never felt annoyed or frustrated at puzzles I could not figure out and that is what I loved about Lyne.
The game's simple, yet soothing atmosphere makes it a pleasure, even when you can't, for the life of it all, figure out the solution. Aside from all that, what I enjoy most about Lyne are the daily puzzles. These are randomly generated each day and vary in difficulty - from easy to extreme. This added feature gives the game replay-ability when you feel like sitting down and cracking out a few puzzles to unwind, or for a mental challenge. If you like puzzle games, I'd suggest Lyne.
Overall, I enjoyed Lyne. I originally bought it for the achievements to use in my profile, but found I got a lot more for my money than just virtual achievements and I was very pleased. If you enjoy puzzle games and are looking for something new, I suggest checking Lyne out.

An absolute treasure.  Cuphead is a run-and-gun style game modeled after Contra but with more emphasis on boss battles than levels.  The bosses all have multiple phases, multiple attacks within each phase, and different patterns of movement to go with them.  This ties rather wonderfully with the game's gorgeous Golden Age of Animation art style.  Like an early Disney, Tex Avery or Fleischer Brothers cartoon things can get wonderfully weird at the drop of a hat.  It's a perfect fit, and the whimsical tone goes along with the steep challenge curve to create an atmosphere of fun.  Even dying is fun.  I should know, I've done it about 200 times (actually closer to 300 by now, I think) and while I haven't finished the game yet I can heartily recommend it to anyone who has played Contra and loved it but thought to themselves, "You know, I wish this looked a lot more like Steamboat Willie and had giant boxing frogs that turned into killer slot machines."  It's a highly specific request, I admit, but Cuphead delivers.
I don't know what the brothers Moldenhauer will do next, but they've done something truly great here, and I hope this is just the first triumph of many for them.

(TL;DR = Great game, albeit very short.  Needs a bit of polish, but if you like light-hearted games, hack n’ slash games, puzzle games, and/or platformers this game is definitely worth the money.)
PRO:
- Lots of gameplay elements; puzzle, hack n’ slash, and platforming.
- All gameplay elements are very well done.
- Fun, cute little story.
- Good visual style.
- Good music.
- Adorable dialog/voice acting (it’s not good, but it’s charming in how silly and earnest it is).
- No recycling; every level introduces new challenges and enemy types.
- Interesting mechanic of having to gather items on each stage to reveal more of the story.
- Full voice acting in-game.
CON:
- The combat could be deeper.
- The lack of a lock-on or ability to adjust mid-strike makes the directed attack all but useless; the game is essentially just one-button combat with the wide area attack.
- The dodge sends you flipping backwards relative to where your character is facing, not the direction you push the left analog stick/what movement key you hit.  This makes the dodge useless as you can’t see where you are dodging and often go flipping off of a ledge.  My advice is to just jump out of the way instead.
- It’s a bit hard to explain, but your character is sort of “floaty.”  It’s almost like she is TOO responsive; trying to land on some of the smaller platforms will often result in her running off them as you try to just adjust yourself slightly.  Maybe this had something to do with me using a controller instead of the keyboard. Regardless, my advice is to stop touching the stick/keys the moment you are about to land.
- VERY short: I was able to 100% complete it in less than two hours and in just one run.
Overall it’s a fun little game with lots of features and a sweet story.  My only complaints are that the combat is rather shallow and it is way too short.  It should be noted that there are many bad games out there that are “anime-like.”  For those games it’s clear the developers made them that way simply because they knew people would gobble them up.  That is not the case with this game; when you play it you really get the sense that Animu Game cared about their project.  Honestly, I recommend buying this game at full price like I did.  Hopefully with more money their next game can be a bit deeper and much longer.

A lot to love, but it's not perfect.
Bioshock is the "spritual successor" to the System Shock games, and it certainly shows in a myriad of ways. From the audio logs left behind, to the hacking system (brillantly done), to the dark, creepy atmosphere of the setting, right down to the "twist" in the plot, this is a game that closely follows the blueprint set forth by the original System Shock.
I've read people feel this game is a bit "uneven", and I think that's an apt way to describe it. Some stuff is wonderfully done, and other parts seem as if they were put together with less care.
For starters, my biggest complaints:
1) The enemies are not varied enough, and in the dark, gloomy lighting they can be difficult to distinguish, so it can be difficult to assess the enemy and determine which weapon is best suited to kill it. Ammo and EVE can be fairly scarce, so one naturally would like to use the most effective means of killing a foe, but when they are nearly indistinguishable from each other, this becomes a chore. THe game provides you with a way to "research" your enemies for damage bonuses, but there is no way to access this information in-game. You must go to an external website somewhere to see pictures of your foes and realize their weaknesses.
2) Combat can be too simplistic, despite the myriad of tools at your disposal.
There are some interesting opportunities to shock groups of enemies standing in water with lightning, or make use of exploding canisters, but for the most part combat is fairly straight forward and boring, since there is little meaningful variation in the enemies.
Only when you need to take down a Big Daddy does the game's environment and combat reall shine. Killing a Big Daddy, especially early in the game when you are weak and underpowered, is a challenge, and requires you to position environmental objects (like canisters and exploding barrels) into makeshift traps. The ability to set traps in your evironment and wait for enemies to arrive is sadly underutilized in the game and within the story. There's a ripe opportunity to set traps once, and that's it. The game could have really benefitted from multiple opportunities to set traps and reinforce your position before a fight. The game gives you tools for this (crossbow tripwires), but sadly the opportunities are simply lacking.
3) The control system - flipping between plasmids and weapons and cycling to the correct one - is clumsy at best, and frustrating most of the time. In a quick-combat environment you'll find yourself swapping to the wrong weapon or plasmid often, and quite frequently wasting precious ammo or EVE.
4) Some of the level designs seem uninspired, which is a shame given the potential of Rapture. There are some great levels with unique designs (a hallmark of the original System Shock, as every level was very unique) and these are welcome and fun when present. But when the area design is boring/uninspired, it drags the game down a notch.
All of that said, it's still a great game. The inspiration from System Shock is apparent. Rapture is a great setting, and dealing with Big Daddy's is fun. I'd give it an 8/10. The graphics are dated a bit, but it's not enough to downgrade it. I think the issues with the game are more with the design and the lack of variety in the enemies. Stil worth getting on-sale this late in its life span.
Oh, and I have dual NVidia cards in SLI. I did not experience ANY issues playing this game that some recent Steam reviews have reported. The game played flawlessly for me. No bugs, no issues, one CTD the entire time.

Possibly one of the best examples of early-access done right, The Long Dark is a fantastic game that just keeps getting better and better.
The premise is simple.  Your plane crashed; it's cold; the wolves are hungry; the bear is angry; no one is around to help; and you've got to do whatever it takes to survive.
What exactly does that mean?  At first, it means following your standard survival game behaviors.  Find shelter.  Find food.  Find water.  Don't let the wildlife eat you as you scour the frozen waste for the things you need.  But what separates The Long Dark from other survival games is that, ultimately, it also means learning the skills to procure those things for yourself.  Want to eat next week?  Better learn to hunt, because the cans of pork and beans you found in that gas station aren't going to last forever.  Want to not die of exposure?  Better learn to tell when a blizzard is coming, because it turns out building a fire in the middle of one is damned near impossible.  Want to look like a rock star?  Better learn to tan a deer hide and sew your own leather pants then--because remember, THERE'S NO ONE AROUND TO HELP.
In this game, you're facing off against Mother Nature one on one.  And Mother Nature may be beautiful (and this game is unbelievably, strikingly beautiful), but Big Mama's also got fists like brick bats, one hell of a long reach, and she's currently undefeated.  So settle in and get ready for a full twelve rounds, Champ.  'Cause you're in for a doozy.

Finally, a good WWII shooter that isn't CoD or Battlefield. This game takes place on the Russia/Axis western front (Red Orchestra 2) as well as the Pacific Front (Rising Storm). Both of these games come with a purchase of either RO2 or RS. The game uses free aim which will keep weapons from centering on your screen until iron-sighting. Bullet drop is taken into account and you can adjust your sights accordingly. While there are 2 more casual modes, most servers run realism in which FF is on, your character can bleed out from wounds, HUD is extremly minimal (only appears when objective is capped or you press a button to bring it up), and you have to worry about the stress of character. Stress occurs when teammates die around you, bullets are shot close or hit close to you, artillery strikes near you, or a commanding officer is killed. It adds a much needed depth which allows for actual fire suppresion to keep enemies down. As you kill with each weapon your character becomes more and more comfortable with the weapon, increasing reload speed, accuracy, etc. You can also unlock a weapon specific attachment every 25 levels with a weapon (unlockables include better scopes, bayonet, cleaner gun). Each team also has different classes such as engineer, marksman, elite rifleman, team commander, squad commander and anti-tank gun. Each class has different abilities and your team must use those abilities to keep ahead of the opposiition. Team commander calls in air strikes, radar planes, and other usefull tools for the team as well as coordinating with the squad leaders to take points and defend certain areas. Gameplay-wise, this game is wonderful but is still slightly arcade-like (battlefield, CoD, etc) and doesn't fully venture into simulator territory like your Arma games.
The game looks ok, with the Rising Storm expansion looking far superior on all fronts (it is also newer than RO2). I don't consider this game well optimized  as most games fall around 40-50 FPS on max settings, vsync and DoF off, but I never felt like fiddling with the options as the game is playable at that framerate (gameplay is slow, high FPS isn't required). I do dislike how there aren't any facial animations, like at all. Spectating games is strange sometimes to see a sniper holding a posiiton and never blinking for a full 30 minutes, but in-game its easy to not notice. Weapons sound impactful and are probably some of my favorite weapon sounds in any WWII game so far. You are also able to turn on each side's actual language, if you dislike Germans and Russians screaming in English.
My only complaints are that I wish there was a radius-based voice chat option instead of all-team, all-squad, and all-game voice channels being the only options. I also dislike how buying the upgrade of RO2 or RS lets anyone have immediate access to automatic weapons. Automatic weapons are mostly given to important classes and many new players tend to pick those classes for the weapon alone and not for learning the abilities. If you do pick up this game, be sure to try out the bolt-action rifles first and unlock one attachment before going up the weapon ladder, as the bolt-action rifles teach you the fundamentals of the game's aiming and bullet drop. Don't assume you will do will immediately, take the time to learn weapons before jumping in guns blazing.

Now THIS is how you make a puzzle game! Both elegant in its simplicity and devious in its complexity, LYNE is a beautiful blend of pick-up-and-play accessibility and fair, reasonable challenge that pretty much never punishes and only rewards. I'm not sure of the exact terminology of every element of the game, so I'm just going to have to wing it and hope it all makes sense...

The easiest way to probably explain it is to say it's a game of join the dots. There are three main coloured shapes, or nodes, scattered across a gridded board, green triangles, red squares and blue diamonds (at least by default, the colour palette can be unlocked and changed throughout the game), with a start and end point for each shape. The object being to drag a line that joins each point whilst also passing through all the faded out nodes of the same shape. So the green line can only pass through the faded green nodes, and so on. There are also neutral nodes that any line can pass through which act as intersections for the different coloured lines. With the exception of these neutral nodes, each node can only be passed through once, either vertically, horizontally or diagonally, and a line can never cross through another line. So, basically, connect each start and end point, and fill in the board along the way. As with most puzzle games, it can sound way more complicated in writing than it really is, but within thirty seconds of actual play you'll perfectly understand exactly how the whole thing works.

The game's first triumph is in teaching itself to the player. With the way it introduces each element of play, the only actions you'll be able to perform are the ones it wants you to learn, further reinforced by brief phases of repetition and minor variation. It won't take long for the series of light bulbs to come on over your head with each new method of covering the board that you learn and you'll soon find yourself steamrolling your way through the opening few stages.

There are 26 sets of puzzles corrosponding to each letter of the alphabet, with each set containing 25 individual puzzles for a total of 650... yeah, you read that right, 650 puzzles. On top of that there are also random daily sets, but unless I'm mistaken, they at least appeared to me to be a mix of various puzzles from the main sets. It's hard to say how long it takes to complete, given that each player will spend a vastly different amount of time depending on their personal skill level, but I reckon about 30 hours would be a reasonable guess, give or take a few hours.

What I really love about this game is how success or failure rests solely in the hands of the player's own determination. With no time limit and no way to technically lose (you either finish a puzzle or you walk away from it), the game is a test of perseverance more than anything. There are a few tricks you can learn to criss-cross your way around a board, but really you'll have to poke and prod at everything and experiment with different routes before honing in on the solution. But rarely will the game leave you hanging, and it'll usually hint as to where you should at least start before working your way out, and from there on it's a gradual process of elimination. It also helps that many puzzles will have multiple methods to solve them, so there is some flexibility in play.
Topping everything off is a slick, clean aesthetic that's minimalist but still appealing. I wasn't a massive fan of the audio as the pinging chimes gradually grated against me and I instead opted to play my own music in the background the entire time, but that's a very minor gripe given how it doesn't really serve any fuctional role in the game play and you can easily live without it. But what I was a massive fan off was the price which is the sweet little cherry on top that should be the final nudge to any fence-sitters still not entirely sure whether or not they should pick this up. Protip, you should.

This is an amazing game! I loved every bit of it, the soundtrack, the art and animation, the frustration, the humor and dark tones...just everything about it. It's a super hard game, but I never got the feeling of "I can never complete or beat this" or "it's too hard, and I don't want to play anymore." It's tough, but the feeling of beating a boss with one hit left or after fighting them upwards of seven or eight times is the real reward here. The run 'n' gun stages are kind of the only thing in the whole package that are pretty average, but I love that they're included and are completely optional. The six weapons in the game all felt unique and interesting, and the charms, while a little annoying that none of them are straight upgrades, they were still an interesting addition. Overall this is a wonderfully tough but fun as hell game. Great game feel, great art style. I'm not one for difficult games where you have to start all the way over, but this one is different. I can't recommend this game enough!

LYNE is an interesting puzzle game, to me. It stands somewhere between Kami (a type of puzzles that I dislike -- not a game's fault, as the game is very well done!) and Hexcells ( a type of puzzles that I very much enjoy!).
It's an abstact puzzle game very tightly connected with Graph Theory. Or, to put it simply, connecting dots.
A big problem, for
, is the sheer amount of puzzles it has. 650. That's... waaay too much. The interesting levels and details get dilluted in this sea of very similar puzzles with no distinct patterns. I'd rather have 50 levels that followed a certain flow and had my think in different ways, rather than just grinding through a lot of them.
All of the puzzles are computer-generated, although the 650 levels were hand-picked, mostly to fit the set's "theme" and difficulty.
There are also daily sets, each with 25 puzzles (2 or 3 sets a day) that are not "curated", so to speak.
The game has 26 sets. Each of these follows some rules of its own. There are no unique mechanics or anything of the sort. The rules consist mainly on "size" and "number of colors". That's fine, it is enough to make some interesting puzzles with some outside the box solutions.
The game doesn't really have anything wrong, inherently. It's just too much, for me.
And the later difficulty wasn't fun, to me. The size of these puzzles went beyond what I could easily process. Like Kami.
The first levels set a pattern in your brain, easing you into it. (It was very weird that I started trying to connect everything, from words in books to coins on my desk haha!)
That's all good, since the levels have enough information to be challenging, but not as much as to overwhelm you.
The last few sets are a bit too crazy, with big boards and far ending points. There are too many entanglements for me to predict it in my head. And that leads to trial and error. And far longer time in each individual level.
Every time I reached a solution I was just relieved. There was no rewarding feeling about it, so I decided to stop playing after 550+ levels.
The daily sets are usually more enjoyable in this regard, although there are certainly some hard ones!
These sets are generated by the date. Early week levels are easy. Mid-week are medium. Late-week are hard. Week-end are random.
If you do enjoy casually solving puzzles, this game will certainly keep you busy for a while! I like shorter experiences. Something like 50-100 puzzles, but each with a very clear objective, and a certain progression between them.
But hey, this is mostly preference. If you think you'd enjoy from the videos, give it a go!
Presentation-wise, it's okay. Not particularly good, in my opinion. Visually, it's cool. It's simple and displays information clearly. (there are also unlockable palettes.)
The music, however, I don't think was all that great. Maybe it's because I recently played Hexcells!
I like the intention! The execution fell a bit short, though. It's a too "on the background". Each time you connect a dot, a sound is played, but things don't seem to flow very well.
Regardless, this is a respectable puzzle game! It kept me playing for far longer than I expected, and it's certainly worth the money! :)

For the 90 hours that I've put into this game (Singleplayer Survival Only), I can tell you that this game has a lot, A LOT, of potential. Of course, this game is all about survival, no happy ending, no cure, no nothing, and this is a concept that a lot of Zombie Survival Game out there forgot. Survivalism isn't that threatening in those other games, but in Project Zomboid, things are different. I mean, as soon as you create a game, you can clearly read "This is how you died".
Of course, some people might say that there is no point at all, no goals, no "missions", etc. This is not entirely true, as the point of the game is to create your own stories after all. How will you die? This question as yet to have been answered by you! Also, when I said that this game has a lot of potential, I was referencing to the future features that it has to offer (it's in Early Access for a reason). To begin with, NPCs (not yet implemented) will have a huge impact on the gameplay, since they will become a huge part in each playthrough. Plus, NPCs will be able to give more goals to the player, as he will be able to interact with them in many different ways.
To sum up, Project Zomboid might be in Early Access for a while, but it will definitely be worth it. From building a community for all survivors to putting them out of their misery when they get bitten by a zombie, Project Zomboid is one of the best, if not the best Zombie Survival Game of all time!

Sir, You Are Being Hunted is the vision of the future if we let mad british scientists loose.
The story in this game is left up to the player to figure out, for the most part. Hidden messages in the randomly generated maps will help you to piece it together if you play enough. But the story isn't the most important part of this game.
This game, because levels are randomly generated, can be either extremely hard or very easy. But for the most part the game has a fairly good difficulty, with enemies becoming increasingly difficult to handle as you spend more time playing. This game is advertised as being a stealth game, but you can choose yourself wether to go down that route or just jump in guns a blazing. Both tactics work well. Some players argue that this should not be the case, but it didn't bother me while playing.
This game can be played with a controller, but I would reccomend sticking with a standard keyboard/mouse setup because it makes inventory management much easier.
The graphics in this game are not to most amazing. They're not bad as such, but they could be made more detailed, especially the "ground" textures. However, the world generator does a good job of capturing what you could call the stereotypical "brittish village" look (amongst other types of land), and when seen from afar, it does look very nice.
The sound in this game is good, the ambiance and such sounds do a good job of immersing you, and it can be very jarring (in a good way) to suddenly hear a robot coming up behind you.
Because things are randomly generated, don't worry about just restarting if you happen to come across a world that places you smack in the middle of an impossible area. The chances of that happening are very low. And if you are finding things too hard or too easy, you can use the newly updated "custom world generators" to swizzle the difficulty.
This is a really fun open-world stealth game, and definitely worth a shot if you like survival horror games.

Incredible. A "walking simulator" enthusiast's dream. An unexpected gut punch of a narrative worth every minute and penny.
I can't begin to stress how deeply this story resonated with me. It drew me in, put me at ease, made me assume, got me uncomfortable yet lazy - then it floored me, made me think about who my narrator is, who I am for listening to them, who I ought to listen to, what any of that even means. Sir, You Are Being Hunted is a stealth exploration game. You've been stranded on a group of small islands, and tasked with finding the scattered pieces of a broken machine, which should help you escape. But the islands are home to strange robots who will attack you on sight.
There are 17 pieces to find, spread across 5 islands whose layouts are randomly generated. They can be identified by a trail of white smoke rising into the air, not high enough to see from behind a building or a hill, but obvious enough that you'll immediately notice if you're looking at it. I like that, instead of just slapping a waypoint marker on each location as some games would do, SYABH trusts the player to actually put some effort in. You might find a scanner that will beep if you're close, but I only had to use it to find the last piece. I found everything else quite easily within 6 hours of gameplay, just by conducting a methodical search.
Along the way you'll need to deal with the various types of robots. To begin with its just a normal human shaped robot with a shotgun, usually hunting in pairs. But over time, more dangerous types start to appear such as robot dogs or robot horse riders. You can decide whether to fight them or avoid them, but you can only save in specific places so you might want to be cautious.
I mostly used the open nature of the islands to keep my distance, only fighting the robots who were guarding the pieces. Guns are not fun to use, they feel slow and weak - probably by design, because the robots struggle with them as well. I had more success by first distracting them either by throwing a bottle or setting an alarm clock, then sneaking up behind and using a powerful axe. Stealth is a tricky thing to get right for me, but I enjoyed this system more than games like Thief or Assassins Creed.
Meanwhile you need to find food, because if your hunger meter reaches zero, your health will start to decrease. If you take damage during combat, your health will automatically regenerate, but only if your hunger meter is high. There is plenty of food available, but you might need to search villages, which are guarded by more robots. Searching buildings can also give various helpful items such as binoculars, matches for lighting a fire to cook raw meat, a map which helps navigation, and more.
Technically the game is solid. Graphics are what you would expect from an indie game, controls are fine on mouse and keyboard, and I didn't suffer any bugs. The most disappointing thing for me was the story. The end was very anticlimactic and failed to really explain anything at all.
Overall I enjoyed SYABH and I would recommend it, if you're looking to play something a bit different to the usual genres.

Finally, a good WWII shooter that isn't CoD or Battlefield. This game takes place on the Russia/Axis western front (Red Orchestra 2) as well as the Pacific Front (Rising Storm). Both of these games come with a purchase of either RO2 or RS. The game uses free aim which will keep weapons from centering on your screen until iron-sighting. Bullet drop is taken into account and you can adjust your sights accordingly. While there are 2 more casual modes, most servers run realism in which FF is on, your character can bleed out from wounds, HUD is extremly minimal (only appears when objective is capped or you press a button to bring it up), and you have to worry about the stress of character. Stress occurs when teammates die around you, bullets are shot close or hit close to you, artillery strikes near you, or a commanding officer is killed. It adds a much needed depth which allows for actual fire suppresion to keep enemies down. As you kill with each weapon your character becomes more and more comfortable with the weapon, increasing reload speed, accuracy, etc. You can also unlock a weapon specific attachment every 25 levels with a weapon (unlockables include better scopes, bayonet, cleaner gun). Each team also has different classes such as engineer, marksman, elite rifleman, team commander, squad commander and anti-tank gun. Each class has different abilities and your team must use those abilities to keep ahead of the opposiition. Team commander calls in air strikes, radar planes, and other usefull tools for the team as well as coordinating with the squad leaders to take points and defend certain areas. Gameplay-wise, this game is wonderful but is still slightly arcade-like (battlefield, CoD, etc) and doesn't fully venture into simulator territory like your Arma games.
The game looks ok, with the Rising Storm expansion looking far superior on all fronts (it is also newer than RO2). I don't consider this game well optimized  as most games fall around 40-50 FPS on max settings, vsync and DoF off, but I never felt like fiddling with the options as the game is playable at that framerate (gameplay is slow, high FPS isn't required). I do dislike how there aren't any facial animations, like at all. Spectating games is strange sometimes to see a sniper holding a posiiton and never blinking for a full 30 minutes, but in-game its easy to not notice. Weapons sound impactful and are probably some of my favorite weapon sounds in any WWII game so far. You are also able to turn on each side's actual language, if you dislike Germans and Russians screaming in English.
My only complaints are that I wish there was a radius-based voice chat option instead of all-team, all-squad, and all-game voice channels being the only options. I also dislike how buying the upgrade of RO2 or RS lets anyone have immediate access to automatic weapons. Automatic weapons are mostly given to important classes and many new players tend to pick those classes for the weapon alone and not for learning the abilities. If you do pick up this game, be sure to try out the bolt-action rifles first and unlock one attachment before going up the weapon ladder, as the bolt-action rifles teach you the fundamentals of the game's aiming and bullet drop. If you are looking for a fun, polished and rewarding MMORPG with a large, active community, I highly recommend this game.

Possibly one of the best examples of early-access done right, The Long Dark is a fantastic game that just keeps getting better and better.
The premise is simple.  Your plane crashed; it's cold; the wolves are hungry; the bear is angry; no one is around to help; and you've got to do whatever it takes to survive.
What exactly does that mean?  At first, it means following your standard survival game behaviors.  Find shelter.  Find food.  Find water.  Don't let the wildlife eat you as you scour the frozen waste for the things you need.  But what separates The Long Dark from other survival games is that, ultimately, it also means learning the skills to procure those things for yourself.  Want to eat next week?  Better learn to hunt, because the cans of pork and beans you found in that gas station aren't going to last forever.  Want to not die of exposure?  Better learn to tell when a blizzard is coming, because it turns out building a fire in the middle of one is damned near impossible.  Want to look like a rock star?  Better learn to tan a deer hide and sew your own leather pants then--because remember, THERE'S NO ONE AROUND TO HELP.
In this game, you're facing off against Mother Nature one on one.  And Mother Nature may be beautiful (and this game is unbelievably, strikingly beautiful), but Big Mama's also got fists like brick bats, one hell of a long reach, and she's currently undefeated.  So settle in and get ready for a full twelve rounds, Champ.  'Cause you're in for a doozy.

There isn't a lot of complexity to this short yet simple indie action puzzle platformer and yet, it has still managed to enthrall me as I progressed from level to level, puzzle to puzzle.
Forward to the Sky is a very charming third person adventure game where you control a princess (whose design is very reminiscent of Saber Lily's from Fate/Unlimited Codes) as you attempt to scale the floating sky tower and confront the evil witch, or so it goes.

If you're looking for a new twist on ghoulies, ghosties, long-legged beasties, and things that go bump in the night, look no further than Ghost Master. Sick Puppies' real-time strategy game stands horror-game traditions on their heads, swapping the spooks and scares of Resident Evil and Silent Hill for supernatural management duties reminiscent of Dungeon Master. It's a great novelty, first of all, but it's also a real success in terms of gameplay, thanks to outstanding scenario design and an irreverent sense of humor.
Some of the haunting stunts you can pull are straight out of Ghostbusters.
Some of the haunting stunts you can pull are straight out of Ghostbusters.
The core elements of Ghost Master are simple. Reverse the stereotypical ghost story and you have a pretty good idea what this game is all about. Unlike in your garden-variety horror game, where you wander the halls of a haunted house waiting to be frightened into a fresh pair of BVDs, here you're some kind of dead civil servant (insert "are there any other kind?" or similar joke here) in charge of the rattling chains and disembodied footsteps. Problems in the small town of Gravenville have attracted the notice of the Haunter Committee, and you're sent to set things right by generally scaring the bejesus out of the flesh-and-blood types.
You do this by recruiting a team of ghosts for each scenario. This spook squad is drawn from six categories--sprites, disturbances, elementals, vapours, frighteners, and horrors--named for the chief characteristics and skills of their members. The sprites class, for instance, consists of minor spirits who mess up electrical appliances, like the cogjammer gremlin and the ghostly spider, clatterclaws. Elementals features aether and earthwall, who have the capabilities of air and earth elementals, respectively. Horrors represents the worst of the worst, such as the mortal-possessing ghastly and the headless horseman. Every sort of spook that's ever made type B-positive run down the walls in a fright flick is at your beck and call here.
Using your team in the field is a balancing act. Ghosts must be fettered to specific objects, so you can't spread them all over the map. Gremlins have to be attached to electronic appliances, such as microwaves and televisions. Apparitions, shadows, and wraiths are stuck to murder scenes. Weatherwitches and headless horsemen are linked to thoroughfares like hallways and roads. And so on.
Role-playing concerns also crop up. While certain types of ghosts are necessities in some situations, there's a benefit to using the same spooks in multiple missions, because they gain experience and become easier to control. They can also be upgraded with new skills, which are purchased in the ghoul room with the gold plasm awarded at the end of each successful scenario. Managing your spook squad is about more than just picking the right ghoul for the job.
Few things will scare homeowners as much as revealing rotting corpses in boarded-up rooms.
Few things will scare homeowners as much as revealing rotting corpses in boarded-up rooms.
Regular plasm consumption is another issue. This is the sole resource in the game, powering your ability to manifest ghosts and all their spectral abilities. Overtax yourself and you can run out of this vital substance, a dire scenario that ends the current haunt and throws you out of the mortal realm. Plasm is earned by scaring people, forcing you to keep a focus on screams and shudders even when the scenario objectives involve something more subtle than driving residents out of their homes.
Even with these physical anchors and resource restrictions, a lot of moving around is required. For starters, your victims don't stand still. Humans in the game communicate in thought balloons and gibberish voices, much like those in The Sims, and are rated in terms of belief, terror, and madness. Build their belief that something out of the ordinary is going on and you'll be able to terrify them or drive them mad. Affect either of the latter categories through something like an eerie laugh, a chill wind blowing through a sealed room, or a ghost playing peekaboo, and the victim will flee, forcing you to adjust your tactics. They even have individual fears, like lightning or insects, which can be revealed with powers like know aura and then used to your advantage.
People will run out of rooms, go from one floor to another, and even dash into the backyard or street to get away from your ghosts, so you need to keep up the assault by locating new fetters. After a little time on each level, you'll get an idea of your victims' escape routes. The level design typically includes lots of locations where you can set up traps to keep mortals so scared that they soon run off into the night or simply go nuts. Needless to say, you can derive a lot of sadistic glee from this. Put a ghastly in a living room, a spook and a cogjammer in a kitchen, and a weatherwitch in the hallway separating them and you can watch your victims slowly lose their minds as they go from one spine-tingling jolt to the next.
Collect gold plasm and you can train your ghosts with different spooky skills.
Collect gold plasm and you can train your ghosts with different spooky skills.
The scenarios themselves are well designed and fairly plentiful (more than a dozen are spread across three acts). Most are more tongue-in-cheek than openly ghoulish, although there are lots of corpses to be unearthed amid the guffaws. All poke fun at movies and TV shows, both horror and mainstream. Scenario names include Ghostbreakers, Poultrygeist, and Phantom of the Operating Room, and plots have been lifted from movies like Evil Dead (faithfully adapted lock, stock, and Necronomicon) and Sleepy Hollow. Look closely at the names of your victims and you'll notice some surprises as well. The Haunting 101 tutorial mission, for example, sees you sending apparitions against Blair, Tootie, and their pals from the '80s sitcom The Facts of Life.
There isn't really an overarching plot, though the people you scare in one scenario often show up in another. You really do get the sense that you're haunting a small town. For example, the Hutz family you haunted in The Calamityville Horror and the kids you drove away from their frat house in Weird Séance show up in the Gravenville police station in The Unusual Suspects. The only problem with this approach is that Gravenville is a little too small, seeing as you have to haunt some places more than once.
The design goes beyond grade-school puns. Scenarios consist of a mixture of puzzles and straightforward rock-paper-scissors design elements, so that you're attempting to complete different objectives each time out. You scare jocks out of frat houses, unveil hidden corpses, assist university students with occult rites, convince a mob boss to believe in ghosts, frighten the locked-up criminals out of a police station, and so forth. Sometimes you even have to avoid scaring people away or driving them mad, as you need them in a lucid state so you can fulfill certain objectives. Puzzles are paramount, as the houses to be haunted always include fettered spirits that can be freed to join your ranks by accomplishing set goals. Some of these are fairly simple--to release Raindance from his toilet prison in the Evil Dead homage Summoners Not Included, all you have to do is clear some bees from in front of a Porta Potti, and to spring Sparkle in The Blair Wisp Project, you just need to start a campfire.
About the only thing missing from Ghost Master is a multiplayer mode, although it's hard to imagine how Sick Puppies could have incorporated such an option into a puzzle-oriented title like this. And the game isn't exactly any poorer for the omission of multiplayer features, since the numerous missions and impressive replay value will keep it on your hard drive for quite some time.

Forward to the Sky is a third person action adventure with platforming
elements and an anime feel.  Graphically the game is sound, and the music does a good job of propelling the atmosphere and the momentum through the story. The game is based around climbing a tower, and there are only six levels to the tower, making the total game time between 1 1/2 and 3 hours. As you ascend the tower, you collect crystals on each level that drop from killing monsters or solving a puzzle.
The gameplay is simplistic, and what combat there is, is not the selling
point of this game.  You are given the option to kill all the enemies, or bypass them, if that is not your thing.  You can make your own path if you wish
to.  I feel that the story was overdone, and a lot of it is unnecessary filler.
When the dialogue happens, the text takes up a large portion of the screen and limits your view.  That coupled with  all the extra story got to be annoying.
What makes this story interesting is the level design.  Each level offers
new, interesting mechanics, making each level unique and keeping the player
involved.  It keeps the gameplay fresh.  The level design offers freedom, with an  open feel that allows the player to bypass parts of the level if they choose.
Overall, the combat is sufficient, there is a large variety of puzzles and
level design mechanics that adds to the possibility of replay, and I never felt
as if the time I put into the game wasted my time.  It respected me as a player, and I enjoyed my time in it.  I would have liked to see more levels, but overall this was an enjoyable adventure.

Review posted on 7/8/2015 Build 32.
To give you a little bit of insight as to the type of person this review is coming from.
I have played a good number of Zombie Apocolypse games with and without the survival element and am a big fan of the genre/concept.
One of my favorite story(s), accounts, or portrayals of this genre would have to be World War Z (the book by Max Brooks, the movie is rubbish in comparision).
No it is not perfect I would not try to tell you otherwise, I see people on the forums who are having issues installing or running the game for various reasons. Personally I had no trouble at all, it runs great except for occasionally closes out of the game completely upon exiting out of the current game, which should have brought me to the main menu.
It is often easy to forget that this game is still in early access. While there are many exciting items and features planned for the future, the game feels and plays almost like a finished game.
Here are some features in the game at the time of this review that I like and/or appreciate and feel add a substantial amount to the immersion of Project Zomboid.
-Crafting & Barricading.
-*Combining.
-Day & Night cycle.
-Logical loot distribution.  In other words you will find loot in places that make sense in the world.
-Hunger & Thirst system.
-character creation process.  Play as a male or femle, name them, choose a pre apocolypse profession (each profession comes with bonuses) or unemployed, plus give them merits and flaws. (I am paraphrasing here, I forget what they are called in game).
-Weather (rain, snow) and yes, seasons!
-Temperature system.
-The ability to create your own "custom sandbox" zombie apocolypse
-Upgrading and repairing. Bat+hammer+nails=Spiked Baseball bat, then use tools to repair it when needed.
-Item conditions. Weapons get damaged and then eventually break.
-Functional L.O.S. (Line of Sight) for both players and Zombies.   In other words you can only see the zombies in the direction your character is facing.
-Multiplayer. Lots of Servers to join.
-Skill system where if you want to improve a skill, you have to keep using it...and live long enough to improve it! Also you can read books related to skills for a xp boost when said skill is used.
*Combining. Example A: I already have a kitchen knife and a jar of peanut butter. Find some bread, use the knife to cut the bread, knife+sliced bread+peanut butter=peanut butter sandwiches.
Example B: Enter a house that still has power. Already have a frying pan equipped. Look in the refrigerator. Frying pan+chicken+peas (perhaps with a dash of salt and/or pepper, optional) = chicken and vegetable stir fry. Turn on the stove, place the stir fry in the pan on the stove, cook, and yum!
Honestly I am glad I paid full price. Yeah I know it might sound crazy, it was just on sale not long ago but honestly the devs deserve every cent.

There is no cure for the zombie virus and I am not sure if that will ever change. Playing Project Zomboid is playing out the story of a character, the story of how they died. This may be a deal breaker for some, which is why I bring it up. There is no way to 'WIN" the game, you just survive as long as you can.
