Okay, with this being a game from the Stanley Parable developer, there's only one thing you can know for certain before diving into it - you can't be certain what to expect. And I guess that's where I could've stopped writing a recommendation, booped that blue upvote button and been done with it. But I want to lay out everything I have brewing in my relatively small mind in order after have just finished the game, and what better place is there for it than a publicly visible recommendation, right? Spoilers (in a sense) follow, so feel free to skip the next paragraph.
And the general idea I carried out is "nobody knows anyone else, ever". Sometimes you have this acquaintance, and you may think you have gained insight into his soul by watching him, his struggles, his life, his work and dreams, but you're viewing it all through the prism of your own perception and worldview, you project yourself onto this person. You must be really careful to not confuse your own reflection for what the other person really is. And in that, communication is integral. Perhaps that's why communication's theme is also brought up so often.
I can see it being called a pretentious walking simulator, and it's probably not far from truth, but it's not important. What is important is that I found something in these small encapsulated levels, then it was not a waste of time for me. It is not a waste of time if it made me ask questions and answer them to myself. Maybe the questions that are not the of kind that developer intended me to ask, but you know what they say, there's "no such thing as a stupid question".
Moreover, the game brought out that curious feeling about the worlds inside games that I had once a long long time ago, as a kid, a feeling that I've lost as I learned more and more about videogames' mechanics, what makes them tick and where their limitations lie. It became dull to try and push beyond their boundaries, to try and reach distant stars that are drawn on the skybox. But with this game, for a moment, I felt something a bit like that long lost emotion.
All in all, the Beginner's Guide can be hit or miss, but it's very short and very cheap so hey, what's the worst that can happen if you play it?

tl;dr version, 8.5/10, still has a ways to go but as it is one of the most intense and realistic zombie survival games in a genre cluttered by easy fixes.
There was no happy ending. This is how you died.
I've been keeping up with Zomboid for longer than I'd like to think about. When it was first announced and gathering attention, the gaming world was abuzz with a zombie survival game the likes of which we had never really seen done well. The initial game they pumped out was fun and the promises of the game to come sounded like a dream come true for hardcore gamers.
But as time went on, I lost interest due to slow updates. The game kept progressing, and every year or so I'd check up on it. I was generally impressed, but eventually just felt like there were enough zombie survival games emerging like Dayz that Project Zomboid had lost its chance. Finally, I decided to check its progress out one last time.
And I was finally hooked.
The experience it delivers is one that no other games to date have really offered. This is a true zombie survival horror game. It does not about action. It is not forgiving. You are thrust in the middle of a zombie apocalpyse with nothing but the clothes on your back and must survive any way you can for as long as you can. There is no happy ending here. The game only gets harder, and you will eventually die.
You create your character picking a profession and using a beneficial/detrimental perk point system, meaning if you want your character to be strong you will have to give something up, such as asmtha or illiteracy. There are tough choices to be made, and many skills that are very useful. There are skills for cooking, gardening, foraging, and of course combat, and you are unlikely to get many of them very high unless you survive a long time. You will have to specialize your character.
If you leave your oven on, it will burn your house to the ground. But maybe that's a good thing as you lured a horde of zombies to a house far from your safehouse and incinerated them all inside. The simple act of climbing through a broken window can give you an infection leading to death if you are not slow and careful. Running is taboo. Fighting every zombie is a chance of being bit and dead.
The music is good ambient music that will set the mood, from a quiet slow terror to a banging intense beat if you are running from a herd. The sounds are functional and also quite terrifying. The graphics look nice while being low enough to be able to handle hundreds of zombies on screen and hundreds more off screen lumbering around. One thing that is not as functional is the animations, most of which are decent but I feel the game could use more of them to make things more clear in a game where there is no room for error.
The game gives you a great amount of customization for your gaming experience, and you can start on a good beginner difficulty to learn how to survive in a safer enviroment or pump up the zombies from Dawn of the Dead to 28 Days Later fast and die quicker. Multiplayer is offered, but at the time of this writing has a long way to go to being something amazing. The potential is there and there are some great encounters to be had with some friends but public servers seem to still be off.
This game is slow to move, but the developers are good about paying attention to the community and I have faith that if/when they finally deliver this game to it's full form, it will be the definitive zombie survival experience.

I do not give a flying ♥♥♥♥ about DLC - I haven't bought any and I'm still having loads of fun.
Two teams, 4 v 1. The 4 are the Hunters, they work together to track, trap and kill the 1. The 1 is a big♥♥♥♥♥super-monster that can kill an unprepared team of Hunters effortlessly.
Gameplay for the Hunters is like a cross between Left 4 Dead, Monster Hunter (google it) and Borderlands (each class has unique class-abilities). You can play as a Medic, Assault, Support or Trapper. Each role has a couple of unlockable Hunters with varying abilities, strengths and weaknesses. Everyone has jetpacks, but there is a bit of a learning curve in using them efficiently (which is a good thing). As long as one Hunter lives, the rest can respawn and dropship in again (this is on a fairly long cooldown, if you die after the dropship has launched, enjoy your wait).
Playing the Monster is also like Left 4 Dead, except that you are alone as the 'special infected' while being much much stronger. You can get around the map much faster than the Hunters, and generally mess with their heads/annihilate them if you have the right mindset and cunning.
The typical Monster game consists of things like ♥♥♥♥♥hit♥♥♥♥♥hitshitnomnonomnomOW♥♥♥♥♥hit♥♥♥♥♥hitnomnomRAAAGH! I win? weee
Currently you can pick from the firebreathing Tank/Fighter, the Teleporting/stealth Rogue, or the ranged/lightning flying tentacle-face dude.
I played the various Alpha and Beta releases and initially found the game to be too similar to Left 4 Dead (far too simple); but after playing the full release for a few days, and the Evacuation mode (multiplayer campaign), I've come to realise that the game is ridiculously well-balanced and really deep - personal experience as a player is a lot more valuable than progression experience (just like Monster Hunter), the maps are big and open enough that you can't predict exactly how the match is going to play out. There's real 'meat' to this game.

Whoever you end up playing, it's easy to pick up the basics, but difficult to master them. The tactics you employ for each match vary wildly depending on your class(es), the environment, and the Hunt type. The maps are awesomely varied (heh, acid maps), and the wildlife is a lot of fun to deal with (fun). The autobalancing is probably the best I've ever seen, even if people drop out, lose a few games in a row, etc, the game stays fun for all involved. Matchmaking is solid, and usually lets you play your favourite role (if you insist on having one) without any trouble.
I'm always impressed by how much work the devs must have put into building up the game world, giving it a unique character all it's own. The Hunter dialogues are pretty good to listen to, especially once you get a good mix of the rarer Hunters together in the dropship.
Basically this is shaping up to be one of the best Coop games I've played since Left 4 Dead. All I need now is a regular crew and some Teamspeak tactics :)
The (overpriced) skins are optional, and the addtional Hunters and Monsters are not available yet (if the devs pay the same attention to balancing as they have done with the rest of the player characters, the DLC PCs won't confer any particular advantage either).
It's easy to underestimate the effort and production values the devs have put into game balancing (it's amazing)  and cutscenes/interactions. I suspect the Season Pass (overpriced) will make more sense as players mature with unlocks and progression - new Hunters and Monsters will affect both game balance and the various cutscenes and player character dialogues, probably a lot of work involved in that.

From all of the games that I have played in my life, Davey Wreden's have had an exclusive tacitly grasping effect on me that is unequal to that of seemingly any other. Much like a book that one can relate to almost entirely, his work conveys a sense of personal understanding that I have never experienced with any other videogame before. This is why I recommend both The Stanley Parable and the Beginner's Guide to anyone, as I'm hoping that they will experience and understand things that I have.
You can probably tell that I'm being pretty vague on what this game actually is about, and that's because I feel as though these sort of games (narrative-driven, walking simulator) are best played without any predisposition or expectation of what is going to take place until you experience it for yourself. However, I do feel inclined to say something that does pertain to how the story is presented: this game is almost entirely narrated and completely self-aware; there is seemingly nothing in the way of inherent fictitious material displayed here, and the entire game is narrated by its creator. For some reason, when I first bought this game, I figured that it would be just like the trailer, in that I would be given the password to someone's computer, and I'd take information from about who this person is from there. So with myself being fooled, I'd imagine that someone, somewhere, also has had the same sense of delusion. Apart from that, all I can say is that you should probably get this on sale, because even though it is indeed a great experience, the price is just a little high for a two hour game.

This game is an extremely complex, somewhat flawed knot of a game.  It's beautiful, and inexplicable in exactly the way that the most personal and painful pieces of art are as made by the most devoted auteurs.
I don't mean any respect to Wreden with the use of that word, of course; but he is, by every definition, an artist creating bizarre works of passion.  While I first encountered his work with the Stanley Parable (The HL2 mod, not the full game, yet,) I was immediately blown away by the high-concept nature of the extremely simple game-- describe precisely what's in the player's mind at the instant they attempt an action, whether it attempts to subvert or follow the intent of the game's creator.  While ultimately it has been done better since, I firmly believe that original mod was the birth of the ludonarrative question of whether or not a player's actions CAN matter in the medium of video games, 'player agency' be danged.
This game follows that track, but not through the player's mind-- rather through Davey's as he seeks out some answers to most of these same questions.  I won't humor any accusation that the game is 'contentless' or 'without gameplay', because-- as usual-- the philosophy of the thing IS the point, even if it ends up linear and 'combatless'.  This means that it ends up very opaque, because it wrestles with such personal issues, but in the same moment that it is unreadable to anyone who isn't its creator, it reflects on so many questions (of identity, of personhood, of the point of even MAKING art) that it can't help but touch anyone paying attention and dwelling close to the subject matter.  If that's the game you need, buy it, love it forever.  If it isn't, you'll blow it off as another walking sim.  If you can't find it in you to wrestle with the same questions Davey's other pieces get to, you won't gain much, but if the philosophy of art and the making of video games is your interest then give it a try.

Forward to the Sky has 6 levels, a weak but family-friendly story, simple combat, and can be finished to 100% in under 2 hours.
However, it is beautiful, controls well with keyboard and mouse, and features some really enjoyable 3D platforming puzzles with new gimmicks introduced in each level.
For combat, you have two combos that are each activated by repeatedly pressing a single button. However, there is still a good amount of enemy variety that keeps things from getting too repetetive. The game also features a multi-stage final boss in which you have to figure out how to defeat each unique part. I tend to prefer combat to be simple in my platformers, so I like the system used in Forward to the Sky, but those who want combat with lots of depth will not find it here.
The goal in each level is easy enough to reach, but there are plenty of hidden areas to reach and plunder to get to 100%. Figuring out how to get to the secret areas tends to take a bit of thought, but not so much that I spent more than a few minutes on any of them which leads to a satisfying experience all throughout the game. The game is short, but it is entertaining from start to finish.

Limbo is…
A dark and scary fall through a dangerous forest as an extremely squishy, but brave young boy. The experience created in this black and white world is one that has me absolutely riding the edge of my seat, stopping at every creaky sound terrified that the spider is waiting just beyond the edge of the screen to stake me,.......once again.
Limbo is a great example of a game that does a fantastic job of creating a truly atmospheric game. The sounds mean something, indicating dangers or useful movement possibilities.
Controls in Limbo are simple, you Move with the  left stick, Jump with A and B to use Action (push/pull). The difficulty in Limbo arrives not in the controls, but instead the unknown. What this means is you don't die because you couldn't time the jump right. You die because you didn't know you needed to jump until it was too late. Limbo is what I call a "Die to Discover" game. The level comes at you with not nearly enough time to react to the hazards so you die. You then know the next hazard exists so you can prepare. You might get through a few more puzzle before you hit this again, but you will inevitably experience this repeatedly, watching this young boy meet his demise over and over and over.
So what does OKG say?
Limbo is only not OKG approved because I can't stomach killing this kid anymore. While it made me giggle at first, I slowly felt less and less comfortable with it as a whole. So if you aren't bothered or can even just get past it, it is easy to control and an engaging experience. I will have to find a playthrough on Youtube, because while looking for screenshots, I saw lots of things that made me curious. so if you can play and enjoy, DO it!!!

I simply had to get this after finding myself drooling at the store page so many times. I'm glad I did!
Dungeon of the Endless fits in the lore of the Endless games, but instead of 4X, it's a dungeon-crawling game with aspects of roguelikes, tower defense games and tactical combat games. Or something like that. It's very unique, I don't think I've ever played a game similar to this.
The game is in alpha, but already very polished and works delightfully well. I have yet to encounter any crashing or even less severe bugs. The gameplay works quite well, the controls are taught in a tutorial but I had to die a few times to realise that there are constructable modules and stuff like that. After I spent a little more time with the UI, the mechanics started to make sense and now I'm hopelessly hooked into the game.
I was initially drawn in by the visual style, which is a really quite original and distinct mix of pixel art and contemporary visual effects, such as dynamic shadows/light and shader tricks. There is quite a lot of empty black space in the trailer, but the dungeon actually spans nicely across the screen and there's not that much empty space around the rooms.
The music and sounds create a nicely moody atmosphere. I have to spend bits of time in the menu screen every now and then simply because the menu music is so good.
Overall, I heartily recommend getting this game, it's already well developed and more content is probably coming as the game matures. One of the best titles I have played in a long time.

I never played Bioshock when it came out originally, but playing it now I can say that it has definitely stood the test of time. Nearly 10 years later and this game plays really well.
Despite it's age, the graphics in the game are amazing. The underwater steampunk atmosphere comes across really well. You get a sense of grandeur about the place, even though it's society has fallen apart.
Each level has a large area to explore, but mostly the game is fairly linear. Given what you learn from the story, this works really well for the game. You can backtrack if you want, but I don't really see much point to that, plus there's a lot [loads] of different weapons and abilities for you to customize to your preferred play style. To the point where I feel it begins to enter RPG-esque areas of character customization.
The enemies are known as 'splicers', that beign genetically modified beings who are essentially hooked on drugs. This is an innovative take on the generic 'zombie', as the game gives an actual explanation as to the situation at hand, rather than some hand-wavy nonsense about some disease. This helps to add some realism to the situation. There are a bunch of different types of enemy, which requires you to slightly alter the way you tackle them, adding a fair bit of variety to the game.
I did seem to have some issues getting the subtitles to play properly. This is a bit of an issue because with lots of weaponry and enemy screeching going on it can be hard to listen to the dialogue. Luckily, the game does offer transcripts of messages in the pause screen.
Definitely one of the better FPS games, and thankfully one that doesn't revolve around your generic military warfare or totally bland zombies.

The core ideas behind Dungeon of the Endless are on the right track and the promise of content to come should turn this into a masterpiece.
The curent look and feel of this alpha indicate a high level of care in the game's development - this is a surprisngly polished release and is very much playable (and re-playable).
What I really liked:
- The graphics are great (and I'm not a pixel graphics fanboy)
- The dungeon generation has been unique and fairly unpredictable each time I re-rolled.
- The heroes are well individualized and you need to adapt your strategy to accomodate their strenghts and weaknesses.
- The gameplay can be challenging and unforgiving however it doesn't feel frustrating.
- I haven't come accross any obvious 'spam this item to win' holes.
- The 'chance' factor works really well with what the game tries to achieve and it forces you to re-think your strategy.
- There's no redundant micromanagement of heroes.
- No redundant micropositioning of turrets either.
- Mobs aren't ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
- No game-crippling bugs that I have encountered (and for an alpha this fresh, that's really surprising)
- Game has potential to become virtually endless in terms of replayability (assuming things go well dev wise).
What I didn't really like:
- Some turrets aren't really useful enough, or rather can be happily ignored throughout the entire game without you missing their utility. I'm referring specifically to the turrets that grant hero bonuses to armor, strength, or heal the hero.
- When the world becomes larger it can get quite tedious to manage heroes on oposite sides of the map. Perhaps a minimap might be useful.
- Switching between heroes can get a bit wonky and it's not always terribly obvious which one you're controling.
- The 'you found the door, there it is!!!!!' pointers are insanely annoying.
The obvious:
- Currently not a whole lot of content is available - early alpha.
- Game won't be for everyone and you might hate it.
All in all, I really like this game and hope it manages to accomplish what it set out to do without needing to get dumbed down or glittered up.

Review written as of 0.1.1:
This game is definitely in alpha, and, as a warning, only 3 stages of the game will feel VERY short. It only took me a couple hours to experience just about all of the in game "behind the door" events, level up all the different heroes, and unlock all the different structures currently available. Ordinarily I would not recommend this title for the average buyer, since there is so little content existing at the present moment. However, as an owner of Amplitude Studio's previous title, "Endless Space", I know this developer as a consumer-oriented, professional studio that sets deadlines and pushes themselves to continue creating content for their games well past the "we could just abandon the game, take the money, and run" phase. I have lots of confidence that the content will continue coming. You will just have to be patient for crucial game elements like the whole research system, all character abilities, the full character roster, DEAR GOD MORE FLOORS PLZ AMPLITUDE, etc...
The graphics and colors of this game are very pleasing to the eye, and shadows look great. FlyByNo is an AMAZING in-house composer, and his work on this game is just as great as his work on Endless Space. I do not know who does the writing at Amplitude but whoever it is, they put such flavor into every tooltip, every item description in all their games that you'll find yourself reading every word that finds its way onto your screen, no matter how dull you may expect the description for an item like "T-Shirt" to be. The founder edition comes with 50% coupons for Endless Space and the new Endless Space expansion (since buying the Disharmony expansion was in my plans already, this practically offset the cost difference between a Founder's Edition and Pixel Edition alone) for a total of about $20 in savings. The Founder's Edition itself costs $20 normally ($15 on sale now) so if you were actually thinking about buying Endless Space and it is not on sale, you may as well buy a Founder's Edition of Dungeon of the Endless and apply the discounts to maximize your Steam Wallet.
In short, this is a fun and unique game with lots of easily visible potential that it doesn't live up to yet. If you are not confident in this developer's ability to deliver content steadily and stay committed to their titles, you will likely feel ripped off for the amount of content currently available and I'd recommend waiting for an official, non-early release. Otherwise, you'll enjoy this, but slowly, and you will wish there was more content available just because you're so enticed by what already exists.

Beautfiul visuals and wonderful soundtrack are the only thing this game has going for it. The actual gameplay is horrendous. Aiming is extremely broken and a huge detriment to the game. The hitboxes, on enemies and Cuphead himself, can be infuriating at times. I often find myself shooting through enemies, only to be struck by them a moment later as my hits somehow phased through them. Enemies will frequently spawn into existence on top of you, instantly causing damage. Or fly in from offscreen when you are near the edges, not even rendering in the game.. just randomly taking a point of health.
It is a very difficult game, but I find no victory satisfying. While I do feel like I get better at fighting each boss, actually winning feels like absolute luck most of the time. Memorizing patterns becomes largely pointless when bosses suddenly switch up their attack to something they hadn't done on previous runs, forcing you between a rock and a hard place where you inevitably die.
A game that is a good kind of difficult should leave you with the feeling of, "Wow. That was really hard, but I made so many mistakes. I can do better." Then you improve and come back stronger each run. Cuphead does not feel this way. Cuphead will make you yell at your monitor for how bullsh**t 75% of your deaths are.
Oh, and local co-op only? Is that a joke? Ridiculous that a game designed for two players wouldn't ship with online capabilities. What year is this?
Side note, what do platformers have against mice? If I could smoothly aim with a mouse instead of the janky 6 directions the game currently allows, it would alleviate half the frustration.

There are some pacing issues, though. In the first half of the game you encounter many interesting creatures and what appear to be other children (who are none too happy to see you). Then the second half takes place in a deserted industrial area. The puzzles become more interesting and complicated, but the absence of other life forms weakens our emotional connection with the game. Limbo's final moment gave me chills -- one of my favorite game endings ever. But the lead up to it needed more of a climax. You work your way through the second half of the game conquering increasingly dastardly puzzles, and then the journey ends unexpectedly.
Limbo is an incredible achievement. Very few games are as original, atmospheric, and consistently brilliant. It belongs in everybody's collection. The journey may be over too quickly, but you will be entertained every minute. This is one of my favorite games.

This is going to be one of those long reviews, so I'll start with a short overview. If you only want a short review, just read that.
Buy this game. It's great. It feels great, controls smooth, looks quite good, has a great atmosphere, some good communities scattered in there, and it takes skill, teamwork, and tactics to play well, but not at the expense of tension or gameplay. It's not quite as realistic as Arma, but it's so much more tense and immersive. It's my FPS dream come true.
Okay, now comes the long bit.
Red Orchestra isn't a perfect simulation of war, but it feels so real, the sense of fear is so palpable, the triumph of finally getting good and learning to hit moving targets, of finally learning how to handle yourself in a combat situation so that you can kill as many of the enemy as possible -
is better than any milsim's realism.
Somebody once asked me if Red Orchestra 2/Rising Storm is as hard as they'd heard. Here's what I told them.
"Let me put it to you this way.
It's not too difficult to learn how to shoot accurately. Not getting shot is the difficult part. You have to learn to check every corner of every room that you enter. Check the ceiling if the building is more than one story, since there are often holes in the second floor. Become obsessive about checking for the enemy. It'll keep you alive longer. Not forever, though. Why would you want to live forever? Make your inevitable death mean something. Never cross open ground if you can avoid it. Move from cover to cover when there is some, which is rare enough, and when there isn't, you'd better hope your squad leader hasn't thrown his smoke grenade yet, because the enemy machine gunner 100 meters away whose muzzle flash is the only thing you can see as your buddy's stomach turns into a large-caliber hole, well, that enemy is going to cut you to pieces if you don't have a smokescreen up. If you see the enemy and you're moving, you're dead already, so don't worry about learning to stop moving and respond.
Shooting accurately is easy if you know when to shoot. Don't try to shoot when you aren't behind some sort of cover. Make sure that it's actual solid cover and not just a piece of corrugated metal or a bush, because bullets go through those, and your muzzle flash will give you away. There's no crosshair. To shoot from the hip and get a kill, you have to be up close and personal, good, in possession of a full-auto weapon, and very lucky. Don't shoot from the hip if you can avoid it. Use your iron sights. No scope for you, unless you earn it with the blood of thousands of enemies. If you've been sprinting for too long, your weapon sways and you can't hit anything. Bullets drop, and they travel at something like 800m/s, though it varies from weapon to weapon, so you have to lead your target (the amount you lead by varies from weapon to weapon as well for the aforementioned reason) and adjust the zeroing on your rear sight if you want your bullets to go anywhere near where you point your weapon. If you are a rifleman, your job is not just to kill the enemy, but to die so that the guy behind you can figure out the location of the enemy who killed you and kill him, making the next 10 meters clear for your squad to advance. The needs of your team outweigh your life. Get used to it.
So you're sure you're in a good firing position. Now line up the shot. Lining up the shot is easy if you can see the enemy. Seeing the enemy is hard. You look for a slightly darker shade of gray or brown in a gray-brown hell that is of no real strategic importance, but your orders are to fight for it anyway, so you do. You look for a slightly different shade of green in a sweltering jungle which has already given you malaria and has rotted your uniform to tatters. If you can see the enemy, assume they can see you. Don't move. The human eye picks up movement much better than it does a slight difference in color. Wait for your chance. Shoot. Wait to see the blood, but as soon as you do, move. You've given away your position. Find a new one.
So you've lined up the shot. It's not difficult to line up the shot if you can do all these things and survive long enough. Pulling the trigger is harder at first. I used to miss on purpose every so often, when I was new to the game. I'm a pacifist in real life, and thought I was doing good, since we're all just scared boys trying to survive in a meat grinder. But no. I've seen too many of my friends die to miss on purpose now. I've been through too much♥♥♥♥♥♥
Everybody around you is going to die. You've accepted this. You're going to die. You're never going to make it home again. But you want to stay alive as long as possible, for some sick, twisted, perverted reason. Part of you would rather die. You've seen men screaming for their mothers as they writhe around in puddles of their blood, staring with soulless eyes at their mangled limbs and exposed intestines. There's no time for a man to be incredulous when he realizes he will never use his legs or genitals again even if he survives. There's only time for pain.
God, you want it to end. But something keeps pushing you onwards, forcing you to do whatever it takes to survive even though you'd rather end it all before the enemy does, because it's all going to end soon anyway. The enemy will never make it home again either. They're all going to die. What does it matter if you happen to kill one of them? From the moment he was assigned to this front, he was dead. You are just the man holding the rifle that causes his death. Somebody else would kill him if you didn't, and maybe if you kill him, you and your friends might survive a few minutes longer. You want those few minutes, even though they will only bring pain, terror, and possibly the shell with your name on it that rips off your arm above the elbow and bathes the snow in warm blood that steams as it cools.
Prepare to die. You are nobody. You are no longer a gamer. You were never a gamer. You used to be a peasant boy from Siberia who dreams of becoming a novelist. You used to be a butcher's son from Bavaria whose sweetheart has promised to marry him when Russia is defeated. You used to be Horace Mann High School's baseball star who joined the Marines since he wasn't good enough for college ball. You used to be the proud child of an old sword-making family from Nakatsu. You used to be these things, but now you're nobody. You don't have a mouse and keyboard. You used to have a plow, but now you turn over the soil with artillery. You used to have a girl's hand to hold, but now you only caress your rifle. You used to have a baseball you played catch with, but now you play catch with grenades. You used to watch your father slide the swords into cold water to harden them, but now you watch bayonets plunge into the warm entrails of your friends. You are cannon fodder. You're not special. You are a cog in a great machine, a machine that has plenty of other cogs willing to take your place when you are no longer useful. You are just one of 25 million cogs.
So, yeah. It's difficult. But be thankful it's not real. For millions, it was."

Used to play this game way back. The premise of each mission is pretty much the same - scare everyone out of the map - with a few twists: almost every map has a few unique npc's that you need some strategy to scare off and at least one ghost that you can unlock. This is where the puzzle elements usually come in to play, because specific conditions need to be met to unlock the ghosts. This is also where some of the drawbacks of the game  are made apparent - npc's sometimes get stuck on the stairs, their pathfinding sometimes is also off. This leads to long periods of waiting for specifc npc's to climb up and down the stairs or randomly wander around the map - even using specific ghost skills which should make it faster don't alway help.
Speaking of skills, when I played this game waaay back I never knew they existed! The upgrade system doesn't feel needed at all in the sense that you can complete all the levels with the default ghost skillset. Some of the skills you can unlock are also copies of skills that other ghosts have so you can have a few almost-all-in-one ghosts.
An interesting game mechanic is the fact that you can switch to the POV of the NPC's or the ghosts, so you can see what they see (note though, that the npc's can't usually see ghosts, but they can see the results from their abilties.
The graphics are dated, especially when it zooms in closer on specific npc's or ghosts. Although, the npc models do not look too bad. The aforementioned bugs are also very frustrating and can even be game breaking.
Having said all that, I would still recommend picking this game up when it is on sale if not only for the fact that it there are not many games with a similar premise and it is very much a play-it-on-halloween type of game.
P.S. I had the very last npc in the very last level get stuck on the stairs ... and then disappear into the ground. I have yet to finish that level  :( .. maybe next Halloween.

"The Beginner's Guide" strings together several independent little computer games. A narrator's voice tells us that these were created by a programmer called Coda. After the first few chapters it becomes clear that all these programs deal with imprisonment and feelings of entrapment. Together with the narrator we slowly start to wonder what kind of guy Coda is. He clearly seems depressive, maybe even suicidal. Actually, I even asked myself at some point whether Coda's sudden stop of releasing games means that he is no longer alive. And even though I didn't like some of the little chapters of the game too much, I nevertheless felt pity for their author.
But wait a minute. The person behind "The Beginner's Guide", the one who obviously introduces us to Coda's world of games, is Davey Wreden. Rings a bell? He was the initial designer of "The Stanley Parable". Remember how hard you tried to get the achievement for clicking on door 430 five times? This surely was a test to figure out what gamers are willing to do in order to get all achievements of the game. This way the gamers themselves became part of the story, test subjects to the designers and programmers of the game.
With knowing this, it seems much more plausible that "The Beginner's Guide" isn't a story about a depressive programmer but just another test for you, the gamer. So, welcome back, test subject! Let's see what you can learn today.
Actually, what I learned was that I don't like any kind of traps at all and that I hate being in a situation where escape seems to be impossible. And I hate to do the cleaning work for people who don't show any intention of even participating in the task. I didn't create that mess! So why should I do the cleaning? But if I don't like this, why did I do it then? Why did I follow orders appearing on the screen and why did I walk into each of the traps even though I knew they were traps?
Because I am curious. And because there seemed to be no way of getting around being imprisoned in these little games. But the worst for me was the cleaning job after making the big mistake of walking into the house in the first place. I tried to avoid it, did nothing of what I was told to do for a while, but couldn't evoke any reaction. The game didn't give me the chance to do anything else besides cleaning up the place as required. And after repeating this task for a couple of times, I got so♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off that I was really close to quitting the game. However, the game designer apparently knew that a gamer's patience can be short at times and so I was finally relieved of the duty and could continue with the next chapter. What did I learn from this? Apparently I am willing to do a lot of stupid repetitive tasks just in the hope to not be stuck in a time warp and in the hope that the game and its story may continue until any kind of planned end. This makes me also ruminate about whether I would do all this in a real situation, too. Would I really walk into an obvious trap out of curiosity? Or did I do it all because I knew there was no real danger for me and because I could escape the situation by simply quitting the game any time I wanted to? But, thinking of it, I actually did this in real life. In real life I let myself get trapped by playing a game. Am I an addict? Why didn't I quit the game but continued till the end?
I guess, you'll have to figure out the answers to all these questions yourself. However, despite these deeply unsettling questions, you shouldn't take the game too seriously. Or maybe you should. It all depends on whether you feel trapped in real life, too. Do you really look for a way to escape? You won't find it in this game.
I really do like the game a lot, even though it isn't funny in the same way as "The Stanley Parable" or "Dr. Langeskov,..." are. But like them, this game draws you deeply into the story. There is no hero or main character behind whom you, the gamer, can hide. You yourself have to deal with being trapped by the game. The only choices for you are between waiting for the programmer to set you free again after a while, or quitting the game altogether without ever finishing it.
Coda may be a real person or not. Maybe Davey Wreden invented him, maybe he feels Coda is a part of his. Since I don't know Davey Wreden, I can't determine the truth or the true intention of the game designer. But I can feel the impact the game has on me. I can feel the borders separating game and reality crumble. And I have to ask myself the question of why I play computer games and whether I feel trapped and entrapped when doing so.

First off, let me say that the game is well put together on the whole, even in its current form. There are some minor tweaks I would add; a better tutorial for instance, and mouseover texts that help beginners out, with the option later of turning mouseover texts from "advanced help" to "minimal help" for instance. I am talking about the utilities you use in the bottom left. Sure trial and error gets you there but it can be frustrating having to work through it yourself.
So, the game. Be prepared to die. A lot. Especially at the start whilst you figure it all out. After that, it does get easier, and you start to hold your own after a few tries.
The game does get a bit repetative, but thats kind of like how dungeon crawlers are. Although the rooms may visually differ, you still have the one aim which is setting up the defences along the way before progressing.
I have to be honest and say, this game isn't for me. It was *quite* what I expected it to be; perhaps a bit more customisation, perhaps when one of your toons levels up, have a mini talent tree going, or simply add the basic stats you want that char to have rather than automatic.
TL:DR
The game is nice, for what it is, no crashes or bugs for me yet, does get repetitive BUT if you do like the dungeon crawler type games with a twist, give it a shot. 7/10 from me.

The King is dead! Long live the King!
Reigns is a port of a mobile game where you get to play as a dynasty of monarchs over hundreds of years, in a centuries long quest to escape a deal with the devil. It's designed very simply, with the gameplay deriving from a card deck that presents different events and decisions to make. When a card comes up with a decision to make, you swipe left or right to indicate what course of action you will take. The deck has hundreds of cards that come up randomly in sequences, so while you will have repeat events, there is a wide variety of scenarios.
It is essentially a resource management game taking the form of a royal choose-your-own-adventure. You play the new King, who has just risen to power in a deal with the devil, that will affect his dynasty for millennia. Your goal is to rule over your kingdom well and keep yourself from being horribly killed. You do this by balancing four resources/factions: the church, the people, the military, and the treasury. The strength of these factions is represented by bars at the top of your screen. Every decision you make adds and/or subtracts from one or more of these factions, raising or lowering the bars. If you ever go too far in the extreme and hit the top or the bottom of any of the bars, you will die based on a scenario related to that extreme. You may last a short time or a long time, but ultimately you will end up dead, most likely not of natural causes. After you die, you'll play the new King, and will have to do the same thing. Throughout all of this, you are trying to meet a few people and accomplish a few things to ultimately break free from the devil. This all continues for around 1400 years (though it's basically only a counter, as technology advancement and history do not really exist). At the end of this time, you get one of three different endings, of which the best ending is very hard to obtain (though there are walkthroughs).
The aesthetics of the game are minimalistic, with simple character designs for its cast, basic Simlish-style voices, and basic background music. I think this was a design choice more than a lack of resources, and actually think the overall aesthetic and ambiance suits the game quite well. Even though the music is sparse, it doesn't really get annoying or feel out of place, and is very much treated as just in the background.
The game is short; about 3-4 hours. Gameplay is extended by trying to obtain all of the different cards and achievements, related to deaths, courtiers, and accomplishments. Since cards randomly come up, it will take time to collect them all; even with over 10 hours played and three playthroughs I have not quite seen all of the cards.
Overall I think this game is quite good for its value. It's simple enough to not be too intense, and us very easy to pick up. At the same time, there is enough depth to keep you interested, and enough to discover in-game and to collect to keep you occupied for awhile. I expect to come back to it every once in awhile to try to collect more cards and achievements.

-[ What is Project Zomboid ]-
Project Zomboid is an open world zombie survival game, you try and survive in one of two small towns located within the state Kentucky. The game uses a style of a top down perspective for players, which they can control the zoom of by either scrolling up to zoom in and scroll down to zoom out.
The Game is featured in Kentucky, you have two spawn points, West Point and Muldraugh both of which are nice towns you can start in!
** Please bear in mind that Project Zomboid (PZ) Is still in Early access, features of the game are subject to change **
-[ What make Project Zomboid so different ]-
Project Zomboid is completely different from any other zombie game out there due to the fact is doesn’t use First Person or third person, the gameplay mechanics of the game are amazing compared to some of the other Zombie games out there.. And finally playing Multiplayer is actually fun!
-[ How do I start ]-
So after you have installed PZ you can either do a short tutorial (recommended!!) after that you can either play on Solo Mode, or you can choose Online. Once you get playing you’re going to want to create you character, so give them a name, make them look all pretty for the zombie apocalypse. After you’ve done that you’ll have to pick an occupation and some traits.. one you have picked a couple you’re ready to rock and roll in the lovely state of Kentucky!
-[ Occupation ]-
As you read above you have to choose your occupation, there is a giant list to choose from which give you certain benefits and when playing with friends you can make sure you’re an asset than a liability! The Occupations range from Carpenter, Electrician, Engineer, Police Officer, Veteran, Unemployed and more! For a full list please click
Most of the Occupations increase certain skills in which you would think common sense right, apart from unemployed. The Unemployed occupation gives you a certain amount of points in which you can spend on traits to “fine tune” your character to how you like and make it fit your playstyle. So Traits.
-[ Traits ]-
Traits are what you select to give your character certain bonuses, unfortunately to get these bonuses you need to give your character some penalties if you like. Some of which make you transfer items from your inventory to a container slower, reading books takes longer, you character can start to panic when you’re indoors due to being claustrophobic. You can see better at night if you select cats eyes, this would help if you like to go out and loot at night time. The List goes on, for a full list please click
-[ Multiplayer ]-
The Multiplayer option is amazing, being able to fight a zombie apocalypse with your friends is awesome. Now you’re probably thinking that you just get KoS’ed all the time on this game? Nope, you have to flag yourself for PvP which is amazing! Although, people can still kill you… if they give you poisoned food.. you’re gonna have a bad time… So make sure to keep your eyes peeled!
The networking infrastructure behind this game is really good, I play on a US Private server, I get a constant 125ms ping. But due to the game being so smooth I don’t ever realise the latency between the US guys and myself, this really does allow the game to be a lot more fun as you’re not stressing about the lag between you guys.
-[ Crafting ]-
Crafting in this game, once you have your head around the GUI is pretty self-explanatory you need certain materials to dis-assemble something and then you need other to create doors and several other things which can be used as boarding windows up, traps in case players get into your house too.
-[ Levelling ]-
In PZ when you certain activities for a certain amount of time, you gain XP for killing zombies, you then also gain XP for let’s say Sprinting.. After you gain 1 skill point, you need to get enough sprinting  XP for the box to go blue, after that box is blue. You can spend the skill point which turns it into a gold box. This now give you a speed boost to your sprinting making you faster, you can do this to several other skills which are in the game too. For a full list please click
-[ Death ]-
When you die, you lose that character, forever. There is a possibility your body can be re-animated and become a zombie, so in order to get your gear back.. You’re gonna need to kill yourself. If not then you’re luck and need to find your body.
So when you die all you need to do is create a new character, pretty much how you did at the start of the game, you can choose a different occupation, traits too! This changes up your gameplay experience allowing you to spend more hours on this amazing game!
-[ My bad points about this game ]-
The tutorial could include more information on how the crafting system works, levelling system too. Other than that I cannot really think of any more bad points of this game.
-[ Conclusion ]-
If you really do enjoy playing zombie games and a few of your friends have this game, You need to buy it! It’s a purchase you won’t regret as you’ll have so much fun! Playing solo can be fun but after a while I can see if becoming extremely stale.. So MP is your best option.
Thank you for reading this review, if you enjoyed it or found it helpful in whether you should buy PZ or not, please be sure to follow my

This is going to be one of those long reviews, so I'll start with a short overview. If you only want a short review, just read that.
Buy this game. It's great. It feels great, controls smooth, looks quite good, has a great atmosphere, some good communities scattered in there, and it takes skill, teamwork, and tactics to play well, but not at the expense of tension or gameplay. It's not quite as realistic as Arma, but it's so much more tense and immersive. It's my FPS dream come true.
Okay, now comes the long bit.
Red Orchestra isn't a perfect simulation of war, but it feels so real, the sense of fear is so palpable, the triumph of finally getting good and learning to hit moving targets, of finally learning how to handle yourself in a combat situation so that you can kill as many of the enemy as possible -
is better than any milsim's realism.
Somebody once asked me if Red Orchestra 2/Rising Storm is as hard as they'd heard. Here's what I told them.
"Let me put it to you this way.
It's not too difficult to learn how to shoot accurately. Not getting shot is the difficult part. You have to learn to check every corner of every room that you enter. Check the ceiling if the building is more than one story, since there are often holes in the second floor. Become obsessive about checking for the enemy. It'll keep you alive longer. Not forever, though. Why would you want to live forever? Make your inevitable death mean something. Never cross open ground if you can avoid it. Move from cover to cover when there is some, which is rare enough, and when there isn't, you'd better hope your squad leader hasn't thrown his smoke grenade yet, because the enemy machine gunner 100 meters away whose muzzle flash is the only thing you can see as your buddy's stomach turns into a large-caliber hole, well, that enemy is going to cut you to pieces if you don't have a smokescreen up. If you see the enemy and you're moving, you're dead already, so don't worry about learning to stop moving and respond.
Shooting accurately is easy if you know when to shoot. Don't try to shoot when you aren't behind some sort of cover. Make sure that it's actual solid cover and not just a piece of corrugated metal or a bush, because bullets go through those, and your muzzle flash will give you away. There's no crosshair. To shoot from the hip and get a kill, you have to be up close and personal, good, in possession of a full-auto weapon, and very lucky. Don't shoot from the hip if you can avoid it. Use your iron sights. No scope for you, unless you earn it with the blood of thousands of enemies. If you've been sprinting for too long, your weapon sways and you can't hit anything. Bullets drop, and they travel at something like 800m/s, though it varies from weapon to weapon, so you have to lead your target (the amount you lead by varies from weapon to weapon as well for the aforementioned reason) and adjust the zeroing on your rear sight if you want your bullets to go anywhere near where you point your weapon. If you are a rifleman, your job is not just to kill the enemy, but to die so that the guy behind you can figure out the location of the enemy who killed you and kill him, making the next 10 meters clear for your squad to advance. The needs of your team outweigh your life. Get used to it.
So you're sure you're in a good firing position. Now line up the shot. Lining up the shot is easy if you can see the enemy. Seeing the enemy is hard. You look for a slightly darker shade of gray or brown in a gray-brown hell that is of no real strategic importance, but your orders are to fight for it anyway, so you do. You look for a slightly different shade of green in a sweltering jungle which has already given you malaria and has rotted your uniform to tatters. If you can see the enemy, assume they can see you. Don't move. The human eye picks up movement much better than it does a slight difference in color. Wait for your chance. Shoot. Wait to see the blood, but as soon as you do, move. You've given away your position. Find a new one.
So you've lined up the shot. It's not difficult to line up the shot if you can do all these things and survive long enough. Pulling the trigger is harder at first. I used to miss on purpose every so often, when I was new to the game. I'm a pacifist in real life, and thought I was doing good, since we're all just scared boys trying to survive in a meat grinder. But no. I've seen too many of my friends die to miss on purpose now. I've been through too much♥♥♥♥♥♥
Everybody around you is going to die. You've accepted this. You're going to die. You're never going to make it home again. But you want to stay alive as long as possible, for some sick, twisted, perverted reason. Part of you would rather die. You've seen men screaming for their mothers as they writhe around in puddles of their blood, staring with soulless eyes at their mangled limbs and exposed intestines. There's no time for a man to be incredulous when he realizes he will never use his legs or genitals again even if he survives. There's only time for pain.
God, you want it to end. But something keeps pushing you onwards, forcing you to do whatever it takes to survive even though you'd rather end it all before the enemy does, because it's all going to end soon anyway. The enemy will never make it home again either. They're all going to die. What does it matter if you happen to kill one of them? From the moment he was assigned to this front, he was dead. You are just the man holding the rifle that causes his death. Somebody else would kill him if you didn't, and maybe if you kill him, you and your friends might survive a few minutes longer. You want those few minutes, even though they will only bring pain, terror, and possibly the shell with your name on it that rips off your arm above the elbow and bathes the snow in warm blood that steams as it cools.
Prepare to die. You are nobody. You are no longer a gamer. You were never a gamer. You used to be a peasant boy from Siberia who dreams of becoming a novelist. You used to be a butcher's son from Bavaria whose sweetheart has promised to marry him when Russia is defeated. You used to be Horace Mann High School's baseball star who joined the Marines since he wasn't good enough for college ball. You used to be the proud child of an old sword-making family from Nakatsu. You used to be these things, but now you're nobody. You don't have a mouse and keyboard. You used to have a plow, but now you turn over the soil with artillery. You used to have a girl's hand to hold, but now you only caress your rifle. You used to have a baseball you played catch with, but now you play catch with grenades. You used to watch your father slide the swords into cold water to harden them, but now you watch bayonets plunge into the warm entrails of your friends. You are cannon fodder. You're not special. You are a cog in a great machine, a machine that has plenty of other cogs willing to take your place when you are no longer useful. You are just one of 25 million cogs.
So, yeah. It's difficult. But be thankful it's not real. For millions, it was."
I cannot recommend this game enough. If you want a story-driven campaign, or good AI, or easy kills, look elsewhere. But give this a shot. It's so damn good. I've never been to war, and I'm so lucky to be able to say that. I'll never kill anybody in real life if I can help it. But this game took me out of my room and put me in the middle of the most brutal war in history better than any tightly-scripted CoD campaign ever could. It's the most immersive game in existence. Try it.

THIS IS A REIEW FOR RO:2
This game is a hardcore, realistic, unforgiving WWII multiplayer with the option to fight with either the Germans or the Soviets during the battle of Stalingrad. Its a bloody battle to capture every point, and you can feel your heartbeat pick up when the artillery stars falling onto you, or your vision blurs and you lose concentration as the enemy bullets fly past your head. The soundtrack is amazing, and sometimes you feel as if you are actually the soldier you are controlling.
Pros:
- Ultra Realistic
- Realistic squad-based battles
- Mostly bolt action rifles (Historical)
- Good Variety of Maps
- Good Community
- Auto kick for teamkillers
- NOT pay to win
- Native Languages (Germans Speak German, Russians Speak Russian)
- Nice weapon sounds
Cons:
- Relatively poor graphics
- Few consistently active servers
- Some maps favor attacking or defending
- Huge learning curve
I suggest you watch at least one hour of WWII propaganda before you play this game

This was original written on my blog, here:
Many stealth games are somewhat of an illusion. Behind the rock throwing, sneaking and stealth assassinations there is essentially a puzzle game, designed to have a few specific solutions. This is where Sir, you are being Hunted differs, the procedural nature of the game gives you a number of situations without an obvious solution. A patrol of 4 guards doesn't necessarily have a blind spot, so completing the game without ever being seen becomes near impossible. This might frustrate some die-hard stealth fans for obvious reasons, but it feels different and somewhat realistic.
The premise is as so, you're stuck on an island with the task of retrieving 17 MacGuffins from 5 different islands. You must take the 17 items to the standing-stones in the center island to repair the "device". You really don't know anything else except you're being hunted by angry English robots.
The English robots match the theme of the environment; the fens, countryside, industrial areas, castles and forests that you stroll through will be familiar to anyone who lives in or has visited the UK. This may not sound exciting in words, but it really is, no other video-game has done anything in this setting. It's dank, dreary, usually raining and very atmospheric coupled with the ambient music. The industrial area in particular has a certain uniqueness about it, the landscape is littered with abandoned towns, villages, churches, factories and ruins. Something very awful happened in this place, and it's never clear exactly what that may have been. The robots speak a number of stereotypical English phrases even talking about their wives. It's as if the personality of the once residents of these islands has been transferred into each robot.
Unfortunately the awful low resolution textures and procedural generation take you out of the game every so often, certain placements don't make sense with roads leading nowhere, walls connected in strange ways and docks located in very small lakes. However this wasn't a large problem for me considering the world is supposed to be in a state of extreme entropy and you don't have much time to focus on the small details anyway. Why don't you have much time? When the game says you're being hunted it doesn't mean it lightly. With sprawling robots which are around every corner don't give you much rest-bite, you're constantly looking behind your back.
This is the one thing that Sir, You Are Being Hunted absolutely nails, the feeling of being on the run. You will relish moments of silence when you can't hear the sinister "bleep-bloop" of the tweed, pipe and top-hat geared robots. Another stand-out aspect is the enemy design. The basic robots can be seen from far away by their glowing red eyes, and even when they aren't in sight each enemy makes a distinct sound. This is clever because you can often get a good idea of how many robots you're facing without even seeing them. The AI is far from intelligent but I wouldn't call it stupid. Even when it does make the odd silly decision, you aren't taken out of the experience like many other stealth games because they're robots. Maybe that's a cheap excuse, but it works. As the game continues more creative enemies are added to the mix, some which create such weird and terrifying sounds you'll never want to go near them. Robots also have a tendency to shoot pheasants and rabbits for their own entertainment and at my scared confusion, wondering what they were shooting at. This creates an unexpected side-effect, making Sir, You Are Being Hunted quite a scary game at times. Avoiding the outlandish looking robots makes it all the more exciting and horrifying when you accidentally bump into them.
The gameplay consists of finding the 17 MacGuffins by following blue will-o'-the-wisps to each location. This works quite nicely as they don't give you a direct way to the MacGuffin, often taking you a longer way around. However I think there are too many will-o'-the-wisps on the islands at a time, reducing your compulsion to explore. Along the way you will find places to loot such as houses, barrels and sheds. To the dismay of many fans it was announced early in the game's development that you won't be able to go inside houses. While this makes sense for a number of technical and economic reasons, it's an obvious shame. Buildings would add a lot to the game in terms of hiding and exploration. Towns are still interesting though, providing a lot of loot and many places to hide. Each town also has a suitably randomized English name that will probably make you chuckle.
The loot consists of random useless objects (of which there are far too many), food, drink, tools, traps, weapons (both melee and ranged) and letters (which provide a bit of context). There is a vitality meter also which you have to keep topped up by consuming food and drink. If you let it drain to 0 your health will start to deplete, in addition to this the lower your vitality is the less quickly your health regenerates. This is never anything to worry about though, in my first playthrough it never went below 20. You can also cook pheasants, rabbits and raw meat on a fire with the disadvantage of the fire attracting robots. But this never becomes a necessity because there is simply enough food that you can eat uncooked.
I did find myself lacking in bandages a few times though. Some of my most tense experiences actually came from those moments when I had no bandages left. I was a sitting duck, getting seen was much more of a consequence, I couldn't risk getting shot, even once. Interestingly enough there is also quite a big chance that robots drop bandages. Giving me a few interesting situations where I risked my bullets for the chance to get a bandage. Despite those moments however there were still far too many bandages, and far too much food for these systems to be of much of an impact. I am happy to role-play a little but some players might resort to charging around the landscape chugging whiskey and eating biscuits, using the health regeneration to tank gunfire.
That said, there is still a great deal of intensity when it comes to fighting robots. Unlike food, bullets are very rare, weapons have lengthy reload times and shooting accurately isn't easy. There was one memorable point where I managed to take out two robots with a hatchet without taking any damage, I had a gun but I wanted to save the bullets. Considering you can't save whenever you want the stakes of dying are quite large too. You can only save at the standing stones where you drop off the MacGuffins and the boats which you use to travel to the different islands. There is a big risk reward element to this system. Either I can grab a MacGuffin and head straight back to a boat to save, or I can save time and head around the island and try to get as many MacGuffins at once. Even though death is usually the players fault your patience is still tested whenever you die, as you are required to do the same thing all over again. Throughout I couldn't help thinking a different save system would work better.
When you come across a MacGuffin there are a few options to get your grubby hands on it. You can throw a bottle to distract the robots near-by, mess it up however and those robots will run to you rather than where it smashed. Alarm clocks are the most effective, hide it somewhere, set the timer and wait for it to go off. Once the guards find it they'll realize it's a trick but usually that gives you enough time...

tl;tr - It was cute and sweet, but sadly short. Beautiful graphics and detail. 9/10 would buy again.
I first purchased the game because the cuteness got me. I was not disappointed. It was quite adorable with a sweet storyline that you uncover as you go. While it is a bit short, it isn't half bad compared to other indie games out there. Especially since it is (i think) the company's first game. But, lets get to the niddy-griddy.
Pros:
It was fairly easy to dive into, you don't have to deal with a tutorial. The graphics are quite beautiful and interesting. The story was good, if not a bit obvious to me. However, it is the characters that make the story, not the story itself. Voice acting was pretty good as well.
Neutral Statements:
The main menu was a bit odd, since it didn't say what each thing was and was only an Icon. But that isn't anything major. (The menu itself was good looking too) There wasn't much combat, and most of it was easy once you got the controls down. The puzzles are relatively easy if you think about them for a few minutes, but as a game that can easily be rated E, thats to be expected.
Cons:
It was short. Took me roughly 1.5 hours to complete. (But, for $8, i feel i got my moneys worth) There is a lack of replayability, as once you complete it nothing really changes from each playthrough, unless you miss crystals going through the levels. (but then again, almost every game has almost 0% replayability for me anyway, lol) The "flying" stuff is kind of wonky. It can be hard to use if you aren't prepared.
Honestly, i'm excited to see where they go from here and look forward to the company's future games. I can easily give it a 9/10.

Forward to the sky is a short and sweet game, even shorter if you don't intend to collect all the gems. The game will take you on a 1-2 hours journey as you slash your way through enemies while traversing through light platforming segments and puzzles. Though combat can get repetitive this is mitagated by the introduction of new elements throughout the levels such as wind tunnels, gravity, and more.
The game uses a chibi/cute anime style which may be off putting to some. While the music isn't very memorable it does it's job and suits the atmoesphere of the game. The voice acting on the other hand will be hit or miss for some. As while it is by no means awful it's certaintly nothing to write home about. At the very least it isn't as bad as some anime dubs I have seen.
Overall the game is an enjoyable time but some consideration should be put into whether it's worth the $8 considering it's fairly short length and fairly minimal replay value. As well as it's fairly easy difficulty, which a child could beat. This may be a good or bad point for you.
I would recommend buying this game on sale, but if you're craving a light-hearted anime game then you certainly can't go wrong with this one.

If any game ever deserved a sequel or rebooted version then it is this one!
There are very, very few games from years gone by that I will play over and over, from start to finish, and not get bored with. This is one of them. If you have a spare bit of cash then try this game out because it is worth it.
Why?
The gameplay is simple, so is the idea, the graphics are fine (I play on a 4k screen at the games best available resolution) and silliness is ramped up to full!

From the catchy soundtrack to the tongue-in-cheek names for some of the mortals (hands up those who got the references to the cast and characters from numerous films and TV series) if you can get past the fact that the game is now in its teenage years then you're in for a treat.
Fancy playing a casual game? Then just relax and have fun using the various ghosts to cause mayhem and mischief to scare your way through the level..
Want a challenge? Use the spooks in a sequence to speed haunt those pesky mortals and scare them all away..
Think you're good? Then instead of making them run in fear try to drive the mortals insane instead by uncovering their deepest fears!
Overall, for the price, well worth it!

If you are looking for a very astetically pleasing, nostagic throwback to the golden age of platformers, minus the frustration. This is a game for you. The art style is beautiful, the levels are fluid, and it can serve as a nice little distraction from a rough day.
Just be warned that it is short, very short, 83 minutes for me from start to finish with a minute or two trying to find the quit button (a little lost amongst all the beautiful visuals, but I'm not complaining).  It was an enjoyable experience, but it really leaves you right after you start getting comfortable. Besides the length, the story is really simplistic and predictable, and the final boss can hit you like a brick considering the combat mostly takes a back seat throughout the other levels.
All in all, very polished and might be worth picking up on a sale, but because of the incredibly short length of the game and lack of replayability it is hard to say it is worth full price. Now pardon me while I go relive my childhood playing some Crash Bandicoot.

Difficult and stressful in the best way possible. The Long Dark challenges you in a way I have never seen before. No zombies, no BS, just nature and all it has to give you. The amount of creativity the devs have put into this game is truly remarkable. As of now, the only available game mode is Sandbox - standard issue survival. No quests, no narrative, just you and the cold. In the future, the devs have shown plans for more features, wildlife, difficulty, and best of all... Story Mode. I can't wait to see what the devs will have in store for the story, after seeing the masterpiece this game already is.
